Trump seen examining printout of apparent Kennedy Center demolition
WASHINGTON - An AFP photo of Donald Trump examining a depiction of Washington’s Kennedy Center apparently being demolished sparked widespread attention Sept 17 after the president threatened to tear down the revered arts venue because he has been blocked from renaming it after himself.
In the image captured by AFP photographer Brendan Smialowski late Sept 16 at Joint Base Andrews, the Republican leader was seen through the windows of Air Force One holding a placard with visible text in red declaring: “Kennedy Center DEMOLIS...”
The rest of the word was obscured by the plane’s window frame but Trump has mused repeatedly about razing the Washington centre.
Below the words is a large picture showing a yellow heavy construction vehicle scooping rubble from a torn-down building.
Smialowski, who was photographing Trump’s return to Washington from a rally in North Carolina, said he was watching carefully as the president appeared to be sitting in a different seat than usual.
“It’s an interesting photo,” said Smialowski, who has covered the White House for 20 years. “The Kennedy Center’s in the news right now, and their future is in the news.”
The AFP images were viewed millions of times on social media and made headlines in many US news outlets.
They were also included as evidence in a court filing on Sept 17 by Joyce Beatty, a Democratic Ohio congresswoman and Kennedy Center board member who is challenging Trump’s overhaul of the institution.
With his approval ratings in the low 30 per cent range amid discontent over the war against Iran and the rising cost of living, Trump has fixated on getting the Kennedy Center renamed in his honour.
He threatened to flatten the venue after a judge ruled this week that his name cannot be added onto the building’s exterior.
The ‘Trump-Kennedy’ Center?
Trump said his administration planned to carry out needed multi-million dollar renovations, then would have to “subsidise it for years to come.”
“I think that the Trump Administration should certainly have recognition because, frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down,” he said on Sept 16.
Judge Christopher Cooper ordered the Kennedy Center on Sept 17 to provide 30 days notice of any planned structural changes “including but not limited to any ‘demolition’ of the Center’s main building.”
Trump and his handpicked Kennedy Center board members have argued that the main building, which was constructed in the 1960s, is in a state of dangerous disrepair.
“As President Trump said last night, without his intervention, the Kennedy Center will inevitably continue to decline,” the White House said when asked about the AFP photo.
The facility was closed on Sept 16 for seven days “to assess existing safety risks,” according to a Trump administration court filing on Sept 17.
Trump installed himself as chairman of the centre, which is named in honour of late president John F. Kennedy, a Democrat who championed civil rights before he was assassinated in 1963.
The venue’s board voted in December to call it the “Trump-Kennedy” Center and installed signage with his name on it.
Judge Cooper, however, ordered Trump’s name removed from the exterior and overturned the board’s decision to rename the institution, saying only Congress can do so.
Workers removed Trump’s name from the building in June, but scaffolding and tarps have remained ever since.
“It’s a memorial to an assassinated president, and that shouldn’t be tarnished by someone else putting their name on it just because they want it,” Keith Chamberlin, a retired NASA engineer, said at the scene on Sept 17.
The Kennedy Center takeover is one of several projects aimed at stamping Trump’s brand on the US capital, including lavish gold trim in the Oval Office, a triumphal arch near the National Mall and a half-billion dollar ballroom at the White House. AFP

At least 26 killed in clashes along Sudan-South Sudan border region
UN Interim Security Force for Abyei strengthens security on the ground after days of deadly fighting.
At least 26 people have been killed and 82 others injured in days of intercommunal fighting in a disputed region on the border between South Sudan and Sudan.
Reporting the death toll on Thursday, the United Nations said it had reinforced its security presence around Abyei town.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2Armed raid on cattle camp kills at least 49 in South Sudan
- list 2 of 2Ambush in South Sudan kills peacekeeping troops
Clashes are frequent in Abyei, and the region’s status has remained unresolved since South Sudan gained independence from Sudan and became a nation in 2011.
The violence erupted at Amiet Common Market in response to separate killings of a Ngok Dinka man on Monday and a Misseriya man on Tuesday, the UN Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) said in a statement.
UNISFA said the initial killings escalated tensions between the two rival communities around the market.
Similar fighting has broken out between Ngok Dinka and Misseriya pastoral communities that often involves grazing lands and watering points for their animals.
The Misseriya, Arab pastoralists from Sudan, migrate south into Abyei during the dry season in search of grazing land, sometimes clashing with the Ngok Dinka, the region’s permanent residents.
”We are actively engaging with the leaders of the two communities who have reiterated their commitment to dialogue and a peaceful resolution to the hostilities,” said Lieutenant General Ganesh Kumar Shreshta of UNISFA.
“Our priority is to prevent further loss of life. We urge all community leaders to embrace dialogue and advance peaceful coexistence.”
In a statement posted on X on Thursday, UNISFA said, “On the ground, we are taking all measures to protect civilians and prevent retaliation”.
The UNISFA force is composed of 3,000 police and soldiers whose mission is to protect civilians.
Abyei is an oil-rich region that is jointly administered by South Sudan and Sudan, with both countries staking claim to the territory.
South Sudan has been mostly at peace since a 2018 agreement ended a five-year conflict during which thousands of people were killed.
The country is due to hold its first elections since independence in December.

Russians set to elect 450 State Duma members in 3-day election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:45:38 UTC
05:45:38 KST

Elena Teslova
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Russian voters will begin voting early Friday to elect the 450 members of the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, in a three-day election that also includes regional and local contests across the country.
The Sept. 18-20 vote will determine the ninth convocation of the State Duma, with parliamentary elections being held for the first time since the beginning of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022.
The elections are being held as part of Russia’s Single Voting Day, with voters in eight regions choosing governors or heads of regions, while parliamentary elections are taking place in 39 regions.
Local council elections are also scheduled in the administrative centers of 10 regions.
111 million eligible voters
According to the Russian Central Election Commission, about 111 million people, including approximately 1.8 million registered voters abroad, are eligible to vote in the parliamentary election.
Voting will take place at polling stations as well as through Russia’s remote electronic voting system.
Polls will open at 8 am local time on Friday, working 12 hours every day until they close at 8 pm on Sept. 20. Russia has 11 different time zones, so in different regions the local time will vary from GMT +2 to GMT +12.
There is no minimum turnout requirement for the election to be considered valid.
The election is expected to be monitored by foreign observers from around 55 countries, including representatives of the Commonwealth of Independent States, Shanghai Cooperation Organization, BRICS, Association of Southeast Asian Nations, as well as countries from Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America.
Russia has not invited the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to observe the three-day vote.
11 parties seeking to capture Duma seats
Eleven political parties are taking part in the State Duma election.
The ballot includes the ruling United Russia party and the four parties currently represented in the Duma — the Communist Party, Liberal Democratic Party, A Just Russia — For Truth, and New People.
Five parties without parliamentary representation are also taking part – Rodina, Pensioners for Social Justice, Greens, Communists of Russia, Direct Democracy, and Yabloko.
The liberal Yabloko party was excluded from the ballot for the State Duma election under the party list system, while candidates nominated by the party in single-member constituencies are taking part in the vote.
The Duma has 450 seats. Half of them are filled through party lists, while the remaining 225 are contested in single-member constituencies.
Parties must receive at least 5% of the party list vote to qualify for seats under the proportional system.
Candidates in single-member districts may be nominated by parties or run independently after collecting the required number of voter signatures.
Vote during continued conflict
The parliamentary vote is taking place while the Russia-Ukraine conflict continues to shape the country’s political and security agenda.
Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian regions have brought security issues into the election campaign, while support for the Russian military has featured prominently in the political messaging of the parties in the race.
Voting is also being organized in Russian-controlled parts of Ukraine, a move that Ukraine and many Western governments reject as unlawful.
The election will determine the composition of the State Duma for the next five-year term.

AUKUS architects say pact on track at five-year mark, but facing challenges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:44:11 UTC
05:44:11 KST

AUKUS on track but faces big challenges at five-year mark, its architects say
In short:
Former top defence officials from Australia, the US, and the UK have assessed the state of the AUKUS pact five years after it was announced.
The pact aims to arm Australia with nuclear-powered submarines, but the slow pace of submarine construction in the US has long been a concern.
"One of the most important consequences of AUKUS is that it has forced us to look deeply at our submarine capacity and infrastructure," former US deputy secretary of state Kurt Campbell said.
AUKUS has forced the United States to confront its "profoundly lacking" capacity to build and maintain naval submarines, but recent progress should inspire confidence in the defence deal, a former top White House official says.
Five years after the pact between Australia, the US and the UK was announced, three of its key architects have assessed its progress towards its goals, which include arming Australia with nuclear-powered submarines to deter Chinese aggression in the Indo-Pacific.
Former US deputy secretary of state Kurt Campbell, Australia's former defence secretary Greg Moriarty and former UK national security adviser Sir Stephen Lovegrove all said they were content with what had been achieved so far.
But they also conceded AUKUS still faced major challenges, particularly in relation to workforce shortages and submarine construction delays.
"I myself remember facing challenges in this process, thinking we'd never get over them, that it was just too hard,"
"Too much bureaucratic, you know, sticking points, not enough money, not enough political will. Each time we have mounted them."
One question that has persistently dogged AUKUS is whether the US can deliver on its plan to transfer several Virginia-class submarines to Australia by the 2030s.
For years, US shipyards have been building the boats far too slowly to maintain the American fleet at target levels.
That has fuelled concerns the US will not have submarines to spare for Australia.
"One of the most important consequences of AUKUS is that it has forced us to look deeply at our submarine capacity and infrastructure," Mr Campbell said.
"In many respects, it was profoundly lacking in the ability to get subs under repair, back out at sea, to be able to turn out new submarines.
"But the fact that we've gone so far gives me that extra confidence that what lies ahead, we will be able to surmount those challenges.
"We have both focused on AUKUS, but we have also, I think, turned our attention more internally to our national sovereign submarine capabilities, and we are much more serious about that at a national level than we were four or five years ago."
Efforts to speed up shipbuilding
Some analysis suggests submarine production in the US is slowing rather than speeding up.
The US is investing heavily to improve the rate of construction, and Australia is contributing more than $4 billion to the effort.
"The Trump administration has driven enormous investment in the submarine industrial base," said Mr Moriarty, who is now Australia's ambassador in Washington.
"It has taken several steps to accelerate shipbuilding capability."
In Australia, Mr Moriarty said, skills shortages remained a significant obstacle.
But hundreds of Australian personnel had now been trained in the US, as well as on visiting American and British submarines in Western Australia, he said.
"There's always heartaches and headaches, but when I think back to five years ago, I'm really pleasantly surprised at how much we've achieved."
The panel discussion was hosted by Washington's Center for Strategic and International Studies.
The think tank also produced its own analysis to mark AUKUS's fifth anniversary.
It noted that the pact's first years were "mainly about building institutions and infrastructure, both of which are now considerable".
"AUKUS has, by any fair accounting, made real progress — more than sceptics on either side of the Pacific predicted,"
"But turning a fifth anniversary into something that lasts still requires, as Australians are fond of saying, some hard yards.
"What has not yet happened — what could not yet have happened, given the timelines involved — is the actual accumulation of boats, sensors, and presence sufficient to create the dilemmas [for adversaries] the partnership was designed to pose.
"That is the conversation still to be had in Washington, Canberra, and London."

The Whole Story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:43:58 UTC
05:43:58 KST

Margarita Calderón and Karen Brock find the gaps that prevent rapid growth in reading for Multilingual Learners!
Are you in the process of implementing SOR (Science of Reading) but find that it needs SOL (Science of Language)? Are you using a popular reading series that seems to be missing something? Are your Multilingual Learners and striving readers rapidly acquiring academic English proficiency? What gaps might you and your colleagues be encountering?
There is a strong body of research on literacy for English Learners/Multilingual Learners (ELs/MLs) that school learning communities can peruse, discuss, and use to begin a roadmap to fill gaps for the new school year.
For more than two decades, we have heard what works for ELs, particularly from the National Literacy Panel on Language Minority Children and Youth (2006, 2008) and the Carnegie Panel on Multilingual Adolescent Literacy (2007). Additionally, empirical studies have compiled and tested these findings; refined instructional methods for teaching background knowledge/academic vocabulary, oracy/discourse, foundational reading, reading comprehension, and writing; and examined how to implement them through school-wide professional learning and coaching.
To date, teachers, school leaders, publishers, and state departments of education have paid very little attention to the evidence-based publications. Instead, confusion stems from the tug of decade-long trends and selective interpretations of the Science of Reading for ELs.
An Overview of Teaching Reading to ELs/MLs
Reading is not the end goal of literacy instruction—it is the pathway. Students first build the background knowledge and vocabulary needed to access the text, then read to construct meaning, engage in purposeful academic dialogue to deepen and refine their understanding, and write to synthesize, communicate, and extend their learning. Background knowledge and vocabulary prepare students for comprehension; reading provides the information; discussion processes it; and writing demonstrates learning. The written product provides the clearest evidence of comprehension.
In 2007, the Carnegie Corporation of New York convened a panel on second-language teaching and learning to focus on multilingual adolescent literacy. The panel concluded that MLs must do double the work of learning a language while also grasping content across disciplines (Short & Fitzsimmons, 2007). An empirical study on multilingual adolescent literacy was also commissioned and published that same year (Calderón, 2007), providing numerous recommendations and instructional strategies not only for reading but also for the components (vocabulary, discourse, reading comprehension, and writing) that support reading comprehension for MLs. These strategies were implemented and tested in secondary schools in Washington Heights, New York City, and Kauai, Hawaii. The four-year study compared the districts’ vocabulary and reading approaches and used a component-building approach to construct a new model for testing in diverse ML classrooms. The new model yielded an effect size of 1.2 for vocabulary and .67 for reading when compared to district models. The empirically tested model helped address multiple issues in multilingual adolescent literacy and for all students, thereby supporting the schools’ transition from low performing to exemplary status in two years.
In this article, we outline some of the gaps that schools across the country are encountering by examining specific components of language and literacy: background knowledge and vocabulary, reading, writing, and the role of student discourse in each. We provide a framework for professional learning that supports quality implementation. We look at the evidence base, ineffective trends, and high-yield practices for background knowledge, vocabulary, reading, and writing to identify solutions.
GOT GAPS IN THE INSTRUCTIONAL METHODS?
Background Knowledge and Vocabulary: Building the Foundation for Reading, Dialogue, and Writing
The books Multilingual Literacy: What You Need to Know About Teaching Reading to Emergent English Learners in K–3 and 4–12 (2026a and 2026b) elaborate on these components and on how they continue to yield successful outcomes for ML and non-ML students and their teachers. Both books emphasize building background knowledge and vocabulary as precursors to reading, discussing, writing, and learning content.
Evidence Base
Reading comprehension begins long before students read the first sentence of a text. Research consistently demonstrates that background knowledge and vocabulary are among the strongest predictors of comprehension because they enable students to connect new information to what they already know. Reading research identifies language comprehension—including vocabulary, syntax, verbal reasoning, and knowledge—as one-half of the reading equation. Without sufficient language and knowledge, students may decode words accurately but still struggle to construct meaning.
Research on MLs further demonstrates that academic language develops most effectively when vocabulary is taught explicitly, practiced orally, and immediately applied within meaningful reading, discussion, and writing. Calderón’s Seven-Step Vocabulary Process exemplifies this approach by providing students with multiple meaningful exposures to new words while preparing them to use academic language during literacy instruction.
Background knowledge is equally important. Students bring diverse experiences to the classroom, and effective instruction intentionally builds shared knowledge before reading so that every learner has access to the concepts, language, and context necessary for comprehension.
Ineffective Trends
Despite decades of research, vocabulary instruction is frequently reduced to isolated word study rather than treated as an integral part of literacy instruction.
Common ineffective practices include:
- Teaching long lists of vocabulary that are disconnected from meaningful reading
- Asking students to memorize dictionary definitions without providing opportunities to use the words
- Relying on worksheets or copying definitions as the primary method of vocabulary instruction
- Using activities such as the Frayer Model as routine vocabulary instruction rather than engaging students in repeated oral language processing
- Teaching too many words instead of selecting two to five high-impact academic vocabulary words that are essential for understanding the lesson
- Treating vocabulary as a one-time activity instead of revisiting words throughout reading, discussion, and writing
- Assuming background knowledge is already present rather than intentionally building it before reading
- Delaying vocabulary instruction until students encounter unfamiliar words during reading
- Providing language scaffolds only after MLs struggle rather than designing lessons around language from the beginning
- Viewing vocabulary instruction as an isolated component rather than as the foundation that prepares students for comprehension, collaborative dialogue, and writing
These practices often emphasize remembering words rather than using language to construct meaning.
High-Yield Practices
Effective vocabulary instruction begins with intentional lesson design. Rather than asking “Which vocabulary activity should I use?” teachers ask “What language will students need in order to successfully read, discuss, and write about today’s learning?”
Teachers intentionally select two to five essential academic vocabulary words before students begin reading. These words become the language students repeatedly encounter and use throughout the lesson.
Examples include:
- Activating and building background knowledge before reading
- Selecting two to five essential academic vocabulary words that are critical to understanding the text and lesson objectives
- Teaching vocabulary through Calderón’s Seven-Step Vocabulary Process, which includes repeated oral practice, meaningful context, student-friendly explanations, word features, partner practice, and planned future use
- Connecting new vocabulary to students’ existing knowledge and experiences
- Using visuals, demonstrations, real objects, and brief explanations to build conceptual understanding
- Revisiting vocabulary repeatedly during close reading
- Encouraging students to use newly learned vocabulary during Turn-and-Learn conversations
- Requiring students to intentionally incorporate academic vocabulary into verbal summaries and collaborative discussions
- Expecting students to apply the vocabulary in written responses, ensuring that language introduced at the beginning of the lesson becomes the language of communication at the end
- Continuously recycling vocabulary across lessons so students experience multiple meaningful exposures over time
Background knowledge and vocabulary are not preliminary activities that occur before “real instruction” begins. They are the foundation upon which close reading, collaborative dialogue, and writing are built. When students enter a text with sufficient language and conceptual understanding, they are better prepared to comprehend, discuss, synthesize, and communicate their learning with confidence.
The 7-step strategy has a large effect size (1.2), and it is even larger when all teachers in the school implement it. The 7-step process takes only two minutes to teach a word or phrase.
Components of Reading: Integrating the Reading Research into Every Lesson
Evidence Base
Skilled reading requires the integration of multiple components. Reading proficiency develops through explicit instruction in phonics, phonological awareness, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension. While each component contributes uniquely to reading success, students become proficient readers when these elements are intentionally connected with student talk during authentic reading experiences rather than taught in isolation. Authentic reading experiences and dialogue are productive for all students and critical for ML students and striving readers. 
In recent syntheses of reading comprehension instruction, Catts et al. (2006) and Duke and Pearson (2021) argue that:
- Oral language is one of the strongest predictors of reading success.
- Oral language development should occur simultaneously with phonics instruction—not after decoding is mastered.
- Vocabulary, discussion, text analysis, and knowledge building are essential for all readers.
- Decoding alone does not produce strong comprehension.
Research from the reading panels further demonstrates that language comprehension—including vocabulary, background knowledge, syntax, and oral language—is equally as important as word recognition in developing skilled readers. Students benefit most when every lesson intentionally strengthens multiple components of reading while engaging them in meaningful interaction with text.
Ineffective Trends
One common instructional pattern is treating the five components of reading as separate instructional “boxes.” Phonics is taught independently of comprehension. Vocabulary is presented as a list of words to memorize. Fluency becomes repeated oral reading without attention to meaning. Comprehension instruction often occurs only after students finish reading.
While textbooks often include supplemental suggestions for scaffolding and word study, this piecemeal approach becomes an add-on rather than the robust instructional approach that is necessary.
Another challenge is passive engagement. Too often, students spend much of the lesson listening to the teacher or completing worksheets instead of actively reading, discussing, and thinking about text.
Some approaches may cover the components of reading, but they rarely integrate them in ways that maximize learning.
High-Yield Practices
High-impact reading instruction intentionally integrates multiple components into every lesson. Students repeatedly engage in reading, language, discussion, and writing while interacting with increasingly complex texts. Research indicates that partner reading plus summarization after each paragraph yields the highest effect size for MLs (.76), as evidenced by these comprehensive models: Bilingual Cooperative Reading and Composition, Expediting Comprehension for ELs, and Reading Instructional Goals for Older Readers.
Examples include:
- Teacher modeling of talk protocols followed by supported practice
- Frequent partner reading and summarizing after each paragraph
- Choral and echo reading with teacher or peers to build fluency and confidence
- Close reading with partner reading and summarizing after each paragraph
- Students formulating text-dependent questions throughout the lesson
- Graphic organizers that support thinking rather than replace it
- Frequent vocabulary highlights or explicit teaching throughout the reading lesson
- Frequent opportunities to summarize, synthesize, and apply learning
Rather than treating the five components (phonemic awareness, phonics, vocabulary, fluency, and reading comprehension) as isolated skills, effective classrooms treat them as interconnected systems that work together to develop proficient readers.
Writing: The Daily Tool for Thinking, Learning, and Communicating
Evidence Base
Writing is one of the most powerful instructional practices available to teachers because it requires students to organize ideas, retrieve information, synthesize learning, and communicate understanding. Research consistently shows that frequent, purposeful writing strengthens comprehension, vocabulary, critical thinking, and long-term retention across all content areas.
Writing should not be viewed solely as a product to assess. Instead, it serves as a thinking process that supports learning before, during, and after instruction.
Ineffective Trends
In many classrooms, writing occurs only during language arts or as lengthy assignments completed after instruction. Students may spend days producing polished pieces, missing frequent opportunities to use writing to clarify their understanding throughout the learning process.
Another common misconception is that every writing task must be lengthy. When writing becomes infrequent or overwhelming, students lose valuable opportunities to process learning.
High-Yield Practices
Effective writing begins long before students pick up a pencil or open a computer. High-impact classrooms embed writing throughout the day using short, intentional tasks that make student thinking visible.
Examples include:
- Exit tickets that synthesize learning in two or three sentences
- Quick-writes before or after reading
- Summaries that capture the central ideas
- Compare-and-contrast responses
- Tables and charts that organize information
- Cause-and-effect explanations
- Reflection journals
- Creative writing
- Evidence-based constructed responses
- Predictions and next-step thinking
- Collaborative writing before independent writing
- Short written responses following Turn-and-Learn discussions
These brief writing opportunities require only a few minutes yet substantially increase student engagement, retrieval, organization of ideas, and transfer of learning. Rather than waiting for students to write at the end of a unit, effective teachers use writing continuously as a learning tool in every lesson and every content area.
Components Before, During, and After Reading to Ensure Learning
Got Gaps in Professional Learning on Reading?
To establish an effective learning context and shift to new approaches, an empirically tested professional learning process facilitates change, adaptation, and high-quality implementation. Exploration, innovation, and implementation call for a comprehensive process.
Why Do Evidence-Based Changes Often Fail?
Making an instructional shift such as integrating the Science of Language with the Science of Reading takes more than a couple of workshops. It means shifting to a comprehensive process.
©M.E. Calderón
Does your Professional Learning Set the Stage for Accelerating Literacy?
When given the time and space to expand their practice, teachers can implement critical components before, during, and after reading that integrate language, literacy, and knowledge. Critical studies of teacher support systems and effective professional learning models have also existed since 1984. The trajectory began with Joyce and Showers (1982, 2002) and Calderón (1984, 2007), then continued with Knight (2018), Brock (2024; Calderón & Brock, 2026a, b), and many others who continue to use data to identify what works for teachers and school leaders in successful schools.
The professional learning/professional development design consists of six essential components that support consistent, continuous learning.
- Present the theory and proven research for the instructional model.
- Provide modeling and practice at each session.
- Discuss classroom implementation.
- Conduct collaborative reflection after each modeling/demonstration and practice.
- Provide coaching for all teachers.
- Involve instructional leadership at every session.
By sustaining a comprehensive learning model year-round, schools quickly turn all classrooms into learning environments where all students demonstrate significant gains in language, literacy, and core content mastery.
Often-Asked Question: Why Didn’t It Work?
Most general education teachers find it takes one to three years to develop efficacy in teaching ELs/MLs in every classroom. Unfortunately, many schools give up on implementing new strategies within the first year, some within the first month. The main reason is that they miss one or more of the six important steps mentioned earlier. That’s when we hear “another one that didn’t work.”
Does your multiyear professional learning plan include these essential components?
Professional Learning Self-Assessment
Reflection
How many boxes did you check?
☐ 6: Your professional learning plan reflects the essential components of sustained, implementation-focused professional learning.
☐ 4–5: A strong foundation is in place. Consider strengthening the remaining components to maximize impact.
☐ 0–3: Lasting instructional change is more likely when all six components work together as part of a coherent, multiyear professional learning system.
Change Is Hard, but Change We Must
Education legislation, policies, and funding are in flux. We don’t know where the changes will land. As educators, we must take advantage of this hiatus to analyze and explore our teaching methods and the school structures that support them.
When we focus on powerful practices, including teaching background knowledge and academic vocabulary, oracy and discourse, foundational reading, reading comprehension, and writing, and support every teacher in school-wide implementation, multilingual students succeed.

Greek parliament lifts Avramopoulos immunity for Brussels corruption probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:43:39 UTC
05:43:39 KST

The former EU Commissioner has himself urged that legal proceedings go ahead, denies any wrongdoing and says he wants to cooperate fully with the authorities.
The Greek parliament on Thursday voted to lift the parliamentary immunity of former European Commissioner Dimitris Avramopoulos, clearing the way for Belgian authorities to continue their actions in the investigation into the affair known as Qatargate.
Of the 266 MPs present, 264 voted in favour of lifting his immunity, while two declared themselves "present". The parliament's Ethics Committee had earlier unanimously recommended the move. The procedure followed the issuing of a European arrest warrant by a Belgian investigating judge in June.
The 73-year-old Dimitris Avramopoulos, an MP for the ruling New Democracy party, served as European Commissioner for Migration from 2014 to 2019 and previously as mayor of Athens. He has categorically denied any illegal activity.
He had himself requested the lifting of his immunity, stating in a memorandum to parliament that he wished to cooperate fully with the competent authorities.
"I have never participated, directly or indirectly, in any illegal activity and I have never acted to serve the unlawful interests of any state or third party," he said.
He added that he is not seeking protection from the investigation, but the opportunity "to present the factual evidence" and to prove that he has no connection with the acts under scrutiny.
Relationship with the NGO Fight Impunity
The Belgian investigation concerns, among other things, Dimitris Avramopoulos's links with the non-governmental organisation Fight Impunity, founded by former Italian MEP Antonio Panzeri, one of the central figures in the case.
Dimitris Avramopoulos sat on the organisation's honorary board in 2020-2021, after the end of his term at the European Commission.
He has maintained that his cooperation with Fight Impunity was entirely lawful and that the related fees were declared to the tax authorities.
"My involvement in the organisation Fight Impunity was entirely lawful, vetted, approved, declared and taxed," he said when the warrant became public in June.
The European arrest warrant relates to allegations of participation in a criminal organisation, public corruption and the laundering of proceeds from illegal activities, according to a document from the Greek authorities cited by international news agencies.
The charges remain the subject of the Belgian investigation and do not constitute a guilty finding.
The long story of the Belgian authorities' investigation
The probe began in December 2022, when Belgian authorities carried out a series of searches and arrests over allegations that foreign governments sought to influence decisions in the European Parliament through money and gifts.
In the course of the case, Belgian authorities have seized around 1.5 million euros in cash. Those arrested included former Italian MEP Antonio Panzeri and the then vice-president of the European Parliament, Eva Kaili.
Qatar and Morocco have been accused of trying to sway European decisions and improve on their public image. Both countries have denied the allegations.
The Belgian investigation has been significantly delayed because of legal appeals challenging the lawfulness of certain procedural steps.

New cat species identified for first time in more than a century in Bolivia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:43:38 UTC
05:43:38 KST

A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living feline species has been formally named and described in more than a century.
The cat, called tilcayo by local communities, is part of a group called tiger cats found across much of South America. It was found in Bolivia’s lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 18in (46cm) long and weighs about 3lb (1.4kg), making it smaller than the average domestic cat.
Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.
“Its fur is light brown … with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body,” said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.
Little is yet known about the cat’s biology and lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it could be more active at night, Nogales-Ascarrunz said.
Tiger cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.
Tiger cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.
Referring to the new species, Lescroart said: “Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records.”
One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives in the Senda Verde wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia after being kept by a local family in their home.
Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because “its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats”, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This made us wonder: what tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?”
The team analysed DNA from 38 cats sampled across several South American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.
“We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise,” Lescroart said.
Genetic analysis suggested that the tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4m years ago.
“The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we estimate those lineages to have been physically separated,” Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.
The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru’s Yungas region, naming it Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca empire that included the area it inhabits.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) red list tracking the status of species currently treats tiger cats as two “vulnerable” species with declining populations.
The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review will assess the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the tilcayo could be considered endangered when assessed on their own.
The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute in the Yungas, one of the region’s most threatened ecosystems.
The mountain forests face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, she added.
“Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats … there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message,” said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study. “There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them.”

05:40:01 KST

EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen says Europe will provide Ukraine with another €3.3 billion for missiles and drones as Russia intensifies attacks on Kyiv and seeks to make daily life in Ukraine's cities impossible.
Ukraine has repeatedly appealed to its partners for more air defense as Russia develops increasingly sophisticated ways to attack Ukrainian cities, while Ukraine’s stocks of air-defense interceptors have fallen to critically low levels.
Following a call with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, von der Leyen said the EU would disburse the funds on 18 September. She also said the EU had approved funding for Patriot air defense systems through its Ukraine Support Loan.
Ukraine needs more air defense
Russia has increasingly combined large numbers of attack drones with ballistic and cruise missiles, forcing Ukraine to defend vast areas while facing shortages of high-end interceptors.
The most difficult targets are Russia’s ballistic missiles, which can reach Ukrainian cities within minutes and require specialized systems such as Patriot to intercept. Ukraine has repeatedly called for more Patriot batteries and interceptors as Russia increases missile attacks.
Ukraine also needs additional air defense capabilities to counter Russia’s increasingly sophisticated drone attacks. Russia is deploying faster, more advanced Geran-type drones that are more difficult to intercept, increasing pressure on Ukraine’s already limited air-defense stocks.
Von der Leyen said the EU had approved funding for Patriot systems last week, but acknowledged that “clearly more is needed.”
The new €3.3 billion package will fund the procurement of missiles and drones for Ukraine, strengthening its ability to defend against Russian attacks.
Europe proposes joint air defense development
Von der Leyen also announced that the EU is prepared to use remaining funds from its Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program to launch a new joint EU-Ukraine defense initiative.
The proposed program would focus on developing a European air and missile defense system, building on the jointly developed anti-ballistic Freya system.
The goal is to combine Ukraine’s battlefield experience and defense innovation with European technology and industrial capacity, according to von der Leyen.
The announcement comes as Ukraine is trying to strengthen its air defenses ahead of another winter of Russian attacks, when strikes against energy and other critical infrastructure could have an especially severe impact on civilians.
The EU has billions in unspent defense funds. It wants to use them for projects with Ukraine
Von der Leyen calls for broader support
Von der Leyen said the EU has already mobilized nearly €15 billion for Ukraine in 2026, with additional support planned. She added that “more is coming.”
She also said Ukraine needs to complete reforms in the Verkhovna Rada to unlock further funding and continue its path toward EU membership.
“Europe is stepping up,” von der Leyen said. “Now others must step up their support too.”

a sequence of colored rooms and a continuous bookcase reshape a madrid apartment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:35:27 UTC
05:35:27 KST

Casa POP reorganizes a standardized Madrid apartment
Casa POP by gon architects is the renovation of a 78 sqm apartment in Vicálvaro, east of Madrid, that had been occupied by its owners for 20 years. The starting point was a typical, heavily compartmentalized home whose layout no longer suited their way of living. The project reorganizes the apartment around a large central storage core, replacing the original sequence of small rooms and corridors with a more open and connected spatial arrangement. A large green bookshelf runs from one side of the home to the other, incorporating sliding doors that can be opened or closed to adjust privacy and change the configuration of the space depending on the occasion.
The apartment is located on the sixth floor of a residential complex built in the 2000s on former industrial land, with exposed brick buildings, shared areas, and a swimming pool. Its elevated position provides views across the surrounding neighborhood, while the compact floor plan gives the apartment a watchtower-like quality. The original layout was based directly on the housing regulations in force at the time, incorporating the domestic rooms required by minimum standards. Designed for a nuclear family with children, it contained two bedrooms, two bathrooms, a small living room, a compact independent kitchen, and extensive hallway space.
For the owners, Santiago and Ángel, this standardized arrangement no longer corresponded to their lifestyle. A hospital nurse and a high school language and literature teacher, respectively, the couple has an active interest in cinema, theater, literature, and other forms of culture. Their daily life is centered on time, leisure, and cultural activities, leading to a different set of spatial requirements. The renovation therefore transforms the narrow and compartmentalized apartment into a more spacious and connected home, while incorporating their request for a cinematic zenithal perspective throughout the project.
The new layout, developed by gon architects studio, is organized as a U-shaped plan around the central storage core, with the circulation moving clockwise. This arrangement allows the domestic programs to unfold as a sequence of physically and visually connected rooms, moving from the more public areas toward the private ones. The apartment can be understood as a series of interconnected rooms of different sizes and functions, forming an open and continuous landscape while maintaining five distinct areas defined by color.
Each of these five spaces corresponds to a domestic program and action, including entering, cooking, eating, resting, and dressing. Within each area, the walls, ceiling, and furniture are painted in the same color, creating a continuous surface and an immersive spatial atmosphere. The approach references the interiors of 18th- and 19th-century European mansions, where color was used to shape perception and alter the apparent scale and character of rooms. Here, the use of color also introduces a playful and sensory quality into the apartment.
From the entrance hall, the sequence continues toward the en-suite bedroom and its lemon-yellow dressing room. A large marble-green walkthrough kitchen forms the central meeting and circulation space, functioning as a place for cooking, gathering, and conversation before leading into the rectangular living-dining room. This space also incorporates a small workspace and a folding bed integrated into the furniture, which can be pulled out when guests stay overnight.
Cinematic references inform the furniture of Casa POP
Throughout the apartment, the different rooms maintain visual and spatial connections with one another and with the exterior. The windows frame views of the surrounding urban landscape, allowing changes in light and time to become part of the interior experience. The apartment is consequently conceived as a space that registers the passage of time through its relationship with the city outside. A large custom-made bookcase, completely lacquered in opal green, occupies the living-dining room, extending from floor to ceiling and across the width of the apartment. Its 27 shelves accommodate nearly 1,500 books and small objects, creating a shared domestic archive that reflects the biographies and interests of Santiago and Ángel. The work of Granadan writer Federico García Lorca holds a particular place within the collection.
The bookcase is perforated at two points to incorporate a system of translucent sliding doors. These doors allow individual rooms to become more independent while retaining flexibility across the apartment. Open, they create long visual diagonals through the connected spaces; closed, they establish more contained and visually abstract interiors. At night, the translucent surfaces allow the individual rooms to read as softly illuminated volumes within the apartment. Alongside the main bookcase, several pieces of furniture were specifically designed and manufactured for the home, including a yellow ceramic headboard in the bedroom and a desk where Ángel grades his exams. By integrating storage and functions into custom furniture, the project keeps the overall furniture arrangement compact. The main living and bedroom areas contain four principal pieces: a table, a sofa, armchairs, and a bed, complemented by the lighting fixtures.
The design also incorporates references drawn from the owners’ personal cultural interests. One of the project’s key visual references comes from a still frame from Pedro Almodóvar’s film The Room Next Door, which Santiago and Ángel presented during their first meeting. The image shows Tilda Swinton and Julianne Moore lying on two lounge chairs, one green and one red. These two colors became part of the project’s imagery and ultimately informed the color palette and narrative of Casa POP. Through its central storage core, continuous circulation, integrated furniture, sliding doors, and color-defined rooms, Casa POP replaces the apartment’s original compartmentalized arrangement with a flexible sequence of connected domestic spaces. The project treats architecture, furniture, color, books, and cinematic references as parts of the same interior system.
designboom has received this project from our DIY submissions feature, where we welcome our readers to submit their own work for publication. See more project submissions from our readers here.

Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case told family that investigation was ‘murdering him’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:33:37 UTC
05:33:37 KST

Days before Nicholas Brandram, the man suspected of being the “Putney pusher”, killed himself, he told his family that the police investigation was “murdering him”.
He had “no fight left” in him, he told his sisters, Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker, and could not see an end to the Metropolitan police investigation, or the online abuse.
Brandram’s lawyers warned the Met last week that his mental health had deteriorated and he was receiving treatment in a psychiatric hospital after renewed press reporting that he had been released under investigation.
“He said a couple of days ago that this investigation was murdering him. Day by day, he was slowly being murdered,” Hicks, 40, said through tears.
“He saw no end to this investigation,” added Voelcker, 45. “My sister and I were keeping a close eye on him because he was telling us he couldn’t go on. He said it more than once in the week before, that he couldn’t keep going. All we could do was just reassure him. We had faith in the system, we had faith in the police, and they neglected him. They failed in their duty of care to him, to the wider family, and we do not want to see another family going through this.”
The pair insisted that Brandram, 44, was not the “Putney pusher” and that he died thinking no one would believe in his innocence.
He was arrested on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm on 15 June, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman headfirst into the path of an oncoming bus on Putney Bridge in south-west London.
The case attracted considerable media attention but appeared to elude detectives, who wound down their investigation in 2018, after interviewing 50 men and arresting three suspects.
But there was renewed interest in the case after Brandram’s arrest, which his family described as heavy-handed and disproportionate. A number of officers in body armour reportedly swooped on his home address, his sisters said, while a reporter who had been tipped off about the arrest filmed the ordeal.
Although Brandram’s name was not published in the media because he had not been charged, his family said that biographical information in reports made him easily identifiable. He was described as a wealthy banker who lived in a £1.4m west London home and an army veteran with links to royalty. Brandram was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, who was a great-granddaughter of Queen Victoria.
While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, he was also arrested on suspicion of possession of class A and class B drugs.
His sisters said there was no forensic evidence linking Brandram to the Putney incident and that he had a prominent military tattoo and a withered calf which, they said, distinguished him from the man in footage of the attack on 5 May 2017.
That morning, Brandram had walked from his home in Notting Hill Gate to his office in Bond Street and sent his sisters an email from his work account, which they said he could only access from his workplace. They said that evidence was passed on to the police.
They added that Brandram had volunteered to take part in an identification parade and provided his DNA for comparison with a sample recovered at the time of the incident. Hicks said detectives told Brandram just days ago that they still did not know when the DNA analysis would be completed.
“Our brother willingly provided DNA in an attempt to obviously help clear his name and to complete the investigation, and for weeks now we’ve been asking the police just to complete the DNA test,” Voelcker said.
“We’ve always maintained that he’s innocent. He always maintained he was innocent. We just needed the police to complete their inquiry, and it just felt particularly egregious that they were just hanging this DNA test over him.”
Hicks said as details of the case kept being reported in the press, her brother became preoccupied by online abuse on forums such as Reddit.
“His reputation within a couple of days was in tatters. People saying he’s the alleged pusher, and you can imagine the vitriol that was coming out online,” Voelcker said.
“You can imagine what people might say about somebody they think tried to push a woman in front of a bus. There was a lot of people had a lot of views about our brother, about his background, about where he worked.”
“And the problem was he was reading it all every day,” Hicks said. “The vitriol is still there and that’s what’s so heartbreaking for us, is that when he took his own life he died thinking that effectively everyone hated him and thought he’d done something awful and that no one would see that he was innocent and he knew that his family were behind him but it wasn’t enough.”
The sisters said Brandram had stayed with them in recent days after his mental health deteriorated following the publication of an update about the case that said he had been released under investigation.
“He was really talking about ending his life and ending things. And he was very low and said he felt like he had no fight left in him. He couldn’t see the end,” Voelcker said.
Brandram was admitted to a psychiatric hospital for six days before being discharged on Sunday.
His family insisted the Met police were warned about his mental health.
Voelcker tried to boost his mood on Tuesday by telling him it was a beautiful day and that he had many friends and his family supporting him. He was found dead at his home in Chiswick, west London, later that day.
The family said their priority was to clear their brother’s name and “to ensure another family does not have to go through what we have as a result of the police delays and leaks to the media”.
Hicks said: “Nick was really very loving, enthusiastic. He had an infectious character to be around, very funny. He was an extrovert, so he loved people. He was a much-loved father and uncle.”
Voelcker added: “He spent a long time in the army before going into the city. And his reputation was important. He was a proud man. I think that’s the thing and even the fact that he needed to seek help from a psychiatric hospital was a big deal for him.”
Ch Supt Dan Knowles, in charge of policing for south-west London, said: “Our thoughts are with Mr Brandram’s family and friends at this deeply distressing time. We recognise the significant impact his death will have on those who knew and loved him. We also understand the strain that being subject to a police investigation can place on individuals and their families.
“The investigation remains ongoing. Following Mr Brandram’s release under investigation, it was made clear that inquiries would continue while officers progressed outstanding lines of inquiry and forensic examinations. This remains the position, and further investigative work is ongoing.
“Investigations of this nature, particularly those involving complex evidential and forensic work, can take a number of months to complete as officers gather and assess all available evidence.”
He added that the force had made a mandatory referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct on 16 September.

Argentina sends Falkland Islands sovereignty bill to Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:31:20 UTC
05:31:20 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
17 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Argentine President Javier Milei’s government sent a bill to Congress on Thursday, seeking to strengthen legal measures related to the country’s sovereignty claim over the Falkland Islands and increase penalties for unauthorized exploitation of natural resources in the area.
“The initiative is based on three pillars: punishing those who illegally exploit our natural resources, encouraging them to stop such activities and giving the state tools to protect itself against external threats,” the Office of the President said in a statement.
The legislation would replace a 2011 law governing activities involving natural resources in the territory and surrounding maritime areas claimed by Argentina.
It would expand sanctions beyond the hydrocarbons sector to cover any unauthorized activity involving the exploitation of renewable or nonrenewable natural resources, according to the government and Argentine media reports.
Penalties proposed under the bill include fines ranging from 4,000 to 500,000 units, or legal monetary reference units under Argentine law, as well as the cancellation or suspension of permits, and disqualification from operating for periods of between five and 20 years.
The legislation would also establish a National Security System coordinated by a National Security Council.
The framework would bring together diplomatic, economic, defense, legal, intelligence and cybersecurity functions, as well as measures related to critical infrastructure and national sovereignty.
The bill comes as Argentina has increased pressure on companies involved in natural resource projects around the Falkland Islands.
The move also follows an Argentine federal court’s decision Wednesday to order works linked to the Sea Lion offshore oil project to be suspended. The project involves Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and British firm Rockhopper Exploration.
The government has opposed the project, arguing that resource exploitation in the area requires authorization from Argentine authorities.
The bill will be reviewed by congressional committees before being considered by the Chamber of Deputies.

Budget day 2026: a renewed drive to safeguard prosperity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:29:50 UTC
05:29:50 KST

The Dutch economy is strong, despite economic shocks and global insecurity. What is more, the government is making funds available to support the purchasing power of households. This is the message set out in the Budget Memorandum and the Tax Plan for 2027 which the Minister of Finance, Eelco Heinen, presented to the House of Representatives today.
The government will seek to stimulate economic growth to safeguard the Netherlands’ continued prosperity. It is placing a strong emphasis on three pillars: investment, reform and international cooperation. Issues relating to grid congestion, regulatory pressure and the permitting system must be resolved in order to encourage private investment. Reforms are needed in order to deliver greater productivity and an increase in the labour supply. And international cooperation is crucial so that the Netherlands remains strong at a time when international relations are under great strain.
Minister Heinen: ‘Whether we’re talking about our security, our public services or the opportunities we want to give future generations, they all depend on the strength of the economy. And it’s that economic strength which is under pressure. So our country must recommit to the task of generating economic growth. That means we have to invest, reform, and step up international cooperation. Sound public finances are a prerequisite, and they will be safeguarded by this budget.’
Key measures
The Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis forecasts that, next year, households will on average be 0.1 percentage points worse off, partly as a consequence of the war in the Middle East and higher prices. The government is taking measures that will on average improve households’ purchasing power by 0.2 percentage points relative to earlier estimates. In addition, lower rates of excise duties on petrol and diesel will provide a reduction in the tax burden at the petrol pump totalling €1.4 billion.
In addition, the government will make a one-off investment of €1.5 billion – and invest €300 million on a structural basis – in infrastructure. As a stimulus to home building, €425 million will be invested annually in housing associations, by means of policy measures, to increase their capacity to build more homes. To foster the energy transition, a subsidy of €1.3 billion will be made available for carbon storage with a view to mobilising investment. In addition, some €370 million will be allocated to international cooperation annually over the next three years, partly for Ukraine.
In the government’s view it is important to look carefully at the final design of the tax on the actual return on savings and investments in box 3. It was agreed in the coalition agreement to evolve the new box 3 system, based on actual return, into a capital gains system. Over the coming period the government will therefore present concrete and broadly supported proposals to work towards this objective in line with the coalition agreement. They will be processed at the next budgetary decision-making moment.
Cooperation with parliament, subnational authorities, civil society and business is crucial in order to effectively tackle the major issues confronting Dutch society. With this Budget Memorandum, the government is reaching out to the social partners (representatives of employers’ and employees’ organisations) to come to the table and discuss these issues. The plan to directly link the state pension age to life expectancy has been definitively abandoned. In addition, the measure included in the coalition agreement to lower the maximum daily wage for the calculation of social security benefits by 20% has been scrapped. It has also been decided to postpone a number of proposed social security measures by a year. This offers scope for discussion between the government and social partners about the reforms to the social security system and to conclude a broadly supported social accord.
Public finances
The government’s commitment to fiscal discipline and a trend-based fiscal policy is undiminished. During the term of this government, the budget deficit will remain below 3% of gross domestic product (GDP) and public debt below 60% of GDP. The deficit will amount to 2.9% in 2027 and fall gradually to 2.2% in 2030. The level of public debt will gradually increase from 45.6% in 2026 to 46.9% in 2027 and 48.9% in 2030. Sound public finances are crucial. Without intervention, expenditure will shift increasingly towards consumption, whereas the government wishes to use the scarce resources to invest in economic growth.
2027 Tax Plan
The Tax Plan presents proposals by which the government seeks to address public concerns relating for example to home building. Besides scrapping the limit on interest deduction, the government also aims to address these concerns by abolishing transfer tax for housing associations. Furthermore, the government intends to reduce transfer tax for investors from 8% to 7% from 2027.
In addition, the government wants to amend the measures for the waste processing sector, so that waste incineration plants will have more time to make their operations more sustainable, and to avoid a situation where Dutch waste is incinerated abroad. To this end, waste disposal charges and the CO2 levy on industry will rise more slowly than previously planned. Measures are also being proposed that will improve the functioning of the tax system and contribute to sound public finances. Tax reliefs that no longer serve their intended purpose or have become too complex for the people for whom they are intended are being abolished. This also helps implementing agencies. Through these measures the government is ensuring that the tax system will continue to improve in 2027.

US: Trump administration weakens Endangered Species Act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:29:00 UTC
05:29:00 KST

US: Trump administration weakens Endangered Species Act
September 17, 2026
The US government is planning a major reinterpretation of the Endangered Species Act (ESA), The New York Times reported and officials confirmed to AFP on Thursday.
The policy shift was delivered in a new memo signed by Brian Nesvik, director of the Interior Department's Fish and Wildlife Service.
In it, the department will reduce the term "take," a term that relates to pursuing, killing or capturing of a species, to simply "affirmative conduct intentionally directed against a particular animal or animals."
This change would no longer treat the unintentional killing of protected wildlife as unlawful.
Wildlife deaths resulting from foreseeable risks posed by activities such as commercial fishing or logging would end up exempt from the landmark 1973 law.
A 'huge loophole'
The wildlife service has historically held people liable for accidentally harming protected species such as grizzly bears, manatees and spotted owls.
"This cuts against the entire history of the Endangered Species Act," Dan Ashe, who led the Fish and Wildlife Service under former President Barack Obama, told the Associated Press. "It just creates a huge loophole. It completely relieves people of any responsibility for their actions, even consequences that can be easily predicted."
The Interior Department confirmed the memo's authenticity to AFP.
"The memorandum accurately reflects the US Fish and Wildlife Service's guidance for implementing the Endangered Species Act following the final rule rescinding the regulatory definition of 'harm,'" the department told AFP.
"Under the guidance, the ESA's prohibition on 'take' continues to prohibit conduct including harassing, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing or collecting protected wildlife," it added.
Broad overhaul of Endangered Species Act
Last year, the Trump administration declared it would consider "economic considerations" when deciding whether to protect species at risk of extinction.
The move is the latest attempt to loosen the landmark ESA's rules. Combined, the changes overturn five decades of precedent in how the law is interpreted and applied.
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has argued that the changes are necessary, claiming the ESA has been "weaponized" to stop economic projects, weaken competitiveness, undermine national security, and ultimately hurt Americans.
Among the changes to ESA is the redefinition of the term "harm," which would allow oil drilling, mining and other activities in endangered habitats as long as those activities do not directly kill or injure the animals.
The automatic application of endangered species protections to those listed as "threatened" was also halted.
Additionally, the Trump administration announced that it was shrinking two vast stretches of protected land in Utah by more than 90%, to open millions of acres of protected land for fossil fuel extraction and mining.
States sue the government
Last week, the attorneys general of 20 Democratic-led states, along with Washington, DC, submitted a lawsuit against the administration over its overhaul of ESA.
One lawsuit tackles the redefinition of "harm," while a second lawsuit challenges a rule that removes protections for newly threatened species, and the new business-related considerations taken into account when declaring "critical habitats."
"The Trump administration is trying to undermine the law, the will of Congress and the will of the people who overwhelmingly support protections for endangered species," Washington Attorney General Nick Brown said.
"Instead of stewardship, this administration's approach to our land, to our water is one of exploitation," he added.

Syria to abolish Assad-era ‘Terrorism Court’ to restore rights in 90,000-plus cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:26:41 UTC
05:26:41 KST

Sahin Demir
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Syria’s People’s Assembly unanimously approved a bill Thursday to abolish the Assad-era “Terrorism Court,” according to state-run SANA news agency.
The move is to reverse the effects of rulings in more than 90,000 cases handled by the court and restore confiscated property and other rights to those affected.
The court was established under Law No. 22 of 2012 during the rule of Bashar al-Assad and had jurisdiction over cases involving civilians and military personnel.
SANA said the exceptional legal framework under which the court operated had drawn criticism because of fair-trial guarantees and the right to defense.
Abdul Nasser Houshan, head of parliament’s Constitutional and Legislative Committee, said the bill abolishes the law establishing the court and assigns the Supreme Judicial Council responsibility for addressing the consequences of its rulings.
Specialized judicial committees will be formed to nullify the effects of previous rulings, including returning confiscated property. Pending cases will be closed or transferred to the competent judicial authorities.
At least 90,560 cases were brought before the court, according to figures cited by SANA from the Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR).
The rights group documented at least 40,602 property seizure and confiscation orders between 2012 and 2024, affecting 320,000 people under the broader seizure and confiscation system established by the Assad regime.
SNHR said the court relied on security reports and confessions extracted under torture in some cases, while imposing restrictions on the right to defense and lacking transparency in its rulings.
The bill also exempts those recovering confiscated property from taxes, fees and other costs associated with transferring ownership back to them. The provision covers property confiscated under rulings by the “Terrorism Court,” Military Field Courts and military courts between March 15, 2011, and Dec. 8, 2024.
The Assad regime abolished the separate Military Field Courts in 2023 and transferred pending cases to the military judiciary.
Following Assad’s fall in December 2024, authorities began reviewing the legacy of the “Terrorism Court.” In 2025, the Justice Ministry referred judges who had served in the court for investigation and established a specialized judicial committee to review rulings and procedures issued by the court and other exceptional judicial bodies.

The upcoming tranche is smaller than the 4.7 billion euros ($5.5 billion) previously promised by EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius on Sept. 11. The smaller disbursement is the result of delays in processing Ukrainian receipts for military equipment.
A senior EU official previously told the Kyiv Independent that the disbursement would likely be lower than $5.5 billion due to this reason. Disbursements from the support loan can only be processed once Ukraine has provided receipts for cross-checking.
Zelensky and von der Leyen have also agreed to meet on the sidelines of the upcoming UNGA in New York, Zelensky said on social media after their discussion.
"We discussed the issue of funding for Ukrainian defense in great detail," the president said. "We are working on solutions to this problem and agreed to meet in New York on the sidelines of the General Assembly."
World leaders will convene at the U.N. headquarters in New York from Sept. 22-28 for the organization's 81st General Assembly. Zelensky is expected to meet with multiple leaders at the event, including a potential one-on-one with U.S. President Donald Trump.
In her statement after the call with Zelensky, von der Leyen indicated that she would lobby Kyiv's non-European allies for increased support during her time at the UNGA.

 Impartiality is sometimes treated by philosophers as if it were equivalent to moral impartiality. Or, at the very least, the former word is often used, without the qualifying adjective ‘moral’, even when it is the particularly moral concept that is intended. This is potentially misleading, since impartiality in its broadest sense is best understood as a formal notion that can be applied in a number of contexts, including non-moral contexts….
