Big space mirrors could bring Earth on-demand light — and upend our night sky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:23:22 UTC
05:23:22 KST

Big space mirrors could bring Earth on-demand light — and upend our night sky
Reflect Orbital satellites could make the darkest skies look like nighttime in the suburbs
Since 1989, astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell has tracked every human-made object in space. McDowell’s meticulously maintained catalog, updated every few weeks, is more comprehensive and detailed than that of most governments.
From his front-row seat, he has watched with growing alarm as private companies launched dozens, then hundreds, then thousands of satellites over the last decade. So when McDowell heard that a space company called Reflect Orbital plans to launch a satellite to reflect the sun’s light onto the night side of Earth, he heaved a deep sigh.
“It’s an insane project,” says McDowell, who retired from Harvard this year and is now an honorary professor at Durham University in England. “There’s a failure to understand that darkness is a good thing.”
Reflect Orbital, based near Los Angeles, hopes its satellite and others like it some day offer “sunlight on demand,” illuminating disaster areas for search and rescue efforts, lighting up nighttime events and festivals and allowing solar farms to run all hours of the day.
“We believe that exploring how new technologies can help the world forgo fossil fuels is a responsible application of the scientific process,” Christopher Buscombe, a spokesperson for Reflect Orbital, wrote in an email to Science News. “We will continue to work closely with scientific partners who share this belief.”
But many space observers and dark sky enthusiasts are in an uproar. The consequences to astronomy could be catastrophic, they say, and the reflected light could threaten human health and safety and disrupt wildlife. In March, the American Astronomical Society petitioned the Federal Communications Commission to deny Reflect Orbital’s request to operate the test satellite. When the FCC granted approval in July, nonprofit organizations including DarkSky International asked the agency to reverse its decision.
The response to Reflect Orbital reflects growing concerns about the crowding of space more generally. The number of active satellites orbiting Earth has ballooned from 2,000 in 2018 to over 16,000 today, McDowell says. Many more are expected to launch in the years ahead.
This traffic jam, along with the proliferation of space junk from dead satellites and discarded rocket stages, has space scientists worried about collisions that could wipe out GPS navigation and other essential tools. The satellites are also a problem for astronomers, interrupting observations by leaving streaks on telescope images.
But there’s not much scientists can do to appeal the launches, says international environmental lawyer Dana Zartner of the University of San Francisco. Space satellite deployments are governed (sometimes loosely) by a patchwork of domestic regulations and international treaties. “The law has not caught up to the reality of what is happening,” Zartner says.
The Reflect Orbital launch, expected this year, could change that. The satellite’s unique brightness and the risks it may bring could mark an inflection point in the way we regulate the night sky. The project “amplifies the issue to the point where it’s impossible to ignore,” says astronomer Stephen Hummel of the McDonald Observatory in West Texas.
Who’s in charge?
Space law’s roots are planted in the Cold War. Some of the earliest international treaties about activities in outer space grew from agreements banning nuclear tests high in the atmosphere.
“People [were] saying, ‘Let’s not nuke the sky, please,’” says Cristian van Eijk, an expert in international space law at Newcastle University in England.
Over 100 nations have signed the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, which declares space “the province of all mankind.” No nation can occupy or claim sovereignty over any portion of outer space, it says, and space must be used for peaceful purposes and be kept clear of harmful contamination. Four other international treaties have dealt with issues such as the registration of space objects and the liability they might cause.
But such treaties are voluntary, and it’s difficult to enforce compliance. “Nobody can make a state do any of these things,” Zartner says. “You cannot throw a state in jail.”
Individual countries have their own regulations about what goes into space and how. In the United States, the Federal Aviation Administration oversees rocket launches and reentries. But the FCC oversees licensing of commercial satellites that communicate with Earth, and it has become the de facto gatekeeper for satellite approval. The FCC has traditionally been required to consider whether applications serve the public interest, but it has not generally considered factors such as light pollution.
The explosion in satellites in low-Earth orbit, between about 100 and 2,000 kilometers in altitude, has exposed gaps in the system, says astronomer Samantha Lawler of the University of Regina in Saskatchewan, Canada. That’s because current approval processes look at launches one by one without addressing what thousands of satellites mean in aggregate. “There are some serious loopholes,” Lawler says.
Bugs on the windshield
To reduce the impact to science, companies like SpaceX have worked with astronomers to dim the appearance of their commercial satellites, by changing their orbits or painting the satellites black, for example. But there are still problems.
Astronomer Meredith Rawls likens existing satellites to “bugs on the windshield.” She and colleagues have spent years preparing the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile to cope with the light streaks left by overhead satellites.
Those streaks can mess with searches for transiting exoplanets, the mysterious sources of gravitational waves, objects in and beyond the distant Kuiper Belt and asteroids that could cross paths with Earth. Satellites in low-Earth orbit, including SpaceX’s Starlink constellations, are mainly visible just before sunrise and after sunset; that’s prime time for many types of astronomical observations.
“One of the most frustrating parts about it is you won’t know what you didn’t discover,” says Rawls, of the University of Washington in Seattle. “We can’t know what we didn’t see.”
The space community is also alarmed by the growing potential for orbiting objects to crash into each other, hurtling space junk toward Earth or creating an unnavigable debris field around the planet. Most commercial satellites have thrusters to avoid such collisions. But the proliferation of objects means those satellites are engaging thrusters frequently, sometimes weekly. Scientists wonder what will happen when they fail.
And there is a growing concern about the potentially hazardous residue such satellites could leave in the atmosphere when they de-orbit. “We are now using space as a species at an unprecedented level,” McDowell says. “A lot of effects that were previously trivial are now no longer trivial.”
Space scientists, amateur astronomers, Indigenous peoples and many others are mourning the night sky as it has existed for millennia — or soon will be. “This represents far more than mere loss of environment,” wrote astronomers Aparna Venkatesan of the University of San Francisco and John Barentine, cofounder of the Center for Space Environmentalism, in 2023 in Science. “We are witnessing loss of heritage, place-based language, identity, storytelling, millennia-old sky traditions and our ability to conduct traditional practices grounded in the ecological integrity of what we call home.” The pair proposed a term for “sky grief”: noctalgia.
That grief could grow as companies put ever more satellites into space. SpaceX alone plans to launch one million as part of orbiting data centers starting in late 2027. Other companies and countries, including China’s space agency, plan to launch hundreds of thousands more. Even if not all of them get off the ground, the number of fake stars in a dark night sky could rival the number of visible real ones by 2030, McDowell says.
Mirrors in the sky
Reflect Orbital’s satellite, named Eärendil-1, is an 18-by-18-meter sheet of reflective material that will fold up for launch and unfurl in space. Motors will maneuver it to bounce light in any direction the company desires. It will orbit 600 to 650 kilometers high, a popular altitude for commercial satellites. Eärendil-1 will be able to shine light on a spot about five kilometers wide, making it as bright as if a full moon were overhead. The mirror will move at about 7.5 kilometers per second, meaning it will illuminate the same spot on the ground for four minutes before disappearing over the horizon.
“Our first demonstration mission will enable Reflect Orbital to test the operation of a commercially built spacecraft and deployable reflector, including the built-in safeguards governing precisely how, where and when the service is delivered,” Buscombe told Science News. “The mission will provide real-world data that shapes the design of future satellites, the markets we serve, how we engage communities and the operational practices we put in place. We expect this to be the first of several test missions.”
This isn’t the first time such a scheme has been proposed or even attempted. In the 1960s, NASA and the U.S. Department of Defense ran a study called Project Able to determine the feasibility of putting a 600-meter-wide mirror into a geosynchronous orbit 36,000 kilometers above Earth. One of the motivations was to light the sky over Vietnam to aid combat.
“They say history doesn’t repeat itself, but it does rhyme,” says Lisa Ruth Rand, a California-based space historian who is writing a book about waste in Earth’s orbit.
Practicalities and cost meant the mirror never got off the ground. But in 1993, the Russian space agency deployed a 20-meter space mirror that swept a spot of light across Europe. The project sought to show the feasibility of lighting up Siberia during long winter nights. Though the beam was mostly blocked by clouds, astronauts aboard the Mir space station filmed the event.
Reflect Orbital says its spotlight will be fully controllable and can be turned off in an instant by tilting the mirror away from Earth. Outside the beam, the light will look like just another star, according to Buscombe. And it shouldn’t shine on places where no one ordered it.
Space scientists aren’t so sure. As light travels from space to the ground, it scatters off molecules in the atmosphere, says astrophysicist Gaspar Bakos of Princeton University. “That is why the sky is blue, why we see the clouds,” he says.
Bakos and colleagues ran computer simulations of the light from a Reflect Orbital satellite overhead under various conditions. Between scattering in the atmosphere and reflections from the ground, Eärendil-1’s beam could appear as a hazy chimney on the horizon from as far as 14 kilometers away, the team reported in a paper posted in August on arXiv.org.
Only one satellite is cleared for operations, Reflect Orbital and the FCC note. But critics worry that there’s nothing in the licensing logic that would stand in the way of more. If the test is successful, Reflect Orbital says it wants to launch 5,000 mirrors by 2030 and 50,000 by 2035. They would be larger, about 54 meters across. Light from such a mirror could brighten the night sky to as much as four full moons. Arranged in a chain, they would keep the lights on longer, because a new mirror would come into view just as an old one sets.
“It’s quite a dance, if you think about it,” Hummel says. “A lot of things need to move very accurately in order to provide the levels of illumination that they’re claiming.”
Within the beam, you’d see no stars. The effect outside the beam would vary depending on distance and existing levels of light pollution. In a dark area, one 54-meter satellite would leave a concentrated glow that outshines the full moon from more than 30 kilometers away, Bakos and colleagues calculate. Even a person in an average suburb could see the beam from 20 kilometers away, Bakos says. For astronomers, the beam would be disruptive from up to 100 kilometers away.
Barentine, who is based in Tucson, has seen renderings of the simulations. “The only word I can think of to describe what they look like is horrifying,” he says. “If you are within a few kilometers of a beam, it looks like the mother ship is landing.”
Meanwhile, the McDonald Observatory is preparing for Eärendil-1 by developing tools to track and avoid the satellite’s path, Hummel says. Staff plan to pause telescope observing as needed. Seeing the beam through a moderate-sized telescope could damage observers’ eyes or harm research equipment, he and others assert.
Reflect Orbital counters that the risk of eye damage is extremely low, and that even intentionally tracking the satellite for 100 seconds through a 12-inch diameter telescope would stay within international eye-safety limits.
The company’s planned fleet could change the night sky dramatically, adding several hundred objects as bright as Venus by 2035, Munich-based astronomer Olivier Hainaut of the European Southern Observatory reported in August in Astronomy & Astrophysics. Because of light scattering, the full fleet could make the night sky three or four times as bright as it already is anywhere within a few hundred kilometers of the beam, Hainaut concludes. That would make skies at even the darkest sites appear more like those in the suburbs.
Reflect Orbital disputes those findings as well as Bakos’.
It’s not just astronomers who are concerned. Glints from rotating satellites could distract pilots or drivers. Nighttime light can also disrupt circadian rhythms, the behavior of nocturnal animals, and migration patterns of birds and insects.
The effects of one intermittent beam are unclear, says biologist Brett Seymoure of the University of Texas at El Paso. “If it’s a few days a year, is that going to have a big effect? Probably not. But we don’t know.” More troubling is the idea of permanently lighting up the night sky, which could alter critical ecosystem services, Seymoure says. “It’s an existential crisis for me.”
Reflect Orbital says it will maintain strict exclusion zones for astronomy and sensitive environments, which the company is developing with the National Science Foundation. It plans to adjust the exclusion zones based on the satellites’ actual brightness post-launch. “We are committed to ongoing dialogue with scientists, astronomers, environmental researchers and other interested stakeholders,” Buscombe told Science News.
Fighting back
Previous efforts to block satellites have relied on arguments about orbital debris and the environmental impact of light pollution. DarkSky International, for instance, challenged an FCC decision that granted SpaceX a license for its second-gen Starlink satellites in 2023, arguing the agency should have required an environmental review. DarkSky lost.
Typically, government-approved projects are subject to the National Environmental Policy Act, which requires environmental impact assessments. But since 1986, the FCC has said that most of its activities are excluded from the act because space is outside of Earth’s environment.
The FCC’s stance isn’t likely to change. In 2025, President Trump directed federal agencies to revise their environmental review processes to “prioritize efficiency and certainty over any other objectives.” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has announced plans to speed the satellite application process by creating a “licensing assembly line” and to clarify that FCC’s space-related activities don’t require environmental review.
But if the FCC won’t consider the environmental impact of satellite operations, critics ask, who will? It “becomes this buck passing thing,” Barentine says. “The FAA says we find nothing wrong with your launch, the FCC says we find nothing wrong with your radio communications, and there’s nothing to check the environmental impacts.” The FCC did not respond on the record to requests for comment.
Mirrors designed to send light to Earth might change the legal landscape, Barentine says. If an individual gets hurt by looking at the mirror through a telescope, that individual could have the right to sue in court. That’s not an ideal strategy for policy making, he says, because “we might actually have to wait for something to happen, for somebody to be injured.”
Scattered light also could count as a public nuisance, depending on where it shines, Zartner says. If it spills over an international border, Reflect Orbital or even the United States could be liable for any harm done in another nation’s territory.
Simply by being so visible, Reflect Orbital’s satellites could bring wider awareness of the concerns over space crowding. “Satellites up in the air are so intangible for most people,” Zartner says. “For the law, you need something tangible. To get support, you need something that people can see and latch onto.”
Zartner, Barentine and Venkatesan have outlined legal strategies to protect the darkness, drawing on individual rights, community rights and the rights of nature. Though those efforts haven’t succeeded to date, “I don’t believe that will be the case forever,” Venkatesan says. “We have to keep trying.”
What follows depends on how the public and policy makers respond. Could they be moved to action by sunbeams at night? Or are people already too acclimated to starless, satellite-filled skies? Spotting artificial objects in space has become a pastime in its own right.
What comes of this moment could determine what future generations experience when they look to the night sky. In one possible future, there’s a sense of awe for ancient celestial phenomena, their light traveling hundreds or thousands of light-years. In another, we may look up and applaud only the stuff we made and sent up ourselves.

Kashmir cracks walnut success code, turns to medium-sized, grafted trees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:19:49 UTC
05:19:49 KST

A street vendor sells walnuts on the occasion of the Sayar festival, in Mandi on Wednesday. (ANI Photo)
KOKERNAG: In Gohan village, around 100km south of Srinagar, Shabir Ahmad was among many harvesting walnuts from a towering tree. The work has become increasingly difficult. “My back aches now,” Ahmad said. J&K produces 3.5 lakh tonnes of walnuts annually, around 90% of the country’s total output.Like other villagers, Ahmad had no safety gear and he was proud of it. “We have been doing it for centuries,” said Ahmad, also a clerk at a local court. However, the bravado doesn’t help in harvesting seasons. Dr. Mohd Yaqoob Bhat, a surgeon at Paras Hospital in Srinagar, said Valley healthcare units treat dozens of patients each year after falls from walnut trees, some with serious spinal injuries. “There is no mechanism to address the issue,” Bhat said.Ahmad’s younger brother sold one walnut for one rupee and no two fruits are similar. For generations, Kashmir’s walnut trees have been grown from seeds. J&K and Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology (SKUAST) are now promoting medium-sized, grafted walnut trees to bring greater uniformity and help the produce compete globally amid competition from soft-shelled varieties grown in California and Chile.
The initiative aims to replace scattered plantations with organised orchards of known varieties, allowing farmers to grow more trees in the same area and produce walnuts more consistent in size and color.J&K has about 80,000 hectares under walnut cultivation, most of it made up of seedling-origin trees. “When someone plants a walnut seed in the ground, whatever grows becomes a tree. Every tree is a variety of its own,” Ashfaq A. Pandit, professor and head of fruit science at SKUAST, said. This natural variation, once considered an advantage, has become a challenge in the modern market where buyers seek consistent produce.Traditional walnut trees can take about 15 years to bear fruit without using pesticides. Unlike traditional seedling-origin trees, grafted walnuts belong to known varieties.Imtiyaz Ahmad Lone, professor and head of SKUAST’s Walnut Research Centre, said the university released new walnut cultivars and grafting-based cultivation had spread over nearly 90,000 hectares despite lack of subsidies.Farmers argued, however, that the grafted varieties are no match for the traditional Kashmiri walnut. “It is no match in taste. The new varieties are brittle, tasteless. They are a no-show,” Mohammad Sultan, a Pulwama farmer in the business for 50 years, said.
Researchers differed. Lone pointed out that grafted trees have early bearing, give faster returns as orchards and nut quality are uniform. “They have higher productivity and better export potential. There is a gradual opportunity to replace unproductive seedling trees,” he said.The transition has impacted walnut woodcraft industries. Walnut trees cannot be cut in J&K without govt permission. The matter was debated in the assembly in March when CM Omar Abdullah opposed a bill allowing landowners to cut walnut trees on private property. Omar defended the restrictions, saying the law served a broader purpose of conserving walnut and chinar trees.

Migrant arrivals to Europe fall 39%, while deaths rise: UN migration agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:15:54 UTC
05:15:54 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Migrant and refugee arrivals to Europe by sea have fallen sharply in 2026, but the number of people dying or missing during the journeys has risen, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Thursday.
Nearly 60,000 people arrived by sea this year, as of Sept. 15, down 39% from last year's 98,040, according to data from the IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix and Missing Migrants Project.
At least 2,292, however, have died or gone missing while attempting the crossings, compared with 1,999 during the same period in 2025.
The IOM cautioned that the actual toll is likely higher because many shipwrecks and disappearances are never recorded.
The sharpest decline in arrivals was seen on the Central Mediterranean route to Italy, falling 55% from 48,231 to 21,393. Deaths on the route climbed from 844 to 996.
"Fewer people are arriving by sea in Europe than at this point last year. But people are still dying and going missing in alarming numbers trying to reach safety," IOM Director General Amy Pope said in a statement.
Greece received 20,428 sea arrivals, about 5,000 fewer than a year earlier, while deaths along the Eastern Mediterranean route rose to 417 from 284.
Arrivals via routes to Spain also declined, with 16,794 people reaching the country through the Atlantic and Western Mediterranean, compared with 22,855 last year. At least 879 fatalities were recorded along those routes.
Pope urged greater international cooperation to save lives, combat trafficking, and expand safe and regular migration pathways.

The Choglamsar flower park will serve as a training, demonstration and model floriculture centre for farmers and youth, where Lilium, Gladiolus, Tulips and other ornamental flowers will be cultivated for national and international markets.

From African shepherd to Australia's marathon record holder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:13:41 UTC
05:13:41 KST

Haftu Strintzos's remarkable journey from shepherd to marathon record holder
Australia's men's marathon record holder, Haftu Strintzos, thrives on hard work but still finds it hard to believe where life has taken him.
Born in eastern Tigray in northern Ethiopia, he grew up standing barefoot in fields for hours, helping provide for his family from dawn to dusk.
"I feel as though I have lived a double life in a way," he said after celebrating his 27th birthday in Melbourne.
"I consider myself very privileged to live this life.
"I spent my early days as a shepherd, herding goats and sheep through the mountains of my local village. I grew up without a TV or running water."
In his remote community, 2,300 metres above sea level, the only source of information he had until age 10 was a mobile phone.
Haftu lost both biological parents by the time he was six, and was taken in by his maternal grandmother, living with his aunt and cousins.
A Greek Australian aid worker by the name of Maria Strintzos came calling, meeting Haftu in 2007 at the age of eight.
After decades working across Ethiopia, she asked him if he'd like to be her son, adopted him and helped him migrate to Melbourne in 2011 — more than 12,000 kilometres from the mountains of Tigray.
Today, Haftu speaks five languages (Tigrinya, Amharic, Greek, Japanese and English), holds a Master of Electrical Engineering from Villanova University in the USA and recently broke the national marathon record.
Feeling the 'weight of the world'
Maria always felt compelled to help others. Growing up in South Melbourne in the 1960s, she found strength in the local Greek community, even while migrant families faced racism.
"We had absolutely everybody there. As much as I loved growing up there, it built a strength in me," she said.
"I grew up knowing what social injustice and inequality looked like."
Her aid work took her through Indonesia, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Sudan, supporting famine relief, water schemes, food security, women's empowerment and communities affected by conflict, spending 35 years around wars and disease, but also hope, in the Horn of Africa.
But something different about young Haftu stood out.
He would walk barefoot through dry riverbeds, guiding his almost blind grandmother, Shifta, through the mountains to meet Maria.
"He was very respectful," she said.
"And he would sit there really quietly … didn't muck around like the other kids.
"He always had this sort of sad and serious look about him. It's like he had the weight of the world on his shoulders.
"But the way he looked after his grandmother and the way the grandmother would talk about him was very moving at the time too."
With the pull of family ties in Australia, Maria found herself at a crossroads.
"I was challenged at that time because I didn't particularly want to leave Ethiopia," she said.
"I loved my life. I loved what I did … I felt like I was achieving something."
Embracing the challenge of two different worlds
Excelling at school and winning education awards, Haftu embraced every opportunity.
When he migrated to Australia in 2011, he took nothing for granted in his new environment.
Growing up without electricity, he became fascinated by anything electrical.
Maria bought Haftu toy cars that he would unpack and dismantle.
"He literally pulled them apart with the motors, everything, and reassembled them," she said.
Having never seen a TV, he would sit on the couch for hours waiting for people to appear outside the screen.
"Sometimes I'd catch him sort of looking behind the TV because he thought there was people in there,"
"I still can't believe it. It was quite incredible that given his background, that he had this innate gift, something about electricity."
Maria said she's most proud of how Haftu had risen above adversity in his life.
"Where he's come from it was a rock hut, and they would sleep on the floor and the animals were next to them," she said.
"The uniqueness of Haftu is that he's managed to retain the positive qualities of his experience. I'm in awe of him."
But the culture shock wasn't easy; different foods, subtle racism and grappling with Western values were also some of Haftu's greatest tests.
"My biggest challenges in assimilating to Australian culture were learning the English language and motion sickness while riding in cars," he said.
"I remember a time in my early days where the only way I would not throw up while Mum drove the car was if I sat in the front passenger seat and kept my eyes on the road in front."
From a school oval to an athlete with no fear
It wasn't until he moved to Australia that Haftu realised his potential in athletics, having grown up in Tigray not knowing it was even a sport or profession.
"My PE teacher at school encouraged me to pursue it when he saw me run a cross-country race at the school oval," he said.
In that school race, he just kept running and didn't stop after the finish line, such was his determination for long-distance.
"I have grown up through this sport and learned my most valuable life lessons through it,"
"Running helped me connect with my local community, just getting out and about and meeting like-minded people."
His talent soon attracted attention, including from Cathy Freeman, who became like a mentor and even attended his birthday party during his teens.
Training up to 190 kilometres a week under coach Adam Didyk, Haftu broke the Australian men's marathon record in two hours, six minutes and 20 seconds at the Gold Coast Marathon in July.
He became the first Australian winner in 20 years, smashed the course record and set a new Oceania record — all on his fourth attempt at the distance.
Didyk, who also coaches Australian women's marathon record holder Jessica Stenson, has guided Haftu remotely from Adelaide for two years.
"He's a fairly no-fuss kind of individual. He'll just take the work and get it done," Didyk said.
"He's obviously very capable when it comes to longer distances and feels confident running at the pace he needs to for the marathon; quite extraordinarily, mind you."
Didyk said Haftu's college experience and early development give him a strong understanding of racing, matched by mental strength.
"He backs himself. He has a lot of confidence in his ability, and he believes in what he can do.
"He's one of those no-fear athletes who sets a goal that looks pretty daunting, but it excites him more and more the scarier he makes it."
Australian records are just the beginning
Haftu's talent comes as a package. Didyk said the physical ability, mental strength and calmness on race day were all put together to make good decisions, ultimately which led to the record-breaking performance at the Gold Coast Marathon.
"He's just a sensible, quite an intelligent young guy, and that all comes together to match what he can physically do as well," he said.
Haftu's calmness and patience on the Gold Coast reinforced Didyk's belief that he had world-class potential.
"There's so many positives about Haftu that he can go and achieve what no Australian has before in the marathon," Didyk said.
"He's very determined to be successful in international level … it was a phenomenally strong close.
"I think what's probably most important to us now with seeing that is if he's going to be competitive at an Olympic or World Championships level, he's going to need that ability to be able to close really fast over those last 10 kilometres.
"He's shown he's got the foundations to do something like that."
"Off the back of that, it started to give us the knowledge of him to go, 'that's the game he can play when he goes to a major championship, he can put himself in there and he can put himself in a competitive situation late in the race'.
"And that's ideally what we're aiming to do with him over the coming years."
From his humble beginnings in Ethiopia, Haftu's dreams of standing on an Olympic podium remain his driving force for motivation for the 2027 World Championships in China, and Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.
Australia hasn't had an Olympic marathon medallist since Lisa Ondieki won silver in 1988.
"I am very fortunate to have the support systems I need to help me to achieve my goals — something that not every athlete gets to have," he said.
"I want to continue to break records. After all, records are there to be broken."

KHARTOUM, Sudan / ISTANBUL (AA) – The Sudanese army said Thursday that it took control of 11 areas in the North Kordofan state in southern Sudan following clashes with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
“Our forces today managed to liberate the areas of Kajmar, Sharshar, Al-Baniya Al-Kurayniya, Al-Qulaiat, Awlad Hazma, Maquldat, Rishan, Al-Qaa, Al-Laqad Forest, Al-Kukaiti, and the area around Al-Mazrub in the North Kordofan state,” it said in a statement.
“The advances came after fierce battles in which RSF forces suffered heavy losses,” it said, adding that army units pursued remaining fighters toward the outskirts of Darfur.
The army also said it carried out wide-scale clearing operations in areas west of El-Obeid, the state capital.
“Operations are continuing with determination and steadfastness until state sovereignty is fully restored, civilians are secured and the areas are cleared of the terrorist militia and its supporters, leading to security and stability across the country,” said the statement.
There was no comment from the RSF on the statement as of 1730GMT.
Military sources told Anadolu on Thursday that the army advanced on fighting fronts in the North and South Kordofan states and took control of several areas in both states.
The army announced on Sept. 6 that it had seized the town of Hamrat al-Wiz in Jabra al-Sheikh, North Kordofan.
Since late July, the army has taken control of large areas in North Kordofan after retaking the city of Bara and the areas of Jabra al-Sheikh and Umm Siyala.
Sudan’s three Kordofan states – North, West, and South – have witnessed fighting between the army and the RSF since last Oct. 25.
Sudan has been engulfed in a war between the army and the RSF since April 2023, which has killed tens of thousands and displaced around 13 million people, according to UN and international estimates.

Why is Trump shifting millions in military aid to South America?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:07:31 UTC
05:07:31 KST

Why is Trump shifting millions in military aid to South America?
The US has decided to redirect $52 million in foreign military financing to four countries in South America, the Associated Press reported on Tuesday.
The funds, which subsidize purchases of American military equipment, are being reallocated from Slovakia, North Macedonia, Tunisia, and Iraq to Panama, Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia, the news agency said, citing a State Department notification to Congress.
The shift comes as US President Donald Trump has placed greater emphasis on the Western Hemisphere under what he has called the ‘Donroe Doctrine’, his version of the 19th-century hegemonic Monroe Doctrine. The Trump administration has said it intends to strengthen US influence in the Americas while preventing rival powers from gaining strategic positions in the region.
The State Department said the previous distribution of foreign military financing did “not align with the administration’s prioritization of” the Western Hemisphere. Spending the money in South America will help recipients “combat narcoterrorism in our backyard and help continue to secure the Panama Canal” and “prevent adversaries from establishing strategic footholds in our hemisphere,” the department explained.
How did the South American recipients align with Trump?
Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, all four recipients have taken steps aligning themselves more closely with his administration’s priorities.
Panama withdrew from China’s Belt and Road Initiative and expanded security cooperation with Washington, though President Jose Raul Mulino pushed back on Trump’s suggestion that the US should retake direct control of the Panama Canal.
Mulino’s government has scrapped contracts with Hong Kong-based firm CK Hutchison Holdings, which Washington cited as evidence of a slow Chinese takeover of critical ports in Peru. The company owned by billionaire Li Ka-shing’s family is seeking $1.5 billion in damages.
Ecuador has signed a trade agreement with the US, lowering trade barriers and making other concessions to American exporters. President Daniel Noboa has also expanded counter-narcotics cooperation with Washington, tacitly endorsing Trump’s controversial tactics that involve airstrikes on boats in international waters that the Pentagon deems suspicious.
Noboa’s proposal to once again allow foreign military bases in Ecuador was rejected by voters last year.
Peru has joined Trump’s signature Shield of the Americas initiative under new President Keiko Fujimori, the daughter and political heir to dictator Alberto Fujimori, and otherwise expanding security cooperation with Washington.
Colombia too took a right-wing turn and realigned with Washington this year, after controversial President Abelardo de la Espriella came to power.
The millionaire nicknamed El Tigre (The Tiger) owns a personal luxury brand and used to represent drug traffickers as a lawyer. He has pledged to be tough on organized crime as president, including by resuming fumigation of coca with herbicides.
How is the ‘Donroe Doctrine’ being enforced?
The Trump administration has also used military and economic pressure elsewhere in the Western Hemisphere.
In January, US forces abducted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, and brought them to the US to face federal “narco-terrorism” charges. Trump subsequently said Washington would temporarily “run” Venezuela and tap its vast oil reserves.
During his first term from 2017 to 2021, Trump recognized opposition politician Juan Guaido as Venezuela’s interim president and supported his bid to replace Maduro.
Washington also tightened its trade blockade of Cuba this year, cutting off Venezuelan oil supplies and threatening retaliation against countries providing fuel to the island nation. The resulting fuel shortage has contributed to prolonged blackouts and a severe energy crisis.
Trump intervened directly in Honduras’ 2025 presidential race by publicly endorsing conservative candidate Nasry Asfura. He also pardoned former President Juan Orlando Hernandez, a fellow member of Asfura’s National Party who had been convicted in the US on drug trafficking charges.
In Colombia, former President Gustavo Petro alleged that the election won by de la Espriella had been digitally manipulated from abroad, pointing to alleged Israeli involvement and criticizing US interference in the campaign. Colombian electoral authorities rejected his fraud claims.
How is the ‘Donroe Doctrine’ different from the Monroe Doctrine?
US President James Monroe declared the Western Hemisphere off limits for European great powers in 1823.
While he framed his policy as anti-colonialist, in practice it prevented any military threat to the US homeland from emerging in South America and ensured preferential treatment of US businesses, particularly their access to natural resources, from bananas grown in Guatemala to copper mined in Chile.
US hegemony manifested during the 20th century in the so-called ‘dirty war’ against left-leaning political projects in South America. Washington supported right-wing dictatorships across the continent as long as they pledged to oppose Communism.
Since the end of the Cold War, Washington has defended its interests in South America under the guise of promoting human rights and democracy and dismantling narcotraffic, with the messaging shifting depending on which of the two US parties was holding the presidency.
Trump’s version distinguishes itself in its blatant approach rather than essence.

A State Department spokesperson said a “core delegation from the Iranian regime” would be allowed to attend the meeting in line with the United States’ obligations as the world body’s host country.

Tehran responded with strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases.
“The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year,” the State Department spokesperson added.
In the past, the US government has barred Iran’s delegation from shops and restricted its movements to travel between the United Nations headquarters, the Iranian UN mission and UN ambassador’s residence and New York’s John F. Kennedy Airport.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment.
Under the 1947 UN “headquarters agreement,” the United States is generally required to allow access to the United Nations for foreign diplomats. But Washington says it can deny visas for “security, terrorism and foreign policy” reasons.
The Trump administration on Sept 16 said it would deny entry to Palestinian officials for the UN meeting, extending a ban in place since 2025, over actions they took to “internationalise the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,” including pursuing cases against Israel at international tribunals.

Russia’s war has devastated Donetsk Oblast, with losses already exceeding $26 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:01:28 UTC
05:01:28 KST

Donetsk Oblast’s preliminary economic losses from Russia’s full-scale invasion exceeded 1.08 trillion hryvnias ($26 billion) as of 1 August 2026, according to data provided by the Donetsk Regional Military Administration to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Donbas.Realities project.
Donetsk Oblast has been at the center of Russia’s war against Ukraine since 2014, with the frontline running through the region and Ukrainian-controlled towns facing daily Russian attacks since 2022. Only about 30% of the oblast remains under Ukrainian control.
Industry accounts for most losses
According to the administration, businesses in the region’s real economy suffered more than 1.08 trillion hryvnias in losses, including lost profits, Donbas.Realities reported.
Industry accounted for 909.4 billion hryvnias ($22 billion) of the estimate, while the electricity and gas sectors suffered 156.5 billion hryvnias ($3.8 billion) in losses.
Agriculture accounted for 11.8 billion hryvnias ($285 million), transport for 1.5 billion hryvnias ($36 million), and other sectors for another 1 billion hryvnias ($24 million).
The losses among businesses operating in the social sphere were separately estimated at 100 million hryvnias ($2.4 million).
Full extent of damage remains unknown
The administration said its Department of Economy is collecting and consolidating information on losses caused by Russia’s invasion.
The regional administration said the figure is likely incomplete, as ongoing fighting and the scale of destruction make it impossible to determine the full extent of the damage.
“Determining the full extent of material damage caused in Donetsk Oblast is currently impossible,” the administration said, citing ongoing hostilities, the scale of destruction, limited access to damaged or destroyed sites, and the loss of documentation from occupied territories and areas of active fighting.
The administration emphasized that the figures are preliminary estimates and do not represent the region’s full material losses.
A final assessment can only be made after the security situation stabilizes and temporarily occupied territories are liberated, allowing authorities to properly document and assess the damage, it said.
Most of Donetsk Oblast remains under Russian control
About 30% of Donetsk Oblast remains under Ukrainian control, according to the regional administration.
The region has been a major battlefield throughout the full-scale war, with Russian forces continuing to attack Ukrainian-controlled areas while large parts of the region remain occupied.
The scale of the damage in Donetsk Oblast forms part of the much broader economic cost of Russia’s invasion. At the beginning of 2026, Ukrainian authorities and international organizations estimated Ukraine’s overall losses since the start of the full-scale invasion at more than $195 billion, Donbas.Realities reported.

Researchers explore the hidden pathways linking problematic caffeine use to sleep loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:00:41 UTC
05:00:41 KST

A study of university students in Bangladesh found associations between specific caffeine use disorder symptoms and sleep problems. The study found that caffeine use disorder symptoms had both a direct effect on sleep problems and an indirect effect on sleep problems through depressive symptoms. The paper was published in Addictive Behaviors Reports.
Caffeine is one of the most widely consumed psychoactive substances. It is commonly used to increase alertness and reduce fatigue. Among university students, caffeine consumption is especially common because of demanding academic schedules, long study hours, and insufficient sleep. Although moderate caffeine use may temporarily improve wakefulness and concentration, excessive or poorly timed consumption can interfere with sleep quality.
Sleep disturbances are themselves associated with impaired daily functioning, poorer mood, and an increased risk of depressive symptoms. Caffeine use and mental health may therefore be connected through several interacting behavioral and psychological pathways. An important factor in understanding these relationships is why individuals consume caffeine, as motives may include increasing alertness, regulating mood, socializing, controlling weight, or relieving withdrawal symptoms.
Some individuals also develop problematic patterns of caffeine use. These patterns are characterized by difficulty reducing consumption despite experiencing negative consequences. Symptoms of caffeine use disorder may be associated with greater psychological distress, anxiety, and sleep problems.
Study author Shekh Tanjina Islam Dola and her colleagues investigated the relationship between caffeine use motives, caffeine use disorder symptoms, depression and sleep problems among university students. In their study, they used statistical techniques that allowed them to map associations between specific symptoms of each of these conditions and to test the direct and indirect pathways between them.
The study participants were 530 students from the Barishal division of Bangladesh. They came from two public universities – Patuakhali Science and Technology University and University of Barisal. Participants’ average age was 22 years. 57% were male. 72% reported caffeine consumption. On average, caffeine consumers reported ingesting 1.9 cups of caffeine drinks (tea/coffee) per day.
Participants completed a survey that contained sociodemographic questions and assessments of caffeine consumption motives (the Caffeine Motives Questionnaire-21), caffeine use disorder symptoms (the Caffeine Use Disorder Questionnaire-10), sleep quality (the Medical Outcomes Study Sleep Scale), and depressive symptoms (the Patient Health Questionnaire-9).
The results showed that caffeine intake was higher among smokers compared to non-smokers. It was also higher among those with loans or debts, those in certain academic years, and those with lower monthly family expenditures. It was not associated with age, gender, residency, income, and several other factors.
More severe caffeine use disorder symptoms were directly associated with more sleep problems and more severe depressive symptoms. Depressive symptoms were, in turn, associated with more sleep problems, meaning depression partially mediated the relationship between caffeine use disorder and sleep disturbances. The researchers also found that craving and withdrawal-related motives were key bridges connecting caffeine use disorder to these negative mental health and sleep outcomes.
“This study found a high prevalence of caffeine consumption among university students in Bangladesh and identified important psychological correlates, particularly depression and sleep problems. Network analysis suggests that certain features, especially craving and withdrawal-related symptoms, may play a key role in connecting caffeine use disorder with mental health and sleep-related outcomes,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the links between caffeine consumption and mental health. However, it should be noted that study participants were exclusively university students, making generalizability of the findings to other demographic groups limited. Additionally, the cross-sectional design of the study does not allow any causal inferences to be derived from the results.
The paper, “From caffeine use motives to sleep disturbance: network and structural equation modeling of caffeine use disorder and depression among caffeine consumers,” was authored by Shekh Tanjina Islam Dola, Farhana Najnin, Md Bony Amin, Md. Shamim Sikder, Md. Joy Vangi, Jannatun Naeem, Md. Jahurul Islam Rony, Mst. Mushfika Rahman Takia, Md. Kamruzzaman, Abu Sayeed, Md. Shajadul Islam, and Saraban Tahura Ether.

The AI ‘Slowdown’ Is an Antitrust Mess
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:58:28 UTC
04:58:28 KST

Following multiple reports of AI agent swarms hacking websites and coordinating via secret message boards, along with a dire message for humanity from an outgoing Anthropic engineer, leading AI companies have called for a coordinated AI development “slowdown.” Alongside various versions of this specific phrase—slowdown—they’ve also expressed concerns that doing so would run afoul of antitrust laws.
Antitrust experts say that while the companies’ charged language isn’t necessarily doing them any favors, the unrestrained development of a rogue killer AI probably isn’t in line with the spirit of the Sherman Act, a key US antitrust law that exists to promote a competitive marketplace. At the same time, getting an official all-clear from the government to move forward could ward off costly investigations down the line.
Radical Rhetoric
Under antitrust law, how a company’s employees talk about business decisions is often as important as the business decisions themselves. Google famously trained its employees not to use certain phrases—even internally—that could imply it was engaging in anticompetitive behavior, and instead instructed them to emphasize the ways that business decisions would improve its offerings and benefit consumers.
So from an antitrust perspective, the use of phrases like “a slowdown” or “a pause” may set off more alarms than the actual activity it represents: developing ways to ensure that advanced AI models don’t go rogue. A collectively agreed-upon slowdown without any particular purpose could be interpreted by regulators as an anticompetitive agreement to reduce trade.
“I think they kind of boxed themselves into a corner with the way they phrase things,” says John Bergmayer, legal counsel for the nonprofit Public Knowledge.
“Usually in antitrust, one of the things that the economists look at is whether you're reducing output,” says Bergmayer, which is to say, whether two or more companies are making a pact to “kind of take it easy.” Rather than talk about some collusive-sounding effort to dial back development, he says, AI companies could have just emphasized their desire to work on safety protocols together to prevent catastrophic risks and treated a slowdown in model releases as a natural side-effect of that.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, whose company recently dodged a massive antitrust suit brought by the Federal Trade Commission, chimed in on the slowdown proposal by not endorsing an explicit “slowdown” at all. Zuckerberg instead argued that AI labs have a “strong natural incentive” to make AI agents behave better because consumers don’t want models doing things people don’t intend—known as “misalignment” in AI industry jargon—and that the companies that don’t take the time to get alignment right “will fall behind” competitively. It’s the difference between two automakers saying “we’ve agreed to not make better cars for a while” and saying “we’re not making faster cars until we figure out how to make them safe, because no one will buy our cars if they kill people.”
(Disclosure: The reporter on this story previously worked at the FTC but did not participate in the Meta case.)
David Lawrence, until recently a policy director of the Department of Justice’s Antitrust Division, wrote on LinkedIn that agreements that prevent catastrophic risks actually “increase output and promote competition” and are already protected under the law by something called the “ancillary restraints doctrine.”
“After all,” a career FTC antitrust attorney commented below the post, “no humanity would result in no competition.”
If anything, collectively agreeing not to implement safety measures could expose the AI labs to allegations of “quality fixing,” says Roger Alford, a professor at Notre Dame Law School and the former second-in-command for the DOJ Antitrust Division. That’s when companies mutually agree not to improve their own products; Alford points to a European antitrust case in which car companies worked together to develop emissions-reducing technology but agreed to not compete on improvements beyond what the law required. They ultimately had to pay roughly the equivalent of a billion-dollar fine.
And of course, self-regulation isn’t new. Bergmayer points out that industries can already limit their antitrust liability via the National Cooperative Research and Production Act of 1993, which lets them stand up a standards-development organization so long as they file a notification to the FTC and the DOJ.
Market Pressures
Trustbusters are typically skeptical of antitrust exemptions, because they say they end up making big players even bigger and preventing newer companies from getting traction in a market. Others have raised eyebrows at the request as well, including David Sacks, the cochair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science & Technology. Sacks accused Anthropic and OpenAI of being a duopoly and said the antitrust exemption request was an “election-season psyop” and an excuse to “form a cartel.”
But many employees of major AI companies have earnestly voiced concerns about how quickly their workplaces are churning out new models, potentially at the cost of safety.
“Sometimes companies want to be regulated as a ploy to pull up the ladder behind them. But sometimes it really is that they feel like the market is pressuring them to act in a way that they think they shouldn't,” says Bergmayer. “Psychologically, maybe the AI labs feel like they don't have the permission of the markets or their upcoming IPO or something to unilaterally take action like that.”
This summer, both Anthropic and OpenAI filed confidential paperwork for initial public offerings and have valuations near or beyond a trillion dollars each. Anthropic is expected to go public next month, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the company would delay its IPO until 2027 because of the recent safety concerns. (OpenAI’s CFO previously told employees that it would be a public company in 2027, according to CNBC.) The Ramp AI Index, which measures AI adoption rates, suggests that the two companies’ models have similar usage rates and are competing neck and neck for the top spot. Neither company responded to a request for comment for this story.
“They, I think, want an exemption because, in their mind, somehow they think they need to coordinate on a slowdown because, let's be honest, they don't want to unilaterally disarm while the others keep going at a breakneck speed,” says Alford.
There’s political pressure to keep moving as fast as possible too. After news about the slowdown proposal, President Donald Trump posted on social media that the government already has “tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!” and that “WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”
The Department of Defense’s chief technology officer account has also been posting “anti-doomer” memes, seemingly in response to the idea of a slowdown.
The DOJ Antitrust Division also isn’t immune to political machinations. Alford was ousted from the agency last year after accusing DOJ leadership of corruption because they approved a merger between two technology infrastructure companies that Alford later described as a “scandal” in a public speech. And a Wall Street Journal journalist reported that Andrew Ferguson, the chair of the FTC, told attendees at an antitrust conference that Trump would “ultimately decide any AI policy.”
If the federal government were to initiate an antitrust investigation into an AI slowdown, it would be considered a “conduct investigation.” Unlike a “merger investigation,” which imposes strict time limits on a government probe, a conduct investigation can take years. AI companies could be required to produce millions of pages of documents, executives and other key employees could be dragged into depositions, and hundreds of other employees could have their devices subject to litigation holds—even if the government ultimately decides it doesn’t have a case.
With no new regulations in sight and likely no antitrust exemption to come, frontier AI labs will have to write the rules of the road themselves, and potentially dodge an investigation or two along the way.

SPACECOM Boss Wants Better Domain Awareness to Target Threats on Orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:57:09 UTC
04:57:09 KST

The Space Force revealed this week that it has space control weapons on orbit, but the head of U.S. Space Command said the U.S. still has “a long way to go” in improving its ability to detect and target threats in the domain.
“To be able to negate threats in space, we must be able to find, fix, track, and target those threats,” SPACECOM Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting said Sept. 16 at the AMOS Conference in Maui, Hawaii. “Targeting in the space domain is maturing, but it still has a long way to go. We don’t have robust target folders like the joint force does in other domains.”
Space domain awareness, which is the military’s term for being able to see and understand what’s happening in the environment, is foundational for military operations on orbit. The better the data, the better decisions commanders can make about how to move through the domain and respond to threats that might impede that freedom of maneuver.
In a roundtable with reporters following his speech, Whiting said there has been some progress within the Space Force to improve the quality and quantity of its object tracking data. However, key shortfalls remain, and closing those gaps is a top priority for his command.
“Do I have all the track quality that I need at all times? No,” he said. “And that is why, in my current list of gaps that we every year go through a process to analyze, in my top five, we have a need for improved space domain awareness for space engagements.”
Whiting highlighted three examples of areas for improvement:
- better integration of commercial and allied data
- stronger linkages between sensors, command-and-and control systems, and effectors, including space weapons
- expanded ground- and space-based surveillance capabilities
Whiting said that while data quality from both commercial industry and U.S. allies has improved significantly in recent years, integration issues and unstable funding have made it hard to take full advantage of those improvements.
“I want to be able to take commercial data, data from our allies, and get it into our programs of record today,” he said. “Right now, we can’t do that. We take that commercial and allied data and do an incredible job of processing it, but in a parallel way to our programs of record. We’ve got to be able to close those two together, for example, to make progress here.”
Fixing that integration challenge, he said, would represent “the biggest initial step we could take—and we could take that in the short term.”
Whiting also highlighted longstanding challenges around tying together the sensors that collect and process information, the C2 systems that analyze it, and the “effectors” that act on that intelligence. Combined, that string of systems makes up what’s called a “space kill chain,” and the Space Force has been focused on closing gaps in key parts of that architecture—many of them classified—for the past few years.
“We really need the acquisition organizations in the services who are delivering space domain awareness sensors, command and control systems, and effectors to work horizontally to make sure that we’re closing the kill chain by providing the space domain awareness target-quality track that the command and control systems and the effectors require to be effective,” he said. “We must be able to reach across all of these vertical program offices to make sure they deliver as an intact kill chain.”
Longer term, Whiting said, there’s a need for better surveillance of orbits beyond geosynchronous, to include cislunar pathways between the Earth and the moon.
“We want to see that scale beyond geosynchronous orbit … out to cislunar space and be able to maintain track of objects in those areas so that we’re not operationally surprised,” he said.

The measures are part of a broader series of sanctions imposed by the Trump administration against Cuban entities and individuals.
The US has maintained broad sanctions on Cuba for decades, while the executive order established a separate sanctions program targeting specified sectors of the Cuban economy.

Parents, privacy, parliaments: The battle begins for von der Leyen’s social media ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:52:30 UTC
04:52:30 KST

BRUSSELS — Ursula von der Leyen's bill to keep young Europeans off social media is an ambitious response to the growing outcry over the potential harm of TikTok, Instagram and other online platforms. Making the restrictions a reality will require a whole new level of ambition.
The European Commission must now negotiate with national governments and technologists to figure out exactly how to impose a law across Europe that would ban kids under 13 from social media, and severely restrict access for those under 15 — all without trampling on privacy of young and old alike in the process of verifying users’ age.
Reducing the harms of social media on youth has been a top priority for the Commission president, a medical doctor and mother of seven who has repeatedly decried the internet's impact on the health of minors since her 2025 State of the Union speech.
Advertisement
“If a platform wants to access the children or the teenagers, the minors, they have to prove first that they are safe,” she told reporters on Thursday as she officially unveiled the EU Kids Act, the day after again touting her leadership on the issue in this year’s annual address.
The EU’s proposed measures come after Australia imposed the first-ever national social media ban in December 2025, blocking under-16s from creating accounts on major platforms such as Instagram and YouTube. Australia’s ban has had limited impact so far, with a large percentage of kids still having access to social media, which Canberra blames on the platforms’ lack of compliance.
A fierce global campaign by parents and mental health professionals has been warning that social media platforms lead to a range of ills including addiction, social isolation and depression.
The "Lost Screen Memorial", an installation of giant illuminated smartphones representing 50 children who tragically lost their lives following harm linked to social media, displayed at Place des Nations, ahead of the 79th World Health Assembly in Geneva, on May 17, 2026. | Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images
Child rights campaigners and some EU governments have argued that blanket bans are not the way to go, violating young people’s rights to information and expression. Their concerns were integrated into the new proposal, which attempts to reconcile sometimes conflicting considerations and targets online channels beyond traditional social media, including AI chatbots and video games.
But the nuances in the legislation will only add to the challenge of making the law a reality.
The EU’s proposal would effectively bar anyone under 13 from creating accounts on social media and video-sharing platforms, while severely restricting teens aged 13 to 15 from using these services independently. Services like video game platforms and AI chatbots have to follow safety-by-design principles that don’t encourage compulsive use among kids.
Advertisement
Balancing act
The proposal also takes into account the different approaches that EU capitals were already developing in their national measures. The two most important capitals to balance are Paris and Berlin, which are calling for bans for under-15s and under-13s, respectively. The Kids Act’s tiered approach, which includes different restrictions at each age, could keep both capitals happy.
Finalizing the rules will be an uphill battle for European legislators. The 55-page proposal needs approval from national governments and the European Parliament. The national bills would effectively be scrapped by the Commission’s EU-wide proposal.
Estonia may be a particularly thorny negotiator, having publicly opposed any such bans or age limits. Rome, a major European player, has also so far decided against social media restrictions. The Netherlands’ digital minister, Willemijn Aerdts, said in comments that the country supports the proposal but would still prefer the minimum age to be set at 15. A spokesperson for Spain’s digital ministry also emphasized their existing efforts to set a threshold at 16.
Still, given the outcry from parent groups and rising popular opposition to tech platforms, many EU capitals have an incentive to get this done quickly.
Ireland’s digital minister Patrick O’Donovan, who last week was very publicly pushing for the ban to be set at 15, struck a conciliatory note Thursday. “I think the nature of these things is that you strive for the highest possible ideals, make your case, and now is the time to examine the implementation and process around delivery of change,” O’Donovan said. “We are united in our shared purpose here.”
The Commission wants to conclude negotiations within the next 8 to 12 months, a senior Commission official told reporters. It’s not the length or complexity of the rules, but the urgency that the various legislators feel that will determine the speed of negotiations, the official added.
Advertisement
Still, the required procedures would bring the implementation date to mid-2028 since the law includes a six-month transition period.
The target is an ambitious one for the EU’s legislative process. Other landmark tech laws, such as the Digital Services Act, have taken more than two years to negotiate.
Child rights groups have expressed trepidation about the proposal’s focus on parental controls. An excessive focus on parents controlling their kids’ online lives could be too invasive and disadvantage kids whose parents are unable to spend much time with them, Sørine Vesth Rasmussen, senior advisor on tech policy and children’s rights at the Danish civil society group Børns Vilkår, said.
In a statement, Greece’s Digital Minister Dimitris Papastergiou said that parents shouldn’t be overly burdened by the legislation, and that primary responsibility should lie with the platforms.
Privacy concerns
A key sticking point, all agree, could be the law's implications for privacy rights. Since the rules mandate age verification to access social media, people will have to prove their age by sharing a digital version of their ID. Privacy activists warn that governments or companies could use this procedure to track what people (of any age) are doing online, while also creating a tempting target for hackers.
"The EU Kids Act is shaping up to be a disaster for the open internet, dressed up as child protection,” said Arya Haager, from digital rights NGO epicenter.works.”It turns identity verification into the price of admission for going online at all.”
Advertisement
Haager said the law would quietly build a “surveillance infrastructure around family data” to prove not only the age of young users, but also connect them to adult guardians who can supervise their accounts. This data could “later be repurposed to exclude people based on ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation,” she said.
Widespread age verification requirements, warned Jurgita Miseviciute, head of public policy with privacy-focused tech firm Proton, would “create an open door through which every law-abiding adult and child in Europe can be at best surveilled, and targeted by criminals at worst.”
Speaking on Thursday, Commission tech chief Henna Virkkunen said the law creates a “robust” age-verification framework. “Proving your age online should be easy, and it should reveal nothing else about you, absolutely nothing else [other] than your age,” she said.
Still, the Commission concedes that the proposed law isn’t perfect, and that circumvention is possible. Instead, they see it as the first step to a long process of changing people’s attitudes about safety.
“This is about getting clearly the message (out) to everyone. It is not about catching every single individual,” a senior Commission official said. “The point is to create a societal change that is stable and persistent.”

Translator Lubov Tsai: I taught myself literary Bulgarian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:52:05 UTC
04:52:05 KST

Author
Daniela Goleminova
Thursday 17 September 2026 20:00
Thursday, 17 September 2026, 20:00
Lubov Tsai
PHOTO Personal Archive
Font size
Lubov Tsai is a Taurida Bulgarian, born in the Bulgarian village of Petrovka in Ukraine’s Azov region. She is married to a Korean, hence her surname.
Tsai graduated in mathematics in Donetsk, making a home in Luhansk for 40 years. In 2014, she and her family moved to Zhytomyr. So they travelled nearly 1,000 km from the far east of Ukraine to the north-western part of the country, stayed there for some time and eventually settled in a village near the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv.
PHOTO Personal Archive
“I saw online that there were many websites and literary portals featuring works translated from Bulgarian. As I read them, I found many mistakes in the translations, and it hurt me. That is how I started translating from Bulgarian into Ukrainian. My list of authors now includes more than a hundred names... The first book I translated was Vaptsarov’s Pesen za choveka (A Song for Mankind). Then came Dimcho Debelyanov’s Svetla vyara (Bright Faith), Mara Belcheva’s Senki (Shadows), Petya Dubarova’s Tam nyakade (Somewhere Out There) and Zdravko Kisyov’s Svetlopis (Lightwriting)... The latest book I worked on is by Daniela Stoyanova. I plunged into this sea of translation, and this is my life,” Lubov Tsai says.
The Taurida Bulgarian proudly says that she taught herself standard Bulgarian.
“I learned the language simply by reading contemporary texts. When I read, I understand everything, and I think my blood helps me. When I am translating and come across a word I don’t know, I immediately look up its meaning,” she explains.
PHOTO Personal Archive
For several years, Lubov attended Sofia University St Kliment Ohridski’s Summer Seminars in Bulgarian Language and Culture for foreign scholars of Bulgarian and Slavic studies, further improving her command of the language.
Is there an interest in Bulgarian literature in Ukraine?
“There is. I have friends who read a great deal and are very interested in Bulgarian literature. And they are not only ethnic Bulgarians – some are people I studied with at university. Now I am trying to translate Ukrainian literature into Bulgarian as well. I have translated several Ukrainian poems that were published on the Literary Club portal. I also donate some of the books I translate to libraries,” Lubov Tsai says.
PHOTO Personal Archive
Are young people of Bulgarian descent in Ukraine interested in learning Bulgarian?
“Since 1991, young people have been able to study Bulgarian at a lyceum in Taurida. They can also come to Sofia and other Bulgarian cities to study the language,” the translator says.
Will learning foreign languages, including less widely spoken ones, continue to be valued in the future? And how is the rise of artificial intelligence changing the translation industry?
“Artificial intelligence has no soul. Besides, it makes many mistakes. I don’t think it can replace the heart and the blood. There is a saying: ‘You are as many times a person as the languages you know.’ I see that young people today have many opportunities to learn foreign languages, and they make use of them. That is a good thing,” Lubov Tsai says.
PHOTO Personal Archive
Does mathematics help when learning foreign languages?
“Mathematics helps with everything. I don’t know many languages. I studied German, but I don’t know it well. I never studied English and don’t speak it. I speak Russian, Ukrainian and Bulgarian. I understand a little Polish and Belarusian because the languages are closely related. Mathematics helps you build a system and find the way of translating that works best for you. One of my teachers used to say: ‘The most beautiful things in the world are music and mathematics.’ I would add poetry. It is built with such harmony, just as God intended,” Lubov Tsai concludes.

Belarus holds military drills around the Suwalki Gap, NATO’s only land link to the Baltics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:45:54 UTC
04:45:54 KST

Belarus sent tank and mechanized battalions to training grounds near Poland and Lithuania for four-day drills that Minsk says focus on border security, counter-sabotage operations, and defense against drones and light aircraft, Militarnyi reported on 17 September, citing the Belarusian Defense Ministry.
The exercise includes tank and mechanized infantry battalions, units typically used in conventional ground warfare. Minsk says their tasks include guarding checkpoints and infrastructure and defending against drones. Some drills are taking place near the Suwałki Gap, the only land route connecting Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia to the rest of NATO. The corridor lies between Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad region, which is separated from the rest of Russia. Belarus denies any offensive intent.
What Belarus says it is practicing
Belarus’s Western Operational Command is holding the exercises from 15 to 18 September under Chief of the General Staff Pavel Muraveyko, according to the ministry’s schedule outlined by Militarnyi.
The drills are taking place at the Gozha range near Lithuania and at the Brest and Ruzhany ranges near Poland. RBC-Ukraine wrote that mechanized and tank battalions are taking part and that the Brest and Ruzhany sites lie about 15 and 60 kilometers from the Polish border, respectively. Reservists have also been called up to local territorial-defense units, the ministry said.
Militarnyi cited the ministry as saying that one unit guarded a water intake, another directed traffic with police, and a mechanized brigade manned a checkpoint with border guards. The ministry also said truck-mounted fire teams were posted around the clock to defend against drones and practiced firing at targets imitating surveillance drones.
Muraveyko said the army was not considering offensive action and called allegations of preparations for an attack baseless, according to remarks quoted by Militarnyi. Belarus has not disclosed the total number of troops involved, and the exercise’s scale has not been independently verified.
The Moscow Times reported that the ministry also claimed the exercise remained below the notification thresholds set by the 2011 Vienna Document, an international agreement requiring advance notice of large military exercises.
How Russia could exploit the Suwałki Gap
In December 2025, security analyst Taras Zhovtenko warned that Russian propaganda had laid the groundwork to cite an alleged blockade of Kaliningrad to justify a limited incursion and the establishment of temporary checkpoints.
A German war game later modeled Russia staging border incidents before seizing key routes, although Baltic officials said the scenario severely underrated their armed forces.
Separately, French open-source analyst Clément Molin found that defenses along the Polish and Baltic borders with Russia and Belarus remained patchy and shallow, with Lithuania the most exposed. These assessments describe possible vulnerabilities, not evidence that an attack is planned.
