'Can't quarantine any sector': Tony Burke warns migration overhaul carries economic risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:45:47 UTC
04:45:47 KST

IN BRIEF
- The home affairs minister says there will be impacts on industry from the migration changes.
- He also suggested farmers should consider hiring Pacific workers amid concerns over backpacker labour shortages.
The Home Affairs Department has engineered a slowdown in backpacker visas to reduce arrivals and is now urging farmers to consider hiring Pacific workers to pick their crops.
The National Farmers' Federation has led a campaign to axe visa bottlenecks amid growing industry anxiety that fruits and other crops will wither on trees without the labour force needed to harvest them.
The agricultural sector is warning the shortages will increase supermarket prices.
As the federal government moves to reduce arrivals to Australia, its visa overhaul includes introducing a ballot system for backpackers hoping to spend more than one year in Australia on a working holiday visa.
It will also cut the available long-term visas. Backpackers from the United Kingdom will be exempt from the requirements because of the UK's free trade deal with Australia.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In an interview with SBS News, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has encouraged any horticulture businesses struggling to secure harvest workers to consider the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme and Pacific workers.
"Our preferred agriculture visa has always been the PALM scheme, the Pacific workers visa. When I was employment minister, we did a lot to improve the rules to avoid worker exploitation on the Pacific, on the PALM visa," he said.
"At the time that we were improving those rules, we had some of the farm organisations say to us, 'If you do this, our members will just go and use backpackers.'"
He maintains there is a Pacific workforce ready to step in.
"Now, if the reason that people are more reliant on backpackers and refusing to use Pacific workers is because they're upset that we've ended exploitation in those areas, I think that is a very different question for a number of operators.
"That doesn't depict the whole of the farm sector, not for a minute, and a whole lot of them still use the Pacific Labour Scheme, but the Pacific Labour Scheme right now has extra capacity. Those extra workers are available."
'I can't quarantine any sector of Australia'
Burke said he can't quarantine any sector of the economy from the impacts of the migration shake-up.
The government wants to reduce the number of working holidaymakers, crack down on visa overstayers and tighten allowances for international students as part of its push to reduce migration numbers.
Farmers and the Nationals have been among the critics of changes set to affect backpackers, who the former rely on to pick fruit in the regions.
Only 45,000 working holiday-makers will be able to stay in Australia for a second year under the system, and only 5,000 for a third year — down from 57,000 and 31,000 respectively.
Burke told SBS News there will be challenges for industry to adjust to the changes.
"No matter what you do, if you are lowering (immigration) numbers, there are challenges across the visa system and across the Australian economy," he said.
"I can't quarantine any sector of Australia. What I can do is make sure —as numbers are lowered, and they need to be lowered because of the challenges we have with housing supply — I want the rest of the economy to have the softest landing possible."
One in five international students to be impacted
The government's plan to stop some international students from bringing their families to Australia could affect about one in five people, amid warnings of an economic hit if some choose to study elsewhere.
International students and those on graduate visas will no longer be able to bring family members with them to Australia under the reforms.
PhD students and some Pacific and ASEAN students are exempt from the proposal.
Burke told SBS News around 19 per cent of the cohort bring in family members to Australia. It's unclear whether that includes PhD students, who are more likely to bring family than undergraduates.
"International students tend to be younger, and so family obligations are a very different issue," Burke said.
Asked whether the proposal, which could affect 19 per cent of the cohort, would amount to a major revenue hit for universities and the economy, Burke insisted demand for student spots will bridge any gap.
"It's actually not, for the very simple reason that at the moment, we have more students wanting to study in Australia than we have places," he said.
"Whereas for skilled workers, everyone who an employer can find, they take, because that's completely demand-driven. There's no planning level on temporary skilled visas at all.
"You don't have the same impact for students, nor do you have the same size of demand simply because people tend to be younger."
There are around 680,582 international students in Australia. About 295,000 new international students are due to commence next year, in student cap figures unchanged from this year.
Universities Australia welcomed the carve-out for PhD students, saying Australia was competing globally for researchers and highly-skilled people.
The Group of Eight representing Australia's research-intensive universities said it educated about half of PhD students — about 12,000, with half of those requiring secondary visas for dependants.
"Most of our undergraduate international students are quite young. They're ... 18, 19, 20, and many of them aren't coming here with their parents, frankly," CEO Vicki Thompson told ABC News.
Other measures that will affect students include preventing so-called 'visa hopping', with a new qualification scale to allow only foreign students transferring to higher-level courses (bachelor's to master's, for example) to extend their visas.

Colin Kaepernick on Threats He Faced, His NFL Exile, and That Jay-Z Lyric
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:45:36 UTC
04:45:36 KST

Following a string of high-profile police shootings of Black men 10 years ago, San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick began protesting such incidents by sitting during the national anthem at preseason games. What began as a quiet action turned into a fevered national debate about freedom of expression, patriotism, and so much more.
In Kaepernick’s new memoir, The Perilous Fight, the quarterback explains that his action was spontaneous. He wasn’t even in uniform on August 13, 2016, the first time he sat during the anthem. “I hadn’t given the anthem a second’s thought before I walked out onto the field that day, but it hit me in that moment that I should find a seat,” Kaepernick writes. “I didn’t want to stand up while that song was playing. Rosa Parks had refused to give up her seat on the bus to a white person in 1955. Muhammad Ali wouldn’t step forward when his name was called by the draft board for the Vietnam War in Louisville in 1967. Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised black-gloved fists in the air during the playing of the anthem at the 1968 Olympics. They didn’t like what they saw, the way this nation touted its commitment to justice and at the same time showed little interest in it, and they took action. Those inspiring Americans had the courage of their convictions and literally changed the world in the process.”
Kaepernick, despite leading the 49ers to the Super Bowl in 2013 and throwing 16 touchdown passes, against just four interceptions, for a bad 49ers team in 2016, hasn’t played in the NFL since that season. In 2019, he and former teammate Eric Reid, who joined Kaepernick in kneeling during the anthem, settled a collusion lawsuit against the NFL. In late August, a decade after he etched his name in history, Kaepernick sat down with TIME to talk about why he hasn’t spoken up much about his protests, his relationship with the anthem today, his differences with Jay-Z, and the state of policing in the United States.
(This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity)
You’ve released a book, The Perilous Fight. Why tell your story now?
One, it's 10 years since the protest. I've gotten so many questions about why did I protest, what happened, what led up to it, the details behind the scenes of all of the moments. Not just the protest, but owners in the NFL, the conversations that were happening there, the workout in 2019 and all the things that transpired around that. Then also just the work that we're doing directly in the communities. It felt like it was a great time to be able to go out, answer some of those questions, and also be able to give insight into how we build, how we move forward together. I think it’s especially critical in a moment like this.
The book starts with a harrowing incident of racial hostility involving the N word that you experienced as a child—one you weren’t comfortable sharing with your parents, who adopted you and are white. Why start there?
One of the reasons we wanted to start with that moment of going through the neighborhood, being tied to a rose tree, and the dynamic of not feeling comfortable telling my parents is it really sets the stage for the rest of the book, and sets the stage for the rest of my life. I had to navigate the realities that you face when you are Black in predominantly white spaces. I had so many questions around, “You lived a privileged life. Everything was all good. Middle-class white family. What are you upset about?” And from the outside looking in, I understand how it can look that way. But also the reality of the experience, and what I went through, is also something that's important to put in context.
You didn't really do any interviews during the heat of 2016 and 2017, and in the aftermath. What was your thinking on not doing these types of interviews then?
Yeah, it's interesting because I get both sides of that question. During the 2016 season, it was like, "Why are you talking so much? Be quiet.” As an NFL quarterback, you're required to speak three times a week. So reporters can ask you whatever they would like. I'm happy to answer any questions as part of that. But post that moment, one thing I realized was, it felt like there was a very, very intentional effort to make me the sole figure, or the sole voice, of the movement. I thought it was important to create space for other voices to be able to step up. And one of the reasons that I thought that approach was so important is looking back historically, yes, we need strong leaders, but we need strong people collectively. That's actually what allows us to be able to sustain over time. Also, as part of that, I thought it was very important as they were very intentional attacks to try to discredit me, discredit what I was capable of on the field, discredit my character. In those efforts of trying to discredit me, they were also trying to discredit the broader movement.
If there's one athlete who has stepped up in the way that you wanted, who would that be?
I think there are voices across the board that have stepped up. I would say my brother Eric Reid. I'm always going to bring him up. Love Eric. He continued the protest after I was blackballed. He himself went through the same reality. His final season, [he] went out, set two franchise records, was cut, and never saw the field again. We had voices throughout the NBA step up. Whether that was LeBron, we saw Steph Curry, we saw Carmelo, we saw KD, all stepping to the forefront. We saw this with Megan Rapinoe, doing that on an international stage. We’re seeing it to this day throughout Europe. I would not have had the insight that this would have had the lasting impact internationally the way it does, and that's just within the sports realm. More broadly, what I think it’s done is created opportunities, whether it is on a national stage, international stage, or within local communities. People saying, "Oh, this actually opened the door for me to be able to do the work in a way I previously wasn't able to.”
In 2016, when you first started sitting, and then kneeling, during the national anthem, you’re in this national spotlight and firestorm. Was there one surreal moment you experienced that we didn’t see during this time?
One surreal moment early on, we had a high school, Castlemont in Oakland. After I took a knee, they went out the next week and took a knee, and I went to go visit them the following week at their game. I had a moment where I was in the locker room with them before the game. They're hyping each other up. It's going to be a big game for them. And one of the players says, "We don't get to eat at home. So we're going to go eat on this field.”
That is too often a reality within communities. Not only navigating threats against their life, but navigating whether or not they're even going to have a meal. For me, that was such a surreal moment that athletes in high school and students in high school are going out, trying to chase their dreams and compete at the highest level. They are willing to stand up and risk themselves to go out and advocate for their community, while at the same time not knowing whether or not they're going to have a meal when they get home. That really encapsulated and painted a surreal picture of how dire this is. While the broader national conversation was happening, this is just the reality on the ground.
Were you physically or psychologically threatened while protesting?
Threats became so normalized that I didn't really think about them too much. You get attacked from the President of the United States. You're getting attacked from senators. You have people trying to send bombs to your home. Online threats and mail threats. My now wife Nessa, as I was getting these threats, was like, “You can't be staying at your house alone.” She was in New York at the time. But that ultimately led to me staying at [manager Tony Ng’s] house for the rest of that 2016 season, just so people didn't know where I was at.
Were you ever scared?
No. I also think you get a little bit of the football mentality. If someone is going to try to do something, they’re either going to try to do it or aren't. My responsibility is to be prepared for whatever that is.
Did you ever worry that what happened to you served as a warning to other athletes? That as a result of you not playing in the NFL anymore, they were quiet rather than speaking up?
Absolutely. I know the intention was to send that message: If you try to advocate for the Black community, if you try to fight against the status quo and create a different and better environment, we will take everything we can from you. And this actually showed up in one of our Know Your Rights camps in Las Vegas. One of our young high school students pulled me aside in the middle of the camp. “Hey, I really love football. I also really want to fight for my community and for that to be better. Which one do you think I should choose?”
The fact that they have made that a conversation, that people feel like they have to choose, that is the very thing that I have to continue to fight against. I don't think there is an either-or. We can be phenomenal at our profession. We also can advocate for our community and a better society, better conditions for our people.
In the last nine years of NFL exile, did deciding to stand for the anthem in order to get signed ever cross your mind?
No.
Why not?
Because I set out with a clear goal and clear objective, and the conditions in our society have not changed. There's been progress made in some areas, but holistically, when we look at the climate and environment that we are living in today, those conditions largely have not changed. There is never going to be a moment where I take a position of, “Hey, I'll stand up so I can get my career back.” Because that then becomes a moral concession: If you threaten my career, or if you threaten my money, I will actually say I don't care about the people, and I will look at this just from an individual perspective. That was a line I was not going to cross.
In the book, you detail conversations you had with a few teams around the league. Which team did you feel closest to signing with?
There were three teams that I thought were close. The first was the Seattle Seahawks. In 2017, flew up there, met with Pete Carroll, John Schneider, the head coach and GM of the Seahawks. When I got there, basically the conversation was, “We know you're a starting quarterback.” I didn't do a
workout while I was there. They're like, “We know you can play. We've game-planned for you the last few years. That's not a question for us.” The entire conversation while I was there was just around my politics, taking the knee, how I thought about policing, how I thought about the military, what their community would think, what potential players would think.
In retrospect, it was fascinating to me on a few different fronts. One, the NFL claims it’s a meritocracy. So walking in a building and telling me you know I'm a starter, and not walking out with an offer makes that fall flat on its face. The second part is I just think about it from a labor-laws perspective. Being the owner of a business, a company, I would never be able to ask those questions and get away with it.
They didn't sign me that year. Reached back out the following year to have me come in for a workout. Had booked the flight, was ready to go out there, and prior to getting on the flight, they called my agent. Said, "Well, before he comes out to work out, will he commit to not taking a knee?” I said no. I won't commit to that. Canceled the flight. Canceled the workout. Never heard from them again. [A spokesperson for the Seahawks did not respond to TIME’s request for comment.]
The second one was the Ravens, and this one came about because we played against the Ravens in the Super Bowl. Jim Harbaugh was my coach during that time. His brother John Harbaugh was head coach of the Ravens, and I reached out to Jim and wanted to get his perspective. “Is there anyone that you know that would be interested? Do you think your brother would be open to a call?” John was on board and was like, "Yeah, let's do it.” John went back, advocated for it, wanted to sign me. “It got shut down from above me. I don't have the power to just outright make that decision. But if it was my choice, you would be here.” [A Ravens representative referred TIME to a 2017 quote from Baltimore general manager Ozzie Newsome—now an executive vice president with the team—who said, “(Ravens owner) Steve Bisciotti has not told us we cannot sign Colin Kaepernick, nor has he blocked the move. Whoever is making those claims is wrong.”]
Then the third one was the Raiders in 2022. Had run into [Raiders owner] Mark Davis at an airport. This was actually the first time I had been face-to-face with one of the owners blackballing me. It was a very interesting conversation because it was almost disconnected from the reality of what was going on. Saw me and was like, "Hey, what's up? How are you doing? What you been up to?” I was like, "What? What are you talking about? I've been trying to play, and you've been keeping me out.”
That led to a follow-up conversation about me trying to play. He came and sat in my living room, and we talked about playing for the Raiders. That led to a workout with the Raiders and Josh McDaniels. Workout went great. Josh McDaniels, after the fact, was like, “He looked bigger, stronger, faster than last time saw you.” Mark Davis came in the room after. “So proud of you. That was great workout.” One of the scouts on the way back said, “I'm surprised they let you walk out of the building without signing you. That’s the best workout we've had in years from a quarterback.” Never heard from him again. [The Raiders declined to comment.]
When Jim, who coached Michigan to the 2023 national title, got the job with the Los Angeles Chargers in ‘24, did you reach out to him? Was there any conversation there?
Yeah.
What happened?
He told me that was a table he was not willing to stand on. It was disappointing because prior to that he had been advocating for me. Said I should be a starter. I can help a team win championships. Had a conversation with him and said, "Look, I don't even care what the role is. Like I know Justin Herbert's there. I know the reality of what you have to navigate as a head coach. Let me take the No. 2 spot then. Let me come in, just show you, show everyone else what I can do.” Wouldn't do it. No opportunity, no workout.
Has that affected your relationship with him?
Yeah. And I'll say, also in part because there was a conversation that was put out that he had offered me a coaching job, which just wasn't true. I don't know where and why that came out. That's made the relationship a little bit different since. [When asked to respond to Kaepernick’s comments to TIME about joining the Chargers as a player or coach, Harbaugh, through a Chargers spokesperson, pointed to a 2024 press conference, in which he said he “pulsed” Kaepernick’s interest in coaching.]
Why are you confident that you are ready to be an NFL quarterback right
now?
Because I train for it. I rely on my training and preparation for any moment. I've grown confident in my ability to continue to stay ready because I've shown that the training works, and I've shown that I've been able to go out and perform.
What’s your relationship with the national anthem today? When you go to sporting events, what do you do?
I don't go out for the Star-Spangled Banner. I’m either seated where I'm at, or I'm not out there at all, and then show up when it's time for the actual game to come on.
Your daughter is 4. When this time is right, what will you say to her about the national anthem?
This is actually a funny and timely question. We just went through the process of moving. We're putting some of the artwork up and pictures up. We have the TIME cover framed. I don't like having any of my stuff in rooms that I'm in. Feels weird to me. But my wife wants to have stuff up. And my daughter found it, and she grabbed it and was like, "Oh, this is going to my room.” But she was like, “Baba, why are you taking a knee like this?” She's showing me how I'm taking a knee. Not a conversation I was expecting to be having at 3 ½ years old.
What did you say to her about it?
“Well, Baba was protesting to try to create a better life for everyone. Thought all people should be able to be successful and have good lives and be treated fairly.”
What are you going to tell her when she asks about why you stopped playing in the NFL?
It's going to be an honest conversation, in part because I also know I have to prepare her for the reality that she's going to walk into rooms and they're going to see her last name is Kaepernick. She's going to get asked questions and she's going to have to have to navigate things that she never asked for. Part of my responsibility as a father is making sure that she's prepared and equipped for that.
Going back to your early life a bit – you credit your parents with raising you and having your back. But there were many moments where they weren't as sensitive to your racial experience and awakenings as you would have liked. You make that very clear in the book and don't spare your feelings about it. Have your mom and dad read the book?
They have not read it yet.
How do you anticipate they'll react to it?
There's moments that they just don't know about. It is also something that, for me, in thinking about a white couple born and raised in Wisconsin, adopting a young Black boy, it is very difficult for them to understand the reality of what that's going to be for me growing up. As far as raising me on strong fundamentals and morals, teaching me to work hard, teaching me to treat people well regardless of what their position or status may be in life, all of those things they did extremely well. But when it comes to understanding being Black, being a Black man, what that means, navigating society, that part largely didn't exist. That's where a lot of the conflicts come in around culture, around perception, around who I actually was. I knew they always loved me as their son. I don't know if they always loved my Blackness. And I think that's an interesting nuance to be able to navigate.
How would you characterize your relationship with them now?
I think we're in a good place. My daughter loves calling them during dinner. That is part of her routine now. They come out, they visit. But there is still some of the complexities there.
At several points in the book, you talk about the business of the NFL in the same breath as slavery. Of being photographed in compression shorts at the draft combine, you write, “My mind immediately went to the scenes I had witnessed in numerous movies depicting slave auction blocks.” You also write, “I fully believe what happened to me was a form of buck breaking. That's a slave term to describe how masters used to whip and sexually abuse enslaved men in front of a crowd to dehumanize them and warn other slaves that they better not step out of line. I was made into a warning to other NFL players and professional athletes: You better not challenge the league's authority.” Were you ever worried that people might be offended by that?
No. I know people would take things in the context that they want to. But the parallels between the two are undeniable. Bill Rhoden wrote a whole book around it, Forty Million Dollar Slaves. This came up for Curt Flood when he was fighting for free agency for professional players. "Well, you're making $90,000 a year, Curt Flood. How can you compare this to slavery?” And I believe his quote around that was, "A well-paid slave is a slave nonetheless,” or something to that effect. Which speaks more to the institutions and practices around how you are treating people and the process that they're going through, and the systems that they have to navigate, as opposed to just taking something in isolation.
Two news stories weren't addressed in the book. One is your decision to wear socks depicting police as cartoon pigs in 2016, before you took your public stance. That offended law enforcement personnel, and police unions in particular. Why don't you, or why do you, regret that specific decision?
When I wore those socks, we were seeing police killing Black people with impunity across the country. This is something that has systemically been in place. It came out of slave patrols, built into modern-day policing. Now, policing in the U.S. exists in a way that we don't see in other areas throughout the world, so to me, that was sending a message around the inhumane practices that police were practicing.
It seemed to have an effect where some people would never forgive you after that. But you knew that was a risk?
The same people who are offended, in a way that, “hey, we're never going to forgive you for that,” why are you so remorseful for police killing Black people? Why are you so accepting of that? A pair of socks is so offensive to you, but the killing of a human life you're OK with. So, if we're really going to have a conversation around it, let's actually put it in contrast to the conversations that we're having. I'm going to choose valuing human life in every instance.
The other story is the shelving of the ESPN documentary about you, directed by Spike Lee. About a year ago, ESPN said in a statement that “ESPN, Colin Kaepernick and Spike Lee have collectively decided to no longer proceed with this project as a result of certain creative differences.” What were those creative differences?
We had approved for the documentary to go out, and that was not something that fit within their timeline. So the documentary is finished. It's ready to go. We're looking for potential partners to be able to place it.
Why didn't ESPN want it?
It's a great question. I know they have shifting priorities, as we're seeing publicly right now. We also know they were, I believe, at that point in time in the midst of negotiating their deal with the NFL. So I can't say that those things are connected. But I believe they’re all factors. [An ESPN spokesperson sent TIME a statement: “Two years ago, the three parties involved in this project came to a mutual decision, based on creative differences, not to move forward. Creative differences are not uncommon when several entities collaborate on a project of this kind. Because multiple parties were involved, we are limited in what we can share publicly. This is not new as the decision not to move forward was agreed upon Monday, July 29th 2024. We are grateful for the work that went into it.”]
In a recent interview, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez seemed to agree with the sentiment that “Woke 1.0 was crazy.” She was referring to the period, after the murder of George Floyd in 2020, where there were calls, for example, to defund the police. You wrote in a 2020 essay “in order to eradicate anti-Blackness, we must also abolish the police. The abolition of one without the other is impossible.” What is your response to AOC's characterization and other political characterizations that sentiments like you expressed went too far?
I understand the political realities that politicians are navigating. I'm not naive to that. I also think the reality is, if we are trying to create better communities that allow us to thrive, our resources shouldn't be going towards policing. They should be going towards resources that allow the community to thrive. When you invest in communities, they get safer. People do better. Crime rates drop. I would not discredit the work that was done around the country during 2020, because that has laid the foundation for the movement that we're seeing now. We're seeing a different wave of politicians show up: “Am I providing direct benefit to the people that I'm serving?” I think that is the most important priority to be able to keep in mind.
Do you still support abolishing policing?
Yes. I think that's the work that we should be doing. Reallocating those resources to directly benefit communities and give them the resources that they need to be able to thrive.
You write in the book about how, in 2016, you met with your San Francisco 49ers teammates to explain in more detail why you were protesting during the anthem. You write: "I told my teammates how law enforcement in this country has always been an enemy of Black people.” In 2026, do you still feel that law enforcement in this country is an enemy of Black people?
The institution has not changed. It still exists in the same form it did in 2016. We're still seeing the same issues come out of it. We're still seeing that fuel and funnel into the prison industrial complex. So until those systems are dismantled and those resources are allocated to benefit communities, the institutions are serving the purpose that they were laid out to do.
How would you characterize how Donald Trump has treated you?
At least to my knowledge, that was the first time I had seen a President use their position and political power to target an individual citizen. And I think that laid the foundation and set the stage for a lot of what we are seeing now. And in many ways, I feel like that was an initial test to see how far things could go. I obviously do not agree with his political views or approach. I do not believe that the work he is doing is actually to benefit people other than himself.
The NFL has reported giving more than $450 million to grassroots organizations to benefit communities in need. Do you see that as a sincere response to your protest or a PR play?
I view that as a PR play. There was a player-owners meeting. Bob McNair, who was the owner of the Texans at the time, said, "You need to tell your compadres to stop that other business,” meaning the protests. Bob Kraft was in that meeting and said, "We need to talk about the elephant in the room and ending the protests.” And Terry Pegula, the owner of the Bills, just said explicitly, “We need a Black face to be at the forefront of this to help us stop this.” If it was actually to try to create change and benefit Black communities, the NFL's response holistically from the start would have looked drastically different. I would have a job. Eric Reid would have a job. The other players that were targeted throughout that process wouldn't have had to navigate that.
NFL commissioner Roger Goodell admitted, in 2020, that the league was wrong for not listening more closely to the message and meaning behind protests like yours. He encouraged a team to sign you. Do you forgive him?
No, because he's still taking those actions to this day. That they have not changed their practices. The NFL just went through navigating race-norming, where they were assessing that the baseline intelligence or cognitive abilities of Black players was lower than white players, so that they could deny them medical benefits after playing in the NFL. It’s important to put it into broader context. This isn't a practice that just exists in relation to me and the protest. [The NFL declined to comment.]
The book details your relationship with Jay-Z, whose company, Roc Nation, partnered with the NFL in 2019 to consult on Super Bowl halftime entertainment and other performances and initiatives. Jay-Z recently brought you up in a rap lyric at Yankee Stadium, saying, “Buddy took a check, I ain’t even mad at him, but along with that check you gotta sign a non-disparagement. I’m the one they can’t control.” How would you characterize how Jay-Z has communicated with you, and used you or brought you up?
The fact that seven years after him cutting a deal to undermine the protest, unprompted, [he] brings me up, sounds like a guilty conscience to me. I would also say, just to make very clear, the distinction here. One, I did not sign a non-disparagement. But the second part of this is these are very different situations. He's trying to create a false equivalency around being blackballed by the NFL and having to go through the grievance process, the legal process that's already laid out by the collective bargaining agreement between the NFL and the players’ union–going through that process, and then reaching a settlement at the end of it, because that is your path towards reconciliation, is very different than cutting a deal with the NFL to create personal benefit and undermine the protests. Trying to conflate the two is very disingenuous. [A representative for Roc Nation and Jay-Z did not respond to TIME’s request for comment.]
Are you surprised that DEI is under fire?
I'm not surprised it's being attacked by this Administration. What I am surprised by is the capitulation by corporations, by organizations to go along with it. What I've seen is when you show weakness, that you'll bow down to them, that you'll capitulate to them, they're going to try to take that further and further.
Did you make any mistakes over the past 10 years?
One that I think about a good amount is, I had intentionally taken an approach of I'm going to do my best to not call out or attack people who I disagree with. I did not want to create an environment or narrative that was centered around Black people fighting and distracting from the intention of the protest. Even with Jay-Z, I didn't go out and do interviews around that. I believe people will see the work, and my hope is in seeing the work, people will look at and say, "Oh, that's how it should be done.” But I don't know if that created additional space for people to take the narrative in places that shouldn't have gone. It's one of those things that I'm very mindful of as I move forward.

UN backs Palestinian President Abbas' video address after US visa refusal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Diyar Guldogan
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
The UN General Assembly on Thursday adopted a resolution allowing Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas to address next week’s high-level debate by pre-recorded video after the US refused to issue visas for Palestine’s delegation for a second year.
 
The resolution was passed overwhelmingly with 152 votes in favor, four abstentions (Colombia, Honduras, Panama and Peru), and three against, including the US, Israel and Paraguay.
 
The move follows Washington’s decision to extend visa sanctions denying entry to members of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) and officials of the Palestinian Authority (PA), days before the fall UN General Assembly is set to convene in New York.
 
The measure, submitted by Palestine, permits Abbas to deliver a prerecorded statement during the general debate of the 81st session of the assembly.
 
The resolution also allows Palestinian representatives to participate by videoconference or prerecorded statements at certain high-level UN meetings.
 
It applies only to the assembly’s 81st session and it does not establish a precedent for future general debates or mandated high-level meetings.
 
Following the vote, Palestine's envoy to the UN Riyad Mansour, thanked member countries that voted in favor.
 
Mansour said the leadership of Palestine rejects and condemns the action of denying the Palestinian delegation headed by Abbas to exercise its “lawful right" to participate in the meetings.
 
"This has happened for the second year in a row, and we sincerely hope that that will be the last time that this illegal behavior to exhibit itself and to deny us our rightful right to be with all delegations, with all of heads of delegations, to exercise our duty in conveying our position to the entire international community," he added.

Pentagon, Lockheed to Expand Production of Secretive New Joint Advanced Tactical Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:44:00 UTC
04:44:00 KST

The Pentagon announced a deal with Lockheed Martin on Sept. 17 to expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, an advanced new Air Force and Navy air-to-air missile meant to equip fifth- and sixth-generation fighters.
The “framework” agreement aims to give Lockheed a “long-term demand” signal, part of a push by President Donald Trump’s administration to build and sustain a more robust munitions manufacturing industrial base.
The announcement “establishes the framework for future multiyear procurement of JATM,” according to the Pentagon release.
“We will deliver JATM at the speed our nation and allies demand while providing value for taxpayers and our shareholders,” Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed Missiles and Fire Control, said in a company release.
A Lockheed spokesperson declined to answer further questions from Air & Space Forces Magazine, deferring to the Department of Defense. A Pentagon press officer also declined any further comment about the announcement.
The announcement should signal to Lockheed and other munitions-makers that a stable market is taking shape, said Mark Gunzinger, director of future concepts and capability assessments at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies.
“It is difficult for industry to justify expenditures needed to accelerate and scale up production,” the retired Air Force colonel said. “This is a key reason why this is an important framework.”
Next-Gen Option
The JATM is the successor to the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, which has been in service since 1991.
The radar-guided, medium-range, supersonic AMRAAM has undergone major upgrades since its inception, most recently in 2020. The F-22 Raptor, F-35 Lightning II, F-15 Eagle variants, and the F-16 Fighting Falcon can all carry it, and the Air Force isn’t looking to stop buying the missile even as it looks to the JATM.
The service is seeking $953 million for 618 AMRAAMs in its fiscal 2027 budget request, while the Navy is asking for $673 million to buy 388 AMRAAMs.
The JATM seeks to overmatch the Chinese military’s PL-15 and PL-17 missiles and will reportedly double the AMRAAM’s range and hit targets in excess of 120 miles away, though much of its capabilities have been shrouded in secrecy for years.
In its fiscal 2026 budget request, the Air Force revealed it had bought 144 JATMs in 2024-2025 and planned to buy at least another 112 missiles. The fiscal 2027 request, still pending before Congress, has $1.5 billion in procurement to scale up production, but budget documents don’t list any quantities.
While upgraded AMRAAMs provide an improved strike option for fighter aircraft, the JATM is necessary for advanced aircraft already fielded and those in the pipeline, such as the F-47 and Collaborative Combat Aircraft variants, the FQ-42 Vengeance and FQ-44 Fury.
“It doesn’t make sense to invest in highly survivable and incredibly capable fifth- and sixth-gen fighters and bombers just to saddle them with payloads of weapons that will not survive to reach their targets in a fight with a peer adversary,” Gunzinger said.
Mix for the Future Fight
Though reports on the current conflict with Iran don’t indicate the U.S. is using large numbers of air-to-air missiles, a future conflict with a peer adversary such as the Chinese military is likely to look much different.
“Multiple Mitchell Institute wargames have spotlighted the need to rapidly grow the U.S. Air Force’s inventory of advanced air-to-air weapons, which could be nearly depleted within a couple of weeks of high-intensity combat with a peer adversary,” Gunzinger said.
This isn’t the first time the Pentagon has announced plans for multiyear procurement of key missiles.
In July, the Pentagon announced a similar framework for a USAF program known as the Family of Affordable Mass Munitions, which will produce lower-cost cruise missiles that experts believe will be needed in future conflicts for higher strike volumes.
That deal anticipates 8,000 missiles annually once production is at full strength. Work is expected to ramp up by 2028 with 5,300 missiles produced, increasing to the 8,000-missile mark by 2031.
While the FAMM deal will bulk up low-cost options for the Air Force, work on more expensive but more capable munitions are an important part of the equation.
“Our air forces will have a future high-low mix of counter-air weapons, but it’s far more important to focus on the cost to achieve an effect in the battlespace like countering an enemy air threat than the unit cost of a weapon,” Gunzinger said. “The key is to determine the right high-low mix based on optimizing cost per effect instead of simply chasing lower unit costs.”
Allies and Partner Purchases
The U.S. isn’t the only country interested in JATM—Australia announced $736 million in spending to equip its Royal Australian Air Force with the weapon.
That move, along with potential deals with other allies and partners, could also help reduce missile costs for the U.S.
“I believe sharing production with key allies as soon as possible is critical to improving their interoperability with U.S. air forces and lead to cost-sharing agreements that can accelerate weapon development and acquisition,” Gunzinger said.
Beyond cost savings, having allies buy the next-generation missile for their fleets also gives the U.S. ways to standardize weapons loaders across a coalition and share munitions when needed, he said.

Rain and strong winds forecast across Finland this weekend
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
22:43:31 EEST
04:43:31 KST

Rain will affect much of Finland this weekend as low-pressure systems move near the country, with strong wind gusts expected in the south before spreading across a wider area on Sunday.
The Finnish Meteorological Institute said in its forecast issued on Thursday that temperatures would remain close to normal September levels despite unsettled conditions.
Friday will bring showers mainly to southern and western Finland during the day, with rain also reaching eastern areas by the evening. Northern Finland will remain drier at first.
There is also a small chance of thunderstorms in southern and western Finland overnight from Friday into Saturday.
“There is a small possibility of thunderstorms in connection with the showers in southern and western parts of the country during the night before Saturday,” Finnish Meteorological Institute meteorologist Eetu Rimo said.
Rain will shift northwards during Saturday. According to the forecast, only northern Lapland is expected to avoid rainfall.
Parts of southern and central Finland will have dry periods during the day, but another area of rain will approach from the south-west on Saturday evening. It will move north across Finland during Saturday night and Sunday morning.
South-westerly winds will strengthen as the rain system arrives.
“Strong gusts are possible over land during Saturday and Sunday, particularly in southern Finland on Saturday and across a wider area on Sunday,” Rimo said.
Daytime temperatures will range from 7°C to 17°C. Overnight temperatures will generally remain between 5°C and 15°C, although some areas of Lapland face the possibility of temperatures falling below freezing.
September temperatures have so far remained close to seasonal averages across much of Finland.
That marks a change from the previous three years. September 2023 and September 2024 recorded the highest average temperatures for the month in Finland’s measurement history. September 2025 also recorded temperatures above long-term averages.
At weather observation stations, average September temperatures during those years were generally between 2°C and 4°C above normal.
Finland has recorded no hot days, defined nationally as days when temperatures exceed 25°C, during September this year. There were four such days in September 2025 and eight in September 2024.
“This September might have felt much cooler than the previous ones, but it is worth remembering that the preceding Septembers had temperatures that differed from normal,” Rimo said.

Ilhan Omar attacker sentenced to more than a year in prison
Assailant sprayed vinegar at Representative Ilhan Omar, admitting political motives were behind the assault during her townhall.
The man who sprayed apple cider vinegar at Democratic United States Representative Ilhan Omar during a town hall meeting in her district in Minneapolis was sentenced to a 14-month prison term after he pleaded guilty to an assault charge.
Appearing before District Judge Joan N Ericksen on Thursday, 55-year-old Anthony James Kazmierczak pleaded guilty to planning the January 27 assault, admitting he targeted the congresswoman over opposing political views. He had been charged with assaulting a US officer.

It has been nearly eight months since Kazmierczak lunged towards the congresswoman and sprayed her with a dark water-and-vinegar mixture from a syringe, which landed on Omar’s clothing and skin.
The attack was captured on video and showed Kazmierczak, who sat in the front row of the town hall, leaping from the audience, after which he could be heard yelling, “You must resign” and that Omar was “splitting Minnesota apart”.
Kazmierczak was promptly subdued by Omar’s security team before being arrested. Omar was not injured in the attack and proceeded with the town hall.
The assault came as Omar had been calling for the abolition of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency and the resignation of then-Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem over her management of federal border agents in Minneapolis during the shootings during “Operation Metro Surge,” President Donald Trump’s federal immigration crackdown in the state of Minnesota. “It’s fuzzy,” he told US Judge Ericksen when asked what he remembered.
The government sentencing memorandum, submitted to the court by prosecutors, said he had texted at least three people indicating his actions were premeditated, though he refused to answer questions about his specific intent.
He also messaged a neighbour to arrange for dog care and contacts for a bail bond company.
The sentencing memo said Kazmierczak had long struggled with alcohol abuse, had “a history of mental and emotional health concerns”, and also had a string of health issues tied to a 2022 diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease. His lawyer, John Fossum, had argued that Kazmierczak had not been taking his mental health medication before the attack, lowering his inhibitions and contributing to what happened.
“I’ve spent enough time in jail thinking,” Kazmierczak said Thursday. “I really apologise to her for having put her through that,” he said, referring to Omar.
Kazmierczak wrote to Omar after the attack, “I’m sorry if I scared you.”
In social media posts, Kazmierczak had denounced former President Joe Biden and referred to Democrats as “angry and liars”, writing that Trump wants the US to be “stronger and more prosperous”.
“This assault is yet another example of a dangerous national trend: people channeling political hatred into criminal acts,” said US Attorney Daniel N Rosen after Kazmierczak pled guilty in May.
Omar, a Somali-American refugee and naturalised US citizen, has faced sustained mocking and anti-immigrant rhetoric from Trump throughout her congressional tenure.

'A struggle every day': There's a hidden side to Australia's student visa debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:41:10 UTC
04:41:10 KST

IN BRIEF
- The government says the changes will help cut net overseas migration to 245,000 this financial year.
- Students and migration experts have raised concerns about how some of the new restrictions could affect migrants.
For almost nine years, Bashshar Khalid has been building a life in Australia.
He arrived as an international student in 2017, completed a three-year bachelor's degree in business and then a two-year master's degree before entering the workforce.
But graduating was only the beginning.
Khalid first moved onto a temporary graduate visa, known as a subclass 485, and recently secured a subclass 482 work visa after finding employment in sales.
He told SBS News that making the transition from international student to skilled worker was far from straightforward.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
One of the biggest difficulties was convincing an employer to invest in someone whose ability to remain in Australia had an expiry date attached to it.
"We basically have to work twice as hard, or we just have to prove our skill set to our employers," he said.
At one point, Khalid's temporary graduate visa was approaching expiry while his employer-sponsored visa application was still being processed.
He moved onto a bridging visa while he waited for an outcome.
"Every day when you wake up, or every day you're going into the office to work, you're not sure whether the application will be approved or not ... It's basically a struggle every day."
Government's migration crackdown
Now, the federal government has announced another suite of changes aimed at tightening Australia's migration system and further reducing net overseas migration (NOM).
The changes include measures targeting so-called "visa hopping", restrictions on secondary applicants on most student visas and stronger measures to ensure people without valid visas leave Australia.
The government will also introduce a 'no further stay' condition on all visitor visas and crack down on migration agents it says knowingly support applications without merit.
Announcing the reforms on Thursday, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the government was targeting people who would "never" meet the requirements for permanent residency but continued moving through the migration system to extend their stay.
"They effectively jump from visa to visa, use the appeals process to be able to stay here as long as possible until it eventually becomes absurd to not just let them stay," he said.
Critics say the crackdown could limit legitimate study and work opportunities.
Khalid said he believes there should be a clearer distinction between people switching courses simply to stay in the country, and migrants legitimately progressing through study and skilled employment.
"We have contributed to the economy. We have paid our taxes. We have done everything right by the book," he said.
"There couldn't be one single hard and fast rule about everything.
"If they could genuinely prove that the change of career is more of a personal choice and not just for a visa hopping case, then I think they should be given a fair chance."
Former immigration department deputy secretary Abul Rizvi also supports reducing visa hopping but cautioned against applying restrictions too broadly.
"As a general rule, I think reducing visa hopping is a good idea," he said.
"The question will be how broadly those measures are applied, because if they're applied too broadly, there will be unintended consequences."
Rizvi pointed to businesses that bring workers into Australia on business visas when they urgently need their skills while waiting for a skilled temporary visa to be processed.
If those transitions are restricted while skilled visa processing times remain lengthy, he said, businesses could face difficulties.
'It would have definitely affected my decision'
For Khalid, the uncertainty of Australia's migration system has already made planning a career difficult.
Khalid said policy changes could mean migrants made significant decisions based on one set of rules, only to find the pathway had shifted.
"If my pathway was not as clear ... it would have been a major decision for me whether I should stay on in the country or leave the country," he said.
Had the pathway been more restrictive when he was studying, Khalid said it "would have definitely affected" his decision.
His recently granted 482 visa now provides a potential pathway towards permanent residency.
"After spending a good amount of time in this country, you sort of feel like it's your second home," he said.
What will the changes mean for students with families?
The government's reforms also restrict secondary applicants on most student visas, potentially affecting students seeking to have family members join them in Australia.
Muath Alqarni, a Saudi master's degree student at the University of Melbourne, told SBS Arabic that he understood the government wanted greater control over migration involving international students' families but was concerned about broad restrictions.
"I recognise there is an issue with international students' families' immigration, and I understand that the federal government is trying to control it," he said.
"However, as an international student who used to live with his family, my situation is different."
Alqarni urged the government to examine the data and circumstances of different groups rather than applying broad measures.
"It's a lifetime chance for me to bring my family to Australia and spend a good time with them in Australia," he said.
Rizvi also raised concerns about students undertaking lengthy courses who may be affected by restrictions on bringing partners to Australia.
"If you're doing a four-year nursing degree or a five-year engineering degree or a six-year medicine degree and you're married, to be without your partner for four or six years is really, really difficult," he said.
He argued Australia risked losing some prospective students to competing destinations if they could not bring their partners.
Will the changes bring migration down?
The government says the reforms are designed to help bring NOM down to 245,000 this financial year and 225,000 in 2027-28.
Rizvi believes those forecasts will probably be achieved if the changes are combined with the high student visa refusal rates he says have been in place since November 2025.
International students have played a significant role in recent movements in NOM, he said.
"The biggest increase in the big surge in net migration in 2023 was students, and the biggest reduction since then has been students," Rizvi said.
Burke said migration also needed to slow sufficiently for housing supply to "catch up", but rejected the suggestion migration itself was responsible for Australia's housing shortage.
"The housing shortage we have is not caused by immigration," he said.
"But immigration needs to be part of the solution for the housing crisis."

Ukrainian Armed Forces Receive Australian 30-mm Slinger Anti-Drone Modules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:39:43 UTC
04:39:43 KST

The Ukrainian military has received and is already deploying Australian Slinger C-UAS remotely controlled anti-drone modules.
Photographer Louis Souvestre posted photos of the system in action in Ukraine on his Instagram page.
The anti-drone system was developed and is manufactured by the Australian company Electro Optic Systems.
The Slinger system is based on the 30-mm Bushmaster M230LF automatic cannon and is equipped with a modern optoelectronic targeting system along with a radar.
The module is capable of detecting and engaging aerial targets, such as kamikaze drones and reconnaissance UAVs, at ranges exceeding 800 meters using specialized 30-mm ammunition with radio-controlled fuses.
Thanks to its low weight (about 355 kg), the system is highly mobile and can be integrated onto various types of platforms.
In Ukraine, Slinger combat modules are mounted on pickup trucks, creating mobile fire teams to shoot down enemy drones.
In addition to wheeled vehicles, the Australian systems can also be integrated onto light armored vehicles and armored personnel carriers to protect units on the front lines.
In 2023, it was reported that Electro Optic Systems will supply 160 such anti-drone modules to Ukraine.
110 systems were to be integrated onto M113s, and another 50 were ordered by the company Praktika.
As early as October, the company prepared the first batch of Slinger systems for shipment to Ukraine.
A batch of ten systems was to be delivered to Ukraine by the end of the year.

Tusk: intelligence sees Russian plan for drone strikes on Poland, allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:39:29 UTC
04:39:29 KST

Prime Minister Donald Tusk outlined in the Sejm the "most likely" scenario for the months ahead, warning of serious events and hybrid attacks on Poland and other Ukraine backers.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk, in a special address to the Sejm, said he was presenting the public and MPs with "the most probable scenario for the coming few months".
"It is a scenario involving serious events and requiring us to be focused, serious and, above all, mentally ready to pass difficult tests," Tusk said.
He stressed that such tests "certainly lie ahead for all Poles".
The head of government pointed out that his comments refer to the period up to early spring, "because, according to all sources, it is late autumn and winter that will be the most critical phase of the Russian-Ukrainian war so far".
Jet-powered drones: Russia's new weapon
He also pointed to a significant development "of a very negative nature": Russia is rolling out on a mass scale a new type of drone – jet-powered drones that travel at much higher speeds and operate at high altitude before dropping and hitting their target. He noted that hardly anyone is effectively prepared to counter them and that "this is work we, too, have to do".
Tusk announced he would travel to Ukraine to talk with President Volodymyr Zelensky "about how we can cooperate within the anti-ballistic coalition and make use of the skills, capabilities and capacities of Ukraine and other countries in this field as well".
He also referred to the unfulfilled promises of an energy truce previously mentioned by US President Donald Trump.
"Since then, there have been many attacks, including on energy infrastructure in Ukraine. We must therefore assume this will continue, which also has consequences for Poland, as these attacks are increasingly targeting installations very close to our border crossings with Ukraine," he said.
According to the prime minister, Russia's aim is to destroy Ukraine's economy and logistics on as large a scale as possible. "For now, Ukraine's," he added pointedly.
Six main Ukrainian cities in Russia's sights
The Polish prime minister said constant strikes of very high frequency and intensity are expected on six key Ukrainian cities, along with the destruction of stockpiles of supplies essential for the country's defence and of railway infrastructure. Tusk recalled that in the past several weeks Russians have destroyed more than 300 Ukrainian railway locomotives.
The head of government said that "in the assessment of intelligence services, Russia's plans also include hybrid strikes with drones and missiles on states supporting Ukraine, including Poland". Such possibilities have been mentioned for some time, but now, Tusk stressed, the information is already "highly consistent and, unfortunately, persuasive".
In the prime minister's view, potential strikes will be "so-called 'accidental'", aimed at paralysing or weakening NATO members' motivation to invoke alliance provisions in the event of aggression.
"There is a real risk that the territory of one or several NATO countries on the eastern flank may be entered by drones or other types of missiles, which may even cause destruction. And the official narrative will be that this is an accident and that there is no reason for anyone to contemplate any response from NATO," he said.
Russia's objective, he said, is "to weaken NATO's overall cohesion and, above all, to convince NATO countries that Article 5 is more theoretical than practical". Such "accidental" strikes may be repeated.
Tusk: on security, we must speak with one voice
Continuing, the prime minister said that Russia's new strategy also envisages possible political changes in some European countries. He recalled the forthcoming elections and the presence of forces that can be described as an openly pro-Russian option. He appealed to politicians, regardless of party colours – addressing in particular MPs from the Confederation party – "under no circumstances to take part, whether inadvertently or deliberately, in promoting narratives that Russia cares deeply about".
"Whipping up hostility towards the European Union, towards our allies, towards Ukrainians, is directly implementing Russia's strategy. Everyone must finally understand this," he underlined.
In closing, Tusk called on everyone present in the Sejm chamber to "speak with one voice, take joint decisions, hesitate no longer and show that, regardless of political views, we are all patriots in a moment of trial" when it comes to the security of borders, Polish airspace and people's homes. He pointed out that some politicians in Europe "are just waiting for an alibi" so that, in the event of conflict, they can argue: "We will not die for Poland, we will not perish for Latvia or Lithuania".
"Article 5, allied loyalty, fidelity to commitments must become our hallmark," he declared. He added that Poland wants and needs certainty that, in the event of a more serious threat from Russia, it can "count on a swift and effective response from the entire bloc".

Türkiye-Azerbaijan relations constitute a vital factor in region, wider world: Aliyev
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:36:16 UTC
04:36:16 KST

Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev has said that activities with neighbouring Türkiye further strengthen stability in their region and beyond.
Aliyev said at a meeting on Thursday with security officials of Organization of Turkic States (OTS) member states in the Azerbaijani capital that relations between his country and Türkiye “occupy a special place and play a special role.”
Expressing that there are “no similar relations anywhere in the world,” Aliyev was quoted by the presidency as saying it is impossible to find a “second pair of countries so closely bound to each other,” with a multitude of factors converging such as historical ties, cultural connections and people-to-people relations.
“That is to say, Türkiye-Azerbaijan relations today constitute a vital factor in our region and the wider world, as a unified space. Our joint activities further strengthen stability in our region and beyond, especially in the current difficult geopolitical situation,” he said.
Aliyev described the Shusha Declaration signed with Ankara in 2021 as representing the “peak of our relations,” saying that while they were allies prior to the signing, the declaration formalised their alliance.
“More than five years have passed since that day, and with every passing year and month, our unity grows stronger and our role in the world is further reinforced,” said Aliyev.
Relations between Baku and Ankara were elevated to the level of an alliance with the Shusha Declaration, which Aliyev signed with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan during a two-day visit to the South Caucasus nation by Erdogan.
The OTS was established in 2009 and adopted its current name at the Istanbul Summit in 2021. Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan are members, while Turkmenistan, Hungary and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus hold observer status.
OTS Aliyev said that the overall sentiment among leaders of OTS member states is aimed at bolstering the role and position of the organisation on the international stage.
He said the potential of their countries is quite substantial and continues to grow, noting they are situated across a vast geographical expanse where crucial energy and transport routes and corridors pass through.
"To the west and east of the OTS region, our organisation is being closely watched with great interest as it strengthens its positive role in international affairs, including in matters related to connectivity, transport security, energy security, and security in general," said Aliyev.
“Therefore, I am confident that these issues will also be discussed at today’s council meeting, because today, without energy security and transport connectivity, it is virtually impossible to speak about overall security.”
He also described the stability, peace and security prevailing in their countries as a key factor in the successful development of the OTS, arguing that it is an important factor for development in today’s political and foreign policy realities.
"It is well known that no country can develop without stability and security. Neither investment, technology nor innovation will come to a country if there is no stability or political and economic security there. Therefore, today this is also a key factor that distinguishes our countries from many of the surrounding regions where we are located," he said.
Aliyev also said OTS countries are demonstrating strong economic growth, particularly at a time when they see opposite trends occurring in various parts of the globe.

See the first new species of cat discovered in more than a century—it’s adorable
Unknown

19:34:46 UTC
04:34:46 KST

Deep in the Bolivian Yungas cloud forests, there stalks an utterly adorable beast: smaller than a house cat and spotted like a leopard, the creature has long been known to local communities as a tilcayo. Scientists, however, have only just formally discovered it—marking the first new wildcat species to be identified in more than a century.
The new species, Leopardus tilcayo, is a type of tiger cat, a group of small felines in the genus Leopardus that are native to South America. In a paper published on Thursday in Current Biology, the researchers identify five distinct species of tiger cats in South America, including the tilcayo.
The discovery came by accident, said the study’s co-lead author Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz to NBC News. A man had brought one of the kitties into the sanctuary that she volunteered at, and she noticed that it didn’t quite match any existing tiger cat species. After a series of genetic tests, she and her team discovered the cat must be a new species that had likely diverged from its closest tiger cat relative some 1.4 million years ago.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The discovery of a new mammal, especially a cat, is rare. It’s even more rare to find an entirely new species rather than a variation of a known species. The study analyzed the genomes of 38 cats, including 26 Leopardus cats, comprising “the most complete genetic study yet,” said the study’s co-lead author Jonas Lescroart, an evolutionary ecologist at the University of Antwerp in Belgium, to Gizmodo.
It’s unclear how many tilcayos are out there, and the authors have said that the study should be a catalyst for intensified conservation efforts across tiger cat species.
“Describing a new cat species after more than 100 years shows how much we still have to learn about the biodiversity around us. But it also reminds us that we need to protect the Yungas forests, which are home to so many species—including some we are only beginning to understand,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said in a statement.

The world is just enough: Ursula von der Leyen goes Bond villain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:32:02 UTC
04:32:02 KST

The world is just enough: Ursula von der Leyen goes Bond villain
As a historian who also happens to be German, that was my spontaneous reaction to Ursula von der Leyen’s annual grand – and always grandiloquent – “state of the union” address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.
It’s not really a “union,” of course, and not really a “parliament,” either: technically, the EU is a confederation messed up by the ideological construct of “supranationalism”; and the parliament has no independent legislative power, but let’s not dwell on the obvious.
At the head of her Commission (read: over-reaching Central Committee) of career bureaucrats, von der Leyen is the unelected de-facto leader and personification of the Frankenstein wanna-be-super-state that has long gobbled up idealistic dreams of European unity.
Once, those dreams may have been about democracy, sovereign equality, prosperity for all, and peace. But real-existing EU-Europe is very different: the European dream has come true as a nightmare, dominated by a smug and self-empowered globalist establishment, thoroughly insulated from popular participation, economically stagnant and crisis-prone, as well as unequal, and ever more militarist.
When von der Leyen boasted that, in effect during her tenure, EU-Europe had become “stronger” and “more independent,” while “securing its prosperity” and increasing armament spending “by 80% in the last five years alone,” only the last point bore any resemblance to reality, as the preponderant majority of the over 450 million EU citizens – really subjects – experience it.
But there is no misery a Eurocrat worth her (or his!) salt cannot make worse. Now von der Leyen seems hellbent to take the worst of bad old German traditions to a whole new, all-EU level. As is well-known from the history of the last two world wars, Germany not once but twice first deftly maneuvered itself into being surrounded by (mostly) enemies and then lost, the first time crushingly, the second one even worse, in fact so badly it took a short half-century (and much Russian good will, as it happens) to put the country together again.
The Kaiser’s Germany and the Fuhrer’s were – to be fair even to the Kaiser – quite different, but what their establishments had in common was a bad case of Germanophrenia, a relative of the contemporary Russophrenia syndrome: The core delusion of Russophrenia, as it is now ravaging Western minds, is to hallucinate Russia as on the verge of collapse and of conquering the world at the same time. Those afflicted by Germanophrenia believed Germany was in existential danger but also capable of taking on Europe at least and, if need be, the world, too.
Enter the all-EU version, compliments of the very, very German von der Leyen. Quoting Charles Dickens’ already much overused “it was the best of times, it was the worst of times” line in her impeccably Germanic version of English, von der Leyen proceeded to do two things: assert that the EU is at peak strength and, at the same time, as precarious as ever. Clearly aware that sane listeners would find that combination of claims extremely counter-intuitive, she insisted that even if they “may seem incompatible,” they are still both true. Orwell for beginners really: two plus two is five, if Big Sister from the Commission says so.
Inducing debilitating cognitive dissonance, though, is the least of von der Leyen’s powers. The real payload of her rambling speech was her combative declaration of if not war then defiance against, in essence, almost everyone who matters on planet Earth.
In true paranoid fashion, von der Leyen first declared that the EU faced a “hostile world,” no less. Then, she got more specific: Russia – surprise, surprise – led her enemy list; and she congratulated, in effect, herself for ridding the EU of a “toxic” dependence on its fossil fuels. What a way to describe cutting yourself off from a reliable and comparatively inexpensive energy source to shift to exorbitant prices and uncertain delivery from, for instance, the unpredictable US and the war-torn and blockade-prone Middle East!
She had tough words and warnings for China as well. Those clearly must be seen in the context of ongoing EU attempts to play trade hardball with Beijing. Desperate to make up for the badly declining competitiveness of European industry and currently especially carmakers, the old continent – once happily exploiting the rest of the world for its own gain – has discovered what von der Leyen and her officials think of as fairness.
But throwing down the gauntlet to China and Russia – the core of the emerging multipolar order – was not enough for von der Leyen in attack-mode. Surprisingly, the same woman who almost literally kissed Donald Trump’s feet at Turnberry, delivering a full, unconditional trade war capitulation – so much, by the way, for her claim that the EU is “the greatest trading power on the planet” – loaded her speech with barely concealed challenges to the US. That is, the much diminished but still regrettably powerful center of the old West, as well as the state on which the EU is, of course, toxically dependent in reality.
The single most aggressive of von der Leyen’s sallies against Washington was her bizarre call for giving Canada “associate membership,” a status that does not even exist under the EU treaties, would need the very unlikely agreement of all 27 member governments, and makes no sense geographically or geopolitically.
But while unrealistic, the idea does have the capacity to make Washington very angry indeed. President Donald Trump has already warned that he considers the idea a “hostile act” and is ready to escalate his economic warfare against the EU. Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was in Strasbourg for von der Leyen’s strange offer, has already switched into damage-control mode.
But then again, von der Leyen’s real motive in suggesting a Canadian-EU play that cannot be but against US interests may be something else entirely. In true von der Leyen spirit, the EU has recently made much noise about claiming interests and, quite simply, a say, in the Arctic. That makes fairly little sense except you count Greenland as “Danish,” which it is formally but hardly in reality. Not to speak of the well-known US ambitions to take it over in one way or the other. Some creative minds may have discovered that adding Canada’s northern coastlines would help make Arctic ambitions more plausible.
And that in turn may very well also explain the speed and ferocity of the US response. In other words, the challenge to Washington may be even worse than “merely” offering Canada a counterweight against traditional and entrenched US hegemony. If the Arctic is the real target, the stakes could not be higher. Way to go, Ursula: your EU against everyone at once. Some of your German ancestors would have been so proud.

Russia ‘sabotaging’ power supply lines at Zaporizhzhia plant: Greenpeace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:30:12 UTC
04:30:12 KST

Russia ‘sabotaging’ power supply lines at Zaporizhzhia plant: Greenpeace
Investigation finds no evidence of Russia’s claims that Ukrainian attacks hit the nuclear power plant.
Russia is sabotaging the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in occupied southeastern Ukraine and blaming it on Kyiv to “confuse and distract” from the threats posed by its “illegal occupation and war”, Greenpeace has warned.
In a report published on Thursday, the environmental group concluded that Moscow is “deliberately sabotaging” the plant’s electricity supply while engaging in a “disinformation campaign” about the attacks.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3India warns new US tariffs over Russian oil could impact ties
- list 2 of 3At least 19 injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine
- list 3 of 3US tariffs against Russian oil buyers pass: What it means for China, India
Greenpeace Ukraine and London-based McKenzie Intelligence Services (MIS) analysed satellite imagery of the site and found no evidence of Russian claims that Ukrainian attacks had occurred.
“The satellite imagery and evidence is clear – Ukraine did not attack its own Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant electricity system,” said Shaun Burnie, a nuclear specialist at Greenpeace Ukraine. “This is part of a massive disinformation campaign, enacted by Moscow to confuse and distract from the real safety threats caused only by their illegal occupation and war.”
“The repeated loss of external power at [the plant] is the result of Russian military attacks on Ukraine’s electricity grid and sabotage operations at [the plant] and associated switchyards,” he said.
MIS analysed several satellite images of the 330 kV Ferosplavna-1 power line near the Zaporizhzhia plant provided by Airbus’s defence and space division. The images were taken between October 2025 and June 2026 and analysed to assess whether damage at the site was caused by Ukrainian artillery fire on February 10 and a Ukrainian drone strike on June 4, as Moscow alleged.
MIS concluded that the damage to the power line was inconsistent with artillery fire or drone strikes.
It added that artillery fire would usually leave a pattern of impact craters and dispersed damage across the targeted area, which was not visible.
MIS also found that the damage allegedly caused by a Ukrainian drone strike on June 4 was already visible before the supposed attack.
According to the United Nation’s nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Ferosplavna-1 is Zaporizhzhia’s only remaining external power line. Last month, the IAEA stressed the importance of a stable electricity supply at the plant to ensure nuclear safety.
Greenpeace echoed that warning on Thursday, saying that a stable electricity supply is crucial to “operate essential reactor safety systems, including pumps that provide cooling for nuclear fuel in reactor cores and spent fuel pools”.
