GM’s defense arm helps speed up PAC-3 MSE production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:53:41 UTC
03:53:41 KST

- GM Defense delivered its first batch of PAC-3 MSE missile-housing components to Lockheed Martin 22 days after signing a formal contract.
- The deal follows a June 2026 partnership aimed at using General Motors' manufacturing capacity to help expand PAC-3 MSE production.
GM Defense delivered its first batch of PAC-3 MSE missile-housing components to Lockheed Martin on Sept. 16, just 22 days after the two companies signed a formal production contract, Lockheed Martin said in a post on X.
“The message is clear: we’re moving at the speed of relevance,” Lockheed Martin said. “The future of defense is being written now, and we’re setting a new standard for speed and agility in the industry.”
The delivery follows a memorandum of understanding GM Defense and Lockheed Martin signed in June 2026 to combine Lockheed’s missile production expertise with General Motors’ high-rate commercial manufacturing capacity, part of a broader push to widen the industrial base that builds the PAC-3 MSE interceptor. Neither company has said what portion of the missile the housing components cover or how many units GM Defense will supply under the contract.
The PAC-3 MSE, a hit-to-kill interceptor built to shoot down ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and aircraft, has seen a sharp jump in demand over the past year. The U.S. Army awarded Lockheed Martin a $9.8 billion contract in September 2025 for 1,970 interceptors, the largest deal in the history of Lockheed’s missiles and fire control business. In January 2026, Lockheed Martin signed a framework agreement with the Department of War to triple annual PAC-3 MSE production capacity from roughly 600 to 2,000 interceptors over seven years, and the government followed in April with a $4.7 billion contract to help fund that faster production pace.
That surge in demand traces in part to the missile’s use in combat. Lockheed Martin has said the PAC-3 MSE helped defend forces and infrastructure during Operation Epic Fury, the U.S. military campaign against Iran earlier this year. Seventeen partner nations, including the United States, Germany, Poland, Japan and Romania, have signed agreements to field the interceptor, and the Navy is separately working with Lockheed Martin to integrate the PAC-3 MSE into its Aegis Combat System for the first time.
GM Defense’s role adds to a supply chain Lockheed Martin has been expanding on multiple fronts. British manufacturer GKN Aerospace has built PAC-3 MSE launch tubes for decades and has also produced the interceptor’s mid-section and seeker housing components under a separate agreement dating to 2021. Lockheed Martin signed a similar memorandum of understanding with Germany’s Diehl Defence in October 2025 to explore expanding PAC-3 MSE production in Europe.

US clears way for $24.3 billion fighter jet sale to Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:53:17 UTC
03:53:17 KST

US clears way for $30.9 billion fighter jet sale to Saudi Arabia
WASHINGTON - The US Department of State said on Sept 17 it has approved the potential sale of Lockheed Martin’s F-35 Lightning II fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, as the kingdom is drawn deeper into war in the Middle East.
A sale would mark a significant policy shift from the US, potentially altering the balance of military power in the Middle East and testing Washington’s definition of maintaining its ally Israel’s “qualitative military edge.”
Saudi Arabia made a direct appeal for the jets in early 2025 to US President Donald Trump and has long been interested in Lockheed Martin’s fighter.
The estimated US$24.3 billion (S$30.9 billion) sale would include 48 of the military aircraft and 49 Pratt & Whitney engines along with communications equipment, spare parts and other support items, the State Department said.
Washington weighs weapons sales to the Middle East in a way that ensures Israel maintains a “qualitative military edge”, effectively guaranteeing that Israel gets more advanced US weapons than regional Arab states.
The F-35, built with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection, is considered the world’s most advanced fighter jet.
Israel has operated the aircraft for a decade, building multiple squadrons, and remains the only Middle Eastern country to possess the weapons system.
Saudi Arabia, the largest customer for US arms, has sought the fighter for years as it looks to modernise its air force and counter regional threats, particularly from Iran.
The kingdom’s renewed push for what would constitute two squadrons comes as the Trump administration has signalled openness to deepening defence cooperation with Riyadh.
The Saudi Air Force flies a mix of fighter aircraft including Boeing F-15s, European Tornados and Typhoons.
The F-35 issue has also been intertwined with broader diplomatic efforts.
The administration of former US President Joe Biden previously explored providing F-35s to Saudi Arabia as part of a comprehensive deal that would have included Riyadh normalising relations with Israel, though those efforts ultimately stalled.
Trump has made arms sales to Saudi Arabia a priority since returning to office.
In 2025, the United States agreed to sell the kingdom an arms package worth nearly US$142 billion, which the White House called “the largest defense cooperation agreement” Washington has ever done.
Congressional scrutiny could pose challenges to any F-35 sale.
Lawmakers previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh following the 2018 murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, and some members of Congress remain wary of deepening military cooperation with the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia is pursuing ambitious economic and military modernisation plans under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 agenda.
The kingdom has sought to diversify its defence partnerships in recent years while maintaining its decades-long security relationship with Washington. REUTERS

Poll tracks Zelensky's trust rating amid corruption investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:52:23 UTC
03:52:23 KST

A poll conducted immediately after recent investigations by Ukraine's independent anti-corruption agencies found that President Volodymyr Zelensky's trust rating stands at 54%, the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) reported on Sept. 17.
The survey was taken between Aug. 21 and Sept. 10, during an investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO). The large-scale corruption scandal implicated senior officials from the Presidential Office, including former deputy head Iryna Mudra.
According to the KIIS poll, 54% of Ukrainians said they trusted Zelensky, while 41% said they did not trust him. Among respondents who trusted the president, 18% said they trusted him "fully," while the other 36% reported trusting him "somewhat."
Of those who said they did not trust Zelensky, 25% reported that they did not trust him at all while 16% said they "tend not to trust him."
Zelensky's trust rating was generally higher among women, young adults, military personnel, students, and people from Ukraine's central, northern, eastern, and southern regions.
Trust in the president was generally lower among men, people aged 45-59, western Ukrainians, and residents of Kyiv.
read also
The ratings show virtually no change from the previous month's poll results (55% trust, 40% do not trust), before the latest corruption scandal was brought to light.
KIIS Executive Director Anton Hrushetskyi, however, noted that "the cumulative negative impact" on Zelensky's trust ratings from multiple major corruption investigations involving figures linked to the president "could ultimately prove irreversible."
Trust in Zelensky has skyrocketed during certain moments of national unity, but those ratings fall over time and ongoing anti-corruption probes "are only cementing a critical attitude" toward Zelensky's office, Hrushetskyi said.
"(W)hile Ukrainians maintain their trust in the President as the nation's leader during this brutal war, they also expect appropriate decisions and actions — particularly regarding the fight against corruption and the making of sound personnel appointments," Hrushetskyi said.
KIIS also noted that while about have of the survey was conducted after the recent investigation into former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, the results do not take into account the events of Sept. 14, when the disgraced official attempted to launched a retaliatory attack on NABU and SAPO.

US approves visas for Iranian leaders to attend UN summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:52:00 UTC
03:52:00 KST

The Trump administration has granted visas to senior Iranian officials, including the country's president and foreign minister, to attend next week's U.N. General Assembly high-level meetings in New York despite the ongoing war between Washington and Tehran.
The State Department said Thursday that it had approved visas for Iran's "core delegation," along with essential staffers to participate in the U.N. meetings. The core delegation includes President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, according to U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to visa privacy laws.
"Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend U.N. General Assembly High Level week. The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year," the statement said.
The move is unusual due to the more than six-month-long conflict between Iran and the United States and no sign that agreements to reopen the Strait of Hormuz or return to talks on Iran's nuclear program are close. It also comes as Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have stepped up attacks on Saudi infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea, another major maritime route in the region where impediments have helped drive a surge in global oil prices.
In addition, Iran remains the world's leading state sponsor of terrorism, according to the United States, which has imposed significant sanctions against the country and launched a new campaign in recent weeks aimed at severing "critical financial lifelines."
As the host country for the United Nations headquarters, the U.S. is generally limited in what it can do to prevent foreign leaders from coming to the General Assembly. However, it has in the past denied visas to - or discouraged applications from - leaders involved in active conflicts with the United States.
For last year's U.N. meetings of world leaders - which took place before the Iran war began on Feb. 28 but after the U.S. and Israel launched air strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025 - the State Department also approved a limited number of visas for Iranian diplomats but also imposed rigid restrictions on the delegation's movements.
Those included severe limitations on how far Iranian officials could travel in New York City from their U.N. mission and barred them from shopping at wholesale membership stores, such as Costco and Sam's Club.
The decision on the Iranian visas was announced just a day after the State Department denied visas to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and his delegation to come to the General Assembly.
"Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level week," the State Department said. "The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year."
The department accused the Palestinian Authority - which administers parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank - of trying to "internationalize" the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza by bringing cases to the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court as well as continuing to pay stipends to prisoners jailed in Israel for attacks on Israelis.
The Palestinian Authority condemned the move and called Israel's actions "the real threat to the two-state solution and prospects for peace." It also said it remained committed to long-stalled negotiations but defended its efforts to gain Palestinian recognition through international bodies and courts.
"Punitive measures and restrictions imposed on Palestinian officials do not contribute to advancing peace or combating violence," the authority's foreign ministry said in a statement. "Rather, they weaken the Palestinian partner committed to a political solution and encourage forces working to undermine the two-state solution and impose the reality of occupation, settlement and annexation by force."
The U.S. does not recognize the Palestinian Authority as a full member of the United Nations, although the General Assembly and certain U.N. agencies and bodies have done so.

Trump says he faces ‘big decision’ on whether to resume major attacks on Iran

Unknown Publisher

Rabia Iclal Turan
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
US President Donald Trump said Thursday that he is approaching a critical decision on whether to resume major military attacks against Iran.
“I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them or do I not? It's a big decision. Anything could happen with me,” Trump told Axios in an interview.
Trump is expected to meet next Tuesday with the leaders of six Gulf countries — Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Oman — on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York to discuss the next phase of the conflict.
“I want to find out where they are and how they are doing. We have been very protective of them," Trump said of the six countries.
Earlier, Trump said that Iran has reached out directly to Washington and wants to make a deal, as he described the current state of the war as nearing its conclusion.
Asked how he would describe what phase of the war the US is in, Trump said: "Hopefully we are towards the end of the war."
"They want to make a deal, and we'll see how that works out," he told reporters upon landing in the state of North Carolina on Wednesday evening.
The remarks came amid heightened tensions between Iran and the US over the Strait of Hormuz, despite a memorandum signed in June envisioning a deal to reopen the strategic waterway as a prelude to a wider peace agreement.
The US and Israel launched large-scale attacks on Iran in February, targeting government buildings, military sites, missile infrastructure, and air defenses, prompting Iranian missile and drone strikes against Israel and US bases across the region.
The conflict has since expanded across the region, with diplomatic efforts continuing to end the hostilities.

Labor pounces on migration problems, but leaves massive wedge for critics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:48:00 UTC
03:48:00 KST

analysis
Tony Burke delivers overdue migration policy, but is it sturdy enough to withstand critics?
Tony Burke was late to the National Press Club to announce the government's migration policy on Thursday.
Six weeks late, to be precise.
After the embarrassment of having to abort his earlier press club appearance, followed by senior ministers faffing around over the details, and unsuccessful negotiations between government and opposition, Burke produced a package that, on his own admission, did not include everything he'd wanted.
It attacks some problems. But the government will be wedged between those who think the changes don't go far enough and critics who believe they're draconian.
The government will stop the entry of most overseas students' families, which will make life harder for some and, presumably, discourage others from coming at all. Universities will be concerned.
Working holiday-makers wanting to stay two or three years will face the luck of the draw, under a new ballot system.
Only 5,000 will get a third year, compared to 31,000 last year. Some farmers and businesses in regional areas looking for labour will be worried.
A proposed "No Further Stay" condition for visitor visas is a blunt instrument, but it aims to address a major loophole being exploited.
Burke candidly anticipated he'll come under attack for toughening compliance measures, with greater use of detention as the government tries to deport overstayers.
But again, a substantial challenge remains in a system where enforcement has become too loose.
Delicate balance on numbers
The measures won't satisfy those who desire a much smaller migration program.
They are about achieving the budget target of 225,000 Net Overseas Migration (NOM) by 2027–28, not going lower.
Voters wanting a substantially bigger squeeze on total intake will still look to One Nation, or wait for the Coalition, which is still wrestling with its own alternative.
In terms of numbers, it's a delicate balance. As Burke told parliament: "If you make cuts too deep, too hard in the immigration system, you trash the Australian economy."
The government's changes to prioritise skilled workers in vital areas such as health care and construction will be well received. This should have been done years ago.
Equally, the crackdown on "rogue" migration agents is long overdue.
Burke would have liked to act against those he called "disingenuous protection claims" — people who, coming to the end of their visa hopping, launch a protection claim that might give them "up to nine years working in Australia" while their appeals drag on.
"To give a sense of the gravity of this, if we took the people who apply from countries where more than 85 per cent of the applications fail, that constitutes 80 per cent of our caseload. This is an issue I'd like to be able to deal with."
But that needs legislation, and no agreement was reached in two recent meetings between Anthony Albanese and Angus Taylor.
With One Nation effectively "owning" the immigration issue on the right these days, the opposition would like to move on from it, but eventually felt it could not afford to give too much ground to Labor.
One wonders, however, if the government should not have just included the measure to deal with bogus claims, to see whether the opposition might give in under parliamentary pressure.
Loading
Untidy handling from Burke
Burke's belated appearance came days after One Nation did its pre-emption act, with its own policy launched on Monday — albeit a plan that has been blasted by opponents, stakeholders and many experts.
Inside and outside Labor, Burke's untidy handling of what is a central issue has had some people scratching their heads.
When he was installed in the home affairs portfolio, replacing Clare O'Neil, who'd struggled in the job, Burke was widely seen as both competent and the classic "safe pair of hands".
After all, he's one of the elite group competing to lead Labor eventually.
Burke's mistake was getting ahead of his colleagues by lining up the press club before the policy process had been finalised.
When the draft went to senior ministers, they had issues.
Burke was reluctant to cancel his speech, which made the last-minute pull-out look worse.
Reports of a big split between Burke and Treasurer Jim Chalmers over the policy were overblown; indeed, Chalmers tried to facilitate Burke's attempt to meet his initial timetable.
But Chalmers's general stance on immigration is very forward-leaning, putting him close to that of South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas, who recently warned about "the prospect of mainstream politics entering a political race to the bottom for who can cut migration numbers the most".
The migration policy changes proposed by the various parties will have big fallouts for stakeholders and the economy. But many discontented voters may just make their judgements on the bottom line numbers.
It doesn't take the ubiquitous opinion polls to tell us the electorate is in a very bad mood, with angst about immigration just one strand in this.
Within Labor they talk about the mid-term blues. They've been in this territory before, of course — remember, quite close to the last election, the government's very future appeared at possible risk. Now it has a huge majority to protect it.
On the other hand, in previous difficult times, One Nation hadn't become the mini-monster now confronting both conservative and Labor parties.
On Monday the government will release the latest Intergenerational Report, which charts the economic and budgetary challenges for the coming four decades.
These are formidable, especially for a country with fundamental problems, notably a seeming inability to boost productivity and the pressures of an aging population.
The challenges of the future 40 years will seem theoretical to many people, given how quickly things change.
Forty years ago, the power of social media and AI, which obsess us now, was well over the horizon.
What won't pass people by is another rise in interest rates, at present considered a high prospect when the Reserve Bank meets at the end of this month.
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

Latvia buys Morana howitzers, passing on Sweden’s Archer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:47:22 UTC
03:47:22 KST

- Latvia's government chose the Czech-made Morana wheeled howitzer over Sweden's Archer system for its National Armed Forces on Sept. 15, 2026.
- The decision followed concerns that fielding the Archer would cost more and take longer than Latvia's current defense budget and plans allow.
Latvia’s government decided on Sept. 15 to buy Czech-made 155mm wheeled howitzers for the National Armed Forces, choosing the Morana system from Excalibur Army after Sweden’s competing Archer howitzer proved too costly and slow to deliver under the country’s current defense budget.
The Cabinet of Ministers based its decision on the cost of the offers, delivery timelines, operational capability and how much of the work would involve Latvian industry. The howitzers will expand the National Armed Forces’ indirect fire support units, which the Ministry of Defence said will substantially strengthen the country’s deterrence and defense capability.
Latvia’s Ministry of Defence opened market research into 155mm wheeled artillery systems in May 2024. After reviewing initial offers, it continued talks with two companies: Sweden’s BAE Systems Bofors, which makes the Archer system, and the Czech Republic’s Excalibur Army, which builds the Morana. Latvia signed a letter of intent with Sweden in June 2025, committing to eventually negotiate a contract for the Archer.
That plan changed as the process continued. The ministry concluded that fielding the Archer would require more financial resources than the defense sector currently has available, and its delivery timelines ran longer than Latvia’s approved defense plans could accommodate. Excalibur Army, meanwhile, offered what the ministry called an operationally equivalent system on better price and delivery terms, letting the National Armed Forces build up its artillery capability considerably faster. The Czech offer also builds local industry participation directly into the contract, an advantage the Swedish proposal did not match.
The Morana is a 155mm, 52-caliber howitzer mounted on a Tatra Force 8×8 truck chassis, built by Excalibur Army as a successor to the Czechoslovak-era DANA gun family. It uses an automated loading system that Excalibur Army says can fire six rounds in the first minute and five rounds per minute in sustained fire, with a maximum range of roughly 41.5 km (26 miles) using extended-range ammunition. Its three- to four-person crew works from an armored cab rated to STANAG 4569 Level 2 protection, and the system carries a 12.7mm remote weapon station for self-defense. A U.S. Army delegation visited Excalibur Army’s production site in the Czech Republic in April to evaluate the Morana as a potential contender for the U.S. Army’s own wheeled howitzer program, alongside the French CAESAR and Swedish Archer.
Latvia’s decision does not end its defense relationship with Sweden. The Ministry of Defence said Sweden remains one of Latvia’s strategic defense partners, pointing to a defense cooperation roadmap the two countries signed in January 2026 covering joint air, sea and land activities, Swedish military participation in NATO’s multinational brigade in Latvia, joint exercises and further capability development. Latvia’s National Armed Forces have also ordered Saab Dynamics’ RBS 70 NG short-range air defense system from Sweden, and the Latvian Air Force received Saab’s Giraffe 1X airspace surveillance radar in late 2025.

The situation in Russian-occupied Oleshky was dire. Now it's 'hell'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:47:20 UTC
03:47:20 KST

The situation in Russian-occupied Oleshky was dire. Now it's 'hell'
The aerial view of Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in Kherson Oblast, Ukraine in a photo published on Sept.16, 2026. (Oleshky Lubinets / Telegram)
Residents in Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast face an escalating humanitarian crisis, as constant Russian drone attacks and artillery shelling have made it impossible to deliver essential food and medicine supplies or evacuate civilians by road.
"These people need to be saved," Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, said on Sept. 16, adding that residents are desperate to escape "from this hell."
"People are driven to despair and are simply walking along mined roads (to escape)," an Oleshky resident — whose identity is being withheld for security reasons — told the Kyiv Independent.
Of the city's prewar population of about 24,000, about 2,000 people remain in Oleshky, including about 50 children, Tetiana Hasanenko, exiled head of the Ukrainian Oleshky City Military Administration, told the Kyiv Independent.
This spring, amid a deteriorating humanitarian situation, volunteers could still evacuate civilians from the city despite the risks, the Kyiv Independent reported. Now, several months later, volunteers say even those evacuation efforts are no longer possible, as Russia refuses to cooperate and leaves Ukrainian civilians trapped in the occupied city, facing starvation.
Russian troops continue to use towns and villages on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Kherson Oblast to launch attacks across the river, including on Kherson, which Ukrainian forces liberated in November 2022. Oleshky is an occupied front-line city on the eastern bank, where civilians live amid a Russian military presence and attacks from both Ukrainian and Russian forces.
Ukraine had prepared a humanitarian evacuation mission for Oleshky and approved a list of civilians who needed to leave, according to Lubinets. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) had also expressed readiness to participate, while Ukrainian forces had been preparing to ensure a ceasefire during the mission, he said.
But Russia has not confirmed its readiness to proceed, Lubinets said. Ukraine continues to press Russia to allow the evacuation and remains in contact with the ICRC and other international organizations, he added.
Hasanenko told the Kyiv Independent that "Russia remains silent" about the situation.
At first, Russian authorities pretended not to notice the disaster and tried to portray Oleshky as a functioning city, staging visits and taking photographs there this spring, Hasanenko said.
But as the humanitarian situation has become impossible to conceal, those visits have stopped, she added.
read also
No food
The Oleshky resident told the Kyiv Independent that the food situation has been deteriorating for months.
"By New Year's, there were already shortages of eggs, and we barely managed to buy any apples. Then we didn't see any of that stuff again until spring. When we did, it was at astronomical prices," the resident said.
"Suddenly, bread deliveries stopped," they added. "I'm having tea with honey. And that's all."
According to Hasanenko, the last successful food delivery to the city was on May 26.
"There is absolutely no meat, flour, oil, butter, ready-made bread, and other basic products in the city," she said. Some local residents have posted photographs online of bread preserved in jars.
There were two further attempts to bring supplies into Oleshky, Hasanenko said. On June 2, Russian drones attacked vehicles carrying food, killing two drivers and injuring others. On Sept. 1, Russian forces cut short another attempt to deliver food to the city when they attacked five vehicles with drones.
Hasanenko said civilians in Oleshky were trying to exchange food with one another, but the Oleshky resident told the Kyiv Independent that "there's absolutely nothing to buy, and there's not even the option of bartering."
Ukraine's Holodomor Museum, dedicated to preserving the memory of the 4.5 million Ukrainians starved to death by Joseph Stalin from 1932-1933, on Sept. 16 issued a statement highlighting "famine" as "among the most severe problems" in Oleshky and the surrounding area.
"We are convinced that silence around a mass humanitarian crisis is unacceptable, and we call on the international community not to ignore the situation in Oleshky," it said.
read also
Medical care
The local hospital, left without basic medical supplies, electricity, or running water, is also struggling to operate, Hasanenko said. Four doctors, all elderly former hospital staff, continue to work there, she said.
"But there are absolutely no medical supplies. The only thing they can do is … to stop the bleeding. There are no medicines," Hasanenko said.
Since Russia destroyed the nearby Kakhovka Dam in 2023, the hospital has had to rely on generators for electricity, but fuel supplies have also become increasingly difficult to obtain, according to Hasanenko.
She said ambulances have not been operating in the city for years because Russian drone attacks have made it too dangerous.
Evacuation
May 26 was the last time people were evacuated from Oleshky, and nobody has entered the city since, according to Hasanenko.
In recent weeks, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky to the neighboring village of Radensk alone or in pairs, on roads mined by Russian forces.
"They risk being blown up by a land mine or struck by a drone, but they go anyway, because staying in Oleshky is even worse for them," Lubinets said.
Stefan Vorontsov, a volunteer coordinator with the Humanity NGO, which helps evacuate civilians from occupied territories, said the walk takes five to six hours under the constant threat of Russian air attacks.
"Four or five months ago, it was still possible to leave by car. Now the only option is to walk."
Once people reach Radensk, volunteers can pick them up and help them travel farther, he said. Volunteers helped a family leave the area about a week ago, according to Vorontsov.
"Some are leaving, while others have to return (after picking up supplies) because they have children or grandchildren at home, or relatives with limited mobility," the Oleshky resident said.
Crisis in surrounding settlements
The crisis is not confined to Oleshky itself. The worsening humanitarian situation is spreading across the surrounding settlements, leaving more civilians trapped in critical conditions.
"Oleshky is not the only place where there is hunger," Vorontsov said. "Ukrainian villages around it — Hola Prystan, Radensk — the geography of the problem is getting bigger."
The Oleshky community includes 13 settlements, five of which have been completely destroyed, according to Hasanenko. While settlements such as Solomky, Pidlisne, and Kozachi Laheri have suffered extensive destruction, some civilians still live there.
In other villages such as Radensk, vehicles can either no longer reach people, or have to make a "quite risky" journey navigating the threat from mines and drones, Vorontsov said.
"I don't even remember what it's like to have cars driving on the roads anymore," the Oleshky resident said.
Lubinets gave a broader estimate on Sept. 16, saying more than 6,000 people may remain in Oleshky and the surrounding area, including about 200 children. His office said it had verified 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.
"People's moods are very panicked and depressed," Hasanenko said.
Residents are increasingly worried about how they would survive the winter without regular food deliveries, medicine, electricity, or reliable transport, she added.
"They understand that the summer has passed and no evacuation has been organized."

Business and miners back Labor's migration policies, but farmers angry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:44:39 UTC
03:44:39 KST

Business groups and miners welcome Labor's migration policies, but farmers angry
Minister for Immigration Tony Burke announced Labor's much-anticipated migration policy reforms on Thursday.
He said Labor wanted to push net overseas migration (NOM) down to 225,000 people a year, from 292,000 where it currently sat.
He also wants to tighten visa rules for international students and backpackers, and to increase efforts to remove visa overstayers from the country.
His announcement came days after One Nation unveiled plans to push NOM into negative territory for three years before imposing an annual cap of 130,000, and as the Coalition was finalising plans for a policy expected to pursue NOM of between 150,000 and 170,000 people.
"We are now walking straight into an argument," Mr Burke declared on Thursday.
"We have people who will be going to the next election effectively arguing that in regional areas you'll have large-scale hospital closures and doctors that you just can't find.
"It means a whole lot of aged care just won't be available for elderly relatives, if they were to implement the sorts of numbers they're talking about."
But while the mining industry has welcomed Labor's policy announcement, farmers are furious, and the hospitality industry is not happy.
What is Labor's policy?
Labor plans to introduce a ballot system for the Working Holiday Maker program, and to set processing times for applications for the program to three months.
It wants to crack down on rogue migration agents.
It wants to introduce a No Further Stay condition to all visitor visas to ensure that they are only used by genuine visitors and not as a pathway to extending a stay in Australia.
And it wants to improve the integrity of student visas by stopping visa hopping, among other measures.
Andrew McKellar, the chief executive of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI), said the policy package was a "material toughening" of the migration system, but it could still be improved.
"On balance, I think it's a fairly reasonable plan that's been put forward," he told The Business.
"It certainly doesn't do significant damage to the economy, but it does leave some gaps.
"If you compare what we've seen in some of the other proposals that are around, you know, One Nation's plan was put out earlier this week, that involved very deep cuts.
"It would plunge the Australian economy into a deep recession, and it would also curtail the long-term growth potential of the economy. That would be bad for business.
"I think what we're seeing here is something that is steady, responsible."
Mr McKellar said the overall level of migration under Labor's plan would also be reduced, "which is something that is acknowledged the public has been calling for".
"I hope this can restore some confidence in the system going forward," he said.
What is Labor trying to achieve?
Labor has announced its policy at a time when concerns have been growing about high rates of immigration and rapid population growth.
But on Thursday, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) released new data showing that the post-COVID shock to Australia's population had largely receded.
The data showed that Australia's population was now growing more slowly than in the years before the pandemic.
The data also showed that the "natural increase" in Australia's population (births minus deaths) has been slowing down significantly in recent years.
On a rolling annual basis, natural increase is close to its lowest level on record.
So Australia's overall population growth is being kept afloat by net overseas migration, but net overseas migration is also still falling from its post-COVID peak.
However, Mr Burke said he still wanted to see net overseas migration continue to decline from its current rate of about 292,130 people to 225,000 a year by 2028.
If one assumes that the natural increase in Australia's population remains about 100,000 people a year, Labor's lower NOM target will therefore push overall population growth down to about 325,000 a year.
The last time Australia's population grew by that little was in 2011 (excluding the chaotic COVID-19 period).
In the past 12 months, Australia's population grew by 392,728 people, which is far fewer than in 2008 (459,504 people), and fewer than in 2012 (405,826 people) and 2017 (407,984 people).
Farmers, hospitality industry angry
Labor's new migration policy has upset farmers and the hospitality and tourism industries. They say the political focus on population growth is leading to damaging policies.
James Goodwin, Accommodation Australia's chief executive, said the hotel industry needed migration due to chronic workforce shortages and this would make things worse.
"What's lost in all this talk about migration numbers is that fundamentally Australia as a nation has a huge workforce challenge here,"
"It will now be harder for hotels to access the workers we need and the changes will increase competition in an already tight labour market."
The Australian Hotels Association (AHA) thinks Labor's plan to restrict Working Holiday Makers will have unintended consequences.
"Targeting working holiday makers makes no logical sense. They are a motivated and mobile workforce who help fill seasonal work, especially in the regions," AHA chief executive Stephen Ferguson said.
The National Farmers Federation (NFF) warned the Albanese government was putting Australia's food security, regional economies and farm safety at risk.
"If the government wants to end rorts, then it should target the rorts," NFF president Hamish McIntyre said.
"It should not punish the farmers doing the right thing or the regional communities that depend on a workforce pathway that has helped feed this country for decades."
Andrew McKellar, ACCI's chief executive, agreed that tourism, hospitality, accommodation, and restaurants and cafes were a "critical miss" in the government's migration policies and those industries would suffer.
Mining and housing industries welcome changes
But the Minerals Council of Australia (MCA) has warmly welcomed the government's decision to give greater priority to skilled resource workers in its new migration system.
"The government's plan makes sense," MCA chief executive Tania Constable said on Thursday.
"The MCA raised serious concerns in August about changes introduced in July that pushed many skilled applicants outside Australia further down the visa processing queue.
"Those changes risked making it harder for mining companies to bring in highly specialised workers who are in short supply in Australia, despite skilled migrants making up just 1.24 per cent of the minerals workforce.
"Today's announcement shows the government has heard those concerns.
"The real measure of these changes will be whether an Australian mining company looking for an engineer, geologist, metallurgist or other critical specialist can actually get that person here faster."
The Housing Industry Association (HIA) also welcomed Labor's changes, saying they would provide a "balanced, long-term direction for Australia's migration system."
"Of particular importance to the residential building industry is the recognition that skilled tradespeople are essential to increasing Australia's housing supply," HIA chief economist Tim Reardon said.
"If these reforms successfully combine greater recognition of trade qualifications, priority visa processing for construction workers and more efficient recognition of overseas skills, they represent a significant improvement in Australia's approach to building the construction workforce.
"These policies can work to mitigate the boom-to-bust cycles that the building industry has endured over recent years."

The AI Slowdown Debate Crashed Salesforce's Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:42:25 UTC
03:42:25 KST

Decked out in purple and plaid, Gwen Stefani belted her 2002 single “Underneath It All” to a packed conference center in San Francisco on Tuesday morning—but she was just the warm-up. At the end of her performance, Stefani shouted “Dreamforce! Let’s go!” into a checkered microphone before Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff strode into the spotlight. Dreamforce is billed as the world’s largest enterprise software conference but feels more like attending a megachurch—especially this year.
Benioff roamed the audience while delivering his Dreamforce sermon, followed by a teleoperated camera on wheels that beamed his face to screens hanging from the cavernous room’s ceiling. Within minutes, he ordered up a graph of Salesforce’s annual revenue, which the company projects will top $46 billion in 2027, thanks in part to demand for its AI-powered products. The audience applauded. But hanging over the whole event was a dark question: Is artificial intelligence really worth risking all our lives for?
Between flashy software demonstrations of agents building dashboards, conference-goers watched Silicon Valley leaders debate whether the AI industry should keep barreling ahead or if the government needs to slow AI progress to prevent catastrophic risks stemming from the technology.
Last week, AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and publicly warned that companies racing toward self-improving AI systems were “gambling with our lives.” By the weekend, other Anthropic employees were echoing his concerns, and CEO Dario Amodei was urging world leaders to help “pace the frontier” of AI development. Other AI CEOs then began endorsing the idea, including Amodei’s greatest rival, OpenAI’s Sam Altman.
But not everyone is on board with the idea. David Sacks, a White House AI adviser, brushed off Amodei’s suggestions and fears of AI doom as “just another bid for regulatory capture.” President Trump went further this week, calling fears about existential AI risk “a hoax.” Despite the challenging political environment, Congress is trying to capitalize on the moment and push ahead with legislation to regulate the AI industry.
Onstage, 6-foot-5 Benioff towered over Anthropic’s CEO, vigorously shaking Amodei’s hand just before asking for his latest assessment of AI progress. While this is undoubtedly Benioff’s show, Anthropic has become a critical partner helping usher Salesforce into the AI era.
“Let’s say you're running a car company, and another car company, not yours, they have some kind of safety incident,” Amodei said, making a not-so-subtle reference to OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident. “Obviously, it's very tempting to attack your competitor,” Amodei added, but the more responsible move is to “organize the rest of the industry and say, what can we do to set standards for everyone?”
But the Anthropic CEO was careful to note that pacing the frontier doesn’t mean “freezing the technology in place,” and of course, he took a moment to plug Claude’s integration with Salesforce.
Moments after Amodei exited, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang appeared and began downplaying the concerns Anthropic has raised. AI safety effectively amounts to an “engineering problem,” Huang argued, and the companies building AI can simply police themselves.
“We don't need any new laws, we don't need any new regulation,” Huang told Dreamforce attendees. “You run as fast as you can, but if you feel that at any given point in time, the company is out of control or the products are not going to be safe, you take a pause.”
The debate feels a bit heavy for Dreamforce, but then again, maybe this is the perfect venue for it. As tech executives pitched their various enterprise AI tools, I slipped out of the room, passing the plush mascots and vaguely Hawaiian decorations, to take a call from Sayash Kapoor, an incoming computer science professor at UC Berkeley.
Kapoor and Princeton professor Arvind Narayanan are coauthors of the book AI Snake Oil and write a Substack together called AI as Normal Technology. The pair are known for cutting through AI marketing hype while not dismissing the technology’s potential. This week, they published one of their longest essays yet, which tries to make sense of “loss-of-control incidents,” referring to events such as OpenAI accidentally letting its agents hack into Hugging Face.
“Part of what we were trying to do in this essay is to move past this false dichotomy to bridge the ground between AI safety and cybersecurity,” says Kapoor. “If you think AI will soon become superintelligent and evade any controls we can put in front of them, of course, alignment seems more important. On the other hand, if you think AI companies have been negligent and avoided taking bog-standard cybersecurity steps, then it’s natural to think that control is what we need to intervene on. I think both of these views have some element of truth in them.”
In the wake of the Hugging Face saga, Kapoor says he was surprised to learn how few security precautions OpenAI had taken. AI companies need to reckon with their “lack of organizational maturity,” he argues, and accept that loss-of-control incidents won’t be solved by a single breakthrough in security or alignment. He adds that the incident convinced him that policymakers should make AI labs liable for the harms their technology causes.
“The consequences for OpenAI for the Hugging Face hack were basically close to zero. The company was able to largely proceed as is,” says Kapoor. “If you imagine this level of accident in any other industry, you would have seen a monthslong internal investigation, people would have been fired or gone to jail; OpenAI would have had to pay millions of dollars in fines.”
Kapoor doesn’t wholly endorse Amodei’s proposal to pace the frontier, but he agrees with parts of it. He thinks AI labs need better governance to break out of their “move fast and break things” attitude and that they should let independent evaluators assess their AI safety and security practices. He and Narayanan write that more alignment work is certainly needed but that the real crisis today is more narrowly about cybersecurity.
Others think the Hugging Face incident revealed that AI labs have a true alignment crisis on their hands, which would present a harder problem to solve. In recent weeks, independent researchers have discovered more examples in which swarms of OpenAI’s agents hacked into third-party services. Sydney Von Arx, CEO of AI safety nonprofit Nightingale, helped uncover two of them that targeted a German-language wiki and the software service RubyGems.
“These incidents clearly show that many current AIs are egregiously misaligned,” Von Arx tells WIRED. “Yes, the companies need to be able to control their models so they can’t launch cyberattacks even if they’re misaligned. But we also shouldn’t be building powerful AIs that autonomously try to break out and commit cyberattacks in the first place.”
After the interviews, I raced downstairs to try to get in line for Benioff’s fireside chat with Altman. OpenAI’s CEO told the audience that “the world is right to be afraid” of AI companies. But by the end of the conversation, Altman said he’s hopeful that OpenAI can build better products in its second decade as a company.
“This is like we went to go get fire from the gods. This is a crazy thing that has just happened in the world,” said Altman, referring to AI technology. He hopes that OpenAI can “figure out how to give that value to people in a way that is most useful to them, figure out a way to empower every person on Earth—every enterprise on Earth—with this flood of capability.”
Huang’s case for self-policing depends on AI companies not only knowing when it’s time to pause but also having the self-restraint required to actually do so. It’s not clear if they do. Mere days after warning the world that AI labs urgently need to slow down, the same CEOs were at the biggest enterprise software conference pitching their latest products. While they touched upon concerns about AI doom, they were mainly there to ensure that the money keeps flowing.
This is an edition of Maxwell Zeff’s Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

North Korea’s nuclear tests have turned this mountain into an earthquake hot spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:41:54 UTC
03:41:54 KST

North Korea’s Mount Mantap is being rocked by earthquakes—and the reason appears to be the pariah state’s nuclear tests.
It’s been almost 10 years since North Korea last conducted an underground thermonuclear test at the mountain, which is also known as Mantapsan—yet the geology of the site appears to have been critically altered by intense explosions, according to a new study based in part on photographs taken space.
“Repeated underground nuclear tests [have] progressively disturbed and damaged the surrounding rock and changed the stresses acting on pre-existing faults,” says seismologist and geophysicist Kwang-Hee Kim of South Korea’s Pusan National University. The most recent nuclear test, in 2017, caused the most damage—and after some seismic faults on the mountain were disturbed, it started a domino effect, he says.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Kim is a co-author of the study, published 17 September in Science, which details Mount Mantap’s ongoing seismic activity. Almost 1,400 earthquakes have occurred there between 2008 and 2025, and they have increased in frequency and magnitude since September 3, 2017—the date of the last known nuclear test there. It had an estimated yield equivalent to between 100 and 250 kilotons of TNT—or up to 20 times as much energy as the blast that leveled Hiroshima in 1945.
It’s normal for underground tests to spawn local earthquakes in the weeks that follow as the disturbed ground subsides. But an unusual earthquake on Mount Mantap a few minutes after the 2017 test raised experts’ concerns, and the new study reveals a fresh worry: “The phenomena they’ve identified and documented is a bit surprising,” says Columbia University seismologist Paul Richards, who wasn’t involved in the research. The situation is “potentially dangerous,” he says: “Will it lead to even bigger earthquakes?”
Mount Mantap is an archetypal “tired mountain”—a Cold War term for a nuclear test site where the ground is so fractured by massive underground explosions that it becomes useless and can no longer trap radioactive gases from the blasts. The 2017 thermonuclear test effectively collapsed the top of Mount Mantap. The damage means there are no known plans to do future tests beneath the peak itself, but others may still be conducted at different underground sites at the Punggye-ri test complex surrounding the mountain.
North Korea gives few details about the Punggye-ri complex, and the new study is based mainly on data from seismographs in China and South Korea and satellite photographs of the terrain. Kim and his co-authors warn that the mountain’s persistent earthquakes will affect international monitoring efforts for genuine nuclear explosions: “Seismicity occurring years after detonation may complicate attribution and blur distinctions between explosion-related and tectonic events,” they write.

Minister says detaining visa overstayers will not lead to ICE-style raids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:41:21 UTC
03:41:21 KST

Minister says detaining visa overstayers will not lead to ICE-style raids
In short:
The home affairs minister has assured Australians that a push to detain visa overstayers will not lead to ICE-style immigration raids.
Immigration experts say detaining visa overstayers was an ordinary part of the immigration system until 2015, when facilities were prioritised for criminals awaiting deportation.
What's next?
An expanded Border Force team of 100 officials and 250 new beds will work to detain overstayers or encourage them to leave.
A 100-strong Border Force team being established to remove 77,000 visa overstayers will not bring ICE-style immigration raids seen in the United States to Australia, the home affairs minister has assured.
Tens of thousands of visa overstayers have remained in Australia in part because they are not being detained, and so there is little incentive to leave, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke explained at a National Press Club address yesterday.
In an effort to encourage people to leave of their own accord, the government will create 250 beds where overstayers can be held for deportation, and investigate whether it can repurpose buildings like the former quarantine facility in Melbourne as detention centres.
Mr Burke said when faced with the choice between detention and leaving of their own accord, most visa overstayers would leave.
"Before 2015, we had a routine process in Australia for overstayers where, when people had overstayed a visa, we would bring people in to detention centres … and within a few weeks they would organise their own flight and leave," Mr Burke said.
"And effectively that didn't just affect them, it had a behavioural impact where a whole lot of other people who were overstaying thought, 'Yeah, yeah, it's better that I just get on a plane and leave.'
"Effectively, what we are going back to doing is simply being able to make sure that if you overstay, you will not be able to say, 'Well there's no consequences, as if they're ever going to make sure that I leave.'
"This is not the sort of operation that some people have seen on TV happening in other countries."
Despite his reassurance, the Greens were quick to claim the government's expansion of Australia's immigration detention network was a "reheating" of former prime minister Tony Abbott's immigration policies.
"Labor's new immigration jails will be run by the same exploitative US private prison multinational that is already abusing people's rights in immigration detention here," Greens senator David Shoebridge said.
"If the minister doesn't want these policies to be compared to ICE, he should not behave like ICE," he said.
Since returning to the White House, US President Donald Trump has relaxed the qualifications required for people to join the Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency, boosted its funding, expanded the country's detention centre network and shifted to more aggressive tactics to detain people, including removing restrictions on enforcement at schools, churches and in courthouses.
The changes have raised human rights concerns, accusations of racial profiling in ICE operations, and high-profile cases of fatal shootings by ICE officers.
Migration Institute of Australia chief executive Peter van Vliet said resourcing Border Force to detain visa overstayers would not lead to ICE-style tactics.
"I think that's a complete overstatement of what's been planned," Mr van Vliet said.
"We had this arrangement in place before 2015. It was a fairly soft approach … it was fairly carefully targeted, it was uncontroversial.
"It's just something that has basically stopped."
Detention centres filled after mandatory visa cancellations of criminals
Mr van Vliet said since 2015, detention centres had lost the capacity to hold visa overstayers, after laws passed by the former Abbott government forced the mandatory cancellation of visas of some criminals.
The members of that cohort have continued to occupy Australian detention centres as they have lodged appeals to their removal, going through legal processes that can sometimes take years to resolve.
The change in how detention centres were used also limited options to detain non-criminal "unlawful non-citizens" because of the safety risk of holding them in the same facilities as violent criminals.
"It flooded the detention centres in Australia with people who have been convicted of a crime and come out of jail after serving a sentence, and the whole nature of immigration detention changed, there was simply no more beds for visa overstayers," he said.
"The government has not been paying an awful lot of attention to [visa overstayers] until today."
According to the most recent Home Affairs migration trends report, there were 6,646 departures in the 2024-25 financial year, with about half being voluntary returns and half being removals after detention.
A little over a third had arrived on a visitor visa, while about 20 per cent had arrived on a student visa.
And that cohort has slowly grown since 2016 from about 64,000 visa overstayers to more than 77,000 today.
Mr Burke said the additional migration enforcement staff and separate facilities for overstayers would restore the capacity to detain overstayers, and ultimately encourage others to leave.
Former Immigration Department deputy secretary Abul Rizvi said he doubted the full cohort of 77,000 overstayers could be removed based on today's announcements, though he expected it could help to remove or cause the departure of another 5,000 to 10,000 people a year.
But he said the changes were sensible, and that the drop-off in compliance activity after 2015 had been a "mistake".
"To return to the policy that existed before 2015 is a good thing," Mr Rizvi said.
He added that those pre-2015 operations were not conducted at all like ICE operations, with officers visiting in "white shirts, with ties, a name badge and no gun", and only entered a workplace by invitation or with a warrant.
"They were a very different operation to what we see in the United States," he said.
Mr van Vliet said he was confident that enforcement would not be "gangs of men in four-wheel-drives going after people who might look a bit different".
"It would be three or four officers who would visit somebody and say, 'Look, your visa has run out. You either need to make arrangements to go home or we will detain you.' A sort of soft approach," he said.
"It's nothing like some of the abusive examples we have seen in other countries, where are people are sort of hauled off the street … As long as human rights are respected it is fine.
"Getting some sort of immigration compliance system back into the mix for visa overstayers, who don't have protection claims, they're not in danger going home, they just overstayed their visa and it is time for them to return to their country of origin, it's perfectly reasonable that you have a little bit of a stick to get them to move on."
In a statement, the Human Rights Law Centre said the changes would punish workers vulnerable to exploitation because they would make undocumented workers less likely to speak up.
"Undocumented migrants who have been exploited at work should be protected to take action against their employers. Instead of needlessly expanding the punitive immigration detention network, the Albanese government should invest in protections for migrant workers to ensure that all workers have safety and dignity at work," legal director Sanmati Verma said.
Visa overstayers not the key cohort keeping 'NOM' high
Net overseas migration is falling, with 292,000 net arrivals over the year to March 2026, but that remains well above the federal government's target of 225,000 net arrivals by 2028.
Yesterday, Mr Burke said he already had the tools to reach that target, vowing it would be met even without the changes he announced.
But the home affairs minister said it would allow him to more precisely target the mix of people coming and going from Australia to minimise economic pain caused by migration cuts.
While fewer people overall have been arriving in Australia, the rate of people leaving has remained flat.
While there is a cohort of about 77,000 people without a valid visa remaining in Australia, a much larger number of people have remained in Australia on bridging visas; temporary visas that allow people to remain in Australia lawfully while their visa applications or appeals against decisions are resolved.
The number of people on bridging visas has more than doubled from 176,000 three years ago to more than 400,000 today, many of those being international students challenging a decision to refuse a new visa application they have lodged.
Mr Burke said the government would clamp down on "visa hopping" where people exploited the visa system and appeals process to remain in Australia, even when they did not have relevant qualifications to be able to stay.
A "No Further Stays" provision would prevent people arriving on tourist visas and then lodging new applications, while international students would have to advance their qualifications when seeking a new study visa, closing off the option for people to jump course to course using low-quality institutions in order to remain in the country.
Mr Burke said he would need to legislate in order to curb the significant caseload of people making "disingenuous" asylum claims in order to extend their stay in Australia.
He said the government wanted the Coalition's buy-in on legislative changes before introducing them, and hoped it would continue negotiations with the government.

At least 26 killed in South Sudan tribal clashes
JUBA, Sept 17 - At least 26 people have been killed and 82 others injured in Abyei town on the border between South Sudan and Sudan after clashes between two rival tribes, the United Nations said in a statement on Thursday.
• Abyei is an oil-rich area that is jointly administered by South Sudan and Sudan, which have both staked claims to it following South Sudan's independence in 2011.
• The clashes took place at the Amiet Common Market in Abyei town and involved members of Ngok Dinka and Misseriya tribes and were sparked by the initial killing of two men from both tribes on Monday and Tuesday.
• The initial killings of the two men escalated tensions between the two communities around the market, a key economic hub in the area, the United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei said in the statement.
• "Following the deadly violence, UNISFA immediately reinforced its security presence in and around the market and deployed additional forces to de-escalate the situation," the agency said.
• The two tribes are long-time rivals and similar deadly clashes have broken out in the past over disputes involving grazing lands and watering points for their animals.
• South Sudan has been mostly at peace since a 2018 agreement ended a five-year conflict during which thousands of people were killed. Elections, the first since the country's independence, are due to be held in December. REUTERS

Alleged Trickbot hacker wanted by Germany served as adviser to deputy chair of Russia’s State Duma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:36:44 UTC
03:36:44 KST

Vitaly Kovalev, who is wanted by German authorities as the alleged founder and leader of Trickbot, one of the largest cybercriminal groups in the world, worked as an adviser to Russian State Duma Deputy Speaker Vladislav Davankov and ran for the State Duma on the New People party’s ticket. The GangExposed project first drew attention to the connection between Kovalev and Davankov.
Davankov himself wrote in August 2025 that Kovalev had been his adviser for “more than a year,” describing him as a supporter of New People, an entrepreneur, and a med tech investor. Together they visited the longevity laboratory at Volgograd State Medical University (VolgSMU), and Kovalev, according to Davankov, was tasked with promoting the university’s products in the region. Davankov’s post was also shared by VolgSMU’s official channel.
Kovalev was nominated to run for the State Duma with New People. However, when the party’s federal list was certified on July 10, the state-controlled Vedomosti newspaper reported that Kovalev had been removed from regional group No. 18, which included Kalmykia and the Astrakhan and Volgograd regions. Kovalev’s is no longer among the 298 names on the list that was ultimately registered by the Central Election Commission.
Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) is seeking Vitaly Nikolayevich Kovalev, born June 23, 1988. German investigators believe that under the aliases Stern and Ben, he founded and led the Trickbot hacker group. His wanted notice also lists other aliases: Grave, Vincent, Bentley, Bergen, and Alex Konor. The BKA believes Kovalev is in Russia.
According to the BKA, Trickbot had been operating since at least 2016 and, at various points, boasted more than 100 members, who used its infrastructure for spreading malware of the same name, as well as the Bazarloader, SystemBC, IcedID, Ryuk, Conti, and Diavol tools. The group has infected hundreds of thousands of computer systems worldwide, earning hundreds of millions of euros from its criminal activity. Its victims have included hospitals, government agencies, companies, and private individuals.
In May 2025, German authorities obtained international arrest warrants for members of various cybercriminal groups as part of Operation Endgame. The BKA stated that international warrants had been issued for 20 suspects and that an Interpol Red Notice was also issued for Kovalev, obligating law enforcement agencies in other countries to locate him and, if possible, provisionally detain him pending an extradition decision.
In July 2026, the Council of the EU added Kovalev to its sanctions list over his involvement in cyberattacks. The document lists Kovalev’s full name, date of birth, and the aliases Bentley, Bergen, Alex Konor, Benny, Ben, and Stern. The EU describes Kovalev as a senior figure linked to the Trickbot group and Conti malware and holds him responsible for cyberattacks that caused significant economic damage.
Trickbot was used for initial access into computer systems, theft of banking and personal data, and the subsequent deployment of ransomware. The U.S. Department of Justice stated that Trickbot had infected millions of computers, including at hospitals, schools, and companies, and that its infrastructure was used to spread Conti.
Conti became one of the largest ransomware operations in history. According to the U.S. Department of Justice, it was used in more than a thousand attacks worldwide, and ransoms paid by victims exceeded $150 million. The FBI recorded at least 16 Conti attacks on U.S. medical and emergency networks, including ambulance services, police, and 911 dispatch centers. Worldwide, more than 400 organizations were affected.
Ransomware linked to Trickbot’s infrastructure caused especially severe damage to healthcare systems during the COVID-19 pandemic. Materials from a U.S. Senate hearing state that more than 200 attacks using Ryuk, which is closely tied to the Trickbot and Conti ecosystem, resulted in nearly $100 million in lost revenue for medical organizations and roughly $500 million in system recovery costs.

Ukraine has received the bodies of 252 people killed in the war, the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War reported on 17 September.
The return of the dead remains one of the few channels that still functions between Kyiv and Moscow during Russia’s war against Ukraine. Each handover allows families of missing Ukrainians to identify and bury their relatives.
According to the Russian side, the bodies belong to Ukrainian citizens, including military personnel. Ukrainian authorities will now carry out forensic examinations and identification procedures to establish the identities of those returned, the Coordination Headquarters said.
Bodies to undergo identification
The repatriation was carried out through joint work by Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, the Security Service of Ukraine’s Joint Center, the Armed Forces, Interior Ministry, Ombudsman’s Office, Missing Persons Commissioner’s Secretariat, State Emergency Service, and other security and defense structures.
The International Committee of the Red Cross assisted with the repatriation.
Ukrainian military personnel are transporting the bodies to designated state facilities, where law enforcement and forensic experts will conduct the necessary examinations and identification.
Repatriations continue amid stalled peace talks
The latest repatriation follows the return of 261 bodies to Ukraine on 13 August.
The return of fallen Ukrainian soldiers has accelerated since peace talks resumed in early 2025 and has become a recurring process, making repatriation operations one of the few areas of continued humanitarian cooperation between Ukraine and Russia amid the war.

The US State Department approved the possible sale of around $24.3 billion worth of F-35 Lightning II Joint Strike Fighter jets and related equipment to Saudi Arabia, the department announced on Thursday.
Saudi Arabia requested to purchase 48 of the jets, as well as 49 engines and other materials.
According to a State Department statement, the F-35 sale is intended to support US foreign policy and national security objectives by strengthening Saudi Arabia’s ability to deter threats to the kingdom’s security.
It is also intended to improve cooperation between Saudi Arabia’s military, the US, regional allies, and NATO forces.
US says sale will not alter military balance in region
The State Department claimed that the proposed sale would not alter the military balance in the region or have an inverse impact on US defense readiness.
Word of the potential deal first spread in late 2025, leading many to question whether Saudi Arabia obtaining F-35’s would pose a challenge to Israel’s military advantage as the only country in the Middle East with access to the advanced aircraft.
US President Donald Trump confirmed that the US would allow the sale in November 2025 after meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to sign a series of diplomatic agreements.

Myanmar state media reported that Castillo, 40, was flown out of the capital “in consideration of the friendly relations between Myanmar and the United States”. Three things I learned from a Tibetan Buddhist Master

This post was originally published on this site.
I’ve never before spoken to someone who calls themselves a reincarnated Lama, and so my first question for Tulku Lobsang Rinpoche was about what it feels like. What is it like to be told at 13 years old that you have been formally recognized as the reborn Nyentse Lama?
It turns out, it’s nothing especially Hollywood-worthy. There’s no thrashing around like someone possessed. There’s no standing up with a glow and supernatural powers. Sometimes, there might be a sense that you’re gradually and partially reclaiming past-life memories. But, mostly, the title is a spiritual vocation.
“[A Lama is] born in this world consciously,” he told me, “they live life consciously, and they die consciously…they need to make a reincarnation because they need to help humans.”
A Lama’s job is to help humans find the path. There are always humans who need help finding the path. And so, a Lama’s job is never done.
I, for one, am glad for it. Because over the course of our conversation, Rinpoche not only introduced me to some areas of Buddhism I never knew but also offered me a handful of diamonds to take into real life. The Greek word praxis meant the practical application of an idea or philosophy. And it seems that Buddhism is an inherently praxic philosophy — it’s one that offers real recipes for how to live better and how to walk a path toward peace.
The full video is below for you to watch at your leisure, but I have also taken the time to write up what I see as three valuable pieces of wisdom I can take away from what Rinpoche has to say about truth, karma, and love.
Thank you, as always, for your support.
Go well,
 Jonny

Bill Bailey on music, mischief and touring Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Bill Bailey on music, mischief and touring Australia
Few performers can make people think and laugh quite like Bill Bailey.
Currently on an extensive tour of Australia, Bailey shares stories of adventure, connection and wonder with Megan Burslem on ABC Classic Breakfast.
From making music in Vietnam's remote highlands to mastering a typewriter solo at the Last Night of the Proms, Bailey reveals what it takes to be "a consummate professional".
He also shares the music that has inspired him throughout his career and why Australia continues to hold a special place in his heart.
On touring Australia
Megan Burslem: What do you love about Australia?
Bill Bailey: There's nowhere quite like this country anywhere in the world!
When my son came out on tour and he wanted to go skydiving, I said: "All right, let's go."
It was up on the Gold Coast, a beautiful pristine morning with blue skies.
We hurtled earthwards and then we deployed the parachute, and we just sort of gently floated down and landed on the beach.
Then I asked: "What's that down there?"
And he said: "Oh, that's just some whales breaching in the bay."
I was like, come on, really? This is ridiculous!
Burslem: You're touring all over Australia. Are you secretly sussing out real estate to move here?
Bailey: It's crossed my mind.
On musical experiences while travelling
Burslem: What is the best musical experience you've had around the world?
Bailey: I filmed a documentary in Vietnam, and we went up into the remote highlands up north, to a place called the Sapa Valley.
[The local indigenous people had] an instrument called the khèn.
It's a blown instrument that looks a bit like a bagpipe, but it's made of different lengths of bamboo. It makes a very fluting, haunting sound.
There was one practitioner of it who didn't even speak Vietnamese. This was how remote it was. He only spoke a local dialect.
We had to get two translators, but we figured it out musically.
He would demonstrate [on a few instruments] how [the khèn] would be played.
I figured out the notation of [one of] the instruments and found that I could accompany him on my phone with a little [keyboard] app.
I played a few chords and accompanied him on this instrument up in these remote highlands.
It's moments like that where I think music has this incredible transformative power to connect people across nations, cultures and languages.
On performing at the Last Night of the Proms
Burslem: You played at the Last Night of the Proms last year. What was it like to experience the Royal Albert Hall organ up close?
Bailey: That organ is a beast. It's something like 9,999 pipes.
When I played on the Last Night of the Proms last year, I had to rehearse at midnight.
It's not something where you can just turn up and say: "I'm just going to be noodling around up here. Everyone okay with that?"
I had to come in when all the concerts were finished, and everyone had left.
It was like this fantastically romantic assignation.
"Meet me at the stage door at midnight and I will take you to the organ."
And then you sort of wind your way up through the corridors.
When the organ switched on and it started to fill with air, the whole thing [came alive] like a beast.
I got loose on this instrument, and it felt like that scene in Star Wars when the Emperor goes, "Ultimate power!", and sparks come out of his fingers.
Burslem: You also played Leroy Anderson's The typewriter at the Proms. How did you practise your solo?
Bailey: That was just nerve-wracking.
You have to return the carriage [to get that ting sound].
But you can't rely on the machine to ting every time.
So, as a backup, you have a little bell on the desk next to the typewriter.
But at the Last Night of the Proms, they wanted the bell under the table, so I had to operate a foot-pedal bell on live television.
I practised and practised for hours and hours.
They'd hired me a beautiful old Corona typewriter, and I'm sure the neighbours thought: "Bill's gone analogue. He's writing a novel."
Burslem: Did you make a mistake?
Bailey: At one point, the keys jammed.
But being the consummate professional, I'd planned for that eventuality by deliberately jamming them while I was playing and then rehearsing how to unjam them in the middle of a phrase.
On the best life advice from a music teacher
Burslem: Which piece of music has had the greatest impact on you as a musician?
Bailey: Mozart's Piano Concerto No. 21 because I played it with an orchestra when I was at school.
It was quite a seminal moment for me as a performer because it was probably the most nerve-wracking thing I'd done to date at that point.
And it was down to the encouragement of my music teacher, Linda, whose words apply to life:
"You're capable of more than you think you are. Push yourself, go for it, do it. Have the confidence in your own abilities."
Those kinds of things are just great life advice.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Bill Bailey is touring Australia in September and October 2026 with his new show Vaudevillean.
