Are best books lists 'reductive and performative' or good for readers?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

A brief history of best-of lists, from the 19th century to Top 100 Australian Books
All best-of lists, from the annual Triple J Hottest 100 to the decennial Sight and Sound Greatest Films of All Time, spark debate.
ABC Radio National's Top 100 Australian Books, set to count down in October, promises to be no different.
Voting for the poll is underway, with readers invited to choose up to 10 titles they hope will appear in the list of the nation's favourite Australian books of all time.
Throughout history, best-of lists have inspired public discourse about the diversity of the literary canon and the books valued by society.
Best-of lists are not without their critics. The Australian writer Rosalind Moran, for one, has argued they are subjective, reductive and performative, demonstrating how we are drawn to "the contemporary language of productivity and completism".
Yet best book lists, however imperfect, play a role for writers and readers in driving sales and animating literary culture.
The American author Jennifer Egan, for instance, has described how the "turning point" for her bestselling novel A Visit from the Goon Squad was its appearance on the New York Times 10 Best Books of 2010 list.
In the struggle for attention in the digital age, best-of lists can also help readers discover books.
Although about 22,000 new books are published here each year, Australians are reportedly reading less than ever before. In a saturated information landscape, best-of lists introduce readers to the books others hold dearest to their hearts.
While reading might be declining, the number of best book lists appears to be rising. From BuzzFeed to Goodreads to BookTok, the internet is replete with lists recommending books to readers.
One website has even created a meta-list through an algorithm that aggregates 759 best-of lists to offer a "definitive guide to the world's most acclaimed books".
'A hundred good books'
As the mass market for reading grew in the 19th century, so did curated lists aimed at guiding readers to the best books in a crowded field.
The cultural influence of these lists extended to the publishing industry and educational sector, with book series marketed as "classics" and "great books" courses established at universities.
One of the most discussed lists was made by British politician and polymath Sir John Lubbock.
In 1886, Sir John gave a talk to the Working Men's College in London where he recommended "a hundred good books".
After the Pall Mall Gazette published his list as "the hundred best books", what started as a private lecture evolved into a public debate about literary taste and cultural value in Victorian society.
The newspaper ran a month-long column, The Best Hundred Books by the Best Hundred Judges, in which public figures such as poet and critic Matthew Arnold, UK prime minister William Gladstone and polymath John Ruskin commented on Sir John's list.
The debate fascinated readers: the column was reprinted as a special edition, selling more than 40,000 copies within a few weeks.
Oscar Wilde was one writer who responded to the list.
With his typical wit, Wilde criticised the idea of a best book list altogether, suggesting that a list of "The Worst Hundred Books" would be more useful in "an age which reads so much that it has no time to admire, and writes so much that it has no time to think".
Australian books on best-of lists
After The Observer published a list in 2003 of the 100 greatest novels of all time, literary editor Robert McCrum noted that "[f]or reasons I have yet to fathom, it excited special notice in Australia".
One reason could be that the list featured a lone Australian entry: Peter Carey's 1998 Booker Prize-winning novel Oscar and Lucinda. (Nobel laureate JM Coetzee, who moved to Adelaide in 2002 and became an Australian citizen in 2006, appears at number 84 with his 1980 novel Waiting for the Barbarians.)
Australian writers have fared little better on recent lists.
When the Guardian published its list of the top 100 books of the 21st century in 2019, Carey's True History of the Kelly Gang (2000) and Helen Garner's This House of Grief (2014) were the nation's only representatives.
No Australian titles made the 2024 New York Times list of this century's best books, which was created by polling hundreds of writers, editors, critics, academics and librarians.
Yet the opinions of experts are not always consonant with those of readers. When the publication repeated the exercise with a popular vote, the Reader's Pick list featured 61 books that did not appear on the original list, including Markus Zusak's The Book Thief (2005) at number 33.
And what of Australian books on the meta-list of the greatest books? Christina Stead's 1940 novel The Man Who Loved Children is the highest ranked, at number 453.
Valuable discussion
More than 280,000 people voted last year in ABC Radio National's Top 100 Books of the 21st Century.
Despite the countdown's international scope, 26 Australian authors made the list, with Trent Dalton's Boy Swallows Universe (2018) crowned the nation's most popular book of this century.
The result inspired thoughtful commentary on the books included and excluded. Author and academic Melanie Saward, for one, noted that the list contained few titles by First Nations writers and felt it "lacked the diversity reflecting our country".
Whatever the result, the Top 100 Australian Books is certain to prompt important conversations about the writing championed by the nation.
As reflected throughout history, this is perhaps the most vital role of best book lists: in his response to critics 140 years ago, Sir John wrote that "[m]y most sanguine hopes have been realized by the valuable discussion which has taken place".
Voting for the Top 100 Australian Books closes on October 1. The countdown will take place on Radio National on October 17 and 18.

The US State Department approved a possible $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, it said in a statement on Thursday.
The package also includes 49 Pratt & Whitney F135-PW-100 engines, along with cryptographic equipment, electronic warfare support, training and logistics packages, according to the notification sent to Congress.

Trump Withdraws ICE Director Nominee After Republican Senator Blocks Confirmation Hearing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:23:19 UTC
03:23:19 KST

President Donald Trump on Thursday pulled his nomination of former Oklahoma Highway Patrol trooper Lance Schroyer to head Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky blocked Schroyer’s confirmation hearing, stalling the process from moving forward.
Trump tapped Schroyer to be the next ICE director in June, calling him a “PATRIOT with real operational experience, and proven leader with DECADES of experience locking up the worst of the worst,” and saying that he would play a “vital role” in the Administration’s immigration crackdown.
The President did not provide an explanation for his decision to withdraw the nomination. The White House did not immediately respond to TIME’s request for more information.
Schroyer’s pick was somewhat of a surprise, given that he has no experience leading a law enforcement agency. He is close to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, whose department houses ICE; Schroyer previously served on Mullin’s security detail, and the Secretary later made him a senior DHS advisor.
Schroyer also helped lead the Oklahoma Highway Patrol’s efforts to train troopers and enforce an immigration crackdown in conjunction with ICE in his state, and was deputized to make federal immigration enforcement arrests last year.
Mullin and Trump both urged Congress to swiftly confirm Schroyer following his nomination.
"Lance is coming straight from the operational field where he ran large scale operations and worked alongside state and federal partners to remove illegal aliens from Oklahoma," Mullin said at the time, adding that Trump “made a great pick.”
But Paul, the chairman of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, said in August that he would delay a confirmation hearing for Schroyer until DHS provided further information regarding the investigations into the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis earlier this year, a major flashpoint in Trump’s sweeping immigration crackdown.
ICE has not had a Senate-confirmed leader since 2017. Schroyer’s nomination followed former acting ICE Director Todd Lyon’s departure from the agency at the end of May. Long-time immigration official David Venturella has headed ICE, also in an acting capacity, since June 1.
“Americans are calling on ICE to deescalate its immigration enforcement tactics, and the Administration needs to nominate someone who will right the ship, provide transparency, and restore the accountability Americans expect from law enforcement,” Democratic Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, said in a statement, in which he called on Paul to bring Mullin and Venturella before the committee.
“Despite the public's urging,” Peters added, “we now have an agency that has been engaging in increasingly questionable and escalatory behavior and refuses to be transparent and accountable to the American people.”

The incident comes as Ukraine continues to face a shortage of military personnel and challenges with recruitment and mobilization.
On Aug. 28, Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov said Ukraine needs to mobilize at least 30,000 people per month, while a parliamentary defense committee official said days earlier that the government was considering changes to the mobilization system amid recruitment challenges.
General mobilization, as part of martial law, has been in place in Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022.
Since the draft ramped up in scope over the last few years as fewer Ukrainians volunteered to fight, mobilization has been a source of simmering tension in Ukrainian society. Cases of attacks on draft officers increased in frequency in 2026.

To replace Netanyahu for real, the opposition will need to learn how to be ruthless

In Israel's election season, every day is an opportunity for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to try and terrify voters with the specter of Gadi Eisenkot, currently leading in most mainstream polls, putting an Arab party in his coalition. Feature: Chinese technology brings new dimensions to classroom learning in Serbia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:18:57 CST
03:18:57 KST

By Zhang Xuan, Nemanja Cabric
BELGRADE, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Holding a virtual reality (VR) controller, a Serbian student conducts a chemistry experiment in an immersive digital laboratory. Elsewhere, students explore marine life through VR headsets, examine 3D images of human organs on interactive screens and interact with an intelligent robot capable of speaking more than 100 languages.
At the Center for Robotics and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Education in Belgrade, Serbia, AI, VR and other technologies have become part of classroom learning, turning the vision of technology-enabled education into interactive learning experiences.
Established in 2020 with support from Chinese partners, including NetDragon Websoft Holdings Limited and Beijing Normal University, the center is dedicated to integrating technology with education. It has trained thousands of teachers and become an important platform for China-Serbia cooperation in technology-enabled education.
Danimir Mandic, director of the center and dean of the Faculty of Education at the University of Belgrade, recalled that a team of Chinese experts spent three months in 2020 integrating advanced technologies into the center's 1,000-square-meter facility.
"The buzz around AI started about 10 years ago. Even then, I firmly believed that we needed to introduce technology and smart systems into the classroom," Mandic said. The result, he recalled, was a center that felt like stepping into a "spacecraft."
Six years on, the technologies showcased at the center have gradually found their way into classrooms through teachers trained there.
Gordana Miscevic, a professor at the Faculty of Education, has been involved with the center since its inception, training teachers from different schools and disciplines.
"Over the past six years, I have witnessed very positive changes brought about by the integration of technology into education," Miscevic said, noting that technology can make lessons more engaging and improve teaching outcomes.
For Sofija Matovic, a researcher and doctoral student, the impact is also evident in feedback from teachers who have participated in the center's training programs.
"We run 'Digital World' workshops to help primary school teachers use educational robots and improve their digital literacy," Matovic said. "Many teachers report a significant increase in student motivation after using these tools in class. That is the best feedback we could ask for, showing that the direction we are exploring is the right one."
For Mandic, the cooperation also points to broader possibilities for the future of education.
"I have visited China and seen the maturity of its education system firsthand," Mandic said. "I look forward to bringing more advanced experiences and technologies to Serbia, helping advance lifelong learning and further bridge education and employment."
Hu Zhiyu, first secretary in charge of science and technology cooperation at the Chinese Embassy in Serbia, said the center exemplifies how China-Serbia cooperation in science and technology is delivering tangible benefits.
Looking ahead, Hu said China and Serbia will continue to deepen cooperation in AI and robotics, expand AI applications into more fields and inject new impetus into the building of a China-Serbia community with a shared future.
The growing cooperation extends beyond education. At the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in China, Nenad Popovic, Serbia's minister without portfolio for international economic cooperation, said Serbia, as a founding member of the World AI Cooperation Organization, is committed to promoting inclusive AI development and contributing to global AI governance.
Stronger cooperation between China and Serbia would create greater opportunities for mutual development and prosperity, Popovic said. ■

The A3 bloc -- Democratic Republic of the Congo, Liberia and Somalia -- demanded an end to unilateral cross-border incursions and the release of detained Syrian nationals.
Bahrain and Pakistan reiterated their calls for Israel to vacate occupied lands.
The US took urged mutual restraint and continued engagement through diplomatic mediation.
Israel has occupied the Golan Heights since 1967 and annexed the territory in 1981, a move unrecognized by the international community. ABUJA, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- The death toll has risen to 48 as suspected poisoning from a locally brewed alcoholic beverage continues to spread in Nigeria's southwestern Ondo State, the government said Thursday.
Banji Ajaka, the health commissioner in Ondo State, told Xinhua by telephone that about 182 confirmed cases were reported at local health facilities, with suspected cases spreading across Odigbo and Irele Local Government Areas.
At least 20 deaths were initially recorded, several days after the incident was first reported in two communities in Odigbo on Sept. 5.
"The source of the death is linked to the consumption of suspected methanol," Ajaka said, noting that methanol is a flammable and toxic alcohol not intended for human consumption. "The urine sample from the victims is pointing to suspected methanol."
A local brewer sold the alcoholic drink to people in the affected communities in Ondo, according to local sources. Most of those who allegedly consumed the beverage were youths.
Ajaka said that the Idogun and Gbogunron communities have so far been affected in Irele Local Government Area, which has now become a flashpoint of the incident.
Local police said Thursday that they had so far arrested 15 people involved in the production, sale and distribution of the alcoholic substance.
Public health authorities in Ondo have intensified their investigation following the surge in casualties, Ajaka said, adding that the investigation involved the World Health Organization, Nigeria's National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, and other agencies.
Local experts have warned that consumption of methanol, also known as methyl alcohol, can cause central nervous system depression, permanent blindness or death.
Chinedu Osuagwu, a local health expert, told Xinhua that there could be severe fatality risks, as many Nigerians continue to consume methanol in the form of illegally mixed counterfeit alcoholic beverages or local spirits. ■

Relations between Baku and Ankara were elevated to the level of an alliance with the Shusha Declaration, which Aliyev signed with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan during a two-day visit to the South Caucasus nation by Erdogan.
The OTS was established in 2009 and adopted its current name at the Istanbul Summit in 2021. Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan are members, while Turkmenistan, Hungary and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus hold observer status.
OTS

He also described the stability, peace and security prevailing in their countries as a key factor in the successful development of the OTS, arguing that it is an important factor for development in today’s political and foreign policy realities.
"It is well known that no country can develop without stability and security. Neither investment, technology nor innovation will come to a country if there is no stability or political and economic security there. Therefore, today this is also a key factor that distinguishes our countries from many of the surrounding regions where we are located," he said.
Aliyev also said OTS countries are demonstrating strong economic growth, particularly at a time when they see opposite trends occurring in various parts of the globe.

Interview: GGI shares similarities with HCCH's multilateralism, says HCCH secretary general
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:18:45 CST
03:18:45 KST

Chinese Ambassador to the Netherlands Shen Bo (R) shakes hands with Christophe Bernasconi, Secretary General of The Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH). (Xinhua/Shao Haijun)
by Xinhua writer Shao Haijun
The Hague, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- China's Global Governance Initiative (GGI) shares many common principles with the multilateral approach pursued by The Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH), particularly in promoting universality, inclusiveness and practical international cooperation, HCCH Secretary General Christophe Bernasconi has said.
Bernasconi and Chinese Ambassador to the Netherlands Shen Bo signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in The Hague on Wednesday between the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of China and the HCCH on cooperation to strengthen global governance.
Bernasconi told Xinhua in an interview after the signing ceremony that he recognized many common elements between the GGI and the work of the HCCH.
"The key points are a vision of bringing as many States as possible together around the table, based on equal sovereignty, and a willingness to develop effective and practical instruments that have a direct impact on people's lives and facilitate cross-border activities and initiatives," he said.
He added that such cooperation should be pursued "while respecting each other and respecting differences, including differences between legal systems, while recognizing the need to connect these systems."
With its origin dating back to 1893, the HCCH is an intergovernmental organization headquartered in The Hague. Its statutory purpose is to work for the progressive unification of the rules of private international law.
The HCCH currently has 95 Members, comprising 94 States and the European Union. China joined the organization on July 3, 1987.
Bernasconi said China has consistently participated in HCCH meetings and contributed to the organization's work both in the development of international legal norms and in the area of good governance.
"China has always been a very active, engaged Member, participating in our meetings and contributing both on the normative side and in the area of good governance," he said.
He said the MoU signed Wednesday would provide a platform for further cooperation between China and the HCCH.
"We also hope to see China join more of our Conventions," Bernasconi said, adding that there was room for China to derive greater benefits from its membership while continuing to contribute to the organization.
He said workshops and seminars can be organized to help relevant authorities in China better understand the meaning and practical benefits of additional HCCH Conventions.
"I look forward to using the Memorandum of Understanding, among other things, as a platform for further cooperation," he said.
Bernasconi said China's role in international legal cooperation is important because meaningful international law, including private international law, can not be developed without China's active participation.
"You cannot develop meaningful international law, including in the field of private international law, without China's active participation," he said. ■

====================================================================================================

AI can recognize animal sound patterns but may miss their meaning: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:18:41 CST
03:18:41 KST

JERUSALEM, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Israeli and German researchers found that artificial intelligence (AI) can recognize patterns in animal sounds but may struggle to understand what those sounds mean, Tel Aviv University said in a statement on Thursday.
In their study, published in Current Biology, the researchers examined a basic problem facing scientists using AI to study how bats, whales, birds, and other animals communicate.
The researchers said that similar sounds can have different meanings, while very different sounds can sometimes carry the same message.
To test the limits of AI, the researchers studied recordings of toddlers who had not yet fully developed speech. The children made sounds while distressed, calling for their parents, or asking for food.
Unlike animal sounds, the researchers could partly determine what the children were trying to communicate.
The team tested the recordings using traditional sound analysis and two advanced AI systems.
Although the AI systems performed better than the traditional method, they still sometimes grouped sounds with different meanings together or separated sounds that conveyed the same message.
The researchers concluded that understanding animal communication will require more than AI, adding that scientists will also need to study animal behavior and how animals hear and respond to sounds. ■

Feature: Mangrove restoration project transforms livelihoods in coastal Kenya
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:18:36 CST
03:18:36 KST

MALINDI, Kenya, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- A lush mangrove canopy stretches along the Athi-Galana-Sabaki River in Malindi, a coastal resort town in Kenya's Kilifi County, attracting local and international tourists thanks partly to a local women's group.
The 21-member Patanani Wito Women Group, all widows living near the estuary, has spearheaded the area's transformation from a site plagued by illegal logging into a thriving mangrove conservation zone.
Today, their conservation efforts are bringing tangible benefits and lasting change to the local community.
Agnes Kache Kahindi, chairperson of the group, said training from Nature Kenya experts helped the women realize that they could protect their local environment while building sustainable livelihoods.
"We teamed up with the sole purpose of earning a living by raising seedlings used in the restoration of the estuary," Kahindi told Xinhua recently.
Kahindi said that all 21 members work on a rotational schedule, allowing them to balance conservation work with parental responsibilities at home.
Alongside raising mangrove seedlings, the group runs an on-site restaurant that serves local meals to visiting tourists.
"We sell mangrove seedlings to buy food and educate our children," Kahindi said, adding that some members had even used their income to invest in livestock.
Beyond financial stability, she said the project had also helped rebuild her social support network, transforming her from a lonely widow into part of a sisterhood of women who have overcome shared struggles.
For 57-year-old Elina Damacharo, who joined the group in 2011, the initiative was a lifeline.
Widowed with seven children, all either in school or of school age, Damacharo initially had no resources to support them.
Today, she proudly says that most of her children have completed their education, thanks to the income she has earned through the group.
"The group gave me a job. From my earnings, I have educated my children, started keeping goats and replaced the grass-thatched hut my husband left me with a proper iron-sheet-roofed house," Damacharo said.
Damacharo now manages the group's mangrove nursery, which sells seedlings to banks and organizations for reforestation projects.
According to Francis Kagema Wathigu, Nature Kenya's coastal conservation programs coordinator, the women's group is playing a key role in mangrove replanting efforts.
Kagema explained that the decline of traditional Giriama community support systems had left many widows vulnerable to social isolation.
The project provides them with greater economic independence, giving members the means to build homes and support their children's higher education.
Kagema added that the widows' conservation work complements a 500-meter boardwalk, complete with a bird-photography hide and a shaded picnic area designed for ecotourists.
"The resulting green ecosystem serves as a crucial nursery ground for commercially important fish, prawns and crustaceans," Kagema noted, adding that it delivers "lasting benefits for the local community, the environment and native wildlife alike."
Joseph Mangi, chairman of the Sabaki River Conservation and Development Organization, said the restoration work is helping attract tourists to the area, where visitors now walk along the 500-meter wooden boardwalk to enjoy views of the estuary and watch hippos in the river.
He said the estuary was once heavily degraded as residents cut down mangroves for quick income, with little regard for the fragile ecosystem.
Mangi noted that the site now attracts hundreds of tourists and thousands of students annually, while local widows earn income by offering guided tours and receiving a share of visitor revenue.
Recognized by Nature Kenya as one of the country's 68 Key Biodiversity Areas, the Sabaki River Estuary hosts more than 240 bird species, including 91 species of waterbirds.
Shaped over decades by shifting sand, silt and sediment, the dynamic mosaic of microhabitats was once severely threatened by unregulated sand harvesting and overfishing before restoration efforts took root.
According to the Kenya Forest Service, mangrove forests line Kenya's 600-km coastline, thriving across creeks, bays, lagoons and river deltas. ■

Peak of DR Congo Ebola outbreak not yet confirmed: Africa CDC
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:18:11 CST
03:18:11 KST

KINSHASA, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Available data do not confirm that the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reached its peak, according to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).
"The data that we have cannot confirm that the peak of the outbreak has been reached," Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya told an online press briefing on Thursday. "The transmission is not yet consistently controlled."
As of Tuesday, the country had reported 7,404 confirmed cases, including 3,577 deaths, with an overall case fatality rate of 48.3 percent. A total of 1,776 patients have recovered, according to the latest situation report by the DRC government.
Despite a slight decline observed in Ituri, the long-time epicenter of the outbreak, Kaseya said the overall situation does not yet amount to a sustained national decline, warning that previous decreases had been followed by renewed increases.
Kaseya said transmission must show a sustained decline, and that any decline must be supported by "complete and comparable" data at provincial, health-zone and health-area levels.
Authorities must also demonstrate effective control of transmission chains, reliable contact tracing, rapid detection of cases and community deaths, and no further geographic expansion, he said, also calling for increased response capacity in the neighboring North Kivu Province, where treatment facilities are under mounting pressure.
Africa CDC data showed 316 patients were being cared for against 220 available beds in the province, putting bed occupancy at 143.6 percent. According to the latest government situation report, 42.1 percent of hospitalized patients in the province were being treated outside facilities meeting required standards.
Kaseya also pointed to significant gaps in contact tracing, saying only about 32,000 people were currently listed as contacts, representing roughly 27 percent of the estimated number that should be under follow-up.
World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Wednesday that the response was beginning to show encouraging signs in some of the worst-affected areas, particularly Ituri.
The current outbreak has become the largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic in the DRC's history and the second-largest globally, after the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa. ■

US officials made rare visit to Myanmar to free American businessman
WASHINGTON, Sept 17 - A delegation of U.S. officials traveled to Myanmar this week and met with the country's military-backed government to secure the release of detained US citizen Adam Castillo, a Department of State spokesman said on Thursday.
The visit appeared to be the most significant engagement with Myanmar since the military deposed elected leaders including Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, plunging the country into chaos.
Myanmar said on Wednesday it had freed and deported businessman and former U.S. Marine Castillo "in consideration of the bilateral friendly relations" between Myanmar and the US.
Washington has avoided sending senior officials to Myanmar or holding talks with the Myanmar government since the coup, which elicited a raft of U.S. financial sanctions against Myanmar's leaders and businesses that support them.
The State Department spokesman said the US maintains a diplomatic presence in Myanmar and "engages with all groups" in the country, including authorities in the capital Naypyitaw, "on issues affecting US interests."
"Throughout our engagements with authorities in Naypyitaw, the United States has and will continue to raise the need to cease violence, allow humanitarian access, and release political prisoners as part of efforts to bring about conditions for durable peace," the spokesman said in a statement, issued anonymously.
The State Department declined to say who was in the US delegation or whom they met with.
The visit comes as Myanmar's government is seeking international legitimacy. Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing -- who brutally crushed protests against the military takeover, sparking a bloody civil conflict -- installed himself as president earlier this year after holding elections widely decried as a sham.
Castillo was detained in June following a business dispute. His sister, Amanda Castillo, thanked President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance for working for his release in a statement on Wednesday. REUTERS

Putin put Russian assets of French supermarket chain Auchan and Swiss food giant Nestlé under temporary management. Neither company had left Russia after the full-scale invasion.
The assets of the Russian subsidiaries of France’s Auchan and Switzerland’s Nestlé have been placed under the temporary management of a company called L.E.V. Management, under a decree signed by Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The same decree also placed under temporary management a 0.007% stake held by the French group Adeo in Le Monlid, the Russian legal entity of Leroy Merlin, which now operates under the Lemana PRO brand.
In mid-August, Kommersant, citing sources, reported that a company called KS Logistika had asked Putin to impose temporary management on five of Nestlé’s Russian legal entities — a step that “could be the first stage in an ownership-transfer process.” According to Kommersant’s source, the request was prompted by “a lack of plans to expand capacity and a halt in exports of goods made in Russia.”
Neither Auchan nor Nestlé left Russia after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Nestlé did scale back its operations, however: the company halted investment, stopped selling some of its brands, such as KitKat and Nesquik, and announced that it did not plan to turn a profit in Russia.
Leroy Merlin’s owner said in 2023 that it was leaving Russia, and the home improvement stores have since operated under the brand name Lemana PRO.

Brazil’s Lula announces welfare increases ahead of presidential election

Unknown Publisher

Brazil’s Lula announces welfare increases ahead of presidential election
Government says that increase represents an adjustment for inflation that has eaten away purchasing power since 2023.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s government has announced a 15 percent increase in welfare benefits ahead of a closely watched presidential election in October.
The leftist president was joined by government ministers in the capital Brasilia on Thursday, where they announced that the “Bolsa Familia” poverty alleviation programme would increase minimum monthly benefits from 600 reais ($116) to 691 reais ($134) next month.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro to institute debt ceiling if elected president
- list 2 of 3Last dance? Inside Lula’s strategy to win a fourth presidency in Brazil
- list 3 of 3Flavio Bolsonaro faces corruption probe weeks before Brazil election
“This is a programme that has changed the lives of millions of Brazilians,” Lula said in a social media post, stating that the adjustment was meant to counter the impacts of inflation, which has risen since 2023.
“It’s income to put food on the table. It’s money circulating in the economy. It’s more dignity for Brazilian families,” he added.
Lula is currently facing a challenge from the political right by presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro.
A Datafolha poll released on Thursday found Lula winning 39 percent of the vote during the first round of voting on October 4 to Bolsonaro winning 36 percent. The poll predicts that Lula would narrowly beat Bolsonaro by 46 percent to 44 percent in a runoff.
The leftist president has faced challenges from rising debt servicing costs. Finance Minister Dario Durigan said the current budget would cover the benefit increase without creating additional expenses.
Planning Minister Bruno Moretti added that higher cash benefits would allow people to maintain their purchasing power amid rising costs.
“Inflation since the [March] relaunch of the programme through August stands at 15.04 percent,” Moretti said.
Benefit adjustments are allowed in Brazil, and conservative governments in the past have also overseen increases in the months leading up to elections. Before the 2022 presidential election Jair Bolsonaro boosted cash payments, totalling about 273 billion reais ($52bn) in 2022 and 2023, according to an analysis by the Reuters news agency.
The new financial aid increase is expected to cost the government 5.8 billion reais ($1.13bn) in 2026 and 22 billion reais ($4.27bn) in 2027.
The Bolsa Familia programme has been a central legacy of Lula and his Workers’ Party, part of Lula’s vision of pairing political democracy with social and economic policies that seek to address poverty and inequality.
Households with a monthly income of 218 reais ($42) qualify for the programme, which offers assistance to millions of poor families across the country.
In an interview published in the Brazilian newspaper Extra, Durigan also stated that the government was considering a debt relief proposal meant to decrease strain on borrowers.
“It is about making it possible for people who today have more jobs, more income and greater access to quality services to start over,” he was quoted as saying.

Macron and Aoun discuss efforts to back Lebanon’s army, end Israeli attacks

Macron and Aoun discuss efforts to back Lebanon’s army, end Israeli attacks
The French presidency said the aim of the Paris talks was to review a Lebanese armed forces deployment plan.
The leaders of France, Lebanon and Jordan convened in Paris to drum up international support for the Lebanese army.
Macron welcomed Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and King Abdullah II of Jordan to Paris for the talks on Thursday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Lebanon security talks in Paris to focus on post-UNIFIL alternatives
- list 2 of 4Israel bombs southern Lebanon as talks postponed
- list 3 of 4How Israel’s destruction of south Lebanon is making displacement permanent
- list 4 of 4US set to approve 60,000 heavy bombs for Israel: What that means
The meetings come after a US-mediated framework deal was agreed between Israel and Lebanon in June. But the agreement did not force Israel to withdraw from the large area of southern Lebanon it occupies, and Israel has continued its attacks on the country.
The agenda also included the creation of a new force to succeed a longstanding United Nations peacekeeping mission in southern Lebanon.
The officials were later joined by chiefs of defence staff from Lebanon, Jordan, France, the United Kingdom and Italy, as well as top US and Saudi officials, a French military source told the AFP news agency.
Macron said that the talks aimed to “strengthen Lebanon’s sovereignty and enable it to fully ensure its security”.
“A sovereign and stable Lebanon is a decisive step toward peace and stability for the entire region,” Macron wrote in a statement on X.
“We support the Lebanese Armed Forces, which are indispensable for asserting the authority of the Lebanese state across its entire territory,” he added.
The French presidency said the aim of the Paris talks was to review a Lebanese armed forces deployment plan based on a “clear, credible and realistic” framework.
Paris said it wanted this as a prerequisite for what it hopes will be “robust” international support, whether in the form of financial assistance, equipment or training.
Earlier in the day, Aoun and Macron also discussed “efforts to put an end to Israeli attacks in light of the Lebanese-American-Israeli negotiations and the ‘framework agreement’”, according to the Lebanese presidency.
Aoun also said the Lebanese army is the “main pillar for protecting Lebanon’s sovereignty”, stressing that strengthening state authority is a Lebanese choice rather than an externally imposed demand.
The Lebanese president expressed his “profound relief” at the progress of the talks, his office said in a statement on X, adding that he also expressed hope that the needs of the Lebanese army would be met by its allies.
Aoun reiterated his affirmation that only the state should have arms and praised the Lebanese army’s role in working towards the country’s stability.
The poorly equipped Lebanese forces have struggled to carry out their mission to disarm Hezbollah in the south.
Aoun has repeatedly stated his determination to disarm Hezbollah, but “without a confrontation”.
Post-UNIFIL alternatives
The talks also come as the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) ends this year after almost half a century of operations dating back to the Israeli invasion of 1978.
Last year, the UN Security Council, under US pressure, decided to end UNIFIL’s mandate on December 31, 2026.
France and Italy have said they want to set up a multinational coalition to succeed UNIFIL. The force has just fewer than 7,500 peacekeepers from 46 countries.
Aoun told the AFP this week that Lebanon wanted a new force, European or otherwise, to prevent a security vacuum after the UN peacekeepers leave south Lebanon.
Israel and the United States attacked Iran in February, setting off a war that has spread across the Middle East, including in Lebanon, with Israeli forces fighting Hezbollah.
Israel invaded southern Lebanon, and its forces continue to occupy what is a stretch of Lebanese territory about 10 kilometres (six miles) deep along the border.
In June, Israel and Lebanon signed a US-sponsored framework agreement that involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon’s south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region.
Fears of a renewed Israeli military campaign, however, are growing in Lebanon after escalating attacks, despite the “ceasefire” agreed to in June.

Weapons and ammunition stolen from Israeli army warehouses during the war in the Gaza Strip have made their way to criminal organizations, including LAW anti-tank rockets, Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported Thursday.
It said the military may not know the full quantity of weapons and ammunition stolen from warehouses and now circulating outside its control.

An investigation by the Israeli police’s Lahav 433 unit also found that companies in Bedouin communities had purchased hundreds of large cargo-carrying drones using fraudulent invoices, according to the report.
The drones have not been located, and authorities do not know where they are being used, said KAN, citing assessments that some may be used in smuggling operations.
The broadcaster said Israeli police, the army, the Shin Bet security agency and the broader security establishment are assessing the scale of the threat posed by drones and developing ways to counter them.

Shares in Raiffeisen Bank International fell 9% after a short seller accused the lender of helping Russia evade sanctions. The bank called the report misleading and factually wrong.
Shares in Raiffeisen Bank International fell 9% during trading on September 17 after the short seller Grizzly Research published a report accusing the bank of helping Russia evade sanctions.
Raiffeisen said the report was misleading and contained factual errors. “We remain confident in the strength of our compliance systems, which have been audited repeatedly,” a bank spokesperson said. The spokesperson also said the company has spent years trying to sell its Russian business and leave Russia.
In its report, Grizzly Research called Raiffeisen and its Russian subsidiary “one of the key channels for evading sanctions.” The report’s authors say $1.19 billion in trade with Russia went through the bank, including trade in sanctioned goods used by Russia’s armed forces.
Analysts at Bloomberg Intelligence say Grizzly Research may be exaggerating Raiffeisen’s sanctions risks. In their view, transactions through the bank’s Russian subsidiary are not in themselves evidence of sanctions evasion.
The bigger risk comes from regulators: any close scrutiny from the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control or the European Central Bank could further complicate Raiffeisen’s already difficult exit from Russia.
Raiffeisen Bank International’s main asset in Russia is its subsidiary, AO Raiffeisenbank. AO Raiffeisenbank remains the largest Western lender in the country and has not been hit by Western sanctions.
Raiffeisen announced plans to wind down its Russian operations as early as the first weeks of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but it has yet to leave the Russian market.
Russian authorities are blocking the sale of Raiffeisen’s Russian business. Any deal requires their approval, but Moscow wants to keep the bank in Russia as a conduit for settling payments with Western countries, chiefly Europe. At the same time, the United States has pressured Raiffeisen over its dealings with Russia.

Series of mysterious explosions rock German region

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:03:34 UTC

Series of mysterious explosions rock German region
A series of mysterious explosions have rocked the central German city of Frankfurt and the surrounding area this week, with police investigating possible links to organized crime.
Two improvised explosive devices detonated within minutes of each other in Frankfurt early on Thursday. One damaged a cafe in the east of the city, while the other struck a popular shisha bar on the Zeil, one of Germany’s best-known shopping streets.
The second blast was powerful enough to damage another bar across the street and a neighboring bank office, according to local media. One resident awoken by the explosion compared the scene to a “war.”
Police arrested a 17-year-old Dutch national following the blasts. No further details about the suspect have been released.
The explosions were the latest in a string of similar incidents in the Frankfurt area. Three blasts occurred within 24 hours between Sunday and Monday, targeting a cafe, a bar and a kiosk in Frankfurt and nearby Offenbach. No casualties have been reported.
A 15-year-old Dutch national was arrested following one of the attacks, according to police.
The Hessian State Criminal Police Office has said a “double-digit” number of similar incidents are under investigation. Authorities suspect some could be linked to so-called “violence as a service,” in which criminal networks outsource violent acts to third parties, often recruiting young perpetrators online or through social media.
Frankfurt police have previously described the practice as an emerging form of organized crime involving the recruitment of minors, including from abroad, to carry out acts of violence.
Hessian police have warned that the trend represents a new dimension of serious organized crime and poses a “considerable” threat to public safety.
The latest blasts coincided with Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt presenting a report on organized crime in Germany, which he described as a “growing threat.”
“Criminal gangs are becoming more professional, brutal, and unscrupulous,” Dobrindt said, pledging to strengthen efforts against criminal networks.
According to the Interior Ministry, almost 700 organized crime investigations were launched last year, involving nearly 8,000 suspects – the highest figure in five years.

Trump says ‘major progress’ made towards establishing US military base in Poland
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump said on Sept 17 there had been “major progress” towards establishing an American military base in Poland, after Warsaw said it was holding talks with Washington on the issue.
“Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland,” Trump said on social media.
“If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great U.S./Polish Alliance.”
Trump’s announcement comes despite his administration launching a formal review of its military presence in Europe, raising fears among allies that it could cut back its forces in European nations.
But Poland, which borders both Ukraine and Russia on NATO’s eastern flank and spends around five per cent of its GDP on defence, is working to strengthen the US presence on its soil.
“We are ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defence cooperation: seriously, responsibly, and always together,” Nawrocki said on X.
“I can assure you that the Polish government will do its utmost to provide the best possible location for the US Army base.”
Polish President Nawrocki is a conservative ally of Trump, and he visited the White House in 2025. During that visit Trump offered to send more US troops to Poland.
Polish deputy defence minister, Pawel Zalewski, said in August that his country was discussing with the United States whether to set up a permanent US base on its territory.
“We have already completed the initial stage (of the process), not to mention the political will, which was expressed long ago,” Zalewski told public broadcaster TVP.
Almost 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in Poland – which is also an EU member state – but almost exclusively on a rotational basis.
Washington has levied heavy criticism against a number of European countries that refused to allow US forces to use NATO bases on their territory in their war with Iran.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had also threatened to reduce his country’s contribution to the alliance’s budget if certain states refused to honour the commitments made in 2025 at the NATO summit in The Hague.
At that summit, NATO allies pledged to devote by 2035 at least five per cent of their GDP to security spending, including 3.5 per cent devoted strictly to military expenditures. AFP

Women diagnosed with ADHD later in life are learning to view hyperfocus as a superpower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:00:39 UTC
03:00:39 KST

A recent study suggests that women who are diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in midlife often endure years of hidden emotional struggles and misdiagnoses before finding profound relief. The research indicates that while these women face unique challenges, such as hormonal impacts on medication and intense emotional sensitivity, a late diagnosis can help them reframe traits like hyperfocus as personal strengths. The findings were published in Journal of Attention Disorders.
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by ongoing patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. In the brain, people with ADHD often show differences in cognitive control, which involves the ability to use prior knowledge and goals to guide attention and behavior. When this mental system is unbalanced, people can experience difficulties sustaining attention, heightened impulsivity, and emotional challenges.
Historically, ADHD has been viewed mainly as a condition affecting hyperactive boys, leading to a gender gap in clinical settings. Girls and women tend to display more internalized, inattentive symptoms, such as daydreaming or mental restlessness, which are easily overlooked or mistaken for personality traits.
Because of this, females often slip under the radar during childhood. This observation aligns with a study covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that females receive their ADHD diagnoses an average of four years later than males, often experiencing higher rates of anxiety and mood disorders in the meantime.
Without a proper diagnosis, women often develop coping strategies to mask their struggles and fit into societal expectations of organization and emotional balance. Over time, this constant self-monitoring can take a heavy psychological toll. In line with this, a 2023 systematic review indicated that women who grow up with undiagnosed ADHD often suffer deep emotional distress and relationship struggles before finally finding self-acceptance through an adult diagnosis.
Hormonal changes across a woman’s lifespan can interact with ADHD traits, complicating matters further. A 2025 review found evidence suggesting that fluctuating female sex hormones alter ADHD symptom severity and reduce how well stimulant medications work. Still, the ADHD experience is not entirely negative, as many people with the condition experience periods of intense concentration, a phenomenon known as hyperfocus, where they enter a deep state of immersion in an engaging task.
The research team, led by Tracy Kelly, who currently works in acute inpatient wards, and Brandon May, an assistant professor in forensic psychology at the Florida Institute of Technology, wanted to explore the lived experiences of women who receive a late ADHD diagnosis in midlife. They aimed to understand how this life-changing information shapes a person’s identity, self-perception, and social functioning, particularly when navigating the specific developmental and societal pressures of middle age.
“In short, we wanted to understand what it means for women to reach midlife before receiving an ADHD diagnosis,” the researchers told PsyPost. “Previous research had documented barriers to diagnosis in women (it is stereotypically characterized as a male disorder), but less attention had been paid to how women in midlife make sense of that experience alongside career demands, caregiving, and changes in identity.”
“We were particularly interested in the consequences of years of misunderstood difficulties, and whether diagnosis changed how women understood themselves and their strengths,” Kelly and May explained.
The scientists conducted their research by interviewing 12 women aged 45 to 58 who had received a formal ADHD diagnosis in adulthood. The participants engaged in semi-structured online interviews lasting an average of 52 minutes. The researchers used a method called reflexive thematic analysis, which involves reading through the interview transcripts multiple times to identify recurring patterns and central themes in the participants’ subjective accounts.
The analysis yielded three main themes, the first being the hidden struggles of discovering ADHD. Participants described years of being misdiagnosed with conditions like anxiety or depression. Many women reported feeling immense social pressure to maintain perfectly organized homes and lives, leading to a deep sense of shame when their ADHD traits made this difficult. To cope, they often masked their natural behaviors, suppressing their tendencies to talk excessively or appear disorganized just to seem socially acceptable to others.
“A person’s outward appearance of coping can conceal considerable effort and distress,” the researchers noted. “Women in our study described masking their difficulties and interpreting problems with organization, attention, and emotions as personal failings.”
The second theme centered on battling intense emotional storms. The women reported experiencing overwhelming emotions and heightened rejection sensitivity, a condition where minor perceived criticisms trigger intense emotional pain. Several participants also noted that hormonal fluctuations during perimenopause and menopause, the transition periods when reproductive hormone levels naturally decline, seemed to worsen their emotional dysregulation. Some women observed that their ADHD medication felt much less effective during specific phases of their hormone replacement therapy cycles, highlighting a need for hormone-aware treatment plans.
The third theme focused on living with ADHD and reframing the condition. Receiving an official diagnosis was described as a profoundly validating experience, with one participant likening it to winning the lottery. The diagnosis provided an explanation for their lifelong challenges, allowing them to replace self-blame with self-compassion. Many of the women also learned to view certain ADHD traits as functional strengths, frequently describing their capacity for hyperfocus as a personal superpower that enabled them to work diligently, complete tasks rapidly, and make spontaneous connections.
The researchers were struck by how much a formal identification could shift a person’s perspective. “Specifically, how receiving a diagnosis could change the meaning women attached to their past experiences,” they said. “Difficulties they had understood as personal shortcomings became more understandable, allowing greater self-compassion.”
“Yet that relief did not necessarily erase longstanding shame or everyday struggles, and that is an area that many women still struggle with (i.e., stigma and misunderstanding of ADHD in women),” the authors added. “Recognizing those strengths can coexist with taking their difficulties seriously. The broader message is to listen to women’s experiences and avoid letting stereotypes determine whose struggles are recognized.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2025. That study found that adults diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood reported experiencing notable personal strengths, such as high energy, unconventional thinking, and resilience developed through managing adversity.
Additionally, the observations regarding hormones align with a study covered by PsyPost in 2026. While that 2026 study tracked daily symptoms quantitatively across menstrual cycles in younger women rather than relying on qualitative interviews with midlife women, both projects indicate that hormonal fluctuations exacerbate ADHD symptoms and diminish medication efficacy.
Finally, the reports of severe emotional burdens resonate with research covered by PsyPost in 2025. Although that prior study used quantitative clinical comparisons between men and women rather than subjective interviews, it similarly found that women with ADHD are diagnosed later than men and tend to experience higher levels of depression, anxiety, and functional disability.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study’s sample consisted exclusively of white women, which means the findings might not capture the experiences of women from more diverse ethnic or socioeconomic backgrounds. The researchers also relied on self-reported ADHD diagnoses and self-identified perimenopausal status, neither of which were independently verified with clinical records or physical assessments.
“It is also worth noting that hormonal changes describe perceived experiences; they do not establish biological mechanisms or demonstrate that a particular medication adjustment works,” they clarified. Similarly, the study did not objectively test superior attention or productivity among the participants.
“The word ‘superpower’ in the title – and we discussed this at length with the reviewers of this paper – reflected how some participants understood aspects of their own experience,” they pointed out. “However, it should not be read as a claim that ADHD is universally advantageous, or that people should feel obliged to find a positive side to it.”
Because the participants were reflecting on their past experiences after receiving a diagnosis, their memories might be influenced by their new understanding of the condition, a phenomenon known as recall bias. Future studies could explore the experiences of a wider variety of women and look more closely into how specific life stages, such as the transition into menopause, physically and psychologically interact with ADHD symptoms.
“The study points toward research with more ethnically and socioeconomically diverse groups, and studies following women over time to understand what changes after diagnosis,” the researchers said. “It also highlights the need to investigate experiences around perimenopause and menopause using clearer clinical measures.”
“More broadly, our findings suggest participants spent years of underdiagnosed ADHD through self-blame, had difficulty obtaining recognition, and finally the importance participants attached to finally having an explanation,” the team noted. “These findings identify issues that deserve closer attention in assessment, ongoing support, and future research.”
“An important contribution is the attention it gives to women’s own accounts,” they concluded. “Their stories show that receiving a diagnosis can change how someone understands decades of experience. That understanding can be incredibly meaningful, even when everyday difficulties persist. Recognition, self-compassion, and continued practical support all deserve attention.”
The study, “Exploring Women’s Experiences of a Late ADHD Diagnosis: Unveiling a Personal Superpower Through Reflexive Thematic Analysis,” was authored by Tracy Kelly, Brandon May, Cody Normitta Porter, and Marek Palace.

US sanctions boost China’s science-driven innovation by over 70%, study finds
US tech restrictions have driven Chinese firms to expand and deepen their scientific research sourcing through citations and research
3-MIN READ3-MIN
18

US-sanctioned Chinese companies are increasingly turning to open-source research to innovate and reverse-engineer restricted foreign technology, with a 72 per cent surge in scientific literature citations in their patent applications, according to a new study.
While the United States said it expanded its Entity List to safeguard national security and preserve its technological edge, an analysis of Chinese patent filings over the 12 years until 2022 showed that US restrictions on access to technology had driven Chinese firms to widely source publicly available scientific knowledge and conduct more of their own research.
“Our analysis reveals that US trade sanctions, such as the Entity List, have generated consequences that US policymakers may not have fully anticipated,” the researchers wrote in a policy article published in the peer-reviewed journal Science on Friday.
“Though hindering the targeted firms’ short-term operations, sanctions may also catalyse these firms’ development of internal capabilities and drive strategic shifts, potentially leading to the emergence of separate technological systems that compete with, rather than integrate into, the current global innovation ecosystem,” they wrote.

A Genetic Mutation May Help Explain Lung Cancer in Nonsmokers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:00:04 UTC
03:00:04 KST

Smoking is one of the biggest contributors to lung cancer, but anywhere from 10-20% of cases in the U.S. each year are diagnosed in people who never smoked. In a new study published in Science, researchers report that for some of those cases, an inherited genetic mutation might be involved.
Scientists co-led by Dr. Jaclyn LoPiccolo, an attending physician and lung-cancer researcher at Dana Farber Cancer Institute, found that people with a mutation in the EGFR gene had a 25-fold higher risk of developing lung cancer compared to people without the mutation, regardless of whether they smoked. When the researchers looked just at nonsmokers, the risk was even higher: carriers of the mutation had a 60-fold higher risk compared to nonsmokers who didn't have the mutation. Since nonsmokers have a lower chance of developing lung cancer than smokers, this jump in risk reflects how strongly this genetic mutation might impact risk, LoPiccolo says.
The findings add to growing knowledge about what is driving lung cancer in people who don’t smoke. A handful of genetic mutations have been linked to lung cancer in nonsmokers, including some that appear to be more prevalent in Asian people who get lung cancer, as well as inherited mutations like BRCA2, but they aren't well understood. While the specific EGFR mutation in question, called T790M, was first discovered in a European family in 2005 with members who hadn't smoked but had developed lung cancer, it wasn’t clear how much the mutation, which is rare, actually contributed to lung cancer.
LoPiccolo and her team used a large data set of genetic samples from the 23andMe Research Institute to determine how much of an impact the mutation has on lung cancer. “While we knew that T790M was associated with lung cancer, we didn’t have a population large enough to determine how common the variant was, how strong its effect, and how the risk varies in different groups,” says LoPiccolo. “This mutation is so rare that we weren’t able to get population-level risk estimates without the size of a database like that from 23andMe.” About one in 15,000 people in the U.S. carry the mutation, but rates are higher—about one in 2,000—in Southern Appalachia, where scientists believe the first carrier brought the mutation to the U.S. from England or Ireland more than 200 years ago.
The findings open to door to considering how genetic testing might fit into lung-cancer screening. Currently, screening—in which people receive a low-dose radiation CT scan to look for lung cancer—is only recommended for people with a heavy smoking history who are above a certain age. “I do think that understanding your risk of lung cancer, especially from a genetic perspective, along with your exposures to things like radon and other environmental factors, would be really valuable,” says Nadia Litterman, executive director of the Susan Wojcicki Foundation, which funded the Lung Cancer Genetics Study that provided data for the analysis. (Wojcicki, the former CEO of YouTube, never smoked, yet she died of lung cancer in 2024.) “That’s the world we are trying to work toward, and this is a major step toward that.”
Litterman points to BRCA genetic testing for breast cancer as a potential model for lung cancer. “The lung-cancer guidelines are not quite there yet, but it’s a pretty clear path of what it could look like for people who are carriers of this mutation,” she says. “They could be screened on a more regular basis, and if they develop cancer, and it’s caught early, they would have a much better trajectory than if they didn’t know about [their genetic] risk.”
That’s what patients like Frank McKenna are counting on. A personal trainer in Virginia Beach, McKenna was diagnosed with lung cancer in 2016, despite never smoking or working in areas where he might have been exposed to environmental risk factors like radon. “I was shocked when I was diagnosed with Stage IV lung cancer after the only symptom I had was a little cough,” the 66 year old says. His doctor ordered a genetic test of fluid drained from his lung and learned he carried the EGFT T790M mutation. A biopsy from his lung lesion confirmed the mutation, and he started on a targeted therapy, which he continues today, designed to specifically neutralize his mutation. “When I started that targeted therapy, which is a pill I take once a day, within a couple of days, I could feel a difference,” he says. “I had lost weight, and there was cancer in various parts of my body, including in my bones, where it had spread. But I could feel my life coming back.”
A few months later, his daughter, who is now 33, was diagnosed with melanoma in her ear and was asked about her family history of cancer. She joined a study and provided samples to look for markers of cancer, and while she did not carry many common cancer mutations, she did carry T790M. But for now, there are no evidence-based recommendations to follow when it comes to how she should be monitoring her lungs for signs of cancer. “That’s why I’m pushing for how we can screen younger people, knowing that she has a genetic risk, and what low-dose screening she should get," says McKenna. "If something were to appear, she can catch it at an early stage, perhaps Stage I, and not go through Stage IV, because there are not as many options, and the outlook is not as positive.”
LoPiccolo is conducting a study, called INHERIT, which includes people from across the country with any inherited genetic risk for lung cancer, including the EGFR T790M mutation. Doctors will work with each participant to understand their family history of lung cancer, smoking history, genetic profile, and any environmental exposures that might contribute to lung cancer before coming up with a personalized plan for how often they should be screened with low-dose CT scans to look for cancer. “The goal is to use CT screening to detect lung cancer at the earliest, most curable stage when it can be removed or cured,” says LoPiccolo.
Such data will be critical to changing lung-cancer screening guidelines and providing families like the McKennas more peace of mind that they are giving themselves the best chance of conquering cancer. “I have scans every six to seven months,” says McKenna. “Because when you read any research on targeted therapies, one of the first things they say is that cancer will find a way to overcome the therapy. Fortunately, my last scan a few weeks ago was still clear, but what if you could catch the cancer early with screening often enough so it’s much easier to treat?"
Correction, Sept. 17
The original version of the story misstates the funder of the study. The study was funded by a group of philanthropic organizations and a government grant, not the Susan Wojcicki Foundation, which funded the Lung Cancer Genetics Study, which provided data included in the study.

In 2024, people across Russia poured brilliant green antiseptic into ballot boxes. This weekend, police in the city of Tyumen have told pharmacies not to sell it or iodine in bulk during the elections.
Pharmacies in Tyumen have been advised not to sell large quantities of iodine and brilliant green antiseptic ahead of the elections, according to the local news outlet 72.ru.
“The police came in and told us not to sell iodine, brilliant green, or anything else that stains from September 18 to 20. Some of our colleagues were told not to sell anyone five or more of these products at once,” one Tyumen pharmacist told journalists.
Other pharmacy workers said they had no strict rules about selling iodine or brilliant green during the elections, though they confirmed that they had received the recommendations.
According to 72.ru’s sources, the police decided to head off possible provocations based on their experience in past elections. The outlet also reported that people buying large quantities of staining antiseptics will be monitored.
During the 2024 presidential election, people across Russia poured brilliant green, iodine, and ink into ballot boxes. According to reports, most of the voters who spoiled ballots this way had been influenced by phone scammers.
Alina Nevmyanova, a Moscow resident who poured brilliant green into a ballot box, was sentenced to a year in a minimum-security penal colony. She said she had been scammed and had received calls from a “police lieutenant,” a “Central Bank employee,” and an “FSB officer.”
Russians will vote in local, regional, and national elections, including for the State Duma, from September 18 to 20.

“[Russian President Vladimir] Putin has ruled Russia for 26 years – longer than Joseph Stalin. During this time, his regime has systematically dismantled anything that resembled democracy,” Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sept. 7, condemning the elections scheduled for Sept. 18-20.
The upcoming elections will be Russia’s first national parliamentary elections held since the beginning of the full-scale invasion launched in February 2022.
Mobile voting under heavy military guard
According to a separate report from Euronews, the voting for Russian-installed legislatures had already concluded on Sunday, Sept. 13, in occupied Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions – parts of Ukraine that Russia illegally annexed in 2014.
Russian authorities have reportedly presented the early voting system as a security measure for frontline territories and said the arrangements were necessary under martial law imposed by Moscow.

“For Russia… it is important to go on with the voting on the illusion of normalcy, despite the fact that the Kremlin does not have full control over the annexed regions,” political analyst Abbas Gallyamov said, according to Euronews.
Limited political competition
United Russia – the pro-Kremlin party holding a dominant position in Russian politics – is widely viewed as the leading force in the election.
Russia’s Supreme Court barred the only registered liberal and openly anti-war party, Yabloko, from participating in September’s parliamentary elections on Aug. 10, while its deputy chairman, Lev Shlosberg, was sentenced to more than 11 years in prison on account of promoting “extremism” because of his public statements against the war.
Despite its anti-war position, Yabloko is not pro-Ukrainian. The party is pushing for an immediate ceasefire that would leave the current front line largely intact.
Still, it brought together not only traditional liberal voters but also servicemembers’ families, men concerned about being drafted, and citizens weary of mounting losses who oppose the continuation of Russia’s war, making it a thorn in the Kremlin’s side.
According to Euronews, some residents of occupied parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions welcomed the Russian authorities’ political efforts, framing the vote as familiar rather than new.
“For the last nine years, we’ve been striving to get closer with Russia, and Russian politicians are well-known to us,” Sergei, a 47-year old resident of the occupied city of Luhansk said, asking that his last name be withheld for security reasons.
“We’re speaking Russian and have felt like part of Russia for a long time, and these elections only confirm that,” he continued.
In occupied parts of the Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions, a different environment was described. Local residents and Ukrainian activists said voters had limited information about the candidates, some of whom reportedly arrived from other regions of Russia, including Siberia and the Far East.
Dead soldiers used in fabricated ballots
The early balloting follows voting that reportedly began on Aug. 29, according to United24Media, who reported that Russian commanders also used the identities of soldiers killed in action to vote for the ruling United Russia party.
Russian authorities allegedly delayed formally recording dead or missing soldiers as casualties.
While their names remained on active unit lists, officers reportedly completed ballots in their names and delivered them to polling stations in occupied Melitopol, Berdiansk, and Tokmak in the Zaporizhzhia region.
Kyiv Post has not independently verified the allegations.
Kyiv rejects vote, while SBU urges residents not to participate
Russia’s electoral process, held on occupied Ukrainian territory, represents a violation of international law. Kyiv has consistently urged international institutions and foreign governments not to recognize it.
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) issued a statement on Monday, urging residents not to participate in the elections and warning that organizing or promoting the vote could lead to criminal liability under Ukrainian law.
Under Part 5 of Article 111-1 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code, the penalty includes up to 10 years in prison and confiscation of property.
Do not “become an instrument of the Kremlin regime in the war against our state,” the agency wrote.

Shortly after the announcement, Mureșan wrote on social media that he accepted the president's proposal, adding that "Romania needs a credible government as soon as possible." | Martin Bertrand / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images
Romanian President Nicușor Dan proposed member of European Parliament Siegfried Mureșan as the country’s next prime minister in a third attempt to wrench Bucharest out of its political crisis.
Following a day of talks with parliamentary parties on Thursday, Dan said in an address that Mureșan had received “the most votes cast today by the parties in the consultations” — although none of the names floated for the role appealed to a clear majority.
“Beyond the fact that he was proposed by the three parties, [Mureșan] is a person who has experience in the European Parliament, who has negotiated important things over time, so he has the expertise for this position,” the president said.
Advertisement
Shortly after the announcement, Mureșan wrote on social media that he accepted the president’s proposal, adding that “Romania needs a credible government as soon as possible.”
Romania has been in political crisis since April, when the Social Democratic Party teamed up with the far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians to topple then-Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan over his austerity policies.
Dan’s first two nominees for Bolojan’s replacement failed to secure enough party support to lead a new administration.
Mureșan now has ten days to form a cabinet and win a vote of confidence in parliament. He is supported by the National Liberal Party, of which he is a member, as well as the Save Romania Union and the Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania.
But he has received an icy welcome from the Social Democrats and the Alliance — the two largest parties in Romania’s lower chamber — who appear to take issue with Mureșan’s position as an EU lawmaker.
The Social Democrats’ president, former Prime Minister Sorin Grindeanu, said in a Facebook post that he was “surprised and disappointed” by the nomination of “a man who, just days before this nomination, was waging a fierce campaign in Brussels against his own country to cut European funds.”
Also on Facebook, using flag and roses emojis, Alliance leader George Simion wrote: “We are not voting Germany, nor France, nor [the Social Democrats]. Only Romania.”
Mureșan has been part of the European Parliament since 2014, a vice-president of the European People’s Party since 2019, and a leading voice on EU budget talks in the European Parliament. He is a co-rapporteur for the upcoming Multiannual Financial Framework — the bloc’s seven-year budget — for 2028 to 2034.

Govt issues SOP to curb stray cattle on highways, allowing fines and penalties for owners.
NEW DELHI: Owners who abandon cattle on highways and expressways could face fines and penalties, with the road transport ministry issuing a standard operating procedure (SOP) to curb the menace of stray cattle and other animals causing road crashes. States and local authorities will initiate “owner-tracing” and take steps to recover applicable fees, fines and penalties from owners.The SOP follows a Supreme Court direction to NHAI to devise a structured mechanism for the safe removal of stray animals from national highways and expressways.The “SOP for Safe Removal of Stray Cattle and Other Animals from NHs/Expressways”, issued this week to highway agencies and state govts, designates NHAI, NHIDCL and state PWDs as nodal agencies for removing stray animals from NHs and expressways. They will arrange their safe transportation to shelters, cattle pounds or gaushalas identified by state govts.The highway agencies will identify and mark stretches where stray cattle and other animals are frequently spotted. They will also arrange and bear the cost of transporting the animals to shelters identified and maintained by state and local authorities.States and local authorities will “maintain cattle-pound records and initiate owner-tracing and action for recovery of applicable fees, fines and penalties under the relevant cattle-trespass legislation”, as per the SOP.
State govts are empowered to initiate action under the The Cattle-Trespass Act of 1871 .State govts can invoke provisions of The Cattle-Trespass Act, 1871 against owners. Section 25 provides for recovery of fines imposed for damage caused by cattle trespassing through the sale of the animals involved. This applies whether the cattle were caught while trespassing or later, and whether they belonged to the offender or were merely in their charge when the offence occurred.
Though there is no separate official data on crashes and fatalities caused specifically by stray cattle and other animals. However, in 2024, 19,082 crashes and 8,917 deaths were recorded under the “run off the road” category. The road transport ministry has said such crashes could result from excessive or inappropriate speed, driver distraction, misjudging a curve or attempts to avoid a collision with another road user or an animal.
