Factors in setting minimum wage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:25 UTC
01:40:25 KST

Taiwan’s minimum wage has risen for 11 consecutive years. When the Minimum Wage Review Committee convenes on Thursday next week, the announcement of a new monthly minimum wage exceeding NT$30,000 is all but certain. The key question is: How should this year’s raise be determined?
Taiwan’s K-shaped economy is in the throes of simultaneous growth and decline, painting very different economic pictures across industries. The challenge lies in ensuring that workers share in the gains of broader economic growth, while at the same time addressing employers’ ability to absorb higher labor costs.
There are good reasons for the continued increases in the minimum wage over the past few years. With rising prices, rent and living costs, a stagnant minimum wage would inevitably squeeze the real incomes of the lowest-paid workers. If economic growth is reflected only in corporate profits and capital markets, but fails to translate into higher incomes for workers, its benefits might never truly be felt by ordinary people.
Semiconductor and some export-oriented industries have enjoyed strong growth momentum thanks to the rapid expansion of the artificial intelligence industry; however, traditional manufacturing, retail, restaurants and some domestic service industries face pressures including labor shortages, rising costs and limited consumer spending. There are also significant differences in the financial health of large corporations, and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
Using the overall economic growth rate as a singular basis for raising wages risks overlooking these disparities between industries. While highly profitable companies might be able to absorb the additional costs, for SMEs operating on thin margins, a minimum-wage increase could strain operations and even affect their willingness to hire. If businesses pass some of these costs on to consumers through higher prices for goods and services, the additional income workers receive could also be offset by inflation.
The review should consider a broader range of economic indicators, including prices, economic growth and conditions across different industries. The size of the increase should reflect these disparities and, critically, be accompanied by supporting measures so that wage policy does not become a burden that SMEs struggle to absorb.
A NT$30,000 minimum wage is likely to become our new starting point. The question is how to gradually translate economic growth into higher incomes for more workers.
The minimum wage review is not simply about deciding on a number; it is also a test of how to strike a balance between raising workers’ incomes and maintaining the competitiveness of Taiwan’s industries.

Accommodation issues continued to plague the lead-up to the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games yesterday with even the hosts looking at alternative arrangements after cases in which male and female athletes were allocated shared rooms.
Local organizers, having decided not to build a dedicated Athletes’ Village, looked to creative accommodation options to house the 17,000 competitors and officials arriving for the Games, which officially open tomorrow.
An Italian cruise ship which is to host 4,000 participants arrived on Tuesday and 2,000 other athletes and officials would be accommodated in shipping-container style huts in the dock area of Japan’s biggest port.
Photo: Reuters
“Since the cruise ship village opened yesterday, athletes have been arriving and going through the entry procedures,” Japanese Deputy Chef de Mission Hisashi Mizutori told a news conference.

India yesterday said that it would continue buying oil from “diversified” suppliers after US lawmakers approved sanctions designed to squeeze Russia over its war in Ukraine.
The US legislation targets Russia’s energy and defense sectors, Russian President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions.
It also gives US President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas — including potentially China and India — in an effort to choke off revenue financing Moscow’s war.
Photo: AFP
However, the Indian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that it “remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people.”
“It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics,” the ministry said.
Moscow is one of New Delhi’s most important strategic partners and military suppliers.
“The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” the ministry said.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran conflict in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s war in Ukraine, and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi held talks in New Delhi last week ahead of a BRICS summit.
“This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors,” the ministry said. “Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship, but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side.”
Indian refiners nearly doubled crude imports from Russia to 2.25 million barrels a day in March — the weeks after the Middle East war erupted — helped by temporary US waivers.
Shipments hit a record 2.81 million in July, trade intelligence firm Kpler said, but have since dropped back to 2.07 million last month.
In Washington on Wednesday, US lawmakers approved the sanctions, sending the legislation to Trump.
The US House of Representatives passed the package by 262-159, giving a final congressional green light to the most substantial US legislative effort against Moscow since Trump returned to office.
Trump has said he will sign the measure, which sailed through the Senate in an 86-11 vote last month.

UNITED STATES
Moon crater discovered
A NASA researcher has found a massive, recently formed crater on the moon, a rare occurrence that only happens “once in a century or even longer,” scientists said. The crater, dubbed “McGetchin,” measures 222m wide, NASA said in a blog post. It is believed to have been created in the spring of 2024 from a comet or asteroid colliding with the moon, with researchers describing the object that caused it to be the size of a building three-to-six stories high. “Scientists estimate that an impact of this magnitude happens on the moon about once in a century or even longer,” NASA said in the blog post. Although the crater had been there for years, it was not discovered until Robert Wagner, a researcher with NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, noticed it in a new scan of the moon’s surface.
Photo: AFP / Handout / NASA
FIJI
HIV emergency declared
The Pacific island nation has declared a national HIV crisis as sexual transmission and illicit drug use help to spread the virus. New HIV diagnoses surged to 2,016 cases last year — 16 times the level recorded in 2019, authorities said, vowing a “whole of government” response. “I am formally declaring a national HIV emergency in Fiji,” Minister of Health Atonio Lalabalavu told reporters on Wednesday. “This decision recognizes the seriousness of the epidemic and the urgent, coordinated response our country now needs.”
AUSTRALIA
Visa rules tightened
Canberra will stop foreign students from bringing partners and children to accompany them while they study and tighten working holiday visa rules, Minister for Home Affairs Tony Burke said yesterday. Burke dismissed suggestions that the changes were politically motivated by the One Nation party, which has promised to cut migration. “It’s simply demonstrably wrong to suspect that somehow this is a recent bit of work done to deal with a political climate — it’s not,” he told reporters. The reforms are expected to bring annual net migration down to about 225,000 by 2028.
BOLIVIA
Paraguay border finalized
The nation and Paraguay on Wednesday finalized the course of their shared border after nearly nine decades of negotiations that began after a territorial war between them, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement. The two countries fought between 1932 and 1935 over the Chaco Boreal region in a conflict that left between 80,000 and 100,000 people dead. Bolivia lost an area equivalent to more than half of Paraguay’s current territory as a result. “Bolivia and Paraguay have completed the delineation of their entire international boundary, a process carried out over 88 years by technical commissions from both countries,” the ministry said.
COLOMBIA
Airstrike ban lifted
A judge on Wednesday lifted a ban on airstrikes on guerrillas, which had been suspended to protect minors, but may now proceed with “caution,” a ruling said. President Abelardo de la Espriella has ordered a series of attacks on guerrilla camps to make good on his promise of flushing out the country’s armed groups. On Sept. 2, a Bogota court ordered the temporary suspension of airstrikes against rebel camps, a document obtained on Wednesday showed. Attacks may now resume, but with “a reinforced standard of precaution” when “there is certain, objective or reasonably verifiable information about the presence of boys, girls or adolescents” recruited by guerrillas, it said.

Ocean acidification shrink squids’ brains, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:24 UTC
01:40:24 KST

At the current pace of climate change, ocean acidification might shrink the brains of squids by the next century, impairing their ability to hunt, an Academia Sinica study showed.
Exposing Sepioteuthis lessoniana, or bigfin reef squid, to projected 2100 ocean acidity levels significantly reduced their brain volume, the academy’s Institute of Cellular and Organismic Biology said in a news release yesterday.
Institute assistant research fellow Tseng Yung-che (曾庸哲) and Acadia University assistant professor of biology Garett Allen coauthored the study, and collaborated with fisheries and scientific research groups affiliated with Taiwanese and Japanese governments, it said.
Photo courtesy of Academia Sinica
Exposing squid to seawater at pH 7.8 increased the time they needed to capture prey by 2.5 times and decreased their predatory willingness, the institute said.
The change in behavior stemmed from a disruption in higher-order neural integration circuits, not due to eye damage, as previously hypothesized, it said.
Being kept in an acidic environment for 90 days decreased squids’ brain size by 49 percent, and the increased acidity in optic lobes reduced the number of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, which transmit visual information, the institute said.
The changes led to problems in energy metabolism and synaptic signaling, it said.
The affected squids were notably slower in defensive inking, finding concealment in corners and catching prey, the institute said.
The impaired cognitive capabilities of an apex predator are highly likely to have negative ramifications for the ecosystem, highlighting the threat climate change poses to the environment, it said.
However, the squids also showed surprising resilience by responding to long-term exposure to acidification with multi-layered neural adaptations involving building ribonucleoprotein complexes, maintaining Golgi apparatus function and transporting vesicles, the institute said.
The research team believes that using magnetic resonance imaging and machine learning could help scientists understand the climate’s impact on the brains of cenopods, which have implications for the ocean’s ecosystem, it said.
The study was published in Communications Biology on Jan. 8, and sparked interest in international publications, including the US-based Time magazine and the UK’s The Times, the institute said.

‘Practical Magic 2’ should have stuck with the original spell book
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:22 UTC
01:40:22 KST

Getting a sequel greenlit nearly 30 years after the original movie floundered upon its release likely required a stroke of magic.
1998’s Practical Magic, led by Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman as the Owens family witches, eventually became a cult classic, finding its footing with a home video release and subsequently, streaming services and social media.
So 28 years later, the original stars are back, the midnight margaritas return and even the iconic coastal Massachusetts home at the heart of the first film was rebuilt for the ultimate punch of nostalgia. Enough time has passed since the original movie that its ’90s wardrobe is back in style.
Photo: AP
But Practical Magic 2 abandons some of the original’s best elements, including the campy fun that helped it find an unlikely second life.
The first movie was a blend of Death Becomes Her and Halloweentown, but the sequel sacrifices some of that whimsy in favor of a more genuinely spooky undertone that doesn’t quite fit. Where a pentagram in the original is forged with whipped cream, it’s done with fire in the sequel.
We pick up shortly after the 1998 film ended, with the Owens sisters seeing the curse that has afflicted their family of witches for generations playing out yet again. Sally (Bullock) becomes a widow once more after her second husband meets an untimely demise, as do all men who fall in love with an Owens woman.
She forces her sister Gillian (Kidman) and her aunts Jet and Franny (Dianne Wiest and Stockard Channing) to swear they won’t tell her two young daughters of their magical abilities or the curse, and casts a spell to make them forget about their witchy childhoods. Fast forward to when those young girls (a terrific Joey King and an underutilized Maisie Williams) are adults taking an interest in romance, and chaos ensues.
Sally’s daughter Kylie (King) propels the at times meandering plot forward through her mission to undo the Owens family curse after her boyfriend, Gideon (Xolo Mariduena), slips into a coma. Sally and Gillian follow her to England to try to keep her safe from dark magic.
This is where the spooky-playful energy of the original is swapped out for a more spooky-creepy tone. Perhaps more eerie elements come with the territory of a major studio’s release during the ever-expanding Halloween season. But Practical Magic 2 lacks the moments of pure fun — like Bullock asking PTA moms to form a coven or Kidman telling neighbors to hang onto their husbands when she’s back in town — that made the original film’s darker moments more admissible.
There are still charming, tender moments in the film, propelled by its strong performances. Bullock and Kidman serve up the comedic high points while the emotional heft is deftly carried by Channing, Wiest and King.
Lee Pace delivers as the charming British scholar of witchcraft and magic who helps Sally and Gillian in their quest to save Kylie, while also serving as a love interest for the romance-resistant Sally.
But the movie’s strongest bond is between Bullock and Kidman, who are good friends offscreen. Their connection to each other, and with director Susanne Bier, who has worked with each of them, keeps the lengthy sequel afloat.
Like the original, the sequel has a strong soundtrack and score that help to carry the story through its back-and-forth between lighter and darker moments. Don’t worry, Stevie Nicks is back. As is Harry Nilsson’s Coconut.

Armenia would not oppose closure of Russian base: Pashinyan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:00 UTC
01:40:00 KST

Armenia would not stand in the way of Russia shutting down its military base in the country, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said Thursday, arguing that the facility was no longer essential to Yerevan's security.
The base, near Armenia's border with Türkiye, has been a key symbol of Moscow's military influence in the South Caucasus.
Pashinyan's comments come as Armenia pursues an increasingly pro-Western foreign policy and distances itself from traditional ally Moscow's orbit.
"We have never put the issue of the Russian military base operating in Armenia on the agenda," Pashinyan told a news conference.
But if Moscow wanted to close its 102nd military base in the northwestern city of Gyumri, Armenia "will not object," he said.
"The 102nd military base adds nothing to Armenia's security."
Russian President Vladimir Putin said earlier this month that Moscow was ready to withdraw the base "even tomorrow" if Armenia decided it no longer needed a Russian military presence.
A 2010 agreement extended Russia's right to operate the base until 2044. It hosts around 3,000 Russian troops.
On Thursday, Russian Security Council Secretary Sergei Shoigu accused Yerevan of seeking to "sever ties" with Moscow and expand cooperation with NATO.
Relations between the longtime allies have deteriorated sharply, with Yerevan deepening ties with the EU and United States after accusing Russia of failing to protect Armenia in confrontations with neighbouring arch-foe Azerbaijan.
Armenia also froze its participation in the Russian-led Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO) in 2024 and has taken steps towards possible EU membership.
Earlier this year, Moscow slapped bans and restrictions on a range of Armenian imports, including fruit, vegetables, flowers and beverages.
Brussels offered Armenia a trade lifeline that would liberalise nearly 80 percent of Armenian exports to the EU, making them tariff-free.
Russia nevertheless remains a major trading partner and Armenia is heavily dependent on Russian energy supplies.

TMC vs TMC: EC bars both factions from using party symbol, name in Bengal bypolls
NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Thursday barred both rival Trinamool Congress (TMC) factions from using the party's name and reserved election symbol in the upcoming West Bengal Assembly bypolls, according to an interim order.The decision comes ahead of the October 6 bypolls in Nandigram and Rejinagar, where factions led by Mamata Banerjee and Ritabrata Banerjee had fielded candidates while staking claim to the TMC identity and its twin-flowers-on-grass symbol.The poll panel has been hearing competing claims from the two factions over control of the party, its name and election symbol. Both sides have submitted documents and appeared before the Commission during the proceedings.The dispute reached the Election Commission in July after the rival factions staked competing claims to control of the TMC. The Commission subsequently sought responses on issues including organisational control, authorised signatories, party assets, name and election symbol.The issue gained urgency after the EC announced the Nandigram and Rejinagar bypolls for October 6. With nominations closing on September 16, the Commission faced a deadline to determine how the rival factions would contest the elections.
The Commission held separate meetings with representatives of both factions on September 12.The Mamata faction was represented by Derek O'Brien, Kalyan Banerjee, Sagarika Ghose, Saket Gokhale and advocate Abhinav Singh. The Ritabrata faction was represented by Ritabrata Banerjee, Akhruzzaman, Arup Roy, Chandrima Bhattacharya and Riju Datt.Both sides maintained that they represented the legitimate TMC and sought recognition of their claim to the party name and symbol.The Mamata faction argued that Banerjee remained the party chairperson and that the national working committee was still within its five-year term.The rival faction contended that the party constitution provided for a three-year term, which it said had ended in February 2025.
On September 13, the EC sought final submissions from both factions by 3 pm on September 16, the nomination deadline for the two bypolls. The Commission indicated that another hearing could be held on September 17.At the time, the Mamata faction said that in the absence of an interim order, it would contest using the original TMC symbol. The Ritabrata faction maintained that the EC alone could decide which side was entitled to use the party name and symbol.On September 15, TOI reported that the Commission was likely to issue an interim ruling on September 17. The EC subsequently scheduled another hearing with both factions on Thursday.

US gold futures contracts rose by 0.54% to $4,410.
The spot price of silver climbed over 4.5% to $66, in parallel with the rise in the precious metal.
Platinum and palladium prices also gained value.
Analysts stated that the drop in oil prices to a one-week low and the easing of the US dollar index from a seven-week high drove the rise in gold prices.

Investors continued to evaluate the Fed's decision on Wednesday to raise interest rates to the 3.75%-4% range and its policy signals for the upcoming period.

17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Israeli military incursions and compounding economic distress continue to jeopardize Syria's fragile transition despite legislative milestones and mass refugee returns, a senior UN official told the Security Council on Thursday.
Relaying a message from the UN chief, UN Deputy Special Envoy for Syria Claudio Cordone told council members that "violations of Syrian sovereignty and territorial integrity must cease, and the 1974 agreement must be respected." He cautioned that security concerns "cannot be addressed in any sustainable way through unilateral military action or an open-ended military presence."
Cordone emphasized that an active Israeli military presence in southern Syria directly breaches the 1974 Disengagement Agreement through "near daily incursions, temporary checkpoints, searches of homes and artillery fire," particularly in Quneitra and western Daraa. The warning follows a Sept. 9 visit by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to Israeli forces deployed on Mount Hermon.
Cordone noted that localized tensions in Suwayda must be resolved by Syrians "without disruptive foreign interference" through the reinvigorated September 2025 roadmap.
Israel has occupied Syria’s Golan Heights since 1967 and unilaterally annexed the territory in 1981, a move not recognized by the international community. Following the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime on Dec. 8, 2024, Israel expanded its occupation of Syrian territory and took control of the buffer zone and positions on the Syrian side of Mount Hermon after Netanyahu claimed that the disengagement agreement had collapsed.
Fuel spikes, maritime chokepoints
On the humanitarian front, UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs Tom Fletcher warned that regional shipping disruptions across the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and the Strait of Hormuz are driving up maritime freight, insurance rates and supply lead times into Syria.
A 40% surge in diesel prices this week threatened bakeries, water pumping and winter heating, said Fletcher. He reported that the minimum expenditure basket climbed 33% since June 2025, forcing aid agencies to halve food rations for the most vulnerable families as critical food and education sectors remain only 26% funded.
Lethal landmines, displacement
Although more than 2 million internally displaced persons and 1.8 million refugees have returned voluntarily since December 2024, Fletcher noted that 5.5 million people remain displaced nationwide, including nearly 800,000 living in camps where women and children make up more than 75% of residents.
Explosive ordnance presents a lethal barrier to recovery, killing 880 people, including 269 children, and maiming 1,616 since late 2024. Fletcher warned that contamination blocks essential agricultural land, emphasizing, "You cannot build an economy over a minefield."
Addressing the council on behalf of civil society, Syrian Forum co-founder Yasser Tabara argued that long-term stability requires merit-based public appointments over political loyalty, urging international donors to convene a dedicated reconstruction conference and help counter private-sector banking overcompliance.

U.S. President Donald Trump plans to sign legislation soon that would allow him to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas, a White House official told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 17, a day after the U.S. House of Representatives approved the bill.
The bipartisan legislation, championed by the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, would give Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and natural gas, as well as five countries helping Moscow evade energy sanctions.
The bill's passage has been closely watched in Ukraine as Kyiv pushes Washington to increase economic pressure on Russia. President Volodymyr Zelensky urged U.S. lawmakers on Sept. 11 to pass the legislation while also calling for strong "personal decisions from President Trump."
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Sept. 17 that new U.S. sanctions against Russia would make efforts to reach a peaceful resolution to the war in Ukraine more difficult.
"This constitutes unfriendly actions," Peskov said.
The House approved the bill on Sept. 16 by a vote of 262-159.
The legislation had already cleared the Senate with overwhelming support in early August, less than a month after Graham died of an illness following his trip to Ukraine.
If enacted, the legislation would target countries purchasing Russian energy products. China, India, and Turkey are among the largest buyers of Russian oil, while the European Union, China, and Turkey are major importers of Russian natural gas.
The list of targeted countries would be reviewed every 180 days. Countries importing less than 15% of Russia's total natural gas exports and actively reducing those imports would be exempt from the tariffs.
Beyond energy buyers, the legislation would impose sanctions on Russian President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as major Russian financial institutions, including the Central Bank, Sberbank, and Gazprombank, and Russian state-owned companies.
It would also target foreign entities supporting Russia's defense-industrial base, major Russian energy projects, and Moscow's so-called shadow fleet, which helps Russia continue exporting oil despite Western sanctions.

Climate change destabilizing factor in deadly Nepal-China flood disaster, say researchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:33:21 UTC
01:33:21 KST

Saadet Gokce
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
A group of expert academics said Thursday that climate change was "a destabilizing factor acting on a pre-existing geological predisposition" behind last month’s deadly flash floods and mudslides along the Nepal-China border.
In a report, World Weather Attribution, including researchers from Nepal, Pakistan, the UK, Ireland, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, the US, New Zealand and the Netherlands, including experts in glaciology, climate science, humanitarian aid, seismology, and social science, examined the range of factors that contributed to the disaster, which killed over 1,400 people, with over 6,000 still missing, according to the latest figures.
"Climate change is thus best understood as a destabilising factor acting on a pre-existing geological predisposition, rather than the fundamental cause of the failure," the report said.
Although Nepal had early warning systems and adaptation measures, the incident "was beyond the design and predictive limits of existing risk reduction measures, and no existing early warning system could have provided sufficient lead time or prevented the scale of impacts observed in the worst-affected areas, highlighting the limits of adaptation," it said.
The disaster struck on Aug. 26 when a glacier on Nepal's Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of 5,200 meters (17,060 feet).
The fracture triggered an ice-rock avalanche that turned into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.
Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal's Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley.
The disaster also buried the Gyirong border crossing in Xizang.
According to the report, the fracture may have been preconditioned by a magnitude 7.8 earthquake in 2015, while warming, permafrost degradation, glacier thinning and retreat, increased rainfall, and unusually warm conditions likely contributed to the incident eventually occurring.
"Rapidly rising temperatures at a rate beyond the global mean as a result of fossil fuel emissions increase the likelihood and severity of such hazards in the Himalayas," it said.
The report called for stronger adaptation measures, including improved high-Himalaya earth observation, hazard monitoring, risk communication, and transboundary data sharing, as well as a rapid transition away from fossil fuels and delivery of climate finance commitments to reduce future risks.

Rental prices in Kyiv, Odesa decline amid enemy shelling - LUN
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:33:00 EEST
01:33:00 KST

Intense enemy shelling over the past month has driven down apartment rental prices in Kyiv by 3% and in Odesa by 11%, the LUN Statistics service has reported.
"Since mid-2022, shelling has had very little direct effect on rental prices, especially in the economically active capital - the market adapted, and demand stabilized despite regular attacks. What we're seeing in Kyiv now is the first signal in a long time that the intensity of strikes on the capital is again affecting people's willingness to pay rent in that particular city," said Liudmyla Kiriukhina, head of LUN Statistics, whose words were cited in the statement.
According to LUN, as of September 2026, the rent for one-bedroom apartments in Kyiv has fallen by 3% over the month, averaging 18,000 hryvnias per month. Over the year, rent in the capital has remained unchanged overall. In Odesa, the price has fallen by 11% compared with a month earlier, to 13,400 hryvnias per month, but is up 12% compared with the same period of 2025.
In the west of the country, by contrast, the trend is upward. In Lviv, for example, one-bedroom apartment rental prices rose by 9% over the month, to 26,900 hryvnias per month. Over the year, rent in the city has risen by 43.5%, the analytics portal reported.
In Uzhhorod, the price rose by 8% over the month (up 40% year-on-year), to 29,100 hryvnias per month, while in Ivano-Frankivsk it rose by 11% (up 42% year-on-year), to 22,400 hryvnias per month.
LUN noted that the rental market in the capital and in Odesa remains active despite the shelling: a one-bedroom apartment in Kyiv is rented out in an average of four days, and in Odesa in five days, while finding a tenant in Lviv takes an average of six days.
"One possible factor is internal migration, both between cities and between districts within the same city. Ahead of the new heating season, the characteristics of the housing itself may also matter more to tenants: autonomous heating and power supply, a nearby shelter, and the building's readiness for possible outages," LUN experts explained.

"There are many domestic issues usually that are predominantly in terms of priority. With the American voter, with the average US voter, there are many other domestic priorities," Boulos concluded.

Britain contracts drone-ship sensors to track air threats
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
17:30:21 BST
01:30:21 KST

Project HORUS, the Royal Navy effort to deploy persistent air-search sensors on uncrewed maritime platforms, is now under contract as the service moves ahead with a distributed system intended to detect and track airborne threats.
The status of the project was confirmed in a written parliamentary answer from Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard, following a question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty asking for the scope of the programme.
Pollard said: “Project HORUS is supporting urgent operational requirements for a rapidly procured, persistent air-search capability using uncrewed maritime platforms fitted with sensors to detect, track, identify and report airborne threats. The project is on contract and is intended to help the Royal Navy generate distributed sensing that reduces risk to personnel, and will inform future procurement decisions.”
The confirmation represents a step forward from the market-engagement stage reported by the UK Defence Journal in March, when the Navy was seeking mature systems that could be brought into service at pace. At that point, the requirement called for “a rapidly procured and persistent air search capability” able to detect, track, identify and report threats including drones, fast jets and cruise missiles from sensors carried aboard maritime platforms.
The original market notice envisaged moving rapidly from industry engagement to an initial capability. It stated that the intention was to select credible solutions, place contracts and deliver the first capability within four to six months, with an emphasis on mature products and suppliers able to work quickly.
HORUS is built around distributing sensors across multiple lower-cost uncrewed platforms rather than relying entirely on crewed ships or a small number of high-value assets.
The earlier requirement described a “System of System Approach” intended to introduce greater mass through numerous lower-cost sensors operating from uncrewed platforms in areas where sending personnel could carry greater risk. Persistence was also central to the concept. The March requirement sought platforms capable of remaining on station for 30 days as a threshold requirement and as long as 90 days as an objective, without in-person human intervention or maintenance.
The performance targets outlined during that earlier market engagement included the detection of NATO Class 2 uncrewed aircraft, anti-ship and land-attack cruise missiles and third and fourth-generation fighter-bombers at distances of at least 15 nautical miles.
Industry was also asked to consider how the system could eventually be expanded to detect surface threats, including fast attack craft and uncrewed vessels. The initial requirement envisaged persistent surveillance across an area of around 2,500 square kilometres, pointing towards several sensor-carrying platforms operating together rather than a single picket.
Alternative commercial approaches were also being considered, including what the Navy described as “SENSE as a service”, potentially allowing industry to provide the sensing effect rather than Defence purchasing every element outright.
Those figures and performance requirements were set out during the earlier market-engagement phase and do not necessarily describe the final contracted configuration. Pollard’s latest answer confirms, however, that HORUS has moved beyond that initial stage and is now on contract in support of an urgent operational requirement.

UN food agency scales up Yemen response as fighting displaces 125,000 people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:29:35 UTC
01:29:35 KST

Sahin Demir
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
The World Food Program (WFP) said Thursday it is scaling up its emergency response in Yemen after renewed fighting along the western coast displaced an estimated 125,000 people within days.
The UN agency said it has already provided food assistance to 45,000 people and is preparing to assist an additional 1.5 million if the conflict intensifies. It warned that critically low funding could limit the scale and speed of the response.
“Every day the conflict spreads, more families are forced to leave their homes, markets are disrupted, and people’s ability to access food becomes severely restricted,” said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP representative and country director in Yemen.
WFP said many displaced families are heading toward Aden, Al Maafer and other areas, with displacement expected to increase as front lines shift.
It said clashes in the port city of Mokha since Sept. 9 have affected its programs, offices and facilities, with WFP premises breached and at least 49 food distribution points becoming inaccessible.
The violence has also forced families to cross into Djibouti, where more than 2,400 people arrived within a few days, with more expected, it added.
WFP warned that more than 18 million people, roughly half of Yemen’s population, face acute food insecurity, while 2.2 million children under the age of 5 are acutely malnourished, including 500,000 suffering from severe acute malnutrition.
The agency said it needs $274 million to sustain emergency food assistance, nutrition programs, school meals and other humanitarian operations through 2027.
Yemen’s western coast has seen a sharp escalation in fighting, with the Houthis recently advancing to the strategic port city of Mocha near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The Houthis have controlled the national capital, Sanaa, and large parts of northern and western Yemen since 2014. The internationally recognized government and allied forces control areas in the south and east.

Italy-sized no-fly zone to be created around Beijing after rare crash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:29:00 UTC
01:29:00 KST

A vast airspace security zone roughly the size of Italy is set to be established around Beijing, barring all but commercial, approved business and emergency flights, a report said Thursday, months after a small aircraft crashed into the Chinese capital's tallest building.
A permanent 600-kilometer-wide circle of "Special Restricted Area" centered around Beijing will take effect from Sept. 20, Reuters reported, citing an aviation notice attributed to Beijing airspace control authorities and available through the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration's public NOTAM search system.
The entire airspace, from ground to unlimited altitude, will be closed for all flights except for commercial airline flights, approved business flights and military, customs, police and fire-rescue flights, the notice showed.
The over 280,000-square-kilometer zone encompasses Beijing and Tianjin, much of Hebei, and extends into parts of Inner Mongolia, Shanxi, Shandong, Liaoning and the Bohai Sea. By a rough geographic estimate, some 100 million people and dozens of airports and smaller airfields fall within its bounds.
The zone is among the largest permanent airspace restrictions imposed over a capital city. It follows a rare breach of Beijing's tightly controlled skies that raised questions about security gaps in the airspace around the Chinese capital.
A light sport aircraft crashed into the 108-storey CITIC Tower in Beijing's central business district on June 26. Local authorities said the crash killed the sole pilot and injured 13 others who were not on board.
The 66-year-old pilot, who authorities said had repeatedly mentioned ending his life in his diary, deviated from his approved flight area and lost contact with a general aviation airport in Beijing's suburbs from which he took off, official reports said.
All exempt flights operating inside the new restricted zone must strictly follow the pre-approved flight plan, report and obtain approval for any potential deviation, and maintain continuous two-way radio communication with air traffic control, the notice showed.
Aircraft are required to have surveillance and identification equipment on board that would allow air traffic controllers to identify and track them continuously and electronically. Pilots must also report "security status" before entering the restricted zone, the notice said.
Chinese state media said over the weekend a "Capital No-Fly Zone" would be established over Beijing from Sept. 20, without specifying the exact size and scope of the restricted area.
"To strengthen airspace security management in the capital region, maintain order in aerial operations, and protect important targets on the ground and the lives and property of the public ... China will designate a no-fly zone in and around the capital," the state-run Beijing Daily said Sunday.

This photo taken on Sept. 16, 2026 shows a view at a side event themed "Artificial Intelligence (AI) Empowering Human Rights Development" during the 63rd session of the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva, Switzerland. TO GO WITH "China hosts event themed 'AI empowering human rights development' in Geneva" (Xinhua/Lian Yi)
GENEVA, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- A side event themed "Artificial Intelligence (AI) Empowering Human Rights Development" was held Wednesday during the 63rd session of the United Nations Human Rights Council.
Co-hosted by the Permanent Mission of China to the United Nations Office at Geneva and the China NGO Network for International Exchanges, the event brought together nearly 100 participants, including representatives from over 20 countries, heads of non-governmental organizations, and experts, and engaged in in-depth discussions on strengthening global AI governance and fostering the advancement of human rights.
Wang Nian, Counselor of the Permanent Mission of China to the United Nations Office at Geneva, said China is committed to responding to the calls of the Global South and uniting the international community to leverage AI in support of human rights protection.
China has presented a series of joint statements at the Human Rights Council regarding the role of AI in promoting human rights and introduced a thematic resolution on "accessibility for all," Wang said.
China advocates for a people-centered, inclusive, and mutually beneficial approach, aiming to empower groups such as persons with disabilities, the elderly, women, and children through AI, while ensuring their equal participation in social life, Wang added.
Liu Zhenzhong, Deputy Secretary-General of the China NGO Network for International Exchanges, shared his insights and practical experiences regarding the use of AI by Chinese civil society organizations in natural disaster relief.
Emphasizing that AI is a double-edged sword offering new opportunities for the advancement of human rights while posing potential governance risks, he called on the international community to fully leverage the role of civil society organizations as bridges and links, improve the global AI governance system, and ensure that the fruits of intelligent technology serve the development of human rights in all countries in a fair and inclusive manner.
Attendees shared their perspectives on how AI empowers the advancement of human rights from various angles.
Lu Xiaoguang, Vice President of Presidium of Beijing Disabled Persons' Federation, outlined how Beijing is advancing the practical application of assistive technologies, such as brain-computer interfaces and smart assistive devices, through a three-pronged approach involving institutional safeguards, technological innovation, and industrial empowerment.
By building a comprehensive ecosystem for technology-driven disability support, the city employs intelligent solutions to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of persons with disabilities -- including convenient living and equal development -- in a holistic and precise manner, he said.
Wu Jianshe, Project Officer of Neijing NGO Network for International Exchanges, addressed the core theme of the "right to be heard."
He shared practical achievements in using AI to help individuals with conditions such as stuttering and Alzheimer's disease overcome communication barriers.
Moreover, he also detailed experiences in developing Beijing's multilingual public service platform, highlighting how intelligent public services can precisely safeguard the basic rights of the public.
Kevin Lau Chung-hang, Founding Convener of the Hong Kong Global Professional Youth Initiative, shared successful practices from Hong Kong, China, in leveraging AI to empower human rights protections across sectors such as healthcare and public welfare.
Highlighting the significant digital and healthcare development gaps facing the Global South, he called for strengthened cross-border and inter-regional non-governmental cooperation to precisely bridge the North-South development divide and promote inclusive development where smart technologies advance human rights for all.
David Lopez, representative of Association AIDHDES, said the current global landscape of smart services is characterized by unequal resource distribution and supply imbalances.
He urged nations to accelerate the development of public AI infrastructure and establish inclusive smart service systems that benefit the entire population, while breaking down technological barriers to ensure that countries and groups from all backgrounds can equitably share the dividends of AI development.
Ayyoub Mihoubi, founder of IBRAA Autism Institute, Algeria, shared innovative applications of AI technology in the early screening, rehabilitative intervention, and family guidance for autism.
Through digital and intelligent support models, these technologies effectively alleviate the caregiving burden on families of individuals with special needs, providing this group with professional and accessible social welfare and developmental support, he said.
Jasdev Rai, director of Sikh Human Rights Group, pointed out that AI holds significant value in areas such as poverty alleviation, public healthcare, and ecological governance, effectively contributing to the improvement of people's livelihoods.
At the same time, he said technological development must adhere to ethical bottom lines and establish robust risk prevention and control mechanisms to ensure that AI develops safely, for the greater good, and in an inclusive manner. ■

BANGKOK, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's primary energy consumption rose 0.9 percent year-on-year in the first half of 2026, as higher electricity and natural gas demand outpaced a slip in oil use amid high prices linked to the Middle East conflict, official data showed on Thursday.
According to Thailand's Energy Policy and Planning Office, the uptick was in line with economic growth of 2.4 percent in the first six months, although growth slowed to 1.9 percent in the second quarter from 2.8 percent in the first.
Nationwide electricity use increased 6 percent to 109,846 gigawatt-hours between January and June, driven by rises of 10.2 percent in household demand and 7.4 percent in commercial demand.
Natural gas consumption climbed 8.5 percent to 4,937 million cubic feet per day, mainly for power generation. Gas-fired plants supplied 61 percent of the Southeast Asian country's electricity generation.
Refined fuel use fell 0.8 percent to 142.7 million liters per day. Diesel demand dropped 2.4 percent owing in part to higher prices, while gasoline and jet fuel each rose 1.1 percent. Jet fuel demand was supported by higher air passenger and cargo volumes.
Coal and lignite use fell 16.5 percent, partly due to reduced operations at a lignite power plant.
The shift toward electric vehicles (EVs) continued. Cumulative pure-EV registrations stood at 491,496 units as of June, up 66 percent from a year earlier, and power use at charging stations surged 87.1 percent.
The office forecasts full-year primary energy demand at 2.04 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, up 1.4 percent after a 1.6 percent decline in 2025.
It expects natural gas use to rise 8 percent, oil use 0.1 percent, and hydropower and imported electricity 5.9 percent, while coal and lignite use is projected to drop 15.6 percent. ■

====================================================================================================

After a Self-Immolation at the UN, Rethinking What Beijing Fears on Tibet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:28:00 UTC
01:28:00 KST

On July 2, Lobga Rangzen, a Tibetan man who had taken the word meaning “independence and freedom” as his name, set himself on fire outside the United Nations headquarters in New York. His act came one day after China’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law took effect. In a video posted before his death, he denounced the law as an erasure of Tibetan identity and called on Tibetans-in-exile to take up their responsibility.
He chose the spot deliberately, too. Tibetans have looked to the U.N. for redress since 1950, when Tibet’s appeal first went to the new global body. The General Assembly passed resolutions on Tibet in 1959, 1961, and 1965. The 1961 resolution explicitly invoked Tibetans’ right to self-determination. Yet after the People’s Republic took China’s U.N. seat in 1971, the issue vanished from the organization’s agenda. Rangzen’s self-immolation was an indictment of six decades of silence.
For weeks after his death, Tibetan communities across the globe marched and demonstrated. CNN, Radio Free Asia, and others covered it; the U.N. secretary-general’s spokesperson offered condolences, and the U.S. State Department reaffirmed its support for Tibetans. Then, within days, the coverage vanished. No government went beyond boilerplate statements of sympathy.
For decades, the Central Tibetan Administration’s envoys and Tibetan human rights organizations have worked in Geneva, Washington, and Brussels with extraordinary persistence, winning legislation like the Resolve Tibet Act. Beijing’s position has never varied: Tibet is an “inalienable part of China.” The one channel that did exist, nine rounds of talks with the Dalai Lama’s envoys between 2002 and 2010, produced nothing, and those talks have been moribund for over 15 years.
The strategy of seeking international support to enact change in Tibet has run its course. The world has heard Tibetans cry out since 1959. Sympathy has calcified into routine: statements, condemnations, calls for dialogue. There is little prospect that external pressure alone will move the Chinese Communist Party on Tibet, and no government has shown any willingness to go beyond words.
But Beijing fears a different kind of pressure, one that comes from inside the Chinese-speaking world.
China’s Real Fear
A year ago, Chinese state security police in Changsha detained Zhang Yadi, a 22-year-old Han Chinese student who had been studying in France, on suspicion of “inciting separatism.” Her offense: writing and editing for Chinese Youth Stand for Tibet (华语青年挺藏会), a bilingual Han-Tibetan exchange platform I founded. Zhang was born and raised in Hunan, Mao’s home province, to Han parents. Nearly all of our members are also ethnically Han.
Many people asked why a Han Chinese person would risk prison for Tibetans. The more useful question is why Beijing treated a small volunteer media project as a state security threat and detained a college student over it.
The CCP understands that its rule in Tibet rests not only on security spending but on the acquiescence of the Han majority – an acquiescence manufactured through decades of disinformation. Since 1959, state propaganda has taught Chinese citizens that old Tibet was a barbaric serf society, that the Dalai Lama was its greatest slaveholder. One particularly enduring myth holds that Tibet’s Buddhist monks made drums out of human skin. A hit 1990s song to that effect, “Sister Drum” (阿姐鼓), was written by a Han composer who knew the story only secondhand, from siblings who had traveled to Tibet. Chinese internet users still cite the song as evidence of Tibetan savagery.
According to the CCP’s preferred narrative, the People’s Liberation Army was Tibet’s savior, and occupation is liberation. Ordinary Chinese people don’t defend the CCP’s Tibet policy out of malice; most sincerely see no case against it.
Han acceptance of this narrative is the foundation for CCP rule in Tibet – but it is more fragile than it looks. In 2025, the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR) raised just 31.8 billion yuan in local revenue against 310 billion in spending. Central transfers of 253.88 billion yuan, more than 80 percent of the budget according to the TAR’s budget reports, filled the gap, funding both livelihood programs and a vast stability-maintenance apparatus. And that budget excludes spending in the Tibetan areas of Qinghai, Sichuan, Gansu, and Yunnan.
There is already simmering resentment of these policies. On the Chinese internet, a segment of Han nationalists already ask why the government grants ethnic minorities college-entrance bonus points and what it derides as “super-citizen treatment.” As China’s economy slows, complaints about the fiscal burden are growing sharper. That resentment is combustible, as ready to turn on minorities as on the CCP.
The party can ignore foreign condemnation, but not a public at home that calls into question Beijing’s rule in Tibet. Han Chinese who speak fluently to that public, using the Chinese language and Chinese platforms, are the CCP’s nightmare on the ethnic frontier. More and more Han Chinese resent CCP policies in Tibet. Our aim is to redirect the questions they are already asking. Instead of “why are we paying for them?” we ask: “What is this money actually buying, and who does it benefit?”
The Dalai Lama grasped the importance of Han Chinese partnerships decades ago. He appointed Chinese liaison officers at Tibetan offices worldwide and built his Middle Way Approach partly around winning Chinese hearts. But the CTA’s Chinese-language capacity has withered; the Chinese sections of exile institutions have become marginal afterthoughts.
Our group, Chinese Youth for Tibet, formed organically on the Chinese-language internet, among young people fluent in its idiom. Tibetans welcomed us because that gap had gone unfilled for so long.
Falling Between “Two Desks”
Other Han Chinese have taken up the cause before. Grace Wang, a Duke student, was buried in nationalist abuse in 2008 for merely trying to mediate between pro-Tibet and pro-China protesters. The late historian Li Jianglin, born into a Communist family, spent years recording exile Tibetans’ oral histories; her “Tibet in Agony” reconstructed why the Dalai Lama fled in 1959. In July, police in Lhasa detained Zhang Yi, a pro-democracy activist since 1989, for displaying a photograph of the Dalai Lama at Sera Monastery, and formally arrested him on July 28.
One by one, Han Chinese keep arriving at a shared sense of historical responsibility. My moment came in 2018, while teaching at a Tibetan middle school; the government forcibly closed that school two years ago.
Yet groups like Chinese Youth for Tibet fall into an institutional blind spot. When Zhang Yadi was arrested, concern stopped at her as an individual; almost no Tibetan or Western outlet has interviewed our organization to ask what we do, or why Han Chinese would stand up for Tibet at all. Our proposals to foundations disappear without reply. A veteran colleague told me recently: you have fallen into the gap between two desks.
In international media, government bureaucracies, and foundations, the “Tibet desk” and the “China desk” are separate worlds. Most China specialists pay little attention to Tibet. Tibet specialists know little of Chinese administration, law, or society – especially in the Tibetan areas outside the TAR, where most Tibetans live.
This gap explains why Chinese-speaking advocates for Tibet working to raise awareness using Chinese language platforms remain unfunded, uncovered, and unprotected – even as Beijing prosecutes our members as state security threats. The CCP takes our work seriously enough to prosecute it. Western foundations and newsrooms have yet to really register our existence.
Han and Tibetan people have been neighbors for millennia. We drink from the same rivers, and our futures are bound together long after this regime is gone. For that reason, I believe the rise of Han Chinese-driven activism is one of the most strategically significant developments in the Tibet issue.
International advocacy kept Tibet’s cause alive for more than 70 years, and that work must continue. But the diminishing returns were made all too tragically obvious by Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation. He burned to death on the U.N.’s front steps and the world barely noticed.
The international community is not going to change Tibet’s fate. What could still make a difference is a growing awareness among China’s Chinese-speaking majority. Whoever wants to change Tibet’s future should start funding and covering the people doing this work, and protecting them.

PROFILE – Magdalena Andersson: Sweden’s first female premier returns to center stage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:27:23 UTC
01:27:23 KST

Sweden's left-wing opposition has won a narrow majority in the country's parliamentary election, paving the way for Social Democratic Party leader Magdalena Andersson to return as prime minister after four years in opposition.
After the final votes were counted, the results showed that the four parties backing Andersson had won 176 of the 349 seats in parliament, compared with 173 seats for the right-wing bloc led by incumbent Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson.
For Andersson, the election opens the way for a return to the job she became the first woman to hold in Swedish history.
"The Swedish people have voted to take Sweden forward, and I want to realize the new direction that you have voted for," she said in her victory speech.
"And to all of you who have chosen to vote for a party other than mine, I want to say to you that you have my full respect. I will work hard to earn your trust as well," Andersson added.
However, the result does not guarantee Andersson a return to office.
Sweden's fragmented parliament means that forming a government could require difficult negotiations between parties with different priorities.
From finance minister to first female prime minister
Andersson's political career has been shaped by economics, government and the Social Democratic movement.
Born in Uppsala on Jan. 23, 1967, she joined the Social Democratic youth movement at 16 and quickly rose through its ranks.
She studied economics at the Stockholm School of Economics and later studied at Harvard University and the Institute for Advanced Studies in Vienna.
Andersson entered government service in the 1990s, becoming a political adviser to Prime Minister Goran Persson.
She subsequently served as his director of planning and later held senior positions at the Ministry of Finance and the Swedish Tax Agency.
In 2014, she became finance minister under Prime Minister Stefan Lofven.
For seven years, Andersson was one of the most influential figures in Swedish economic policy.
Then, in November 2021, she made history.
After Lofven stepped down as Social Democratic leader and prime minister, Andersson succeeded him and became Sweden's first woman prime minister.
Her path to office, however, was anything but straightforward.
Turbulent start
Andersson's first experience as prime minister lasted only hours.
After parliament rejected her proposed budget and adopted an opposition-backed alternative, the Green Party left her government.
Andersson resigned rather than lead a government whose parliamentary legitimacy she believed had been undermined.
Days later, she was back.
She was successfully re-elected as prime minister on Nov. 29, 2021.
She returned as head of a Social Democratic minority government and became Sweden's first female prime minister.
Andersson promised to strengthen the welfare state, tackle segregation and gang crime, and restore what she described as greater democratic control over schools, healthcare and elderly care.
Under Andersson, Sweden abandoned its longstanding policy of military non-alignment and applied to join NATO.
She remained prime minister only until the 2022 election.
Since losing office, Andersson has remained leader of the Social Democrats and one of Sweden's most prominent political figures.
Comeback
Her political message in 2026 has focused heavily on the cost of living, welfare, healthcare, schools, economic growth, security and social cohesion.
Her party argues that Sweden has become more divided and that government policy should put greater emphasis on ordinary working households.
She pledged to raise taxes on banks and high earners to strengthen the welfare system, including reducing healthcare waiting times and helping struggling families cover their bills.
The Sept. 13 election has given Andersson something she did not have after the 2022 vote: a plausible route back to government.
The election has given Andersson the first move.
Now she must turn a razor-thin parliamentary advantage into a functioning government.
Among supporters and opponents alike, Andersson is known for her directness.
Her forceful political style has earned her the nickname "Bulldozer", a reflection of her reputation for pushing through negotiations rather than avoiding confrontation.
That style could prove useful in the negotiations ahead.

French PM to propose €54B budget squeeze for 2027

Sébastien Lecornu after the weekly council of ministers in the main courtyard of the Élysée Presidential Palace in Paris. | Bastien Ohier/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said his government’s budget for 2027 will include a staggering €54 billion in savings as he attempts to contain the country’s growing deficit in a year that’s seen little to no economic growth.
In an excerpt of an interview published by French daily Le Figaro, Lecornu said that without any cuts, the budget deficit would spike to 6.5% of gross domestic product — making it all but impossible for the government to keep its promise to the European Commission to get that figure to 3% of GDP by 2029.
“These savings will serve to considerably curb the growth of spending, which has been rising inexorably year after year” due to an aging population which increases health and old-age-related costs, Lecornu added.
Advertisement
France has in recent years struggled to rein in spending and a debt burden that has grown from €2.3 trillion to more than €3.5 trillion and is becoming increasingly expensive to service as interest rates spike across the world. Lecornu, who vigorously opposes tax hikes on any segments of the population, said the country needs to find an additional €10 billion to finance the debt.
“The debt burden is weighing increasingly heavily on the budget equation,” he said.
Lecornu said the 2027 budget deficit target was 5%, while the hope is to contain this year’s deficit to less than 5.5%
The French government had initially planned on reducing its deficit to 4.7% of GDP this year — but acknowledged last week that the figure would ultimately land above 5%. It also cut its growth forecast for this year and next year to 0.5% in 2026 and 1% in 2027.
The government targeted €30 billion in the 2026 budget and €60 billion the year prior.
Lecornu’s minority government will present its budget bill to lawmakers in the coming weeks, but getting it passed will be difficult without a governing majority and as the spring 2027 presidential election gets closer, which will incentivize parties to stake out their positions ahead of an electoral cycle.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim reaffirmed earlier this week that his country would not allow shipping linked to Israel's military to transit, amid reports that several Israel-bound containers had been seized.
“Malaysia’s position is clear and unequivocal. We will not allow our country to be used as a conduit for any shipment that supports or contributes to Israel’s military capabilities and its atrocities against Palestinians and other innocent lives," Anwar said in a statement on X.
“Any suspicious shipment will be subject to inspection and investigation in accordance with Malaysian law. Where a violation is established, decisive action will be taken".
On Tuesday, Bloomberg reported that three Israel-bound containers were seized in mid-August at Malaysia's Tanjung Pelepas port, citing anonymous sources. Manifests seen by the financial news outlet said that the containers carried electric bike parts from a Chinese manufacturer.

Malaysia has no formal diplomatic ties with Israel, and is prohibited from trade with Tel Aviv by its own customs regulations. The country's 2010 Strategic Trade Act also bans transhipment of military and strategic dual-use goods.
The latest seizures by Malaysia's government indicate a tightening of transit controls in the Southeast Asian country, which has long been vocal on the Palestinian cause.

Jeffrey Epstein’s estate is facing a new lawsuit filed by two women who allege that Epstein possessed child sexual abuse material (CSAM) of them. They want a judge to order that a program be set up to identify and notify all individuals whose “unlawful sexualized images” might have been in Epstein’s collection, and are also seeking monetary damages.
The complaint was filed this week in the US district court for the southern district of New York on behalf of two plaintiffs, who are anonymous in the filing but described as survivors of Epstein’s CSAM crimes. The lawsuit was filed against Epstein’s former lawyer Darren Indyke and Epstein’s former accountant Richard Kahn, who are being sued in their capacities as co-executors of Epstein’s estate. Attorneys for Indyke and Kahn, who have both said that they had no knowledge of Epstein’s crimes during their employment, did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the complaint on Wednesday.
The complaint claims that for more than two decades, Epstein, who died in a Manhattan jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges, possessed, transported, produced and distributed “child pornography and/or child sexual abuse material of countless children”. It alleges that Epstein “acquired by theft” nude or partly nude images of the first plaintiff, referred to in the document as Jane Doe, and that he transported the material across state lines and retained it.
The lawsuit argues that many of those depicted in the CSAM that they say was possessed by Epstein have never been identified or notified through the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s victim-identification program.
With regard to the second plaintiff, identified in the complaint under the pseudonym “Amy”, the lawsuit alleges that “upon information and belief, Epstein acquired CSAM images” of her.
The complaint alleges that beginning in the 1990s, Epstein “created and kept” in his locked safe in his New York City home a “‘modeling book’ of sexualized images of children”. It further alleges that beginning in “at least in the 2000s, Epstein had his assistant take nude, sexualized photographs of multiple children, paid them for the images, and then used those photographs for his own sexual gratification and perhaps that of others”.
Jane Doe alleges that she was around 12 years old when Epstein stole photographs of her partly nude, which the complaint claims had originally been taken “as part of an artist study for and catalogued, numbered and maintained by the artist in a lockbox”.
The lawsuit alleges that Epstein also “stole nude or partially nude photos of another minor” and transported these images across state lines. The complaint also alleges that “despite contemporaneous reports made to law enforcement, specifically alerting law enforcement that Epstein had obtained these photos of Jane Doe, and similar photos of another minor, no one in law enforcement took action to prosecute anyone or even investigate these reports”.
It adds that “upon learning that Epstein had possessed sexualized images of her as a child, Jane Doe suffered and continues to suffer severe emotional distress”.
“Amy” alleges in the complaint that she is a victim of “actively traded CSAM which has been in distribution since the late 1990s to present day”. The lawsuit alleges that “on information and belief” images of her are contained within the CSAM collection seized from Epstein’s properties.
In a statement to the Guardian, one of the lawyers representing the plaintiffs, Margaret Mabie, of Marsh Law, said that according to the released files, a report completed on Epstein’s collection identified 15 or more hits of known series like Amy’s and that “to our knowledge, none of the victims identified in that report, or in any other CSAM discovered in Epstein’s collection, have ever received notice”.
The complaint also alleges that other people, “including Epstein’s employees and/or coconspirators, had access to, viewed, or otherwise received from Epstein, the CSAM images in his possession, including images of Jane Doe and ‘Amy’”.
The two plaintiffs are bringing the lawsuit both individually and on behalf of a proposed class of other survivors they seek to represent, who are described as “all persons who were under the age of 18 at the time they appeared in any visual depiction of child pornography, including CSAM, contained within any image, video, or electronic media collections seized from properties or devices controlled by Jeffrey E Epstein, including the media identified in the Epstein Files Transparency Act productions and the materials described in the July 6, 2026, FBI and [justice department] memorandum”.
In a statement this week, Hillary Nappi, of AWK Survivor Advocate Attorneys, said that their goal with the lawsuit “is accountability and identification”.
“We want the estate to preserve and account for everything seized from Epstein’s properties, and we want a real, court supervised process to identify and notify every survivor depicted in that collection,” Nappi said. “Many of them have no idea their images exist in his files, and they deserve to know, and they deserve the chance to seek justice.
“Survivors have waited years for accountability, and this case opens the door for others depicted in his collection who don’t even know they’re in it,” Nappi added.

"When farmers' profit margins are weak or in many cases negative, throughout the US and for many farmers in the world, the depression of those margins leads to less output and ultimately that will feed into less food production globally."

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said Thursday that hate speech is exploiting new technologies and "spreading fast and striking deep" across societies worldwide.
Addressing a UN event on intercultural dialogue and countering hate speech, Guterres said the UN Charter's founding promise that "We the Peoples" would "practice tolerance and live together in peace with one another as good neighbors" has long been challenged by hate speech, which he said is now "taking on new forms … finding new pathways," and "weaponizing new technologies, from digital platforms and algorithms to artificial intelligence."
He said the growing reach "is testing our shared humanity," pointing to rhetoric that is "eroding trust, dividing communities, and dehumanizing entire groups" across continents.
Guterres urged renewed global action. "We must raise our collective voice and reject hatred," he said.
Efforts to counter hate speech must address "root causes and drivers as well as the consequences," and must be "grounded in respect and equity" while "shaped by women, men, and youth," he said.
"Reining in hate speech does not mean extinguishing freedom of expression," he said. "But freedom of expression must never be an excuse for causing or compounding harm."
He urged unity "to end the tragic cycles of fear, hatred, and violence" and to build "the cohesive and stable societies envisioned in our Charter."
UN General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman echoed the appeal, saying hate speech "rarely begins with words alone."
"It often grows from fear and a lack of understanding, or even contact with people of different faiths, cultures, and creeds," he said, warning that the sentiments are later "weaponized" by those with "malicious intent."
Rahman said dialogue and tolerance "are some of the strongest tools we have to wipe out the root causes of hate speech, and to cultivate trust, one of the strongest antidotes against prejudice, misinformation and hostility."
He added that restoring trust is "at the heart" of his vision for the 81st General Assembly session.

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: British settlers in occupied West Bank to face sanctions
The British government has already warned British Jewish settlers living in settlements in the occupied West Bank that they will fall under a new sanctions regime targeting illegal settlements, The New Arab has learned.
The warning included a reminder that people should be "aware of any new sanctions imposed under [the sanctions] regime", sources familiar with the ongoing discussions told TNA.
The warning was issued as part of the UK's latest position on the illegality of Israeli settlements under international law, the sources said, adding that London also urged people to take note of current official advice against conducting economic and financial activities in settlements.
There are no precise figures for the number of British citizens living in settlements in the occupied West Bank.
However, the British Foreign Office previously confirmed that its records indicated between 20 and 30 British citizens were living in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.
It cannot be confirmed whether those figures account for all British citizens living in settlements, as Britons are not required to notify British authorities of their presence there.
Around 840 Britons emigrated to Israel in 2025, according to recent data, marking the highest number since the 1980s. According to the latest estimates, around 40,000 British citizens live in Israel.
The Foreign Office said in 2025 that its estimates also showed that 80 British citizens who held only British nationality were serving in the Israeli military one month before the start of Israel's war on Gaza on 7 October 2023.
However, it did not indicate what roles they held in the Israeli military or whether any of them were serving in the occupied West Bank.
Earlier this year, official documents disclosed to British media outlets under the Freedom of Information Act showed that more than 2,069 British soldiers who held dual or multiple nationalities had served in the Israeli military.
Warnings about the new sanctions regime were also sent to British nationals in both Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories, sources told TNA.
The punitive measures target "specific trade and activities linked to settlements" and "do not target British citizens travelling to Israel or Palestine in general", the sources added.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament on 8 September that the government was working to establish a sanctions regime targeting illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.
According to Miliband, the regime, which he said would be implemented within six to nine months, includes a ban on trade in goods originating from illegal settlements.
It also includes a ban on advertising in Britain for the sale or promotion of land and property in those settlements.
Miliband also announced that the sanctions regime would include "appropriate religious exemptions", without explaining the nature of those exemptions.
Under the British government's new policy towards settlements, the sanctions regime will give British authorities powers to take action against individuals and companies that support, facilitate or profit from settlement activities.
Miliband said the government would also target companies and individuals providing services such as construction, infrastructure, financing and real estate for settlement expansion.
When Miliband was asked following his announcement in the House of Commons about the government's position on British Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank, he did not respond at the time, saying he would write to MPs on the matter.

Germany: Third malaria death linked to Frankfurt Airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:16:00 UTC
01:16:00 KST

Germany: Third malaria death linked to Frankfurt Airport
September 17, 2026
A person living near the Schwanheim district of Frankfurt died of malaria, local authorities said on Thursday. The incident is the third such death after a recent cluster of malaria cases linked to Frankfurt Airport emerged.
Two airport workers died of the disease in July and August.
Malaria is a life-threatening disease transmitted by mosquitoes and causes hundreds of thousands of deaths per year, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa. The disease is not common in Germany.
Schwanheim district, which borders the airport, registered two new malaria cases on Tuesday this week. Neither of the two infected individuals, both living in different households, had previously visited a malaria-endemic area and they did not work at Frankfurt airport.
Frankfurt health authorities extended their condolences to the relatives of the latest victims and said the two latest cases in the Schwanheim district were linked to an infected Anopheles mosquito that arrived in Germany by plane.
Germany's public health institute, the Robert Koch Institute, said malaria mosquitoes can fly between 5 and 10 kilometers (3 to 6 miles). The registered infections occurred some 5 kilometers away from the airport.
What is airport malaria?
Malaria cases in Germany normally involve people who have contracted the disease while traveling abroad. But in this instance, the cases are attributed directly to Frankfurt Airport.
Airport malaria can occur when an infected mosquito is transported on an aircraft or in luggage and then infects someone on the plane, at the airport or in the immediate surrounding area.
The RKI describes such cases as very rare, with the last documented case at Frankfurt Airport having been recorded in 2023.
Because patients may not have traveled to a malaria-risk area, the disease can also be diagnosed later than usual.
Mosquito traps have been installed at the airport. Mosquitoes captured there are being genetically analyzed at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp to determine their species and origin.
Still, Frankfurt Airport urged employees at the airport to seek medical attention if they develop symptoms.
