‘Bucha massacre’ a false flag orchestrated by UK – Moscow
Britain orchestrated the ‘Bucha massacre’ narrative to prolong the Ukraine conflict in 2022, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has said, citing a new investigation into the alleged victims.
Zakharova said new evidence proves that Bucha was a “brazen falsification” commissioned by Kiev’s foreign sponsors and amplified by the Western media to eliminate any chance of a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine.
She singled out the UK government as the primary organizer of the false flag operation, adding that the “key role” of spreading the story was assigned to the BBC.
In March 2022, Russian forces withdrew from Kiev Region, including Bucha, as a good-will gesture in support of a potential settlement at the Istanbul peace talks. Bucha Mayor Anatoly Fedoruk and residents initially said everything was calm and peaceful in the town, which is around 20 km from central Kiev.
Days later, images of bodies strewn across the streets of Bucha were broadcast by the Western media, supported by NATO-aligned OSINT fact checkers, triggering a storm of international accusations against Moscow that contributed to the collapse of peace talks.
Zakharova noted that there is still “no single website, no single figure, no lists – neither consolidated nor fragmented,” that would provide any verifiable information about the alleged victims of the Bucha ‘massacre’. The UN, Kiev, international organizations, and Western media have never provided a list despite repeated Russian requests.
The unverifiable nature of the incident strongly implies that it was falsified, and suggests that UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres knowingly made himself “part of this provocation,” Zakharova said.
Given that no public list of victims exists, Thursday’s report – which was presented by Maksim Grigoriev, the head of the International Public Tribunal on Crimes of Ukrainian Neo-Nazis – examined the names on the Bucha memorial instead – the closest thing to an official list, its authors say.
The memorial contains over 500 names and has repeatedly served as a backdrop for visits by Western leaders.
Grigoriev said researchers cross-checked the names against Ukrainian media, military records, and social-media accounts, and found that those they traced were Ukrainian servicemen, including Azov and territorial-defense fighters, rather than civilians allegedly murdered by Russian troops.
The soldiers were also found to have had little or no connection to Bucha, and were killed and buried nowhere near the town.
Among the examples cited were Evgeny Petrash and Vladimir Bisaga, who the investigation identified as Azov fighters buried in Kiev and Uzhgorod, respectively. Two other names, Ruslan Belousov and Roman Dovgalyuk, were identified as Ukrainian military pilots killed when their aircraft was shot down near Berezovka – far from Bucha.
The report also features a number of eyewitness accounts from several conflict-zone towns, pointing to a wider pattern of Ukrainian forces killing civilians and then blaming Russia once Western reporters arrive.
One witness said Ukrainian troops opened fire on civilians collecting water, with journalists arriving to film the aftermath within minutes.
Grigoriev said these testimonies show that Kiev repeatedly used civilian deaths to manufacture material for the Western media and claimed that the same method was used in Bucha.
Zakharova stated that the new findings will be submitted to Russian law enforcement, international organizations, and international courts. The investigators behind the report also urged foreign journalists to conduct their own examination.

Royal Navy ice patrol ship replacement still undecided
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:45:51 BST
00:45:51 KST

The procurement method and timetable for replacing HMS Protector remain undecided, more than two months after Defence confirmed that funding had been allocated for a successor to the Royal Navy’s Antarctic patrol ship.
The latest position was set out in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked when a decision would be made on both the method of procurement and the exact replacement timeline.
Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard said: “The Defence Investment Plan announced plans to replace HMS Protector with a more modern variant to maintain this essential presence and support Government activities in the Arctic and around the British Antarctic Territory. Decisions on the method of procurement and the exact replacement timeline will be taken in due course.”
The answer follows an earlier exchange in July, when Pollard confirmed that funding had been allocated for the replacement but said the schedule depended on a procurement route that had yet to be selected. At the time, he said: “The Defence Investment Plan has allocated funding to replace HMS Protector but the exact timeline for this replacement is subject to further work. This will depend on the method of procurement which is yet to be decided.”
The answer, in public at least, leaves the programme broadly where it stood in July, with a replacement funded in principle but the acquisition route and delivery schedule still to be settled. HMS Protector is the Royal Navy’s specialist ice patrol ship and operates primarily in the Antarctic, supporting British interests in the region, hydrographic survey work and wider government activity around the British Antarctic Territory.
The vessel began life as the Norwegian-built Polarbjørn, entering service as a commercial polar research and subsea support vessel before being chartered by the Royal Navy in 2011 as a temporary replacement for HMS Endurance. The ship was subsequently purchased outright in 2013 and has since become the Navy’s permanent Antarctic patrol vessel.
Protector is ice strengthened and designed for work in polar conditions, providing the UK with a regular naval presence in one of the most remote operating environments faced by the fleet. The Defence Investment Plan now commits the Government to replacing her with what Pollard described as a “more modern variant”, with the successor intended to maintain Britain’s presence not only around the Antarctic but also support activity in the Arctic.

The Bank of England is shaking up its bond sales – why does it matter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:45:42 UTC
00:45:42 KST

The Bank is selling off hundreds of billions of pounds worth of government bonds it bought via the emergency policy of quantitative easing during the financial crises and Covid. Photograph: Bank of England/PAView image in fullscreenThe Bank is selling off hundreds of billions of pounds worth of government bonds it bought via the emergency policy of quantitative easing during the financial crises and Covid. Photograph: Bank of England/PAExplainerThe Bank of England is shaking up its bond sales – why does it matter?What the plan to sell £146bn in gilts back to the Treasury means for the public finances Bank of England holds interest rates Burnham’s talk of ‘breathing space’ at odds with reality of future rate rises Mixed in with the Bank of England’s decision on Thursday to hold interest rates at 3.75% was a surprise announcement that it was shaking up its programme of quantitative tightening.So why is this apparently arcane change to QT important, and what does it mean for the public finances?What is QT?It is the Bank of England’s controversial process of selling off hundreds of billions of pounds worth of government bonds that it bought via the emergency policy of quantitative easing (QE) during the financial crises of 2008 and Covid.The Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) sees QT as the necessary unwinding of the massive balance sheet it built up. Its stockpile of bonds, known as gilts, has already been reduced from a peak of £895bn in February 2022, to £488bn.But critics on the right and left have complained that selling off significant quantities of government bonds costs the Treasury, as they are being sold at a loss.There have also been concerns that in a febrile bond market, large-scale sell-offs risk depressing prices – and thus driving up the yield, or interest rate, the government has to pay to borrow.What is the Bank looking to change?Instead of looking for private-sector buyers for its stock of gilts, the Bank plans to sell them directly to the Treasury instead.The Treasury’s debt management office (DMO), which has the job of doing the government’s borrowing for it, will then issue new bonds to cover the costs of those it has bought from the Bank.The Treasury sees this as simplifying what can be a messy process. As the chancellor, John Healey, put it in a letter to the Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, on Thursday: “This sales model … would see a return to a single public-sector supplier of gilts to the market.”It also has the advantage of allowing the DMO to tailor gilt sales to market demand, which currently favour gilts that mature over a shorter period, rather than the Bank having to sell off the 20- and 30-year dated gilts it still has on its books, for which there is less investor appetite.The yield, effectively the interest rate, on 30-year gilts dropped sharply on Thursday after the decision was announced, to 5.745% – and was on course for its biggest drop since 2020.No final decision has been made, however, despite the fact the Treasury, Bank and DMO have apparently been discussing the idea for a year. Healey has promised to make a final ruling in April – and until then, QT will be paused.Wasn’t QT already being slowed down?Yes. The Bank has run down its stock of gilts by £70bn this year. That included £20bn of actual sales; and another £50bn worth that reached their maturity date.Over the coming years, it plans to sell off £20bn of government bonds annually, alongside retiring gilts that reach maturity.That’s because the Bank is keen to avoid the risks of exacerbating already-fragile bond markets. The minutes of the MPC meeting revealed that members discussed offloading bonds at a faster rate; but “at a time when bond markets globally had been volatile, this risked destabilising markets”.The Bank also announced it would set aside about £120bn of the longest-dated government bonds it holds, as these are used to back the issuance of the UK’s bank notes.In total, the Bank expects to sell a total of £146bn of gilts between now and 2034 – at a steady pace of £20bn a year – back to the government, if Healey gives the plan the thumbs up.What’s the impact for the public finances?Analysts expect it to be modest. The Treasury may be able to finance its borrowing a bit more cheaply when the Bank is not selling a slew of long-dated bonds into the market. As analysts at the investment bank Jefferies put it: “Taken together, the changes imply a materially lower future supply burden, particularly for [long-dated gilts].”And to the extent that the pace of sales is slowing, the losses on those bonds, which is borne by the Treasury, will crystallise more slowly – another marginal upside.Jefferies also suggested that, by making its future plans clear, the MPC’s decision could “ease some of the pressure that had been building for changes to the Bank’s QT approach”.Explore more on these topicsQuantitative easingBank of EnglandBondsGiltsGovernment borrowingEconomic policyEconomicsexplainersShareReuse this content

cantilevered roof extends over frank lloyd wright’s concrete usonian house
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:45:20 UTC
00:45:20 KST

a frank lloyd wright house built partly by its owners
Frank Lloyd Wright’s Samuel and Dorothy Eppstein House has returned to the market in Galesburg, Michigan, with an asking price of $2.1 million. Completed in 1953, the low-slung Usonian residence sits within The Acres, a community Wright planned for a group of Upjohn scientists outside Kalamazoo. A broad cantilevered roof stretches across hand-cast concrete block walls, while mahogany-framed glazing opens the interiors toward the surrounding landscape.
The Eppsteins had a unusually hands-on relationship with the house. Samuel and Dorothy were both research scientists at Upjohn, and Dorothy had flown military aircraft during World War II as a Women Airforce Service Pilot. The couple helped fabricate some of the roughly 3,000 concrete blocks used in the construction. They also pushed back on parts of Wright’s original plan, asking for larger children’s bedrooms and a bigger kitchen with a window. Wright agreed.
Inside, the materials do much of the work. Cherokee red concrete floors run through an in-line plan with radiant heating embedded below, while the concrete block continues across interior walls. Mahogany frames the windows and doors. At the living area, tall glazing pulls the wooded site close to the rooms, reinforcing the long horizontal lines of the roof above.
The current listing records three bedrooms and two bathrooms across 2,500 square feet. Built-in furniture remains part of the architecture, alongside Wright-designed pieces that have stayed with the house. Its spaces retain the compact proportions associated with his Usonian work, opening outward through broad expanses of glass where the plan reaches the landscape.
Frank Lloyd Wright completed the Samuel and Dorothy Eppstein House in Galesburg in 1953
the eppstein house returns to market
The setting gives the house another layer of interest. Wright conceived The Acres across roughly 70 acres, with circular homesites surrounded by shared open land. Twenty-one houses were planned, though only four Wright-designed residences were ultimately constructed there. The Eppstein House occupies a two-acre property within that larger landscape.
Marika Broere and Tony Hillebrandt acquired the house in 2016 after years of deterioration and completed an extensive restoration the following year. The work renewed the roof and building systems while repairing the concrete floors and Wright-designed woodwork. Now listed by Signature Sotheby’s International Realty, the 1953 residence is back on the market for $2.1 million.

Russia launched a large-scale missile and drone attack on Ukraine overnight on 17 September, striking Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, and Odesa Oblast, among other regions.
The attack damaged civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, including apartment buildings and educational facilities, while water infrastructure was also affected. Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko reported 20 people injured, including at least two children.
Water infrastructure hit as winter concerns grow
The overnight strikes affected Kyiv’s water infrastructure, temporarily disrupting water supply on the left bank and reducing pressure in some areas on the right bank.
Kyivvodokanal said its specialists restored operations and that water supply is now fully functioning across the capital.
The damage comes as Ukrainian authorities have warned that Russia could target critical water infrastructure as winter approaches, potentially adding another major threat to civilians alongside attacks on Ukraine’s electricity and heating systems.
Russia has repeatedly used winter strikes to target Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, particularly electricity and heating, leaving civilians without power, heat, and basic services during freezing weather.
This winter is expected to bring a heavier campaign: Russia has intensified its attacks since the summer, increasingly targeting food-related infrastructure and supplies in addition to energy facilities.
No missiles intercepted, once again
Russia launched ballistic and cruise missiles alongside 157 Shahed-type attack drones and decoy drones, according to Ukraine’s Air Force.
The ballistic missiles included Iskander-M, S-400 and North Korean KN-23 missiles launched from Russia’s Bryansk and Voronezh oblasts. Russia also launched four Kalibr cruise missiles and Oniks missiles.
Ukraine’s air defenses reported destroying or suppressing 131 aerial targets, but none of the ballistic weapons were among those intercepted. The 131 targets consisted of seven Bandеrol/Dan-T missiles and 124 Shahed, Gerbera, and other drones.
Once again, Ukraine intercepted none of the Russian ballistic missiles, underscoring the country’s shortage of high-end air-defense interceptors needed to defend against Russia’s increasing ballistic missile attacks.
However, Ukraine’s General Staff reported strikes on two of the S-400 systems that Russia uses to launch ballistic missiles from Bryansk Oblast.
Ukraine strikes two Russian S-400 launchers in Bryansk. The same systems were used to attack Kyiv overnight.

The victims included a 10-year-old girl and a 12-year-old boy.
Kyiv’s military administration also reported a strike on a warehouse building in Podilskyi district.
The Air Force said Russian missiles and attack drones hit 36 locations across Ukraine, while debris from intercepted targets fell at five locations.
Russia also hits Odesa and Zaporizhzhia

Zaporizhzhia was also hit by Russian missiles, with three people injured – a woman and two men. The missiles struck industrial facilities, partially damaging buildings and causing a fire at one site.

One bomb hit a private house and outbuildings, killing a 51-year-old woman and injuring a 70-year-old man. Unknown Publisher

DAR ES SALAAM, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- The 28th Chinese medical team to mainland Tanzania provided specialized training in minimally invasive surgery for cerebral hemorrhage for neurosurgeons at Muhimbili Orthopedic Institute (MOI), Tanzania's national super-specialized hospital for orthopedics, trauma and neurosurgery.
The training, conducted on Wednesday and led by Ma Junwei, a neurosurgeon on the Chinese medical team, focused on using a portable surgical visualization device donated by a Chinese medical equipment company.
Ma said the device can connect directly to computers and mobile terminals, providing real-time, high-definition visualization during surgery without relying on large precision equipment such as operating microscopes and endoscopes.
The technology helps reduce intraoperative bleeding and postoperative infection risks, shorten surgery time, minimize surgical trauma and accelerate patient recovery while lowering treatment costs, Ma added.
Laurent Mchome, director of the neurosurgery department at MOI, described the training as practical and closely aligned with clinical needs. He said the donated equipment is easy to operate and will help address gaps in the department's equipment and technical capabilities.
Liu Jia, head of the Chinese medical team, said the training and equipment donation demonstrated the deepening healthcare cooperation between China and Tanzania.
The team will continue providing technical training, hands-on instruction and medical equipment support to strengthen Tanzania's healthcare capacity, Liu said. ■

LIMA, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The 3rd Congress of Latin American Sinologists has brought together experts and researchers from China and Latin America in the Peruvian capital to discuss development, connectivity, innovation, and cooperation between China and the region.
Under the theme "From Dialogue to Convergence: Institutionalization, Connectivity, and Common Horizons between Latin America and China," the forum aims to deepen understanding of China and explore new forms of cooperation amid growing global economic, technological, and diplomatic interdependence.

Waldo Mendoza, academic vice rector of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, said that the congress addresses issues shaping Latin America-China relations, including trans-Pacific connectivity, Chinese-language teaching and cross-cultural exchanges.
The three-day congress, which will last through Thursday, is organized by the Confucius Institute and the Center for Oriental Studies of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, together with the World Center for Sinology at Beijing Language and Culture University. ■

Pakistan announces austerity, fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel costs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
23:42:38 CST
00:42:38 KST

ISLAMABAD, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Pakistan's federal government Thursday announced a fresh round of austerity and fuel conservation measures effective immediately, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division, as authorities move to curb public spending amid rising fuel costs.
The measures, approved on the recommendations of a government committee tasked with monitoring fuel conservation and austerity, include a 50-percent cut in fuel provision for official vehicles for three months. The armed forces, civil armed forces, law enforcement agencies, essential services and the Federal Board of Revenue are exempt, except for their administrative or non-operational formations, and development projects remain unaffected.
The government has also ordered a 5-percent reduction in the non-employee-related expenditure for the current fiscal year 2026-27, to be deducted monthly, a measure that will extend to Pakistani missions abroad and staff posted there, though their rent, education and medical costs will still be covered.
A complete ban has been placed on the purchase of vehicles and durable goods, with the exception of information technology procurements. All foreign travel has been suspended for three months, including for otherwise mandatory engagements, with limited exemptions for scholarships and training arranged through official channels. Pakistani ambassadors will represent the country at important events abroad in place of visiting officials.
Under the new rules, government meetings will be held via teleconferencing where possible, official dinners have been suspended except for visiting foreign delegations, and government-funded seminars and conferences have been banned. Only a single dish will be permitted at wedding functions, according to the notification.
The directive also reaffirmed market closing times set earlier this year, requiring shops, malls and restaurants to shut between 9 p.m. and 11 p.m., while hospitals, pharmacies, gyms and IT-related businesses remain exempt.
The provincial and regional governments have also been encouraged to adopt similar measures.
Pakistan has repeatedly tightened public spending in recent years as it grapples with a difficult external financing position and elevated energy import costs. ■

Turkish authorities reassure investors after sharp stock sell-off

ISTANBUL, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Turkish financial authorities reassured investors on Thursday that there is no fundamental or structural risk to the country's stock market following a sharp sell-off, pledging swift measures to ease a liquidity squeeze concentrated in part of the fund market.
The Financial Stability Committee, chaired by Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek, convened early Thursday to assess developments in the capital markets after the benchmark BIST 100 index plunged more than 7.5 percent at one point on Wednesday.
In a post-meeting statement, the Ministry of Treasury and Finance said recent volatility stemmed from credit and liquidity problems at some funds managed by a limited number of portfolio management companies.
"There is no fundamental or structural risk concerning the functioning of Borsa Istanbul and our capital markets. The problem is concentrated in a specific segment of the fund market and is temporary and manageable," the ministry said.
The committee also discussed measures to ease liquidity pressures and prevent contagion risks while maintaining financial market stability, adding that regulatory and supervisory bodies would continue to act decisively against those engaged in market-disruptive activities, the statement said.
The online economy news platform Ekonomim attributed the sharp market downturn primarily to liquidity shortages at mutual funds following regulatory changes introduced by the Capital Markets Board on Aug. 28, which prompted increased redemption requests and added to liquidity pressures in the market.
According to Borsa Istanbul data, heavy selling on Wednesday triggered an index-based circuit breaker in the afternoon, with the BIST 100 ultimately closing 5.54 percent lower at 13,122.58 points. ■

Chinese intangible cultural heritage exhibition in London showcases contemporary design
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
23:42:16 CST
00:42:16 KST

This photo taken on Sept. 17, 2026 shows an exhibit on display in an exhibition titled "Reviving Craft: Reflection of the Mind," in London, Britain. An exhibition bringing together Chinese intangible cultural heritage and contemporary design opened at Somerset House in London on Wednesday, featuring nearly 150 works and sets of works by more than 70 Chinese and international artists. Titled "Reviving Craft: Reflection of the Mind," the exhibition is part of the 2026 London Design Festival and runs until Sept. 27. It features works in ceramics, lacquer, embroidery, glass, fiber art, furniture and installation. (Xinhua/Li Ying)
LONDON, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- An exhibition bringing together Chinese intangible cultural heritage and contemporary design opened at Somerset House in London on Wednesday, featuring nearly 150 works and sets of works by more than 70 Chinese and international artists.
Titled "Reviving Craft: Reflection of the Mind," the exhibition is part of the 2026 London Design Festival and runs until Sept. 27. It features works in ceramics, lacquer, embroidery, glass, fiber art, furniture and installation.
The exhibition is jointly curated by Su Dan, professor at the Academy of Arts and Design of Tsinghua University, and Yang Lan, chairperson of Sun Media Group.
Following previous editions in Paris in 2024 and Milan in 2025, the London exhibition focuses on the relationship between people and their inner world. It is divided into three sections themed around the Chinese concepts of Chengxin, or clearing the mind, Xiuxin, refining the mind, and Yangxin, nourishing the mind.
Among the works on display are Chinese sculptor Zhi Min's ceramic and metal work Moon, Shi Hui's paper-fiber work Seal Stone, lacquer artist Xue Xiaodong's screen inspired by The Ode to the Goddess of the Luo River, and Suzhou embroidery artist Yao Jianping's double-sided embroidery screen Nine Carps.
Traditional techniques including lacquerware, cloisonne, Suzhou embroidery, gambiered Guangdong silk and glassmaking are presented alongside contemporary art and design. Some works also bring traditional craftsmanship into furniture, fashion and other objects intended for everyday use.
Yang said the exhibition takes on particular meaning at a time when artificial intelligence is changing the way people create.
"Through making things by hand, we can rediscover human embodied intelligence and feel a connection that is tangible," she said at the opening ceremony. "It gives us strength and inspiration."
Yang said China and Britain both value craftsmanship and cultural heritage, expressing hope that the exhibition could help promote exchanges between the two countries, especially among younger people.
Li Liyan, minister counsellor at the Chinese Embassy in Britain, said intangible cultural heritage today carries significance beyond preservation and inheritance.
"It also needs to become part of contemporary life and face the future," Li said. He added that the exhibition offers overseas audiences a way to learn more about contemporary China and provides a platform for exchanges between China and Britain in culture, art and creative design.
Su has described design as "an important medium for transforming intangible cultural heritage," saying contemporary design can help traditional craftsmanship find new expressions and enter modern life.
The London exhibition is also a special project of this year's London Design Festival, which brings together exhibitions, installations and design events across the British capital. ■

Oscar-winning Russian director offers $1mn diamond prize at Moscow film awards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:40:49 UTC
00:40:49 KST

Oscar-winning Russian director offers $1mn diamond prize at Moscow film awards
Russia’s Oscar-winning film director Nikita Mikhalkov has chosen Moscow to host his Diamond Butterfly film awards for a second year despite several other countries looking to stage the ceremony.
The ceremony will take place at Mikhalkov’s Workshop 12 theater in Moscow on November 12, he announced on Thursday.
“This year, as last year, the awards ceremony will take place in Moscow, in our theater,” Mikhalkov said. “I am convinced that the mechanism for holding the ‘Diamond Butterfly’ needs to be refined where it was born.”
“Despite the fact that many countries would like to host the ceremony, we decided that this one and possibly the next one will be held in Russia,” he added.
The Diamond Butterfly is the main prize of the Eurasian Film Academy, an initiative founded by Mikhalkov to promote filmmaking and cultural exchange among participating countries. The award is organized by the Russian Culture Foundation with support from the Culture Ministry.
Films entered for the prize have been screened in Russia and abroad over the past year. Mikhalkov said that the screenings had introduced audiences to movies which previously received little attention internationally.
“The principles by which films are selected for the ‘Diamond Butterfly’, its key meanings and values, are attracting more and more attention to the film award today,” he said.
The Diamond Butterfly is billed as an alternative to mainstream Western film awards, placing emphasis on traditional values.
The inaugural ceremony was held in Moscow in November 2025, with an expert jury judging 34 films from 17 countries. Prizes were awarded in 12 categories.
Winners receive a Diamond Butterfly statuette designed by Russian artist Yuri Kuper and decorated with nearly 5,000 lab-grown diamonds. The Best Film winner also receives the ten-carat Yakut diamond worth $1 million.
Winners in other categories, including Best Director, Best Screenplay, Best Actor, and Best Actress, receive five-carat Yakut diamonds valued at $250,000 each.

Ireland boycotts Eurovision for second year over Israel’s inclusion

Ireland boycotts Eurovision for second year over Israel’s inclusion
Public broadcaster RTE says the country’s participation cannot be justified amid ‘appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza’.
Ireland has become the second country, after the Netherlands, to announce a boycott of next year’s Eurovision Song Contest over Israel’s participation.
Irish public broadcaster RTE said in a statement on Thursday that the country’s participation could not be justified “given the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza” and that the humanitarian crisis in the enclave “continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Justice prevailed’: Is the Netherlands shifting its stance on Israel?
- list 2 of 3Eurovision to bar countries at war from hosting: What that means
- list 3 of 3Dutch public broadcaster to boycott ‘no longer’ neutral Eurovision
RTE, which manages Ireland’s selection and participation in Eurovision, added that it remained “deeply concerned by the continued denial of independent access [for] international journalists to the territory”.
The decision marks the second consecutive year that Ireland will neither participate in nor broadcast the competition, which is the world’s most popular television music show.
Earlier this month, Eurovision organisers said they would exclude any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.
However, Dutch public broadcaster AVROTROS said the measure was not “sufficient”.
AVROTROS announced last month that it was withdrawing from the 2027 competition.
It said Eurovision could “no longer be considered neutral” given Israel’s participation in “a large-scale military conflict” in Gaza.
Both Ireland and the Netherlands were among five countries that withdrew from Eurovision 2026 in Vienna earlier this year. Spain, Slovenia and Iceland also decided not to participate.
‘The correct and principled decision’
Sinn Fein, Ireland’s main opposition party, welcomed RTE’s decision. The party’s spokesperson for Culture, Communications and Sport, Joanna Byrne, told Al Jazeera that Israel’s behaviour “cannot be normalised”.
“RTE’s decision to again boycott the Eurovision Song Contest is the correct and principled decision in the face of Israel’s ongoing genocide against the Palestinian people,” Byrne said.
She added that Israel is an “apartheid state” and accused it of engaging in “ethnic cleansing”.
“Israel, as an aggressor nation just like Russia, should have been banned when they engaged in genocidal actions, just like Russia.”
The European Broadcasting Union organises the annual music competition. It has faced accusations of applying a double standard for refusing to exclude Israel, despite banning Russia following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Eurovision Director Martin Green said on Thursday that organisers “fully respect” Ireland’s decision and that they “will be missed”.
“The Eurovision Song Contest is at its best when broadcasters and their artists from different countries come together to share music, celebrate creativity and create connections between audiences,” Green said.
“That power to bring people together is at the heart of what makes the Contest so special, and is even more important now in an increasingly difficult and divided world.”
The 2026 show, which Bulgaria won, attracted 132 million viewers, 34 million fewer than its 2025 edition.
Thousands of protesters had gathered outside the venue in the Austrian capital during the final in mid-May to oppose Israel’s participation.

Saudi Arabia, Houthis exchange blows as conflict escalates
September 17, 2026
At least five people were killed in the escalation between the Iran-backed Houthirebel group and the internationally recognized Yemeni government, supported by Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of a "cowardly" strike on Mecca, the holiest city in Islam and the site of the hajj and umrah pilgrimages, this week.
The rebel group denied the accusations.
Meanwhile, the Houthis claimed Saudi warplanes targeted three telecommunication towers in Taiz in southwestern Yemen.
According to the Almisrah TV channel, backed by the Houthis, one civilian was killed in the town of Abs in the northwest, with the channel later reporting that three children were killed by strikes carried out by Yemen's internationally recognized government.
In Saudi Arabia, one person was killed by shrapnel from a downed drone in the Mecca area, the country's civil defense agency said. Damage was also caused to buildings and vehicles.
This was the first reported death in Saudi Arabia in the current escalation between the two sides.
Houthis advance along coast after collapse of truce
A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia collapsed in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace. As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen's more populous western areas since the start of Yemen's civil war in 2014.
The rebel group has reported dozens of Saudi strikes since its recent offensive to secure control over the coastal areas near the Red Sea's Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes, from government hands.
The strait's importance has increased since Iran put restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz over the US and Israel's war with Tehran.
The conflict in Yemen has forced more than 100,000 people to flee their homes, according to UN figures.

How Russia’s liberal opposition broke the public’s trust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

How Russia’s liberal opposition broke the public’s trust
Russia’s liberal opposition has evolved from the optimism of the early post-Soviet era to exiled figures backing Western sanctions and calls for regional self-determination, RT’s Marina Kosareva reports. Some have gone as far as advocating Russia’s breakup into multiple states.
In a report aired on Thursday, Kosareva traces the movement from the hopes surrounding the collapse of the Soviet Union to the increasingly confrontational positions adopted by some opposition figures abroad.
”It all started with lots of hopes and dreams,” Kosareva says, recalling aspirations for “a better future, freedom, democracy.”
After Boris Yeltsin won Russia’s first presidential election in 1991, his government launched sweeping market reforms, including price liberalization and privatization. The transition brought severe economic disruption, soaring prices, and falling living standards, eroding public confidence in both the reforms and the political forces associated with them.
Throughout the 2000s and 2010s, opposition politicians continued to campaign for competitive elections, freer media, and political change.
”Some of them set up their own media outlets, often with Western funding, which led to the now infamous Foreign Agent Law,” Kosareva said.
As relations between Russia and the West deteriorated after 2014, some opposition figures began openly supporting Western sanctions and military aid to Ukraine.
”Russia must be kicked from all international organizations, including Interpol. Financial blockade must be full,” former world chess champion and opposition figure Garry Kasparov said in 2022.
Others went further, advocating self-determination for Russia’s national republics. A 2026 declaration backed by opposition figures called for transforming “imperial Russia into a modern democratic state or several democratic states.”
Kosareva asks whether liberalism has become permanently associated with foreign influence in Russia, or whether the problem lies with those who came to represent it.
”Either way, the trust has been broken,” she concludes.

ICC incapable of delivering ‘real justice’ – expert to RT (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:38:44 UTC
00:38:44 KST

ICC incapable of delivering ‘real justice’ – expert to RT (VIDEO)
The international community cannot expect “real justice” from the International Criminal Court (ICC), University of Indonesia international law professor Hikmahanto Juwana has told RT.
Juwana argued that the tribunal has undermined its claim to universal justice by disproportionately targeting weaker countries while powerful states evade accountability.
His comments came as former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte made his first in-person court appearance since his arrest in March 2025 on an ICC warrant. He faces crimes against humanity charges over alleged killings linked to his anti-drug campaign, which he has denied.
Juwana described the Hague-based ICC as “not a workable system,” arguing that political power inevitably shapes its ability to operate.
”There’s going to be a political domination of how the ICC will work,” he said in an interview aired on Wednesday. “The big states may use [their] influence and force not to abide with the ICC… And it is because of that […] we cannot expect real justice to be delivered by the ICC.”
Juwana questioned the court’s claim to represent “world justice,” noting that “most” of those brought before it come from countries “that are not powerful.” He argued that this imbalance was rooted in the ICC’s creation, which he said was driven by “European countries, especially the Western European countries.” From its inception, he added, the court appeared to target less powerful states, calling this “the failure of the ICC from the beginning.”
From the inception of the ICC, it was as if they were TARGETING countries who weren't very powerful — Hikmahanto Juwana Professor of International Law University of Indonesia to RT
'This is the ICC's FAILURE from the very beginning' pic.twitter.com/mhR4x3Hg7y
The ICC was established under the Rome Statute in 2002 to prosecute genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and aggression. It has 125 member states, but major powers including the US, China, India, and Russia, as well as Israel, remain outside the court and reject its authority.
Washington has sanctioned ICC President Tomoko Akane, along with judges, prosecutors, and other court staff, over cases involving US and Israeli nationals. Under President Donald Trump, it has pledged to “systematically dismantle the threat posed” by the ICC to US sovereignty.
The tribunal has also faced accusations of political bias and selective justice from member states. Venezuela and Chad have taken steps toward withdrawal, while Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger recently began the year-long process of leaving the court, branding the ICC an “instrument of neocolonial repression.” Burundi and the Philippines withdrew from the Rome Statute in 2017 and 2019, respectively.
SUB What’s going on with Duterte?
Duterte’s arrest came after the Philippines withdrew from the ICC, but despite his lawyers challenging the court’s jurisdiction, the tribunal maintains it retains authority over alleged crimes committed while the country was a member.
Wednesday’s pre-trial hearing marked Duterte’s first in-person appearance before the court since his detention. He remained silent as judges discussed his health, evidence disclosure, and preparations for trial.
Duterte had missed earlier proceedings on medical grounds, with his lawyers arguing that cognitive decline had left him unfit to participate. His defense says serious memory problems prevent 81-year-old former Philippine leader from reliably recalling the past.
According to AFP, citing his medical assessment files, Duterte believes he is living in 2007 or 2008, thinks he is 84 or 85, and cannot recall the name of the sitting US president.
Judges, however, have allowed proceedings to move forward, with the trial set to begin on November 30. On Wednesday, the ICC ordered Duterte to remain in custody until then, citing an increased risk that he could flee or interfere with witnesses or proceedings.

A Magistrates Court in Brisbane, Australia, sentenced Matthew Alexander Donald De Campo, 32, to six months in prison on Thursday for ramming his vehicle into the gates of the city's Great Synagogue in February.
Despite the prison sentence, Magistrate Megan Power ordered De Campo’s immediate release on a good behavior bond, crediting him for the 83 days he had already spent in custody.
De Campo pleaded guilty to willful damage and two drug-related offenses. Queensland Police initially charged him with willful damage aggravated by the circumstances of a hate crime, but during the hearing that concluded with sentencing, the prosecution asked to remove the aggravating circumstance.
De Campo caused AU$12,000 of damage
The incident occurred on February 20, shortly after 7:15 p.m. Security camera footage shows De Campo’s vehicle arriving at the synagogue on Margaret Street in central Brisbane, then accelerating in reverse into the gates. One of the gates was torn from its mountings, and the resulting damage was estimated at approximately AU$12,000.
No one was injured during the ramming, but a person standing behind the gate at the time spotted the vehicle and quickly moved out of its path just moments before the gate collapsed.
Following the impact, De Campo fled the scene. Police tracked his vehicle with the aid of a helicopter and arrested him shortly thereafter.
At the time of the incident, police stated that the impact on the gates was deliberate; however, there was no indication of an intent to harm anyone or to enter the synagogue, and the case was not investigated as an act of terror.
De Campo allegedly suffered from severe mental health issues
The court heard that De Campo was in a severe mental state at the time of the incident. The judge noted that his conduct toward police indicated that he appeared paranoid and was suffering from delusions.
The defense argued that he had deteriorated into cannabis and methamphetamine use and that his condition at the time of the incident had been affected by the drugs.
After he was released on bail in May, De Campo entered a three-month rehabilitation program. The defense presented the court with his rehabilitation progress, and he pleaded guilty to the charges against him.
The judge sentenced him to six months in prison for causing the damage, but ordered his immediate conditional release. The 83 days he had already spent in custody were recognized as part of the prison term, and he will serve the remainder of the sentence under the release conditions imposed on him.

Argument PA not producing 'sufficient' results evidenced by US Abbas sanctions, expert tells ‘Post’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:37:46 UTC
00:37:46 KST

The Palestinian population may view renewed US sanctions against the Palestinian Authority (PA) as another sign that the current leadership’s approach to Washington has “not produced sufficient political results,” Nabil Kukali, president and founder of the Palestinian Center for Public Opinion (PCPO), told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday.
The US State Department confirmed on Wednesday that the Palestine Liberation Organization and the PA had failed to maintain their commitments under the PLO Commitments Compliance Act of 1989 (PLOCCA) and the Middle East Peace Commitments Act of 2002 (MEPCA), resulting in sanctions against Palestinian officials.
Beyond citing the PA’s continued stipends to Palestinian terrorists (“pay-for-slay”) and failure to reform textbooks to remove the glorification of terrorism, the department said that the PA and PLO were initiating and supporting actions at international organizations that undermine or contradict prior commitments.
These have included efforts to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ), as well as attempts to bypass negotiations by seeking unilateral recognition for a Palestinian state.
As a result, the department announced that the United States would deny visas to PLO members and PA officials.
The sanctions will prevent PA President Mahmoud Abbas from attending the UN General Assembly in New York in person for the second consecutive year.
Kukali said he would be “cautious” about determining whether the sanctions alone would be enough to weaken Abbas’s camp electorally, given that there is not yet “enough evidence to isolate their effect from the much broader set of factors shaping Palestinian voters’ attitudes,” including the economic situation, security, the war and its consequences, governance, institutional performance, and the prospects for a political solution.
However, Kukali said there may still be significant domestic political consequences beyond the potential impact on the Palestinian Legislative Council (PLC) elections, particularly among Palestinians already critical of the PA.
“The US measures may reinforce the argument that the PA’s diplomatic approach and its relationship with Washington have not produced sufficient political results,” he said, arguing that the recent announcement could develop into a broader debate over Palestinian political strategy.
Pro-Abbas Fatah supporters may see sanctions as external pressure effort
Fatah supporters in the pro-Abbas camp may instead view the sanctions as an attempt to apply external pressure on the Palestinian leadership, following its efforts to take Israel to international courts, Kukali said. In such a case, he explained, it would be inaccurate to assume that Abbas would suffer a domestic political loss.
Kukali noted that while over half (57.2%) of Palestinians polled by PCPO previously said that Washington would continue to support Israel, only 20.4% said they believed the US would adopt a “more balanced role in the future.”
At the same time, he said there are significant indications that American voters support recognition of Palestinian statehood.
“The recent US measures toward Palestinian officials themselves illustrate how official Washington policy may continue to move differently from some of the trends emerging within American society,” he said, suggesting that the sanctions could potentially generate a greater reaction among American voters than among Palestinians.
“Some Palestinians may increasingly perceive a gap between attitudes within American society and the policies of the US administration toward Palestinians. Whether that perception will actually affect how they evaluate President Abbas or Fatah is a separate question, and I do not think its outcome should be assumed in advance.”
While Kukali said he doubted the measures would have an automatic impact on Palestinian politics, he acknowledged that the timing of the sanctions was important. The PLC elections are scheduled for November 28, and “any developments affecting the Palestinian leadership’s international standing, its relationship with Washington, or public perceptions of the effectiveness of its political strategy” could form part of the electoral debate.
Though Kukali was uncertain about the impact the sanctions would have on the elections, Prof. Kobi Michael, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) and a visiting professor at the International Centre for Policing and Security at the University of South Wales, told the Post that he thought Hamas would use Abbas’s failures as a way to demonstrate to voters that Fatah’s political struggle has been ineffectual compared to Hamas’s armed “resistance.”
Michael: Fatah reform bloc, Hamas will use Abbas's failures against him
The Fatah Reform Democratic bloc and Hamas “will use it to claim that [Abbas] is history and must leave and only they will be able to make the changes [needed] to recruit international support,” he suggested.
Despite viewing the restrictions for Abbas as a potential avenue for Hamas to market itself as a more powerful and effective alternative, Michael said that he doubted the PA president would allow the elections to go ahead in November as planned.

Lawmakers, faith groups urge passage of Right to Worship Act on Capitol Hill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:37:26 UTC
00:37:26 KST

Lawmakers joined faith-based leaders and community advocates for a press conference on Capitol Hill on Wednesday to push for the swift passage of the Right to Worship Act, a bipartisan, bicameral bill that would establish federal protest-free buffer zones around houses of worship.
The legislation would create a 100-foot perimeter around religious institutions during services, making it unlawful to knowingly disrupt, impede, threaten, or intimidate individuals attempting to practice their faith.
The proponents emphasized that rising incidents of harassment and targeting at religious sites necessitate federal intervention to protect worshippers across denominations.
"Exercising your right to worship should not require you to exhibit particular courage as you enter your synagogue, church, mosque, temple, mandir, or gurdwara," said Representative Tom Suozzi. "I will always stand up for people's right to protest peacefully, but attendees of religious services should not be harassed, threatened, intimidated, or targeted for practicing their faith."
The bill is sponsored in the House by Suozzi and Representative Brad Knott, alongside a companion measure in the Senate introduced by Senators Ted Cruz and Elissa Slotkin.
The legislation also imposes civil penalties for violations and authorizes individuals, the US Attorney General, and state attorneys general to file suit against violators, while explicitly excluding peaceful expression protected by the First Amendment.
Supporters at the press conference highlighted that the pressure facing religious communities extends across the political and geographic spectrum. "The breadth of support for the Right to Worship Act is very gratifying," Suozzi said. "So many groups recognize the horrifying reality that the threat to the freedom to worship is not unique to any one faith or congregation. Every religious community feels it, which is why this bill will protect everybody."
Knott echoed those sentiments during the conference, stating that the proposal strikes a necessary balance between safeguarding public assembly and ensuring safety. "The Right to Worship Act protects peaceful speech while restoring essential protections for Americans by empowering worshippers against those who seek to intimidate them."
The legislation has garnered endorsements from more than twenty national religious and civil rights organizations, including the Anti-Defamation League, the American Jewish Committee, the Islamic Society of North America, and the Hindu American Foundation.
Alyza D. Lewin, President of US Affairs for the Combat Antisemitism Movement, emphasized the vulnerability faced by congregants since late 2023. "In the aftermath of October 7th, Jews have had to endure violent threats and intimidating harassment just to enter synagogues to practice their faith and gather as a community," Lewin said. Drawing a parallel to existing protections, Lewin added, "We place buffer zones around polling stations so that individuals can complete their ballots in peace, without being heckled or intimidated. Surely religious worship, an activity covered by the First Amendment, deserves as much protection as voting. Americans must be able to practice their faith free from harassment and intimidation."
Jonathan Greenblatt, CEO of the ADL, stressed the urgency of the measure given recent security challenges. "No one should have to push through a hostile crowd or shout over a bullhorn in an attempt to pray," Greenblatt said. "The Right to Worship Act gives law enforcement and communities the tools they need to prevent these disruptions before they escalate, while still respecting every American's First Amendment rights."

US deployed more than 50,000 troops during Iran war, inspector general report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:37:22 UTC
00:37:22 KST

The US helped evacuate 9,000 US citizens in the first months of the war with Iran. In addition, Iran carried out 600 attacks in Iraq, either directly from Iran or using proxies.
A Lead Inspector General Report to the United States Congress regarding the US war on Iran has provided new details about the extent of the war effort and the challenges involved.
Although some of the details were known, such as the Iranian attacks on US bases around the region, the report provides new data on aspects of the campaign. It covers the period April-June 2026. Usually these kinds of reports are released several months after the period they cover.
One of the key pieces of information provided is the extent of the US deployment in the region.
The report says that “more than 50,000 US Service Members were deployed throughout the US CENTCOM area of responsibility (AOR) in support of OEF [Operation Epic Fury].”
Report details scale of US military buildup in region
The report noted that “force flows continued into the region in the days after major combat operations began. CENTCOM reported that force presence and disposition have changed throughout the conflict.”
During the conflict, more than a dozen fighter squadrons, along with a similar number of navy destroyers and air defense batteries, were in the region.
The US also deployed the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) ballistic missile defense batteries. Some of these have already been deployed in the region over the years to counter missile threats. For instance, Iran launched large numbers of ballistic missiles at Israel in 2024 and 2025. The US also deployed the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) and elements of the 82nd Airborne Division.
The new report provides some spotlight on the funding for the war. This has been one of those issues that has popped up in Washington during hearings. The report says that the “Office of the Under Secretary of War (Comptroller) Chief Financial Officer (OUSW[C]) estimated the cost of OEF to be $33.4 billion as of June 29.” This includes more than 20 billion in munitions. The costs do not include all the needs for repairs of various bases and sites. New photos have revealed some of the destruction caused by Iranian attacks since February.
One of the issues the US had to address because of the Iranian attacks was to shift some military assets around the region. For instance, it is known that the US has used Jordanian bases and also moved refuelers to Israel.
The report says that while “Bahrain had been US Navy Central’s (USNAVCENT) main logistics hub to sustain operations in the Persian Gulf region…during major combat operations, Iran targeted Bahrain with OWUAS [attack drones] and ballistic missile strikes.
US shifted naval resources amid Gulf base vulnerabilities
CENTCOM stated that it initially shifted naval sustainment resources from Bahrain to alternate hubs.” This illustrates a key theme that has been raised during the war regarding the vulnerability of bases in the Gulf near Iran. Iran has targeted US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, and other places. It also targeted diplomatic facilities in Iraq.
The US supported local partners in the Gulf to counter the Iranian threats. “This has included the provision of military sales, training, and information-sharing to Gulf partners.” The US says that the Gulf partners demonstrated “significant air defense capabilities.”
This would likely refer to Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia.
The battle helped cement cooperation. “US forces embedded in partner air operations centers across the region, which supported coordination, deconfliction, and synchronization of air defense efforts. The Middle East Defense Network, an integrated missile defense architecture in the region, intercepted more than 6,000 OWUAS and more than 1,500 ballistic missiles that targeted US and partner forces.”
CENTCOM likely learned a lot from this conflict, and this also impacts CENTCOM's work with the IDF. This work has been ongoing for years.
However, a real conflict situation, much like the conflict with Iran in 2025 and the missile barrages, helps militaries learn to fight in real time. US Central Command “reported that Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict. In addition, dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged during [Epic Fury].”
Iran also targeted US diplomatic facilities. This included 600 attacks in Iraq.
The inspector’s report notes that “the US Consulate General in Erbil’s new consulate compound suffered damage to multiple buildings. The US Embassy in Baghdad suffered damage but to a lesser extent.
The Baghdad Diplomatic Support Compound, located near Baghdad International Airport, suffered extensive damage, but the facility was already in the process of closing due to a decision that was made before the current conflict began.”
US evacuation effort moved thousands out of conflict zones
Due to the war, the US helped citizens evacuate. In total, around 9,000 were evacuated, with 6,500 of those evacuating from Israel. While the cost of evacuating people from Israel was quite low, the US did pay millions to evacuate people from other places such as Jordan and Iraq.
It was not clear why it was so expensive to evacuate people from Jordan, but not Israel. Around 50 people were evacuated from Jordan, while 850 left Qatar and 16 were evacuated from Bahrain. These were people in contact with the US State Department.

UAE presidential adviser Gargash says trust with Iran will take years to rebuild
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:37:21 UTC
00:37:21 KST

The diplomatic adviser to the UAE president told a session in Dubai that relations with Tehran must continue, but that confidence broken by the attacks on the Gulf will take years to restore.
Trust between the United Arab Emirates and Iran will take years to rebuild, UAE president's diplomatic adviser Dr Anwar Gargash said on Thursday.
Speaking at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai, he said relations with Tehran had to continue because the two countries were neighbours, but that confidence was a separate question after the attacks on the Gulf states.
Gargash said the UAE was managing the crisis while also assessing the future of the relationship.
“At the end of the day, we are neighbours, geographically neighbours. We have very complex relations with Iran, and certainly there is a collapse in the security regiment in the region. Thus, we have to find some new channels of understanding,” he said.
He set out the UAE approach in three parts. “Our role, or rather our approach, is based on three elements. First, to defend our sovereignty, and then to be flexible,” he said. The third was continuity of economic development through the crisis, he said, citing the president's visit to Germany.
“We have to try. To maintain our development, our economic uproar, and the visit of our president to Germany was successful because we don't want to stop our economy in the midst of this crisis,” he said.
Asked about his 7 September statement that UAE confidence in Iran was broken, Gargash said he had drawn a deliberate distinction.
“Actually, I differentiated between the relations and the trust, and I said that the relations are a must and we should have communication and relations with Iran based on open dialogue and a dialogue that would overcome the daily matters,” he said.
“Confidence building, I believe, will take us a long time. We need years to rebuild this trust.”
“The Iranian president said that the aggression from Iran on the GCC countries was a big mistake,” he said.
“I think it is a geostrategic mistake that created a more complex situation for Iran that would affect its future.”
'UAE is a nice country but not an easy target'
He said Iran's use of proxy militias kept it close to the aggression, and that the Gulf states would be the parties to broker Tehran's return to its international place, trade and commerce, once the attacks stopped.
“They can't negotiate a new future while they are still threatening and being aggressive against the neighbourhood,” he said.
Asked whether the UAE had taken any measures of its own against Iran, financial or political, he said it had not.
“No, we have only defended ourselves, and we continue to defend ourselves, and we still extend our hands for friendly relations”, he said.
Gargash said Iran was made of different circles and that decision-making there was no longer held in one place, as it had been under the previous Ayatollah Ali Khamenei since 1989, and that the voices arguing against confrontation with the Gulf needed to be louder.
On the meeting between Sheikh Khalid bin Mohamed and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian at BRICS, Gargash said the two sides had agreed on the direction if not on everything.
“There was not a complete agreement between them. But there was an agreement on the fact that we should start a new page and look to the future,” he said.
“The future should never be like what we have now. It is not in the interest of Iran nor the GCC countries.”
He said President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed had set the balance between flexibility and strength from the beginning of the war.
“The UAE is a nice country, but we are not an easy target,” Gargash said. “He was so clear in saying that Iran is going to be away from stability for decades to come.”
Houthi control of Bab el-Mandeb 'concern for everyone'
Asked about the drone and rocket fire that triggered alerts in Saudi Arabia's city of Jeddah and Islam's holiest site of Mecca, Gargash said that "targeting Mecca is completely denounced and rejected.”
“The security and the sovereignty of Saudi Arabia is part of our security, and the stability of the GCC countries is interconnected,” he said.
The region had suffered from militias, Gargash said, naming Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen, and that “any arms outside the state are harmful for the countries and the region”.
“Yes, the channels are open. And as you are aware, and strategically speaking, the safety, security, and prosperity of Saudi Arabia is in our interest,” he said, asked whether relations with Riyadh remained open.
On the Houthis' offensive to take control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, Gargash said that "the Houthis' control over the strait is a concern for everyone," and not just a regional issue.
"This is not related to the region, but rather to the international economy," he said. “We go back to the basic principle that these straits are international. This is the international definition."
Gargash set out no timetable for further contacts with Tehran, saying the UAE did not choose the war but defended itself when it started, and that “this is a beginning for a political dialogue that should be started”.

US House approves Russia sanctions bill allowing Trump tariffs of up to 100% on Kremlin partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:37:19 UTC
00:37:19 KST

The US House of Representatives passed a Russia sanctions bill on Wednesday intended to pressure the Kremlin to end the war in Ukraine.
The bill, called the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," passed by 262 to 159. It passed the Senate in August and is now en route to President Donald Trump’s desk for his signature.
The US sanctions bill targets Russia's energy and defense industries, as well as its "shadow fleet" of tankers that evade existing sanctions, in order to deprive Moscow of revenues to finance the war.
It would also place sanctions on Russian President Vladimir Putin, several senior Kremlin officials, Russian financial institutions, and state-owned companies.
It would allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on buyers of Russian energy, such as China or India, in order to reduce their dependence on Russian oil and gas.
What do the bill's critics say?
Notably, the bill had critics on both sides of the aisle.
Republican critics of the bill privately expressed to party leadership that the tariff powers would drive up prices before the contentious midterm elections in November, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) rejected their request for changes, the sources added.
Democrats and a few Republicans argued that the bill gives Trump too much broad presidential power on tariffs.
“Why in the world would this Congress give this president additional authority to visit that kind of economic harm on the American people?” asked House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York).
“The manner in which this bill has been written doesn’t require the president of the United States to impose sanctions on Russia. In fact, there are so many loopholes written into the bill, I believe, that it’s very unlikely that the sanctions relief contemplated in the legislation will ever see the light of day.”
However, the bill’s supporters say that it is a necessary punch to the Kremlin before winter sets in, and argue that Trump would not end up with more power on trade.
"Today, we are now one step closer to securing Lindsey's vision of enduring peace in Ukraine and beyond," Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas).
Zelensky praises Russia sanctions bill as a 'powerful tool' to stop war
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky voiced his support for the bill on Thursday, saying that it was “an extremely powerful tool that can stop this terrorist war and bring Russia to the necessity of establishing peace.”
“I thank the members of the House of Representatives, senators, and leaders of the US Congress for supporting this bill. Russia needs to end this war of its own," he wrote on Telegram.
The Kremlin said that if Trump signed the sanctions into law, it would make it harder to reach a peace deal in Ukraine.
"We are, of course, monitoring the progress of this document. It falls under the category of unfriendly actions, and of course the imposition of any additional sanctions by the US would certainly complicate efforts to find a peace settlement in Ukraine," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

Israeli F-35s to Receive SPICE 1000 High-Precision Munitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:36:03 UTC
00:36:03 KST

The Israeli company Rafael, in collaboration with Lockheed Martin, is accelerating the integration of the SPICE 1000 high-precision munition into the F-35I Adir fighter jet.
Rafael announced this during the Air, Space, and Cyber Symposium conference.
The work is being carried out at Lockheed Martin facilities in the U.S. The integration process is expected to take several months. Rafael notes that in the future, the SPICE 1000 may become available not only to Israeli F-35I fighters but also to other operators of the F-35 family of fighter jets.
The integration of this munition was previously mentioned in official U.S. Department of Defense documentation. In an August report on the F-35 program, the munition is designated as the Israel-unique Smart, Precise Impact, Cost-Effective 1000B—SPICE 1000B.
The document noted that plans are in place to accelerate its integration using the so-called “SPICE Lite” process. Details of this approach were not disclosed.
SPICE is a family of high-precision air-launched munitions equipped with an electro-optical guidance system. It includes the SPICE 250, SPICE 1000, and SPICE 2000. The numerical designation roughly corresponds to the munition’s weight class.
The SPICE 1000 is based on a 1,000-pound (approximately 454 kg) class aerial bomb. After release, it deploys its wings, allowing it to engage targets at a range of about 125 km. According to the manufacturer, the stated circular error probability is approximately three meters.
For guidance, the munition uses inertial and satellite navigation in combination with an electro-optical homing head. During the terminal phase of flight, the system can compare images of the terrain with preloaded images of the target.
Thanks to this, the SPICE 1000 is capable of continuing guidance even in the absence of or when GPS signals are jammed. After being dropped, the munition can autonomously guide itself to the target. Additionally, prior to deployment, the approach direction and angle of attack can be set to strike fortified targets from above.
The SPICE 1000 has been in service with the Israeli Air Force since 2017. The munition is integrated with the F-16C/D Barak, F-15I Raam, and F-15 Bazs fighter jets.
Currently, Israel is the only foreign operator of the F-35 that has been granted expanded authority to integrate its own systems into the aircraft. The F-35I Adir version is equipped with Israeli communications, electronic warfare, and software components and is adapted for the use of national weapons.
In November 2023, the United States announced the provision of SPICE precision-guided bombs to Israel totaling approximately $320 million.

Ninth woman’s body found as South Africa probes series of killings
All female victims in their 20s and 30s were killed on the outskirts of Johannesburg in the past two months.
Police have found the body of another murdered woman on the outskirts of South Africa’s commercial capital – after the discovery of eight female corpses in the same area of Johannesburg in the past two months.
Police said they found the body of a ninth woman and imposed a lockdown in Kempton Park in the Ekurhuleni municipality on Thursday. Three of the partially naked bodies were found in the area this week.
The string of murders has stoked public anxiety that these crimes may have been carried out by a serial killer. Police earlier said that some similarities in the killings of the first eight victims were “sufficiently concerning” for the police to issue a public warning.
“Investigators are considering all possibilities, including the possibility of multiple suspects or separate perpetrators,” said Fred Kekana, the police commissioner for South Africa’s Gauteng province.
The first five bodies were discovered in or near Kempton Park; the others were found in separate locations 25-35km (16-22 miles) away.
“Police are comparing the evidence, timelines, locations, victim profiles and circumstances of each case,” Kekana said, adding that while it is too early to connect the killings to a serial killer, “the similarities in the cases were concerning”.
All were women in their 20s or 30s, and all were found either naked or partially clothed, police said. Some of the bodies had similar bruising.
The first body was discovered on July 17, naked and restrained with cable ties. A suspect believed to have been the victim’s boyfriend was arrested and taken into custody, according to police, though no charges were filed against him.
One of the other victims was identified as 38-year-old Elizabeth Tsontso Moselakgomo, who went missing while out jogging. She was reported missing after her eight-year-old daughter alerted family members that she had not returned from her daily afternoon jog, and she was found dead several days later.
Another body was found naked and in an advanced stage of decomposition, authorities said.
The youngest victim has been identified as a 20-year-old woman.
‘We cannot continue picking up bodies’
South Africa’s President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed “no stone will be left unturned” in the investigation into the deaths, and authorities are now offering a reward of 400,000 South African rand ($25,000) for information leading to the apprehension of the perpetrator or perpetrators.
Women in the vicinity of where the bodies were discovered have also been advised to be “extremely cautious” and not to go out alone.
“We cannot continue picking up bodies,” Tebello Mosikili, the deputy national commissioner for policing in the South African Police Service, told journalists at the scene of the latest discovery.
The killings have highlighted the high rates of violence against women in South Africa, which has one of the highest femicide rates in the world, according to the United Nations.
South African police recorded 9,782 reported rapes between January and March 2026, along with 12,590 sexual offences. That amounts to roughly 108 reported rapes every day.
Almost half of those reported rapes, 4,620, or 47.2 percent, took place at the home of the victim or the perpetrator, according to police statistics.
In November last year, South Africa’s National Disaster Management Centre classified gender-based violence and femicide as a national disaster following sustained pressure from civil society organisations.
A study in 2022 by a South African think tank found that more than 35 percent of South African adult women had experienced physical or sexual violence at some point.

US assured Houthis it would stay out of Yemen war, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:33:21 UTC
00:33:21 KST

Breadcrumb
US intervention in Yemen war 'off the table' despite Saudi pressure
Saudi Arabia has been pressing the United States to intervene against the Houthis after the Iran-backed group seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, but Washington appears reluctant to enter the conflict.
American military intervention in Yemen is "completely off the table" before November's US midterm elections, a senior Yemeni researcher has told The New Arab, despite Riyadh's calls for military assistance to halt the Houthi advance.
Abdulghani al-Iryani, a senior researcher at the Sanaa Centre, told TNA that unless Iran and the Houthis dramatically escalate the situation, President Donald Trump is likely to stay out of the conflict in a bid to limit potential electoral damage for the Republican Party.
"I don't see a reason for the Republicans to give up their electoral chances for the sake of the Saudis," he said.
His comments come as American and Houthi officials held Oman-mediated talks over the weekend, during which US officials reportedly assured the group they would not intervene in the Yemen conflict.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reportedly urged President Trump to launch airstrikes against the Iran-backed group, which seized control of the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait on the Red Sea last week.
But sources say the Trump administration reached an understanding with the Houthis that Washington would stay out of the conflict even as the group attacks Saudi energy infrastructure and targets its ships in the Red Sea.
The Oman-mediated discussions saw the Houthis assure US officials that they would not target American ships and would uphold the 2025 ceasefire, according to Reuters.
A Yemeni source said Houthi officials also committed not to attack Israeli vessels or commercial ships that are not linked to Saudi Arabia.
The discussions, held at the US embassy in Muscat, involved senior Houthi officials Mohammad Abdulsalam and Abdelmalik al-Ajiri, sources said.
The Trump administration designated the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation in March 2025 before launching a two-month bombing campaign against them to halt their attacks on Red Sea shipping. That conflict ended after the two sides negotiated a ceasefire brokered by Oman.
The Houthis and the Yemeni government have engaged in fierce fighting since the collapse of the ceasefire in July.
The group has declared a blockade on Saudi ports and targeted Saudi ships in the Red Sea. It has also struck several Saudi energy sites, including oil refineries and pipelines.
The Houthis last week captured Yemen's entire Red Sea coastline, including the historic port of Mokha and Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb.
Since taking control of the area, the group has said it would uphold freedom of navigation through the strait but would continue to enforce its blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Few military options
Trump's refusal to intervene comes as the Houthis and their allies in Iraq attempt to shut down Saudi oil exports. Shipments via the Red Sea have been completely cut off after a drone strike last week took the East-West pipeline offline. The kingdom is now reliant exclusively on covert shipments via the Strait of Hormuz, assisted by the US military.
Saudi Arabia has escalated airstrikes against the Houthis in the week since they captured the Red Sea coast. The Houthis have reported more than 450 strikes as Riyadh tries to help government forces retake the area.
But analysts say Saudi Arabia's military options are limited. Airstrikes have done little to weaken the Houthis since Riyadh first launched its air campaign more than a decade ago, and it is hesitant to deploy ground troops inside the country.
Other allies have followed the US in declining to get involved in the conflict. Turkey and Pakistan have shown no willingness to intervene despite the three countries signing a mutual defence pact last month. Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi is also unlikely to weigh in after discussing the situation with bin Salman in Cairo this week.
"I don't think Saudi military escalation will help the Yemeni cause or the Saudi cause," Al-Iryani told The New Arab.
"The best bet for Saudi Arabia is to try to help the government hold its ground until the US-Iran war is over, when it will be in a better position to negotiate with the Houthis," he said.

Romanian Liberal MEP Siegfried Muresan nominated as prime minister
