The West’s pretend outrage won’t save Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:07:49 UTC
23:07:49 KST

The West’s pretend outrage won’t save Palestinians
On September 2, without warning, Israeli bulldozers destroyed the homes of 12 Palestinian families in Khirbet al-Tabban, a herding community in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, leaving 70 people homeless, nearly half of them children.
RT’s Charlotte Dubenskij visited the community soon after, interviewing the families and the head of Masafer Yatta council, Nidal Younis. Younis described the demolition as the erasure of this village. He said that in addition to the destroyed homes, “water sources were also targeted, including rainwater collection wells and the families’ small water tanks.” They also destroyed the ten pens housing their 600 animals.
Terrain in the South Hebron Hills is desert-like, dry and hot, and the families’ livelihoods mainly depend on the sheep, goats and chickens they raise and the vegetables they grow – all of which requires water.
According to Israeli rights group B’Tselem, in the 1980s, around 3,000 hectares of the South Hebron Hills were declared a “restricted military zone.” It notes that the expulsion of the roughly 700 residents of 12 villages occurred in 1999, “on the official grounds that they were ‘illegally living in a firing zone’. This flimsy argument blatantly ignored the fact that the families had been living in the area for many years, since before Israel occupied the West Bank and afterwards, with the full knowledge of Israeli authorities … These are false claims, meant to conceal Israel’s aspirations to take over the land for its own purposes and use it to benefit the Jewish population only.”
Just days after razing Khirbet al-Tabban homes, Israeli bulldozers erased another Masafer Yatta community, Khirbet al-Fakhit, leaving 32 more people homeless, and also demolished the home of seven people in still another community, Khirbet Khallet a-Dabe’.
The UN reports that between January 2023 and 31 August 2026, “130 Palestinian communities experienced full or partial displacement. Of these, 48 communities have been fully displaced, including 12 so far in 2026. Overall, more than 6,400 Palestinians, including over 3,100 children, have been displaced in this context since January 2023. Of them, more than 2,500 people, including over 1,200 children, were displaced in 2026 alone.”
All the while Palestinians are being forcibly displaced from their homes, there are upwards of 800,000 Israeli settlers, internationally recognized as illegal, in ever-expanding colonies throughout the West Bank.
Siege as a tool of forced displacement
These colonists further aid in Israel’s ethnic cleansing project by surrounding, blockading, and starving Palestinians. And they do so with the help of the Israeli army and government.
Take the case of Qusra, a village south of Nablus, where Palestinian homes have been cut off and besieged by colonists since August 9.
When activists or others try to bring food, water, medicine and other vital basics to the besieged families, the settlers and the Israeli army usually prevent them from entering, often detaining those trying to help. On September 4, Israeli soldiers blocked a group of around 100 peace activists trying to deliver humanitarian aid to the families.
TRT’s Zena Tahhan reported on September 7 on the twelve Palestinians trapped inside their homes in Qusra. She explained, “The illegal Israeli settlement outpost at Qusra was established in January when settlers took over a nearby building under construction. In August, illegal settlers erected an outpost directly outside one family’s home, blocking the only road, cutting off their electricity and water.”
According to TRT, the families have received some food and basic necessities on several occasions through rights groups. “The army has said they can leave, but have given no guarantee they will be allowed to return to their home.”
Palestinians know that if they do succumb and leave their homes, they almost certainly will never be allowed to return. “In July, a Palestinian family in the neighboring village of Jalud was forced from their home after a similar three-month siege.”
This siege is not only fully allowed by the Israeli government, but also assisted by Israeli soldiers and police. In effect, the fanatical settlers are doing the work for the Israeli authorities, setting the stage for still further forced expulsion of Palestinians.
Colonists continue deadly attacks
On August 6, a Palestinian activist posted of an attack just two hours prior by settlers who “launched a pogrom on the village of Tuba in my community Masafer Yatta, attempting to burn a family alive in their home. At least six people were injured, including two children.”
Almost every day and night there are new attacks by colonists who maim and kill Palestinian civilians by any means possible, from point-blank shooting to burning Palestinians alive. The ferocity and frequency of these attacks is so immense that it is difficult to keep up with their endless terrorism.
And terrorism it is, not only in the opinion myself and others who have watched the abuse of Palestinians for years, but even of one Israel’s own military chiefs, who earlier this year described settler violence as “Jewish terrorism.”
I’ve written countless times over many years on this insane violence. While there has been a dramatic increase in attacks in the past few years, they have been ongoing for decades, aided and abetted by the Israeli military, police and government.
The UN’s OCHA reported that as ofAugust 31, “82 Palestinians, including 19 children, have been killed and about 1,900 injured by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank,” since the start of 2026. It notes, “Of these, 23 Palestinians were killed and over 1,100 injured in the context of settler attacks.”
By September 9, the number of Palestinians reported killed by armed colonists and Israeli forces since the start of the year had risen to 100. This is in the West Bank alone, and does not include the over 1,355 Palestinians killed in Gaza by Israeli forces since October 2025, in violation of a ceasefire that the Israelis never intended to adhere to.
Far from the front pages of Western media who are always ready with a story about alleged human rights violations in Iran or North Korea, over three hundred Palestinian children from the West Bank languish in Israeli military detention – “the highest number in eight years,” according to UNICEF, which notes, “Nearly half – 164 – are held under administrative detention without charge or trial.”
They are among the nearly 10,000 Palestinian hostages ignored by Western media and rights groups, many being starved, beaten, tortured, denied medical care, and nearly 3,200 of who were never actually charged with any crime but are being held under administrative detention.
These are the brutal realities of daily life for Palestinians in the West Bank undergoing Israel’s ethnic cleansing project of depopulating Palestinians from their homeland by any means possible. In full sight, for the world to see.
Once again, it is useful to ask the rhetorical question: What would the reaction be by global media and politicians if this scenario was playing out over and over again in Iran, China, or another state vilified and targeted by the West?
The UK ban on illegal colony goods is mere lip service
When British foreign minister Ed Miliband on September 8 announced plans to ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, it was wrongly perceived by some as concrete action, solidarity, or even a victory.
Reports citing Bloomberg say Miliband assured Washington that the measures would be “largely symbolic.” This is the only truth in the charade: It would put absolutely no pressure on Israel to stop expanding the colonies, and would not cause Israel to prevent the colonists from continuing their attacks on Palestinian civilians.
As Palestinian author and writer, Ali Abunimah, noted, Miliband’s statements in Parliament and on X, “reveal that Britain’s overriding priority remains protecting Israel as a racist Jewish state...This ‘solution’ offers Palestinians disconnected enclaves under permanent Israeli military, economic and political domination – the equivalent of apartheid South Africa’s Bantustans. They would be expected to call these fragments a state, renounce their right to return and accept Israel’s permanent existence as a Jewish supremacist entity.”
Back in 2007, after my eight months in different West Bank communities afflicted with near-daily violence from the Israeli army and from colonists, I understood the notion of a two-state solution has long been dead and has never been just.
Abunimah argues, and I agree, that the joint official statement which Canada, France and several other European countries support explicitly says the objective is to “protect” the two-state solution. “This is coordinated action to rescue a segregation plan, not end Israel’s racism. This is not solidarity with Palestinians. It is just the latest Western attempt to rescue the genocidal Jewish supremacist state that Britain created.”

Baby found wrapped in 1910 newspaper was killed with twine, UK inquest concludes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:06:48 UTC
23:06:48 KST

A baby boy who was found with twine looped and knotted round his neck and wrapped in a 116-year-old newspaper was unlawfully killed, a coroner has concluded.
Crispin Oliver on Thursday said the child, known only as Baby Auckland, had been garotted by an unknown person.
He said it was an “unusual case, legally and evidentially”. The whole story, he added, was “very sad and singular”.
Oliver said: “Clearly, this was a terrible thing that happened to a defenceless infant. It happened in our community. But it happened over a century ago, and it is heartwarming how the public and individuals in this community have stepped up to do the right thing by Baby Auckland.”
The inquest heard that the skeletal remains of the baby had been found during renovations on the second floor of a late 19th-century house in Bishop Auckland, County Durham, on 29 July 2024.
They were found by the house owner, Peter Moody, while he was laying a new floor. In a statement he said he had made the discovery when he lifted up a floorboard. He contacted the county council, unsure of whether he needed to call the police.
DCI Mel Sutherland told the inquest he had been on duty in Bishop Auckland when he was alerted to the discovery of skeletal remains in a town centre house.
After they were confirmed as human, he supervised the sealing of the house to keep it forensically sterile, while a forensic anthropologist was contacted. That scientist, Dr Micol Zuppello, travelled up that evening and spent two days at the house investigating.
The baby’s skeleton was mostly complete, the inquest in Crook heard, bar a missing toe tip. The remains were partly mummified. Carbon dating could conclusively establish only that the baby died between the 17th century and 1955.
A postmortem of the skeleton was carried out by Zupello and Dr Louise Mulcahy, a Home Office pathologist for north-east England based at the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle.
Mulcahy said the baby had been 38-40 weeks, with no signs of traumatic injury, and had twine looped around his neck. She said it had been looped around the neck three times, knotted, and then looped again.
It was not possible to say, she added, if it had been tight or loose. The medical cause of death, she said, was “unascertained”.
The skeleton was too old to be able to confirm or refute the presence of natural disease, she said. In the absence of soft tissue it was not possible, the inquest heard, to say if there had been any assault or trauma. Equally, it was not possible to say with any certainty if the baby had been stillborn or not.
Oliver said police had “had to think laterally” during their investigation. He praised Sutherland for “leaving no stone unturned”.
Sutherland described some of the techniques they had used to investigate further, including DNA testing. All were inconclusive.
He said the newspaper was very brown, but articles could be seen. It was called The Umpire and dated June 1910.
Sutherland said that in 1911 census data, the building was described as dining rooms, meaning “a cafe-type establishment”.
A public appeal was made for people who thought they might be related to come forward. Two sisters came forward who believed they were related to a servant at the house, but DNA testing revealed no match.
During the whole investigation, Sutherland said, there had been “very little to go on”.
Oliver asked if the twine might have been used for a religious artefact, but nothing like that had been found, Sutherland said. There was also no evidence to suggest any link to midwifery practices of the time.
A knot specialist could not be used, the inquest heard, because the nearest person was in the Netherlands and would have been too expensive for this type of investigation.
Baby Auckland was laid to rest at Bishop Auckland cemetery in April this year, with professionals involved giving their services for free.
Sutherland said it had been two years of investigating, “challenging and frustrating at times, but heartwarming to see the send-off he got at the end”.

The fight to preserve Lebanon's history before it's lost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:06:08 UTC
23:06:08 KST

Breadcrumb
A war of narratives: Why these archivists are fighting to preserve Lebanon's history before it's too late
When Monika Borgmann heard about Israel’s evacuation orders for Tyre in June 2026, she decided she couldn’t wait any longer.
As the co-founder of UMAM Documentation and Research, one of Lebanon’s largest private citizen archives based in Beirut’s southern suburbs of Dahiye, she feared the project she had spent decades working on could be at risk.
"I was afraid that if they could call for the whole evacuation of Tyre, they could call for the whole evacuation of Dahiye," she tells The New Arab.
Despite withstanding previous wars and near misses, Monika mobilised her network and made the difficult decision to relocate tens of thousands of books, records, photographs, audiovisual materials, and periodicals that chronicle Lebanon’s complex modern social, cultural, and political history.
"I'm glad I took this decision because ten days later a building next to us was bombarded without any warning," she continues. "Also, I feel that the war is maybe not finished."
Monika now sits in a small office spanning two floors in Beirut’s Badaro neighbourhood, stacked with boxes overflowing with Lebanon's cultural history. It’s a temporary home.
Each day, a team of dedicated archivists meticulously sorts through the records, preserving fragments of a past that might otherwise disappear — while the other half of the collection sits elsewhere in a metal container.
Like other private archives in the country, UMAM remains displaced by the risk of war and uncertainty about the future.
It’s a poignant reminder of the fragility surrounding Lebanon’s relationship with history — and the emotional weight that comes with the responsibility of preserving memory.
"We are going around with our history on our backs in the boxes… waiting until they can go back home," says Chaza Charafeddine, the founder of Athar, an archive containing 2,624 artefacts documenting public life in Tyre that was similarly evacuated from southern Lebanon this year and is now being stored at her home in Beirut.
"It's a difficult situation," she adds.
Lebanon lacks a complete record of its national history, and private archives play a vital role in filling the gaps — often remaining independent of political influence and powerful actors.
Through decades of instability, archives in Lebanon have been targets of looting, destruction, deliberate erasure, as well as underfunding and age-related deterioration. And this ultimately limits memory itself.
During Lebanon’s civil war — an era of history that still isn’t spoken about in some history books — some 1,200 precious manuscripts reportedly “disappeared” from Lebanon’s National Library, while cultural centre Dar el Fan wa-l-Adab was completely looted.
In 1982, Israel also seized the Palestinian Liberation Organisation archives in Beirut, confiscating crucial photographs and documents.
More recently, in 2023, unknown assailants stole a server from Lebanon's state-run National News Agency containing historical records dating back to 1961.
"What Lebanon is living today is a war of narratives, and in this sense, archives have a major role to play," Monika adds. "They should be even more present in the public discourse than they are today."
At UMAM, the work is also personal. Monika’s husband Lokman Slim — a prominent activist, publisher, and UMAM co-founder — was assassinated in 2021 in a case that remains unsolved now, five years on.
At the Badaro office, research and archiving continue, even as questions remain about its future home.
Incredible daily discoveries, tiny threads unravelling a moment of Lebanese citizens' history, are deeply exciting for those at the heart of this work.
Ayman Nahle, for example, focuses on audiovisual archives, including decades of moving images and Lebanese cinema from Baalbeck Studios — work full of discoveries. Sometimes the delicate film is impossible to restore, but other times, the results are breathtaking.
He tells The New Arab that through his work, which includes reactivating old footage, he encounters ‘wow’ moments "each hour, each minute."
"It's just the role of the archivist," he adds. "It's become a kind of lifestyle. What is so beautiful here about the historical construction, how we construct history from the fragment itself."
Beyond the visuals, countless audio recordings also share intimate portraits of Lebanese life.
"You have this huge Lebanese diaspora, and a lot of families, instead of sending letters, they were sending tapes," Monika says. "I was listening to some, and it really was a beautiful experience."
Marie-Claude Souaid, another member of the team, has been working on a special archive from the Carlton Hotel, a legendary Beirut hub and site of memory with decades of prominent guests and events from the 1960s until the 2000s.
"These archives are confronting me with two contradictory things," the anthropologist tells The New Arab. "The prestige of the country in one hand and the collapse of the country in the other."
Such history, in many ways, offers a window not just into the past but into the essence of Lebanese identity itself.
"Lebanon was already prestigious in the Golden Age and now… we are collapsing. But in between, in some qualitative approach, the archives of UMAM… are the citizen archives that can enlighten the citizen story of this country," says Marie-Claude.
These days, people are racing to preserve the documents and history, particularly in southern Lebanon, where conflict continues, as a way to remember and learn from the past.
More broadly, efforts are also underway to digitise the archival material at UMAM and in other private archives across Lebanon.
Many feel it’s more important than ever to hold on to physical copies — especially given the rise of AI.
"The originals and not only the digital copies are becoming more and more important," Monika says.
Chaza explains that many of the women in her archives from Jaafaria College in the south aren’t veiled, and physical photos cannot be doctored in the way digital files can.
"This is my only security, my only evidence that this era existed in this way," she says. "These people were doing these things at the time in the 40s, in the 50s. This is the only real, real evidence. So that's why absolutely, it's very, very important."
Efforts and conversations have been underway, most recently involving Lebanon’s Ministry of Culture, to try to find a home for some of Lebanon’s displaced archives.
But hopes of a collective, creative space remain uncertain for now.
Yet amid another period of uncertainty, the mission to preserve Lebanon’s history has become increasingly tied to the meaning of identity.
"There are a thousand Lebanons," Chaza adds. "Shias have their Lebanon, the Sunnis have their Lebanon, the Christians have their Lebanon. And all of a sudden, the idea of unity, the idea of Lebanon, of this one country, was completely blurry."
She adds, "I think that's why many people started to grasp moments in history because they want to understand who they are."
Tamara Davison is a British freelance journalist reporting across the Middle East on humanitarian issues, post-conflict resolution and migration
Follow her on Instagram: @tamaradavison_

Jetten refuses to pick a side as opposition warns of drama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:06:04 UTC

Jetten refuses to pick a side as opposition warns of drama
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Prime minister Rob Jetten has declined to say whether his minority coalition will seek support from the left or right to pass its first budget, telling MPs on the second day of debates that making that choice now would be “short-changing the country”.
Instead of committing one way or the other, Jetten said the cabinet would send invitations on Thursday evening to seven opposition parties – Pro, JA21, ChristenUnie, SGP, BBB, Volt and 50PLUS – for a new round of talks on support for the current budget and tax plan.
But the two parties whose votes matter most, which are pulling left and right, have said they see little point in such talks. Opposition party Pro leader Jesse Klaver said more discussions would be a repeat of the ones that collapsed in the summer.
Far-right JA21 leader Joost Eerdmans said the cabinet had to choose. “Broad isn’t going to work,” he told Jetten. “Which way are you going?”
Jetten admitted the cabinet had underestimated how much time it needed in August to work opposition demands into the budget, and said it wanted to keep talking in the coming weeks. He again said a broad agreement was his preference, but did not rule out seeking support for individual budgets if needed.
“A drama for the Netherlands”
 Klaver said the coalition is “divided to the bone”, and told Jetten “lock yourself in a room,” because “if you don’t make the choice, it will grind to a halt and this autumn will be a drama for the Netherlands.”
ChristenUnie leader Mirjam Bikker said it was “hard for us to talk” to a cabinet that could not agree with itself.
On the first day of the debates yesterday, Eerdmans said a total deal with the cabinet was no longer realistic and JA21 would judge each departmental budget separately, ruling out support for the climate budget and probably the asylum budget so long as the spreading law for asylum seekers remains in force.
Klaver responded that Pro would withhold support from every budget if the cabinet struck separate deals with JA21. The coalition of D66, VVD and CDA has 66 of the 150 seats in parliament and needs 16 extra votes in the senate.
Siding with Pro would give it the easiest chance of a majority, but the right-wing VVD does not want to concede to them on many issues.
Stabs in the back 
 PVV leader Geert Wilders opened the day by confronting Jetten with an article in the newspaper AD, in which unnamed ministers criticised the prime minister for failing to take charge, one saying the only direction he took was the visual direction””, managing the image.
Wilders said Jetten’s colleagues had “stuck three daggers in your back” and asked what he thought of not being trusted by his own party.
Jetten said he was proud of his team and “we are making the best of it”.
Tax plans
 In mid-November parliament will vote on the tax plan. Pro and ChristenUnie have both said they will not back it as it stands, because the burden falls largely on people in work, and Eerdmans said there is no way the plan can satisfy both JA21 and Pro at the same time.
The Council of State, the government’s main advisory body, said this week that €5.8 billion of the €6 billion in tax rises planned for 2027 would be paid by workers, while the burden on companies and wealth falls slightly. A decision on the tax on savings and investments, known as Box 3, has been postponed until next year.
Jetten said the cabinet would spend an extra €10 billion on infrastructure in the coming years and told Pro that the nitrogen plans would not be watered down, though “improvements” were possible provided they delivered the same reduction in emissions.
MPs will vote on motions, including a motion of no confidence tabled by Wilders, at the end of the debate on Thursday night.

Türkiye has condemned a drone attack targeting Saudi Arabia last weekend and actions carried out by the Houthis, while welcoming steps by 12 countries to restrict trade and business ties with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Speaking at the National Defence Ministry’s weekly press briefing in Ankara, ministry spokesperson Zeki Akturk said on Thursday that Ankara condemns the drone attack targeting Saudi Arabia, as well as actions carried out by the Houthis.
He said such actions threatening regional stability should end as soon as possible, warning that the continued Houthi threat in the Red Sea and Bab al Mandab Strait adversely affects not only regional security but also international maritime trade and global stability.
Turning to Israel’s actions in the region, Akturk said Israel was further deepening instability by continuing simultaneous attacks on Lebanon, Syria, and Palestine.
He welcomed steps taken by 12 countries, led by the UK, France, and Canada, to prohibit trade and business relations with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Akturk also called on the international community to go beyond statements and take “concrete and deterrent measures” in response to Israeli attacks targeting camps sheltering displaced Palestinians in Gaza and residential areas in southern Lebanon.
“We once again emphasise that Israel must immediately end its actions that violate international law in order to ensure peace and stability in the region,” he said.
Mecca defence alliance
Responding to questions following the briefing, the ministry said the Mecca defence alliance between Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia was based on the countries’ longstanding relations and defence cooperation, as well as the principles of defence and collective deterrence.
“The agreement is not directed against any country, nor does it constitute an alternative to the parties’ existing relations with third countries,” the ministry said.
It added that activities aimed at enhancing military cooperation, increasing interoperability, and strengthening defence capabilities were being carried out in coordination among the three countries, while efforts to institutionalise the alliance were continuing.
Greek premier's Meis (Kastellorizo) visit
The ministry also criticised Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’ visit to Meis (Kastellorizo), saying Ankara had closely followed his contacts with military personnel stationed on the island.
It said the presence of military personnel and a warship on Meis, which was transferred to Greece under the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty on condition that it remain demilitarised, was incompatible with the island’s status and did not contribute to peace and stability.
Türkiye urged Greece “to comply with its obligations arising from international treaties and refrain from activities incompatible with the demilitarised status of the islands.”
The ministry said Ankara supports developing relations with Greece on the basis of good neighbourliness and dialogue, while remaining determined to protect its rights and interests under international law.
US arms embargo decision
On Washington’s decision to extend the lifting of its arms embargo on the Greek Cypriot Administration for another year, until September 30, 2027, the ministry said the move could negatively affect the “sensitive balances and environment of trust” on the island.
The ministry urged third parties to avoid actions that could undermine the delicate balance on the island and to abandon practices that disregard the Turkish Cypriot people.
“Türkiye, as a guarantor country, will continue, as it has in the past, to take the necessary measures in cooperation with the TRNC (Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus) authorities for the security, peace and prosperity of the Turkish Cypriots,” it added.

'Powerful explosion' occurs near Polish border amid Russian drone attack on western Ukraine, Tusk says
A Russian jet-powered drone crashed or struck a target about 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from the Polish border during a Russian attack on western Ukraine, Polish authorities said on Sept. 17.
Ukrainian monitoring channels and the Air Force reported at around 12:45 p.m. local time that the jet-powered drone was flying from Rivne Oblast toward Volyn Oblast, which borders Poland to the west.
The threat of another Russian incursion into Polish airspace prompted the Polish Air Force to scramble fighter jets.
Residents of counties in the Lublin and Podkarpackie districts received government alerts warning of a potential air attack, Polish media RMF24 reported. Airports in Lublin and Rzeszow also temporarily suspended flight operations.
"I received another message: The Russian attack on the western part of Ukraine has ended," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said during a Polish government meeting on Sept. 17.
"Very close to the Polish border, not far from Dorohusk, a gas station was probably attacked again," Tusk said. "There was a very powerful explosion. Our planes took off. This Sept. 17 is an exceptional day, including from the point of view of today's security."
Sept. 17 is a significant date in Poland, marking the anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939. The invasion, launched without a formal declaration of war, came 16 days after Nazi Germany invaded Poland from the west.
The State Border Guard Service of Ukraine denied reports that a Russian drone struck a border crossing with Poland during the attack. Polish authorities, meanwhile, said that the country's airspace was not violated during the Russian attack.
Incursions by Russian munitions into Polish airspace have become increasingly frequent as Russia's war in Ukraine continues, while Russian strikes on Ukrainian targets near the Polish border have intensified in recent weeks.
On Sept. 13, a Russian drone struck a truck about 800 meters (0.5 miles) from the Polish border near the Yahodyn border crossing. The same day, Russian forces struck the locomotive of a passenger train traveling to Warsaw.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki will convene a meeting on Sept. 18 to discuss the country's security situation, Bartosz Grodecki, head of the National Security Bureau, said on Sept. 16, amid heightened tensions between Russia and Poland.

Australia is considering banning the use of smart glasses that can record from federal government workplaces amid growing privacy and security concerns, media reports said Thursday.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher asked the Australian Public Service Commission for advice on the use of smart glasses in Commonwealth workplaces, including whether the devices should be prohibited and what exemptions may be needed, according to ABC News.
"Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information," said Gallagher. "We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants.”
The proposal concerns Commonwealth workplaces and is not a nationwide ban on the possession or use of smart glasses.
It comes as several Australian local councils have separately restricted the technology in public facilities because of concerns that camera-equipped glasses can record discreetly.
Yarra City Council in Melbourne has restricted smart glasses in facilities, including playgrounds, childcare centers and gyms. Brisbane City Council has prohibited non-consensual recording using camera-enabled wearable devices at public swimming pools.
Other councils are considering similar measures.
The federal government has stopped short of pursuing a broader ban on importing smart glasses.
Attorney General Michelle Rowland said last month that an import ban was not currently being considered, although the government was examining privacy issues surrounding wearable technologies.
The privacy commissioner has also been asked to give smart glasses "priority consideration" amid their growing availability and privacy implications.

Switzerland returns ancient golden mask to Egypt (PHOTOS)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:01:37 UTC
23:01:37 KST

Switzerland returns ancient golden mask to Egypt (PHOTOS)
Switzerland has returned a more than 2,000-year-old funerary mask to Egypt after it was intercepted by Swiss customs four years ago, the Swiss Embassy in Cairo said on Wednesday.
The ancient mask dates back to Egypt’s Ptolemaic period and was seized by the Swiss customs authorities in 2022. It was subsequently examined and authenticated as an Egyptian artifact. Egypt’s Foreign Ministry described the artifact as “a golden mummy mask.”
The artifact was formally handed over in Bern by Swiss Federal Councilor Elisabeth Baume-Schneider to Egypt’s ambassador to Switzerland, Mohamed Negm.
“This return is another milestone in the longstanding cooperation between Switzerland and Egypt to protect cultural heritage and fight the illicit trafficking of cultural property,” the embassy said. Bern has returned around 80 cultural objects to Egypt since 2011, according to the statement.
It comes as the North African country steps up efforts to recover antiquities taken abroad illegally. On Thursday, the Egyptian Embassy in Beirut received 74 archaeological artifacts from various historical periods from the Lebanese authorities ahead of their repatriation to Egypt. Cairo said the handover was part of work with Lebanon to protect cultural heritage and combat the illicit trafficking of antiquities.
Egypt has also recovered antiquities from the US as part of its repatriation drive. In April, the country retrieved 13 artifacts that were illegally smuggled abroad, following work with the authorities in New York. The objects included an alabaster jar for oils and perfumes from the 7th century BC, as well as cosmetic containers shaped like animals from the Middle and New Kingdoms of Ancient Egypt.
Also last year, Egyptian officials said 13 artifacts were returned from the UK and Germany. The items include a mummy’s skull and hand, ankh and baboon-shaped amulets, a bronze Osiris crown, and a beaded funerary mask.

FBI warned ICE agents could be targeted by fake ‘tradwife’ dating profiles, memo reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:00:52 UTC
23:00:52 KST

The FBI internally warned that a group of women were creating fake online dating accounts with “tradwife” aesthetics in an effort to lure US immigration agents and “dox” them.
The FBI in Chicago disseminated a brief memo to other law enforcement officials across the US on the potential threat to agents in February, warning that “as of late January 2026, a small group of women allegedly were creating fictitious online dating profiles with the purpose of attracting and then doxxing law enforcement participating in immigration enforcement”. The report, which was shared with the Guardian, provided few details about the alleged scheme and did not explain the source of the information.
“These profiles were incorporating imagery of a ‘traditional wife’ aesthetic and listing specific interests in an attempt to appeal to … individuals in law enforcement,” the FBI continued. “The objective was to lure affiliated law enforcement personnel into an online or in-person interaction under the guise of a date, after which the individuals would be publicly exposed and doxed online. The tactic is intended to generate public embarrassment and deter immigration enforcement activity.”
Property of the People, a government-transparency non-profit, obtained the document through a public records request, one of many internal records the group has collected revealing internal law enforcement concerns about activists organizing against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
The FBI’s “situational information report” did not list the dating sites allegedly used by the women or where they were located, nor did it specify whether agents had actually been exposed. The memo aimed “to raise awareness” about this doxing “technique”, the FBI wrote, adding a disclaimer that the report was “not finally evaluated intelligence”.
The FBI’s “tradwife” comments were a reference to the trend popularized in recent years by influencers promoting traditional gender roles, with women romanticizing domesticity. “Doxing” generally refers to publishing someone’s private information online without their consent, though the administration has used the term loosely, claiming doxing includes posting videos of officers.
The FBI declined to answer detailed questions about the memo, saying the bureau doesn’t generally comment on intelligence briefings. A spokesperson added in an email: “The FBI regularly shares information with our law enforcement partners to assist in protecting the communities they serve as well as protecting those who serve and protect communities. The FBI is committed to ensuring that law enforcement officers are safe from threats or violence while performing their duties.”
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement after publication that its officers are “under constant threat from violent agitators” and “publicizing their identities puts their lives and the lives of their families at serious risk.”
The memo was sent weeks after the New York Post, a conservative outlet, ran a story saying that “lefty TikTokkers” were “orchestrating groups of women” to “chase dick picks and selfies of ICE agents in a twisted scheme to dox them”. That story cited Libs of TikTok, a rightwing account that had posted a screenshot of someone claiming to be part of a Facebook group dedicated to going on dates with agents to expose them. The article listed a handful of posts and videos from users discussing this tactic, though it did not include interviews with anyone who claimed to be duping agents and there was no evidence agents had been tricked.
The news coverage did not mention women using “tradwife” imagery, so it’s unclear whether the FBI may have received direct accounts from targeted agents or was simply summarizing social media trends.
“It’s absurd the FBI issued a thinly-sourced security alert about ICE agents’ online dating troubles,” Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People, said in a statement. “It’s equally ludicrous the FBI is spending taxpayer dollars to protect ICE agents from possible ‘embarrassment’ at the hands of a supposed ‘small group of women’ who might name and ridicule them online.”
Mike German, a former FBI agent and longtime civil liberties advocate, reviewed the document for the Guardian and said it was odd the briefing did not have footnotes or citations. The briefing said the intelligence came from a “collaborative source”.
“The rightwing echo chamber creates threats and the government’s intelligence apparatus just repeats those threats without any context, more detail or any instruction of how agents or officers should respond,” said German, arguing it seemed likely the briefing was inspired by the New York Post story. “They must have run out of other threats.”
The document, German added, “reinforces the paranoid ‘us versus them’ mentality within law enforcement”.
The briefing comes as US law enforcement has raised increasing alarms about officials, and ICE agents in particular, being “doxed”. More than a dozen internal law enforcement reports, obtained via records requests by Property of the People, include similar warnings about doxing.
An October 2025 report from the US army said there was “credible intelligence” that “cartels” had offered to pay gang members and others in the US to dox, assault or kidnap immigration officers. That report cited charges against a man accused of a murder-for-hire plot targeting a top border patrol leader, but the man was found not guilty months later.
In a November 2025 report, the FBI warned that AI, facial-recognition and automated data-scraping tools had “increased the scale and accuracy of doxxing attacks” targeting ICE officers. The alert said people had published ICE officers’ names, photos, license plates, locations and family details, citing various crowdsourced efforts by activists to report ICE sightings.
In a January 2026 New York police department “terrorism brief”, the NYPD warned of “violent rhetoric” and “extremist messaging” on social media after the killing of Renee Good, including “calls to ‘hunt down’, ‘dox’, and kill ICE personnel”. The report cited a small number of online posts that appeared to call for violence.
And a May 2026 alert from Customs and Border Protection (CBP), a branch of DHS, warned that smart glasses, which have cameras, could be used to surveil, record and potentially dox CBP personnel. A CBP spokesperson did not comment directly on the document, but said in an email that smart glasses “pose unique security and intelligence risks because of their ability to discreetly capture audio and video” and the agency continues to monitor technology trends. Property of the People shared records with the Guardian earlier this month showing law enforcement across the US have grown increasingly concerned that smart glasses could be used against officers.
Other law enforcement agencies that have raised concerns about ICE agents being doxed in internal records include the FBI in Los Angeles, the Amtrak police department, an Idaho law enforcement consortium, a Florida fusion center of local and federal agencies, and the Federal Protective Service, which is also part of DHS.
There can be safety concerns if agents’ home addresses or family information is exposed, and two activists were convicted of “stalking” in California after prosecutors said they followed an agent home and publicly disclosed the location.
But German argued law enforcement’s claims about doxing were misguided, noting that ICE officers are domestic servants, not “secret agents” whose identities must be shielded: “These are agents working on the public dime. The public has a right to know who they are and what their qualifications and training are.”

Iran expels Swedish diplomat in tit-for-tat after Stockholm's move
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:00:50 UTC
23:00:50 KST

Tehran summoned Sweden's ambassador and ordered one of its diplomats to leave within 48 hours after Stockholm expelled an Iranian embassy official for activities "incompatible with the Vienna Convention."
Tehran has ordered a Swedish diplomat to leave Iranian territory within 48 hours, after Sweden expelled an Iranian diplomat from its embassy in Stockholm on Wednesday over activities described as incompatible with diplomatic norms.
Alireza Yousofi, director-general for Western Europe at Iran's foreign ministry, summoned the Swedish ambassador in Tehran on Thursday to deliver the reciprocal expulsion order and convey what he described as Iran's protest at Sweden's "destructive policies and its hosting of terrorist groups."
Iran's foreign ministry said in a statement that Sweden's decision to restrict the activities of an Iranian diplomat was "baseless" and attributed it to alleged Israeli influence, describing the move as an attempt to disrupt normal operations at the Iranian embassy in Stockholm.
Tehran warned that any disruption of the embassy's work would engage Sweden's international responsibility under the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.
Sweden's foreign ministry had summoned the Iranian ambassador in Stockholm on Wednesday and ordered the expulsion of one of his embassy's diplomats, citing "improper activities incompatible with the Vienna Convention." It gave no further details of what those activities involved.
Sweden and Iran have a history of diplomatic confrontations. In June 2024, two Swedish citizens, Johan Floderus and Saeed Azizi, were released in a prisoner swap in exchange for Hamid Nouri, a former Iranian prison official who had been serving a life sentence in Sweden.
Nouri was arrested at Stockholm Airport in November 2019 under universal jurisdiction and convicted for his role in the mass execution of political prisoners in Iran in 1988.
In July 2025, Sweden joined several European countries, the US and Canada in accusing Tehran of orchestrating plots to threaten, abduct and harass dissidents, journalists and activists abroad.

Long-term study links childhood screen time to slightly better cognitive skills in teenagers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:00:27 UTC
23:00:27 KST

A long-term assessment of physical habits from childhood to adolescence suggests that higher amounts of screen time and lower amounts of unsupervised physical activity are associated with better cognitive performance in teenage years. The findings, published in Pediatric Exercise Science, highlight how different types and measures of daily movement relate to brain development in unexpected ways.
Cognition refers to a set of high-order mental processes that allow us to navigate daily life. These processes include working memory, which involves holding and manipulating information over short periods, attention, which is the ability to focus, and psychomotor speed, which is how quickly the brain processes and reacts to a stimulus. Childhood and adolescence are sensitive periods for the development of these cognitive skills.
During these formative years, physical activity often decreases while sedentary behaviors and screen time tend to rise. Past research exploring how these shifting habits affect the developing brain has yielded mixed results. Some studies suggest that physical activity boosts cognition by increasing blood flow and releasing beneficial brain chemicals, while others find no such link.
There is also a growing understanding of how broader physical health outcomes influence the brain. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that physical health factors like stiffer arteries are associated with weaker working memory in teens. To better understand the daily habits that often drive these physical outcomes, researchers wanted to look at long-term, cumulative exposure to both physical activity and sitting time.
Prior studies had largely relied on snapshots of behavior at a single point in time. “Existing studies on adolescents have reported mixed findings on how physical activity, sedentary time, and screen time relate to cognition,” Petri Jalanko, a doctoral researcher at the University of Jyväskylä, told PsyPost.
“Most prior work has focused on a single time point, even though children’s movement behaviors change substantially as they grow,” Jalanko added.
To address this gap, the research team, led by Jalanko, tracked the cumulative impact of these movement behaviors over many years. They drew on data from the Physical Activity and Nutrition in Children study in Finland, analyzing a sample of 260 adolescents who were initially recruited between the ages of 6 and 9.
Over an eight-year period, the participants underwent assessments at a baseline visit, a two-year follow-up, and an eight-year follow-up. The researchers also wanted to compare data from self-reported questionnaires with objective data gathered by wearable fitness devices, as the two methods often capture different aspects of physical behavior.
To capture physical activity and sedentary behavior, the researchers used two distinct methods. First, participants and their parents filled out questionnaires detailing the frequency and duration of various activities. This included organized sports, unsupervised physical activity, screen time, and non-screen sedentary time, such as reading or doing arts and crafts.
Second, the children wore a specialized monitor on their chests for a minimum of four consecutive days at each of the three assessment periods. This device recorded heart rate and body movement to objectively measure time spent in light, moderate, and vigorous physical activity, as well as total sedentary time.
At the final eight-year follow-up, when the adolescents were around 15 to 17 years old, they completed a computerized cognitive test battery. This testing software measured their reaction times and accuracy across tasks designed to evaluate psychomotor function, attention, working memory, and associative learning.
The self-reported data yielded some surprising associations. Accumulating more unsupervised physical activity over the eight years was associated with poorer working memory accuracy in adolescence. The authors noted that this specific link was relatively weak from a statistical standpoint, but it presented an interesting contrast to common assumptions about exercise.
“We were also intrigued by the finding that some types of physical activity context (for example, unsupervised activity, as defined in our measures) showed a negative association with working memory,” Jalanko said. “That result should be interpreted cautiously and needs replication, because it may reflect unmeasured factors—such as what the activity is displacing (sleep, homework), or differences in social/educational context—rather than an adverse effect of activity itself.”
More self-reported screen time over the years was linked to faster reaction times in working memory tasks and better overall cognitive scores. Similarly, higher amounts of self-reported non-screen sedentary time were associated with faster reaction times, though this came at the cost of poorer accuracy on working memory tasks.
“One result that stood out was that more screen time was associated with better cognition in our models, because public discussion often assumes screen time is uniformly harmful,” the researcher noted.
“In our data, higher screen time was associated with slightly better performance on some cognitive measures at age 16,” Jalanko explained. “This does not mean that ‘more screen time makes teens smarter’—screen time is a broad category, and different content and contexts likely matter a lot.”
Instead, some screen activities, such as schoolwork, learning-oriented use, or cognitively engaging hobbies, might support or reflect cognitive skills. “More broadly, families shouldn’t view screen time as automatically harmful in all cases, but it’s still important to keep a healthy balance: protect sleep, make room for physical activity, and encourage screen use that involves active thinking rather than passive scrolling,” Jalanko said.
The objective data recorded by the chest monitors showed a different picture. Overall, cumulative device-assessed physical activity and sedentary time were not related to cognitive performance in the general group of adolescents. The physiological intensity of movement, recorded purely by heart rate and acceleration, did not show a broad association with brain function.
When the researchers looked at boys and girls separately, distinct patterns emerged. For boys, engaging in more self-reported organized sports was related to better working memory. At the same time, more self-reported unsupervised physical activity was linked to poorer working memory in boys, but not in girls.
For girls, higher amounts of self-reported screen time were associated with better overall cognition, a pattern not seen in the boys. Additionally, the objective device measurements indicated that more light physical activity was associated with better working memory in girls, but not in boys.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. Because cognitive tests were only fully administered at the end of the eight-year period, the researchers cannot determine cause and effect.
“This was an observational longitudinal study, so we cannot conclude that screen time causes changes in cognition,” Jalanko emphasized. “In terms of practical importance, the observed associations were small—they are meaningful for understanding population patterns, but cognition is influenced by many factors (sleep, education, family environment, mental health, etc.), and screen time is only one part of that picture.”
It is possible that children with naturally stronger cognitive skills simply choose to spend more time on certain screen-based tasks or less time on unsupervised physical play. The study also relies heavily on how behaviors are categorized.
“‘Screen time’ includes many very different activities; some may be beneficial or neutral, and others may be harmful,” Jalanko pointed out. “So it would be a misinterpretation to take our findings as a recommendation for unlimited or purely entertainment-focused screen use.”
He added that prior research suggests that highly passive or rapidly changing short-form content might relate differently to brain health outcomes than educational or interactive use. There are also limitations related to how the behaviors were measured.
Questionnaires rely on memory, which can introduce errors. Parents might not know exactly how much time their child spends playing unsupervised, or they might underestimate screen time. On the other hand, chest-worn devices cannot tell the difference between sitting down to read a book and sitting down to watch a movie.
The researchers suspect that the context of the activity plays a major role in these results. Activities grouped under screen time or sedentary time often include cognitively stimulating tasks, such as reading, doing homework, playing strategy-based video games, or socializing with friends. Unsupervised physical activity might actually replace time that could otherwise be spent on these mentally engaging tasks.
Future studies will need to track both physical behavior and cognitive performance repeatedly from early childhood into adulthood. This approach would help scientists map out exactly how daily habits and brain development interact over a lifetime.
“A key next step is to move beyond observational associations and test causality more directly,” Jalanko told PsyPost. “We are currently analyzing data from our VERNA randomized cross-over study to examine how different intensities of physical activity affect cognitive performance acutely in adolescents.”
“Together, the longitudinal and experimental approaches can help triangulate which relationships are likely causal, and under what conditions,” he concluded.
The study, “Associations of Physical Activity and Sedentary Time From Childhood to Adolescence With Cognition in Adolescence: The PANIC Study,” was authored by Petri Jalanko, Marja H. Leppänen, Bert Bond, Jari A. Laukkanen, Timo A. Lakka, and Eero A. Haapala.

Column: Development as common aspiration: enduring bond between China and India
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:59:10 CST
22:59:10 KST

by Mohammed Saqib
When President Xi Jinping visited New Delhi for the BRICS Summit 2026, the first such visit in seven years, it was more than a diplomatic event. It was a symbol of renewal, a reminder that China and India, two civilizational giants and largest developing countries, share a responsibility to cooperate for development. In this uncertain world, development stands out as the greatest common denominator binding our nations together.
From the spread of Buddhism across the Himalayas to centuries of trade along the Silk Road, histories of the two countries are deeply connected. These ties are not just relics of the past; they remind us that cooperation is part of our shared heritage. Today, as both nations modernize, these connections gain new significance. Development serves as a bridge linking our past to our future.
The meeting between Xi and Narendra Modi in New Delhi represented a commitment to stabilizing their relationship and focusing on shared interests.
Economic engagement could be a major aspect of bilateral cooperation. China's strength in manufacturing and infrastructure aligns well with India's dynamic services sector and innovation ecosystem. Collaborations in renewable energy, digital platforms and green finance could unlock significant potential and accelerate shared prosperity. However, development goes beyond economics; it also involves investing in people. Expanding student exchanges, cultural festivals and joint research programs can help deepen trust between the two nations.
Beyond bilateral relations, the Global South views China and India as pillars of hope. In forums like the BRICS, SCO, the G20 and the United Nations, China and India can amplify the voices of developing countries. The Global South looks to China and India to demonstrate that cooperation among major developing nations is not only possible but also essential.
The vision for shared prosperity is clear. China and India must embrace development as the greatest common denominator. By cooperating in trade, technology, infrastructure and cultural exchanges, they can inspire the Global South, strengthen multipolarity and shape a fairer international order.
Xi Jinping's visit to New Delhi reminded us that civilizational ties and modern aspirations converge on one point: development. It is the bridge that connects our histories, the mission that unites our peoples, and the hope that inspires the Global South. By embracing development as the foundation of cooperation, China and India can move beyond differences, strengthen exchanges and work together to build a brighter and more inclusive future for the world.
We must recognize that what unites us is far stronger than what divides us.

====================================================================================================

Global freshwater storage declines, glaciers continue to retreat: WMO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:59:08 CST
22:59:08 KST

GENEVA, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Rivers around the world had one of the driest years in more than three decades in 2025, according to a new report released by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) on Thursday. The report warns of a continuation of the long-term decline in freshwater storage and glacier retreat, trends with serious implications for the future of the planet, its people and economies.
The WMO State of Global Water Resources Report shows that the water cycle has become more erratic and unpredictable, swinging between too little and too much. The past seven years have seen the fewest rivers with "normal" flows since 1991.
For the seventh year in a row, the number of river basins with "normal" conditions was in a clear minority: ranging between 34 percent and 38 percent, compared to an average of 46 percent between 1991 and 2020.
Terrestrial water storage -- the total amount of water stored in groundwater, lakes and rivers, soil moisture, vegetation and ice and snow -- has been in decline since the mid-2010s.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said that the planet's water reserves used to act as a "savings account" that absorbed the occasional dry season, thereby avoiding a water crisis. "One of the central stories of the 2025 report is what is happening to that savings account. And the simple answer is that we are depleting it," she told journalists at the launch of the report in Geneva.
The year 2025 marked the fourth consecutive year with widespread glacier loss across all regions, leading to short-term hazards such as flooding, and water insecurity in the long term. Between 2023 and 2025, glaciers lost mass in each reporting year with cumulative global glacier mass loss at 1400 gigatons of water. This is roughly equal to about one third of annual freshwater withdrawals.
"All 19 glacier regions around the globe lost ice; in Central Asia, Iceland, the Russian Arctic, and western Canada and the United States. It was among the three worst years on record," said Wayne Jenkinson, the WMO's Director of Hydrology and Cryosphere, at the conference.
In each of the last five years, National Meteorological and Hydrological Services around the globe have reported record-breaking floods and droughts. Some places have had no recovery time between one event and the next, the report noted.
"Water respects no borders. A river basin's water balance depends on what happens in another country. A glacier's retreat in one country reshapes water availability for populations hundreds of kilometers downstream. This is precisely why we need shared data, shared standards, and shared early warning, the exact function WMO exists to perform," said Saulo. ■

Western Thrace Turkish minority takes religious rights concerns to UN Human Rights Council
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:59:00 UTC
22:59:00 KST

Ayhan Mehmet and Seyit Kurt
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
The Federation of Western Thrace Turks in Europe (ABTTF) has raised concerns about the Western Thrace Turkish minority’s right to elect its muftis and the status of its religious institutions before the UN Human Rights Council.
The federation submitted a written statement to the council’s 63rd regular session, being held in Geneva, Switzerland, from Sept. 7 to Oct. 7.
In the statement, titled “Ongoing interference with the religious autonomy of the Turkish minority in Western Thrace in Greece and violations of freedom of religion,” the ABTTF said the minority’s religious status and rights were guaranteed under the 1913 Treaty of Athens and the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne.
It said these arrangements gave the minority the right to elect its muftis and administer its religious institutions.
According to the federation, the minority elected its own muftis until 1985, but after a legal change in 1991, the Greek state began appointing them, effectively ending the community’s ability to choose its own religious leaders.
The ABTTF said that Law No. 4964, enacted in 2022, changed the status of the mufti offices by turning them into public institutions under Greece’s Education, Religious Affairs and Sports Ministry.
The federation said a state-appointed mufti was installed in Didymoteicho in 2026, while similar appointment procedures were underway in Xanthi and Komotini.
It argued that while followers of other recognized religions in Greece can select their religious leaders, the religious institutions of the Western Thrace Turkish minority remain under state control, raising concerns about freedom of religion or belief and equality.
In Greece, the state appoints the religious leaders, or muftis, of the Western Thrace Turkish minority and the administrative boards of minority foundations.
The Turkish minority opposes the practice and calls for community-elected muftis to be recognized.

Belgian Court Rules Treasury Lacked Authority to Reject Release of Russian Assets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:59:00 UTC
22:59:00 KST

Belgium’s supreme administrative court has ruled that a decision by the country’s treasury department refusing to release frozen Russian assets was illegal.
The court, known as the Council of State, ruled that the Administrator General of the Treasury lacked the proper legal competence to determine whether or not to release the assets.
The September 11 ruling was first reported by De Tijd on Wednesday, and shared with OCCRP.
The case originates from a request submitted by Russia’s BCS Bank in January 2023 to unfreeze its securities and cash, which had been blocked at Brussels-based securities manager Euroclear.
The assets were frozen following E.U. sanctions imposed in 2022 on Moscow's main securities holder, the National Settlement Depository, in response to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In July 2024, the Belgian treasury rejected BCS Bank’s request to unfreeze its securities and cash. The treasury alleged that the lender had failed to prove it had fully severed ties with Russia’s National Settlement Depository.
The Council of State ruling does not necessarily mean the frozen funds will be released.
"We are studying the judgment and examining its possible consequences," Ilse Coopman, a spokesperson for Belgian Finance Minister Jan Jambon, told De Tijt. "Once that analysis is completed, we will be able to communicate further."
The judgment arrived amid ongoing legal battles over funds caught in a web of Western sanctions, which OCCRP, De Tijd and Follow the Money previously reported on. Over 200 petitions have been filed with the Council of State challenging treasury decisions on frozen assets and blocked transactions.
Reporters found that much of the 258 billion euros’ worth of blocked transactions and frozen assets (about $270 billion) does not actually belong to Kremlin cronies, or Russian state or corporate entities. Instead, a lot of it belongs to investors who are not sanctioned.

‘My whole family is either dead or injured’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:57:36 UTC
22:57:36 KST

‘My whole family is either dead or injured’
At least 21 killed in Gaza building collapse, dozens missing
At least 21 people, including six children, were killed when a war-damaged residential building collapsed in Gaza City on Wednesday, local rescue officials said.
At least 14 others were injured, and dozens are feared trapped beneath the rubble.
With heavy machinery in short supply after months of conflict, rescue workers have been digging by hand in search of survivors.
Authorities say multiple families were sheltering in the building, and the death toll is expected to rise as recovery efforts continue.
Leaning heavily on the arm of a relative, Hayat al-Ajlah moves slowly between the hospital beds, scanning the faces of the injured.
She is looking for her eight-year-old daughter, Dalia.
Hayat has not seen her since they were pulled from beneath the rubble of the al-Saada building in western Gaza City early on Wednesday, when the war-damaged structure collapsed over their heads.
“I woke up to check my phone,” Al Jazeera quoted the 37-year-old Hayat as saying. “Suddenly, I heard a sound like something cracking. It felt like something was falling from underneath us.”
Moments later, the building came down, killing at least 21 Palestinians.
Hayat found herself trapped beneath the rubble, surrounded by dust and darkness, with family members screaming for help.
“I heard my 74-year-old father calling for my 12-year-old son Yasser. ‘Yasser, Yasser,’ he was calling, and then his voice disappeared,” she said. “I panicked and started screaming for my four children.
‘We survived by a miracle’
For nearly an hour, neighbors and civil defense workers worked to pull Hayat, her children and some of the other residents from the rubble. But Hayat knew that others were trapped deeper inside the building.
“My father and mother’s voices disappeared because they were in the part where the floors collapsed on top of each other,” she said through tears.
“We were closer to the side of the building that tilted, so we survived by a miracle.”
Nine members of Hayat’s extended family were killed, she said, including her parents, four of her siblings, and three of her nephews and nieces.
Her four children survived, although her daughter Dalia was taken to hospital with a serious head injury.
The collapse had come suddenly, but Hayat said there had been warning signs.
“My mother was afraid of the building, and my father was planning to find another place,” she said.
The family had been displaced from Gaza City’s Shujayea neighborhood to Deir el-Balah, in central Gaza, during an earlier phase of Israel’s genocidal war, before returning about two months ago.
With few alternatives, and many in Gaza still living in tents because of Israeli restrictions on reconstruction, the family moved into an empty apartment on the third floor of the damaged residential building after a friend of Hayat’s father told him it was available.
“My father’s friend told him there was an empty apartment on the third floor. It was severely damaged, but my family wanted to get out of the tent and escape its harsh conditions,” Hayat said.
Many members of her extended family were in the building when the tragedy struck because they had been preparing for a celebration – a family wedding planned for next week.
“We never expected this tragedy. The whole family is either dead or injured,” Hayat said.
Families wait at al-Shifa
At Gaza City’s al-Shifa Hospital, relatives of the victims have gathered in grief and shock, waiting for the lengthy recovery operation to continue and for news of those still missing.
Among them was the Saada family.
Umm Mahmoud Saada, in her 70s, stood crying for her son Mahmoud, his wife and their children.
Mahmoud, 38, was the father of six girls and a boy. Neither Mahmoud nor his family survived.
He had been living displaced in southern Gaza and only returned to Gaza City a month ago, she explained.
“He had a tent in the middle of the street and was exhausted [living in it], and his financial situation was very difficult,” his mother said. “A relative showed him this place, so he settled there temporarily. We did not know it would be his end.”
She recalled seeing her son the day before.
“Yesterday, he visited me. We prayed the noon prayer together, ate together and then he left,” she said. “All our loved ones are leaving us, and our hearts are breaking day after day. Why is all this happening to us?”
Rescue with little equipment
The search operation has been prolonged by a severe shortage of heavy machinery and other essential equipment, a direct result of Israeli restrictions on imports into Gaza and reconstruction.
Palestinian Civil Defence said its teams had worked for hours to reach people trapped beneath the building, but had been forced to rely on limited and basic tools. The shortage made it difficult to clear the large amounts of concrete and rubble and reach those still underneath.
Mansour Bakroun, 56, had been sitting in front of his tent when the building collapsed before dawn.
“The building is around 150 metres [about 500 feet] away. At first, I ran back, calling for my family to flee,” he said.
Once the dust began to settle, he ran towards the building, where residents were already trying to rescue those trapped.
Mansour said the building had been visibly damaged since the beginning of the war.
“Every day, something would fall from it … a piece of a wall, a stone,” he said.
“People left, but those who stayed had nowhere to go,” he added. “They had no other place.”
Another man living nearby, Huzaifa Mohammed, said that he had long been afraid of a collapse.
“Every day, I imagine these buildings collapsing,” he said. “Every day, pieces of stone and walls are falling, and people ask: Where should we go?”
Huzaifa said the sight of children being pulled from the rubble had left him struggling to understand what he was witnessing.
“When I see a little girl brought out with her head crushed, I ask myself: What if this were my daughter or my son?” he said.
Huzaifa said people had spent years living among damaged buildings and warnings of danger, with few places to go.
“How long are we going to keep living like this?” he said. “Are we only going to come out and condemn what is happening? We need solutions. We need someone to look at our situation and ask: How much longer can this continue?”

From F1 to FIBA, Qatar unveils packed calendar of global events
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:54:07 UTC
22:54:07 KST

More than 560 events are planned through 2027, with major sports, concerts and festivals on the programme as Qatar looks to build on record visitor numbers.
From Formula 1 and the FIBA Basketball World Cup to concerts and food festivals, Qatar has unveiled a calendar of more than 560 events stretching through 2027.
The programme comes as the Gulf country looks to build on record visitor numbers following a period of regional uncertainty.
Qatar welcomed 5.1 million visitors last year, according to Visit Qatar. Jassim Al Mahmoud, Director of Communications at Visit Qatar, said another 2.9 million arrived in the first half of this year.
“The biggest number of visitors arrived to Qatar last year, so this is something that drives us to have such a rich calendar in order to enhance their experience, to have more options, more variety, to bring more visitors to Qatar,” Al Mahmoud said.
The Qatar Calendar brings events across sport, culture, entertainment and food together on a single platform, allowing residents and visitors to see what is happening and plan ahead.
A busy roster of events
Sport features heavily, with several major international competitions on the schedule.
The FIFA U-17 World Cup Qatar 2026 will run from 19 November to 13 December, while MotoGP returns to the Lusail International Circuit from 6 to 8 November.
The Qatar T100 Triathlon World Championship Final follows from 10 to 12 December, with the Doha Marathon on 15 January 2027.
Top-tier tennis returns in February with the Qatar TotalEnergies Open, scheduled from 8 to 15 February.
Later in the year, Doha will host the FIBA Basketball World Cup from 27 August to 12 September 2027.
Formula 1 is also set to return to Lusail in 2027, with the Qatar Grand Prix scheduled from 3 to 5 December.
Beyond sport, the calendar also includes concerts, festivals, food and cultural events.
Oscar-winning composer Hans Zimmer is among the international artists highlighted, alongside performances by Angham and Saint Levant. A Harry Potter film music concert is also on the programme.
Other events include the Qatar International Food Festival, Art Basel and the Al Ruwais Festival.
The idea is to give visitors a mix of experiences throughout the year rather than focusing solely on major sporting events, with shopping, food, culture and entertainment included alongside them.
Steve Harvey returns with more events
One familiar face at the launch was US TV host and comedian Steve Harvey, who has already hosted several events in Qatar.
Harvey said his previous experiences in the country helped bring him back.
“When it comes to beauty and architecture and landscape and the people, it’s just a great place to come,” Harvey said.
“I travel the world. And so this is a great place to come and do business and share the culture.”
Harvey said he had signed a multi-year deal to bring more entertainment events to Qatar, including the return of FuelFest, a new comedy series and Family Feud.
He also outlined plans to eventually stage what he called a Family Feud World Cup, bringing families from different countries to Qatar to compete in the game show.
Building the tourism sector
The calendar is also part of Qatar’s longer-term tourism strategy.
Doha has set a target of increasing tourism’s contribution to GDP to 12% by 2030, according to material released alongside the calendar launch.
Al Mahmoud said the range of events was intended to give visitors more options during their stays, spanning sport, culture, shopping and food.
“We believe that we have the offering,” he said. “We have lots of options, a lot of variety.”
He said the launch was also intended to signal continuity in Qatar’s events programme.
“By revealing the calendar, we are saying to the world that we are ready, we are open, we have a rich calendar,” Al Mahmoud said.
“Qatar remains fully operational.”

Pakistan announces austerity measures as Gulf conflict drives up fuel prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:53:42 UTC
22:53:42 KST

Pakistan has announced a new package of austerity measures to conserve energy and reduce government spending as the Gulf conflict pushes up fuel prices and disrupts liquefied natural gas supplies.
Thursday’s measures include cuts in fuel use by official vehicles, a ban on government purchases of vehicles and other durable goods, and restrictions on foreign travel by officials and official dinners.
The government will also switch to teleconferencing for meetings, with IT procurement exempt from the ban on durable goods, according to the measures.
Pakistan is facing the prospect of gas and power shortages as disruptions to LNG supplies and higher petrol and diesel prices put pressure on energy security.
The measures are the second austerity package introduced this year. In March, the government closed schools for two weeks, cut fuel use across government and encouraged office workers to work from home.
Pakistan also introduced a subsidy on Wednesday for motorcycle, rickshaw and small-car owners, offering 100 rupees ($0.36) per litre on a capped monthly quota to ease the impact of rising fuel prices.
The latest energy pressures follow disruptions to oil and gas exports through the Strait of Hormuz after attacks by the US and Israel on Iran.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis has also raised concerns over trade through the Red Sea, adding to pressure on regional energy and supply routes.
