‘Amazing community’: how people are making new friends and connections as adults
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:53:28 UTC
22:53:28 KST

Amid growing concern about loneliness and social isolation, new research from the Institute for Public Policy Research found the number of young people in England with no close friends has risen fivefold since 2014, with one in 20 now reporting having none at all.
Making new friends as an adult is not always easy. We spoke to people who have taken deliberate steps to make new connections about what worked for them.
‘If I was in trouble in some way, I’ve now got people I could actually call’
For Rhiannon, a 35-year-old ghostwriter from East Sussex, joining a local knitting and crochet group has become “a lifeline” after separating from her husband and moving a few towns away, and finding connections harder to maintain.
In February, she joined the Yarners, a weekly group in Mayfield. Having only started crocheting a month earlier, she was “absolutely terrified” they would judge her for being a beginner. “But they didn’t care.”
The group quickly became an important part of her life. “No matter what is happening at home, I know for two hours a week I can just sit in a calm and supportive space with people who share my hobby. It’s more than just a group. It’s a real community.”
Having local friends to rely on is one of the biggest perks. “If I needed something, if I was in trouble in some way, I’ve now got people I could actually call and say: ‘Hey, can you help me?’”
‘It just blew up. There are 70 people in the group now’
Ria, 27, moved from Mumbai to London five years ago, but after later moving to Reading, she found it harder to maintain the friendships she had made in the capital.
“I faced acute loneliness,” says Ria, who now works in mergers and acquisitions in London. “When people move away from their home, it gets tough at this age to make friends.”
In May, she created a WhatsApp group to bring her London friends together. It soon expanded through friends of friends and Instagram. “It just blew up. There are 70 people in the group now.”
The London Coffee Club holds meetups in cafes for groups of five to 10. “I’m slightly introverted, so I don’t prefer big groups. It’s a relaxed vibe. There’s no agenda.”
‘She’s helping me and I’m helping her’
Working from home left Rebecca, a 31-year-old NHS project support officer in Bristol, missing everyday social interaction. “I completely underestimated how much I would miss face-to-face contact, even informal conversations such as: ‘How was your weekend?’”
A few months ago, she joined exercise classes at her local leisure centre “as a way to make friends”. Although “absolutely terrified” at first, she now attends pilates, weights and body conditioning classes about three times a week.
“Even though you’re doing an exercise class, there’s that informal aspect where you are having a bit of a joke and a laugh. Working from home, you don’t get that sort of office banter. To me, this is my new equivalent.”
Rebecca has also met a new friend through Bristol Girls, a local Facebook group, and encouraged her to join the classes. “She’s helping me, and I’m helping her,” she says.
‘I have met some of my closest friends here’
After leaving his job as a primary school teacher Ben, 35, suddenly had more free time so thought he would use it to “meet new people” and get back into stage performance.
“It was something I loved at school and at university,” says Ben, who lives in Gateshead and works in education.
In 2017, he joined the People’s Theatre in Newcastle upon Tyne, a non-professional community theatre company, and has since performed in about 20 productions.
“The first year was non-stop as I jumped from play to play and met so many fantastic people,” he says. “It’s been nearly a decade, and I count some people, even people I only met less than a year ago, as some of my closest friends.”
The friendships now extend well beyond rehearsals and performances, with regular social gatherings.
“It’s a huge community, and everyone involved, whether it’s performing, set building, or costume design, does it for the love of it,” he says. “It’s so inspiring.”
‘It’s vital for people to have a safe third space’
Chris, 32, says a combination of growing older, the isolation of Covid and having no similarly aged peers at work led to a point where he “essentially had no local friends any more”.
The systems manager from Kent decided to revive his interest in board and card games and found a local games shop holding £3-a-session games evenings. Although “terrified” before his first event, he “couldn’t have asked for a better environment”.
“I feel like it’s not the impossible feat I thought it was to make new friends as an adult on your own,” he says. “The joy it brings me to be able to take part in a fun activity while getting to know people and enjoying good humour is priceless.
“I think it’s vital for mental health for people to have a safe third space where they can develop relationships, skills and experiences without being dependent on work or partners to fill that void.”
‘It’s brought me this amazing community’
When Chloe, 27, moved back to Hertfordshire after living in the Midlands, the change left her feeling lonely.
But instead of joining a group, she created one.
“All I wanted was just a friend to go for coffee or go to the cinema with,” she says. “I thought: there’s nothing for local women to make local friends. It’s so important to have that community.”
With this in mind, Chloe, a content creator, and her friend Sarah, 30, a nail technician, created the Girls Collective, organising activities where women can meet while trying something new, from keyring making to line dancing.
To drum up interest, they posted content on social media which caught people’s attention.
“We had 65 people for our first event just from our TikTok videos,” she says.
Engaging in an activity, Chloe and Sarah believe, helps to cut through any nerves and awkwardness.
The group now has 500 women in its community chat, and more than 250 have attended events. “They’ve made their own friendships and hang out outside of us [too], which is brilliant,” says Sarah.
Chloe adds: “I had thought having to move back was the worst thing. But now I’m like, no, because it’s brought me this amazing community.”

Swedish premier resigns after left-wing bloc wins election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:52:47 UTC
22:52:47 KST

Melike Pala
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson submitted his resignation Thursday to the parliament speaker after preliminary election results showed the left-wing opposition bloc secured a majority in the parliament.
The left-wing opposition led by Social Democratic Party leader Magdalena Andersson won 176 seats in the 349-member parliament, compared with 173 seats for the four parties supporting Kristersson's government -- the Moderates, Sweden Democrats, Christian Democrats and Liberals.
The opposition also won the election by a margin of 50,359 votes, according to preliminary results cited by public broadcaster SVT.
Kristersson announced that he had requested to be relieved of his duties as prime minister shortly after the votes were counted.
"The election result may have created complicated conditions for the formation of the next government, as the parties' different statements before election day could constitute obstacles to all conceivable government formations and coalitions," Kristersson wrote in a letter to the speaker.
He said the process of finding a prime minister who can secure the support or tolerance of the parliament would require "constructive openness" from the parties represented in parliament.
"In order for that work to begin immediately, I hereby request to be relieved of my duties as Prime Minister," he wrote.
The resignation opens the way for the speaker to begin consultations with political parties on forming a new government.
Kristersson and the other Cabinet ministers will remain in office until a new government takes office.
The election leaves the opposition with three more seats than the parties that have supported Kristersson's government, but the formation of the next government could depend on negotiations among the parties in parliament.

From Macklemore to Azeez Al-Shaair: How stars are paying a price for speaking up for Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:52:39 UTC
22:52:39 KST

- Despite professional repercussions, many public figures continue using their platforms to condemn Israel’s war in Gaza and advocate for Palestinian rights
The removal of US rapper Macklemore from Ed Sheeran’s stadium tour has brought renewed attention to the professional risks faced by artists and athletes who publicly support Palestinians or criticize Israel’s war in Gaza.
For some public figures, speaking out for Palestinian rights has come with significant professional consequences- from cancelled performances and lost advertising deals to dismissal from film productions, termination of employment and, in the case of athletes, financial penalties.
Here are some of the most prominent cases in which artists and athletes have faced reported backlash and repercussions.
Macklemore removed from Ed Sheeran tour
Macklemore was removed from the remaining eight dates on the US leg of Sheeran's Loop Tour after speaking about Gaza and the occupied West Bank during two concerts at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sept. 4 and 5.
The Grammy-winning rapper called for a "free Palestine" and performed Hind's Hall, his protest song named after Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israeli forces in Gaza in January 2024.
Messina Touring Group, the promoter of the US tour, said in a statement to music magazine Rolling Stone that venues scheduled to host the remaining concerts had said they would not allow the shows to proceed with Macklemore on the lineup.
Following his removal, Macklemore pledged his $1 million in net earnings from the tour to six organizations providing humanitarian assistance to Palestinians.
Finneas, Danish band Lukas Graham, Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe and Irish folk group Beoga, which has toured and performed with Sheeran, subsequently withdrew from the tour in solidarity with Macklemore.
Melissa Barrera fired from Scream VII
Mexican actor Melissa Barrera was dismissed from the film Scream VII in November 2023 after posting and resharing messages about Israel’s war on Gaza, genocide and ethnic cleansing.
Barrera responded to claims by Spyglass Media Group, the company behind the film, by condemning both antisemitism and Islamophobia and saying she would continue using her platform to advocate for human rights.
Her dismissal removed Barrera from a franchise in which she had become one of the principal stars through Scream in 2022 and Scream VI in 2023.
She later described the following months as the most difficult period of her life and said work largely dried up for about 10 months.
Barrera has since begun rebuilding her career through independent films and a Broadway role in Titanique.
In September 2026, actor Matthew Lillard said he was ashamed that he had returned for the seventh film without speaking out against Barrera’s dismissal, calling the decision to fire her wrong.
Susan Sarandon dropped by agency
In September 2026, Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon said at the Venice Film Festival that film roles had recently been taken away from her because of her political views.
Sarandon added that some agencies were still advising clients or studios not to hire her because of her support for Palestinians.
She said the resistance was particularly strong among major studios, although she continued to receive support internationally and from independent filmmakers.
Sarandon was dropped by United Talent Agency in November 2023 following remarks she made during a pro-Palestinian rally in New York.
Bella Hadid says brands stopped working with her
American model Bella Hadid has been one of the most prominent international celebrities to publicly support Palestinians, including since the start of Israels war on Gaza.
In July 2024, Adidas removed Hadid from a retro shoe campaign referencing the 1972 Munich Olympics after Israel criticized her inclusion.
Hadid subsequently hired a legal team, according to reports.
Adidas later apologized to Hadid and other campaign partners, saying: "We made an unintentional mistake. We also apologize to our partners, Bella Hadid, A$AP Nast, Jules Kounde, and others, for any negative impact on them, and we are revising the campaign."
The company did not reverse its decision to remove Hadid, prompting calls for a boycott on social media.
The model as early as 2022 said that her pro-Palestine advocacy had cost her both professional relationships and friendships.
In an interview on the Rep podcast, Hadid said multiple companies had stopped working with her because she spoke publicly about Palestine.
She said friends had also cut ties with her but that she was unwilling to remain silent about her family's heritage and the treatment of Palestinians.
Zara Larsson reports losing deals and award-show appearances
Swedish pop singer Zara Larsson has said her public support for Palestine cost her brand partnerships and invitations to awards shows.
Larsson told the Guardian in April 2026 that companies had dropped her and that she had lost industry opportunities because of her political positions, including her advocacy for Palestinians and women's rights.
She also said she declined an invitation to perform during the 2024 Eurovision Song Contest in protest against Israel's participation.
Azeez Al-Shaair fined over Hind Rajab tribute
Houston Texans linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair was fined by the NFL after writing “Hind Rajab” on his eye black during the team’s Sept. 13 game against the Buffalo Bills. 
The league imposed a fine of more than $11,000.
Al-Shaair had previously been fined $11,593 after displaying “Stop The Genocide” on his eye black during a playoff game in January.
The latest penalty drew support from Dallas Mavericks star Kyrie Irving, who said he would cover Al-Shaair’s fine.
Anwar El Ghazi dismissed by Mainz before winning court battle
Dutch footballer Anwar El Ghazi was suspended and then dismissed by German club Mainz 05 in 2023 after publishing pro-Palestinian posts on social media.
The club initially announced that El Ghazi would return after it said he had expressed regret and affirmed Israel's right to exist. El Ghazi disputed the club's account, saying he had not authorized its statement and had no regret for standing with Palestinians. Mainz terminated his contract shortly afterward.
El Ghazi challenged the decision in court and won. The Mainz Labour Court ruled in July 2024 that his dismissal was invalid. The litigation continued through appeals, but Germany's Federal Labour Court rejected Mainz's final complaint in 2026, leaving the ruling in El Ghazi's favor legally binding.
Kehlani loses major performances
Grammy-nominated R&B singer Kehlani faced professional repercussions in 2025 following public statements supporting Palestinians and criticizing Israel’s actions in Gaza.
In April 2025, Cornell University canceled Kehlani’s scheduled appearance at its annual Slope Day celebrations.
A separate planned Kehlani concert at New York’s Central Park in June 2025 was also canceled.

Lavrov says Western countries preparing for war with Russia while promoting ‘myth’ about a Russian threat'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:52:35 UTC
22:52:35 KST

Elena Teslova
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Thursday that Western countries are preparing for a war with Russia while promoting "a myth about a threat emanating from Russia."
He said Russia would be able to respond adequately to external challenges to its security.
"Today, the ruling circles and elites of most Western countries are promoting a myth about a threat emanating from Russia, actively preparing for war against our country and condemning us, among other things, for undermining European values, he said at the opening of the fourth congress of the International Russophile Movement in Moscow.
He contrasted the approach of US officials with that of European leaders, in that Washington was prepared to maintain dialogue even when the sides held fundamentally different positions.
"There is an important difference between the US and European elites. They are ready to talk. Even when positions are radically, diametrically opposed, it is always important," he said.
Lavrov said Moscow is open to serious discussions with those prepared to engage, and that foreign officials should not visit Russia merely to repeat public criticism of the country.
“Condemnation does not require coming here. But we are always open to serious conversations,” he said, adding that it is how the US dealt with Russia.
Despite the dialogue between Moscow and Washington, however, Lavrov said there had been no material change in relations, and that he did not expect one in the near future.

Immunity of Greek ex-commissioner lifted amid Qatargate probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:52:29 UTC
22:52:29 KST

Dimitris Avramopoulos was previously summoned for questioning by Belgian authorities but failed to appear on several occasions. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
ATHENS — Greece’s parliament voted Thursday to lift the immunity of ex-commissioner and current New Democracy lawmaker Dimitris Avramopoulos after Belgian authorities issued an arrest warrant in connection with the Qatargate scandal.
Avramopoulos was previously summoned for questioning by Belgian authorities but failed to appear on several occasions. A European arrest warrant was issued in June and the MP formally requested that Greece's Supreme Court block its execution while questioning its legal basis.
The court refused his request, and in a legal note to MPs, dated Sep. 17 and seen by POLITICO, he called for his immunity to be lifted to facilitate the judicial investigation. In the note, he also denies any connection to the illegal acts under investigation.
Advertisement
Greek parliament then voted unanimously to lift his parliamentary immunity, and, in response to questions from POLITICO, Avramopoulos said he would appear before the Belgian authorities once a date has been set.
He added that he regrets not appearing when he was first summoned around a year ago, stating that had he testified then, there would be no arrest warrant today.
The Belgian arrest warrant for Avramopoulos, dated June 21 and seen by POLITICO, accuses him of membership in a criminal organization, bribery of an official, and money laundering. It also alleges a financial benefit totaling approximately €73,000.
Allegations center on Avramopoulos’ cooperation with Fight Impunity, a non-governmental organization and which the arrest warrant links to the ongoing Qatargate investigation. Avramopoulos was an honorary board member of the NGO and resigned as soon as the scandal broke.
The Qatargate scandal broke out in December 2022 — after Avramopoulos had left the Commission — when Belgian police launched a series of raids on properties and offices in Brussels, arrested key suspects, and seized bags of cash in one of the biggest corruption investigations to hit the EU. The core allegations are that suspects linked to the European Parliament accepted money or gifts in exchange for doing Qatar’s bidding.
Pier Antonio Panzeri, a former MEP from Italy who founded Fight Impunity, Greek former MEP Eva Kaili, and her husband, Francesco Giorgi, were arrested in Belgium in 2022. They are facing charges of corruption, money laundering, and participation in a criminal organization as part of the Qatargate investigation.
They have been released from jail pending trial, but there has been little progress in the case over the last couple of years. Panzeri admitted guilt and has struck a plea deal with the Belgian prosecutor to exchange information for a reduced sentence. Kaili has repeatedly maintained her innocence.

Türkiye's National Intelligence Organization (MIT) chief Ibrahim Kalin visited Pakistan following his trip to Afghanistan, holding talks with senior Pakistani officials on bilateral ties, regional security, and ongoing tensions in the Middle East, Turkish security sources said on Thursday.

Processing of Iranian asylum cases can resume
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:52:15 UTC
22:52:15 KST

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said Monday that she is “quite optimistic” Denmark, Greenland and the USA can reach an agreement on security and defense in Greenland.
Frederiksen spoke at a news conference in Finland, where she attended a European summit focused on security in the Arctic.
“We have agreed to start a high-level working group on closer cooperation on security and defense, also in Greenland,” Frederiksen said.
“As long as the working group between Greenland, Denmark, and the USA continues its work, it is too early to draw a conclusion. But I am quite optimistic that we will succeed in finding a way,” she said.
Frederiksen visited Greenland last week with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Denmark is among 10 NATO countries conducting a joint military exercise in Greenland. The exercise is intended to show that Denmark and NATO are protecting Greenland and the Arctic.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Denmark for not doing enough to protect Greenland from threats posed by Russia and China.
During the first weeks of September, 400 soldiers from 10 NATO countries are operating on land, at sea and in the air near Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq. They are training to operate in Arctic conditions as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry surveillance and deterrence mission.
“If one is to be able to operate in the Arctic, one has to train up here,” Søren Andersen, head of Denmark’s Arctic Command, told the Danish news agency Ritzau last week.
Andersen said the temporary Arctic Shield exercise is part of a long-term strategy for Greenland and the Arctic.
“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.

Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.

'If I open my mouth': Decoding deepening fault lines between allies-turned-rivals - Akhilesh Yadav &amp; Jayant Chaudhary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:51:07 UTC
22:51:07 KST

Akhilesh Yadav and Jayant Chaudharywere once allies. Now, every exchange between them seems to make their fallout a little more bitter and also personal.Their ongoing face-off touched a new low this week after Jayant unleashed another strong attack on his former ally. "When we had an alliance with them, we knew many things, but all those details are not supposed to be shared. It is my ‘gravity’ that I don’t talk about those things. If I open my mouth and share all those details, he won’t find space to even stand in Uttar Pradesh," Jayant warned Akhilesh.The RLD chief's angry reaction came after he was asked about Akhilesh’s remarks on number of seats Jayant should get to contest in the 2027 assembly elections as part of the BJP-led NDA.Akhilesh, who has often targeted Jayant ever since they parted ways in 2024, had mocked the RLD's current standing within the NDA and suggested that the BJP should give it many more seats than what it got under SP alliance if it truly respected the legacy of Chaudhary Charan Singh, Jayant’s grandfather and former Prime Minister.Jayant hit back strongly and accused Akhilesh of making "light remarks."
"Chaudhary Charan Singh's legacy cannot be decided by the number of seats RLD gets to contest as part of the NDA alliance. There has always been respect for him in people's hearts and that respect will always be there. Even if RLD does not get even one seat, it will not impact the respect for Chaudhary Charan Singh."
RLD chief Jayant Chaudhary
Jayant also tried to turn the Chavvani jibe against Akhilesh and said: "PDA (which refers to backwards, dalits and minorities) plank of Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav was aimed at reaching out beyond the party's traditional vote bank, but people would also judge on how much respect and unity the party had maintained with its earlier supporters.”
The RLD allies once again came out strongly in support of Jayant and attacked the SP leadership.Chief minister Yogi Adityanath led the counter-attack on behalf of Jayant and termed the SP chief's comments an "insult to democracy". He accused Akhilesh of making a "mockery of democratic discourse" by resorting to cheap language against political opponents. The UP CM also labeled Akhilesh’s remarks as an insult to the entire farming community and the legacy of former Prime Minister Chaudhary Charan Singh. Other UP ministers also jumped to the defence of Jayant Chaudhary.The latest exchange comes after an ugly war of words last month triggered by Akhilesh Yadav’s “chavanni” jibe at Jayant over walking out of the SP alliance ahead of the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and joining the BJP-led NDA.
The 'chavanni' story
The origins of Akhilesh’s Chavanni jibe go back to January 2022. Jayant, who was then allied with the Samajwadi Party, was asked about attempts by the BJP to bring him into its camp."Main koi chavanni hoon jo palat jaunga" (I am not a 25 paise coin that will flip), Jayant had said then. But two years later, the “chavvani” did flip.
Jayant slammed Akhilesh
Ahead of the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, the RLD walked out of its alliance with the SP and joined the NDA. This happened after the Modi government conferred the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honor, posthumously to former Prime Minister Chaudhary Charan Singh in February 2024, months before the Lok Sabha elections.At a recent event, the SP chief recalled Jayant’s political switch and said: "Jaane kahan-kahan se aa gaye the log gathbandhan banane. Humne chavanni ka rupya bana diya tha, tab bhi humein chhod kar chale gaye wo. (“People from all sorts of places had come to ally with us. We had raised their political worth from a ‘chavanni’ to a full rupee, yet they left us and walked away.”)."Akhilesh did not take names, but the reference was obvious.Jayant had reacted strongly to Akhilesh’s jibe and accused the SP chief of making 'cheap' remarks. “If he wanted to attack me politically, he should have taken my name directly instead of making indirect references,” Jayant had then said.The RLD chief had then received strong support from his allies, with the BJP coming out in his defence. Even BSP chief Mayawati backed Jayant. They quickly turned Akhilesh’s attack on Jayant into an attack against Chaudhary Charan Singh, the farmers and the Jat community.
Battleground Western UP
So, why is Akhilesh targeting Jayant? Is he still trying to settle political scores for the RLD chief’s betrayal in 2024? Or is Akhilesh trying to drive a wedge between RLD and BJP ahead of the assembly elections?Akhilesh knows that the stakes are high for all political parties in Western Uttar Pradesh. With the RLD no longer on his side, the SP chief plans to go all out to strengthen its presence in the region ahead of the 2027 polls.Jayant Chaudhary, meanwhile, has been trying to broaden the RLD’s social base and extend his party’s areas of influence in Uttar Pradesh. This is important for him to show his clout within the NDA. Western UP, with its sizeable Jat, Muslim and farming communities, has traditionally been an important electoral battleground for Jayant and RLD.The politics in the region is already beginning to get tense. Last week, Akhilesh had to cancel his Western UP outreach in the region after a party meeting planned in Bulandshahr could not be held. The local administration, citing waterlogging, refused permission for landing of his chopper. The SP alleged that the waterlogging was an "excuse" and that the BJP-led government was behind the denial.The SP reacted by announcing that the party will organise a series of rallies in Western UP, beginning from Bulandshahr. "Sometime later this month, the national president will visit Bulandshahr and he will also tour every district of western Uttar Pradesh. Saharanpur will also be included in the programme in due course," senior SP leader and party spokesperson Rajendra Chaudhary said."The public is watching and understanding everything. When the time comes, they will teach the BJP a befitting lesson," he said.Saharanpur is also expected to figure in the SP's upcoming political outreach. The district has recently witnessed a political and legal controversy following the demolition of a mosque structure in the collectorate premises.So, the SP’s aggressive pitch against Jayant could be part of its political offensive to dominate the region.
Why is Akhilesh speculating RLD seats?
Is Akhilesh’s ploy of linking RLD seats to the legacy of Chaudhary Charan Singh an attempt to drive a wedge between Jayant and the BJP?When Jayant contested the 2022 assembly elections with Akhilesh, the RLD had got 33 seats as part of the SP alliance. Now, by linking seats for RLD to Chaudhary Charan Singh’s legacy, Akhilesh could be trying to pile pressure on both Jayant and the BJP when they sit to negotiate a workable formula to divide seats, especially in Western Uttar Pradesh, where RLD has a strong presence.But will this work? Political analyst J P Shukla says no. “If Akhilesh Yadav hopes to gain from trying to create differences between RLD and BJP, he is not going to succeed. It is now too late for any major political realignment. By now, they would have settled most of the issues among them,” Shukla says.
Shukla terms these political face-offs as an attempt by leaders to keep their cadres engaged and energised for the political battle.Senior political analyst Anand Vardhan Singh says Jayant would not mind the attention from the war of words with Akhilesh. “His strong remark against Akhilesh is posturing for a greater share of seats. And to that extent, the confrontation with Akhilesh helps,” he says.Singh says Jayant has little room to manoeuvre as most of the Jats would stay with the BJP even if the RLD chief decides to leave the NDA.Explaining Akhilesh’s attacks, Anand Vardhan Singh says, “Akhilesh is desperate for Dalit votes and would not mind being branded anti-Jats.”
Could Akhilesh end up helping Jayant?
While Akhilesh may be stepping up his political attacks on Jayant to push him on the back foot, the SP chief should be wary of his strategy being counterproductive. His remarks have already prompted BJP leaders to rally behind Jayant Chaudhary. From chief minister Yogi Adityanath to several UP ministers, BJP leaders have hit back at Akhilesh, presenting his attacks on Jayant as an insult to Chaudhary Charan Singh, farmers and the Jat community.Even BSP chief Mayawati came out openly in support of the RLD chief after the Chavvani face-off. Mayawati condemned Akhilesh Yadav and sought his apology."The public statement made by the Samajwadi Party (SP) chief regarding his former ally party, the Rashtriya Lok Dal, and its leader, the Union Minister--that "Hum logon ne chavanni ko rupaiya bana diya, phir bhi chhod ke chale gaye"--is utterly indecent, unbecoming, and extremely shameful.
For such arrogant and undemocratic rhetoric, he should immediately apologize not only to that party and its leader but also to the entire Jat community for insulting the family of the late Chaudhary Charan Singh Ji; that would be appropriate," wrote Mayawati in an X post.For the RLD, the attacks may end up doing more good than harm. They give Jayant Chaudhary another opportunity to underline his political relevance in western Uttar Pradesh and, in turn, strengthen his hand when the NDA sits down to work out its seat-sharing formula for 2027. If that happens, Akhilesh’s attempts to put Jayant on the defensive could very well boomerang.

Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov recently awarded the commander of the corvette Soobrazitelny a Medal “For Combat Distinction” after the ship fired two signal flares toward a Danish military helicopter in the Baltic Sea. Russia’s Defense Ministry described the commander’s actions as “skillful and decisive” and credited him with preventing what it called a “provocation” by the Danish Air Force.
According to the Russian ministry, the incident occurred at 2:22 p.m. on Sept. 14 while the Baltic Fleet corvette was in international waters in the southwestern portion of the Baltic Sea. The ministry said a Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter was approaching the ship and allegedly failed to respond to calls on an international communications channel. The ship’s commander then ordered the launch of two red signal flares, after which, according to the Russian account, the helicopter left the area.
The Danish military said the helicopter was carrying out routine photography of the Russian ship in international waters near the town of Gedser in southern Denmark. According to Denmark’s Armed Forces, the Russian vessel fired two flares toward the helicopter, with one passing at close range. The Danish military said the flares were pyrotechnic devices normally used for signaling at sea.
Following the incident, Russian Ambassador Vladimir Barbin was summoned to Denmark’s Foreign Ministry, where Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen called the incident “unacceptable.”
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen linked the Russian ship’s actions to what she described as an intensifying hybrid campaign against Europe, saying Moscow was testing NATO while trying to intimidate Europeans and sow division.
Russian pilots were also decorated after 2023 incident with U.S. drone
The Insider found that in March 2023, Russia’s then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu similarly awarded Orders of Courage to Su-27 pilots following an incident involving aircraft from a NATO country — a U.S. MQ-9 Reaper drone over the Black Sea. According to U.S. European Command, one of the Russian fighters struck and damaged the drone’s propeller during the encounter, forcing the U.S. military to bring the aircraft down in international waters.
Russia’s Defense Ministry denied that a collision had occurred and said the drone crashed as a result of its own sharp maneuvering. The ministry said the pilots were decorated for preventing a violation of the boundaries of an area where Russia had imposed temporary restrictions on airspace use after the start of the full-scale war.
John Kirby, then a spokesperson for the U.S. National Security Council, mocked the Russian ministry’s decision at the time:
“I don’t know of another military in the world, another Air Force in the world, that would award a pilot for smashing into a drone. If that’s bravery, then I guess they’ve got a different definition of it. It's ludicrous, it's insulting.”

Editor's Notes: The IDF needs to be accountable for unanswered military queries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:48:43 UTC
22:48:43 KST

In December 2024, The Jerusalem Post asked the IDF about two strikes in Gaza that killed Hamas commanders Ibrahim Biari and Wisam Farhat. Reports about the operations alleged large civilian casualties. Our military correspondent, Yonah Jeremy Bob, asked for the details behind those decisions.
The army explained its approval procedures. It said it had no fixed casualty ratios, and that commanders had to assess whether each strike was proportionate. We published those explanations in Yonah’s analysis.
He also asked about the two operations themselves. Yonah tells me he pursued those questions then and on at least two further occasions. Sometimes officials refused specifics. Sometimes they said they did not know and might get back to him. The information never arrived.
Nearly two years have passed. I would like to know who is responsible for getting him an answer.
The documentary NAZA has now made allegations about Israeli targeting decisions an international story again. Its directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, drew on anonymous testimony about the civilian deaths anticipated before airstrikes. The IDF said the testimony could not be verified, and that humans approved targeting decisions.
Questions reached the army long before 'NAZA' broke
Our questions reached the army long before the current argument over NAZA. Officials have had time to investigate, consult their lawyers, and work out what can be released.
I believe the IDF is the most humane army in the world.
In November 2023, a Palestinian dentist named Mahmoud Shaheen told the BBC that Israeli intelligence officers had kept in touch with him for hours while he helped evacuate neighbors from buildings in Gaza’s al-Zahra neighborhood. When he needed more time, they allowed it. When his phone battery ran low, an officer reached him through a neighbor’s phone.
The BBC found Shaheen through other residents and checked details against community posts and satellite images, although it could not independently verify the calls. The army could tell us how it organized those evacuations and how often officers delayed strikes to give people more time.
In September 2024, humanitarian pauses agreed to by Israel and Hamas helped health workers vaccinate almost 560,000 children against polio. WHO documented nine-hour daily pauses in designated areas. Palestinian medical teams and international agencies administered the vaccines, with Israeli cooperation helping them reach children during the fighting.
I get frustrated reading commentary that has little interest in those efforts or in Hamas’s use of civilian areas. We should challenge it with the fullest record we can provide, accepting that some of what we publish will be painful.
Seven World Central Kitchen aid workers were killed in April 2024. The IDF found serious errors and breaches of procedure, dismissed two officers, and reprimanded senior commanders. WCK demanded an independent investigation. We should be asking what changed after that investigation and whether anyone checked that the changes worked.
Human rights violations around the world
The Americans have faced such questions. Their August 2021 drone strike in Kabul killed 10 civilians, including seven children. The man they had followed was an aid worker. A Pentagon review found failures in communication and target identification; no troops received disciplinary punishment.
Six years earlier, an American gunship attacked a Doctors Without Borders hospital in Kunduz, Afghanistan, killing 42 people. The organization had supplied its coordinates and contacted military authorities during the attack. Sixteen personnel received administrative punishments, with no courts-martial.
The Pentagon concluded that the Kabul strike was a tragic mistake and found no misconduct or negligence. That distinction was available to the Americans after they killed seven children. It should be available when assessing an Israeli operation, subject to the same examination of the evidence.
In the Netherlands, it took four years for journalists to expose Dutch responsibility for a 2015 strike on an ISIS bomb factory in Hawija, Iraq. Secondary explosions were reported to have killed 70 civilians. Subsequent disclosures showed that the Defense Ministry had access to casualty information years before the public knew what had happened.
These cases rightly sparked outrage. In the Netherlands, officials also had to explain why they had withheld information for so long.
Our military should consider how much harder it becomes to defend an account once journalists discover what was left out.
Earlier this week, I argued for opening more of Israel’s October 7 massacre archive to foreign journalists. Their work could reach audiences who distrust Israeli officials. It could also expose Israeli failures, which the government would have to accept.
I don’t know whether the full record of the Biari and Farhat strikes will vindicate the decisions made. If it reveals mistakes, including serious ones, I want us to publish them. The families whose relatives were killed deserve an explanation, and Israelis deserve to know what their army established.
Intelligence sources and methods need protection. Officials can redact sensitive material and arrange independent scrutiny where public disclosure would endanger someone. They should explain which questions they can answer now and what prevents them from answering the rest.
Yonah raised a possibility that ought to worry the people making those decisions: an American administration restricting military sales to Israel in three years because allegations we could have answered had gone unanswered. I hope the officers insisting on bitachon mida, information security, are also considering that possibility.
The army should publish its estimates of civilian and combatant deaths, explaining how it calculated them and what remains uncertain, and release completed investigations into disputed strikes. If the investigations into Biari and Farhat are still unfinished, tell us what is taking so long.

Former Wolfson doctor sentenced to six years for rape, sexual assaults
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:48:37 UTC
22:48:37 KST

The Tel Aviv District Court sentenced Prof. Aryeh Levin, a former senior doctor at Wolfson Medical Center, to six years in prison on Thursday for raping the mother of a patient and committing sexual offenses against two patients.
The sentence was less than half the 13 years sought by prosecutors, who said they would study the ruling and consider their next steps. The court also ordered Levin to pay NIS 750,000 in compensation to four women affected by the offenses for which he was convicted. He had deposited the money before sentencing.
Levin, 69, formerly headed Wolfson’s pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition unit. He was convicted in February after admitting to an amended indictment under a plea agreement that left his prison term for the judges to decide.
The conviction covers the rape of a patient’s mother, five indecent acts involving two patients, and a separate offense involving a fourth woman. In that case, Levin performed invasive examinations on her when she was a child without her or her mother’s informed consent. He was convicted of abusing his authority as a doctor for those examinations.
In 2013, Levin asked the mother of a boy he was treating to come to his Wolfson office to collect medical documents. After she entered, he locked the door and raped her, according to the facts he admitted.
Amended indictment details offenses from 2010 to 2021
Four of the indecent-act convictions concern a woman Levin treated over many years. The amended indictment describes incidents in 2017 and 2018 in which he touched her sexually during or around medical appointments, despite her efforts to move away. The fifth concerns a teenage patient he touched without her consent following an examination at Wolfson in 2021.
The offenses in the amended indictment span 2010 to 2021. Some took place at the hospital and others at Levin’s clinics.
Prosecutors argued that Levin’s standing as a specialist gave him access to women who depended on him for care. In a statement after the sentence, they said the complainants had seen him as “a savior” and argued that he exploited their trust at moments when they were especially vulnerable. They sought a prison term of at least 13 years.
Levin’s lawyer, Lior Epstein, argued for a substantially shorter sentence. He pointed to the difference between the original and amended indictments, Levin’s admission, the compensation, and the consequences the case had already had for his medical career. The plea agreement was reached late in the prosecution’s case, after the women had testified.
Court stresses gravity of sexual offenses by medical professionals
In explaining its sentence, the three-judge panel said sexual offenses by medical professionals carry particular gravity because patients must trust them at moments of vulnerability. The judges also considered the harm described in the women’s victim-impact reports, including damage to their ability to trust medical care.
The court weighed Levin’s admission, his age and lack of previous convictions, the changes to the original charges, and the compensation he had deposited. It imposed suspended prison terms in addition to the six years and credited him for 34 days previously spent in detention.
Under the plea agreement, Levin also told the Health Ministry he would no longer practice medicine and requested permanent cancellation of his medical license.
Rape crisis center chief criticizes Levin’s sentence, says it fails to reflect gravity of offenses
Orit Sulitzeanu, chief executive of the Association of Rape Crisis Centers in Israel, criticized the sentence. “The sentence handed down to Arieh Levin does not at all reflect the gravity of his appalling acts or his disgraceful exploitation of his role and status,” she said. She called on hospitals to “take every complaint against a doctor with the utmost seriousness and examine it thoroughly” so patients can feel safe.
The court informed Levin that he has 45 days to appeal.

The Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) will hunt down every single Hamas member involved in the October 7 massacre, no matter where they are or where they are hiding, Shin Bet Director David Zini said Thursday at a ceremony honoring Shin Bet agents for their exceptional service.
“To the planners of the slaughter, to its implementers, and to all who took part in the disgrace of the honor and blood of the State of Israel, and to all who seek our destruction, we have one uncompromising message: There is no place in the world too far, there is no forgiveness, and there is no expiration date,” he said.
“We pursued, we are pursuing, and we will continue to pursue you down to the last co-conspirator,” Zini said. “The long and determined arm of the Israeli defense establishment will reach all who harm us – deep in a tunnel, in concealed command centers, and in every corner of the globe.”
“This is our sacred duty to the nation and for humanity,” he said.
The Israeli government promised the Trump administration after a failed attack on Hamas officials in Qatar last September that it would not attack them on Qatari soil again. But if those Hamas officials were to leave Qatar, Zini’s threat might still apply.
Zini told the Shin Bet operatives: “You are the proof that even from a great fall, we can rise up, improve, [and] flourish. This agency rises, learns, and wins every day.”
Netanyahu, Herzog attend Shin Bet award ceremony
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Isaac Herzog attended the ceremony.
The Shin Bet had succeeded in stopping about 1,000 terrorist attacks in the West Bank, and it had hunted down the vast majority of the Hamas terrorists responsible for the October 7 massacre, Netanyahu said.
Zini said the award winners were operatives from various missions, including agents who fought Iran and Hamas, those who stymied terrorists in the West Bank, and some who protected Israel’s cybersecurity.
There were 18 awardees, including three women.
For example, one of the awardees was a female agent given the alias “A.” She is a desk analyst in the Counter-Espionage Division and is a mother of four.
“‘A’ operates against highly complex targets and has achieved security success by configuring a sophisticated intelligence picture,” the Shin Bet said in a press release. “She demonstrated exceptional capabilities in translating her analyses into operational outcomes.”
Another one the awardees was a male agent, also listed as “A,” who is a handler and recruiter of agents in the Shin Bet’s Southern Division. He is a father of five.
“‘A’ significantly expanded the roster of agents in his area of responsibility and recruited high-value, significant sources who have provided a wealth of invaluable intelligence in recent years,” the Shin Bet said.
Shin Bet must work on non-partisan basis to help preserve election integrity, Herzog warns
Herzog said the Shin Bet must work closely, effectively, and on a nonpartisan basis to preserve electoral integrity as Election Day on October 27 nears.
In the past, Zini made statements that led to questions about whether he would attempt to use his position to curry favor with Netanyahu.
There has been no evidence of such an act to date, although he ignored a Knesset advisory committee that told him to grant Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot a special security detail.
Previously, Zini had said if there was not a threat to Eisenkot’s life, there was no obligation to grant him such security protection because he neither holds office nor is the current opposition leader.
The Knesset’s Shin Bet oversight committee, led by government officials, endorsed Zini’s position over those of its own advisory committee.

Kyiv Independent wins 2026 Online Journalism Award for innovation in revenue strategy
The Kyiv Independent has won a 2026 Online Journalism Award for Innovation in Revenue Strategy in the Medium Newsroom category, recognizing a membership model that keeps the newsroom's reporting free to read while inviting readers to sustain it.
The award was announced on Sept. 3 by the Online News Association during this year's virtual awards ceremony.
The judges praised the Kyiv Independent for building "an authentic and transparent membership model around a powerful principle: keeping independent journalism freely accessible during wartime," pointing to its membership growth alongside real-time reporting from a war zone, and its commitment to listening to readers through its Discord community, live events, and newsletters.
read also
The award recognizes the Kyiv Independent's reader revenue results in 2025: membership grew 78% over the year, from 14,300 members at the end of 2024 to 25,500 by December 2025. Monthly recurring revenue rose 69% over the same period while average monthly churn held at 1.64% — below common industry benchmarks — and nearly 90% of members rated their experience 4 or 5 out of 5 in the newsroom's member survey.
Currently, Kyiv Independent has a community of over 35,000 paying members.
"We are proud of this recognition of our reader revenue work, and we owe it to our members. They are the reason a free-to-read newsroom in a country at war can pay its own way," said Zakhar Protsiuk, chief operating officer of the Kyiv Independent.
Reader support made up about 70% of Kyiv Independent’s funding in 2025.
At the core of the model is a simple principle: in a country at war, quality information must stay free and accessible to everyone. Rather than putting reporting behind a paywall, the Kyiv Independent invites readers to become partners in sustaining it — not subscribers, but part of a global community built around a shared cause.
It is the Kyiv Independent's second consecutive Online Journalism Award in this category, following the 2025 award for building a sustainable business model during wartime.
The Kyiv Independent's growth is driven by the community behind it. Consider becoming a member or making a donation to help us keep covering Ukraine's story.

Space economy report: Who's winning the race in Europe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:43:25 UTC
22:43:25 KST

In the past 15 years, Rome has doubled its civilian space budget. Where is it putting the money?
Once considered a niche, the space economy is now a major, mature industrial force supporting innovation, public policy goals, and services in Europe and beyond.
EU countries currently invest a bit more than 0.04% of their GDP in space, but some countries are moving faster than others.
Regarding civilian space projects, Italy now spends more relative to its GDP than any other European country except Luxembourg, overtaking France after a major spending boost over the past 15 years.
The OECD's latest Space Economy at a Glance report claims that Rome's space economy "is now a strategic high-value industrial and digital ecosystem, comparable to specialised niches in aerospace, electronics, telecommunications, software and advanced engineering", with an estimated output of €8 million.
Japan has doubled its budget as well, becoming the top spender relative to GDP among OECD countries.
Another impressive growth, though on a smaller scale, took place in Luxembourg, which tripled its budget since 2010.
When it comes to overall public investments, however, France and Germany are Europe's leading space-faring nations, according to new OECD data.
In 2025, they allocated up to €2.4 billion and €2.5 billion respectively in civilian space spending, followed by Italy with around €2 billion.
The number of activities funded by government space budgets varies greatly across countries and can include, for example, the manufacture and operation of space infrastructure, the use of satellite data, signals and equipment, and any associated research and development.
Military space: Germany on course to be Europe's top investor
Paris and Rome are putting a lot into research, with space accounting for 14% of each government's civil research and development funds in 2024.
That's more than twice the OECD's 6.3% average.
However, when it comes to military spending, it's a different story. Alongside plans to become the most powerful army in Europe, Germany is by far the top spender.
Public demand is increasingly shaped by defence and security requirements, "although comparisons remain difficult as many programmes are classified or dual-use", says the OECD.
Berlin plans to invest €35 billion in space-related defence capabilities by 2030, much more than France, which has allocated around €10.6 billion between 2024 and 2030, with a 25% rate of its government's space spending in 2025.
For a cross-Atlantic comparison, the US spent 46.3% last year.
As for China, the report says Beijing's spending remains "particularly difficult to estimate, as civilian, commercial and military activities are closely integrated under the country’s military-civil framework", adding that rough estimates suggest it could be the world's second-largest government space spender, but the "figures remain indicative".
Satellites: UK far ahead in Europe thanks to navigation market
France, however, boasts a large satellite fleet, with 104 compared to Italy's 80 and Germany's 65, the report says.
The largest one, though, belongs to the UK, with 757 satellites in orbit as of June.
The industry already plays a significant role in the British economy, underpinning around 18% of UK non-financial GDP in 2022, compared with 16% in 2021.
"The largest estimated contribution came from industries relying on positioning, navigation and timing services provided by navigation satellites, at 14% of GDP, followed by industries supported by meteorological satellite services at 11%, and by satellite communications and earth observation services, each supporting around 7% of GDP", says the report.
The overwhelming majority (98%) of British satellites belong to the private sector.
Speaking of which, Europe has some serious private space players, but the reality check on the big picture is pretty stark.
In 2025, only about 12.8% of global private space investment went to European recipients, compared to 67% directed to the US.
This gap is significantly wider when it comes to satellite launches.
Last year, the US attempted 181 orbital satellite launches. Europe managed just eight, well behind China at 92.

US seals big uranium investment in Niger, two years after troops left
DAKAR, Sept 17 - The US government has approved up to $414 million in financing for a uranium project in Niger, according to the project's developer, in what sources described as a win for Washington two years after the West African nation expelled all US forces.
The US Development Finance Corp approved the debt facility for Canadian miner Global Atomic's Dasa project, which the company describes as the highest-grade uranium deposit in Africa, according to a company statement on Wednesday.
The investment could bolster US access to a strategic uranium supply at a time when Niger, the world's seventh-largest uranium producer, is locked in a dispute with French state-backed miner Orano, which long dominated the country's uranium sector.
The financing is being viewed by people familiar with the matter as a diplomatic and commercial breakthrough for Washington, whose relations with Niger deteriorated after the military government that seized power in a 2023 coup ordered US forces to leave in 2024. Niamey's new leaders have relied on Russian paramilitaries for security instead of the West.
Sources briefed on the effort said the US ambassador had urged Washington to rebuild ties with Niamey and back the project after the Trump administration took office with a renewed emphasis on deal-making in Africa.
The project was seen as an opportunity to secure access to a strategic energy resource that might otherwise fall into the orbit of rival powers, they said.
One source familiar with discussions involving Global Atomic and the DFC said a breakthrough came this summer when Chief Executive Stephen Roman travelled to Washington to resolve remaining issues holding up approval.
The project could also provide a rare bright spot in US-Canada relations, which have come under strain amid a trade war between the neighbors.
Niger's government did not respond to a request for comment.
SECURITY AND LOGISTICAL CHALLENGES
Despite the financing commitment, the project faces significant security and political risks.
Jihadist attacks have repeatedly targeted Niger's government and security forces over the past year. Last month, mutinous soldiers attacked a key military airbase and the presidency.
Global Atomic has been exploring alternative routes to export uranium from the landlocked country as transport corridors to the coast have become increasingly risky, a source briefed on discussions said.
One idea has been to invest in a route north through Algeria and across the Sahara Desert.
Algeria sent aircraft to Niger this summer to help the government respond to the latest coup attempt, underscoring improving ties between the neighbouring countries.
Uranium was added to the US critical minerals list last year, prompting renewed interest in Niger's reserves.
Those reserves include uranium stockpiles caught up in a dispute between Niger's government and Orano, which has launched international arbitration proceedings after losing control of key mining assets in the country. REUTERS

Burak Bir

- 'Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world,' says Nvidia CEO
Hosting an artificial intelligence summit on Thursday, Britain’s King Charles warned AI leaders of the "existential dangers" posed by such technologies.
Charles hosted a gathering of leaders from the artificial intelligence industry, including Nvidia's Jensen Huang, at the Scottish headquarters of his King’s Foundation charity.
Speaking at the opening, Charles pointed to the ongoing row over AI, saying that those who have created these technologies are now “increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities.”
The British monarch urged tech bosses to protect humanity and “not lose control of our destiny.”
"In this regard, if I may say so, there seems urgency in adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways," he said.
The king added: “Surely, we need sufficient means of control before it is all too late.”
He touched on the importance of two questions, first "how can we harness the benefits of AI, with safety at its heart," and second, “how can we build international cooperation and consensus to achieve this, so no nation is left behind – but the human race is left in place.”
Saying that the development of AI, its substance and its pace, are both intriguing and deeply concerning in equal measure, Charles added: “Our humanity must remain sacred.”
The public is "anxiously seeking your reassurance that we will not lose control of our destiny, or our souls," he noted.
In recent months, a series of incidents in which AI went beyond what many thought possible and artificial intelligence insiders raised the alarm have led to calls for the technology to be slowed down and more tightly regulated.
Safety is ‘paramount’
Nvidia boss Huang told the summit that he believes safety is "paramount," and that firms should hold back a product and "keep engineering" if it was not safe enough.
The BBC reported that the Nvidia boss also highlighted the value of open models -- systems which give users direct access to the software -- as a way to “ensure that people and countries are not left behind.”
He noted that the systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications “none of us would have imagined alone.”
"Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," he was quoted by the British broadcaster.
Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the UK AI lab DeepMind that was later acquired by Google, offered a more cautious view on the pace of development.
He said the systems that are believed could be as good as or better than humans at multiple tasks, were "probably only a few short years away" and could have an effect “ten times that of the Industrial Revolution.”
The chance of something going wrong was "definitely non-zero," he said.
But he advocated for "a sensible middle way," saying humanity could address risks if collectively given the space and time to mitigate them.
"The future is not yet written," he said.

China has privately urged Iran to help rein in Yemen’s Houthis after Saudi Arabia appealed to Beijing for help as the Iran-backed group’s rapid advances raised new concerns over Saudi oil exports and shipping through the Red Sea, three Iranian sources familiar with the discussions told Reuters.
Riyadh approached China after Houthi forces advanced along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important shipping chokepoints. Iran’s Foreign Ministry and the Saudi government’s media office did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
Oman ceasefire channel reportedly explored
In a parallel diplomatic effort, Hezbollah-affiliated Al Mayadeen reported, citing a senior source, that Saudi Arabia had asked Oman to approach the Houthis about a two-week ceasefire.
According to the report, talks during the proposed pause would focus on what the Houthis call the “humanitarian issue,” including their demand that Saudi Arabia lift its naval blockade of Yemen. The source claimed that an agreement on those issues could be announced during the truce. The report did not cite public confirmation from Saudi or Omani officials.
Oman has played a central mediation role in Yemen for years, maintaining channels with the Houthis while also working with Saudi Arabia and international mediators seeking to contain renewed fighting.
One killed by falling drone debris in Saudi Arabia
The diplomatic push came as attacks continued inside Saudi Arabia. Saudi Civil Defense said a Yemeni resident was killed Thursday when debris from an intercepted Houthi drone fell in Taif. A Saudi citizen and a Pakistani resident were injured, with the Pakistani national reported in critical condition. Buildings and vehicles were also damaged.
The incident followed several days of intensified missile and drone attacks. Saudi authorities said earlier this week that 13 civilians had been wounded in Houthi strikes on Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif, while seven homes and two vehicles were damaged.
Saudi air defenses also said they intercepted a Houthi drone south of Mecca on Tuesday before it entered restricted airspace over the holy city. The Houthis denied targeting Mecca.
Why China has leverage
Saudi Arabia’s appeal to Beijing reflects China’s unusual position in the crisis. It has been Iran’s largest trading partner for more than a decade and remains the main buyer of Iranian crude, giving it economic influence over Tehran while maintaining close ties with Gulf Arab states.
Chinese purchases accounted for more than 80% of Iran’s seaborne oil exports in 2025, averaging about 1.4 million barrels a day, according to data from commodities analytics firm Kpler cited by Reuters. China also brokered the 2023 agreement that restored diplomatic relations between Iran and Saudi Arabia after years of hostility.
Beijing now faces a more immediate economic concern. Houthi advances around Bab el-Mandeb threaten a route linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, while disruption at the Strait of Hormuz has already complicated the flow of Middle Eastern energy to Asian markets.
China has previously sought guarantees for its own shipping as tensions around Yemen intensified. Chinese state-controlled tanker operators have also avoided both Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb during the current crisis, according to Reuters reporting last month.
Whether Tehran will act on Beijing’s request remains unclear. Reuters’ Iranian sources said China’s interests carry significant weight in Tehran but remain only one factor among competing military, political and economic considerations.

Modi pitches India as ‘trusted’ global chip hub
India is preparing to become a “trusted” global chipmaking hub as it expands its government-backed semiconductor program, Prime Minister Narendra Modi has told an industry conference, while laying out a vision to build a broader hi-tech industry in the country.
“The world needs new and trusted locations for chip manufacturing and India is preparing itself for this,” Modi told the SEMICON India 2026 conference in New Delhi on Thursday.
The pitch positions India to benefit from the surge in demand for chips – driven by the boom in artificial intelligence and data centers – which has outpaced production and driven up prices. It also offers up the country as an alternative manufacturing destination for companies amid global supply-chain worries and geopolitical tensions.
The start of commercial production at two Indian semiconductor facilities was announced at the event, taking the number of chip production units in the country to five. Canada PM Carney embraces EU associate membership pitch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:39:00 UTC
22:39:00 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday backed the prospect of Canada becoming the European Union’s first associate member, saying closer ties with Europe would prevent any country from controlling its markets or undermining its sovereignty.
Carney’s speech to the European Parliament repeatedly extolled cooperation between Europe and Canada – but the relationship with the U.S., which has defined Canada’s economy for decades and has increasingly soured, hung over the address.
Trump’s tariffs , demands for economic concessions, and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have pushed Ottawa to reduce its dependence on its neighbor and seek a far deeper economic, security and political relationship with Europe.
Carney told the parliament that he welcomed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal, unveiled Wednesday, though he acknowledged that "associate membership” remains to be defined.
He outlined what he was proposing: deeper integration across trade, defense, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, energy, space, research and financial services to make both sides less vulnerable to economic and geopolitical pressure. He later told reporters he was not pursuing full membership of the EU.
"We do not seek power to dominate others," he said. "On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”
The prime minister received an ebullient welcome when he walked into the chamber in Strasbourg, France - with many lawmakers approaching him to shake his hand and ask for selfies - and a standing ovation after he spoke. One parliamentarian had donned a Canadian hockey jersey.
On Wednesday, von der Leyen proposed making Canada the EU’s first associate member - a status that does not currently exist in the bloc’s treaties and would have to be created. She said Europe wants to take its relationship with Canada to "the highest level possible.”
Carney, sitting in the front row of the chamber, nodded and rose to embrace von der Leyen as lawmakers gave the proposal a standing ovation.
Von der Leyen said Canada and the EU should move beyond their existing free trade agreement and create an "Alliance for the Future” encompassing a "common prosperity and economic security space.”
Carney will host EU leaders for a summit in Montreal on Oct. 29-30, when the two sides are expected to discuss the proposed new relationship in more detail.
Canada sends roughly 70% of its exports to the United States, making it highly exposed to Trump’s tariffs. Ottawa has retaliated and rejected demands that Carney says threaten Canadian sovereignty.
Europe took a different path, shelving retaliation and accepting tariffs of up to 15% on most EU exports to the U.S.
Trump suggested the proposed EU arrangement could be a "hostile act” and threatened heavy tariffs on Europe if he judged its intentions to be unfriendly - raising the stakes ahead of Carney's speech.
Asked about Trump’s comments, Carney said Canadians were united in rejecting outside attempts to dictate the country’s choices.
"Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak. No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally,” Carney said.
Carney has repeatedly urged what he calls middle powers to resist economic coercion. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, he warned that when countries negotiate alone with a dominant power, "we negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered.”

22:35:55 KST

MOSCOW, September 17. /TASS/. Russia's international reserves rose by $4.7 billion over the week, reaching $758.2 billion as of September 11, 2026, according to official data released by the Bank of Russia.
"As of the end of the day on September 11, 2026, international reserves stood at $758.2 billion, an increase of $4.7 billion – or 0.6% – over the week, driven primarily by positive revaluation," the regulator noted.
As of September 4, the volume of reserves was $753.5 billion.
Russia’s international reserves are highly liquid foreign assets available with the Bank of Russia and the Russian government. They comprise foreign currency, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), a reserve position in the International Monetary Fund and monetary gold. Following the onset of Moscow’s special military operation in Ukraine Western countries slapped sanctions against the Bank of Russia. Apart from freezing Russia’s gold and foreign currency reserves, all transactions related to management of the regulator’s reserves and assets, as well as transactions with any legal entity, organization or body acting on behalf or at the direction of the Central Bank, were prohibited.

Tripoli busts Gaddafi-shaped pill shipment as al-Assad's captagon appears in Libya's east
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:33:47 UTC
22:33:47 KST

Tripoli intercepted 100,000 tablets bearing the late Libyan leader's image shipped via Europe in a Renault Master van, while Benghazi's investigators separately seized captagon tablets assessed to have originated in Syria, where the al-Assad regime once industrialised the billion-dollar trade.
Tripoli government’s security forces have seized some 100,000 ecstasy tablets in the shape of Libya’s late leader Muammar Gaddafi, as a separate drug bust in the rival-controlled east discovered a shipment of captagon, the ousted Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad regime's narcotic of choice.
The tablets in Tripoli, intercepted on Saturday by the Deterrence Apparatus for Combating Terrorism and Organised Crime known as Rada, featured Gaddafi’s bust decked out in his characteristic garb, according to Libyan news agency LANA.
Rada said investigators received information about a criminal network pushing the pills through an undisclosed European country. The shipment came by sea through an unnamed port, hidden inside a Renault Master van.
Suspects were apprehended and referred to the public prosecutor’s office, according to reports.
Libyan authorities identified the tablets as ecstasy, commonly associated with MDMA, a popular clubbing stimulant known for causing a state of euphoria and emotional warmth.
Although Tripoli did not disclose the street value of the pills, the 100,000 tablets could be worth between 500,000 and 1.5 million in the broader Mediterranean region, according to available data and informal sources.
In a separate operation in Benghazi — controlled by forces aligned with Marshal Khalifa Haftar and his LNA armed faction — the Criminal Investigation Agency stated this week it seized an undisclosed number of tablets it described as captagon, assessing that Syria was the likely manufacturing point of origin.
Captagon is a cheap and highly addictive amphetamine-type stimulant that flooded Middle Eastern markets throughout the civil war in Syria, quickly becoming a major source of income for the al-Assad regime.
Analysts at the New Lines Institute estimated Syria's captagon trade generated up to $10 billion (€8.6bn) per year at its peak, with the networks around the al-Assad family earning an estimated $2.4 billion (€2bn) annually.
The regime's total earnings from the trade, which became industrialised around 2018-2019, remain difficult to calculate with precision.
Multiple governments, including the US and the UK, have sanctioned al-Assad’s brother Maher and a network of associates for their alleged role in overseeing the drug's production and export from regime-controlled facilities in Latakia and the Qalamoun Mountains in cooperation with Hezbollah.
A narcotics trading link between Latakia and Benghazi has been long established. In December 2018, Greek authorities intercepted a vessel carrying more than 3 million captagon pills from Latakia en route to the eastern Libyan port city, while separate reporting documented containers from Syria arriving in Benghazi carrying millions of tablets.
Ecstasy meets Gaddafi
Gaddafi-shaped tablets have also appeared in Libya before. In August 2025, Benghazi authorities seized an undisclosed quantity of captagon-type tablets bearing Gaddafi’s image.
Forensic experts identified them as MDMA-type narcotics, and investigators stated that the manufacturing source was believed to be Syria. MDMA and captagon are both amphetamine-based stimulants.
In a separate bust that same month, Benghazi said it found 45 ecstasy tablets in the shape of Gaddafi's face among a larger seizure of 1,355 assorted pills.
It is unknown whether the different sets of Gaddafi tablets are linked to the same manufacturing or trafficking networks.
Gaddafi, who ruled Libya for 42 years as its “Brotherly Leader,” was captured and killed by rebel fighters in October 2011 following a popular uprising backed by NATO airstrikes during the Arab Spring.
Gaddafi's image has become increasingly visible in parts of the country 15 years on, often on clothing and at public gatherings marking the anniversary of his 1 September 1969 revolution.
The United Nations drug watchdog UNODC said in its 2026 assessment that Libya was an increasingly significant regional transit point for synthetic drugs due to its political fragmentation and weak border controls.
After al-Assad's fall in December 2024, the new Syrian authorities led by interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa destroyed multiple large-scale captagon production and storage facilities, including those found on the al-Assad regime’s former bases.
However, some of the production and trade still persist after fragmenting into smaller networks mostly linked to al-Assad's loyalists with ties to Hezbollah in neighbouring Lebanon. UN experts reported in late 2025 that significant stockpiles remained in circulation across the wider region.
