Inside the House That Suggests History Got Sad Spinster Lizzie Borden All Wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:32:54 UTC
22:32:54 KST

After she was acquitted for the murders of both of her parents, Lizzie Borden did not adopt a pseudonym and disappear into obscurity. Instead, she spent her ample inheritance (equivalent to about $10 million dollars today) exactly as she’d always wanted to before her parents’ untimely demise: On an imposing 4,000-square-foot, seven-bedroom Queen Anne Victorian mansion in the swankiest neighborhood of her hometown of Fall River, Mass. She named her new abode “Maplecroft.”
Borden—the subject of the latest installment of Ryan Murphy’s Netflix Monster anthology, which has previously dramatized the stories of Jeffrey Dahmer, the Menendez brothers, and Ed Gein—lived out the rest of her life at Maplecroft and died there almost exactly 100 years ago. The home’s a mere mile from the so-called murder house where Andrew and Abby Borden were famously axed to death in August 1892, when Lizzie was 32 years old. Some 50,000 true-crime fanatics flock annually to the macabre site (now a museum and bed and breakfast), but few know to trek up “The Hill,” as Fall River locals call it, for a glimpse of Borden’s other home. Now, as then, it’s a private residence whose owners would prefer looky-loos walk on.
Current owners Brooke and Michael Doherty bought the notorious property in 2021, reluctantly. “When Michael first showed me the house, I said I didn’t want to live in the house of a hatchet murderer,” admits Brooke, whose family previously lived 20 minutes away in a home they were quickly outgrowing. Maplecroft offered plenty of indoor and outdoor space, but with three young children in tow, they worried about unwanted publicity, strangers peeking through windows, and even ghosts haunting the halls.
But it was those hallways—and the grand and back staircases, six carved fireplaces, original crown molding, Tiffany sconces, and stained glass windows throughout—that kept the Dohertys returning to the French Street home. “Soon enough I was convinced I could absolutely live in this old Victorian house that was basically a museum,” says Michael. When the previous owner’s plans to turn Maplecroft into a bed and breakfast fell through during the pandemic, the asking price lowered to $800,000 and the Dohertys made a successful (undisclosed) offer.
Borden moved in just three months after a jury of 12 men freed her from the 9-by-7-ft. cell at the county jail, having decided a mere woman couldn’t possibly have committed the murders. Her new digs were upgraded spectacularly from the much humbler home that was the scene of the infamous crime: Maplecroft was completely modern (in 1893, at least) and comparatively luxurious, with electricity, running hot and cold water, and flush toilets in all of its three-and-a-half bathrooms. Borden would later own one of the first automobiles in town, a black Ford Model T fittingly nicknamed the “Tin Lizzie,” which she stored in her carriage house—now Brooke’s art studio—with a private gas pump and customized turntable; America’s most notorious alleged murderer, it seems, couldn’t reverse park.
Fabulous real estate aside, popular culture paints post-trial Borden as a lonely outcast who was shunned by her neighbors and taunted by local kids who threw rotten eggs. But that’s not quite true: Borden lived at Maplecroft, for a time, with her sister Emma, nine years her elder, and their many pets—three Boston Bull Terriers and a black cat named Daisy. She had few if any friends among the townspeople, who had come to a slow acceptance, despite the jury’s verdict, that their Sunday School teacher had almost certainly committed the gruesome crime. Borden rarely ventured out except to go to the theater, where she could sit unnoticed in the darkness, and in 1904 the spinster fell into and found camaraderie with an inarguably more interesting bunch: the roving and booming Massachusetts theater community, including famous starlet Nance O’Neil, with whom Borden developed a close friendship.
Since she was shunned anyhow, Borden had slowly stopped complying with rigid social rules and norms. She didn’t attend church and quit her previously prominent role in the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union. Both disapproved whole-heartedly of Borden’s rowdy theater friends, whom polite society considered similarly disreputable and immoral. Behind her tall fence, Borden hosted loud, lavish parties in Maplecroft’s basement, decked out as what the Dohertys call a speakeasy with, in Brooke’s words, “a nice wood floor big enough for dancing and floor-to-ceiling wainscoting wood panelling.” One latched panel, meanwhile, conceals a shallow hidden cupboard ideal for a Prohibition-era party. “Just enough space to hide a few whiskey bottles,” adds Michael.
Whatever went down in the basement, prudent Emma upstairs didn’t approve of the shenanigans. With the Fall River Herald reporting on the sisters’ every sighting (even their clothing—Emma wore all black in eternal mourning while Lizzie defiantly refused to wear black as decorum dictated), Emma thought they should live discreetly. Lizzie disagreed and, following a particularly offensive week-long bash in 1905, the eldest Borden sister packed her bags and left forever. “The happenings at the French Street house that caused me to leave, I must refuse to talk about,” Emma later told the Boston Post before speaking rather freely: “I didn’t go until conditions became absolutely unbearable.” On the advice of their reverend, Emma cut ties with her sister and moved away. They never met or spoke again, but died days apart in 1927 and were buried next to one another in the family plot.
Upon her death, the childless Lizbeth Borden (as she called herself in later years) gifted property, jewelry, books and furniture to some distant friends and family members but left most of her money to Fall River’s Animal Rescue League. To the Dohertys, it’s all more evidence that their home’s previous owner was kind and generous, a woman with good taste and an appreciation for fine workmanship, but most importantly—despite what most Borden historians and public opinion and Ryan Murphy says—an innocent one. “The longer we live here,” says Brooke, “the more we’re convinced she didn’t do it.”

Film scenes with drug consumption, trafficking to carry anti-drug warning label
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:31:18 UTC
22:31:18 KST

Movie scenes depicting drug consumption or trafficking will carry the warning: "Illicit Narcotics Destroy Health and Guarantees Imprisonment. Say No to Drugs" (Representative image: Reuters).
NEW DELHI: Films depicting consumption or trafficking of drugs will now carry an anti-drug warning, the broadcast ministry notified on Wednesday.According to the guidelines amended under the Cinematograph Act, such movie scenes will carry the warning: "Illicit Narcotics Destroy Health and Guarantees Imprisonment. Say No to Drugs".The move follows a similar direction issued to OTT platforms by the ministry last month, asking them to prominently display the same warning during scenes showing the consumption or use of narcotic drugs. A similar advisory was also issued to private satellite television channels.The latest change marks a departure from the earlier film certification guidelines, under which the central board of film certification (CBFC) was required to ensure that scenes that could "encourage, justify or glamorise drug addiction" were not shown. However, those guidelines did not mandate a specific warning to be displayed on screen.The film certification guidelines set out the principles that the CBFC must follow while examining films for public exhibition under the Cinematograph Act. They were last amended in May 2025, when the government added three age-based parental guidance categories — U/A 7+, U/A 13+ and U/A 16+. Introduced through amendments to the Cinematograph Act in 2023, the categories require parental guidance for children below seven, 13 and 16 years, respectively.
The guidelines also require the CBFC to ensure that anti-social activities, including violence, are not glorified or justified, while criminal methods that could encourage offences are not depicted. They also prohibit scenes that encourage, justify or glamorise drug addiction.
In addition, the guidelines cover depictions of violence, cruelty and sexual content, as well as material that could affect public order, the security of the State or India's relations with foreign countries.On Wednesday, the Centre also reconstituted the CBFC, appointing actors Preity Zinta, Pankaj Tripathi, Suniel Shetty, Pallavi Joshi and Prosenjit Chatterjee, filmmaker Priyadarshan and Grammy-winning musician Ricky Kej, among others, to the new 18-member board.

Father of Noah, three, thanks those who searched for his son as village reels from loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:30:34 UTC
22:30:34 KST

The father of Noah, the three-year-old boy who was found dead after going missing from a playground, has spoken of his heartbreak and thanked the community who launched a tireless search for his son.
Rhys Woods said there were “no words to describe the pain of this loss”, adding that the family was “absolutely heartbroken”.
The small village of Brantham, in Suffolk, had mobilised on Tuesday, when Noah went missing after becoming separated from a relative at 2.37pm. He is thought to have gone down a woodland path towards the pond where his body was found.
More than 1,300 people from the village and beyond descended on the area to search for Noah. They scoured the woodlands and fields around the area close to the River Stour on the Essex border as helicopters flew overhead. On Wednesday afternoon, a body was discovered at the pond, a short walk from the playground.
Woods said: “Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much. It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation.
“The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives.”
On Thursday, the normally busy playground from which Noah disappeared was silent, save for the crying of people leaving bunches of flowers, which lined the length of the wooden fence surrounding the park.
“We didn’t know you, but we helped to find you,” read one note propped up against the fence. Another read: “We are sorry we couldn’t get to you sooner.” One person from the village wrote: “Little Noah, may you rest in eternal peace. You will remain in the hearts of the village and of all your friends.”
The mood on Thursday morning was muted. The leisure centre had been turned into a makeshift community hub, with a response centre consisting of councillors, local police and volunteers having meetings in the adjacent village hall.
Goldie, who did not want to give her surname, was volunteering to help run the community hub, where a handful of people chatted quietly. She said: “We’re providing a place for people to gather, and we’ve made a tribute book. Tributes are pouring in online, but for the family there is frankly some abuse online so we want them to have something to look at while avoiding that. The community is reeling.
“It’s a small village, and 1,300 people came to volunteer. If there was a chance for him to be found he would have been. Everyone did their very best. Obviously, we are all very upset today.”
The police ran out of hi-vis vests because so many people turned out to help find Noah, and the force was not entirely prepared for the logistics of a huge search party descending on the small area.
Sgt Claire Connick told the Guardian: “I feel so grateful for the community. The way people pulled together was just phenomenal. A man explained to me that he had been up all night until 4am searching. We even had people volunteering to control the traffic. The traffic and parking was something we didn’t factor in, just the volume of people asking how they could help.”
The love for the family and sorrow at the loss was evident. The local Co-op ran out of flowers, and the branch in the next town over, Manningtree, was also running low.
Noah apparently loved the cartoon dog Bluey, and was wearing a T-shirt depicting the character when he went missing. At the playground people had left stuffed toys depicting Bluey, and flowers with Bluey stickers on the cellophane.
Candles had been lit, but the drizzle had snuffed many of them out. A fundraiser gathering donations to support the family stands at £21,000, and Ipswich Town football club arranged to lay a wreath at the playground.
Specialist police officers were supporting Noah’s parents, who had to identify their son’s body on Wednesday night. Connick said: “The nurses and doctors lined up to walk the family into hospital which was a wonderful thing. There really has been so much support for the family.” She added that there would be an increased police presence in the area to help support the community.
Louise Madley, the manager of Brantham leisure centre, said: “There are far too many people to name individually, but to every single person who searched, donated, organised, sent messages of support, delivered supplies, supported the emergency services or helped in any way, thank you so much. Brantham, over the last 24 hours, we have witnessed something truly extraordinary in our village. Something I will, and I am sure others will, never forget. Noah, your memory will forever live on.”
Wood added: “This was the most heartbreaking outcome for us. We were just hoping that he would be hiding somewhere obvious where someone could find him, that’s what we kept telling ourselves the whole time. With our love and deepest gratitude, from his daddy and mummy and little brother, Noah you will be loved forever, you will never be forgotten and we miss you so so much. It has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short three years you were with us.”

The Potential Mismatch Between Japan and the US on China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

As the two most powerful countries in the world today, it is incredibly important that U.S. President Donald Trump will meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on September 24. But before that, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae of Japan is hoping to gain a meeting with Trump during her own visit to the United States for the U.N. General Assembly.
Both Trump and Takaichi are scheduled to address the General Debate in New York on September 22; as of September 17 “nothing has been decided” regarding a potential meeting, according to Takaichi.
The China-U.S. summit will have broad implications across a variety of policy areas, and there is no shortage of things for Trump and Xi to talk about. But it will be especially important for Japan, given not just its alliance with the United States, but also its close geographic proximity to China. Takaichi thus hopes to meet with Trump and share Japan’s perspective on China, in order to make sure Japanese interests are considered by its foremost partner.
For Japan, China is a significant threat to its national security that needs to be managed with help from the United States. The security environment in the Indo-Pacific region is under pressure as China continues developing its military capabilities. According to Japan’s defense white paper released last month, “China has been intensifying its activities in the region surrounding Japan [and] extending beyond the so-called first island chain to the second island chain.”
There are numerous examples of China putting pressure on Japan’s national security and ability to respond. It has upped its coast guard patrols around the island of Taiwan, creating a situation that could threaten Japanese security in the event of a contingency. Japan had to deploy fighters after Chinese and Russian planes were detected in airspace close to the Miyako Strait by Okinawa in June. And Beijing continues to send coast guard ships to patrol inside waters surrounding the disputed Senkaku Islands, claimed by China as the Diaoyu.
While bilateral Sino-Japanese relations have always vacillated over historical disputes and national security concerns, the current state of the relationship is particularly frigid. It is critical for Japan that the United States – its principal ally and partner – stays on the same page regarding the challenge from China.
The U.S. shares some Japanese concerns about China. Like Tokyo, Washington remains concerned about Chinese assertiveness in the Indo-Pacific region. The U.S., Japan, and other states released a joint statement in August that was critical of China’s unannounced launch of submarine-based long-range ballistic missile.
The U.S. continues to participate in multilateral military exercises focused on the Indo-Pacific, hosting the Rim of the Pacific exercises in Hawai’i in July, and participating in the May Balikatan exercises with the Philippines. Official references to the Indo-Pacific region are sparser than during the first Trump administration, but the U.S. continues to share its allies’ concerns about Chinese expansion in the region.
At the same time, there are differences between the U.S. and Japan. The conflict in Iran is arguably the Trump administration’s top priority. A report by the Department of Defense inspector general said the conflict was depleting U.S. supplies of important munitions. It has also necessitated the reassignment of the aircraft carrier USS George Washington to the Middle East from the Indo-Pacific region.
Trump is not a Sinophile, and the U.S. continues to have interests at odds with China’s. But the long-term competition with China may not be as prominent in the mind of Trump, who is bogged down in Iran and related problems. He may be looking for China’s help to ameliorate the worst economic impacts of the war. For example, although the price of oil continues to rise because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, lowered Chinese demand is believed to have a moderating effect on the global oil market.
To be sure, Washington can talk and chew gum at the same time. And it is not uncommon for allies to have different priorities in diplomacy. This means that the real question is to what extent the U.S. president will take into consideration the equities and viewpoints of allies like Japan. If there is a mismatch in those expectations, it will be critical for the alliance to deal with that friction.
Two years into his second term, Trump seems to have established a cordial relationship with Takaichi. The broader alliance also remains a firm and important part of national security and diplomacy for both sides. But Japanese wariness about the upcoming Trump-Xi summit and its implications for the Indo-Pacific region are palpable. “With the decline in the U.S. military’s presence in Asia, aren’t China and North Korea taking advantage of this situation?” asked the Yomiuri Shimbun in a September editorial.
It is difficult to see a major or irreversible rift developing between Washington and Tokyo. But a China-U.S. summit that leaves Japan’s interests out in the cold will be an unneeded challenge for the alliance at a critical time.
Takaichi undoubtedly knows that Trump is a free agent, and that he will do whatever he thinks will “make America great again.” When she meets with Trump ahead of his summit with Xi, her challenge will be to impress upon the U.S. president Japan’s perspective and why it is critical for the Japan-U.S. alliance to continue functioning at a close level. Although the alliance remains strong, a failure to coordinate could lead to friction in this relationship despite its importance to both Washington and Tokyo.

Hackers Demand $3M Ransom in Revolut Data Leak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:27:00 UTC
22:27:00 KST

Reported by
A group claiming responsibility for a recent Revolut data breach has demanded 6,000 Monero—an untraceable, privacy-focused cryptocurrency—worth about $3 million, threatening to sell sensitive information belonging to hundreds of the fintech company’s customers if it is not paid within 24 hours.
The group, calling itself “iamnotavillain,” posted the ultimatum on its website on Wednesday alongside a countdown clock. It threatened to sell the information to other criminal groups if Revolut failed to pay.
A Revolut spokesperson told Reuters late Wednesday that the company had received no direct contact or ransom demand from the people claiming responsibility for the breach, and that there had been no negotiations with them.
The company first confirmed the breach on September 12, saying an unauthorized party had submitted fraudulent requests for customer information using an email account on the legitimate domain of a government agency. Revolut said its own systems and customer funds were not compromised and that it blocked the address after discovering the fraud.
The compromised information could include names, dates of birth, home and email addresses, phone numbers, passports or driver's licenses, verification selfies, bank statements and transaction histories, including Bitcoin transactions, according to notifications sent to affected customers and reviewed by TechCrunch.
The breach is understood to have affected around 680 customers, according to a source familiar with the incident cited by Reuters. The attackers told the Financial Times they had used a compromised Italian government email system to pose as law enforcement officials and request information about specific Revolut customers over several months. They said they used blockchain analysis to identify customers with significant cryptocurrency holdings. Revolut has not independently confirmed those details.
The attackers have also begun publishing information allegedly belonging to individual Revolut customers, including several high-profile clients. They have accused the company of improperly disclosing customer information across jurisdictions, although that claim has not been independently verified and no regulator has publicly concluded that Revolut breached data-protection rules on that basis.
Italian authorities have since stepped up their investigation. Prosecutors in Reggio Calabria opened an inquiry into suspected unauthorized access to a computer system of public interest after investigators linked the fraudulent requests to an institutional email account belonging to the Reggio Calabria prefecture. Investigators are still trying to establish whether the government email system was actually breached or whether the account was cloned.
Italy’s National Anti-Mafia and Anti-Terrorism Directorate has also become involved because the suspected intrusion involved a government entity. Postal police are analyzing the claim made by “iamnotavillain” and monitoring the dark web for any attempt to sell the stolen Revolut customer data.
The latest $3 million demand differs sharply from an earlier claim circulating online that Revolut was being asked to pay 10,000 Bitcoin. That demand was associated with another account calling itself “Revolut Smilik.” The “iamnotavillain” group has said that the other claimant was an impersonator or former associate who had obtained only part of the stolen data; that account of the dispute has not been independently verified.

What is behind the timing of the Houthis’ new offensive in Yemen?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:26:11 UTC
22:26:11 KST

The Houthis, an Iran-backed Shia group, have recently captured Mocha, a Red Sea port near the Bab al Mandab Strait, as well as key islands adjacent to the critical waterway, expanding their control across southwestern Yemen against Saudi-backed forces.
On Wednesday, Houthi accounts published a video showing the debris of an apparently Saudi F-15 fighter jet shot down by the group, which has controlled Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, and other areas in the country’s west with large Shia populations since 2014.
The Houthi expansion along Yemen’s Red Sea coast has alarmed the internationally recognised government, which fought the Iran-backed group during the civil war, and its Saudi backers, already pressured by Iran’s Strait of Hormuz blockade.
Hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces had largely subsided since a UN-brokered truce in 2022.
The following year, Tehran and Riyadh agreed to restore diplomatic relations in a China-brokered deal. While the US-Iran war has heightened tensions, the Houthis have largely stayed away from the confrontation in the Gulf.
So why are the Houthis escalating against their enemies now?
Tensions between the two sides began escalating in July after Iran resumed direct flights to Houthi-controlled Sanaa for the first time in about a decade.
An Iranian aircraft initially flew a Houthi delegation to Tehran, but when a Mahan Air flight later sought to return the delegation, Saudi-backed forces struck Sanaa airport to prevent it from landing.
The aircraft was eventually diverted to Houthi-controlled Hudaida.
The dispute went beyond a single flight. Riyadh viewed direct flights between Tehran and Sanaa as a challenge to arrangements governing the airport that had accompanied the 2022 truce, while the Houthis framed the issue as a question of Yemen's sovereignty over its airspace.
Earlier this month, the Houthis launched a lightning offensive against Saudi-backed forces.
Domestic and regional factors
Behind the ongoing Houthi offensive, experts see a combination of domestic and regional factors emboldening the Yemeni group, which appears to have used the truce period to strengthen its military capabilities more effectively than its Saudi-backed rivals.
Esam Alahmadi, a Yemeni political analyst and sociology PhD researcher at Selcuk University, sees three interrelated motives behind the Houthis’ current escalation in Yemen.
First of all, the Houthis want “to convert territorial control along Yemen’s western coast into broader political and military gains,” Alahmadi tells TRT World.
With its ongoing offensive, the group has gained territory around the Bab al Mandab Strait, giving it greater leverage over a chokepoint that handles about 12 percent of global shipping.
The Iran-backed group also wants to take advantage of the current regional conflict, in which Tehran backs the Houthis, “in an effort to establish themselves as an actor that cannot be ignored,” Alahmadi says.
Finally, the Houthi advance around Bab al Mandab strengthens the group’s “domestic mobilisation narrative by portraying itself as a force confronting regional and international adversaries, rather than merely a party to an internal Yemeni conflict,” he adds.
The sophistication of recent Houthi attacks also suggests that the group used the truce period to enhance its missile and drone capabilities, bring in Iranian experts and Hezbollah operatives, and take control of military infrastructure previously established by government forces on islands and coastal areas overlooking Bab al Mandab, according to Alahmadi.
In recent years, conflicts across the Middle East have seen regional actors, including Israel and Iran, seek to extend their influence beyond their borders through alliances with armed groups and other regional partners, particularly in areas surrounding strategic waterways
This regional environment has also encouraged groups such as the Houthis to seek regional and international leverage to promote their interests.
“The Houthis increasingly feel they are in a stronger position after demonstrating their ability to project power beyond Yemen through their Red Sea campaign. This has encouraged them to raise their demands and increase pressure on Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government,” Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at International Crisis Group, tells TRT World.
While Tehran helped restrain the Houthis following the 2022 truce amid the China-brokered Saudi-Iran rapprochement, that calculation has changed following the US-Israel strikes on Iran, with Tehran now having “less incentive” to hold the Houthis back, Nagi says.
With Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz already disrupting global oil shipping, Tehran would also benefit from further disruption around Bab al Mandab under Houthi pressure, particularly if it drives energy prices higher, he adds.
The Houthi offensive has also unfolded amid shifting regional alignments. Iran and the UAE, despite being on opposing sides of several regional conflicts, have agreed to strengthen ties and expand cooperation.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE, meanwhile, have pursued competing agendas in Yemen.
The UAE backed the Southern Transitional Council, while tensions with Riyadh became particularly apparent in January when Saudi forces struck UAE-backed forces during a weapons shipment.
Both the Iran-UAE rapprochement and Tehran’s “attempt to alleviate pressure on itself in the Strait of Hormuz by shifting the theatre of conflict to the Bab al Mandab Strait” played a role in the emergence of the current Houthi offensive, Adel al-Shuja'a, a former spokesman for late Yemeni president Ali Abdullah Saleh, tells TRT World.
Saleh was killed by the Houthis in 2017.
The Houthi offensive has also altered regional calculations, allowing Israel to increase pressure on Saudi Arabia to normalise relations with Tel Aviv, according to al-Shuja'a.
“Saudi Arabia possesses significant strengths, yet it is hampered by indecision and a tendency to look to Washington for solutions. It has yet to realise that Washington’s perspective on its own interests differs fundamentally from the kingdom’s.”
What is next?
Despite the Houthi advances, it would be difficult for the Shia group to extend its rule across Yemen, a country with a non-Shia majority that is already grappling with a deep humanitarian crisis, according to analysts.
“The greatest danger is that Yemen’s western coast could shift from being a local front into an arena for open regional conflict,” says Alahamdi, referring to opposing agendas between Israelis, Saudis, the UAE and Iran in the middle of the already high Gulf tensions.
“If there is no effective containment or political arrangement, there is a risk that this becomes a broader escalation rather than a battle confined to the Bab al Mandab area,” says Nagi.
Other experts share those concerns.
“The trend seems to be toward a sustained confrontation. Houthi territorial gains around Bab al Mandab increase their leverage but also make a stronger Saudi, Yemeni and potentially international counter-response increasingly likely,” says Luciano Zaccara, a Doha-based expert on Iran.
While the Trump administration, which has recently signalled that Iran wants to talk to Washington, has downplayed ongoing Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and Riyadh-backed forces in Yemen, that stance “may change in the future”, Zaccara says, pointing to the tit-for-tat attacks between the US and Iran and the rapidly changing military environment in the Gulf.
But the analyst also sees that “expelling the Houthis from greater Yemen would be extremely difficult” because the group is militarily stronger than before, while their Yemeni opponents remain fragmented despite the Saudi support.
“The quick advances and the heavy attacks against Saudi cities demonstrate their recent military build-up.”
Also, a fragmented country like Yemen, where various external actors support different local forces, forcing out the Houthis from their strongholds in western Yemen seems to be a real challenge for both Saudis and their allies.
Doing so would require several measures at once, Alahmadi says: unifying Yemeni anti-Houthi forces under coherent political and military leadership; building professional ground forces rather than formations driven by competing interests and divided loyalties; cutting off arms-smuggling and funding networks; and developing better local governance.
But whether the Houthis can hold on to their recent gains will also depend on how quickly their opponents can regroup.
“The battle is not over,” Nagi says.
While the Houthis now control Mocha, parts of the approaches to Bab al Mandab and several surrounding islands, “that does not necessarily mean they will be able to consolidate these gains,” he says.
“It is about whether the Houthis can turn their recent military gains into durable control and whether the government and its allies can rebuild a coherent defensive line.
“The coming days and weeks will be important in determining whether the current Houthi advance becomes a lasting shift in the military balance or the beginning of another cycle of territorial reversals.”
Without a unified front, it will be difficult to reverse the Houthi advances, Nagi says, noting that recent developments show the Iran-backed group has a more coherent military strategy than the fragmented Saudi-backed forces.
“The immediate question is less whether the Houthis can be pushed back in principle, and more whether their opponents can overcome the organisational weaknesses that allowed the recent advance to happen in the first place.

Ukraine Repatriates 252 Bodies From Russia

Ukraine has repatriated the bodies of 252 people whom Russia claims are Ukrainian citizens, including military personnel, Ukrainian officials said on Thursday.
According to a statement from Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, the remains were returned following another round of repatriation measures.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“According to the Russian side, the bodies belong to Ukrainian citizens, including servicemen,” the headquarters said.
Ukrainian authorities have not yet independently confirmed the identities of the deceased.
Identification process to begin
Law enforcement investigators and forensic specialists working under the Interior Ministry will conduct the examinations needed to identify the repatriated remains.
After identification, the bodies can be handed over to their families for burial.
The operation involved the Coordination Headquarters, the Security Service of Ukraine’s Joint Center, the Armed Forces (AFU), the Interior Ministry, the Ukrainian parliament’s human rights commissioner, the Secretariat of the Commissioner for Missing Persons, the State Emergency Service, and other security and defense agencies.
The headquarters thanked the International Committee of the Red Cross for assisting with the operation.
It also thanked AFU personnel responsible for transporting the bodies to designated state facilities and transferring them to law enforcement officers and forensic experts.
‘It Is a Pity’: China Could Stop the War but Leans Toward Russia, Zelensky Says
Previous repatriations
Ukraine and Russia have continued returning bodies despite the absence of broader progress toward ending the war.
In July, Ukraine received 501 bodies that Moscow claimed belonged to Ukrainian military personnel. Another 522 bodies were returned in June, while Ukraine repatriated 1,000 bodies in April.
The large-scale repatriations followed an agreement reached during earlier negotiations in Istanbul under which Ukraine and Russia committed to returning thousands of bodies.
Identification can take months or even years. Ukrainian investigators have reported receiving damaged or mixed remains, while some bodies returned by Russia were later found to belong to Russian troops.
Police have also discovered explosive devices inside repatriated bodies on several occasions, making safety inspections mandatory before forensic examinations and DNA testing can begin.

India-Pakistan navy ship collision sparks alarm over unintended escalation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:25:25 UTC
22:25:25 KST

India-Pakistan navy ship collision sparks alarm over unintended escalation
Pakistan says an Indian warship entered its EEZ, while India says the collision occurred in international waters.
Islamabad, Pakistan — More than 16 months after India and Pakistan fought a four-day air war, firing missiles and drones at each other, the South Asian neighbours came the closest since then to a military face-off — this time in the Arabian Sea.
Indian and Pakistani naval vessels collided on Tuesday, setting off tit-for-tat accusations. Pakistan’s government summoned India’s top diplomat in Islamabad on Wednesday, mirroring action New Delhi had taken hours earlier when it summoned Pakistan’s charge d’affaires and lodged a protest of its own over the incident.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4India summons Pakistani diplomat after incident in Arabian Sea
- list 2 of 4Are India and Pakistan preparing for a naval face-off in a future conflict?
- list 3 of 4Two wins, two losses: What India, Pakistan have learned a year after war
- list 4 of 4Why Pakistan overhauled its military command structure after five decades
The collision is the first direct military encounter between the nuclear-armed neighbours since their four-day conflict in May 2025, when Indian air strikes and Pakistani retaliation brought both countries closer to full-scale war than at any point in decades.
So far, details of what happened remain disputed. Neither government has released video, track data or an independent account – and each statement places the blame on the other’s vessel.
But analysts say it underscored the risks of unintended incidents in the seas that could potentially escalate into broader crises, when India and Pakistan have few military and diplomatic mechanisms left in place to defuse tensions.
Two accounts
According to Pakistan’s Foreign Office statement issued on Wednesday evening, the navy has been conducting its biennial SEASPARK-26 exercise inside its exclusive economic zone since September 1 .
A country’s EEZ extends 200 nautical miles (370km) from its coast. Its territorial waters are only 12 nautical miles (22km) from the coast, with the rest of the EEZ in international waters. While vessels from other countries can pass through a nation’s EEZ in international waters unencumbered, they cannot exploit the waters economically: that right belongs only to the country whose EEZ it is.
Pakistan said that an Indian vessel, identified as the guided-missile destroyer INS Kolkata, had “repeatedly” tried to enter the exercise area since September 7 .
On September 15 , it said, Kolkata made a “dangerous” change of course that brought it into contact with a Pakistani vessel identified in local media as PNS Hunain, an offshore patrol vessel.
“Pakistan strongly rejects this belligerent Indian action,” the Pakistani Foreign Office said, calling it a violation of a 1991 bilateral agreement requiring warships to stay at least three nautical miles (5.5km, 3.4 miles) apart in international waters.
India’s Ministry of External Affairs said the warship was on “routine surveillance” in international waters when a Pakistani vessel approached at high speed and manoeuvred unsafely.
Neither government has named the vessels in its own on-record statement, and India has not confirmed or denied the Kolkata identification.
The two navies last collided in June 2011, when Pakistani frigate PNS Babur brushed against Indian frigate INS Godavari in the Gulf of Aden, while escorting a merchant vessel freed from Somali pirates.
Each side blamed the other then too. That row faded within weeks.
The risks
Retired Vice Admiral Ahmad Saeed of the Pakistan Navy said the pattern — two ships pressing close without a clear intent to collide — was familiar from Cold War-era “bumping” incidents between Soviet and US ships in the Black Sea.
But he argued that India and Pakistan are worse placed to manage similar encounters.
“There’s no bilateral Incidents at Sea agreement, the kind the US and USSR signed in 1972, and no navy-to-navy hotline,” Saeed told Al Jazeera. “Article 10 sets a distance, but it gives no manoeuvring rules and no procedure for investigating an incident afterwards. That gap is exactly why each side can just accuse the other.”
Article 10 of the 1991 confidence-building agreement between the two nations requires warships to stay at least three nautical miles (5.6km, 3.5 miles) apart in international waters.
Saeed said the greater risk was what might follow the collision: sharper tactics such as fire-control radar lock-ons or helicopter overflights and eventually “a contact with actual casualties.”
Muhammad Shareh Qazi, a Lahore-based security and maritime analyst, however, pointed to the same 1991 agreement, which he said requires 30 days’ written notice before a military exercise, as well as international collision regulations that apply to both countries as signatories to the UN maritime convention.
“If this collision really had the potential to escalate militarily, you’d have noticed by now,” Qazi said. “There’s a tool for that, called chaff, fired just above the bow or stern purely to signal you could escalate if needed. Nothing like that happened here.”
Both navies also have their own internal accountability channels, he added, with a captain found to have acted without authorisation facing a court martial process separate from any diplomatic protest.
On fishermen routinely detained for straying across the Sir Creek boundary, which is not demarcated between India and Pakistan further south, Qazi said the link to incidents further out at sea was indirect but real.
“Clear demarcation could help close those ambiguities over time, by reducing the ambiguity around where and how these interactions are expected to occur,” he added.
Saeed was more cautious about how contained an incident like this would remain.
“This hasn’t stayed quiet. Both governments went public with protests within a day of each other,” he said, adding that what made the moment riskier than 2011 was that “both publics are primed after last year’s conflict, which was not the case in 2011.”
Similar close-quarters confrontations have become more frequent between China and the Philippines in the South China Sea.
In the most recent flare-up, on July 24 , Philippine officials said a Chinese vessel came within about seven metres (23 feet) of a Philippine fisheries boat near Scarborough Shoal, the Philippine-claimed reef that China has controlled since 2012, and that Chinese coast guard ships fired water cannon at Philippine vessels.
Whether this week’s collision follows that pattern or fades like the 2011 incident depends less on the ships than on what comes next diplomatically, Qazi said.
“If, in the next 24 to 48 hours, an official statement suggests there was a genuine cause to manufacture an incident for the purpose of escalation, then yes, there may be a real possibility of this happening again,” he added.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday welcomed the prospect of Canada becoming an “associate member” of the E.U., just hours after U.S. President Donald Trump dismissed the proposal as “laughable.”
Addressing the European Parliament as a guest of honor in Strasbourg, France, Carney insisted “Europe and Canada are stronger together” and said “Canada and the European Union can anchor our ground to hold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive.”
Carney’s pivot toward Europe comes as he seeks to establish stronger international ties and curtail Canada’s reliance on the American market amid an all-out trade war. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs came into effect last week, matching the economic pressure imposed by the U.S. after negotiations collapsed last month. Trump’s repeated threats against Canadian sovereignty and calls to make it the “51st state” have added to the months-long tension.
While Carney did not directly mention Trump or his Administration while addressing European lawmakers, he appeared to make nods to the current volatility of Canada-U.S. relations and condemned economic coercions. Speaking about the "current geopolitical rupture," he said a "new dimension was needed.”
“Economic integration is now being weaponized, tariffs being used to exert pressure,” he said. “Financial mechanisms have been used for coercion. Supply chains constitute weak points to be exploited.”
Championing the burgeoning E.U. alliance, Carney focused on what he said were shared values between Canada and the bloc, insisting: "We are not fair-weather allies. We believe that our prosperity grows when it is shared."
“I'm not proposing a third bloc in order to become a 'great power' rival, only with better manners,” Carney continued. “We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”
Carney, who began his speech in French—one of Canada’s official languages—before continuing in English, with splatterings of German, welcomed how European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen had on Wednesday opened the door for Canada becoming an “associate member” of the 27-member bloc.
When speaking about forging closer ties with the E.U., Carney referenced seeking strategic autonomy through “deep co-operation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defense industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space and payments.” He insisted Canada and Europe must not be dependent on “individual nations or individual companies” as this “creates vulnerabilities, particularly when supposedly global companies prove national in the breach.”
He also hinted at a potential freedom of movement between the E.U. and Canada that would allow “youth to work, study, and live where they want, on either side of the Atlantic.”
Carney’s passionate advocacy for the deepening of ties with the E.U.—a move he says Canadians have shown they’re in support of—came after Trump lambasted the idea of a new European dawn for Canada.
Speaking to reporters Wednesday, Trump called the proposal “laughable” and threatened economic punishments if the E.U. moves forward with von der Leyen’s plan.
"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump said en route to an event in North Carolina. "If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”
In response to Trump’s remarks, a European Commission spokesperson told TIME: “As president von der Leyen made clear [on Wednesday], the proposed strengthening of our partnership with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”
Carney welcomes new alliances on visit to Europe
Carney's speech to the European Parliament came on the final day of his stay in Europe, where he sought to cement and deepen Canada’s international relationships.
The E.U. is Canada’s second-largest global trading partner for goods and services, with bilateral trade worth approximately C$178.6 billion in 2025.
The Canadian leader also traveled to Liverpool, England, to meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The pair attended a football game and watched Everton—the team they both support—secure a victory against the Wolverhampton Wanderers.
"The leaders began by underscoring the close co-operation between the U.K. and Canada and emphasized the importance of building similar close ties with European partners, particularly on trade and defence,” a Downing Street spokeswoman told TIME.
Ahead of the meeting, Burnham called Carney a “great progressive leader” with whom the U.K. shares “so many values, but also with whom we have a shared opportunity on defense co-operation, on trade” and AI.
Canada applies to join U.K.-led military coalition
Following Burnham and Carney's meeting, it was announced that Canada has applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military coalition.
The force, formally launched in 2014, consists of 10 North Atlantic NATO member states that deliver rapid response and security operations.
“Prime Minister Carney announced that Canada has formally applied to join the Joint Expeditionary Force and welcomed the U.K.’s support for Canada’s participation in this important initiative,” Carney’s office said in a statement.
Canada, already a NATO member, is seeking to diversify its defense dependency from the U.S. with new partnerships across the Atlantic.
In February, Canada became the first non-European country to participate in the "Security action for Europe” (SAFE) instrument, which provides up to €150 billion in low-interest loans to help member states purchase military and defense equipment.
What happens next as Canada seeks "associate" membership with the E.U.?
Following von der Leyen’s proposal, a European Commission spokesperson told TIME that the executive cabinet will work “in close coordination with [its] member states and the European Parliament” to “create a new form of partnership that has not existed until now–building the closest imaginable form of association with a partner outside Europe.”
The proposed alliance is set to include deeper economic ties, a technology alliance, greater integration of defense industrial bases, and efforts to make the Arctic a flagship joint project. It could also expand cooperation on energy, critical minerals and batteries, as well as AI, quantum technology, cybersecurity, and economic security.
The E.U.-Canada summit set to take place in Montreal in late October will “provide the first meaningful opportunity to discuss these issues further,” the spokesperson told TIME.
The proposal has been welcomed by many European lawmakers across the bloc.
Member of the European Parliament (MEP) for Spain Javier Moreno Sánchez, who also serves as chair of the parliament’s delegation for relations with Canada, told TIME the decision to bring Canada in as an “associate member” was “politically and symbolically significant,” but warned it “must now be followed by concrete actions.”
Irish MEP Barry Andrews told TIME that the announcement is a clear “win-win for both sides,” adding that “in an ever more insecure world, truly democratic countries must come together and stand up to Trump, [Chinese President] Xi Jinping, and [Russian President Vladimir] Putin.”
Germany, the E.U.’s largest economy, also embraced the move, with government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius saying Berlin “welcomes the initiative for a particularly close partnership with Canada.”
The E.U., much like Canada, is seeking new partnerships amid a weakening alliance with the U.S. under Trump, following disputes over tariff threats, his lashing out at the NATO alliance, and his push to annex Greenland.
Espen Barth Eide, Norway’s Foreign Affairs Minister, told TIME the world is "living through the most serious security situation since the Second World War.”
“At a time like this, it is welcome that the E.U. is strengthening cooperation on European security. We also welcome the E.U.’s efforts to involve Norway, the United Kingdom, Canada and Iceland. Such an approach strengthens European security,” he said.
Norway and Iceland are not members of the E.U., but both belong to the European Economic Area (EEA), giving them close economic ties to the bloc through trade and free movement—a model from which Canada could draw inspiration.
Elsewhere, the “associate” membership proposal faced backlash.
French MEP Manon Aubry, co-chair of The Left group, told TIME there was “a serious question of method,” arguing that “a decision of such magnitude cannot be made by the president of the European Commission alone.”

Swiss parliament vote on UBS capital rules postponed

Swiss parliament vote on UBS capital rules postponed
The Swiss Senate has not yet taken any decisions on the future capital requirement rules for systemically important large banks with foreign holdings. Due to time constraints, it was unable to conclude its deliberations on the bill on Thursday. The debate will continue next week.
The regulation, which would currently affect, in practice, only the major bank UBS, is controversial. Accordingly, the members of the Senate took time to exchange their arguments. So much time, in fact, that it was not yet possible to vote on the minority motions tabled.
The federal government wants banks to be required to underpin their subsidiaries abroad with 100% hard core capital (CET1 capital). UBS is vehemently opposed to this. According to the bank, it would be obliged to hold around $22 billion (CHF18 billion) in additional core capital.
+ UBS global units must be backed by ‘hard capital’: SNB
However, the majority of the Economic Affairs Committee (WAK-S) of the Senate has now put forward an alternative proposal to tighten the “too big to fail” framework. On the one hand, the WAK-S is proposing that 50% of overseas holdings be backed by hard core capital, rather than the current 45%.
For the remaining 50%, additional core capital in the form of AT1 bonds (Additional Tier 1) should be permitted. The current rule is: 45% core capital plus 17% in AT1 bonds. UBS also rejects this proposal.
A sizeable minority – in line with the government’s approach – would like to see a 90% capital requirement for foreign holdings. Representatives of left-wing parties, on the other hand, spoke in favour of the federal government’s proposal.

Since its launch in 1955, Eurovision has become the ultimate pop platform, catapulting Swedish icons ABBA to worldwide fame and boosting the likes of Celine Dion, Cliff Richard and Olivia Newton-John.
This year's competition was watched by 131 million viewers, down by 35 million from the year before, after five countries boycotted it over Israel's participation.

Next year's event will take place on May 15 in Bulgaria's Black Sea city of Burgas.
Israel’s genocide in Gaza has killed more than 73,700 people as Tel Aviv continues to kill Palestinians in the territory and violate a US-brokered ceasefire in place since October 2025.

How far will Egypt go to help Saudi Arabia secure the Red Sea?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:24:10 UTC
22:24:10 KST

How far will Egypt go to help Saudi Arabia secure the Red Sea?
Regional analysts highlight the growing security alignment between Cairo and Riyadh amid escalating Red Sea tensions.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s latest meeting with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi this week came at a highly sensitive moment for both countries.
Mere days before Tuesday’s meeting, Iran-aligned Houthi rebels seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, gaining significant control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2Egypt’s el-Sisi meets MBS, backs Saudi call for secure Red Sea navigation
- list 2 of 2‘They called us’: Has Trump abandoned Bab al-Mandeb to the Houthis?
This precipitated a Saudi air campaign over Yemen and repeated attacks by the Houthis on the kingdom’s oil infrastructure.
Analysts say Riyadh is looking for help to protect the kingdom and Red Sea shipping, and that Egypt, whose Suez Canal revenue depends on the same traffic, is an obvious partner.
The deepening bilateral relationship carries significant implications for the region, from the conflicts in Yemen and Sudan to Egypt’s close ties with the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia’s new defence pact with Turkiye and Pakistan.
Purpose of the visit
Abdel Monem Said, a member of Egypt’s Senate who is close to decision-making circles in Cairo, told Al Jazeera the visit had political, economic, strategic and military dimensions.
He said it came as Iran escalated regional conflicts through what he called its proxies, chief among them the Houthis. Their advance directly threatened Egypt’s economy and the Suez Canal, he said.
Said stressed the need for joint strategic and military thinking between Egypt and Saudi Arabia that would act as a strong deterrent against Iran-backed groups from Iraq to Yemen.
He added that Egypt is eager to prevent Iran and its allies from imposing control over the region, especially over maritime traffic in the Red Sea, given the direct repercussions this has for the Suez Canal.
Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at King’s College London, said Cairo increasingly sees one continuous security space stretching from the Suez Canal to Bab al-Mandeb.
If that southern gateway becomes unreliable, he said, Egypt stands to lose shipping, hard currency and strategic leverage.
“I do think Cairo now has a very strong interest in substantive cooperation with Saudi Arabia on Red Sea security,” he told Al Jazeera over email.
‘A new Arab order’
In the lead-up to the meeting, the chairman of the Arab Affairs Committee in Egypt’s House of Representatives, Mohamed Salah Abu Hemila, told Al Jazeera that the Saudi crown prince’s visit may produce a new roadmap for political and strategic cooperation on a number of Arab and regional issues.
The alliance between the two nations would serve as the cornerstone for building a new Arab order — more robust, cohesive, and capable of safeguarding its interests and defending its just causes, he said.
The foremost issues would be Red Sea security and freedom of international navigation, but they would also include the Palestinian cause and the situations in Yemen, Libya and Sudan.
A statement released by el-Sisi’s office after the meeting also affirmed that “relations between Egypt and Saudi Arabia can only be exemplary within the Arab framework,” and linked Egyptian and Gulf security.
Tarek Fahmy, professor of international relations at Cairo University, told Al Jazeera that Saudi Arabia is increasingly acting within an Arab framework after the United States’s reaction to the Houthi escalations fell short of what the kingdom expected. Reports suggest that Saudi Arabia asked the Trump administration for military help in combatting the Iran-backed group, but that Trump refused. Neither Saudi Arabia nor the US has officially commented on these reports.
Red Sea security
No details of specific military cooperation between the two countries were announced during or after the meeting.
However, Egypt is already a party to a Saudi-led coalition for Red Sea maritime security launched in August. The grouping was created as a consequence of international fears that the Houthis could close Bab al-Mandeb while Iran had the Strait of Hormuz choked off.
The coalition, whose founding document stresses it is purely defensive in nature, has not taken military action against the Houthis so far. The rebel group, too, has not taken measures to shut down shipping after its recent advances.
Krieg says Saudi-Egyptian military cooperation is likely to entail intelligence sharing, maritime surveillance, protection of commercial shipping and greater coordination around the Red Sea.
But there is a “very hard ceiling” on how far Egypt will involve itself inside Yemen, he said. “The Egyptian preference will be to defend the maritime system without becoming responsible for Yemen.”
Historical memory likely plays a role in that preference. In the 1960s, Egyptian leader Gamal Abdel Nasser sent tens of thousands of Egyptian soldiers to participate in the North Yemen Civil War, a long and costly endeavour that yielded few results and many casualties.
“Yemen taught Egypt that an apparently limited intervention can become a strategic trap very quickly,” Krieg said.
A broader convergence
It’s no surprise that the two nations should seek to deepen cooperation at this moment, say analysts. The Iran war is only the latest – and perhaps greatest – in a series of regional crises that the two states have found themselves roughly aligned on.
In January, weeks before the war began, el-Sisi met Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud in Cairo. Afterwards, the Egyptian presidency said the two countries held “identical” views on solutions to regional crises that focus on preserving the unity and sovereignty of states.
This was reiterated on Tuesday, when the two sides “stressed that any threat to Sudan’s unity and territorial integrity poses a danger to the collective security of Egypt, Saudi Arabia and all countries of the region”, according to Egypt’s State Information Service.
“Both are deeply uncomfortable with the fragmentation of states and the rise of militias, separatist movements and externally sponsored sub-state actors,” Krieg said. “You can see that in Sudan, Libya, Somalia and increasingly Yemen.”
However, this strategic vision for the region has run contrary to Abu Dhabi’s preferences and policies.
That pre-war meeting between el-Sisi and Prince Faisal came only days after Saudi Arabia launched strikes on a United Arab Emirates-backed separatist group in Yemen, which was widely received as a repudiation of Abu Dhabi.
The UAE is long faced accusations of sponsoring the Rapid Support Forces rebel group in Sudan, driving a devastating civil war that has negative ramifications for Egyptian security. Cairo has supported Khartoum’s efforts to combat the group and restore its sovereignty. The UAE has rejected accusations that it has provided military, logistical, financial or political support to the RSF.
At the same time, the UAE is far and away the largest investor in the Egyptian economy. In 2025, its net investments in the country were more than double that of the second-biggest investor, the United States.
“This is where the Saudi-UAE rivalry becomes difficult for Egypt. Cairo does not want to choose between Saudi Arabia and the UAE,” Krieg says.
Instead, Krieg expects Egypt to compartmentalise, siding with Riyadh on security matters while preserving its economic relationship with Abu Dhabi.
Riyadh “does not need Cairo to publicly attack Abu Dhabi”, he said, but to use its geography, intelligence and influence to make certain regional strategies harder.
Multilateral limits
Saudi Arabia’s urgent need to contain the fallout from the US-Iran war has led it to embrace an increasing number of partners and allies.
Since the war began, it has signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement to include Turkiye in a bilateral mutual defence treaty it had with Pakistan.
It has organised a multilateral maritime security coalition for the Red Sea, sought assurances from the United States and the European Union and signed a defence agreement with Ukraine.
These measures, however, have been more form than function, say analysts. They have not deterred Iran and its regional allies from launching direct attacks on the kingdom, nor have they empowered Yemeni allies to keep the Houthis in check.
Tuesday’s meeting seemed to tacitly acknowledge the lack of a ready military solution for Yemen. Egypt expressed support for “efforts to reach a comprehensive and sustainable political solution to the Yemen crisis”.
They may, however, indicate the kind of security architecture that will emerge once the war is over.

MOSCOW, September 17. /TASS/. Ukraine lost about 1,260 troops in the special military operation zone in the past day, according to Russian Defense Ministry data.
In particular, the Ukrainian army lost up to 220 troops in the area of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North, over 200 troops in the area of responsibility of Battlegroup West, up to 170 troops in the area of responsibility of Battlegroup South, more than 400 troops in the area of responsibility of Battlegroup Center, over 240 troops in the area of responsibility of Battlegroup East, and up to 30 troops in the area of responsibility of Battlegroup Dnepr.
Russian forces strike metallurgical enterprises, Ukraine’s energy facilities
Russian forces launched a massive overnight strike on enterprises of Ukraine’s metallurgical and radio-electronics industries, the country’s defense industry, and energy infrastructure facilities in Kiev, Zaporozhye and the Odessa Region, the Defense Ministry said.
"Tonight, Russian forces, in a massive strike using high-precision weapons based on land, sea and air, as well as unmanned aerial vehicles, hit enterprises of the metallurgical and radio-electronics industries, Ukraine’s military-industrial complex, and energy and transport infrastructure facilities in Kiev, Zaporozhye and the Odessa Region," the ministry said. Vessels being used in the interests of the Ukrainian military were also hit.
Russian forces hit three Ukrainian dry cargo ships, ferry at Chernomorsk port
The Russian army struck three dry cargo ships and a ferry used to deliver military cargo to Ukrainian troops in the port of Chernomorsk in the Odessa Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Footage shows Russian forces striking three dry cargo ships and a ro-ro ferry used to deliver military cargo to the Ukrainian army with Geran-4 Seeker drones at the port of Chernomorsk in the Odessa Region," the report reads.
Russian aviation destroys Ukrainian troop positions in Kharkov Region, DPR
Russian forces struck temporary deployment sites of Ukrainian units in the Kharkov Region and the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR) with guided aerial bombs, the Defense Ministry said.
"Video footage shows strikes on the temporary deployment site of the 4th Border Guard Detachment in the settlement of Fyodorovka in the Kharkov Region, using four FAB-500 aerial bombs equipped with a universal glide and guidance module, and on the temporary deployment site of the Ukrainian army’s 100th Separate Mechanized Brigade in the settlement of Druzhkovka in the DPR, using five FAB-500 aerial bombs equipped with a universal glide and guidance module. All targets were destroyed," the ministry said.
Russian forces strike major data center supporting Ukraine’s military
The Russian Armed Forces have struck Ukraine’s major data center, which supported servers used for military purposes, the Defense Ministry reported.
"The strike targeted the De Novo Data Center, a major facility supporting server equipment used for military purposes, as well as for the processing, transmission, and storage of data, including intelligence data, for the Ukrainian armed forces," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces hit drone production facilities in Kiev, surrounding region
Russian forces struck facilities used to produce and store drones in Kiev and the surrounding region, the Defense Ministry said.
"The strike hit the following facilities in Kiev and the Kiev Region: a facility for producing and storing various types of unmanned aerial vehicles, including RAX-2X medium-range UAVs; a facility operated by Pegasus Arms LLC for producing and storing long-and medium-range fixed-wing UAVs; and an industrial facility producing components for long-and medium-range UAVs and preparing ground-based robotic systems for deployment," the ministry said.
Russian forces strike dry cargo ship with cargo for Ukrainian military at Chernomorsk port
Russian forces struck a dry cargo ship delivering military supplies to the Ukrainian armed forces troops at the port of Chernomorsk, Odessa Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"In the Odessa Region, a dry cargo ship carrying military supplies was struck at the Chernomorsk port, the Artsiz electrical substation, powering the Izmail port, was hit, and two road bridges across the Dniester River in the area of Mayaki, used for the transit of military cargo from Romania and the port of Izmail, were also struck," the ministry stated.
Russian forces hit Brovary energy storage facility supplying military sites in Kiev Region
Russian forces struck the Brovary energy storage facility, which supplied electricity to military sites in the Kiev Region, the Defense Ministry said.
"The strike hit the Brovary energy storage facility, which ensures uninterrupted operation of military sites in the Kiev Region," the Defense Ministry said.
Russian forces strike two road bridges across Dniester River in Odessa Region
Russian forces have struck two road bridges across the Dniester River in the Odessa Region that were used to transport military supplies, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Two road bridges across the Dniester River, which were used to transport military supplies from Romania and the port of Izmail, [were hit in the Odessa Region] near Mayaki," the statement reads.
Russian Armed Forces strike Zaporozhstal metallurgical complex in Ukraine
The Russian Armed Forces have struck the Zaporozhstal steel mill in the Zaporozhye Region, which produces steel for defense enterprises in Ukraine and Europe, as well as an electronic industry assembly facility, the Defense Ministry reported.
"In the Zaporozhye Region [the following have been struck]: the Zaporozhstal steel mill, a key enterprise of Ukraine’s metallurgical industry that produces cast iron and rolled steel used by defense enterprises in Ukraine and Europe; the Zaporozhye electronic assembly facility (the state-owned enterprise Iskra Research and Production Complex), which manufactures radio engineering reconnaissance equipment and electronic warfare systems for the Ukrainian armed forces, as well as components for anti-aircraft missiles," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian air defenses down 956 Ukrainian drones in 24 hours
Russian air defenses shot down 8 guided aerial bombs and 956 fixed-wing drones belonging to the Ukrainian armed forces over the past 24 hours, the Defense Ministry has said.
According to the ministry, since the start of the special military operation, a total of 674 aircraft, 284 helicopters, 237,803 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 30,941 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,778 multiple rocket launcher vehicles, 36,480 field artillery guns and mortars, and 72,091 special military motor vehicles have been destroyed.
Ukraine loses 40 soldiers, self-propelled gun encircled in Kharkov Region in 24 hours
Over the past 24 hours, the Ukrainian troops trapped in the Kharkov Region have lost up to 40 soldiers and a self-propelled artillery piece.
"Over the past 24 hours, losses among Ukrainian armed formations within the encirclement amounted to up to 40 military personnel, one armored combat vehicle, and one self-propelled artillery unit," the Defense Ministry said in a news release.
The ministry noted that, in total since the beginning of September, over 650 troops, 16 armored combat vehicles, 9 motor vehicles, 13 quad bikes, and 25 ground-based robotic systems have been destroyed within the encirclement.
Russian forces take control of Malaya Volchya, liberate Rozovka
Units of Russia’s Battlegroup North have taken control of Malaya Volchya in the Kharkov Region, while service members from Battlegroup East have liberated Rozovka in the Zaporozhye Region, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Battlegroup North units operating in the Kharkov Region continue to tighten the encirclement and expand their external control zone. Through active operations, Russian forces took control of the settlement of Malaya Volchya in the Kharkov Region. <...> Units of the Battlegroup East moved deeper into enemy defenses and liberated the settlement of Rozovka in the Zaporozhye Region," the statement reads.
Russian army thwarts trapped Ukrainian troops' attempts in Kharkov Region to break out
Over the past 24 hours, the Russian Armed Forces have thwarted all attempts by Ukrainian units to break out of encirclement in the Kharkov Region.
"Enemy personnel sustained losses in the areas of Khripuny and Buzovo in the Kharkov Region. All attempts by Ukrainian units to break out of encirclement were thwarted," the Defense Ministry said in a news release.
Russian forces strike Ukrainian army’s infrastructure sites, ammo depots
Russian forces struck infrastructure facilities used by Ukraine for military purposes, as well as ammunition depots and drone assembly sites, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Russia’s tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile forces and artillery units struck Ukraine’s energy and transport facilities used by the Ukrainian armed forces, ammunition and supply depots, as well as assembly and storage sites for drones and their components, along with the temporary deployment points of Ukrainian formations and foreign mercenaries in 152 areas," the statement reads.
Russian aviation strikes Ukrainian troop concentrations in forest belts in Kharkov Region
Russian aviation carried out airstrikes on Ukrainian troop concentrations in forest belts near the community of Serdobino in the Kharkov Region, the Defense Ministry said.
"During reconnaissance operations, Russian forces detected concealed positions of Ukrainian personnel in forest belts near the community of Serdobino in the Kharkov Region. Russia’s Aerospace Forces crews conducted airstrikes on the identified targets using FAB aerial bombs equipped with universal glide and guidance modules. Live recording footage confirmed that the designated targets were successfully struck," the ministry said.

Russia is escalating its hybrid attacks on the West. Moscow will make Europe’s life ‘hell’ for supporting Ukraine, Kremlin insider tells Bloomberg.

Unknown Publisher

Russia is escalating its hybrid attacks on the West. Moscow will make Europe’s life ‘hell’ for supporting Ukraine, Kremlin insider tells Bloomberg.
Russia’s hybrid attacks on European countries are growing more aggressive and reckless, the Bloomberg news agency reports in an extensive investigation. European officials who spoke with the outlet said it is only a matter of time before the attacks cause civilian casualties.
Russia was once accused of interfering in elections and weaponizing migrants trying to reach Europe. Now it is suspected of sabotage, arson, attacks on critical infrastructure, cyberattacks, and airspace violations.
Many incidents — particularly cyberattacks and hacks — go publicly unreported, meaning the true scope of the hybrid campaign is far larger than what’s known.
Over the past two months, Russia has focused its attacks on defense-industrial and logistics targets directly tied to support for Ukraine, a NATO official told the agency. The campaign has grown more aggressive and carries higher risks, the official said, adding that Russia’s hybrid attacks pursue strategic goals rather than aim to cause direct physical harm.
“Russia is consistent in identifying weaknesses in NATO’s infrastructure and is willing to attempt multiple tactics and targets in a flexible and increasingly risk-taking manner,” said Emily Ferris, an associate fellow at at the UK’s Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
European officials are confident Moscow is behind these operations, which are structured to give Russian authorities plausible deniability. The actual perpetrators are typically hired through intermediaries for money.
Russia is acting out of desperation after Ukrainian drone strikes on logistics hubs and the fuel and energy sector damaged its economy, according to Bloomberg’s sources in the intelligence services. The more painful Ukraine’s strikes become, the louder the calls within Russia’s leadership for Europe to pay for its support of Kyiv.
A Bloomberg source close to the Kremlin said outright that Russia intends to “make life hell” for Europe through asymmetric hybrid operations over its support for Ukraine.
So far, however, the outlet says, the campaign has backfired. Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said the country is becoming a “daily target of hybrid warfare,” yet Germany has announced it will supply Ukraine with missiles for its air defense systems and has launched serial production of drones for the Ukrainian military.
The war in photographs
Russia continues to attack Ukraine daily with drones and missiles. Overnight on September 17, Russian strikes damaged warehouses, office buildings, and multistory apartment buildings in Kyiv, injuring 20 people, according to the latest data. In Odesa, a strike damaged a 19-story building and injured six people, including two children. Meduza is publishing photographs of the aftermath of the strike on Odesa.

MOSCOW, September 17. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova pointed to oddities and contradictions surrounding the appearance of names of victims of the Bucha events on a city memorial, while the Kiev regime has still not provided a list of the dead.

1,700-year-old fragment of "Odyssey" discovered inside library book
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:22:26 UTC
22:22:26 KST

1,700-year-old fragment of "Odyssey" discovered between pages of a library book
A researcher in the Netherlands found an incredibly rare fragment of Homer's epic "Odyssey" that is over 1,700 years old sandwiched between the pages of a library book.
The find was made by Dr. Mark de Kreij, of Radboud University in the Netherlands, while he participated in a project to study and publish ancient manuscripts held by Utrecht University. He made the find about two years ago, local media reported, but the university only announced the discovery this week.
De Kreij identified the tiny slip of paper while looking at a collection of early Christian manuscripts purchased by the university in the mid-20th century, according to a news release from the institution. At first, researchers thought it was a piece of paper from the 7th century. Several similar fragments, in Egyptian, had already been found in the collection.
But De Kreij, a Greek teacher, recognized some of the the language on the paper and identified it as a part of Homer's "Odyssey."
"Everyone who learns Greek learns Homer," De Kreij told Dutch media outlet RTV Utrecht.
Researchers were able to date the fragment back to about 300 AD, the university said, and only about 30 such fragments exist worldwide.
"I have the best job in the world," De Kreij told RTV Utrecht. "I am a treasure hunter. Every day you find something nice. This is one of them."
The piece of paper would have come from a pocket edition of the complete poem, the university said, owned by someone living in Egypt's Faiyum oasis. RTV Utrecht described the fragment as about the size of a playing card. The fragment is discolored and has moisture stains, according to the outlet. Both sides have writing on them.
The fragment is from the 12th book of the "Odyssey," where Odysseus tells the tale of his starving sailors devouring cattle that are sacred to the Sun God, Apollo. This moment comes about halfway through the poem. De Kreij told RTV Utrecht that because books wear from the outside in, it makes sense that the fragment would be from that portion.
"There are so many boring parts in the "Odyssey," De Kreij said. "This happens to be a really fun passage."
