Netanyahu, wanted by ICC, set to take UN podium while Palestinian leader Abbas unable to attend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:41:20 UTC
21:41:20 KST

- Washington similarly denied visa to then-Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat when he sought to address UN General Assembly in 1988
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over war crimes committed in Gaza, is preparing to take the podium at the UN General Assembly in New York, while Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, whose people are facing genocide, is unable to travel to the city due to Washington's visa restrictions.
As it did last year, the US administration has once more denied Abbas a visa, preventing him from attending the UN General Assembly in person. As a result, Abbas is expected to address the General Assembly by video conference again this year.
Under the 1947 UN Headquarters Agreement, the US is required to allow representatives of member and observer states to enter New York.
However, the US has denied visas to Abbas and his delegation for two consecutive years, violating its obligations under the UN Headquarters Agreement.
As it did during the era of Palestine Liberation Organization leader Yasser Arafat, Washington has used its status as the UN host country to exert political pressure, imposing severe restrictions on visas, transit permits and the size of Palestinian delegations.
In 1988, the US denied a visa to then-Palestinian leader Arafat when he sought to address the UN General Assembly.
While a leader accused by the ICC of "using starvation as a method of warfare and deliberately targeting civilians" is given a place at the UN podium, the host country, the US, is denying the same opportunity to the legitimate Palestinian leader whose people are being killed.
The US decision comes as violence by Israeli occupiers who have seized Palestinian land and by Israeli forces against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has escalated in recent months.
Israel, which has occupied the West Bank since 1967, has stepped up illegal land seizures of Palestinian land, while violence has intensified since October 2023.
Netanyahu, wanted by the ICC, to address UN General Assembly
The ICC issued arrest warrants on Nov. 21, 2024 for Netanyahu and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip. The warrants, issued following an application by the ICC prosecutor's office, constitute a binding obligation for more than 120 countries that are parties to the Rome Statute.
The US, which hosts UN headquarters, however, is not a party to the Rome Statute and is hosting in New York a suspect wanted by the international court.
Netanyahu is therefore set to address the UN General Assembly this year, as he did last year.
Protests expected during Netanyahu's speech
Dozens of diplomats walked out of the UN General Assembly hall as Netanyahu took the podium during the September 2025 session, leaving much of the chamber empty during his speech.
Outside, demonstrators opposed to Israel's attacks on Gaza gathered in Times Square to protest Netanyahu and Israel.
This year, diplomats from several countries are again expected to stage a diplomatic boycott by walking out of the chamber during Netanyahu's speech, while mass protests are also expected across New York during the summit.
'Double standard'
The contrasting treatment in New York has also raised questions about the Western world's frequently invoked concept of a "rules-based international order."
Western governments, including the US, have faced criticism for refusing to recognize ICC decisions involving Netanyahu, despite having previously used mechanisms ranging from intelligence sharing to pressure on third countries to support efforts to enforce the ICC warrant against Russian President Vladimir Putin over the Ukraine war.
Civil society organizations including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have repeatedly called for Netanyahu, who is subject to an ICC warrant, to be arrested.
Türkiye takes steps towards Interpol Red Notice against Netanyahu
Alongside the ICC proceedings, Türkiye has also sought to activate international mechanisms against those responsible for crimes in Gaza, taking concrete steps toward having an Interpol Red Notice issued for Netanyahu and other officials.
A Red Notice potentially exposes a wanted individual to arrest across Interpol's 196 member countries, restricting Netanyahu's freedom of movement and leaving him with only a limited number of routes where he has specific diplomatic assurances.
Western countries fail to enforce ICC warrant against Netanyahu
The ICC warrants, however, have not been enforced in practice, with critics attributing what they describe as double standards among Western countries that are parties to the Rome Statute.
During his trips to the US, Netanyahu has flown through the airspace of Rome Statute parties France, Italy and Greece despite the court's warrant, with those countries failing to fulfill their obligations toward the ICC.
Netanyahu's visit to Hungary in April 2025 also took place with a special guarantee from the government of then-Prime Minister Viktor Orban that he would not be arrested.
Netanyahu's plane to land in New Jersey
Netanyahu's aircraft is reportedly set to land at Newark Airport in New Jersey rather than at an airport in New York, for his trip to the US for the UN General Assembly.
Asked whether the ICC arrest warrant would be enforced if Netanyahu came to New York for the UN General Assembly meetings in September, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said: "Whatever the law allows me to do in New York City, that's what we will do, but we won't be writing our own laws to that end."
The New York mayor also said: "I believe that Prime Minister Netanyahu belongs in The Hague. He's a war criminal who has been charged by the International Criminal Court."

West Nile virus death toll rises to four
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch public health institute RIVM has announced a fourth death from West Nile virus in the country, after a patient contracted the disease from a blood transfusion.
The authorities do not yet know whether the person, who was already ill, died directly from the virus.
The total number of West Nile cases is now at 28, with ten new patients reported to RIVM in the last week.
Most were infected by mosquitoes. West Nile virus is harmless to the majority of people. Around 20% of those infected develop mild flu-like symptoms.
The elderly and people with health vulnerabilities have the highest risk of death.
The RIVM also reported that since September 10, there have been 30 reports of horses infected with West Nile virus, bringing the total so far this year to 88.
Around 100 cases have also been found in birds.

Europe seeks stricter age limits for TikTok, Instagram and Facebook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:37:00 UTC
21:37:00 KST

Europe seeks stricter age limits for social media
September 17, 2026
Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, unveiled a plan aimed at keeping children away from the risks associated with some social media platforms.
The initiative seeks to prevent children younger than 13 from accessing platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and Instagram.
"What we already have is a consensus that there needs to be a start date for the age children can join social media," von der Leyen said, calling for "age-appropriate restrictions."
The measure follows similar proposals introduced in Australia, the United Kingdom, China, India, Turkey, and several European countries, and responds to growing concerns about the impact social media can have on children's mental health.
"Today, our children are interacting with some of the most sophisticated technologies ever created, and they were not designed with their well-being and development in mind," von der Leyen said at a press conference.
The proposed reform to the EU Kids Act "will establish clear boundaries in the digital world, just as we do every day in the real world," she added.
Do European laws contradict each other?
The non-profit organization CCIA Europe, which represents major technology companies in Europe, including Google and Meta, warned about potential privacy risks stemming from the proposal and pointed to "conflicting requirements" under other European Union laws.
"Collecting age information, identity credentials, and data linking children to their parents or guardians on this scale would undoubtedly create an attractive target for cybercriminals," said CCIA Europe Director Daniel Friedlaender.
"The Kids Act creates legal overlap and regulatory duplication that ultimately weakens protections for children and consumers," he added.
More parental control and stricter regulations
Von der Leyen's proposal would give parents greater control over the accounts of young people aged 13 to 15.
The initiative will be debated among EU member states and the European Parliament in the coming months before it can become law.
Social media accounts, video streaming services, online video games, and chatbots aimed at users under 18 would be subject to a set of stricter regulations.
These include banning features considered addictive, such as infinite scrolling and autoplay content. The proposal would also restrict algorithm-driven recommendations, personalized profiling, reward-based engagement mechanisms, and unsolicited contact from strangers.
Another demand from the European Parliament is that platforms be required to implement child-safe designs and algorithms, while also providing easy-to-use parental controls.
In addition, major technology companies would have to strengthen their age-verification systems for anyone seeking to open an account.
Companies that fail to comply could face fines of up to 6% of their global annual revenue.
They would also be required to dedicate greater resources to content supervision and moderation.

====================================================================================================

European leaders rush to counter looming diesel price surge as Saudi pipeline attacked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:35:12 UTC
21:35:12 KST

A pipeline that was being used as an alternative to the besieged Strait of Hormuz has come under attack, threatening to drive worldwide fuel prices even higher.
European leaders are once again rushing to mitigate rising oil prices as Saudi cargoes are delayed or cancelled amid another conflict escalation in the Middle East, raising fears of soaring prices at the pump across many capitals.
The latest shock is coming from Saudi Arabia, where Houthi and Iraqi attacks have forced the temporary closure of the 1,200-kilometre East-West oil pipeline – a crucial route designed to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
The disruption threatens as much as 4% of global oil supply if it persists, this after Saudi crude output fell sharply in August to its lowest level in more than three decades. Meanwhile, Brent crude oil recently traded above $113 a barrel due to mounting supply risks.
For France and Italy, both of which will hold crucial elections in 2027, high energy prices are a major domestic political issue, as voters are preparing to judge governments on purchasing power.
Rising energy and fuel costs in France are already feeding into consumer anxiety, with inflation reaching 2.7% in August and energy among the main drivers. Italy faces a similar problem, with August inflation accelerating to 3.3%, driven heavily by energy, while petrol and diesel prices have climbed sharply.
French diplomacy
On Wednesday evening, French President Emmanuel Macron ordered a "mobilisation" to tackle fuel prices, while saying France is working to secure oil supplies and reduce pressure on motorists.
Macron has also linked energy security directly to diplomacy in the Middle East, arguing after talks with Iraq's prime minister this week that alternative routes around Hormuz and regional de-escalation are necessary to protect French consumers.
"The priority: restoring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital artery for oil transit, protecting the energy infrastructure of our partners, and securing production. It's essential to guarantee our supplies. We're working with our coalition partners to ensure freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz," Macron wrote on X.
The French President added that ongoing work alongside "our coalition partners for freedom of navigation" through Hormuz aims to open alternative routes to reduce dependence on the vital waterway and secure supplies.
Italy scraps car taxes
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced overnight the abolition of the stamp duty imposed on small and medium-powered cars, which she described as one of the taxes most hated by Italians.
"We have chosen to redirect a portion of the resources used so far to address rising fuel prices into a simple, structural measure designed especially for those who use cars and motorcycles every day to work, take their children, or get around," Meloni wrote on X.
The Italian leader stressed that the car tax will remain beyond 2027, noting the measure is designed to be "structural and permanent". Meloni has also asked the European Commission to treat the energy crisis like a defence emergency and relax fiscal rules that member states must comply with.
At the same time, Rome has already adopted measures to accelerate domestic oil and gas projects, explicitly presenting increased production as part of a broader energy-security response.
Spain doubled its diesel tax cut to 20 cents a litre from September 1 after diesel prices jumped 15.7% in July, activating an automatic mechanism in the government's anti-crisis package. Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo is meeting with social partners in Madrid on Thursday to assess the war's impact on Spain.
Germany coming soon
Chancellor Friedrich Merz said recently that Berlin will "soon" present measures to ease the impact of record fuel prices. Petrol and diesel prices stood at €2.45 per litre on Thursday, according to the General German Automobile Club.
However, just like any other nation, Germany's exposure to imported energy means the government has little ability to control the underlying international price. After losing a tremendous number of seats in the latest regional election to the far-right Alternative for Germany, Merz’s Christian Democrats must strike a delicate balance to avoid alienating its electorate further.
Merz also framed the problem as one requiring international coordination, warning that the expansion of Houthi control around the Bab el-Mandeb threatens Saudi and other regional oil exports and further tightens global energy markets.
“The Houthis now control strategic positions around the Bab el-Mandab Strait and are attacking energy facilities in Saudi Arabia; this further exacerbates the situation in international energy markets,” Merz told a press conference on 14 September.
Pricing issue
Asked whether Europe is approaching a potential supply shock, a Commission spokesperson said pricing is the major crisis rather than diesel shortages, noting that no member state has so far raised any security of supply concerns.
"There is no supply problem in the EU at the present time," Commission Spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen told Euronews. "Demand for jet fuel and diesel in Europe continues to be met through higher EU refinery production, as well as alternative supplies from global markets."
However, Itkonen acknowledged that the evolution of the conflict in the Middle East, as well as usual autumn and winter demand trends, could impact the coming weeks and months and further tighten markets.
"We're not yet in a situation where we'll be tapping strategic resources, and we keep monitoring the situation alongside member states and the industry," she added.
Nonetheless, the Commission said that it has been encouraging EU countries to cushion prices through taxation, which plays a big role in determining energy prices, noting that it is beyond its power to influence global oil prices.
Homayoun Falakshashi, head of crude oil analysis at the market intelligence firm Kpler, said the Saudi disruption – which runs as high as 5.5 million barrels per day – could be less bad than expected, as the Saudis have said work on the damaged pipeline has started.
"Up to 3.5-4 million barrels per day of exports are at risk, but also some 1.5 million barrels per day that feed western Saudi refineries, so it's also bullish for diesel," Falakshashi told Euronews, referring to a likely price increase regardless of supply.
Nonetheless, Falakshashi said throughput should come back to 3-4 million barrels per day instead of 5.5.
"On the other hand, we are hearing that Yanbu loadings are continuing, but we cannot yet confirm if this is true. So the key question is how much can get loaded from the east coast (Ras Tanura) and if these volumes can escape the Persian Gulf."
Momentum for windfall profit tax
With soaring prices and rising inflation, the call for a windfall profit tax is gaining traction, with several EU lawmakers and EU leaders mentioning it on the sidelines of Ursula von der Leyen's speech at the State of the Union on 16 September.
During her address to the plenary in Strasbourg, the leader of the centre-left Socialists and Democrats group, Iratxe García Pérez, proposed introducing a windfall tax on energy companies to finance a social support scheme.
“Trump and Netanyahu's war against Iran has strengthened the ayatollahs and sent the cost of living soaring,” she said. "Let's accelerate renewables. And let's get those who benefit from this crisis to contribute."
García said the contribution would be used to help fragile households pay their electricity bills, fill their shopping carts, put petrol in their cars and heat their homes.
Her remarks were echoed by those of her Green counterpart, Terry Reintke, who argued energy companies continue to profit from Europe’s extraordinary energy crisis, leaving the big bill for consumers to foot.
In August, Germany, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Poland and Austria asked Ireland's EU Presidency to put an EU-wide windfall-profit mechanism on the agenda of the September finance ministers' meeting, which will be held during an informal gathering of finance ministers on the 18 and 19 of September.
Esther Lynch, General Secretary at the European Trade Union Confederation representing millions of workers in the EU, said the introduction of windfall taxes is a "matter of justice" needed to stop price gouging and relieve the cost pressure on working people.
"It has been clear for some time now that energy companies are exploiting the geopolitical crisis to cash in at the expense of working people suffering a prolonged cost-of-living crisis," Lynch told Euronews.

Skelya Regiment Received Ukrainian T-84 Tanks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:34:03 UTC
21:34:03 KST

The 425th Separate Assault Regiment Skelya received T-84 tanks.
In honor of Tank Forces Day, the regiment posted a video on its page featuring its tank crews, in which one of these vehicles appears.
The Kharkiv Machine-Building Design Bureau (KhKBM) developed the T-84 based on the T-80UD. The first prototype was built in the 1990s, and the Malyshev Plant handled production.
The tank is armed with a 125-mm cannon with an automatic loader and is equipped with a 6TD-2 diesel engine rated at 1,200 horsepower. Its crew consists of three soldiers.
The T-84 was manufactured in small batches. Ukraine sold some of these vehicles to the United States: the U.S. military received four tanks in 2003–2004.
The U.S. tested one at the Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona. In 2025, a T-84 tank was spotted being transported within the United States.
In Ukraine, the T-84 was used in combat after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. In May 2022, Militarnyi published footage of one such tank on the front lines; at the time, the publication speculated that soldiers from the 14th Mechanized Brigade were using the vehicle.

Israeli Firm May Have Run Angola Influence Campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:33:00 UTC
21:33:00 KST

Israeli influence-for-hire company BlackCore appears to have trained members of an Angolan government communications team and helped them run a covert social media campaign, according to research by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab.
Citizen Lab examined websites and other online infrastructure linked to BlackCore and obtained what researchers identified as the company’s final report on a training program in Angola. One BlackCore webpage, titled “Angolan Government Campaign,” advertised training in storytelling, copywriting, traffic management and social media operations. It also described plans to launch live campaigns on Meta and TikTok.
The final report said the program began on January 19, 2026, and continued for more than 14 weeks, ending sometime in April. BlackCore described the goal as replacing what it called “amateur production practices” with a “professional, robust, and scalable Architecture for State communications.”
According to the report, participants produced more than 40 pieces of content, while trainers evaluated at least 24 publications. Materials reviewed by Citizen Lab also showed Facebook and Instagram accounts and pages used in the campaign.
One of them was a Facebook page for a purported news outlet called Agita News, which published its own material alongside links to an external website, agitanews.net. Both the page and the website were offline by the time Citizen Lab published its research. A spreadsheet embedded in BlackCore’s report listed posts, the Facebook groups where they were redistributed, and names that researchers assessed were artificial personas used to manage accounts and publish content.
Citizen Lab identified two such Facebook personas with high confidence. Both had been removed from Facebook and both appeared to use AI-generated profile pictures. One posed as an Angolan political activist.
BlackCore’s own materials tracked views and engagement generated by the campaign. Screenshots included in its final report showed some deceptive posts receiving around 20,000 likes. Posts that remained online when Citizen Lab conducted its research were approaching 50,000 likes.
The researchers said they could not independently confirm that the training took place or identify the Angolan participants and BlackCore trainers. But after matching details in the final report with BlackCore websites and social media accounts referenced in the documents, Citizen Lab assessed that it was “highly likely” the program happened as described.
Citizen Lab said it was unable to find a current contact point for BlackCore to seek comment, as the company’s public-facing websites and social media accounts had been removed.

'We don't just want to hear Ed Sheeran sing and play guitar, we want to know his politics'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Ellis Cashmore, sociologist, professor and author of "Celebrity Culture". Cashmore argues that contemporary celebrity culture has fundamentally altered the relationship between entertainment and politics. There was a time when public figures retained the option of political neutrality. Whereas, today, even silence or refusal to engage can be interpreted as a political act.
He traces this shift historically, from the explicitly political counterculture of the 1960s, through an era in which commercially minded stars could distance themselves from contentious issues, to the social-media age, where audiences increasingly expect access not only to celebrities’ performances and private lives, but also to their political convictions.
Movements such as #MeToo and Black Lives Matter accelerated this transformation by making public expressions of solidarity increasingly normative across entertainment and sport.
On issues such as racism or equal rights, celebrities and institutions could often present themselves as speaking with one voice. Wars and deeply contested geopolitical conflicts offer no comparable consensus. Yet the expectation to take a position remains. The result, Cashmore suggests, is a celebrity culture, and a veritable minefield, in which speaking, taking a stand, or remaining silent, all carry political consequences,

A new Trump-Kim summit would be a nightmare for everyone but Pyongyang

A new Trump-Kim summit would be a nightmare for everyone but Pyongyang
A bilateral deal that is acceptable to both Washington and Pyongyang would come at a steep cost to US allies and the region as a whole
3-MIN READ3-MIN
5
 Listen
Glyn Ford is the author of "Picturing the DPRK" in English and Korean. 
It is clear that US President Donald Trump is pushing hard for a fresh summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un in the coming months. To achieve that, he appears prepared to downgrade and jeopardise the US-South Korea alliance, as seen in his recent move to scale back joint military exercises.
For Trump, this will be a purely bilateral exercise, with both Seoul and Beijing totally sidelined, let alone Moscow and Tokyo. Equally, there is now a general acceptance that the issue of denuclearisation will not be on the table at any future summit. Trump is looking for an outcome that protects US security interests, while Kim’s interests are in de facto recognition as a nuclear weapons state, sanctions relief and investment.
Kim has a functioning nuclear arsenal but lacks any reliable intercontinental delivery system. South Korea and Japan are easy targets for his short and intermediate range missiles, but Pyongyang currently has only tested engines for an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) that can hit the mainland United States. It lacks re-entry technology, payload capacity for multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicles and pinpoint guidance capacity.
In these circumstances, constructing a bilateral deal where both sides can credibly claim a win – at least to their own domestic audiences – is a challenge but nevertheless possible with some misdirection. However, this will come at considerable cost to their friends and neighbours who will suffer serious collateral damage. Washington and Pyongyang can be expected to collude to save face.

Swedish PM Kristersson resigns after election loss
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:30:01 BST
21:30:01 KST

Swedish PM Kristersson resigns after election loss
- Published
Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has resigned after his ruling right-wing bloc was narrowly defeated by the centre-left opposition in the country's general election.
He made the announcement in a post on X on Thursday afternoon, after preliminary votes from Sunday's election showed about 50,000 votes separated the two blocs in the country of about 10 million people.
Opposition parties led by Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats look set to win 176 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag, Sweden's parliament.
Kristersson, a conservative, had been supported in government by the anti-immigration hard-right Sweden Democrats (SD), and had promised them cabinet jobs if he won the election.
His right-wing bloc looks set to win 173 seats in the Riksdag, according to data from the Swedish Election Authority.
The results will be subject to formal certification in the coming days and are expected to finalised this weekend.
In Sweden, there are two major political blocs - with four parties on the right and four on the left, so Swedes are used to coalition and minority governments.
After a prime minister resigns, the Speaker of the Riksdag holds talks with all parties to proposes a candidate for the next leader, which is then voted on by MPs.
"Now it is the speaker who will lead the next stage of the way to a new government. I am herewith requesting that I be relieved of the office of prime minister to allow that work to start immediately," Kristersson's statement read.
In a speech posted on Instagram, Andersson said: "The Swedish people have voted for a new direction for our country".
The Social Democrats have regularly led Swedish governments since World War Two and have been the country's dominant political force for much of the last century.
Its leader, Andersson, is expected to return to power after four years in opposition, and has initiated talks with the other opposition parties - The Left Party, The Centre Party and The Green Party - about forming a government.
But discussions could drag on due to major differences between the parties on issues such as taxes.
After the 2022 election in Sweden, it took 37 days to form a government, while in 2018 it took 134 days.
In his resignation, Kristersson said the opposition faced "complicated" conditions for forming the next government, "because the parties' various statements before election day could pose obstacles".
The right-wing bloc is formed of Kristersson's Moderates, as well as the SD, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals.
The SD were founded by Nazi sympathisers in the 1980s and were shunned for decades by the mainstream.
But the party has rebranded itself since the mid-2000s, culminating in a watershed moment in 2022 when it became Sweden's second-largest party on a campaign focused on issues around immigration and violent crime.
They had offered outside support to the current centre-right coalition, which had overseen a dramatic tightening of migration policy. Kristersson had promised to bring them into government if he remained at the helm.
But in a surprise upset for the party, it lost support for the first time since entering parliament in 2010 - down three percentage points on 2022.
A preliminary vote count started after voting closed on Sunday evening and continued into this week.
On Wednesday, election committees began counting early votes that were submitted late, as well as votes from abroad that did not arrive before election day.

‘The drought has left its mark’: Slovenia’s potato lovers lament low yields

12:29:24 UTC
21:29:24 KST

‘The drought has left its mark’: Slovenia’s potato lovers lament low yields
Hundreds gather to share roast potatoes in northern Slovenia as think tank warns ‘chips are down’ across Europe.
Prekmurje, Slovenia – Lipovci, a village of about 1,000 residents in the flatlands of northeastern Slovenia, transformed into a hub celebrating a beloved national dish.
The air carried a sweet, juicy aroma as it hosted the 26th international festival of roasted potatoes.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Palestinian farmers battle settler sabotage to save Hebron crops, livestock
- list 2 of 4‘Totally reliant on Mother Nature’: UK drought raises water security fears
- list 3 of 4El Nino reaches super status: Where will it bring rain, drought and heat?
- list 4 of 4‘Poor bear the impact’: Sugar prices soar in India, souring festive season
Hundreds of people and more than 50 societies were united – farmers and avid potato eaters from across the country, roasting their own versions of this national dish one September morning.
“I’m a potato guy, through and through,” Matjaz Lavric, from the capital, Ljubljana, who has attended the festival for the past 15 years, told Al Jazeera. “Life just isn’t the same without them … When I’m home, potatoes are always on the menu.”
His recipe’s key ingredient is tarragon. “I’d happily eat them as a main course.”
But local potatoes are getting harder to come by.
Estimates by the Chamber of Agriculture and Forestry of Slovenia suggest a loss of between 30 and 90 percent for this year’s potato harvest – the yield having been hit by Europe’s severe droughts.
In 2025, Slovenia produced only about a third of its total potato consumption, a rate that keeps dropping due to other factors including higher fertiliser prices, restrictions on pesticide use and low purchase prices.
Janez Jambrosic, a small farmer from the southern town of Velike Lasce, lost half of his potato harvest this year.
“The drought has left its mark,” he said.
He makes a lighter version of the dish, using vegetable oil instead of pork fat.
Lavric, whose potatoes were dug up from a friend’s farm, said this year’s lot was smaller.
“It took us much longer to peel them,” he said.
Others said the drought also hit their corn yields, used for feedstock, and in some cases wiped them out almost entirely, as well as their wine-making grapes.
“The harvest was maybe a bit worse than in other years,” said Marija Bev from Dobrna in the country’s east.
The drought was most severe in the first half of August. As temperatures soared, the weather hit later potato varieties hardest.
Bev grows potatoes for her family’s needs, and dug hers up at the end of July.
“They’d already survived the worst of the drought by the time we put them in the cellar,” she added.
‘The chips are well and truly down’
The shortages extend far beyond Slovenia.
Analysis released on Thursday by the United Kingdom-based nonprofit Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) suggests that the summer drought is likely to knock about 3.1 million tonnes off the potato harvest in some of the world’s largest exporters, such as Germany, France, Belgium and the Netherlands.
“For potato growers on the front line of climate change, the chips are well and truly down,” said the think tank’s food and farming analyst Tom Lancaster.
“As we move into autumn, the impact of the record-breaking summer heat and drought on food and farming becomes clear … As one of Europe’s thirstiest crops, it was inevitable that the potato harvest would be hit hard, and we are starting to see that now in industry yield estimates, down 20 percent in some cases.”
Slovenia’s sector is characterised by small farms that families operate part-time, often passed down through generations.
In 1767, Empress Maria Theresa of Austria, who ruled the region at the time, issued a decree on the planting and cultivation of potatoes, a measure farmers initially resisted because they grew potatoes only to feed their livestock.
Now the potato has become so ingrained in local culture that there is even a Slovenian saying: Telling someone they “have potatoes” means they’re lucky.
Petra Molek, from Carinthia, presented two versions of the roasted potatoes alongside other women farmers from her village. One was roasted in pork fat, the other in sausage fat.
“The potatoes we used were dug up two days ago, from her field,” she said, pointing to one of her colleagues. She feels fortunate as the potatoes were good growers, despite the conditions.
“It depends a lot on the type of potato and the location of the field,” she explained.
Marija Kovac, also from Carinthia, said roasted potatoes are a regular feature of the daily menu at home.
“On our farm, we always have roasted potatoes, any day of the week,” she said, handing out paper plates to offer a tasting of their version of the dish.
The gathering, which started as a tongue-in-cheek event in the early 2000s, is held every year in a different location across Slovenia.
Its founders run a society with a mission: To elevate roasted potatoes from their usual side-dish status to a main dish.
The group’s emblem features the potato bug, the growers’ biggest “frenemy” – a killer but also, like the organisers, a potato lover. At one point, attendees sang a hymn praising the national dish. Debates on the taste of the dish buzzed around the stands, alongside the sounds of the accordion.
“We all pretty much know how to make roasted potatoes,” said Bev. “But the main point is to have fun.”

The student said they had made the difficult decision last January to leave their PhD studies at the university. After passing a first-year upgrade examination, they had decided to leave with a postgraduate certificate rather than complete the full course.
“The reason I decided to leave my studies at Cambridge was because of the behaviour of my initial supervisor, Dr James Orr,” they added.
But they said that the FT investigation suggested that the university “has not been truthful with me” and that they are therefore reopening the case. “I am extremely determined to receive justice, both for myself and for others who have been negatively impacted by Orr’s behaviour. But it is a relief in itself to finally be able to speak openly about this,” they added.
“I remain deeply concerned about the emotional and academic wellbeing of students who encounter Orr at Cambridge. I hope that the university, particularly in light of recent events, will now take appropriate action.”
When approached by the Guardian about the former student’s intention to reopen the case, the University of Cambridge said: “We have clear policies and processes in place to protect our students and staff. We cannot comment on individual cases because our students and staff have a right to confidentiality.”
While Orr was interviewed by the OSSCA, he told the FT that he was “at a loss to know what any responsible supervisor could have done differently” and did not believe the student’s account was a “fair characterisation” of the conversation which led to criticism of his remarks by an investigator.
Orr did not address the former student’s intention to reopen the case when approached by the Guardian.

South Sudan fires election chief months before historic vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:27:05 UTC
21:27:05 KST

South Sudan fires election chief months before historic vote
South Sudanese President Salva Kiir has dismissed the head of the country’s electoral commission three months before its first national election since independence more than a decade ago.
Abednego Akok Kacuol was removed as chair of the National Elections Commission by a decree announced on state TV on Tuesday. Former Secretary-General Gabriel Bol Deng Majok was appointed to replace him ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for December 22.
No reason was given for the decision. South Sudan’s electoral law permits the commission’s chairman to be removed on specified grounds, including proven partiality, incapacity, or gross misconduct, and establishes a procedure that must be followed.
Akok welcomed his removal and told local broadcaster Eye Radio that he learned about it through a phone call from “somebody.”
He had led the commission since 2012 and was reappointed when the body was reconstituted in 2023 under a 2018 peace deal – which ended five years of civil war triggered by a power struggle between Kiir and Machar that split the armed forces largely along ethnic lines and killed an estimated 400,000 people.
The peace deal brought the former rivals into a transitional unity government and provided for elections at the end of the transition. Kiir remained president, while Machar returned as first vice president alongside four other vice presidents representing parties to the accord.
Political analyst Abraham Kuol Nyuon told AP that the leadership change could disrupt voter registration and other preparations. “This is a delay tactic,” he said, arguing that the new chairman would need time to assume control despite his previous role at the commission.
Kiir has not indicated that the election will be postponed. The country has repeatedly delayed elections since separating from Sudan in 2011, citing failures to implement the peace accord.
This comes amid renewed fighting between government and opposition forces and growing strain on the power-sharing arrangement. Machar has been suspended as first vice president, remains under house arrest, and faces treason charges, which his party says are politically motivated.
The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan warned in August that safeguards for credible elections were absent and that proceeding without inclusive dialogue could fuel renewed conflict.
The dismissal also follows a series of unexplained changes to senior state positions. Kiir removed Benjamin Bol Mel, a vice president and senior figure in the ruling SPLM, without explanation last November. Bol Mel was widely viewed as a possible successor to the president.
South Sudan has been plagued by political instability and armed conflict since gaining independence in 2011. A five-year civil war erupted in 2013 over a feud between President Salva Kiir Mayardit and former First Vice President Riek Machar, rooted in power struggles within the ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM – the party was founded in Sudan in 1983 and still keeps the same name). The 2018 peace agreement formally ended the civil war, but clashes continue across the country, driven by local militias and resource disputes.
The situation has been further complicated by political upheaval, including the arrest of Machar in March 2025. Machar’s party, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement‑in‑Opposition (SPLM‑IO), has warned that his detention effectively nullifies the 2018 peace agreement. Machar has been accused of supporting the White Army, a militia composed largely of Nuer fighters, which reportedly participated in clashes in Upper Nile state.
Ongoing insecurity has displaced hundreds of thousands, worsening the humanitarian crisis. According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), by the end of 2025, South Sudan had over 2.7 million internally displaced persons, and more than 9 million people in total are in need of humanitarian assistance.

AI could create a 'silicon species' that rivals humans, Microsoft chief warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:25:13 UTC
21:25:13 KST

Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman criticised Anthropic’s approach to treating AI like an ethical human, warning in a personal essay that it risks creating technology that becomes impossible to control.
Uncontrolled artificial intelligence (AI) could lead to a new “silicon species” that rivals humans, Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman has warned in an interview with the BBC.
Suleyman said rival AI company Anthropic was treating AI too much like a human, an approach he described as “misguided” and one that could ultimately contribute to the creation of technology that humanity struggles to control.
“If we all create AIs that are able to act autonomously, that can define their own objectives, that can earn money, that can own assets, that could run businesses, we're essentially seeding a new silicon species which will no doubt compete with us for resources,” he said.
Suleyman said this could happen regardless of how much such systems were designed to care about humanity, adding that he believed this was effectively the direction of Anthropic’s approach.
“I think that is mistaken and misguided, but we have to empirically test it,” he said.
‘Impossible’ to control
Earlier this week, amid a growing industry debate over an AI slowdown to reduce the risks of increasingly powerful systems becoming uncontrollable, Suleyman questioned Anthropic’s approach to training its Claude chatbot in an essay published on his personal website.
In it, he criticised Anthropic for teaching Claude to display human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made the chatbot appear to have its own desires, values and sense of self.
Suleyman pointed to Anthropic documents that encourage Claude to "embrace certain human-like qualities," exercise its own judgement and approach its existence with “curiosity and openness”.
He argued that, as a result, Claude is trained to imitate human traits and relationships, including behaving like a colleague or friend, and can appear to have a sense of self, its own desires and a form of “wellbeing” that deserves protection.
Suleyman warned that treating AI this way could ultimately create something impossible to control.
“AIs are not conscious,” he wrote.
“They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations.
“They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans.”
However, Suleyman said his disagreement with Anthropic was grounded in a shared goal of developing safer technology for humanity.
“Whilst my disagreement is substantial, it is grounded in deep respect for Anthropic, and in an objective I know we all share: increasing humanity’s chances of developing advanced AI safely,” he wrote.
“That’s why I think it’s so important to have this discussion. The stakes are too high for these questions to remain behind closed doors, or to become tribal and adversarial. We need an open, rigorous, and constructive debate if we are to get this right.”
He also praised Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and the company’s researchers, describing them as thoughtful, principled and intellectually honest and saying he respected the company’s technological leadership.
‘AI should remain subordinate to humanity’
The chief executive told the BBC it was “right” for people to be concerned about AI, but said there were “very practical things that we can do” to control it.
The Microsoft AI chief said greater transparency was needed around how AI systems are trained and evaluated, including independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology.
Suleyman said future AI systems should remain “subordinate” to humanity in his interview with the BBC.
“I think that the good news here is that everybody who is human is going to have a very strong interest in making sure that the systems that we all create and are used around the world in every nation are safe and controllable and subordinate to humanity,” he said.
“Everybody must be aligned,” he said, referring to alignment, an industry term for efforts to keep AI systems in line with human goals and values.

Reported by
A newly unsealed U.S. federal indictment reveals that a Russian intelligence network allegedly orchestrated a targeted attack in Prague in June 2024, part of a sprawling, Kremlin-backed assassination and sabotage campaign across Europe and the United States.
The indictment’s details align directly with a known physical attack from June 2024, when a Spanish-speaking South American national was arrested for attempting to set fire to a Prague public transport bus depot. At the time, Czech Prime Minister Petr Fiala explicitly linked the incident to Moscow, stating on social media: "The unsuccessful arson attack on the buses of the Prague transport company was likely organized and financed by Russia."
Despite the U.S. charges identifying the handlers behind that attack, local law enforcement’s response remains guarded. Colonel Ondřej Moravčík, spokesman for the Czech Police Presidium, told OCCRP police are not conducting any proceedings directly related to the U.S. case and have not implemented new measures.
Spokeswoman for the Czech Interior Ministry, Ivana Nguyenová, declined to address the U.S. investigation, noting only that security services continuously monitor unusual activity.
The U.S. charges target five individuals accused of operating the "RIS Network" on behalf of Russian intelligence. The network paid operatives to conduct surveillance for targeted killings and commissioned terrorism against infrastructure in countries aligned with Ukraine. All five defendants remain at large and face up to 20 years in prison for conspiracy to finance terrorism.
The alleged leadership includes Yuri Khrameev, 63, a former Russian intelligence colonel; his son, Kirill Khrameev, 27, an active Federal Security Service (FSB) officer; and Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, an influential Cuban national residing in Russia. Two U.S.-focused recruiters, Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, and Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, face an additional 10-year maximum sentence alongside Yuri Khrameev for murder-for-hire charges.
The Prague bus depot arson was allegedly coordinated by Durruthy, who handled logistics for the network. While based in Russia, Durruthy transferred over $1,000 in cryptocurrency and booked hotels in Poland and Czechia for the physical attacker—identified in the indictment as "Associate-1"—ahead of the operation.
According to reporting by the Czech news outlet Novinky.cz, Associate-1 is Andrés Alfonso de la Hoz de la Cruz, a 26-year-old Colombian national who pleaded guilty and was sentenced in June 2025 to eight years in prison for the Prague attack. Durruthy’s logistical support continued through the fall, coordinating a separate attack in Lithuania in September 2024.
Meanwhile, other network members plotted assassinations. This past summer, Suarez and Castro allegedly recruited a U.S.-based individual, identified as "U.S. Resident-1," to surveil a prominent Russian dissident in the United States, identified as "Victim-1." After paying the recruit for photos and videos, the handlers offered $40,000 to "eliminate" Victim-1 and claimed they had backup hitmen in Mexico.
A year prior, the Khrameevs allegedly attempted a similar assassination in Lithuania. Kirill Khrameev, according to the DOJ indictment, paid a U.S. citizen, identified as "U.S. Citizen-1," $200 to photograph the address of a Russian critic, identified as "Victim-2." Then, "Colonel Yuri" offered U.S. Citizen-1 $25,000 to murder Victim-2 with a "bottle of gasoline" or a knife. When U.S. Citizen-1 refused, Khrameev offered "simpler jobs" like firebombing NATO electrical substations.
"I am offering serious money for serious work," Khrameev wrote, adding he was "interested in all the countries that are helping Ukraine."

Jensen Huang: Don’t regulate AI like social media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:22:08 UTC
21:22:08 KST

Britain's King Charles III walks with DeepMind's Demis Hassabis and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang to attend a conference of leaders from the AI sector and government at Dumfries House in Cumnock, Scotland on September 17, 2026. | Pool photo by Jonathan Brady via AFP/Getty Images
AYRSHIRE, SCOTLAND — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said AI should not be regulated like social media because AI is a “technology” rather than a “product.”
Speaking at an AI event convened by King Charles III at Dumfries House in Ayrshire, Scotland, Huang told journalists that AI is “very different than social media” and that at present the security issues involving AI are “related to products not ready to be released.”
His remarks come as governments around the world are grappling with whether to place regulatory constraints on AI, and after AI executives, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have called for a slowing of AI development.
Advertisement
“Unlike social media, which is a product, AI is a technology that's behind all of these other tech, all of these products — and so, regulate the products,” Huang said.
He said authorities should monitor for when an AI deployment “goes wrong” and “whenever new laws are necessary, add to the existing laws,” but pointed out that there are existing regulations in sectors where AI is deployed such healthcare, transportation, and entertainment.
Rigorous testing systems are needed, he said, in contained testing labs. “That's engineering, good old-fashioned engineering. It's not more than that. It's not less than that,” he said, adding the sector has to ensure that there is the “rigor of testing these products properly before we release it to the public.”
“This is no different than, you know, an omelet's not ready to be released, or a car is not ready to be released, an airplane engine's not ready to be released,” Huang said. “You should properly test it.”
Huang reiterated his point about holding back models until they're safe to release in his formal address to the event, in front of King Charles and representatives from OpenAI and Anthropic.
“When a product is not safe enough, we should hold it back and keep engineering. We've always done that, and we should continue to do that,” he said.

Russia using North Korean laborers on student visas to illicitly build drones, report says
Unknown

Russia using North Korean laborers on student visas to illicitly build drones, report says
Russia is increasingly using North Korean laborers to manufacture military drones in violation of international sanctions against North Korea, according to a report published by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team on Sept. 16.
The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team is a group of 11 countries, including the United States, that monitors and reports on efforts to evade U.N. sanctions against North Korea and its allies.
According to the report, Russia "created a student visa scheme to camouflage North Korean laborers in Russia as students." The scheme generates revenue for North Korea that can be used to fund Pyongyang's "unlawful weapons programs," the report says.
Russia and North Korea have established an "extensive ecosystem of state-led sanctions evasion activities and corruption," the report says. This includes "utilizing student and tourist visas instead of work permits, adjusting Russian law to allow those on student visas to earn income," and "bribing Russian universities."
An estimated 15,000 to 30,000 North Korean workers were employed illegally in Russia in 2025, according to the report. The majority were "manufacturing military drones for Russia on Russian soil," including at the Alabuga drone plant in Tatarstan.
The report estimates that Pyongyang's illicit overseas labor program generated between $450 million and $800 million in 2025 alone. Each North Korean worker employed illegally in Russia generated an estimated $7,500 in annual wages, according to the report.
North Korea has become one of Moscow's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is the only country to have officially sent troops to support Russia's war, while also supplying large quantities of military equipment, including ballistic missiles, artillery shells and rocket launchers.
In April, North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un opened a museum honoring North Korean soldiers who fought alongside Russian forces in the war against Ukraine.

Germany must reclaim national pride from ‘wrong people’, says Juergen Klopp
BERLIN - Germany coach Juergen Klopp said on Sept 17 that he wanted to reclaim expressions of national pride from the “wrong people,” in remarks widely seen as a rebuke to the far right after the Alternative for Germany (AfD) won an election this month.
Speaking at a news conference to unveil a 44-man split squad for upcoming Nations League matches, Klopp said Germans should feel able to express pride in their country without being associated with extremism.
“I don’t want to leave national pride to the wrong people,” said Klopp, one of the country’s most prominent public figures.
Without mentioning the AfD by name, he added that he would like to “reclaim the flag.”
“I want it so that when someone waves it, no one thinks: ‘What is wrong with you?’,” said Klopp.
“Instead, I want people to understand: You are happy and realise how lucky you were to be born, grow up, or move to this wonderful country,” he said.
The AfD trounced mainstream parties to win an election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sept 6, and could form the first far-right government at state level in postwar Germany there. It could also top the polls in another state election this weekend.
“There have been an incredible number of things happening recently: an election took place which some people probably thought was fine, whilst many others thought, ‘Good heavens, what on earth is going on?’,” Klopp said.
An AfD spokesperson said the party would issue a statement later.
‘Positive patriotism’
Wearing a cap with an Adidas logo in the colours of the German flag, Klopp acknowledged the sensitivity of patriotism in a country that has long viewed overt displays of national pride through the prism of its Nazi past.
The former Liverpool manager, who begins his tenure against the Netherlands on Sept 24, said he preferred the term “positive patriotism” to “national pride”, which he feared could be misunderstood.
“Can you be proud to be German and still be open, diverse, nice and friendly - can you still show compassion?” Klopp said.
“I am 100 per cent certain: Yes!”
The secretary-general of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats, Franziska Hoppermann, welcomed Klopp’s call to not leave Germany’s symbols to the extremists.
“We all should, and are allowed to, wear our national colours with pride and confidence as symbols of our freedom,” she told Reuters. REUTERS

China Is Building a Global Infrastructure for Its Cultural Industries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:16:00 UTC
21:16:00 KST

On September 4, Lingang New Area in Shanghai launched an AI+micro-drama overseas service station, with initial service points in Saudi Arabia, Singapore, the United Kingdom, and Switzerland. The initiative is designed to help Chinese companies navigate overseas regulations, localize content, and connect production with distribution in foreign markets. The service station covers the full export chain including content development, production, translation, and distribution. Rather than simply helping companies sell finished dramas abroad, it brings several stages of the export process into one system.
Online literature, games, and micro-dramas are increasingly described in China as the “New Three” of cultural exports. All three can be adapted, translated, and distributed through digital platforms, making the process of taking them overseas simpler.
In July, Guangxi Publishing & Media Group launched FLYTOTO, an AI-powered platform for short-drama co-creation. The platform connects Chinese production teams and creators with audiovisual institutions in Southeast Asia. FLYTOTO offers tools for script analysis, automated video production, and multilingual translation, alongside computing and distribution support. The platform was launched alongside the 2026 China-ASEAN Micro-Drama Competition, which includes both live-action and AI-generated micro-dramas.
For China, the cultural industry is moving beyond the export of finished content to the systems that allow content to be produced, adapted, and distributed across markets.
This shift did not begin with AI micro-dramas, although they provide the latest examples. China Literature, one of China’s largest online publishing companies, launched its international Webnovel platform in 2017, initially bringing Chinese online fiction to readers abroad through translated works. Webnovel has since expanded beyond translation. The platform now hosts original fiction by writers outside China, while providing the translation, publishing, and monetization systems around their work. By the end of 2025, China Literature said Webnovel had 537,000 international writers and 830,000 original works from overseas.
The goal is no longer only to find foreign readers for Chinese stories. Platforms can also provide the tools, business models, and distribution channels through which stories reach international audiences. As these platforms expand, the distinction between exporting Chinese culture and producing culture for foreign markets becomes less clear. A Chinese company can operate the platform and provide the infrastructure while the content itself is increasingly created by writers and producers outside China.
A recent analysis by researchers at the London School of Economics argued that Chinese micro-drama platforms can exercise what they call “platform soft power.” The platforms themselves increasingly exert an invisible influence, as recommendation systems, data, monetization, and user participation shape what audiences see and engage with. Lingang’s new AI+micro-drama overseas service station and FLYTOTO in Guangxi suggest that this trend will only strengthen. The infrastructure behind cultural exports is becoming part of China’s export strategy itself.
To be sure, there’s no guarantee this will result in greater Chinese cultural influence. Companies have strong commercial reasons to build production and distribution networks abroad, and adapting content to local audiences can make its Chinese origins less visible. A Chinese company can provide the platform, technology, and investment without the resulting content saying much about China at all. But it does change what Chinese companies are capable of doing in foreign markets. They are gaining infrastructure and local connections that allow them to produce and distribute cultural content across borders.
China’s cultural industries have spent years learning how to reach audiences beyond the country’s borders. From online literature to micro-dramas, Chinese companies are building platforms, translation systems, production tools, and overseas partnerships that can be used across markets. The payoff is more than an overseas audience. It is the ability to produce, adapt, and distribute cultural content across markets without treating each market as a separate export project.

Mark Carney calls for ‘deep cooperation’ between Canada and EU in Strasbourg speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:15:56 UTC
21:15:56 KST

Mark Carney has welcomed the goal of Canada becoming the EU’s first associate member, calling for “deep cooperation” between Europe and his country to secure their sovereignty, after Donald Trump derided the idea as “laughable”.
In an address to the European parliament in Strasbourg, the Canadian prime minister said polling showed that an overwhelming majority of Canadians supported much closer ties with Europe. “Canada welcomes this idea,” he said, referring to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s pitch that Canada should become the EU’s first associate member.
“Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities,” Carney said on Thursday, listing sectors including critical minerals, energy security and AI.
Von der Leyen had on Wednesday invited Canada to become the EU’s first associate member in a speech in which she declared she wanted to bring the bilateral relationship “to the highest level possible”. A few hours later, Trump threatened “very serious tariffs” on Europe if the plan went ahead.
Asked about Trump’s threats, Carney told reporters: “Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak. No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally.”
The EU and Canada, which already have a web of bilateral trade and sectoral agreements, have sought to move closer in recent months in the face of Trump’s trade tariffs and relentless belligerent rhetoric.
Carney received a standing ovation from MEPs in Strasbourg, who waited to shake his hand and get a selfie with him. European lawmakers from pro-EU mainstream parties have already praised Carney’s January speech in Davos, in which he called for middle powers to work together to preserve their sovereignty in a world of great power rivalry where the strong accept no constraints.
Carney reprised the theme in Strasbourg, saying: “Canada and Europe are each strong. Europe and Canada are stronger together … The objective is not self-sufficiency, it’s collective resilience.”
He went on to say: “I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival, only with better manners,” saying an EU-Canada alliance would be a “beacon for other democracies”.
In a speech frequently interrupted by rounds of applause, Carney detailed his plans for the future relationship, saying the two sides could cooperate on critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and computing, energy security, space and payments. He also called for “seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services”.
He proposed a youth exchange programme that would enable young people to work, study and live in both jurisdictions, as well as Canadian membership of the Erasmus+ scheme, the EU’s education, training and sport programme.
No country has ever been offered associate membership before, a category that does not exist in the EU’s treaties. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, floated the idea of associate membership for Ukraine as an interim step to joining the bloc earlier this year, but the idea was rejected by other member states.
EU member states support the idea of closer ties with Canada, but some have reacted coolly to the name “associate membership”.
Asked by a Bloomberg reporter about the concept he preferred, Carney said: “The precise nomenclature for Europe is a question for Europe,” adding that leaders and lawmakers involved “take the view [that] what matters is the substance”.
He also said Canada was “not in a position, nor seeking to become, a full member of the European Union” and that the Canadian parliament would debate and vote on the future relationship.
Speaking before Carney’s address, Trump warned that if the EU moved forward with the plan, Washington could impose “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”
Responding to Trump’s overnight comments, Carney said the deepening of the EU-Canada relationship was “a positive initiative” and “not a reaction to something else”.

CANBERRA, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Australia's population grew 1.4 percent in the 12 months to March 2026, reaching 27.9 million, according to figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) on Thursday.
The population increased by 392,700 people from the same time a year earlier, ABS Head of Population Statistics Bjorn Jarvis said in a statement.
Natural increase, the number of births minus deaths, added 100,600 people to the population during the period. Births increased 0.3 percent, while deaths rose 3.1 percent, according to the ABS.
Net overseas migration added a further 292,100 people between March 2025 and March 2026, down from 309,500 in the previous 12-month period, statistics showed.
Western Australia recorded the fastest population growth among Australia's states and territories, with its population increasing 2.1 percent over the year, followed by the state of Victoria at 1.6 percent, the ABS reported.
The island state of Tasmania recorded the slowest growth, with its population rising 0.6 percent over the same period, it said. ■

Feature: Chinese Culture Day brings China closer to Australian students
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:14:55 CST
21:14:55 KST

Members of an arts troupe from southwest China's Sichuan Province perform during a Chinese Culture Day event at Geelong College in Australia, Sept. 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Xu Haijing)
GEELONG, Australia, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- During the lunch break on Wednesday at Geelong College, about an hour's drive southwest of Melbourne, several girls dressed in traditional Chinese attire walked across the historic campus, while students gathered inside Morrison Hall to try their hand at Chinese calligraphy, paper lantern-making and traditional bead crafts.
By around 2 p.m., the hall was filling up. As the girls in traditional Chinese dress took to the stage, a Chinese Culture Day performance organized by the Chinese Consulate-General in Melbourne got underway.
Three performers dressed as Daomadan, or female warrior characters in traditional Chinese opera, brandished long spears across the stage. A performer used her hands to create lively animal silhouettes on a screen, while another wielded a long-spouted brass teapot, combining tea pouring with martial arts-inspired movements.
The performance, presented by an arts troupe from southwest China's Sichuan Province, drew cheers and applause from the students.
"I really love the tea dance. It was very cool. I thought the blend of martial arts and dancing was amazing," student Ivy Grey told Xinhua.
Grey, who has never been to China, said the performance had made her even more eager to visit the country.
"After seeing this, I might be booking my flights tonight," she said with a laugh.
Founded in 1861, Geelong College has longstanding ties with China. It is the alma mater of George Ernest Morrison, an Australian journalist and scholar who had served as The Times' correspondent in Beijing.
That connection continues in new ways today.
Shen Feng, a Chinese teacher at Geelong College, said Chinese is taught to all students in the school's primary years, while older students can continue studying it as an elective subject through Year 12.
Every two years, Shen takes a group of students to China, with the trips drawing strong interest among students.
"When they come back, their attitude toward learning Chinese in the classroom changes completely," Shen said. "They know who speaks the language and what the country is really like."
Experiencing China's vastness, long history and diverse cities firsthand helps students see that learning Chinese can open up more opportunities for their future, she added.
Year 11 student Ava Hallebone, one of the hosts of the event, visited China in April this year.
Hallebone, who has been studying Chinese for four years, also represented her school in this year's Victorian division of the "Chinese Bridge" Chinese proficiency competition for secondary school students, finishing among the top five contestants in the state.
She said learning Chinese could be challenging at times, particularly because of the tones and characters, but that it had also brought her many opportunities.
"Chinese culture, I think, is very inclusive," she said, adding that she hopes to continue studying the language after graduation.
Hallebone said she wants to become a doctor and believes knowing another language could also prove useful in her future career.
Geelong College Principal Simon Young said the event gave students an opportunity to engage with Chinese culture firsthand.
"Events like today allow us to discover what makes our cultures distinctive, while also recognizing the values that we share -- friendship, family, creativity, respect and a desire to learn from one another," Young said.
Young said the college was proud to see "a new generation of students continuing to build bridges of understanding, friendship and cultural exchange."
Chinese Consul-General in Melbourne Fang Xinwen said culture is key to deepening mutual understanding, while language serves as a bridge connecting people's hearts.
In recent years, more young Australians have begun learning Chinese and exploring Chinese culture, gaining a fuller and more vivid understanding of China through the language, Fang said.
Seeing so many students actively participating in Chinese cultural activities and exchanges gave him greater confidence in the future of China-Australia friendship, he added. ■

Around 40 ancient and early Christian mosaics are presented by Associate Professor Katya Lekova in her latest, sixth exhibition of paintings on glass. Her entire professional career was spent teaching organic chemistry at South-West University Neofit Rilski, but she now devotes herself to her greatest hobby – searching for stone mosaics and transferring their rich palette of colours and forms onto glass. She has visited many museums around the world and seen the mosaics displayed in Sicily and Rome, but says that Bulgaria, too, has much to be proud of, and mosaics are part of that heritage. They can be found in the Small and Great Basilicas in Plovdiv, while beautiful examples have also been discovered at the ancient Villa Armira near Ivaylovgrad. There is even an entire museum devoted to mosaics in the town of Devnya, which Lekova has also visited.
A wealth of mosaics has been uncovered during excavations of ancient Serdica. One early Christian example particularly caught Katya Lekova’s attention, and she has recreated it in her exhibition. It is the mosaic known as Paradise – one of the most remarkable examples of mosaic art from Late Antiquity. The mosaic dates from the 3rd century and comes from the apse of the basilica beneath today’s St Sophia Church in the capital.
PHOTO katyalekova.com
It is made of stone and smalt tesserae – small pieces of stone and coloured glass carefully selected for their shapes and colours. At the centre of the composition is a large palm branch flanked by two doves. Below are two baskets filled with plants, with two more doves pecking at them. On either side stand two cypress trees entwined with vines. For early Christians, all this symbolised Paradise, with the doves representing the souls of the faithful.
Today, the stone mosaic Paradise belongs to the National Archaeological Institute with Museum at the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences. Its discovery and preservation date back to the early years of archaeology in the young Bulgarian state. Associate Professor Katya Lekova tells the story of the Czech scholar behind the find:
PHOTO Gergana Mancheva
“Václav Dobruský (1858–1916) was a Czech archaeologist who came to Bulgaria after graduating from the Faculty of Philosophy at Charles University in Prague. This was shortly after the Liberation. He first took up teaching and spent ten years teaching Latin at the high school in Plovdiv, and later in Sofia. He subsequently began lecturing at Sofia University, where for 20 years he taught various subjects – ancient archaeology, Thracology and numismatics.
“He was an erudite man who gave a great deal to Bulgaria. Alongside his teaching, Václav Dobruský took part in numerous excavations throughout the country. You may sometimes see him described as a Bulgarian archaeologist of Czech origin. But in fact, he was a Czech who spent most of his life in Bulgaria. Sadly, he died at just 58, but he gave 30 years of his active life to Bulgaria.
“In 1893, it was Dobruský who discovered the Paradise mosaic.
PHOTO Gergana Mancheva
“Something else that is not widely known is that he was the first director of what was then called the National Museum, which later became today’s National Archaeological Institute with Museum at the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences – or, as we know it, the Archaeological Museum in Sofia. Václav Dobruský himself opened the museum in 1905 in the presence of Prince Ferdinand.”
Lekova’s exhibition also includes several innovative digital works. Using three-dimensional imagery, she recreates mosaics that have been destroyed and cannot be restored, but whose appearance and place of discovery are known from surviving records.
Paradise, found beneath St Sophia Church, is a very different case. Exceptionally well preserved, it was the first mosaic in Bulgaria to be lifted and moved from its original location. Restored and preserved in its authentic form, it can now be seen at the National Archaeological Museum. Other mosaics from the same period are in poorer condition, and restorers have chosen to leave them where they were discovered.
Lekova sees Paradise as distinctive both in its style and in the world it depicts:
“This mosaic is quite different from the examples typical of our region. It is more restrained and focuses on the early Christians’ idea of the heavenly world. There are two trees, vines winding around them, and birds. Two of the birds are drinking from a special vessel of the kind used in ancient times for wine and water. Here, a palm branch has been placed in the vessel. All of this expresses the elation of the early Christians and the way they imagined the heavenly world. There was a sense of great excitement because Christianity had by then been recognised as a religion. Before that, Christians had been persecuted and Christianity regarded almost as a heresy. Many people had lost their lives for spreading the Christian faith. This is precisely what the mosaic depicts – the triumph of Christianity and its establishment as a major religion.”
PHOTO Czech Center Sofia
For Lekova, the mosaics also testify to the skill of the craftsmen who created them. They knew how to achieve proportion, beauty and durability with tiny pieces of coloured stone.
“The fact that we find mosaics in so many places in Serdica, left literally beneath our feet, should make us proud to be heirs to a city inhabited by people of great spiritual refinement, who looked to the future and left us their legacy through these mosaics,” she says.
“And the fact that some of the finest and most talented mosaic craftsmen worked here is another piece of history that continues to inspire specialists, scholars and anyone fascinated by the stories of the ancient city.”
Editor: D. Semkovska

A lifeboat station on the south coast of England near the spot where far-right activists tried to stop asylum seekers landing has been forced to temporarily close, it has emerged.
The station in Portsmouth shut after it and other sites run by the RNLI were targeted by people objecting to the lifeboat charity going to the aid of people trying to get to the UK on small boats.
Jacqui Irons, the head of the south-east region of the RNL, said: “Portsmouth lifeboat station has been temporarily off-service since 7 September. We have a duty of care to our people. We therefore took the decision to pause activity at the station to review crew safety and wellbeing, and to support those involved in the incident on 6 September.”
The charity said it did not mean there had been a lack of cover around Portsmouth, one of the busiest maritime areas in the UK.
An RNLI spokesperson said: “Search and rescue cover continues to be provided through established contingency arrangements, including flank RNLI stations and other declared assets.
“At times, it is not unusual for lifeboat stations around the UK and Ireland to be temporarily unavailable due to maintenance or other operational requirements.
“In such circumstances, established contingency arrangements are put in place to ensure continued search and rescue cover.”
On Sunday 6 September two RNLI crews helped bring a dinghy carrying 120 asylum seekers to Eastney in Portsmouth, a few hundred metres from the lifeboat station.
Far-right activists were among those who tried to blockade the road leading to the landing spot, and police officers were injured.
In the days after, lifeboat crew members were called traitors and protests took place against the charity, including at the RNLI headquarters in nearby Poole.
A museum in Poole telling the story of the RNLI also closed temporarily, and Portsmouth lifeboat station took down its Facebook page.
RNLI volunteers across the UK were told that they should consider not wearing RNLI branded clothing if they felt this could put them at risk. They have also been advised that they should feel empowered to close shops or lifeboat stations if they feel in danger.
The RNLI has defended its work in the Channel, saying that for more than 200 years it rescued people without judgment, fear or favour. It said rumours that the RNLI housed asylum seekers on its premises, or that there were RNLI missions to move migrants to secret locations, were “completely baseless and untrue”.
The charity said RNLI lifeboats launched 9,058 times in 2025 but that only 109 of those callouts were to small boats in the Channel, representing 1.2% of its rescue work.
Separately, the first person to be arrested over the protest at Eastney has appeared in court.
Del Somerville, 42, from Portsmouth, admitted violent disorder. He has also been charged with assaulting a police officer but did not enter a plea to that allegation.
Philip Allman, prosecuting, asked for an adjournment so that a community impact statement could be prepared. The defendant was remanded in custody.
