Klopp wants Germany football team to 'reclaim the flag'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:41:00 UTC
20:41:00 KST

Klopp wants Germany football team to 'reclaim the flag'
September 17, 2026
Jürgen Klopp used his first squad announcement as Germany's new head coach to deliver a stirring speech in favor of what he described as "positive patriotism."
"I'd like to reclaim the flag for myself — or for us," Klopp said.
"I want us to always wave it in a way that makes no one think: 'What's wrong with you?'" he said. "But, rather, that people simply get the feeling that you're happy and understand how lucky you are to have been born, raised or moved to this wonderful country."
This was an apparent reference to the recent state election in Saxony-Anhalt, which the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won in a landslide victory.
Klopp said of the election "that some people probably thought it was OK, while many others thought: 'Good heavens, what's going on there?"
The former Borussia Dortmund and Liverpool head coach was quick to say he is not a political expert and that he doesn't want to talk about politics at every press conference, but that he doesn't want to "leave national pride to the wrong people."
Rather than leaving that up to misinterpretation, something Klopp said was possible, he turned toward the concept of "positive patriotism."
"I can be proud to be German and still be open-minded, diverse, kind and friendly," he said. "I actually think we're a wonderful country."
The 59-year-old added that, just as he had selected the current squad by looking at what the country had to offer in terms of football talent rather than what it was lacking, it might help to do the same when looking at the country as a whole.
This echoed a similar sentiment of former Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann, who spoke emotionally after Germany's Euro 2024 exit.
"Being together must become more important again. We must not be consumed with envy, always paint everything in a negative light and not begrudge our neighbors anything," Nagelsmann said.
"I believe that if everyone starts within their own small circle — on their street, helping their neighbors when something comes up [...] [we can] support one another, integrate everyone, welcome them, and help them feel at home, and bring people together to work with us toward a better future."
Klopp highlights power of football
Klopp was quick to turn to the power of football, while also recognizing its place in wider society.
"It's more important that we have doctors. It's more important that we have nurses. It's more important that we have a great, great many people in a wide variety of professions," he said, before adding that football can "foster a sense of community that lets us truly feel the power of sports."
Klopp cited the recent successes of Alexander Zverev, the world champion field hockey team, the home World Cup in women's basketball and the success of athletes at this summer's European Athletics Championships as further positive examples of the power of sport.
"That's our mission. We have to create the right atmosphere — I know that. But to do that, we need people who are willing to embrace it," he said.
Master class in communication
Klopp's delivery was a textbook example of how to create alignment across his messaging. His squad, made up of 44 players including 11 new faces, is a reflection of the diverse society that Klopp proudly referenced.
His engagement with the media was also strategically smart. After laying down clear boundaries in his first press conference that included him saying he would quit if coverage strayed into the personal, Klopp this time opted to seek to include the media as part of the process while also subtly reminding them of what he sees as their role.
When explaining his choice to name such a large squad with so many new and young players, Klopp said he wasn't going to tell members of the media how to do their job when it comes to assessing players, but said that he knew how he would do it. In between the lines, this was an indirect appeal to the media to choose coverage that would foster the development of this new era of players rather than hinder it by being overly critical or negative.
On top of that, Klopp did all of this while wearing a baseball cap with the words "one of 83 million" written on the front. This is in reference to a Germany's approximate population and an expression about how everyone has an opinion on the Germany team and so is therefore a "Bundestrainer" (national team coach). It also came across as an attempt to assign a shared responsibility for the team's success.
Germany's Euro 2024 campaign briefly instilled some pride over the flag again, as did Germany's women in the Euro 2022 final. The most impactful though, was the 2006 World Cup in Germany, which provided the biggest positive cultural shift in the general German attitude toward national pride since World War II.
Now, through the vehicle of football, Germany's new head coach has declared a desire to restore that pride. Klopp said his whole career had brought him to this moment.
After these words, it felt like all the disappointments the Germany team — and their fans — have endured over the last few years may also have brought them to the right leader.

German court holds Meta liable for 'fraudulent' ads on Facebook, Instagram
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:38:14 UTC
20:38:14 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
A German court has ruled that US technology company Meta can be held legally liable for "fraudulent" advertisements published by third parties on Facebook and Instagram.
The Frankfurt Regional Court said Thursday that Meta must stop the publication and distribution of fake advertisements that unlawfully used the logo of a financial information portal and the name and images of its well-known founder.
The case was brought by a company operating an online portal offering comparison calculators, product reviews and consumer guidance on financial products, as well as its founder and managing director.
The portal has more than 600,000 followers on Instagram and around 29,000 on Facebook.
According to the court, unidentified users used the company’s registered logo and images of its founder to promote purported financial investments, directing users to external links in what appeared to be fraudulent schemes.
Several affected users subsequently contacted the plaintiffs.
The company reported nearly 260 violations to Meta in August 2024 alone, but identical or substantially similar advertisements continued to appear. Meta took up to 62 days to remove some of the content.
The court found that the advertisements seriously infringed the company’s corporate personality rights and the founder’s personal rights.
Meta exercises control through algorithms
The court rejected Meta’s argument that it could avoid liability under the EU’s Digital Services Act because it had no prior knowledge of the fraudulent content.
Referring to a recent ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union, the judges said liability protections do not apply in the same way when a service provider exercises control over displayed content.
Meta determines the ranking and timing of advertisements through an automated auction process and controls the distribution of content in users’ feeds through algorithms, the court said.
Unlike platforms that offer purely chronological feeds, Meta therefore exercises control over the advertising content shown to users, it added.
The court ordered Meta to compensate the plaintiffs for future damages arising from the distribution of identical or similar fraudulent advertisements.
The company must also provide information about the advertisements and disclose the revenue it generated from them.

Although Salam opened and closed the session by discussing his government’s commitment to financial and economic reform, asserting a state monopoly on weapons, the 2027 budget, reconstruction in southern Lebanon, and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the country, only the latter seemed to prompt heated outbursts and personal insults on the floor.

Its losing wars have led to occupation. Hezbollah’s refusal to disarm weakens the state in the face of Israel.”
MP Ziad Hawat also accused Hezbollah of bringing the IDF back into the country, an accusation that was interrupted by Hezbollah MP Hussein Jachi, who shouted, “Some of our colleagues think Israel is not an enemy.”
Hezbollah continued to receive criticism from other lawmakers throughout the session. Hours after the initial confrontation, Tripoli-born Sunni MP Achraf Rifi and Hezbollah lawmakers argued over the position of Syrian refugees in Lebanon and Hezbollah’s involvement in the civil war.
Hezbollah refuses to disarm, cede land to government forces
Independent Beirut MP Paula Yakoubian also questioned why Hezbollah had not handed over areas of southern Lebanon without an Israeli presence to the LAF.
“Why doesn’t Hezbollah hand over a map of its weapons to Lebanese negotiators so that they can secure an Israeli withdrawal and the return of displaced people?” she asked.
Independent Beirut MP Ibrahim Mneimné said: “We hear criticism of Hezbollah, but after everything that has happened, they must acknowledge their responsibility.”
Lt.-Col. (res.) Sarit Zehavi, founder and president of the Alma Research and Education Center, told The Jerusalem Post the developments and widespread condemnations of Hezbollah in the Lebanese Parliament were not a surprise, especially given the widening rift between the pro- and anti-Hezbollah camps in Lebanon.
While the recent vote and comments made during the session were important demonstrations of the attitudes held in Beirut, they did not change the fact that the Lebanese government had failed to take meaningful action to disarm Hezbollah and establish a monopoly over its weapons, she said.

'Yemen was already suffering', NGOs tell TNA as crisis deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:36:21 UTC
20:36:21 KST

Breadcrumb
'Yemen has already been suffering': aid groups tell TNA renewed war will deepen crisis
Yemen's renewed fighting is deepening an already desperate humanitarian crisis, aid groups have warned The New Arab, as clashes across the country displace tens of thousands of people and international funding cuts leave relief organisations struggling to respond.
Heavy fighting broke out across Yemen on 3 September after Ansar Allah, commonly known as the Houthis, launched an offensive to seize the country's Red Sea coast from the UN-recognised government, triggering battles around Taiz and Marib.
Khanzad Shah, Islamic Relief's acting country director for Yemen, told The New Arab that the organisation was "extremely worried that this new escalation will now make the humanitarian crisis here even worse, and make it even harder for families to get food and healthcare".
"The crisis in Yemen has largely been forgotten by the world, and this is a wake-up call that the people of Yemen are still suffering," he added.
Aid groups have been forced to navigate shifting frontlines and a precarious security situation while responding to a crisis already strained by deep cuts to international assistance.
Frontlines reignite: The Fall of Mokha
On 3 September, Yemen's frontlines, dormant for four years, reignited after the Houthis launched an offensive in Taiz governorate aimed at capturing the Red Sea port city of Mokha.
After around a week of back-and-forth fighting, the Houthis made a rapid advance along the coast on 10 September, capturing Mokha and later reaching the outskirts of Lahj province.
As the fighting raged, civilians fled south, Shah told The New Arab.
"People are moving from around Taiz to Lahj and then onto Aden to try and find safety and support," he said.
"Many of these families don't have enough food or water as they had to flee with whatever they could carry. In some areas, whole villages have reportedly emptied."
According to the UN refugee agency UNHCR, around 100,000 people have been displaced by the fighting across the country, with 2,400 crossing the Red Sea to Djibouti.
The agency told The New Arab that 63% of all newly displaced households originate from Taiz, while refugees displaced to Djibouti are being registered in Markazi refugee camp.
The fall of Mokha shocked the UN-recognised government because of the speed with which the city and surrounding coastline were captured. Fighting is expected to continue after the government declared a "kill box" in the area and, backed by the Saudi Air Force, launched strikes on Houthi targets.
The capture of the coast has also raised international concern over the potential impact on global shipping and energy markets following major disruption around the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Iran war and previous Houthi attacks on shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb since the start of Israel's war on Gaza.
For MSF, however, the fall of Mokha has prompted more immediate concerns over the city's civilians and the safety of its team operating at Mokha General Hospital.
In a statement released on Friday, MSF's Yemen country coordinator, Lou Cormack, said the Houthi takeover of the city "has had a major impact on both medical activities and the needs of the population in recent days".
"The rapid advance of Ansar Allah [Houthi] forces has fundamentally changed the situation," she said, forcing MSF to alter plans to reopen a former field hospital in Mokha, provide water to displaced people and establish cholera isolation and treatment units in Mokha and Khawkah to the north.
Instead, MSF has focused on keeping Mokha General Hospital operating after Yemeni healthcare workers fled alongside civilians. Only 30 healthcare workers remain at the hospital, providing minimum services.
"Almost all other healthcare facilities in the city have stopped functioning, largely because their staff had left," Cormack said, adding that bombardments were continuing and that MSF would remain to provide healthcare to civilians amid uncertainty over what comes next.
Mobilising a response despite fighting and funding cuts
Alongside the fighting on the coast, the International Rescue Committee told The New Arab that the conflict had rapidly spread across the country.
"Frontlines have reopened across five governorates in a matter of days, key roads have been cut, and many families are once again being displaced into areas with little capacity to receive them," Carol Sekyewa, the IRC's Yemen country director, said.
Sekyewa said 18 million people across Yemen were already facing acute hunger before the latest escalation and warned that disruptions to essential supplies or restrictions on access could have catastrophic consequences.
"The IRC is continuing to provide vital, life-saving health and protection services, but every road that closes makes it harder for people to reach treatment and for humanitarian organisations to deliver assistance."
Fighting is also raging around the hills and peaks surrounding the partially besieged city of Taiz, the capital of the governorate where Mokha is located. The Norwegian Refugee Council is mobilising there to assist newly displaced people.
"Several families who were already in displacement and were residing [in] displacement sites that are in frontline areas in Taiz have fled to new locations," Alison Bottomley, an advocacy adviser with the NRC based in Yemen, told The New Arab.
"NRC is responding to the emergency needs of these displaced families in their new locations," she added, noting that people need shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene, with many having fled in the middle of the night.
"We met families who told us they had to leave home at three o'clock in the morning before walking 15 kilometres to find safety."
Bottomley said that despite the four-year ceasefire that paused much of the fighting, Yemen remained in the grip of a humanitarian crisis, particularly after deep cuts to international aid programmes at the beginning of US President Donald Trump's second term.
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development estimates that aid spending from Development Assistance Committee countries fell 23.1% in 2025 from 2024 levels, with a further 5.8% decline projected for 2026.
The funding cuts have affected the NRC's ability to respond. Bottomley told The New Arab that "the number of stock and emergency resources is limited, with overall humanitarian response deeply underfunded".
This includes Houthi-controlled northern Yemen, which accounts for 70% of the population, where funding reductions have led to cuts in food, nutrition and health services.
"It is critical that there is a commitment to support vulnerable people in Yemen," Bottomley added.
The UNHCR told The New Arab that alongside limited stockpiles, the fighting is "raising broader concerns over humanitarian logistics" as potential closure of the Bab al-Mandeb could affect humanitarian and commercial shipping serving Yemen, Sudan, and other operations in the region.
Oxfam has also had to scale back operations around Taiz. Fatma Jaffar, the organisation's advocacy media manager in Aden, told The New Arab that it had been forced to shut down one intervention in the area, where it helped run a community centre with a local partner.
Jaffar said Oxfam was continuing to provide services in other parts of Taiz, "but still we're in a kind of emergency, like we're anticipating something to happen, and of course taking into consideration our staff and operations and the safety of them".
"Until now, we're not seeing massive access issues," she said, adding that the organisation was coordinating with authorities in both the north and south. However, "the security situation is what's stopping us from intervening in certain areas when we're trying to gather content, when we're trying to gather data around impacts".
"It's very sad as a Yemeni to see all of these people fighting, and unfortunately the victims are the civilians in the middle of the chaos."
Oxfam, which has operated in Yemen since 1982 when the country was still divided between north and south, has increasingly shifted from civil society and governance projects towards humanitarian and resilience work since the civil war erupted in 2014.
The breakdown of the relative calm brought by the four-year ceasefire has again disrupted the organisation's humanitarian work, with Oxfam now focusing on supporting internally displaced people across the country. Jaffar said there were two million displaced people around Marib alone, where Oxfam has an office, as well as in Taiz.
"For us right now, the priority is to respond to the IDPs that we're seeing in the districts that we're intervening in and trying our best to mobilise sufficient resources," Jaffar said, adding that the organisation was struggling with funding but stepping up advocacy efforts to secure more.
"Yemen has already been suffering a decade-long conflict, so being dragged further into this conflict only puts us at risk," she said.
"My only hope is that it doesn't escalate further, and we see all of the conflict parties reaching an agreement."

Possible U.S. war crimes in Iran cited by U.N.-backed experts

U.N.-backed experts allege U.S. war crimes in Iran
Geneva — Human rights experts commissioned by the United Nation's top human rights body say they have found "reasonable grounds" to believe the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including on a school in the southern city of Minab.
The international fact-finding mission on Iran says the findings center on a pair of airstrikes that killed scores of civilians, including women and children.
A preliminary U.S. assessment suggested that the United States was "likely" responsible for the deadly February attack on the school but did not intentionally target it and may have hit it in error, possibly due to the use of dated intelligence that wrongly identified the area as still part of an Iranian military installation, a person briefed on the preliminary intelligence told CBS News.
The Trump administration has not directly accepted responsibility or released findings of a Pentagon investigation into the attack on the school on the war's first day, using Tomahawk missiles.
Iranian health officials and state media said about 170 people were killed, most of them schoolgirls between the ages of 7 and 12.
"Following the United States and Israeli attacks on 28 February, the mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects," the fact-finding team said in a statement. It said the school in Minab was "clearly identifiable."
The U.N.-backed team also alleged the U.S. had committed war crimes in relation to a missile strike that dispersed tungsten pellets over a "clearly identifiable sports complex and residential area" in the southern city of Lamerd, also on Feb. 28.
The U.N.-backed team said 22 civilian men and women were killed. U.S. Central Command has denied responsibility for the strike on Lamerd.
The team also said Iran's state security forces had committed killings on a "staggering scale," referring to a January crackdown on nationwide anti-government protests, and alleged that their actions amounted to "crimes against humanity."
It said civilians were caught between "gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's deadly conflict with the United States and Israel."
The fact-finding mission on Iran, chaired by jurist Sara Hossain of Bangladesh, is made up of independent experts and was created in 2022 by the Human Rights Council, the U.N.'s top human rights body.

“I am here to advocate for the incorporation of Judeo-Christian history and values within our standards,” she told the board. “It was upon Judeo-Christian values that this great nation was built.”
The curriculum overhaul drew opposition from Muslim advocates. In a separate statement Wednesday, CAIR’s Austin office called for the board to reconsider the standards, arguing that their treatment of Islam would encourage prejudice against Muslim students.
PJTN projected that the Texas changes could eventually influence instruction for as many as 25 million students nationwide, citing the state’s influence on educational materials. The statement provided no calculation or supporting evidence for that estimate.
Cardoza-Moore traced her textbook advocacy to 2012, when she challenged a passage in a Pearson human geography textbook used in Tennessee that she said legitimized the 2001 Hamas suicide bombing at Jerusalem’s Sbarro restaurant. PJTN said the disputed reference was subsequently removed.
“Students cannot fully understand America if they do not know and understand the laws, history, ideas, and traditions which shaped America,” she told the Texas board.

MOSCOW, September 17. /TASS/. Testing of a new antenna complex for superlong-range communication will take place in the Donbass region, the Center for Unmanned Systems and Technologies (CUST) told TASS.
"Participants in the CUST resident Antelekon project are continuing to test a new antenna complex based on the series AN5200-5800Sh17 helical broadband directional antenna. These tests will be conducted in the Donbass region in the near future. Previous tests took place in urban areas, at the BARS-Sarmat special-purpose training ground, and directly in combat conditions. Military personnel highly praised the antenna for its ease of use, reliability, signal quality, and communication range," the company stated.
The AN5200-5800Sh17 series antennas are designed for use in ground-based control stations, electronic warfare systems, mobile command posts, repeaters, radio links, monitoring and video surveillance systems, and other equipment. The "dish" in the CUST resident’s antenna system significantly increases the communication range. The estimated range of the equipment in the gigahertz frequency band can reach 130 km. The antenna system has a low voltage standing-wave rate and low radar visibility," the CUST added.
The system also extends the operational range of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). "As the developer notes, the technical solutions implemented in the product ensure stable video communication during sharp drone maneuvers (somersaults, rolls, barrel rolls). In addition, this Antelecon innovation makes it possible to extend the operational range of Russian UAVs and the distance at which enemy drones can be detected and countered," the company noted.

Left-wing Zionists must understand what should be an axiom in an updated “Ethics of the Zionists”: Who is wise? Anyone who appreciates genuine friends while recognizing evil enemies. And who is not so wise? Anyone who cannot see how faux friends embolden our jihadist enemies.

EU plans social media ban for children under 13
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:34:00 UTC
20:34:00 KST

The European Commission on Thursday adopted the EU KIDS Act to restrict social media access for children under 13 and set an EU-wide minimum age of 15 for minors to open their own accounts.
“The proposal prohibits social media platforms from accessing children under the age of 13 and sets an EU-wide minimum age for minors to open an account of their own at the age of 15,” a written statement noted.
The act proposes that children can create personal social media accounts only from the age of 15, while allowing parents or guardians of children aged 13 and 14 to set up “mini accounts” that the children can access through their guardians’ accounts.
“This would allow them to access age-appropriate social media and video-sharing platforms,” the statement added.
The proposal also stressed the need for services available through the mini accounts to be designed with safeguards, “such as limited social contacts and limited screen time up to one hour per day”.
While prohibiting access to social media for children aged between three and 13, it allows access to “specially designed child-friendly video-sharing services” through accounts managed by their guardians.
Platforms would also be required to provide parents or guardians with easy-to-use tools to limit children’s access on adult devices to child-friendly services and cap their use at one hour per day.
The act also imposes obligations on online services, including social media, video-sharing platforms, online games, AI companions and chatbots, to protect users under 18.
It aims to ban addictive features and profiling-based recommender feeds that drag minors into “rabbit holes” of harmful content. It also seeks to prohibit infinite scrolling, reward tricks, night-time push notifications and unsolicited contact from strangers.
“In addition, AI companions and chatbots must be turned off by default and cannot simulate interpersonal relationships in ways that create emotional dependency,” the statement further underscored.
Minors’ profiles would be private by default, with geolocation, camera and microphone access disabled.
Platforms are also called on to offer easy ways for minors to block and mute users, effective time-management tools and safe recommender systems.
Online services and app stores will also be required to use age-assurance tools, while the Commission offered the use of an EU age-verification app “which does not retain identity documents or biometric data, thereby meeting the highest privacy-preserving safeguards”.
“The proposal reverses the ‘burden of proof’, making the providers of very large online platforms responsible for proving that their services are ‘safe by design’,” the statement added.
The platforms will therefore be obliged to submit a compliance plan to the Commission and an independent auditor, who must thoroughly assess the new service, feature or functionality.
‘It is time for EU to act’
Speaking at a news briefing on the act, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pointed out that too many children are exposed too early to an online world “they are not ready to navigate”.
“Today, our children are engaging with some of the most sophisticated technology ever created, and it was not created with children’s well-being and development in mind. Platforms are designed to capture attention,” she noted.
She described such addictive features as part of business models designed to keep children online and monetise their attention.
“Parents cannot compete or keep up against algorithms, and they should not have to. (...) It is time for the European Union to act,” von der Leyen underscored.
She further cautioned that the proposed age limits would not let tech companies “off the hook” for their platforms’ content.
“Platforms have been playing fast and loose with our children’s mental health. Now we are reversing the burden of proof. Now they have to prove to us that they are safe,” von der Leyen said.
She reaffirmed that the EU is changing the years-long practice of platforms denying the harm they cause and trying to avoid prescriptive rules while setting their own rules at their own pace.
“So instead of authorities proving harm after the fact, the biggest platforms must submit detailed child safety plans in advance, and that means again that safety will come first,” von der Leyen added.
She noted that the act “puts the parents in the driving seat, and the burden of proving safety on the platforms where it belongs”.

Bell Chung rings changes for future of Taiwanese language
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:33:18 UTC
20:33:18 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — When singer Bell Chung's (鐘綺) 6-year-old nephew sings along to her music, she catches a glimpse of what the Taiwanese language could sound like in the next generation.
Her approach is somewhat counterintuitive: If Taiwanese is to stay alive, she believes it cannot remain frozen in the past. Instead, it needs to sound contemporary enough for a new generation to hear it as part of their own lives.
For Bell, that means challenging some of the conventions that have long shaped Taiwanese-language music, from how melodies follow the tones of the language to the words and themes used in songs.
Taiwanese has long been closely associated with nostalgia and older generations. This has left some people with the impression that it is something their grandparents listen to rather than a language that belongs to them.
“If you really want Taiwanese music to grow, or if you really want the world to recognize it, I really think we should step out of that circle and box,” Bell told Taiwan News.
One of the challenges Bell sees is the expectation that Taiwanese melodies should follow the tones of the spoken language, a convention known as “tau-im” (倒音). She deliberately does not always follow the rule.
For her, the question is not whether the language itself can work in contemporary music. Taiwanese, she said, is “beautiful” and offers plenty of possibilities for artistic expression. The bigger obstacle is the expectation of what Taiwanese songs are supposed to sound like.
Bell said artists who move beyond familiar practices can face criticism that their music does not sound sufficiently Taiwanese or that they are using the language incorrectly. But she believes following those practices too closely can create another problem: making the music feel distant to people who did not grow up with it.
“I want my music to be a part of their lives,” she said. That means making choices not only about melody, but also about the words and phrases she uses.
Some vocabulary commonly used by older generations can give a song an old-fashioned feel, Bell said. She cited words such as “yao-giao” (妖嬌), a term used to describe someone as charming or coquettish, which she would be unlikely to use in her own songs because younger listeners may associate it with their grandparents’ generation.
“The lyrics that you choose really affect how a song makes you feel,” she said.
Bell also wants contemporary Taiwanese music to speak to contemporary experiences. She points to older songs that portrayed women as obedient or expected them to endure unhappy relationships.
In her view, a new generation of Taiwanese-language music should be able to tell different stories, including ones that encourage women to be more independent and assertive.
That idea also shapes Bell’s social media content. She regularly posts videos featuring Taiwanese phrases, often explaining them in English.
The motivation is personal. Taiwanese is Bell’s mother tongue, and she grew up speaking it with her family. She has become increasingly concerned that fewer children are growing up speaking Taiwanese at home.
“I decided to make videos that teach foreign people, or even people in Taiwan, simple Taiwanese phrases,” she said. For Bell, making the language approachable is another way to encourage the public to engage with it.
Her music and social media work therefore serve the same purpose, even though they take different forms. “When I am making music, I feel the most like myself when I write in Taiwanese,” she said. “And when I am making videos, I feel like I am spreading my mother tongue to people around the world.”
The response has given her reason to keep going.
Bell said she has received messages from people in Taiwan who previously did not listen to Taiwanese music but began doing so after hearing her work. She has also heard from people overseas who became interested in learning Taiwanese because of her music.
To her, those reactions show that people can connect with the language through curiosity and enjoyment, rather than simply seeing it as something they are expected to preserve.
Bell sees a similar dynamic in the global popularity of K-pop and J-pop. Listeners do not necessarily need to understand every lyric to connect with music in another language. A melody, an artist’s image or simply the feeling of a song can be enough to make someone want to listen again.
She hopes Taiwanese music can create the same kind of connection. That is also why Bell is interested in the idea of “T-pop,” although she does not think its identity has been fully established yet.
She imagines a future in which people around the world associate Taiwan not only with Mandarin-language music, but also with Taiwanese-language music as a distinct part of the country's cultural identity.
“What would be really cool is when the world thinks about Taiwan, they wouldn’t automatically think of Mandarin music,” she said. “They would actually think about Taiwanese music as something that’s unique to Taiwan.”
For Bell, making that happen means creating music that feels contemporary enough to become part of popular culture, rather than being seen primarily as a link to the past. She wants Taiwanese to feel like something people actively want to listen to and identify with, not simply something they are told to preserve.
Bell’s commitment to creating music in Taiwanese did not begin with a desire to create T-pop. It began with her grandfather.
“Before he passed away, he told me Taiwanese is our root. So if you like singing, if you love music, just use your talent to keep the language alive.”
For Bell, his message was about more than the language itself. Her grandfather also spoke to her about their history, culture and where they came from. “It is our identity, our sound,” she said.
Her parents have also supported her vision, even when people in the music industry questioned her decision to sing in Taiwanese. After leaving her label, Bell wrote a song for her parents, which became the first Taiwanese song she released after the move.
She said her parents, sister, and boyfriend, whom she said has also played a major role in her music production, have all given her the confidence to continue pursuing music in Taiwanese. That community is now extending beyond her family and into an audience she hopes will carry the language forward.

Nearly a year since a ceasefire ended major fighting in Gaza, reconstruction of the devastated territory has yet to begin. Most buildings were completely destroyed by Israeli airstrikes or bulldozed by Israeli forces, and nearly all of the rest have suffered damage.
The population of more than 2 million lives confined to a third of the enclave's territory, mainly housed in makeshift tents or in overcrowded rooms in damaged buildings.
Bulldozers were at work at the site on Thursday, removing rubble to prepare the ground for tents, where survivors from among more than 110 people who had been living in the building could be housed. Residents sifted through the rubble picking up belongings, including food.
"We were in shock from the scene we witnessed. Imagine seeing your family members under the rubble — some of them (torn to) pieces, others killed," said Nader El-Ejlah, a survivor who said several of his relatives were killed in the collapse.
El-Ejlah said the family had moved into the damaged building because they could not find any other shelter. Unless a solution is found to provide displaced people with new shelters, the collapse would not be the last, he said.
"We have lost our family, there are still people (whose fate is) unknown to this day. There are several buildings in Gaza, until now, that are on the verge of collapse," he said.
Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for the Palestinian Civil Defense Service in Gaza, told Reuters there were eight children among the dead, and around half of the wounded were also children.
"We don't have the needed equipment. Despite that, rescue teams did a heroic job and rescued 45 people from under the rubble and moved them to hospitals for treatment," Basal told Reuters by phone from Gaza.
Palestinian and U.N. officials blame Israel's restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery to clear rubble and rebuild homes. Israel says its curbs aim to keep equipment out of the hands of militants.

Canada's PM Carney welcomed the invitation to become the first "associate member" of the European Union, but emphasised that the intent is not to become a full member nor to cede sovereignty.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's invitation to become the EU's first "associate member", with some caveats.
In her State of the Union address on Wednesday, von der Leyen floated the idea of the unprecedented arrangement, which has yet to be fully defined.
In his own speech before the European Parliament, Carney welcomed the move, pointing to opinion polls showing an overwhelming majority of Canadians favour much closer ties with Brussels. At the same time, he spelled out some limits in how far Ottawa is willing to go.

Asked after the speech whether he felt comfortable with that precise connotation, he noted that "the precise nomenclature is a question for Europe," arguing that what mattered was the substance.
At the same time, Carney also seemed to trace a line for any potential relinquishment of sovereignty from Canada's side, insisting that "we are looking for partnerships that are complementary, that reinforce our sovereignty".
Canada is locked in a trade war with the US after talks on a bilateral agreement collapsed. In response, Carney has been seeking closer ties with Brussels, which he sees as a blueprint for other democracies to follow.
During his speech before MEPs in Strasbourg, he pointed out what he sees as the potential areas of deepening collaboration with the EU, such as critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space, and payments.
"An alliance is not defined by what we oppose, but by what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability. An alliance that builds resilience for what it allows us to do for our citizens, and our citizens to do for themselves," he added.
At the same time, he stressed that he did not intend to form a third bloc "with better manners" to enter the great power rivalry.
"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law."

One pincer stalled a year ago, the other has just been broken near Kostiantynivka—Russia’s ring will not close, Ukrainian commander says

Russia's attempt to encircle the fortified cities of Donetsk Oblast has lost its northern pincer, the commander of Ukraine's Third Army Corps, Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, said in a television interview reported by Ukrinform. He described where the two Russian pincers were meant to meet, far behind the front line, and what Moscow must do now that one of them is gone. He also named what the Ukrainian operation there is meant to achieve, after declining to do so when he revealed it two days earlier.
Two pincers that were to meet in another oblast
Biletskyi set out the Russian design "to envelop the so-called fortress cities from the north and from the south"—the four cities, Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka, that have been the backbone of Ukraine's defense in the oblast since 2022..
"From the south it was an envelopment through Dobropillia, and from the north through this salient, which is now being cut off, it went to the city of Sviatohirsk and further, to the settlement of Barvinkove, where these two claws of the Russian army, the Dobropillia one from the south and the Sviatohirsk one from the north, were supposed to close," the commander said.
Barvinkove sits in Kharkiv Oblast, west of the fortified belt. The distance from there to the current front line shows how far behind Ukrainian lines the ring was meant to close.
Neither pincer got near it. Ukrainian forces stopped the Russian infiltration near Dobropillia last year, Biletskyi said, and the situation there remains difficult but under control. Russian assault groups have kept pushing toward the town in recent weeks, though Ukrainian troops have mined or destroyed the main approaches.
On the northern pincer he was blunt:
"The northern claw has effectively been routed and destroyed," he said.
“Only the first season” – Ukraine unveils secret counteroffensive in a region Russia has been trying to seize for 12 years
Now the cities have to be stormed
Holding that result now depends on Russian supply, Biletskyi said. The critical task is "paralyzing logistics, paralyzing the rear areas, not letting the Russians restore this offensive."
He then set out what the failure costs Moscow.
"Then they will have to storm the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk and the Druzhkivka-Kostiantynivka agglomerations head-on," he said. "And storming these cities head-on is a far more painful and costly business for them than trying to envelop them and effectively take them without a fight."
Russia has taken none of them: it has been fighting for Kostiantynivka since October 2025 and has not reached the other three. Ukraine reinforced the sector last month, placing two newly formed groupings under Azov commanders. One of them has since warned that Russia may mobilize up to 600,000 troops for its next offensive.
Ukraine’s Vivaldi counteroffensive disrupts Russia’s plan to encircle Donetsk Fortress Belt – ISW
What Vivaldi is actually for
Two days after the operation was made public without a stated objective, Biletskyi gave one, and it is defensive.
"Our main strategic task for the Armed Forces of Ukraine is defense on the Donetsk and Luhansk axes, the defense of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts," he said.
Ukrainian forces are not trying to take as much ground as they can, he added.
"We are not fighting there just for tens or hundreds, and at one time thousands, of kilometers. We are fighting first of all for favorable defensive lines."
Vivaldi is meant to put the troops on exactly those lines. That sets a different yardstick than captured settlements: the operation will be judged on the ground Ukraine ends up holding, not on how much of it there is.

The Iranian Foreign Ministry said it summoned Sweden’s ambassador in Tehran, Mathias Otterstedt, and informed him that one Swedish diplomat would have to leave Iran within 48 hours, according to the official news agency IRNA.

The ministry also accused Sweden of pursuing “hostile policies” toward Iran and hosting individuals and groups opposed to Tehran.

On Wednesday, the Swedish government said it had expelled an official from the Iranian Embassy after summoning Iran’s ambassador.
Stockholm said the official was asked to leave Sweden over “activities that are not compatible with the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.”
Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard said the decision was taken to protect Swedish citizens and interests, while Justice Minister Gunnar Strommer said, “We know Iran has for a long time been conducting security-threatening activities in and against Sweden.”

Social media platform Snapchat would be "willing to implement" time limits for teenage users, Evan Spiegel, CEO of its parent company Snap, said Wednesday.
Speaking to the BBC at the company's California headquarters, Spiegel said limiting the time young users could spend on the app could be "an important step forward for the industry."
"That's something we've talked about internally," he said, without committing to a timeline. "I don't have more to share today."
His comments followed calls from Meta for other social media companies to adopt restrictions similar to those it agreed to introduce under a multibillion-dollar settlement with US states.
Under the August settlement, Meta agreed to pay $12.7 billion and introduce a default two-hour daily limit for teenage users across its platforms, mute notifications during school hours and restrict nighttime access.
"I think that would be beneficial overall," Spiegel told the BBC. "We've looked really thoughtfully at the terms."
Meta said it would introduce stricter time limits and pay an additional $5.3 billion if YouTube and TikTok follow suit. It denied wrongdoing as part of the settlement.
Last month, a Meta spokesperson expressed hope that Snap would adopt similar measures.
Spiegel noted that Snap's Family Center already gives parents tools to monitor aspects of their teenagers' Snapchat use.
"We want to figure out how we can be part of the solution," he added.
Lawsuits against Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap accuse the companies of harming young people’s mental health through their platforms. Snap has also been accused of facilitating illegal drug sales.

U.S. House passes Russia sanctions bill granting Trump tariff authority
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:29:43 CST
20:29:43 KST

NEW YORK, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. House of Representatives on Wednesday passed a bill imposing sanctions on Russia and Iran, sending it to President Donald Trump for his signature.
The House passed the bill 262-159, with support from most Republicans and dozens of Democrats. The bill passed the Senate in August by an 86-11 vote with bipartisan support, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky met with lawmakers and urged its passage.
The measure would impose sanctions on Russian officials, banks and vessels used to transport Russian energy. It also authorizes Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian oil or natural gas.
The measure also extends the Iran Sanctions Act by five years, maintaining sanctions targeting Iran's energy and weapons sectors.
Since beginning his second term in January 2025, Trump has largely relied on executive authority to impose tariffs and sanctions rather than pursuing such measures through legislation in Congress.
Among Republicans, 203 voted for the bill and seven voted against it. House Democrats were divided over the legislation, with 58 voting for the bill and 152 against it, while one Independent voted for the bill. ■

Xinhua Commentary: Hong Kong's first 5-year blueprint charts clear course for development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:29:20 CST
20:29:20 KST

HONG KONG, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- The first five-year plan of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) is of milestone significance in advancing the practice of "one country, two systems" and marks a crucial step for Hong Kong to expedite the transition from stability to prosperity and achieve high-quality development.
The guiding document unveiled on Wednesday charts a clear course for Hong Kong's economic and social development from 2026 to 2030.
The formulation of the plan reflects a profound shift in Hong Kong's governance approach and development model, demonstrating the notable improvement in the governance capacity of the HKSAR government under "one country, two systems."
Built on consensus from all sectors of Hong Kong society, the blueprint will further enhance the HKSAR's governance efficacy, making the development direction clearer, resource allocation more efficient, and social expectations more stable, and providing stronger safeguards for the well-being of its residents and the interests of investors.
The plan will consolidate and enhance Hong Kong's status as an international financial, maritime and trade center, and develop the region into an international innovation and technology center and a global hub for high-caliber talent.
The blueprint comes as Hong Kong's economic growth gains momentum, with social stability and prosperity providing an indispensable environment and foundation for the city to implement medium- and long-term planning. The Hong Kong society has been calling for a more forward-looking and holistic blueprint for development.
One of the underlying principles of the plan is to uphold the two-pronged approach of "effective market" and "capable government." Far from weakening the market, this governance innovation strengthens strategic guidance, unleashes market vitality, and turns institutional advantages into real development gains. It provides Hong Kong with a powerful tool to tackle long-standing deep-seated problems and gives full play to the advantages and vitality of the "one country, two systems" policy.
This year marks the start of the national 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), which includes arrangements for promoting the long-term prosperity and stability of the HKSAR and the Macao SAR by supporting the two regions in consolidating and enhancing their competitive advantages, and helping them better integrate into and contribute to the country's overall development.
Aligned with the national five-year plan, the HKSAR's blueprint seeks to turn the country's strategic opportunities into the region's development drivers.
Hong Kong's plan will leverage the vast mainland market and its comprehensive industrial system, while exerting the city's role as an international platform. It aims to further develop Hong Kong as a gateway and bridge between the country and the world, and as an international metropolis that is more attractive, vibrant and rich in opportunities.
A blueprint is only as valuable as its implementation. As long as all sectors of the Hong Kong society fully and faithfully uphold "one country, two systems," adhere to the principle of "patriots administering Hong Kong," maintain and improve its executive-led governance, enable a capable government to deliver results and an effective market to unleash its full potential, and make concerted efforts, the HKSAR will surely translate its grand blueprint into reality. ■

New Zealand job ads rise in August: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:29:10 CST
20:29:10 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand job advertisements rose 0.6 percent in August from the previous month and were up 9.7 percent from a year earlier, according to a report released Thursday.
Applications per job ad also increased 0.9 percent in July, the sharpest monthly rise in 18 months, "despite being spread across a rising number of opportunities," said the report by employment marketplace SEEK.
The consumer services sector drove monthly growth, with job advertisements in hospitality and tourism rising 3.4 percent and retail and consumer products increasing 3.3 percent, the report said, adding that mining, resources and energy recorded the strongest annual growth, with job ads up 46.7 percent.
Artificial intelligence (AI) skills were referenced in 4 percent of job ads in New Zealand, with mentions up 4.4 percent month-on-month and 93.3 percent year-on-year, it said, noting that AI was most commonly referenced in information and communication technology, marketing and communications, and consulting and strategy roles.
Separately, SEEK's Advertised Salary Index showed advertised salaries rose 0.6 percent in the three months to August and 2.6 percent annually.
Government roles recorded the fastest annual advertised salary growth among industries at 10 percent, nearly four times the national rate, the index showed. ■

Researchers develop self-repairing coating to extend rust protection
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:29:08 CST
20:29:08 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia are developing a "smart", self-healing coating that could dramatically extend rust protection for steel structures, including buildings, bridges, and cars.
The powder-like particles, designed by nanoarchitects at Australia's University of Queensland (UQ), can turn water-based paint into self-repairing corrosion shields, with nanoparticles acting as tiny containers that release rust-inhibiting molecules when damage is detected on the coating surface, according to a UQ statement released Wednesday.
Electrochemical testing indicated the new self-healing coating could restrict corrosion to 37 nanometers per year, 600 times more effective than many existing high-performance rust-protection products, which report an ability to restrict annual corrosion to 0.025 mm, according to the study published in Small Science.
"What we have created is a barrier that is constantly sensing if something is wrong so it can patch any scrapes and cracks itself, greatly extending the duration of protection," said UQ researcher Asep Nugraha.
The researchers encased the common rust inhibitor benzotriazole in a nanostructure that, when added to waterborne polyurethane coatings, creates a composite with an extreme responsivity to changes in acidity.
"It is not a coating that will last forever, but coatings that contain our technology will have a greatly expanded lifetime, meaning far less maintenance and a much longer time between applications," Nugraha said, adding that researchers aim to produce a commercial product within the next five years. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: China backs live-action dramas as AI-made micro-dramas dominate releases
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:29:02 CST
20:29:02 KST

The State Council Information Office holds a press conference on accelerating high-quality development of the radio, television and online audio-video sector during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Pan Xu)
BEIJING, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- China's audiovisual regulators on Thursday voiced support for live-action dramas in the face of AI-made productions accounting for more than 90 percent of the country's micro-dramas released in the first eight months of 2026.
"Our position is clear: live-action dramas are the mainstay of quality productions and should receive strong support," said Wang Xiaoliang, an official with the National Radio and Television Administration (NRTA), at a news conference on the sector over the next five years.
Authorities will step up the implementation of a program to support the production and distribution of quality works, guide platforms to create dedicated sections for live-action dramas, and provide financial support to ensure that such productions find an audience and generate returns, according to Wang.
His remarks came as micro-dramas -- series whose episodes run for less than 20 minutes -- have surged in popularity in China and gained a growing following overseas.
Official data show China released 430,000 micro-dramas from January to August, 13 times the number released in all of 2025. The country now has more than 800 million micro-drama viewers, while the market exceeded 100 billion yuan (around 14.8 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025.
Chinese regulators, however, are not opposed to using AI in screen production.
AI technology has opened new possibilities for creative expression in micro-dramas, while helping cut costs and improve efficiency, but it has also posed challenges for content quality and the protection of rights and interests, Wang said.
Such dramas must carry clear content labels, and efforts are underway to push platforms to follow rules on authorizing the use of people's likenesses and voices, he added.
China identified micro-dramas as an emerging form of cultural business to be vigorously developed in its 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030).
The country implemented a policy document on the development and management of micro-dramas on Sept. 1, while introducing a unified label as part of efforts to bring the sector under proper regulation.
At the news conference on Thursday, officials said China will step up efforts to expand the global reach of micro-dramas, leveraging AI to strengthen their leading edge in overseas markets.
Chinese micro-dramas have gained popularity in more than 200 countries and regions, accounting for more than 80 percent of the overseas micro-drama market, according to He Biao, deputy head and spokesperson of the NRTA.
Shao Jiang, an associate professor at Beijing Union University, said Chinese micro-dramas are shifting from a scale-driven approach focused on downloads and paid traffic to one centered on content, intellectual property and cultural resonance.
Released late last year, Chinese micro-drama ENEMY quickly climbed the trending drama charts in the United States, Mexico, Thailand and other countries and regions, and many overseas viewers took to social media to dissect the plot and discuss its cultural details.
The micro-drama weaves traditional Chinese cultural elements, including opera and ancient architecture, into key moments in the story rather than presenting them as standalone cultural showcases, allowing viewers from different backgrounds to appreciate their appeal as the plot unfolds.
In the early stages, most exported productions relied on translated versions of Chinese hits. Now, more companies are shifting toward locally produced content overseas, working with local partners in casting and production to better integrate into target markets.
Technology is giving Chinese micro-dramas a digital boost overseas, according to industry insiders. AI is being used in scriptwriting, visual effects, multilingual dubbing and audience analysis, significantly improving production and distribution efficiency.
Li Ruoqie, head of a micro-drama production company, said his team entered the North American market in May and has since completed eight productions. An AI micro-drama about vampires has surpassed 15 million views on TikTok.
"AI micro-dramas featuring Western elements such as vampires and werewolves cater to North American audiences' interest in gothic romance and supernatural stories, while costing far less to produce than live-action dramas," Li said.
Liu Xingliang, a digital economy scholar, said AI tools reduce the cost of operating across languages and cultures while improving the efficiency of large-scale content production and optimization.
He added that AI is also playing a growing role in creative processes, including script development, scene design and editing, reshaping the industry's cost structure and making it easier to tailor content to different markets. ■

19:28:54 CST
20:28:54 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Participants at the 13th Beijing Xiangshan Forum hailed the event as a key platform for different parties to engage in dialogue as China seeks to play a constructive role in peacefully settling conflicts amid rising global uncertainty.
Themed "Build Consensus on Stability, Advance Security Governance Together," the forum, which runs from Tuesday to Thursday, has drawn guests from more than 100 countries, regions and international organizations.
Noting that this year marks the forum's 20th anniversary, Yao Yunzhu, a senior adviser to the forum and retired major general of the Chinese People's Liberation Army, said she was pleased to see its growing scale over the past two decades.
Yao stressed that the forum has brought together representatives from different sides, including those at odds with each other. "It allows them to voice their respective views and even engage in heated exchanges while maintaining mutual respect."
Co-hosted by the China Association for Military Science and the China Institute for International Strategic Studies, the Beijing Xiangshan Forum has become a track-one-and-a-half dialogue event, where officials and scholars engage in semi-official talks.
Unlike some global forums that have banned Russian official delegates since the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the Beijing Xiangshan Forum provides a more inclusive space for military personnel, security scholars and observers from different parties around the world.
The forum hosted eight closed-door seminars covering a wide range of hotspot issues.
Jean Christophe Baron von Pfetten, chairman of the Royal Institute for East West Strategic Studies in Britain, participated in a closed-door seminar last year, where he found that Ukrainian and Russian people sat at the same table.
"It's really remarkable. I cannot solve conflicts, but at least not escalate this conflict," said Baron von Pfetten, who returned to the forum this year.
Not shying away from sensitive topics, the forum seeks to help participants find common ground and facilitate dialogue toward peaceful solutions, rather than fuel tensions and confrontation, said Zheng Hao, a Chinese news commentator who took part in a session as a speaker at the event.
Through such dialogue, participants can gain new insights and perspectives and explore possible solutions to difficult problems, said Oleksandr Chalyi, Ukraine's former first deputy foreign minister.
Baron von Pfetten emphasized that the forum's distinctive strength lies in its broad representation. "It's fantastic that China is organizing something like this, which can not be organized anywhere else."
The forum exemplifies China's approach -- maintaining engagement with all parties, facilitating dialogue, and pursuing political settlement -- as demonstrated in both the Ukraine crisis and the Middle East issue, said Baron von Pfetten.
However, participants cautioned that despite the forum's role in facilitating dialogue and mutual understanding, some problems and disputes in today's world are deeply rooted and cannot be resolved overnight.
"You can bring a horse to water, but you cannot make it drink. Whether the horse drinks is up to itself," Carice Witte, founder and executive director of Sino-Israel Global Network and Academic Leadership Group, told Xinhua.
Mutual understanding is the first step toward solving problems, Yao said, adding that such exchanges may not yield immediate results, but the empathy developed over time provides a solid foundation for lasting relationships.
"Dialogue and consultation are the only right way forward," said Chinese Defense Minister Dong Jun at the opening ceremony of the forum on Wednesday. He spoke about finding solutions to protracted conflicts and hotspots around the world.
"It may not resolve all issues at once, but with wisdom and patience, things are going to work out," Dong added. ■

This will underpin long-term electricity demand growth, although the scale and pace of expansion will depend on market and execution risks, Moody's said.
To meet the additional demand, Malaysia's utility firms and independent power producers will need to add at least 14-17 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity over the next decade, requiring 80 billion ringgit (19.52 billion U.S. dollars) to 95 billion ringgit of investment.
"The data center-led demand growth will be credit positive in the long term if utilities can execute generation, transmission and distribution projects effectively. In the meantime, financial leverage of the rated utilities will rise during the development phase, reducing financial headroom," said Moody's. ■

China unveils crop farming plan to boost grain capacity by 2030
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:28:50 CST
20:28:50 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- China will steadily enhance its comprehensive grain production capacity by 2030 and hold the bottom line of basic self-sufficiency in grains and absolute security in staple foods, according to the national crop farming development plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) released by the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs.
Under the plan, by 2030 China will consolidate and enhance the production capacity of soybeans, oilseeds, cotton and sugar crops to maintain a reasonable level of self-sufficiency, and ensure balanced, diverse and safe supplies of vegetables, fruits and tea.
The plan also sets targeted measures for different crops and regions.
Placing strong emphasis on the green transition, the plan calls for agricultural water conservation and more meticulous use of fertilizer and pesticides.
It also highlights the leading role of new quality productive forces in agriculture, including breeding and promoting breakthrough varieties and applying intelligent machinery.
Technology already contributes more than 64 percent to China's agricultural output growth.
The crop farming plan is aligned with the plan to accelerate agricultural and rural modernization during the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) period, which sets a target of increasing the country's comprehensive grain production capacity to 1.45 trillion jin (about 725 million tonnes) by 2030.
"The 15th Five-Year Plan period is critical for basically achieving agricultural and rural modernization," said Zhao Changbao, director of the Rural Economy Research Center of the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, in a recent article.
"Continuously raising the land output rate, resource utilization rate and labor productivity is an inevitable choice for responding to changes at home and abroad, consolidating the foundation of agricultural development and safeguarding national food security," he said.
Zhao noted that the plan dovetails with the requirement of the plan to accelerate agricultural and rural modernization during the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) period to boost output and production capacity, production and ecology, and output and income simultaneously.
China's grain security foundation has continued to strengthen. The country's grain output reached about 714.9 million tonnes in 2025, marking the second straight year with grain output above 700 million tonnes.
The plan comes as global food security faces mounting headwinds. The 2026 State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report, released in July by five United Nations specialized agencies, estimated that about 645 million people, or 7.8 percent of the global population, were affected by hunger in 2025.
China feeds nearly 20 percent of the world's population with less than 9 percent of its arable land, and has kept its grain self-sufficiency rate at a high level. ■

Fiji declares national HIV crisis as new cases spike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:27:34 UTC
20:27:34 KST

Fiji has declared a national HIV emergency after a surge in new cases, with the government and international agencies racing to contain a crisis driven by sexual transmission and injection drug use.
Fiji has declared a national HIV crisis as sexual transmission and illicit drug use help to spread the virus, now infecting an estimated one in 60 adults in the Pacific nation, up from one in 167 five years earlier.
“I am formally declaring a national HIV emergency in Fiji,” Health Minister Atonio Lalabalavu told reporters on Wednesday. “This decision recognises the seriousness of the epidemic and the urgent, coordinated response our country now needs.”
New HIV diagnoses surged to 2,016 cases in 2025 — 16 times the level recorded in 2019, authorities said, vowing a “whole of government” response.
Among HIV cases with a known mode of transmission, more than half were linked to sexual transmission and more than 42% to injecting drug use, the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) said in a press release on Wednesday.
HIV transmission rates began to increase around 2019 when a group of “very high-risk” injecting drug users emerged, primarily in the sex worker community, Renata Ram, United Nations’ HIV/AIDS country director in Fiji, told AFP earlier this year.
Two in every 100 pregnant women carry the virus, and of the 59 babies born with HIV in 2025, 18 died before their first birthday, as HIV can be transmitted to the fetus or the newborn during pregnancy, during labour or delivery, or by breastfeeding.
Scaling up efforts
The government said it was expanding access to free HIV testing, prevention services and treatment.
“This includes rapid testing, prevention medicine for people at higher risk, harm-reduction measures for people who inject drugs, and free treatment for people diagnosed with HIV.”
Fiji said it was receiving external support in the effort, including from Australia, New Zealand, India, the Global Fund and the United Nations.
“Fiji has recognized the urgency of the moment and is stepping up its response,” said Winnie Byanyima, executive director of the in a press release, adding that the current situation is a reminder to the world that AIDS is not over.
“HIV epidemics can change quickly, and countries need health and community systems that are ready to respond urgently,” she said.
The UN agency welcomed Fiji's plans to introduce legislation for a needle and syringe programme.
“Fiji still has an opportunity to change the course of this epidemic,” said Eamonn Murphy, UNAIDS director for regions including Asia and the Pacific.
He added that the national crisis declaration is a call for action, not fear. “HIV is not transmitted through everyday contact, and people on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load do not sexually transmit HIV,” Murphy said.
He called for stronger cooperation across the Pacific and sustained international solidarity to reinforce the national effort and help accelerate action.
A hub for regional drug trafficking
The roots of the crisis lie partly in Fiji’s position as a drug trafficking hub. Pacific islands, including Fiji, have been transit hubs for drugs from Latin America and Asia destined for lucrative markets in Australia and New Zealand.
The flow of highly addictive drugs such as methamphetamine and cocaine rose sharply after a lull during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime.
Those drugs are increasingly seeping into the Pacific's domestic markets — in part due to foreign criminal syndicates opting to pay their local facilitators in kind.

2026-09-17
11:26:00 UTC
20:26:00 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday, Sept. 17, that China is not politically on Ukraine’s side in Russia’s war and instead leans toward Moscow, despite having enough influence to push Russian leader Vladimir Putin toward negotiations.
Zelensky made the remarks in an interview with Japanese public broadcaster NHK, excerpts from which he published on his official Telegram channel.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is a pity that China is not on our side in this war – politically. It is not even about weapons,” Zelensky said in the final excerpt.
He argued that China’s position was not neutral because Beijing appeared more open and willing to help Russia than Ukraine.
For a country as large and influential as China, being even “a little more” on Russia’s side has major consequences, Zelensky said.
China has leverage but has not used it
Zelensky said he had personally seen a North Korean-made missile in Ukraine but had not seen a Chinese missile used by Russia.
However, he said Chinese technology and equipment were reaching Russia, possibly together with specialists and technical expertise.
The Ukrainian president said he had never seen China publicly pressure Moscow to stop the war. He acknowledged that Beijing might be raising the issue privately during bilateral meetings but said there had been no visible result.
Zelensky pointed to Russia’s growing isolation from international energy and banking systems, Western sanctions and restrictions targeting its shadow fleet as areas in which China could exercise significant leverage.
6 Russian Aircraft Hit as Ukraine Strikes Deep Inside Russia
In his assessment, Beijing could find a way to push Putin toward negotiations but had chosen not to do so. He questioned whether refusing to act despite possessing such influence amounted to support for Moscow.
Zelensky said strong global leaders, including China’s leadership, could help stop the war quickly if they demonstrated sufficient political will.
Ukraine has repeatedly raised concerns about Chinese-origin technology found in Russian weapons. In July, Beijing had not visibly responded after Ukraine provided serial-number evidence linking Chinese-made components to Russian missiles and drones.
Kyiv Post also reported in August that Chinese components, including small turbojet engines, had helped Russia develop faster Shahed-type attack drones that are more difficult for Ukraine to intercept.
China says it strictly controls exports of dual-use goods and has opposed sanctions imposed on Chinese companies accused of helping Russia’s military industry.
Kyiv seeks Drone Deal with Japan
In another excerpt from the NHK interview, Zelensky called for deeper military-technology cooperation between Ukraine and Japan at both the government-to-government and business-to-business levels.
He noted that more than 70% of Ukraine’s defense industry is privately owned and said closer cooperation could increase bilateral trade, particularly in the defense sector.
Zelensky acknowledged differences between the two countries’ legal systems but argued that “when it comes to defense, there are no neutral countries.”
He identified maritime-surveillance, reconnaissance and demining drones, as well as air defense, cybersecurity and food security, as potential areas for cooperation.
Ukraine would like to conclude a Drone Deal with Japan, Zelensky said, adding that Ukrainian defense equipment could also prove useful to Tokyo.
Any decision to acquire it would, however, be up to Japan, he added.
North Korean training raises Pacific threat
Zelensky also warned that North Korea had sent between 30,000 and 50,000 soldiers to Russia, where they were able to obtain experience in real combat rather than through digital simulations.
In the second interview excerpt, he said the North Korean forces had suffered significant losses when they fought Ukrainian troops during the Kursk operation.
Afterward, Zelensky said, they avoided entering Ukrainian territory directly but continued training inside Russia, including alongside drone operators.
“They are training, working with drones and drone operators,” Zelensky said, describing the experience they were gaining as a major threat to security in the Pacific region.
Ukrainian military intelligence previously said that North Korea had deployed a new contingent of approximately 8,500 troops to Russia, including around 400 drone operators and 1,000 engineers and deminers.
Ukrainian intelligence estimated in August that around 25,000 North Korean personnel had served in Russia and that Moscow could seek tens of thousands more.
The growing partnership allows Russia to obtain additional troops, ammunition and missiles while giving Pyongyang practical experience in drone warfare, electronic warfare and modern high-intensity combat.

Magdalena Andersson waves to supporters during an election party at the Waterfront Conference Center on Sept. 11, 2022. | Jonas Ekstromer/TT News Agency/AFP via Getty Images
Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson resigned after narrowly losing a closely fought election, paving the way for a new center-left government to take over.
Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson is now expected to begin formal negotiations with other parties in her bloc and, if she can get a deal, she will become Sweden’s new prime minister in the weeks ahead.
“The Swedish people have voted for a new direction for our country,” Andersson said in a video posted on social media. She said the election showed voters wanted “cohesion” and not “division” and promised to work for unity as prime minister.
Advertisement
Anderson said she would seek to prioritize a fair migration system that stops unfair deportations, a climate policy that sees green transition as an opportunity for Sweden, better elderly care and healthcare, and a revitalized economy to boost growth and reduce unemployment.
The contest offered voters a choice between Andersson’s center-left and socialist alliance of four parties, and Kristersson’s rightwing grouping of four parties, which included the far-right anti-immigration Sweden Democrats.
During the campaign, Andersson, who previously served as prime minister until the 2022 election, warned voters against handing power to the Sweden Democrats after Kristersson said he would offer the far-right party ministerial jobs in his next government.
But the result capped a bad election for the Sweden Democrats who were hoping to enter power as for the first time but lost votes, seats and influence instead.
The Swedish Election Authority’s final tally of the preliminary vote count gives Andersson’s left bloc 176 seats to Kristersson’s 173.

Advertisement
That may not be easy as two of these potential allies are at odds: The Left Party has named its price as having ministers in the government — and that’s something the liberal Center Party says it cannot accept.
Andersson said “a new era of cooperation between the political parties” would be needed.

“A constructive openness will now be needed from the parties in the Riksdag for a prime minister to be tolerated — and for a new government to gain support for its state budget,” Kristersson wrote. “Talks will need to be held with all parties to find ways around these deadlocks and create the conditions for a stable and effective government.”
One option sometimes discussed by commentators in Sweden is for the main center left and center right parties — Andersson’s Social Democrats and Kristersson’s Moderates — to come together to form a grand coalition, removing the need for support from either end of the political spectrum.
But even if they did agree to work together, these two parties would still need backing from a third to get a majority, and collaboration between the two rival camps is seen as highly unlikely by political insiders.
Negotiations could last weeks. The earliest a new prime minister can be sworn in is Sept. 29. Barring an unlikely unravelling of those negotiations, the result heralds the end of conservative Kristersson’s hopes of holding onto his job.
