Textbooks may have misdrawn this basic brain structure for 100 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:54:28 UTC
19:54:28 KST

Textbooks may have misdrawn this basic brain structure for 100 years
- Date:
- September 17, 2026
- Source:
- Johns Hopkins Medicine
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered that brain-cell axons may not be smooth tubes as textbooks have shown for more than a century, but instead naturally resemble strings of tiny pearls. Those pearl-like structures can change with neural activity and may help control how quickly electrical signals travel through the brain.
- Share:
The brain's microscopic wiring may need a different kind of textbook illustration. Instead of the smooth, narrow tubes commonly drawn extending from nerve cells, some axons resemble strings of tiny pearls. These repeating bulges are not simply decorative details. Their shape appears to influence how electrical messages travel.
Researchers at Johns Hopkins Medicine brought this unexpected architecture into focus in a study published online in Nature Neuroscience on December 2, 2024. Working with mouse neurons, they found evidence that a familiar picture of brain cell anatomy may overlook an important feature of the cells' signal-carrying extensions.
Related research has since documented pearled axons in human brain tissue, extending the observations beyond mice. Together, the findings raise questions about how the physical structure of the brain's wiring helps regulate communication.
"Understanding the structure of axons is important for understanding brain cell signaling," said Shigeki Watanabe, Ph.D., an associate professor of cell biology and neuroscience at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, in the university's 2024 announcement. "Axons are the cables that connect our brain tissue, enabling learning, memory and other functions."
A Different Picture of Brain Cell Axons
Axons are the long extensions that allow neurons to transmit electrical signals to other cells. The conventional illustration shows a relatively uniform tube interrupted by occasional bulges (synaptic varicosities that hold globs of neurotransmitters, which enable signaling to other brain cells).
Beaded axons themselves are not an unfamiliar sight. Scientists have long observed pronounced swellings in dying neurons and in neurodegenerative conditions, including Parkinson's disease. In those settings, the beading can accompany damage to the cell membrane and the internal framework that helps maintain the axon's structure.
What stood out in the Johns Hopkins study was the presence of much smaller, repeating swellings in axons examined under conditions intended to preserve their normal structure. The researchers called these regions "non-synaptic varicosities." Unlike the familiar bulges associated with communication sites, these swellings were not synapses.
The distinction matters: the study did not suggest that every beaded axon is damaged. Instead, it pointed to a form of nanoscale pearling that may be part of the normal architecture of the axons studied.
A Clue From Worms
Watanabe's interest began with observations of repeating pearls along axons in worms. A conversation with Swiss scientist Graham Knott, Ph.D., prompted him to investigate further. One possible explanation involved the axon's internal skeleton, a supporting network of proteins.
A Harvard University team had reported repeating "skeletal" components within axons in a study published in 2012. Watanabe and Knott wondered whether disrupting that framework would make the pearls disappear. Jacqueline Griswold, a Johns Hopkins graduate student and the study's first author, tested the idea. The pearling remained.
That result redirected their attention toward the axon's physical properties. Watanabe and Griswold joined forces with theoretical biophysicist Padmini Rangamani, Ph.D., a professor of pharmacology at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine, to investigate how the surrounding membrane might shape the axon.
Freezing Brain Cells Reveals Hidden Detail
Studying these extensions of brain cells (neurons) requires imaging structures far narrower than a human hair. Johns Hopkins described them as roughly 100 times smaller than a hair's width. The researchers used high pressure freezing electron microscopy to preserve their delicate shapes before examining them with beams of electrons.
The preparation method was important. Standard electron microscopy commonly involves chemically fixing and dehydrating tissue, steps that can alter the structures scientists are trying to observe. Freezing offers a way to retain a shape closer to the original.
"To see nanoscale structures with standard electron microscopy, we fix and dehydrate the tissues, but freezing them retains their shape -- similar to freezing a grape rather than dehydrating it into a raisin," Watanabe said.
The team examined mouse neurons grown in the laboratory, neurons from adult mice and neurons from mouse embryos. Their axons were nonmyelinated (they were without the myelin insulating cover that surrounds the axon). Across tens of thousands of tissue images, the researchers repeatedly encountered the same pearled appearance.
They also observed pearling with high resolution imaging of living neurons, providing evidence that it was not simply produced by freezing the samples.
"These findings challenge a century of understanding about axon structure," Watanabe said.
How Membrane Physics Shapes Axons
To explain the pattern, the researchers built mathematical models of the membrane surrounding an axon. Relatively simple mechanical models reproduced important features of the pearls, suggesting that physical forces could help determine the shape without requiring a rigid internal mold.
Experiments supported that interpretation. Increasing the sugar concentration in the solution surrounding the axons made the swollen regions smaller. In the model, increasing membrane tension also reduced their size.
Cholesterol provided another way to change the membrane's behavior. Removing it made the membrane less stiff and more fluid. This altered the pearled structure in both the models and mouse neurons and reduced the speed of electrical signaling.
"A wider space in the axons allows ions [chemical particles] to pass through more quickly and avoid traffic jams," Watanabe said.
However, bigger pearls did not invariably mean faster signals. The dimensions of both the swellings and their narrow connecting segments mattered.
Electrical Activity Changes the Pearls
The researchers also tested whether neural activity could reshape the axons. After high frequency electrical stimulation, the pearl-like regions became an average of 8% longer and 17% wider, with enlargement lasting at least 30 minutes.
The published paper reports that electrical signals slowed after this stimulation, with the effect lasting at least an hour. When cholesterol had been removed beforehand, some structural changes still occurred, but the pearls remained smaller than those in untreated cells, and the same significant slowing was not detected.
The findings suggest that axons are not merely fixed cables. Their physical structure can respond to activity and help adjust how messages move through them.
Later Research Finds Pearled Axons in Human Tissue
When the original findings were announced in 2024, the team planned to examine axonal "arms" in human brain tissue obtained with permission from people undergoing brain surgery and from people who had died with neurodegenerative diseases.
A related study subsequently reported pearled axons in human cortical tissue obtained during epilepsy surgery. Led by Chelsy R. Eddings and colleagues, including Watanabe, the work appeared online in Neuron on November 24, 2025, and in its February 4, 2026, issue.
The researchers combined electrical stimulation with rapid freezing to capture tiny membrane changes in mouse and human brain slices. Alongside the pearled axons, they found evidence of ultrafast endocytosis, a process through which nerve endings quickly retrieve membrane after releasing chemical messages.
These observations extend the evidence to human tissue, but they do not establish that every axon has the same shape. Nor do they show that pearling has identical effects on signaling throughout the human brain. The human study primarily investigated membrane recycling at synapses.
The Broader Search for What Controls Axon Shape
The relationship between axon structure and function also became the focus of a National Institute of Mental Health Multiple Principal Investigator grant awarded to Watanabe and Rangamani and highlighted in 2024. The project supports computational models of how a neuron's physical properties and incoming signals affect its axon, followed by tests in mouse tissue and cell cultures.
Separate research is exploring other ways to investigate the dimensions of this microscopic wiring. In a study published in PLOS Biology on July 17, 2026, University of Edinburgh researchers used automated imaging of living zebrafish to screen 880 compounds for effects on axon diameter. They identified 33 initial hits and confirmed that compounds affecting particular chemical signaling pathways could increase axon width. This was not a direct replication of the pearling study, but it provides another tool for investigating how axon size is controlled.
For the Johns Hopkins team, an important question remains how the structure seen in functioning axons relates to the damaging beading associated with neurological disease. Understanding that distinction could help researchers separate normal changes in neural wiring from signs that the system is breaking down.

Guidance: Spousal employment - Supplementary Agreement Germany
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:53:37 BST
19:53:37 KST

Spousal employment - Supplementary Agreement Germany
The NATO Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) and the Supplementary Agreement are the international legal agreements that enable UK Defence to operate in Germany.
Documents
Details
The NATO SOFA is a multinational agreement between nations enabling the operation of a nation’s defence task in the territory of another nation.
In Germany, the stationing and operation of UK Defence personnel is governed by the Supplementary Agreement to the NATO SOFA. The Supplementary Agreement expands upon the provisions of the NATO SOFA and forms part of German domestic law, providing the detailed legal framework under which UK Defence operates in Germany.
Overview
Neither the NATO SOFA nor the Supplementary Agreement provides a direct legal entitlement for accompanying spouses or family members to undertake employment in Germany.
The agreements provide a basis for lawful residence and status in Germany for eligible dependants accompanying members of the force or civilian component. Any employment activity undertaken by a dependant must, however, comply with applicable German law.
The UK Ministry of Defence cannot grant authority, permission, or exemptions allowing spouses or dependants to work in Germany. Responsibility for ensuring compliance with host nation legislation rests with the individual and, where applicable, their employer.
There are several routes through which accompanying spouses may lawfully undertake employment within Germany, subject to the relevant legal and regulatory requirements.
Employment within the German Economy
The status of an accompanying spouse is recognised under German immigration arrangements associated with the Supplementary Agreement and NATO SOFA framework. Consequently, accompanying spouses generally do not require a separate residence permit or work permit to seek employment in the German economy.
Individuals employed by German or other locally established employers will be subject to German legislation and jurisdiction. This may include:
- employment law
- taxation requirements
- social security contributions
- health insurance obligations
- pension arrangements
- other statutory and regulatory requirements
The decision to undertake employment within the German economy is a personal one. Individuals are responsible for ensuring that their employment arrangements comply fully with German law.
Neither the Supplementary Agreement nor the NATO SOFA provides exemptions from German employment, tax, social security, healthcare, or other legal obligations arising from employment.
Operating a Business or Undertaking Self-Employment in Germany
Accompanying spouses may be able to establish and operate a business, trade, profession, or other self-employed activity within the Federal Republic of Germany, subject to the relevant approvals, registrations, and regulatory requirements imposed by the German authorities.
Any business activity undertaken for commercial gain and participating in the German economy will ordinarily be subject to applicable German legislation. This may include taxation, social security obligations, health insurance requirements, licensing provisions, and other regulatory controls.
Individuals considering self-employment or the operation of a business should seek appropriate professional advice from qualified German legal, tax, and financial advisers before commencing any activity.
Care should be taken to maintain a clear distinction between any commercial activity and the rights, privileges, or status derived from dependant status under the NATO SOFA and Supplementary Agreement.
International remote working (IRW)
Neither the NATO SOFA nor the Supplementary Agreement establishes a legal framework for International Remote Working (IRW).
Remote working arrangements are a matter between the employee and their employer. The UK MOD cannot authorise or validate remote working arrangements undertaken within the territory of another sovereign state. This includes those attracting the term Crown Servant (Civil or Military) not assigned to Germany for the purpose of their employment.
Before commencing any form of remote working from Germany, both the employee and employer should satisfy themselves that the arrangement is lawful and compliant with all relevant German legal requirements.
Consideration should be given to matters including:
- employment legislation
- taxation obligations
- social security requirements
- healthcare obligations
- health and safety legislation
- data protection and privacy regulations
- any other relevant regulatory requirements
Depending on the circumstances, German law may impose obligations on either the employee or employer, even where the employer is established outside Germany and the work is undertaken remotely.
Employees and employers are strongly encouraged to seek independent legal and professional advice from appropriately qualified German advisers before commencing any remote working arrangement.
Where the work involves access to official, government, or sensitive information, additional security considerations may apply. Individuals should ensure compliance with all relevant departmental security policies and seek advice from their employing organisation where necessary.
Key Principles
- The Supplementary Agreement and NATO SOFA do not provide a right to employment for accompanying spouses.
- Any employment, self-employment, or business activity in Germany must comply with German law.
- The MOD cannot grant permission or exemptions for employment activities in Germany.
- International Remote Working is not covered by the Supplementary Agreement or NATO SOFA.
- Individuals and employers are responsible for ensuring that any employment arrangement is lawful and compliant with applicable host nation requirements.

Why is inflation rising again around the world?

19:50:54 KST

Counting the Cost
Why is inflation rising again around the world?
Rising energy prices are pushing inflation higher again, forcing major central banks to raise interest rates.
For decades, central banks treated oil shocks as temporary, something to wait out, not hike rates over.
And that’s because raising rates in this case can slow growth without bringing down the price of a single barrel of oil.
But this time might be different.
Oil surged past $100 a barrel last week.
Six months into the Iran war, the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted and Houthi advances threaten Saudi oil supplies, too.
Energy costs are feeding through into household and business bills.
That is forcing policymakers to reconsider the old rulebook even though tighter policy means higher borrowing costs.

====================================================================================================

from the picturesque to the smartphone: architecture’s obsession with being seen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:50:36 UTC
19:50:36 KST

before the building, the image
Before the Crystal Palace existed in Hyde Park, it appeared in the newspaper. Joseph Paxton sketched his proposal in June 1850 and sent a view to the Illustrated London News while the scheme was still awaiting approval. It appeared on July 6th. The Royal Commission accepted his design nine days later. Thousands of panes of glass and miles of iron structure still had to follow, but the public had already seen the building in the form of that image.
This sequence still happens now. We regularly meet architecture first as an image, often long before visiting it, and sometimes without ever visiting at all. But this second existence developed over centuries. Buildings occupy sites, and they occupy pictures. Sometimes the picture begins doing so much of the architectural work that it’s hard to separate the two.
Little Island, Heatherwick Studio, New York, 2021 | image by Michael Grimm
before the camera
At Stourhead in Wiltshire, a walk around the English estate frames ever-changing scenes. A Pantheon sits across the water between trees, and an arcaded bridge stretches beyond. Henry Hoare II began to design and build the garden in the 1740s with architect Henry Flitcroft, and drew on classical landscapes and paintings by Baroque-era artists like Claude Lorrain and Nicolas Poussin. Buildings were strategically sited to emerge into view, disappear into nature, and then return beautifully from another angle.
The picturesque had already made the ‘view’ into something that was to be curated by architects and landscape designers. John Macarthur’s writing on the subject follows the way this ‘pictorial’ thinking entered landscape and architectural design, as special importance was given to the viewer in motion. Space could be walked through while certain moments within it behaved almost like finished pictures. Even while the technology of photography would arrive later, architecture already understood the joys of situating someone in exactly the right place to look.
a view of Stour Head in the County of Wiltshire, the Seat of Henry Hoare Esq. (The Temple of Flora) | image courtesy Yale Center for British Art
architecture learns to travel
Of course the picturesque estate was reserved for only a select few. London’s Great Exhibition of 1851, the world’s first international world’s fair, brought this type of experience to mass culture. Millions eventually entered Joseph Paxton’s Crystal Palace, though illustrated newspapers had already given the building another audience.
Paxton understood the usefulness of that audience early. His newspaper image helped build excitement for a proposal still competing for approval. This way, representation became part of the project’s public understanding before it was even built.
World’s fairs were filled with these split existences. Their pavilions were temporary by design, but photographs and printed images gave them an eternal life. The Eiffel Tower remained in Paris, while many structures surrounding it at the 1889 Exposition survive only through their representations. Architecture could vanish from a site and remain alive as a still image.
Crystal Palace, illustration of the transept of the Crystal Palace, designed by Sir Joseph Paxton, at the Great Exhibition of 1851, Hyde Park, London | image courtesy Britannica
modernism finds the page
By the early twentieth century, architecture and mass media were growing together. Le Corbusier selected photographs, edited them and arranged them across books with an understanding that the page could construct its own architectural experience. A house became a sequence in itself as the reader entered through one photograph, turned a page and found another. At this time, experiencing built space in this way was relatively novel.
Historian Beatriz Colomina highlighted this relationship as part of her reading of modernism in Privacy and Publicity. She wrote: ‘modern architecture only becomes modern with its engagement with the media.‘
Her argument places publications and other systems of representation inside architectural production itself. Le Corbusier’s buildings existed on their sites, while another version was being assembled through photographs and printed pages for a much larger public.
‘Le Corbusier: Architect of Books’, Catherine de Smet, archival interior photograph of the L’Esprit Nouveau Pavilion, 1925 | image courtesy Nostos
photography begins changing the building
Claire Zimmerman, Professor of Architecture at the University of Toronto, describes an even more consequential exchange in Photographic Architecture in the Twentieth Century. Architects first turned to photography because it reproduced lines and planes so effectively and helped their work circulate. That relationship soon moved in both directions.
‘Photography altered the material that it represented,‘ Zimmerman writes. Her study follows the overlap between how modern buildings looked and how photographic images made them look.
Once architects spent years seeing architecture flattened onto magazine pages, those pages inevitably entered the visual imagination of architecture itself. Glass became reflection, and white walls became fields of light and shadow. A corner could take up an entire spread. Even though buildings were still rooms and structures, they were being designed inside a culture that was beginning to understand what a camera could extract from them.
Lucia Moholy. Bauhaus Workshop Building from Below. Oblique View. September 1926 | image courtesy MoMA
the pavilion that survived as photographs
Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich’s Barcelona Pavilion makes this exchange especially strange. The original structure stood for only a short time before it was dismantled in 1930. For the decades that followed, architects encountered its marble planes and chrome columns through a limited body of black-and-white photographs. The building became foundational to modern architectural culture while remaining physically absent.
When the pavilion was finally rebuilt in 1986, generations had already spent more than half a century looking at it. Through photography, the project was at once preserved and reinvented. Those images determined the pavilion’s most familiar views, flattened its colors into tones, and established an object that existed outside of built space. The reconstruction eventually gave visitors a building they could walk into, but those photographs had reached them first.
Barcelona Pavilion, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich, 1929 | image © Marcin Jezyk
‘a picture of a mood’ becomes the house
Pierre Koenig’s Case Study House #22 offers a more intimate version of the same phenomenon. Julius Shulman arrived to photograph the house in May 1960 while the Stahls were still waiting to move in. Construction dust remained, and was surrounded by incomplete landscaping. During the photoshoot, Shulman noticed two young women sitting in the cantilevered glass corner and rebuilt his composition around them, with Los Angeles glimmering below.
The now-iconic photograph feels effortless because the moment was authentic and temporary. Shulman later described the image as ‘a picture of a mood.’
For millions of people, Shulman’s photograph is their first encounter with Case Study House #22. The image has circulated so widely that Koenig’s architecture and Shulman’s construction of it have become almost inseparable. The house had rooms, changing daylight and years of family life. The photograph compressed all of that into one corner at one hour and somehow gained the greater cultural reach.
Julius Shulman, Case Study House #22, Pierre Koenig, Los Angeles, California | image courtesy Sotheby’s
las vegas reads at highway speed
Denise Scott Brown’s photographs of Las Vegas capture a landscape built to be read in motion. Motel signs hang against huge skies, lettering often larger than the buildings it advertises. In Learning from Las Vegas, Scott Brown, Robert Venturi and Steven Izenour described this as ‘an architecture of communication over space,’ where ‘communication dominates space as an element in the architecture and in the landscape.’ The Strip had to make itself legible before the driver passed it.
Photography was central to how Scott Brown studied that condition. She documented roads, signs and commercial strips. She said: ‘I am not a photographer. I shoot for architecture.‘ The camera became a way to isolate the visual logic of the city. With a vibrant sign floating against the sky, or a parking fronting a low box, architecture is compressed into an image quickly enough to be understood at speed.
Denise Scott Brown, Architettura Minore on The Strip, Las Vegas, 1966 | image courtesy Carriage Trade
from a handful of images to thousands
For much of the twentieth century, a major building entered architectural culture through a small set of photographs. Photographers chose the views, editors repeated them, and certain angles slowly became inseparable from the buildings themselves. Shulman’s Stahl House and the familiar photographs of Mies’s Barcelona Pavilion gained their authority partly through this scarcity.
The smartphone broke open that small circle of image makers. A visitor can photograph a building, edit the image and publish it before leaving. Theorist Lev Manovich calls Instagram ‘the perfect medium of the ‘aesthetic society,’ where image-making has become far more accessible. Architecture now enters a stream of pictures produced almost continuously by the people moving through it.
Corinne Vionnet’s Photo Opportunities combines repeated tourist photographs into a collective image
the visitor enters the frame
MVRDV’s Depot Boijmans Van Beuningen makes this shift especially obvious. Its mirrored facade absorbs Rotterdam and everybody standing around it. Before the building opened, Winy Maas was already watching passersby search for ‘the best place to stand to take a good selfie.’ The visitor becomes part of the architectural image almost automatically.
Case Study House #22 became famous through one highly controlled photograph. A contemporary museum can generate thousands of competing views in its first week. One person photographs the facade while another turns the camera toward themselves. Architecture now often circulates through a constantly feed of images rather than a single iconic frame.
Depot Boijmans Van Beuningen, MVRDV, Rotterdam, The Netherlands, 2020 | image © Ossip van Duivenbode
architecture learns from its own image
This sense of abundance also feeds back into design. Openings frame views, mirrors multiply scenes, and circulation creates new positions between bodies and buildings. Of course these elements physically exist in space, but they also lend themselves to be easily photographed. A building can keep offering images as people move through it.
Claire Zimmerman’s line that ‘Photography altered the material that it represented’ captures the longer exchange. Architects designed buildings, saw them returned as photographs, then designed the next buildings with this image-centric culture in mind. In this way, the camera became part of how architecture understood itself.
Le Corbusier, Beistegui Apartment-external terrace on the 4th and last floor (from Le Corbusier, Oeuvre complète 1929-1934, Paris 1947) | image via Research Gate
the camera moves inside
For most of photography’s history, some distance remained between a building and the production of its public image. Shulman arrived to LA with equipment, Scott Brown photographed Las Vegas as research, publications gradually carried those pictures elsewhere, but the smartphone compresses those stages almost completely.
Buildings now see versions of themselves circulating within hours of their public openings. The smartphone — and social media — accelerated a generations-long exchange between buildings and their representation. Architecture spent the twentieth century learning what it looked like in photographs. Now, the camera walks through the door with everyone else.
Louvre Abu Dhabi, Atelier Jean Nouvel, United Arab Emirates, 2017 | image © Laurian Ghinitoiu
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

Sudan gold mine collapse kills 82
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:50:13 UTC
19:50:13 KST

Sudan gold mine collapse kills 82
At least 82 people have been killed after an informal gold mine collapsed in Sudan’s West Kordofan state, with dozens more still missing, according to several news agencies, citing local officials.
Rescue efforts are continuing at the al-Zara mine near the town of Nuhud, an area controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The collapse began in one shaft on Sunday and spread to interconnected tunnels.
Rescuers recovered 82 bodies by Wednesday afternoon, Suleiman Abu Hmeida, a member of Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms, told AP. “But dozens remain unaccounted for,” he said.
The Emergency Response Rooms is a grassroots network that provides assistance to communities and monitors developments during Sudan’s ongoing conflict. A local administration official separately confirmed the same death toll, according to AP.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army (Sudanese Armed Forces, SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). This occurred after months of tension between their commanders, army generals Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo ‘Hemedti’, respectively, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands and displacing millions.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi–US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. Sudanese officials have named Colombians and Ukrainians among mercenaries backing the RSF against the army. Officials have also accused Ukraine and the United Arab Emirates of involvement and recently claimed the European Union has an “incomplete understanding of the complex situation” in the country.
Khartoum has also accused authorities in neighboring Kenya of backing the RSF and has broken ties with the East African grouping IGAD amid mistrust of regional mediation. In July, TASIS, a political coalition aligned with the paramilitary, announced the formation of a rival government months after its members signed a charter in Nairobi. It named Gen. Dagalo as chairman of a 15-member presidential council, a move rejected by the UN and AU.
The Sudan Doctors Network earlier reported 67 recovered bodies and said the death toll could rise as the search continues. The medical group said the informal mine employed unregulated workers and lacked basic safety and protective measures.
“The Network emphasizes that mining activities in areas under RSF control, in the absence of safety standards and adequate protection and rescue equipment, turn mining into a direct threat to the lives of civilians,” they said.
The Kordofan Observatory monitoring group said the mining area extends for more than a kilometer over fragile sandy soil.
Gold is one of Sudan’s most valuable commodities, with official figures showing gold exports generating more than $1.5 billion in the first ten months of 2024, despite the ongoing conflict. The country produced 70 tons of gold in 2025, according to the figures from the state-owned the Sudanese Mineral Resources Company (SMRC).
Deadly mine collapses have occurred elsewhere in Africa. In August, more than 100 people were reported killed when an artisanal gold mine collapsed in Zamboye in the Central African Republic, near the border with Cameroon. Several underground tunnels caved in while miners were working below ground.

Burning tires, empty pumps: $100 oil sparks global unrest as Iran war drags on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:49:20 UTC
19:49:20 KST

With no clear end to the war with Iran, most shipping through the Strait of Hormuz still disrupted and escalating fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis placing additional pressure on alternative oil routes, the global energy crisis is increasingly spilling into the streets. Oil has again climbed above $100 a barrel, protesters have burned tires and vehicles, workers have gone on strike and governments from Asia to Europe are scrambling to contain public anger.
The strain is especially acute in developing economies that rely heavily on imported Middle Eastern oil and gas. Many governments already accumulated debt trying to cushion households and businesses from earlier price increases during more than six months of war. They now face the same politically dangerous calculation again: allow higher energy costs to reach consumers and risk accelerating inflation and unrest, or expand subsidies and relief programs at the cost of larger deficits and pressure on local currencies.
“How much fiscal capacity does Asia or the developing world have in general to manage this geopolitical crisis?” Sana Jaffrey, an Asia conflict expert at Australian National University, told The New York Times. She warned that when governments begin exhausting that capacity, the consequences will spread well beyond the countries now struggling with fuel shortages.
Syria erupts after fuel prices jump
Some of the most dramatic protests have unfolded in Syria, where demonstrations broke out across several cities after authorities announced increases of as much as 40% for fuel and gas. The government attributed the move to soaring global prices and work at the country’s largest refinery that has reduced domestic production and increased reliance on imports.
For a country still struggling to recover from more than a decade of devastating civil war, the increase proved explosive. Protesters blocked major roads with burning tires, including routes around Aleppo, and demonstrations continued for several days. In Kurdish-majority Qamishli, protesters carried signs declaring, “No to the policy of starvation.” One demonstrator, 56-year-old Abdel Rahman Khalil, said the public would no longer remain silent and demanded that authorities respond to people’s demands.
Other governments in the region are confronting the same pressure. Lebanon has reported sharp increases in gasoline and diesel prices, while Iraq has seen long lines at filling stations and growing criticism of the government’s ability to secure domestic supplies.
Israel chose another approach. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich temporarily cut the excise tax on gasoline by half a shekel per liter, reducing the regulated price from 8.25 shekels to 7.75. The measure, which runs through Oct. 31, has been criticized by opponents as “election economics” because it comes shortly before Israel’s Oct. 27 election.
Shortages, strikes and blackouts across Asia
The energy shock is particularly severe across Asia, where many economies depend heavily on Middle Eastern supplies.
In Makassar, the capital of Indonesia’s South Sulawesi province, residents have reported shortages of gasoline and cooking gas alongside rolling blackouts. Drivers have been seen pushing motorcycles after running out of fuel or abandoning them in long lines at filling stations. Taxi drivers protested against fuel rationing, while a student demonstration against rising prices in Yogyakarta was broken up.
Line at a gas station in Makassar:
In the Philippines, transport workers launched protests demanding fuel subsidies and lower taxes. Fishermen around Manila Bay, already kept ashore for weeks by monsoon rains, have found that soaring diesel and gasoline costs make returning to sea unaffordable.
“Many were raring to go back to fish, but have no money to buy gas,” fishing association leader Fernando Hicap told The New York Times. Bus drivers have described similarly punishing economics, with some saying shifts of up to 18 hours now barely cover the cost of a meal. The government has offered one-time assistance of about $80 to public transport drivers, but industry representatives say it falls far short of what is needed.
Ride-hailing drivers in Vietnam have also called for protests over fuel costs. Demonstrations have been reported in Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, where the energy crunch has compounded an already serious gas shortage. Textile and other industrial plants around Dhaka have been forced to suspend or sharply reduce production, threatening jobs in one of the country’s most important industries.
For Asian governments, the danger is that subsidies meant to prevent immediate unrest may only shift the crisis onto national balance sheets. Public debt in several countries has already risen as governments absorb costs that consumers cannot bear.
French fishermen block fuel depots
Europe is feeling the squeeze as well. In southern France, fishermen have repeatedly blocked oil terminals and fuel depots to protest soaring diesel costs and deteriorating working conditions.
At Fos-sur-Mer, police cleared fishermen from a fuel depot earlier this week. The protests then moved to Frontignan, where around 100 fishermen blocked access Wednesday before police intervened. On Thursday, fishermen returned, burning pallets and tires and preventing fuel trucks from entering or leaving as their representatives prepared to meet the government.
The demonstrations have centered on a simple complaint: at current fuel prices, fishermen say going to sea is becoming economically impossible. The French government has responded by extending targeted fuel assistance through the end of the year and raising aid available to fishermen.
In Portugal, drivers organized through social media have staged slow-moving convoys, deliberately creating traffic jams while sounding their horns. One convoy reportedly blocked access near the major refinery at Sines. The government has announced measures aimed at easing pressure on taxi drivers, transport companies and emergency services as diesel prices reach record levels.
Cars burned in Guatemala
The protests have also reached Latin America.
In Guatemala, truckers, trade groups and other demonstrators have blocked roads over fuel prices, with some protests turning violent. Vehicles and barricades have been set on fire, and two police officers were shot and wounded during clashes on Sept. 11.
President Bernardo Arévalo has accused criminal groups and political rivals of exploiting legitimate public dissatisfaction to provoke violence and destabilize his government. Lawmakers are considering legislation that would cap diesel and gasoline prices and trigger government subsidies once prices cross a specified threshold.
The scenes in Guatemala, Syria and elsewhere illustrate how an oil supply shock that begins thousands of miles away can quickly merge with local grievances over poverty, inequality, taxes and distrust of government.
In the US, no protests but growing political pressure
The United States has so far avoided the street protests seen elsewhere, but fuel prices are becoming an increasingly significant political problem for President Donald Trump and Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
A New York Times/Siena poll conducted Sept. 8-13 found a sharp deterioration in perceptions of the economy even among Republican voters. In January, 72% of Republicans said the economy was better than it had been a year earlier; by September, that figure had fallen to 29%. The poll also found widespread dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of the cost of living and the Iran war.
Fuel prices help explain the anxiety. Diesel has climbed above $6 a gallon and gasoline has hovered above $4 nationally, while economists warn that expensive energy can feed through into transportation, food, electricity and home-heating bills.
Trump has repeatedly insisted that the Iran war will end soon and that fuel prices will fall sharply when it does. At a campaign rally in North Carolina this week, he again sought to reassure voters as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress.
The president has also argued that temporarily higher energy costs are justified by the objectives of the war, presenting them as a price Americans must bear for the campaign against Iran.
For governments elsewhere, however, there is less room to absorb that price. If disrupted energy supplies persist into winter, when heating demand rises across the Northern Hemisphere, pressure on households, businesses and public finances could intensify further.
The question is increasingly no longer whether the Iran war will raise the cost of energy around the world. It is how much economic and political strain governments can absorb before the anger now visible on streets from Syria to France and Guatemala spreads further.

‘So many loopholes’: Democratic House leader Jeffries flags concerns over Russia sanctions bill – US politics live

United States Institute of Peace files emergency motion to block carving of Trump's name on its facade
While Donald Trump ponders demolishing the Kennedy Center unless his name is added to the memorial for the slain president, the United States Institute of Peace filed an emergency motion in federal court on Thursday asking a judge to block his administration “from carrying out plans to carve President Trump’s name into the façade of the iconic USIP headquarters building.”
The filing was made in a court battle that began in May 2025, when a federal judge ruled that Elon Musk’s so-called “department of government efficiency”, or US Doge service, illegally took over the the non-profit thinktank created and funded by the US Congress through “blunt force, backed up by law enforcement officers from three separate local and federal agencies”.
Musk’s Doge staff fired most USIP employees in a late-night email in March 2025, and then forcefully entered the thinktank’s building after cancelling its contract for private security.
In court, the USIP has maintained the organization is an independent creation of Congress and outside the president’s executive authority. The administration argues it is an executive branch organization, and pushed ahead, last December, with affixing Trump’s name to the exterior of the building, using bolted-on lettering. That change already offended the USIP board members who filed the suit, but carving Trump’s name into the stone, they argued on Thursday, “would cause irreparable harm”.
In the new filing, lawyers for the USIP argue that the administration, including Trump and his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, have not followed the court’s order to maintain the status quo at the institute:
Rather, they continued to dismantle USIP and to actively undermine the organizational independence enshrined in USIP’s organic statute— including by affixing the President’s name to the building. Unsatisfied with the relative impermanence of external lettering, Appellants apparently now intend to carve President Trump’s name into the façade of USIP’s privately owned headquarters building while this litigation is pending. The building—which was largely funded by private donations to USIP as a tax exempt nonprofit corporation— is a work of expressive architecture designed to be “symbolic of USIP’s “independent “mission.”

A canvasser for a Maine political action committee who was paid to knock on doors in support of Republican senator Susan Collins faces criminal charges after being caught on a doorbell camera stealing a package from an absent homeowner’s porch in Woolwich, Maine on Wednesday afternoon.
Video of the man, dressed in a red T-shirt with the name of the PAC, Stronger Maine, on the front and the name of the candidate, Susan Collins, on the back went viral after it was posted on Facebook by the homeowner.
Stronger Maine called the police and fired the canvasser immediately, a source who has worked with the group told the Bangor Daily News.
The Collins campaign said that the man was not employed by them.
According to Federal Election Commission records, more than half of Stronger Maine’s $2.6m in fundraising this year has come from from the Virginia-based conservative dark-money group Stronger America, which donated $1.4m.
Andy O’Brien, the former managing editor of a Rockland, Maine newspaper, pointed out on social media that the canvasser did a poor job of covering his tracks, because, before he grabbed the package and ran to his car, he left a flyer for Collins hanging on the homeowner’s front door.

The US Postal Service has stopped work on developing a computer system that was central to Donald Trump’s effort to limit mail voting after the supreme court rejected the planned to change to how mail ballots are delivered this week, postmaster general DavidSteiner told the Associated Press.

'I don’t know what the hell that means', Trump says of executive order he signed to let hunters use lead ammunition
Donald Trump signed a pair of executive orders to expand hunting and fishing on Thursday which, he told a gathering of outdoor industry leaders in the White House Rose Garden, mean “opening up millions of acres of federal land for our hunters and fishers.”
The orders seek to expand fresh and saltwater fishing and direct the secretary of the interior and other federal agencies to find ways to expand hunting, including of species not subject to certain endangered protection laws, within 90 days.
Those agencies will then have 180 days to propose rollbacks to federal restrictions against hunting and fishing on federal land and to find ways to expand using that land for recreation.
“This builds on our actions in August that opened up another 92 million acres of federal land across 32 states,” Trump said in remarks he largely read, and even hinted he did not entirely understand.
“We believe that public lands belong to the American people and to the public and hunters, fishers, and outdoorsmen should be able to access them and they weren’t able to,” Trump read aloud from a text he suggested his interior secretary, Doug Burgum, had prepared for him. “And this order also protects the use of affordable, traditional le-” Trump read, and then stopped to comment on what were supposed to be his own remarks.
“Well, this is pretty good. Is that- I never knew this was a problem, Doug. You’re going to have to educate me, but you put it in,” he said to Burgum, before continuing to read the text: “lead ammunition.”
The president then paused and looked up again to comment: “Is ammunition, lead ammunition was a problem, huh? Is it better than other ammunition? I assume, huh? That’s uh pretty good. I don’t know what the hell that means, but I know one thing: you wanted it, you wanted it, and I’m here for you,” he told the industry leaders assembled before him, who burst into applause.
“So, the order protects the use of affordable traditional lead ammunition,” Trump continued reading.
“That sounds good to me,” he said.
As Trump spoke, the website of the US Fish and Wildlife Service, an agency within the Department of the Interior, still officially encouraged hunters to go “lead-free”, urging hunters to take advantage of “Lead-free ammunition incentives available at 26 refuges across 19 states” for the 2026–2027 hunting season.
“Protect wildlife by choosing lead-free ammunition this hunting season. Encourage other hunters to choose lead-free ammunition for all hunting, including big game,” the agency urged hunters, as of Thursday night.
The agency’s website even answers the question Trump apparently failed to ask: “Why choose lead-free hunting ammunition?” with the following information – now apparently to be discarded at his order:
Lead fragments on impact. Lead ammunition loses weight as small pieces strip from the front of the bullet or shot as it passes through an animal. These fragments are found farther from the wound channel than you may expect, and many are too small to see with the naked eye, making them difficult to remove.
Fragments reach scavengers. Lead fragments may be left in the remains after harvesting an animal, even after field dressing. Remains from field-dressed animals provide a food source for scavenging wildlife, including bald and golden eagles.
Lead-free ammunition leaves less behind. When ingested, a lead fragment no bigger than a grain of rice can sicken and even kill an animal the size of a bald eagle. Lead-free ammunition leaves little or no fragments behind that could be consumed by scavenging wildlife.

The US Senate on Wednesday blocked an effort by Sen. John Kennedy to fast-track legislation requiring developers of advanced artificial intelligence systems to install an emergency “kill switch,” amid growing debate in Washington over the potential risks posed by increasingly autonomous AI.
Kennedy, a Republican from Louisiana, sought unanimous consent to advance his AI Emergency Button Act, arguing that humans must retain the ability to shut down an AI system if it becomes uncontrollable, according to The Hill.
“Well, I’ve got a bill, and it basically says that if you’re going to sell an advanced AI model in the United States of America, it has got to have a kill switch,” Kennedy said.
He said the legislation would leave responsibility for activating the switch with the companies developing the systems rather than the federal government.
A “kill switch”
Kennedy warned that advances such as recursive self-improvement could, in a worst-case scenario, allow an AI model to operate beyond effective human control.
“What I would like to see us do is to figure out a way to strike a balance between innovation and public safety,” Kennedy said.
Sen. Rand Paul, a Republican from Kentucky, objected to the request, saying Congress should seek a better understanding of the technology before imposing broad requirements.
Paul warned that an open-ended mandate could affect AI systems used throughout the economy, including search engines and medical applications.
“AI is going to be throughout the economy and so many facets. Are doctors going to have to build a kill switch into drug prescription analysis?” Paul said.
Paul proposed establishing a bipartisan committee to study the risks posed by superintelligent AI and possible safeguards. Kennedy rejected the proposal, arguing that another congressional study could further delay action.

‘A really scary place for children’: English hospitals have chronic lack of health play staff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:45:29 UTC
19:45:29 KST

Children in English hospitals with serious illnesses are being exposed to avoidable trauma because too few health play professionals are being employed, analysis by a leading charity has found.
These workers help to support children through the trauma and anxiety that can come with receiving medical treatment while in hospital by providing play opportunities through games, toys and activities.
However, the hospitals are facing a shortage of such staff, leaving children without the relief such organised play and games can provide for those having treatment for serious conditions.
Across NHS hospitals, there are only 955 full-time equivalent health play professionals currently supporting 21 million child hospital admissions each year, according to figures obtained by the charity Starlight Children’s Foundation via freedom of information requests. This equates to a ratio of about one professional for every 22,061 admissions, far below the recommended staffing levels of one professional per 2,230 hospital admissions. In England, there are 820 health play professionals supporting almost 17m admissions.
Health play professionals can also help to provide positive healthcare experiences for children, which research has shown can help to reduce distress, improve cooperation and help to prevent lifelong healthcare avoidance and mental health problems associated with traumatic childhood healthcare experiences.
At the age of three, Lyndsey Hookway’s daughter Filly was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. She spent 26 months in and out of hospital undergoing treatment including chemotherapy.
Now 13, Filly recalls the positive impact health play had on her when she was younger.
“I definitely did feel less anxious and less nervous, and they definitely did help me overcome stuff like losing my hair, such as playing with a lion teddy called Ollie the Brave who had removable wigs,” Filly said. “I was definitely bored and so having the play specialists really did help with that.
“They really do make a big difference and it really did make a difference on the days that they weren’t there.”
She added: “They should be considered the same priority has other hospital staff because I think especially for children who they’re mostly for, the hospitals can be a really scary place. So it really does help.”
For Hookway, the play professionals also gave parents of seriously ill children relief at a time that was incredibly overwhelming for the whole family.
“Having the health play professionals was a nice break for Filly to have someone who wasn’t me, who was falling apart” Hookway said. “Filly was bored and scared and in pain and unwell, during all of her admissions. But she’s also got a mum who’s probably traumatised and stressed and spinning plates at home as well.”
She added: “We’ve seen the difference between the hospitals that were well-resourced by play specialists and the ones that weren’t.”
Alongside the shortage of specialist staff, Starlight also found that only 23% of NHS trusts and health boards across the UK had dedicated budgets to train health play professionals, resulting in a postcode lottery with inequitable access to therapeutic play support. Furthermore, no integrated care board (ICB) has a dedicated health play budget.
Only 5% of ICBs include health play within their children and young people’s strategies.
Cathy Gilman, the chief executive of Starlight, said: “Every child deserves healthcare that is compassionate as well as clinically excellent. Yet for too many children, hospital is frightening, overwhelming and, ultimately, traumatic. We know those experiences can stay with them for life, affecting their mental health and even whether they seek healthcare as adults.
“Play changes that. It helps children understand what is happening, gives them a sense of control, builds trust with the healthcare team and reduces fear before, during and after treatment. It isn’t entertainment and it certainly isn’t a luxury. It is an essential part of safe, effective children’s healthcare.”
An NHS spokesperson said: “The NHS has worked closely with Starlight to produce the health service’s first guidance aimed at improving health play services across England. This guidance developed with dozens of healthcare professionals is helping local health systems design services which are a welcoming and therapeutic environment for babies and children.”

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks to the members of the Parliament at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, September 17, 2026. | Ronald Wittek/EPA
STRASBOURG — Mark Carney used an address to the European Parliament to sketch out what Ottawa would want from closer ties with the EU but declined to give full-throated approval of Ursula von der Leyen’s surprise “associate member” plan.
Speaking a day after the Commission president floated the unique relationship status, the Canadian prime minister acknowledged the offer and instead of accepting it outright, listed potential individual areas of cooperation, including critical minerals, defense, AI, energy security, and space.
He also called for more seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and services, as well as Canadian participation in Erasmus+, the EU's student exchange program.
Advertisement
"We welcome this ambition," he said, after name-checking the idea of von der Leyen, who was sitting in the audience. "Polling shows an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties."
Carney's list of potential tie-ups was an early attempt to put substance behind what, for now, remains a largely undefined political proposition.
The “associate member” idea had caused confusion on Wednesday because the Commission hadn't run it past European capitals in advance and no such status currently exists. Later on Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump said he might respond with “serious tariffs” if Canada were to become closer to the EU.
"An alliance for the future is a unique, positive approach that we will define together, building on our common strengths and based on shared values," Carney said.

Advertisement
Before von der Leyen dropped the “associate member” label, Carney advised Canadian reporters that there would not be a “big reveal” in Strasbourg.
“The real deepening and discussions will be launched with our summit in Montreal … towards the end of October,” he said in Toronto on Tuesday on the sidelines of his global investment summit.“And then go for it from there.”
Europe is a top priority for the Carney government because the EU is viewed as the easiest way for Canada to deepen an existing free-trade relationship, one that was debated in Parliament a decade ago.
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly dropped a hint to reporters in Toronto on Wednesday that Ottawa is looking for additional guarantees on trade — which could require new legislation.
When asked about the possibility of “associate” EU membership, Joly observed that countries with free-trade agreements tend to become more insular to protect their own industries when targeted by tariffs.
She singled out the EU specifically.
Advertisement
“We want to make sure that markets are still opened between us and that not only a free trade agreement holds, but that we align our industrial policies, particularly in sectors impacted by the tariffs,” she said. “That’s really important.”

Quadcopters: Israel's weapon for indiscriminate killing in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:44:09 UTC
19:44:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Quadcopters: Israel's weapon of choice for indiscriminate killing in Gaza
Since 7 October 2023, the Israeli military has increased its use of drones known as "quadcopters" in the Gaza Strip, after previously deploying them in eastern and border areas.
This type of drone has been used extensively and on an unprecedented scale, are of multiple types, and their use has are not limited to attacking resistance fighters.
The Israeli military has relied on quadcopters in its field operations. Some emitted disturbing sounds or sent messages to civilians about displacement and movement, while others carried weapons. Particular types were designated for assassinations, either by detonating themselves or dropping explosive munitions.
Quadcopters have played an active and significant role in the context of this war, after previously appearing during the Great March of Return protests along the Gaza Strip border, which Palestinians organised from 2018 to 2023.
60 killed
A report issued by the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor on 12 September this year found that the Israeli army had killed at least 60 civilians with fire from these drones or with munitions they dropped since the ceasefire came into effect on 10 October 2025 until early September 2026.
According to the report, Israel has used small multi-rotor quadcopters and tactical drones in the Gaza Strip, which can be equipped with daylight and thermal cameras and systems for identifying and tracking targets.
It said some models can, depending on the mission, be fitted with 5.56 mm and 7.62 mm weapons or 40 mm explosive munitions.
Palestinians recently documented a video that was widely circulated on social media and described as "terrifying". It showed a quadcopter landing in Gaza City's eastern Tuffah neighbourhood at extremely low altitudes among residents' homes, filming inside homes and taking advantage of the absence of windows.
The footage reflects one of the typical ways this drone operates. The aircraft has become part of Palestinians' daily routine in Gaza, whether through its filming operations, deliberate or random gunfire towards areas where displaced people are staying, or the occasional dropping of inciting leaflets aimed at Palestinian resistance factions.
The Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor said field monitoring had identified three main patterns in the use of these aircraft.
The first involved precise and direct gunfire at individuals whom the operator could see and identify.
The second involved dropping explosive munitions on civilian gatherings and tents housing displaced people.
The third involved imposing fire control over areas adjacent to what is known as the "yellow line" by targeting civilians as they attempted to reach their homes and land or carry out their work there.
Ramy Abdu, head of the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, said the group had documented a rise in the Israeli army's use of quadcopters as a tool for precise killing in the Gaza Strip.
He stressed that they had not been used only to assassinate activists or people Israel claims are wanted but had also been used to target civilians, including children, directly.
He told The New Arab that the danger of using quadcopters lies in "their technical capabilities, which allow the operator to monitor the targeted person, verify their identity and track their movements before opening fire, greatly narrowing the margin for error in identifying the target and increasing the obligation to refrain from attacking when their civilian status becomes apparent, or there is any doubt about it".
He added that the repeated targeting of children, displaced people, farmers and shepherds with direct fire or munitions dropped from these aircraft, despite the clarity of their civilian status and their lack of any direct participation in hostilities or any imminent threat, collectively provides strong indications that targeting civilians was deliberate and was not the result of an error in identifying the target or an accidental attack.
He noted that these attacks are "prohibited from the outset" and cannot be justified on the grounds of military necessity or subjected to a proportionality assessment.
He further said that direct attacks on civilians are already prohibited and are not permitted by claims of military necessity or the rules of proportionality, and Israel's use of this weapon, according to the group's documentation, violates the principle of distinction under international humanitarian law, which requires parties to a conflict to distinguish between civilians and combatants.
Abdu stressed that the situation differs from weapons that may lack the ability to distinguish, as "the decision to open fire on civilians despite having the full ability to distinguish them is not related to the weapon's inability to distinguish, which means systematic, deliberate and intentional targeting".
On the ground, quadcopters are constantly present in the skies over the Gaza Strip, including areas where displaced people are staying.
Palestinians in displacement areas see these aircraft flying at different hours of the day and descending to extremely low altitudes.
Use of drones
Brigadier General and military affairs expert Naji Melaab said Israel had developed its use of small drones in the Gaza Strip, so they were no longer limited to reconnaissance and intelligence-gathering missions but had become a tool for carrying out precise targeting and killing operations.
Melaab told The New Arab that these drones are distinguished by their small size and ability to move in places that are difficult for soldiers to reach.
He said that they have been used inside tunnels and buildings in Gaza, where they can film the location and transmit information and images directly to the control centre.
He added that the drone can be operated by a single soldier and has advanced capabilities, including capturing sounds and transmitting them to the operator.
It can also create noise or broadcast messages depending on the mission assigned to it.
Melaab also said the most significant development was equipping the drone with a machine gun that allows the operator to control gunfire with precision.
He explained that it can also destroy itself if it crashes or reaches a designated location, and that Israel has used these drones in the Gaza Strip, particularly for reconnaissance operations, as well as for assassinations. The use represents a shift from drones designed for surveillance to systems capable of carrying out direct offensive missions.
This development reflects an advanced use of artificial intelligence and military technology in the war on Gaza, as the drone now combines reconnaissance, target identification and the ability to carry out strikes, thereby allowing killings to be conducted from a distance without soldiers entering the targeted location, according to Melaab.
He warned of the danger of this type of operation, particularly when relying on inaccurate intelligence.
Targeting a building or home with a drone can result in civilian deaths amid the difficulty of verifying information on the ground before carrying out the strike.

Le Pen is leading the polls ahead of a high-stakes presidential election next spring to replace Emmanuel Macron. One of the campaign's main issues is France's increasingly strained finances, with a public deficit that could exceed 5% this year.

National Rally officials privately say that Ukraine will never be able to repay the EU loan and it will ultimately fall on the bloc's capitals to do so.
"You can't say, on the one hand, that there isn't a single euro … to adjust pensions for inflation, but, on the other hand, that there are billions for the net contribution to the European Union," Le Pen said.
While the National Rally is internally divided over Russia, Ukraine and NATO, Le Pen's rivals have on multiple occasions accused her party of playing into the Kremlin’s hands in order to undermine the National Rally's credibility. The media has also repeatedly asked top party figures to clarify the party's line on assistance to Kyiv.
In Wednesday evening's interview, Le Pen stressed that France under her presidency would organize a conference for peace that would bring Russia, Ukraine and other European countries such as Germany and Poland to the table. The goal, she said, is to put an end to the war.
She also pushed back against proposals made by her presidential rivals, such as former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, to protect Ukraine's skies with French fighter jets — an option Paris has also so far refused to contemplate. "That would make us co-belligerents," Le Pen told LCI.

Every Iranian strike came with a cyberattack, UAE cyber chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:42:36 UTC
19:42:36 KST

Dr Mohamed Al Kuwaiti told Euronews the UAE was hit online and from the air at the same time, and says international law still has no answer for it.
Every missile and drone strike on the UAE during the Iran war was matched by a cyberattack on the same target, the head of the UAE Cybersecurity Council told Euronews on Wednesday.
In an interview at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai, Dr Mohamed Al Kuwaiti said the strikes and cyberattacks went hand in hand and that the mix of methods used against the UAE was, to his knowledge, unmatched anywhere.
"Whenever we see a kinetic attack on any of the ports or on any refineries or the airport, there is always a cyberattack towards many of those entities," he said.
"Cyber-crimes, cyber terrorism, cyber warfare, all of it came together during this crisis."
Dr Al Kuwaiti did not attribute the cyber operations to any state.
He listed supply chain compromises, ransomware, fraud, advanced persistent threats and deepfakes.
Electricity, water and aviation were all targeted. Most of that infrastructure is privately owned. Al Kuwaiti said its operators, Emirati and foreign, held it alongside the state.
"Local private sectors or international private sectors, they all came together into this solidarity," he said. "We are one of the global leaders in cyber defence."
He said a second campaign ran online, where false material spread faster than verified reporting.
"We saw during the crisis how many rumours came out here and there," he said. "Now it's no longer seeing is believing."
Al Kuwaiti wants international law to catch up. No treaty sets out what a state may do when it is attacked through a network rather than by a weapon.
"There is still no Cyber Geneva Convention that protects based on the laws, as in the physical laws," he said. "A nation that gets attacked by cyber, does it actually have the right to attack back? Those laws are blurred."
He said security should be built into systems from the start, including AI agents and large language models, and that governments, companies, universities and civil society should share what they know.
"Countries might really spend so much in doing their digital transformations, but yet with a simple attack all of this could go down," he said.
The UAE is targeting AI-driven nation status by 2071 and is building data centre and cloud capacity to match. Al Kuwaiti said he would keep pressing for agreement on cyber norms through the United Nations and the International Telecommunication Union.

Yemen escalation displaces more than 57,000 children: UNICEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:38:41 UTC
19:38:41 KST

Yemen escalation displaces more than 57,000 children: UNICEF
Renewed fighting in Yemen is deepening an already severe humanitarian crisis in a country where more than 12 million children depend on aid, after more than a decade of conflict.
The warning comes from the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) which said that more than 57,000 children have been displaced in just the past two weeks while others have been killed, injured or reported missing.
“Children in Yemen were already living through one of the world’s most grave humanitarian crises, and many have known little but conflict and displacement,” said Edouard Beigbeder, UNICEF Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa.
“For children who have already endured years of hunger, displacement and disrupted schooling, this latest violence is eroding what little stability they had left.”
Children killed and injured
Yemeni Government forces, supported by a Saudi-led coalition, and Iran-backed Houthi militia have been at war since 2014, but the country had experienced relative calm following a UN-backed truce in 2022.
The new escalation has forced tens of thousands of families to flee their homes, triggering widespread displacement across several governorates, including Taiz, Hudaydah and Marib.
Since 3 September, at least nine children have been reported killed and 12 injured while three others are missing following an attack on the road from Yemen’s western coast to Aden.
Healthcare and education disrupted
The fighting has also cut children’s access to healthcare and education. UNICEF said services at 26 health facilities that it supports have been disrupted, while 243 schools have closed or suspended classes, affecting more than 137,000 students.
The agency is expanding its emergency response to reach up to 231,000 people. Teams have supported health facilities and distributed hygiene kits and water tanks in Taiz, while providing additional water and hygiene supplies in Marib.
Nine health and nutrition mobile teams have been redeployed to displacement sites and affected communities in Aden, Marib and Taiz. Emergency water and sanitation teams also aim to reach more than 200,000 people with safe water and hygiene supplies and carry out urgent repairs to damaged systems.
Meanwhile, child protection teams are providing psychosocial care and case management, including for unaccompanied and separated children. They are also helping make communities aware of the dangers posed by unexploded ordnance.
Supporting arrivals in Djibouti
UNICEF is also working with authorities in Djibouti to support Yemeni families who have fled there after making the dangerous journey across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. More than 2,000 people, including many children, have now arrived in the country.
The UN agency recalled that even before this latest escalation, roughly 12.2 million children in Yemen needed humanitarian assistance. More than 2.2 million under-fives are acutely malnourished, including over 515,000 suffering severe acute malnutrition.
Across Yemen, around 17.8 million people lack adequate access to healthcare, water and sanitation services, and only 60 per cent of health facilities are fully functional. Some 3.2 million school-age children are out of school.
UNICEF echoed the UN Secretary-General’s call for all parties to protect civilians, including children, respect international humanitarian law, and facilitate safe and unimpeded humanitarian access to communities in need.

As freshwater reserves shrink, countries must prepare for a new water reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:38:16 UTC
19:38:16 KST

As freshwater reserves shrink, countries must prepare for a new water reality
The world is entering a period in which abnormal water supplies are becoming the norm, with river flows, groundwater and glaciers all showing signs of sustained disruption, the UN weather agency warned on Thursday.
“This is not a single bad year, but a persistent decade-long signal,” said Celeste Saulo, Secretary-General of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), presenting the agency’s latest State of Global Water Resources report.
The assessment shows that 2025 was one of the driest years for river flows worldwide in 35 years, with below-normal discharge across 36 per cent of the world’s river basin area.
It was also the seventh consecutive year in which rivers with historically “normal” flows were in a clear minority, underscoring what WMO describes as an increasingly erratic and unpredictable water cycle.
“Water-related extreme events continue to devastate communities and economies,” Ms. Saulo underscored.
Water ‘savings account’
Groundwater, glaciers, snow, soil moisture, lakes and other freshwater stored on land, act as a buffer during droughts and dry seasons. Ms. Saulo described these slower reserves as the planet’s “savings account”.
Traditionally, she explained, they have absorbed bad years so that a single dry season does not immediately become a water crisis.
“We are depleting that savings account,” she said, noting that terrestrial water storage has been declining since around 2014–2016, while groundwater levels in many regions have fallen over several years.
Nearly two-thirds of monitored groundwater wells were outside their normal range in 2025, with conditions shifting further towards deficit, than recovery.
There were, however, some positive signs. Parts of South America saw a partial recovery in water storage after a severe multi-year deficit, while central and southern Africa maintained much above-normal water levels across several major lakes.
Glacial melt
Every major glacier region on Earth lost ice for the fourth consecutive year.
“All 19 glacier regions around the globe lost ice; in Central Asia, Iceland, the Russian Arctic and western Canada and the United States, it was among the three worst years on record,” said Wayne Jenkinson, WMO’s Director of Hydrology and Cryosphere.
In 2025 alone, glaciers lost around 408 gigatonnes of ice, while cumulative losses between 2023 and 2025 reached roughly 1,400 gigatonnes – equivalent to around one third of the freshwater the world withdraws in a year.
Some regions with smaller glaciers such as Central Europe, the Caucasus, the western Canada and the United States may already have reached “peak water”, Jenkinson warned.
“After this point, the glacier gives less meltwater each year simply because there is less ice left to melt. That matters for every community downstream that relies on water during hot, dry summers,” he said.
Narelle van der Wel, WMO’s Head of Cryosphere Monitoring, Predictions and Services, stressed that while some further glacier loss is unavoidable, the eventual scale of the decline is not predetermined.
“Some glacier loss is inevitable, but total loss of glaciers is not yet inevitable,” she said, pointing to emissions reductions as central to limiting future losses.
Moving the baseline
The report does not attribute every observed change to climate change alone. WMO says pressure on water resources and natural variability also contribute.
Mr. Jenkinson said governments need to prepare for “moving baselines” as historical patterns become less reliable.
“The situation 30 years ago is not where we are today,” he said. Countries, he added, need to prepare “for those changes that have really already arrived”.
Over the past five years, Asia and Africa accounted for at least half of reported water-related extreme events and more than 80 per cent of associated deaths, yet both remain among the regions with the largest gaps in water observations.
Water monitoring has improved significantly since WMO began publishing the report five years ago, with 52 countries now providing data from more than 3,100 river-flow stations, compared with just seven countries and 14 stations in the first edition.
However, WMO says better monitoring, data-sharing and early warnings will be increasingly important as countries adapt to water conditions that are already radically changing.
The recent China-Nepal disaster, which WMO described as a “catastrophic compound crisis” involving a rock and glacier failure, showed how difficult such hazards can be to anticipate.
“Water respects no borders,” Ms. Saulo said. “This is why we need shared data, shared standards and shared early warnings.”
