Trump slams EU touting Canada membership as 'hostile' act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:12:00 UTC
17:12:00 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened action against the EU if it moves forward with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal to make Canada the bloc's first associate member.
"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina, calling the proposal "laughable."
"If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe," he added.
The European Commission said von der Leyen's proposal – which is yet to be fleshed out and will need to be approved by EU member states to go forward – was not a hostile act.
"As our President (von der Leyen) made clear yesterday, the proposed strengthening of our partnership with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength," said Olof Gill, a European Commission spokesperson.
France's Europe Minister Benjamin Haddad said the United States has no power to veto the EU's geopolitical choices.
"It is not up to the United States – or anyone else – to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans," he told Public Senat TV.
Von der Leyen made the proposal Wednesday during her annual State of the Union speech, attended by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, as she sought to deepen ties among allies in what she called "an openly hostile world."
The EU faces the risk of war on its borders due to Russia's invasion of Ukraine, while both the bloc and Canada have grappled with trade tensions with the United States and an increasingly assertive China.
Earlier this month, Carney had said he was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU as relations between Ottawa and Washington have deteriorated since Trump's return to the White House, leading to tariffs on tens of billions of dollars in cross-border trade.
It is unclear at this stage whether von der Leyen's proposal of associate membership would be backed by EU member states or by Canada.
One EU diplomat expressed surprise Wednesday at the proposal, saying "nobody really knows what it means," adding there were concerns that the European Commission chief "is overpromising and won't be able to deliver." The EU has historically resisted such flexible alliances that have no legal status.
On Thursday, another European diplomat called it an "unfortunate proposal, which has never been discussed with Member States."
A third European diplomat said Trump's reaction said more about how he views international relations than about von der Leyen's proposal.
"If this is described as a hostile act, it suggests that partnerships are a zero-sum game where closer cooperation with one means loss of sovereign choice for another," the diplomat said. "And it also hints that the U.S. sees Canada as part of its sphere of influence rather than an independent actor."
Another European diplomat added: "It’s a good thing that we learned in the meantime to not take every statement of President Trump seriously."

17:12:00 KST

President Donald Trump said he hoped the seven-month war with Iran was nearing an end as the conflict escalated, with Saudi aircraft striking Yemen and Houthi fighters launching drones and missiles at Saudi cities.
The Iran-backed Houthis' lightning advance in Yemen along the Red Sea, their attacks on Saudi Arabia and damage to Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline have extended Tehran's reach in the war and heightened global oil supply risks.
As the war expands into a new theater, the U.S. tightened its travel warning for Saudi Arabia, banning government employees from traveling within 30 kilometers (20 miles) of the Yemen border.
Still, just hours after reports of fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, Trump told reporters Wednesday evening: "Hopefully we are toward the end of the war."
Referring to Iran, he said: "They want to make a deal. We'll see how that works out." He also said he had heard directly from Iran, without elaborating, reiterating previous comments.
Trump has offered shifting goals and timelines for the war, which began Feb. 28 when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran and Tehran struck Israel and U.S. bases in Gulf states.
The war's extension into Yemen threatens to worsen the global energy supply shortage caused by the conflict, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The strait carried about 20% of global oil and LNG before the conflict.
Traders say a prolonged closure of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline could cut off as much as 4% of global oil supply. Saudi Arabia has not said when operations might resume.
The price of Brent crude hovered about $108 a barrel Wednesday, close to its highest levels since May. The politically sensitive average retail price of diesel fuel in the U.S. hit another record high, above $6.30 a gallon for the first time.
But oil prices fell in early Thursday trading as reports that Saudi Arabia was offering extra crude cargoes through Oman reduced fears of supply disruptions in the Middle East.
Brent crude futures dropped $1.24, or 1.2%, to $104.59 a barrel by 0049 GMT, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were down $1.14, or 1.1%, at $101.29.
The rise in oil and gas prices due to the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran has become a major issue for Trump's Republican Party in the run-up to the November midterm elections.
Axios reported late Wednesday that Trump was expected to meet Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly next Tuesday to discuss the next steps in the conflict.
Citing unidentified sources, the news outlet said Trump would meet with leaders or foreign ministers from the Gulf Cooperation Council countries: Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman. The State Department and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.
The Houthis Wednesday released battlefield video of fighters seizing armored vehicles from Saudi-backed forces. The video also showed warplanes flying overhead and huge explosions billowing into the sky from desert dunes.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said his group had launched new drone and missile strikes on the major Saudi Red Sea oil port of Yanbu and at a southern Saudi airbase at Khamis Mushait. He did not say when the strikes took place.
Saree said Saudi forces had carried out as many as 450 airstrikes on Yemen this week. Officials in the Saudi-backed government controlling southern Yemen acknowledged their forces and Saudi Arabia's forces were conducting airstrikes on Houthi positions, though Riyadh has not confirmed them.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition battling the Houthis since 2015. The conflict had largely quieted under a cease-fire in recent years but reignited when the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in July and fired at southern areas in the kingdom.

Lockheed hopes to sell a new F-16 to U.S. Air Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:11:22 UTC
17:11:22 KST

Lockheed Martin is pitching the U.S. Air Force on a new version of the F-16 fighter, designated the F-16G, as a way to replace aging Fighting Falcons faster than the F-35 production line can keep up.
Multiple people familiar with the aircraft told Aviation Week that the F-16G builds on the current Block 70 F-16, Lockheed’s newest production version, and would add conformal fuel tanks, 600-gallon wing tanks, an infrared search and track pod, a Sniper targeting pod and a drag chute. Those additions would extend the jet’s range and give it added sensor capability compared with earlier F-16 models still flying in Air Force squadrons.
The idea of buying new F-16s to fill out the fighter fleet is not new. Then-Air Force Assistant Secretary for Acquisition Will Roper raised the option back in 2021, pointing to the active F-16 production line in Greenville, South Carolina, as a way to add capacity while the F-35 program worked through its own delivery pace. Lockheed builds F-16s and F-35s at separate facilities, but the F-35’s more complex production process has left the Air Force short of new airframes to replace F-16s reaching the end of their service lives.
Lockheed Martin would not confirm details about the F-16G when asked on Sept. 16. The company said only that it remains ready to support the Air Force’s mission needs and described its aircraft as central to the service’s fleet. The Air Force likewise declined to comment on the F-16G specifically, saying it is still in the early stages of reviewing options for its next Future Years Defense Program and has not yet settled on requirements.
The push comes after a 2025 Air Force study identified a need for more fighter production to close a growing capacity gap. The Congressional Research Service says the service wants to grow its fighter inventory from 1,098 aircraft in fiscal 2026 to 1,558 by fiscal 2035, a target the Air Force has described as necessary to keep risk to its operations at an acceptable level under the National Military Strategy.
Other outlets have reported similar signals in recent months. Inside Defense reported in December 2025 that the Air Force was considering a new F-16 variant as a lower-cost way to fill capability gaps than buying more F-35s, and Air and Space Forces Magazine has reported that the F-16G is expected to come up for discussion at an upcoming Corona conference, the periodic gathering of the service’s top generals.
Neither the Air Force nor Lockheed Martin has said when a decision on the F-16G might come, or how many aircraft such a program could involve.

US Congress passes broad new sanctions bill to pressure Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:11:00 UTC
17:11:00 KST

U.S. lawmakers approved sweeping new sanctions Wednesday to pressure Russia over its war in Ukraine, sending the legislation to President Donald Trump after months of delay.
The Republican-led House of Representatives passed the package 262-159, giving final congressional approval to the most substantial U.S. legislative effort against Moscow since Trump returned to office.
Trump has said he will sign the measure, which cleared the Senate in an 86-11 vote last month.
The legislation targets Russia's energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow's so-called shadow fleet of tankers circumventing Western sanctions.
It also gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, including potentially China and India, to choke off revenue for Moscow's war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed the legislation's passage as "symbolic" and thanked U.S. lawmakers.
The bill is "an extremely powerful tool that can stop this terrorist war and bring Russia to the point where it has to make peace," Zelenskyy wrote in a statement.
"Sanctions must be strong so that all efforts for peace, including our joint diplomatic efforts with the United States, Europe, and our other friends, can succeed," he added.
The bill would also target companies and foreign actors supporting Russia's military and extend sanctions involving Iran.
India said Thursday it would continue buying oil "through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics."
Moscow is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners and military suppliers.
The legislation's sweeping tariff powers produced an unusual split among Democrats, who overwhelmingly support Ukraine but have resisted handing Trump greater authority over trade.
Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called the bill "deeply flawed."
"White House lawyers drafted the current text to maximize President Trump's authority to impose new import taxes on the American people, and to minimize any obligation to impose new sanctions on Russia or its enablers," he said.
Dozens of Democrats nevertheless backed the measure, offsetting opposition from a handful of Republicans who objected to sanctions on free-market or non-interventionist grounds.
Supporters argue that tougher economic pressure is needed, with Russia's full-scale invasion now in its fifth year and no peace settlement in sight.
Pro-Ukraine activists celebrated the House vote, pointing to continuing Russian attacks, including drone strikes Wednesday on civilian transport in the south that officials in Kyiv said killed five people.
Trump has generally preferred to retain control over sanctions and tariffs rather than have Congress dictate policy, which helped delay the measure for more than a year.
Its sponsor, Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly in July, had pushed the legislation since April 2025.
Wednesday's vote came just before House lawmakers were to leave Washington to campaign ahead of November's midterm elections.
"Once the bill is quickly signed and becomes law, we hope for strong U.S. enforcement to finally end the cash flows to the Kremlin's war chest," said Svitlana Romanko, executive director of Ukrainian energy lobby group Razom We Stand.
"Every day of delay is a day we in Ukraine must bury more people."

He says that’s why Poland must be very openly ready to follow through on its allied commitments.
“Article 5, loyalty within the alliance, and faithfulness to our commitments must become our hallmark,” he says.
Tusk says Russia is not prepared or willing to get involved in any serious discussions about ending its aggression against Ukraine “at least until the end of winter.”
“They are convinced that this winter will be a time of dire crisis for Ukraine,” he says.
Intelligence shows Russian 'plans for hybrid strikes ... against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,' Tusk says
Tusk says that intelligence assessments show “plans for hybrid strikes using drones and missiles against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland”.
He says the latest intelligence on this is “very consistent and convincing”.
He says that Russia is expected to pretend that any incidents are “accidental” in a bid to “paralyse or at least weaken Nato’s resolve to invoke the relevant provisions” of the Nato treaty.
“There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles could be launched into the territory of one or more Nato countries on the eastern flank, and could even cause damage, and the official narrative will be that this is an accident and that there is no reason for anyone to consider any response from Nato.
The aim … will be to weaken Nato’s integrity in general and, above all, to convince … member states that Article 5 is more theoretical than practical – that is, the assumption that no one will want to die for Latvia or Lithuania, given that we are dealing with incidents rather than a declaration of war.”
He says he expects Russia to use “recurrent” incidents to use them as “an increasingly stark illustration of Nato’s helplessness” to respond in a united manner.
Coming autumn, winter will be 'most critical moment' in Russian war against Ukraine, Tusk says
Tuskis now speaking in Polish parliament,speaking about what he believes Poland and Ukraine’s other allies should be expecting in the coming months as Russia ramps up pressure and threats against Nato.
He says he wants to outline “the most likely scenario for the next few months, as it is a scenario involving serious events and one that requires us to be focused, serious and, above all, mentally prepared to face difficult challenges.”
He says “late autumn and winter” are expected to be “the most critical moment” in the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine so far.
Tusk noted that Russia is increasing its attacks using jet-powered drones, which he believes “very few [countries] are currently prepared to effectively counter.”
“Russia’s objective today is to destroy Ukraine’s economy and logistics on as large a scale as possible. … Ukraine is expected to face constant strikes of very high frequency and intensity. This includes the six main Ukrainian cities, with the destruction of warehouses containing all types of products essential, first and foremost, for the country’s defence, as well as – as we have witnessed in recent weeks – very severe damage to the railway infrastructure.”
'If anyone dares to attack us, they will face a resolute response from us and allies,' Poland's Tusk says
Meanwhile, Polish prime minister Donald Tusk warned that “if anyone dares to attack us, they will face a resolute response from us and our allies,” as he responded to growing tensions and aggression from Russia.
In a sombre speech marking the 87th anniversary of the 1939 Soviet invasion of Poland, Tusk said he would “prefer to speak only about the heroic deeds recorded in the history books,” but “Russia’s escalating aggression is not letting me do that.”
“History, as we know, does not repeat itself, but it does rhyme, and we must interpret these rhymes of history today with due seriousness,” he said.
Responding to recent Russian incidents in and around Poland – including last year’s drone incursion into Poland, a Russian missile straying into Poland in July, and recent incidents at the Polish-Ukrainian border – Tusk insisted that Warsaw “will not be intimidated.”
“Russia does not need to cross our border. It is already waging a hybrid war against us using drones, acts of sabotage and disinformation on the internet. We know from our allies that the coming months may bring further provocations,” he said.
He said he was “neither afraid nor naive” about the dangers posed by Russia.
In a strong speech, he continued:
“I am from Gdańsk. In May 1939, a certain French politician – a future Nazi collaborator – asked in the French press why anyone should die for Gdańsk. A few months later, the whole of Europe was dying.
To those who say today that this is not our war, I would like to remind them of this lesson from history. In 1939, our alliances existed only on paper, really. We were left on our own. Today, we are members of Nato and the European Union.”
We spend almost 5% of our GDP on defence. This is almost twice as much as Germany and twice as much as France. We are building one of the strongest armies in Europe; we secured €44bn from the EU’s SAFE programme, the most from all EU countries. And Polish borders are today the best marked borders on the entire continent.
Europe, which in 1939 did not want to die for Gdańsk, today funds Polish armaments.
But we are aware that even the largest army is not enough if the nation is not ready.
Therefore, I address all those who look at the future with anxiety:
We are not seeking war, but if anyone dares to attack us, they will face a resolute response from us and our allies. Long live a free and secure Republic of Poland.”
He is also speaking in the Polish parliament now, promising to set out further details on the threats facing Poland.
Germany, US sign 'letter of intent' on close defence cooperation, despite previous clashes
Kate Connolly
Berlin correspondent
Following months during which the German government has sought to convince the public that militarily (and otherwise) Germany must stop relying on its erstwhile trustworthy partner, the United States, due to the erratic, rude and unruly behaviour of its president, the defence ministers of both countries signed a “letter of intent” this week, signaling close cooperation after all.
Germany’s defence minister, Boris Pistorius, visibly surprised at the warm reception he received in Washington earlier this week, said after his first meeting with US war minister Pete Hegseth he had only heard warm words of praise for Berlin over its contribution to joint defence goals.
This was in sharp contrast to the bitter tirade Hegseth had delivered to European defence ministers just weeks ago, accusing them of abandoning the US in the Iran war, or to the message disseminated by president Trump earlier this year when he announced the withdrawal of thousands of US troops who are stationed in Germany, in what was interpreted as a clear snub to Berlin.
At a time of dwindling military stocks – the US looking at its war against Iran, Germany, focused mainly on helping to defend Ukraine - the counterparts’ intention, so the letter states, is for “enhanced bilateral cooperation in the defence sector to support transatlantic industrial production and maintenance capacities” and although using slightly wishy-washy terminology, it suggests quite a political U-turn.
From accepting that the Trump administration had mentally withdrawn itself from Nato, and Berlin should become more independent from Washington as a result, the government of Friedrich Merz has now signed up to the statement “Germany and the United States agree that the current political challenges require a robust and mutually beneficial, closely integrated defence industry base on both sides of the Atlantic,” as the declaration reads.
The powerful industries of both countries “can and should” complement each other more closely in the future in the production of “state of the art” weapons systems, components and complex munitions.
Pistorius has sought to play down accusations that this is a contradiction, painting it instead as a pragmatic and direct reaction to current tensions. (What we sometimes refer to as Realpolitik.)
Today he will take delivery of F-35 fighter jets manufactured for Germany’s armed forces in Texas, before heading home tomorrow.
Romanian EU lawmaker Siegfried Muresan proposed as Romania's next prime minister
Sweden is not the only European country working to change its prime minister.
Following a day of consultations with political leaders, Romania’s president, Nicușor Dan, has nominated EU lawmaker Siegfried Mureșan to become the next prime minister.
Romania has had a caretaker government since early May, when prime minister Ilie Bolojan lost a vote of confidence in parliament.
“Romania needs a government,” Dan said, adding that “people’s lives depend on it.”
However, he acknowledged that none of the prospective candidates can currently command a clear majority in parliament, as political parties remain cannot agree on the way forward.
Dan said he had seen “a great deal of concern amongst the parties about the elections and far less concern for national interest.”
He added that Mureșan, 44, had the necessary experience to take on the role and attempt to break the political deadlock.
The MEP has been a member of the European parliament since 2014. Born to German and Romanian parents, he is also a vice-president of the centre-right European People’s Party, the European parliament’s largest grouping.
Elsewhere, the EU and China are continuing efforts to avert a trade war after an hour long call between EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart Wang Wengtao.
The EU reiterated the need to move from “rhetoric to results” with a “credible” solution that will curb China’s growing €1bn a day surplus in trade with the bloc.
Extensive work mapping the potential safeguards including quotas and price floors and possible retaliatory measures by the Chines have already been carried out in advance of Sefcovic’s planned meeting with Wang on 8 October.
A spokesperson said the call lasted more than an hour and took stock of the work carried out by officials so far covering the management of Chinese exports to the EU, the EU’s access to the Chinese market and export controls on rare earths.
Restrictions on exports of rare earths were imposed by Beijing in April 2025 but were suspended for a year last November after Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Xingping in Korea last October.
Experts expect that suspension to continue after the Trump Xi summit next week in Washington but the EU will be pushing for a crave out for the bloc.
“While genuine engagement remains a priority, it is equally important that first concrete outcomes are delivered at the second session of the Trade and Investment Council in Beijing in Cotober which the commissioner will co-chair – a signal that we are moving from rhetoric to results,” said the EU’s deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill.
Centre party leader thanks outgoing PM, says will be 'a constructive force' to keep government 'rooted in the centre'
Meanwhile, Centre party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist also thanked the outgoing prime minister Ulf Kristersson praising his “efforts and leadership during the past term.”
“He has led Sweden through a tumultuous time with a changed security situation and Sweden’s historic entry into Nato. Being prime minister is Sweden’s most important role, and it deserves respect regardless of political divides,” she said.
Speaking about what’s next, she added:
“Now Sweden is entering a new political phase. The Centre party will be a constructive force to ensure Sweden gets a functioning government with a policy rooted in the centre.”
What that will actually mean in practice, we will have to wait and see.
SVT reported that the leaders of the four opposition parties are planning first meetings already.
The current parliament speaker Andreas Norlén is also hoping to individually speak with party leaders tomorrow, SVT said, getting ahead of the formal schedule (14:10).
Right-leaning bloc 'ready to continue governing Sweden if they fail,' liberal leader says
Liberal party leader Simona Mohamsson praised Kristersson’s time in government, saying he led “Sweden’s most liberal government ever,” and hailing what she sees as its successes on education and crime.
Her Liberal party, part of the outgoing government led by Ulf Kristersson, cleared the 4% threshold into the new parliament with 5.3% of the vote last Sunday.
Mohamsson thanked Kristersson for “four important years,” and giving Sweden “a fresh start when it needed it the most.”
“Now it is up to Magdalena Andersson to show whether she can put together any government foundation from the opposition’s mixed bag of left socialists, cultural relativists, and Centre Party members. My teammates to the right and I stand ready to continue governing Sweden if they fail,” she said, echoing the sentiment expressed by Kristersson earlier (13:57).
Christian Democrat leader Ebba Busch also posted a message in a similar tone, conceding the result, but praising the outgoing government’s track record.
“At present, there is no one who commands a majority in the parliament. The red-greens have not automatically won the government power. Various parties’ red lines before election day can lead to a complicated government formation,” she said.
Similar to Kristersson earlier, she also hinted at possible alternative majorities formed along the economic policy lines.
Sweden's election winner Andersson vows to 'move Sweden forward'
Meanwhile, the leader of the left-wing bloc that won Sweden’s election, Magdalena Andersson, vowed Thursday to lead the country in a “new direction” after four years of right-wing rule backed by the far right.
“The Swedish people have voted for a new direction for our country. Voted for unity and against division. The Swedish people have voted to move Sweden forward, and I want to realise the new direction that you have voted for,” she said in a speech posted on social media.
In the address, recorded in a prime ministerial aesthetics and with a Swedish flag in the background, she said she wanted to lead Sweden “away from conflicts from the sake of conflicts, and in a direction based on unity” between key parties as political talks about the new government are set to begin.
“It is up to all political parties to put the party politics aside and put Sweden and the Swedish people first,” she said.
She also talked about priorities on climate, schools, health care, and social care as examples of areas where she wanted to change the government’s policy.
Kristersson's language suggests he still hopes left-leaning bloc will fail to form government - snap analysis
Jakub Krupa
It’s worth noting that the language used by Kristersson in his resignation letter – particularly a reference to irreconcilable differences in the various parties’ stated positions (13:57) – is not accidental.
The left-leaning bloc – led by former prime minister Magdalena Andersson and her Social Democrats - consists of four parties, and there are significant friction points between them, particularly between the Left Party and the Centre Party.
The Centre Party had previously suggested it would not accept ministers from the Left; the Left, particularly now emboldened by its strong election result, is unlikely to agree to no top jobs in a government it is expected to support.
If either party drops out of the arrangement, the bloc will struggle to form a government, as there are no viable alternatives.
But their voters generally expect them to work together.
And a leading figure from the Centre Party implied on Monday (Europe Live, Monday) that they could probably find a way of working with the Left, confirming the party would take part in exploratory talks led by the Social Democrats.
Still, the discussions are likely to be tricky and could take weeks before they agree on a path forward.
Outgoing PM Kristersson is clearly hoping those discussions fail.
His supporters repeatedly pointed out before the election that you could often see the four leaders of the four right-leaning parties in his bloc together – in fact, they also had a dinner together Monday night – and they marketed themselves a “stable” arrangement that was sort of ready to go.
But same didn’t really apply for the red bloc amid some apparent internal divisions between the leaders, leaving lots of questions mark to solve only now.
Kristersson appears to be keen to exploit some of these differences.
On election night, he suggested forming an alternative coalition against socialist economic policies – widely interpreted as an attempt to woo the Centre Party back to his side.
Even then, huge questions remain over how he could secure a majority without the far-right Sweden Democrats, an option that remains unacceptable to centrists.
Expect these talks to pick up speed now that we have the official results – and a looming vacancy at the top.
Timeline for next steps after Kristersson's resignation - snap analysis
Jakub Krupa
In terms of next steps, there is a bit of time before the formal process of electing the new prime minister will get under way.
The new Riksdag is expected to convene on 28 September and elect its speaker on the same day.
The new prime minister can be proposed the next day, 29 September. That leaves just under two weeks for informal talks between now and then, and Kristersson will stay in post until a new PM is picked.
As explained in our live blog on Sunday, Sweden has a slightly unusual system of “negative parliamentarism,” which means that “if there’s a prime minister proposed, then if there is the absence of an absolute majority in parliament against the proposal, it’s interpreted as support.”
As Nicholas AylottofSödertörn University explained it to me on Sunday:
“So a party that doesn’t really want to give full support to this proposed candidate – maybe because it’s not going to be part of the coalition, but which can just about live with it, and doesn’t have a better alternative – it can abstain from the vote, and that’s counted as passive support. This makes it much easier to form minority governments.”
Meanwhile, Swedish public broadcaster SVT reported that just before Kristersson’s statement was published online, someone brought four cakes into the Social Democrat’s HQ in central Stockholm.
Guess we now know the reasons behind the delivery.
Swedish PM Kristersson resigns after election defeat
And in the last few minute, Sweden’s prime minister Ulf Kristersson has resigned from the post after official results confirmed that his right-leaning bloc lost last Sunday’s parliamentary election.
The four left-leaning parties, with former prime minister Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats as the largest party, won by just 50,359 votes, the final count showed.
The four left-leaning bloc will have 176 seats in the new parliament to 173 for Kristersson’s three-party coalition government and the far-right Sweden Democrats who were expected to join the administration after the vote, the Tidö bloc.
In a letter posted on X, Kristersson said that following the tight election results “may have complicated the conditions for the new government to be formed” with contradicting statements from different parties on their positions.
“Constructive openness from the parties in parliament will now be needed for a prime minister to be accepted, and for a new government to be able to receive support for its state budget.”
“Discussions will need to be held with all parties to find ways around these deadlocks and to create the conditions for a stable and effective government.
“It is the speaker who will lead the next steps towards forming a new government. In order for that work to begin immediately, I hereby request to be relieved of my duties as prime minister.”

Swiss Senate rejects tax on short-haul flights

Swiss Senate rejects tax on short-haul flights
The Swiss Senate does not want a tax on short-haul flights. On Wednesday, it voted 20 to 17 against taking forward an initiative from the canton of Basel-City to that effect.
While temperatures soared this summer, the country’s airports also reported record passenger numbers in July, noted parliamentarian Maya Graf from the Green party.
She added that air traffic causes noise pollution for local residents. In the densely populated Basel metropolitan area, many people are affected on a daily basis by Basel-Mulhouse Airport. However, some of these flights bring no significant added value to the region’s economy, tourism or leisure sector. An incentive tax on airline tickets for short-haul flights would help reduce unnecessary flights.
The cantonal initiative proposed defining the routes concerned on the basis of whether destinations were reasonably accessible by rail, rather than on the basis of a fixed number of kilometres.
More
A Swiss initiative wants flyers to fund trains
Speaking on behalf of the committee, Severin Brüngger from the Radical Liberal party expressed doubts about the measure’s effectiveness. Passengers would simply be likely to switch to airports in neighbouring countries, in particular Basel-Mulhouse Airport (EuroAirport). What is needed instead are measures coordinated at the international level.
Admittedly, international coordination is needed for kerosene taxation, but using this argument to oppose Swiss measures does not hold water. France has banned short-haul flights and Belgium has introduced a tax on flights of less than 500 km. This shows that it is possible for a country to take action, countered Eva Herzog from the Social Democratic party, to no avail.
The House has yet to give its verdict.
The senators subsequently rejected a petition calling for a ban on private jets in Switzerland.

UN mission finds grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran, and Tehran crimes against humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17

UN mission finds grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran, and Tehran crimes against humanity
- A UN fact-finding mission found reasonable grounds to believe the US committed war crimes in Iran by striking a school and sports centre, causing numerous civilian deaths.
- The report accused the Iranian authorities of crimes against humanity during a violent crackdown on anti-government protests, including unlawful killings and torture.
- The mission highlighted failures in US military intelligence and described Iran's response as a severe escalation, with a likely higher death toll than official figures suggest.
AI generated
GENEVA – A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said on Sept 17 it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.
It also found that the Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.
The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined the US’ conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government’s response to nationwide unrest that began in late December.
The Pentagon declined to comment on a report conducted by an outside organisation.
“Our investigation remains ongoing, and we have nothing to announce at the moment,” it said in a statement. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in response to the report that the UN Human Rights Council had “accomplished nothing for human rights,” adding that Iran was the only party in the current conflict that had committed war crimes.
The Iranian permanent mission in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
US officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.
UN Fact-Finding missions are investigative, not judicial bodies, and therefore do not initiate any criminal cases. Their findings, however, can be used in criminal investigations by national courts or international tribunals such as the International Criminal Court.
States will discuss the findings of the report when it is presented to the Human Rights Council in Geneva on Sept 21.
Minab school strike
The UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe US forces were responsible for an attack on Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the city of Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.
The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.
According to the report, the US failure to update information in relation to the school, which was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval complex, in its targeting databases and to confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.
“Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen.”
In June, US President Donald Trump said that “nobody” purposefully attacked a girls’ school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident.
Reuters first reported that an initial internal US military investigation showed US forces were likely responsible for the fatal strike in Minab in southern Iran.
The Pentagon has since elevated the probe but it has not published any preliminary findings.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.
The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed or injured 22 civilians.
It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
US Central Command said in a statement in March that US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.
Iran abuses
The UN mission probe found that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December 2025, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shi’ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution.
Tehran blamed “terrorists and rioters” backed by exiled opponents and the US and Israel.
The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the numbers of dead and injured were likely far higher than official figures, which state 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 injured.
The government’s response to the protests – including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty – marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said. REUTERS

Unemployment virtually unchanged in August
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The unemployment rate remained at 4% in August, the same as July, with around 408,000 people out of work, according to new figures from Dutch statistics bureau CBS.
While the total number of unemployed people in the Netherlands has risen, on average, by around 3,000 per month since June, the number of people leaving the labour force has also increased.
During the same time period, the number of people outside the labour force decreased by an average of 4,000 per month. Retirees and those who are unable to work due to disability or illness make up the majority of the non-labour force.
Since 2023, the number of unemployed people in the Netherlands has been slowly rising. In April, 343,000 were unemployed.
The Dutch unemployment agency UWV registered around 195,000 people on unemployment benefits. That was slightly higher, around 1.4%, than it was in July.

Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappé breaks silence on Ceuta shirt controversy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:06:18 UTC
17:06:18 KST

Real Madrid's striker has for the first time explained why he, Vinícius Jr and Ibrahima Konaté partly covered up a message on a t-shirt backing Ceuta.
Kylian Mbappé has explained for the first time why he, along with teammates Vinícius Júnior and Ibrahima Konaté, only partially wore a shirt in support of Ceuta before Real Madrid's match against Elche. The French forward insists the gesture was not meant as a rejection of the people of Ceuta, and has expressed solidarity both with the city's population and with the migrants who have died.
"I want to explain it properly so that people understand," Mbappé told the newspaper AS. He explained that the initiative to wear the shirt had come from the clubs, and that the players were expected to put it on. "The first thing I want to say is that I stand in full solidarity with Ceuta and with all the victims. Because before being a player, I am a human being," he said.
Mbappé said he had also wanted to use the gesture to remember the migrants who have died and those still in difficult situations. "I also wanted to have a gesture and a thought for all the migrants who have lost their lives and who are also living in harsh conditions," he said.
The striker acknowledged that it was a "difficult" position, and denied that his decision meant he was against the people of Ceuta. "I have nothing against them, and I support them 100 percent — my thoughts are with them. But I also wanted to spare a thought for all the people who are suffering," he explained.
The controversy began before Tuesday's match, when the three players only partially put on the shirt, covering the message "We are all mackerel" — a reference to the nickname for Ceuta's inhabitants. The slogan was completed by the phrase "Our city, our homeland."
The initiative had been proposed by Elche, as the home side, and accepted by Real Madrid. LaLiga president Javier Tebas later criticised the three players for not wearing the shirt properly.
Mbappé insisted his intention had been to convey a broader message of solidarity. "I'm a guy who wants the best for the world we live in. I am trying to send a message of positivity and peace, and I hope this is resolved quickly," he concluded.

Girls make a comeback — What India is doing about the women shortage | DW Documentary
For decades, many families in India and China did not want daughters. Girls were often aborted, killed as infants, abandoned or sold.
In recent years, things have started to change.
Political decisions aimed at curbing rapid population growth in India and China, together with a widespread preference for boys for economic reasons, have led to a situation where both countries now have more men than women.
As early as 1990, Indian economist Amartya Sen, who would later win the Nobel Prize in Economics, warned that more than 100 million women were "missing" in the developing world, and especially in India and China, in the ratio to men.
But slowly, there has been a shift in thinking in both countries — both in politics and society.

Happy birthday, Narendra Modi: BJP competes for leader's affection
Today is Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's birthday, and his Bharatiya Janata Party is pulling out all the stops to celebrate the milestone.
The leader's 76th birthday has turned into an unofficial race by BJP-ruled states, with each arm of the political party attempting to outshine each other via campaigns that involve lighting candles, elaborate social media output, drawing competitions, motorbike rallies and more.
BJP-led state governments have launched a month-long series of celebrations marking the birthday and 25 years in public office, a move not usually associated with heads of state in recent years.
In Delhi, schools have been directed to hold earthen lamp-lighting ceremonies on campus, The Wire reported, with schools also told to record and upload video footage of the events.
The celebrations, branded the "Seva Sankalp Abhiyan" — meaning "Service and Resolution Campaign" in Hindi — run from September 17 to October 17. Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta has said the campaign will also include blood donation drives — also being run in other states — as well as the inauguration of development projects worth roughly 13,820 crore rupees (around €1.25 million or $1.45 million).
The lamp-lighting ceremony, dubbed the "Ashirwad Ka Diya" or "lamp of blessing" programme, will also take place across other BJP-led states, including West Bengal, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, and more.
In Odisha, party leadership has asked people to light the lamps and upload photographs and videos on social media, local media reported.
In Modi's home state of Gujarat, Interior Minister Amit Shah has launched a bike rally from the PM's birthplace of Vadnagar to his constituency, Varanasi.
There were also prayers conducted at several temples across the country.
With the BJP's state arms running their own social media campaigns to celebrate the leader, who will be the real winner?
Supreme Court rejects government's appeals against disabled veterans' pensions
India's Supreme Court dismissed 271 appeals filed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government challenging disability pensions awarded to former armed forces personnel, ruling that the government still bears the burden of proving a serviceman's disability was unrelated to military service, local media reported.
A two-judge bench of Justices PS Narasimha and Alok Aradhe held that while the 2008 pension rules removed an earlier presumption that a soldier was fit upon entering service, this did not shift the entire burden of proof onto the serviceman.
The court said the "onus to prove that the member's disability is not attributable to service still lies on the employer."
The appeals stemmed from cases where military release medical boards had classified disabilities as "neither attributable nor aggravated" by service, only for the Armed Forces Tribunal or high courts to overturn those findings and grant pensions.
The bench also criticized the government for pursuing appeals it said were largely time-barred, and cited Right to Information data showing the vast majority of departmental pension appeals from ex-servicemen are rejected at earlier stages.
The court referenced a 2015 defense ministry report that had recommended withdrawing such litigation against disabled soldiers, noting the recommendation was never fully implemented.
India's Foreign Ministry slams reports that world leaders fell ill after BRICS summit
India's Ministry of External Affairs has rejected social media claims that several world leaders fell ill after attending the BRICS Summit held in New Delhi on September 12-13, calling the reports "fake" and warning against "malicious" posts.
The MEA's fact-checking unit posted on X: "Fake Alert!!! 🚨🚨🚨 We caution against such malicious posts on social media platforms!" This included a social media post by Polymarket, one of the world's largest prediction market platforms.
The clarification followed genuine confirmation from South African President Cyril Ramaphosa's office that he had withdrawn from public engagements after returning from the summit, having been advised to rest due to ill health.
Separately, unverified posts claimed Chinese President Xi Jinping fainted and left the summit early for medical treatment. The claim originated from Wanjun Xie, chairman of the China Democracy Party, and was not confirmed by Chinese or Indian officials. Beijing has banned the party.
Xi is confirmed to have attended the summit and met bilaterally with Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
India vows to protect trade and economic interests amid threat of US's Russia-linked tariffs
India said Thursday it remains committed to securing energy supplies for its 1.4 billion people and will keep sourcing oil from diverse suppliers, hours after the US House of Representatives passed a bill authorizing tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue buying Russian oil and gas, including India, along with new sanctions tied to Russia's war in Ukraine.
The bill now goes to President Donald Trump for signature.
India's Ministry of External Affairs issued a statement responding directly to the legislation: "India remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people. It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics."
The ministry said it had raised the issue with US officials in recent months, adding, "Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side."
"The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests," the statement added, saying it would work with trade and industry bodies on the legislation's implications.
India is the world's third-largest oil importer, and Russia has become one of its largest suppliers as well as a longstanding strategic and military partner. New Delhi has consistently defended the relationship as necessary for its energy needs, resisting outside pressure to scale it back.
What do we know about the sanctions?
The package targets Russia's energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials. It also targets Moscow's so-called shadow fleet, old tankers it uses to circumvent sanctions.
More controversially, the legislation allows Trump to impose secondary sanctions on countries that rely on Russian oil and gas, in the form of tariffs. Beijing and New Delhi are expected to be the main targets of such measures.
The bill would also extend sanctions on Iran.

US judge dismisses oil trader's Swiss smears complaint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:04:00 UTC
17:04:00 KST

US judge dismisses oil trader’s Swiss smears complaint
The United Arab Emirates won dismissal of a lawsuit by an oil trader who alleged the state directed a smear campaign that pushed his company into bankruptcy.
The lawsuit, filed in January 2024 by oil trader Hazim Nada, claimed that his company, Lord Energy, was targeted by a misinformation campaign orchestrated by Swiss private investigative firm Alp Services, and ultimately directed by the UAE and its president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed.
United States District Judge Amy Berman Jackson ruled that the UAE is immune from the suit under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act. She also dismissed other defendants, including Alp, on various legal grounds.
“Notwithstanding its length and unnecessary detail, the amended complaint is nothing more than a defamation case in search of a legal theory,” Jackson wrote Tuesday in Washington federal court. “It is also an action in search of a basis to require a foreign sovereign and other foreign entities and individuals to defend themselves in the United States.”
The complaint, based on more than 8,000 hacked documents, shone light on the world of private intelligence agencies for hire. Nada alleged that Alp hired journalists and academics to write articles falsely accusing Lord Energy of being a front company to fund terrorist organizations, which led its banks to stop working with it. The company declared bankruptcy in April 2019.
Nada, a 43-year-old citizen of Italy and the US, said he was disappointed by the ruling and is considering an appeal.
“We’re basically telling foreign governments that it’s OK to work in a way where you appoint a third party to do the dirty work for you,” Nada said in an interview. “It’s become a modus operandi for all these states to do the dirty job by hiding behind consultants and mercenaries, so where are we going?”
Nada said he is trying to restart Lord Energy, but he said “it’s tricky with all the things that have happened.”
The UAE embassy in Washington and Alp didn’t respond to requests for comment.
Nada formed Lord Energy in 2008 to trade coal, grain, cement and steel, and he expanded into oil in 2014. His lawsuit claims that the business was seen as a threat by the UAE and its state oil company, Abu Dhabi National Oil, in the spot market for light crude oil in Asia. He sought $2.8 billion in damages.
The lawsuit claimed Nada didn’t know the “scope and scale” of the campaign against him and his company until hackers “obtained tens of thousands of documents from Alp’s servers and shared some of them” with him in April 2021, according to the opinion.
The story of the smear campaign against Nada and Lord Energy was the subject of a New Yorker article in 2023.
The case is Nada v. United Arab Emirates, 24-cv-00206, US District Court, District of Columbia.

Girls make a comeback — What India is doing about the women shortage | DW Documentary
For decades, many families in India and China did not want daughters. Girls were often aborted, killed as infants, abandoned or sold.
In recent years, things have started to change.
Political decisions aimed at curbing rapid population growth in India and China, together with a widespread preference for boys for economic reasons, have led to a situation where both countries now have more men than women.
As early as 1990, Indian economist Amartya Sen, who would later win the Nobel Prize in Economics, warned that more than 100 million women were "missing" in the developing world, and especially in India and China, in the ratio to men.
But slowly, there has been a shift in thinking in both countries — both in politics and society.

Happy birthday, Narendra Modi: BJP competes for leader's affection
Today is Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's birthday, and his Bharatiya Janata Party is pulling out all the stops to celebrate the milestone.
The leader's 76th birthday has turned into an unofficial race by BJP-ruled states, with each arm of the political party attempting to outshine each other via campaigns that involve lighting candles, elaborate social media output, drawing competitions, motorbike rallies and more.
BJP-led state governments have launched a month-long series of celebrations marking the birthday and 25 years in public office, a move not usually associated with heads of state in recent years.
In Delhi, schools have been directed to hold earthen lamp-lighting ceremonies on campus, The Wire reported, with schools also told to record and upload video footage of the events.
The celebrations, branded the "Seva Sankalp Abhiyan" — meaning "Service and Resolution Campaign" in Hindi — run from September 17 to October 17. Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta has said the campaign will also include blood donation drives — also being run in other states — as well as the inauguration of development projects worth roughly 13,820 crore rupees (around €1.25 million or $1.45 million).
The lamp-lighting ceremony, dubbed the "Ashirwad Ka Diya" or "lamp of blessing" programme, will also take place across other BJP-led states, including West Bengal, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, and more.
In Odisha, party leadership has asked people to light the lamps and upload photographs and videos on social media, local media reported.
In Modi's home state of Gujarat, Interior Minister Amit Shah has launched a bike rally from the PM's birthplace of Vadnagar to his constituency, Varanasi.

Switzerland raises economic growth forecast significantly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:02:58 UTC
17:02:58 KST

Switzerland raises economic growth forecast significantly
According to the federal government’s economists, the Swiss economy is likely to perform significantly better than previously expected. They are therefore raising their forecast substantially.
The federal government’s expert group has revised its forecast for 2026 to predict growth in real gross domestic product (GDP, adjusted for sporting events) of 1.7%, up from the previous estimate of 0.9%, as announced by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) on Thursday. The forecast for 2027 of 1.6% has been confirmed.
According to the statement, the reason for the revision is the latest data from the Swiss economy, which showed surprisingly high growth. GDP grew exceptionally strongly in the second quarter.
+ Swiss economy grows surprisingly fast in Q2
‘A certain counter-movement’
However, according to federal experts, this growth is unlikely to continue unchecked. On the contrary, a “certain counter-movement” is expected in the second half of the year.
This is because, according to the press release, almost half of the strong growth in the second quarter was attributable to the highly volatile value added in the chemical and pharmaceutical industry. “This is likely to have overstated the underlying economic momentum,” the statement continues.
Weakening of the franc helps
Nevertheless, the Swiss economy remains fundamentally on a path to recovery. The recent depreciation of the franc is also helping in this regard, as it benefits the export sector.
As for inflation, the federal government’s economists continue to forecast a rate of 0.6% for both 2026 and 2027. The unemployment rate is forecast at 3.1% for 2026 and 3.0% for 2027.
The expert group emphasised that the conflict with Iran, high energy prices and ongoing trade policy uncertainty pose significant risks to the economy. Persistently high oil prices could therefore place a significant strain on the global economy, and according to the statement, inflation in Switzerland would also be higher as a result.

Xi stresses sustained efforts to expand, strengthen advanced manufacturing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:02:41 CST
17:02:41 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has urged sustained efforts to expand and strengthen advanced manufacturing to provide strong support for advancing Chinese modernization.
Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a recent instruction, which was conveyed at a national conference on advanced manufacturing held in Beijing on Wednesday and Thursday.
Efforts should be made to ensure both high-quality development and greater security, pursue smart, green and integrated development, and make the country's industrial chains more self-supporting and risk-resilient, Xi stressed.
He emphasized the need to accelerate the development of a modernized industrial system with advanced manufacturing as the backbone, and reinforce the foundations of the real economy.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, delivers a speech at a national conference on advanced manufacturing held in Beijing, capital of China. The national conference on advanced manufacturing was held in Beijing on Wednesday and Thursday. An instruction of Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, was conveyed during the conference. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen)
Premier Li Qiang, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, delivered a speech at the conference.
Xi's important instructions provide essential guidance for developing advanced manufacturing, Li said, noting that China must treat developing advanced manufacturing as a major strategic task, and press steadily to boost its strength in manufacturing.
Li stressed that next-generation intelligent manufacturing should serve as the primary direction, with greater emphasis on digital and intelligent empowerment, high-end manufacturing and self-reliance, green and low-carbon development, and cross-sector integration.
Efforts should be made to continuously strengthen the innovation capacity, competitiveness and overall strength of advanced manufacturing, Li said.
Li called for deepening the "AI plus manufacturing" initiative, stepping up guidance and support for enterprises' digital and intelligent transformation, and consolidating the foundation of intelligent software and hardware.
China should also advance the deep integration of advanced manufacturing and modern services, foster service-oriented manufacturing, and cultivate advanced manufacturing clusters according to local conditions.
Chinese Vice Premier Zhang Guoqing, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, delivers a concluding speech at a national conference on advanced manufacturing held in Beijing, capital of China. The national conference on advanced manufacturing was held in Beijing on Wednesday and Thursday. An instruction of Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, was conveyed during the conference. Officials urge public to rely on official information
The committee urged investors and the public to rely only on statements issued by official institutions as authorities respond to the recent volatility.

Netball's unprecedented suspension as Diamond pleads guilty to assault
Australian netballer Sarah Klau has been sanctioned by the sport's governing body after pleading guilty to assault and failing to disclose the matter prior to the Commonwealth Games.
Following an investigation into the incident over the past couple of weeks, Netball Australia has handed Klau a $5,000 fine and a two-game ban that is wholly suspended for 12 months.
The goal keeper will also be required to complete additional education.
Klau breached the sport's code of conduct by failing to behave in a professional manner while in public and engaging in conduct that could bring the game into disrepute.
In a statement, Netball Australia said it took into consideration Klau's "individual circumstances and her otherwise exemplary personal history", as well as her apology to the victim and venue, but the seriousness of the charge and breach of standards warranted formal disciplinary action.
Chief executive Mark Falvo described it as "a significant but momentary lapse in judgement … that has been mitigated by her otherwise excellent character".
This means Klau will still be eligible for selection in the Constellation Cup.
The Australian squad set to face New Zealand in a four-game bilateral series in October will be announced in the coming days.
This is believed to be the first time a Super Netballer and national team member has been in trouble with the law, and the decision now sets a precedent for the sport at the elite level.
Klau fronted Sydney's Downing Centre Courthouse in early September facing a common assault charge from June 7, when she allegedly kicked a security guard in the back outside a pub.
The 31-year-old reportedly attended a Sydney Swans AFL match before arriving at the Paddington Inn and retaliated when she was denied entry due to being too intoxicated.
This took place a day after Klau was ruled out of the NSW Swifts' penultimate game of the Super Netball season to manage an ongoing leg injury.
The assault shocked the netball community and was dubbed "out of character" by many who know Klau.
The charges were laid five weeks after the incident, ahead of Klau's departure with the national team for the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
Netball Australia's investigation aimed to determine whether the veteran knew about the charges before she left.
There is a possibility that she was notified in writing at her Sydney address while in camp in Melbourne, then flew straight to Scotland to compete completely unaware.
Klau has played 67 caps for her country and has been a mainstay in the squad since her international debut in 2019.
Despite being hampered by injury throughout the recent Super Netball season, Klau was still named and made her second appearance at the tournament, albeit with limited court time.
The Diamonds won bronze after defeating England 68-50 in the medal matches.
Klau then spent time abroad on holiday before returning home and fronting court.
Following the investigation, Netball Australia would not disclose the timeline of events but confirmed it did not find out about the incident until a week before the court appearance on September 3.
Commonwealth Games Australia's (CGA) athletes must agree to their ethical by-laws, which state that an athlete cannot engage in any conduct — whether publicly known or not — that brings the relevant person's sport into disrepute.
The behaviour policies also outline that an athlete must not deliberately withhold information in relation to any possible prohibited conduct and is expected to notify the CEO or CGA President of any potential breach.
When contacted by ABC Sport, CGA said it was aware of the court proceedings but was waiting on the findings of Netball Australia's investigation before determining any impact they may have on Klau's relationship with the Australian CGA team.
Up and coming defender Jessie Grenvold earned her first call-up for the side and travelled as a reserve. Had all of this come to light, Grenvold could have taken Klau's place.
Importantly, Klau has avoided a conviction, likely due to her status as a Diamonds player, as the judge said it would be a "terrible setback" to "everything you have achieved".
"It's always such a shame to see fabulous sports men and women compromise themselves, really, on nights out," the judge said during sentencing according to NewsCorp.

Speaking in a statement issued via the Australian Netball Players' Association, Klau expressed deep regret.

"I am committed to learning from this and ensuring my actions reflect the standards expected of me and our sport.
"I am grateful for the support I have received, I care deeply about netball and the values it represents."
Two years ago, the Swifts parted ways mid-season with long-time player Sam Wallace-Joseph due to behavioural issues that happened internally and were never publicly disclosed.
Considering the nature of these charges, the guilty plea and the timing of the incident while Klau was in season and supposed to be resting a leg injury, fans thought the club might also make an example of this incident.
Instead, Klau has missed out on a penalty entirely in club land.
The Swifts re-signed their two-time premiership player for a fifth Super Netball season before the trial and later defended her integrity, confirming no further action will be taken.

‘It’s beautiful when it’s clean’: the Argentine neighbourhood saving a contaminated river
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:00:44 UTC
17:00:44 KST

Twenty-three years ago, María Monges looked around her flooded neighbourhood and knew something had to be done.
Founded in 1998 in Buenos Aires province’s San Martín district, the community of Costa Esperanza sits on the banks of the Reconquista, Argentina’s second most-polluted river and owes its name to the fictional location of a hit Argentine youth telenovela of the time, Verano del 98. But the real place is very different from the idyllic coastal city where the protagonists of Argentina’s answer to Dawson’s Creek met their first loves or sang around bonfires.
“You don’t know what it was like – when we started cleaning up, all the streams were blocked up everywhere: rubbish, dead dogs … a bit of everything. It was unsanitary, but we carried on working anyway,” says Monges, now 61. She started knocking on doors, getting people out to work with her, and in 2005 got the provincial administration to give them tools, uniforms and training. Now Monges leads 9 de julio, a workers’ cooperative that, from Monday to Friday, cleans up streams flowing from the river. “Every day, we will find rubbish,” says Monges. “It’s like people don’t understand.”
The Reconquista is 51 miles (82km) long, located in the north-east of the province of Buenos Aires and flows through 18 municipalities. About 4-5 million people live in its basin. It flows into the Luján River, which then connects with the Río de la Plata estuary.
Since at least the 1970s, the river has been a dumping ground for untreated sewage, industrial waste and landfill leachate. It has the state sewage company on its banks, along with homes that lack adequate infrastructure, residents connecting their drainpipes so that waste is discharged directly into the water. Several factories located in the district of San Martín, known as “the Industrial Capital”, also throw their waste into the river.
“All of this not only pollutes the water, but also the soil and the air. In this area there’s no access to drinking water … all the aquifers are contaminated,” says Natalia Gavazzo, an anthropologist and researcher at the National Scientific and Technical Research Council. Gavazzo directs the Migrantas en Reconquista project, which conducts research and carries out initiatives in the region to strengthen the socio-environmental strategies employed by women in the neighbourhoods of the Reconquista river basin. She adds that the environmental activism in Costa Esperanza is carried out primarily by women. “They are not just victims,” she says. “They are also the key agents of mitigation and adaptation; they possess a wealth of knowledge that is central to the survival of their communities.”
But the Reconquista is just one of the troubled rivers in La Plata, the giant system that connects multiple waterways across Uruguay and Argentina. According to the World Meteorological Organization State of Global Water Resources report, out on Thursday, major parts of La Plata river basins have experienced recurring below-normal water levels between 2021 and 2025, caused by persistent multi-year drought conditions.
La Plata basin includes the Paraguay River, which has consistently recorded water levels at their lowest since 2020. Analysis of WMO data shows that the Paraguay River’s water levels have been consistently below normal for the last six years, with its 25 driest months since 1991 registered after 2020.
The drought and pollution issues plaguing La Plata and the Reconquista are affecting many more of the world’s rivers. As Gavazzo puts it, “climate change has an uneven impact around the world – the north produces the emissions, but we in the south foot the bill.” For the anthropologist, the same is true at a local scale. “People in gated communities throw out rubbish, but it ends up here,” she added.
Juan Borús, who recently retired from the National Water Institute and is one of the country’s leading hydrologists, says that governments should “tackle every one of these sources of pollution individually, which is an extremely costly, painstaking task that requires regulation”, but that “companies that discharge complex effluents evade the rules … They’ve been doing it all their lives.”
In 2001, the Buenos Aires province created the Reconquista River Basin Committee (Comirec) to clean it up, but it had limited impact, and parts of the river where Costa Esperanza is located still exhibit “severe deterioration”, according to its early 2026 reports. High levels of E coli (a bacterium that indicates the presence of fecal matter) and low levels of oxygen make it “not a suitable environment for aquatic life” and “a risk to the population”, according to Patricio Carmona, a biochemist specialising in environmental analysis.
“The smell is like an acid,” says Lorena Batista, 47, a neighbour who works at the National Institute of Industrial Technology. “It is nauseating,” adds Zulma Monges, María’s daughter. The stench, they agree, becomes unbearable in summer, and when the wind blows they have to close their windows. It is not only the smell – neighbours have suffered from skin conditions such as hives, rashes, sores and scars, respiratory and lung problems, and gastrointestinal diseases, although Zulma says the skin conditions have become somewhat rarer since her mother’s community squad started picking up the rubbish.
Once a month, residents meet to discuss problems and contact representatives from the local government, to whom they address their concerns – accumulated rubbish or water cuts, for example. “It’s very much a part of our lives; it’s already become an integral part of the neighbourhood’s culture,” says grocer Rosa Valencia in her shop, laden with coconuts, plantains and yerba mate.
And there are other efforts under way to clean up the river. The San Martín University’s School of Habitat and Sustainability is developing artificial wetlands – a nature-inspired method that could be installed on site to help filter out persistent pollutants and restore the area’s biodiversity. A group of several local organisations, Foro por la Recuperación del Río Reconquista, is campaigning for the creation of an ecological preserve. “Many years ago, before the landfill was built, that area was a large marshland with beaches,” they claim in their petition.
“Older folks used to tell us: ‘we’d go fishing there, we’d spend our weekends there; there were always, always, always lots of animals’,” says Zulma Monges. The area, she says, is overpopulated, and “the few green spaces we do have, we’re maintaining them as a community”. Then she pulls out her phone and shows a picture of one of the streams, just after it was cleaned by her mother’s squad.
“It’s beautiful when it’s clean,” she says. “The thing is, you have to stop the rubbish from reaching the neighbourhood. But this whole area … look, it’s beautiful.”
- 
  Over the next year, in the Our Rivers series, we’ll be focusing on the environmental challenges facing the world’s rivers, looking at the waterways around the planet that are overengineered or suffocating and drying up, and those that are being opened up again and given new life.
