‘Like a Disney movie’: Three wild dog brothers make Africa’s longest journey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
04:00:39 UTC
13:00:39 KST

It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all brothers, on an epic journey to find a home of their own after their family tells them to leave. They dodge cars and hunters in search of a new life, navigating bushmeat snares and the hostility of a human-dominated landscape until they find a new haven on the African savannah.
But this is exactly what happened in Zambia last year, when three endangered African wild dogs made the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent. The brothers travelled more than 2,500 miles (4,100km) over eight months in their “dispersal” – when a young dog comes of age and must establish new territory to find a mate and start a family of their own.
From point to point, starting in Kafue national park in western Zambia to their final destination in the Luangwa valley in the east of the country, the brothers covered 340 miles (546km), which is also a record.
The epic single journey is almost equivalent to travelling the length of Chile by foot and farther than the famous wildebeest and zebra migration across the Serengeti in east Africa. The previous record was 2,418 miles, also made by African wild dogs, which moved between Loliondo, in northern Tanzania’s Ngorongoro district, and Tsavo West national park in southern Kenya in 2012.
Dr Matt Becker, chief executive of the Zambian Carnivore Programme (ZCP), whose scientists were monitoring the wild dogs and have published their findings in the journal Ecology, says: “These extraordinary journeys show that natural connections between Africa’s wildlife strongholds still exist. But they also reveal how difficult and dangerous those journeys have become.
“Rather than relying solely on fenced protected areas, these findings reinforce the value of investing in connected landscapes. The dogs are showing us that connectivity still works; now we need to do more to protect and strengthen it.”
The researchers tracked 19 separate groups of wild dogs to monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the three brothers who were far less successful at finding a new range. Two of the sisters died, probably caught in snares, but not before they had a touching final encounter with their siblings.
Two months into their journey, the group of brothers and sisters came across each other deep in Zambia’s copper-belt mining region, spending the day together before going their separate ways again. Related dogs do not form new family packs, and typically have to travel long distances through the landscape to find prospective mates.
Only 6,600 or so adults remain of 39 distinct populations of African wild dogs, and the species is classified as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list. Habitat loss, declining numbers of natural prey, bushmeat hunters’ snares and human conflict are among the biggest threats to their survival.
But researchers say the three brothers’ epic journey shows the wild dogs can still survive in a human-dominated landscape despite the enormous challenges they face. Alongside African savannah elephants, whose ancient migration routes are increasingly being blocked by human development, African wild dogs need to be able to make long journeys to find new homes.
“These long-term studies provide key evidence that connectivity between large landscapes is still there,” says Dr Nyambe Nyambe, director of the Kavango-Zambezi transfrontier area secretariat, a key conservation region that spans five countries, including Zambia, where governments are trying to keep space for wildlife to move through the landscape.
“If we conserve and continue to improve these connections – spanning the range of national parks, community areas, nations and regions – a lot of species like wild dogs can make the rest happen,” Nyambe says.

English Heritage trains new generation of scythers to maintain meadows and craft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
04:00:39 UTC
13:00:39 KST

It sounds like something out of a Thomas Hardy novel: a merry band of men and women roaming the West Country cutting meadows by hand in exchange for hunks of bread and cheese.
But the conservation charity English Heritage is recruiting a team of volunteer scythers to maintain 21st-century meadowland in the old-fashioned way.
The first scythers have been trained and will use their new skills in the meadows around an abbey in Somerset, where it is hoped that as well as helping to keep the age-old practice alive, they will protect a rare type of bumblebee.
Ginny Slade, who has completed the training, said she found there was something therapeutic about scything.
“You need a level of physical fitness but it’s also about enthusiasm and the passion to learn heritage skills,” she said. “It’s a repetitive movement. You find your rhythm and zone into it. You can really connect with the meadow, the landscape.”
The first volunteers have also found that using the scythe is something of a sensual treat – the sound of the blade cutting, the scent of the meadow.
Slade said: “Scything is a wonderful example of how traditional skills can still have a role in addressing modern challenges. We hope to help create the diverse, flower-rich habitats that pollinators need while also preserving knowledge and skills that have shaped our landscapes.”
Slade, a volunteer and community engagement manager with English Heritage, is one of the first to be trained by professionals at the Exmoor National Park Authority in the art of using and maintaining a scythe. “You want a really good scythe,” said Slade. “If you look after them, they can last generations.”
English Heritage rewards volunteers with bread and cheese (it also thought about providing West Country cider but thought this was not a good idea on health and safety grounds).
The first group of scythers will help care for the meadow at Muchelney Abbey, in Somerset, which was once a wealthy and important monastery with features including a thatched two-storey monks’ lavatory, which is unique in Britain.
They will work on a three-year project with the Bumblebee Conservation Trust to improve habitat for the shrill carder bee, a species that has declined significantly because of the loss of flower-rich grasslands.
As part of the project, English Heritage volunteers have been trained by the bumblebee trust to carry out wildlife surveys.
Rather than simply recording numbers, volunteers will monitor the relationship between bees and the meadow ecosystem, including which flowers are in bloom, which plants they are using, how far bees travel from their nests and how the habitat changes over time.
Hardy wrote about scything in prose and poetry: in Far From the Madding Crowd, Bathsheba Everdene watches haymaking, and the farm hand Mark Clark is described as “humming a tune to the strokes of his scythe”.
In his poem Four in the Morning, Hardy wrote about the “to-and-fro/Wheezed whettings of a scythe apace”.
The meadow at Muchelney is one of 100 that English Heritage pledged to create and enhance to mark the coronation of King Charles in 2023.
Slade said Muchelney was the pilot site but the idea was for the volunteers to travel to other English Heritage sites to use their skills. “We’re really at the beginning of this journey, but we’re very excited about it.”

Turkey detains dozens in crackdown on LGBTQ+ activists and journalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
04:00:38 UTC
13:00:38 KST

Turkish authorities have used accusations of obscenity to justify a wave of raids and arrests targeting the LGBTQ+ community, which has grown to include journalists as well as more than 150 arrested during protests against the raids.
Starting in the early hours of Sunday, Turkish police carried out simultaneous raids on the offices of LGBTQ+ rights organisations and HIV-advocacy groups in the cities of Istanbul, the capital, Ankara, and the coastal city of İzmir, as well as the cities of Aydın and Mersin.
“This is the widest crackdown on LGBTQ+ people in recent years,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, of Human Rights Watch.
Video released by the Turkish interior ministry showed police rummaging through filing cabinets, grabbing rainbow flags and leading people away in handcuffs, as well as raiding nightclubs and the homes of activists.
Prosecutors in Istanbul said officials seized digital equipment, drugs and a firearm, as well as arresting dozens of people in the raids.
Rights groups tracking the arrests believe that 62 people have been held on remand, but more than 100 were detained. Sinclair-Webb, who accused authorities of attempting to smear and criminalise LGBTQ+ advocacy, said: “We believe this includes others not associated with LGBTQ+ groups [detained] for drug and prostitution offences.”
While homosexuality is not illegal in Turkey, prosecutors in Ankara have accused LGBTQ+ rights groups of violating laws prohibiting “obscenity”, and those governing NGOs, although formal charges remain opaque.
Turkey’s justice minister, Akın Gürlek, said the raids and arrests across the country were part of an operation entitled “My Family is Safe” and claimed the sweep was intended to “protect our children, the institution of the family and the social order”.
As a result, Gürlek said, authorities targeted venues they claimed were associated with prostitution, distribution of obscene material “and activities exposing children to such content”.
A Turkish press freedom group, the Media and Law Studies Association, said this included seven members of the executive board of Kaos GL, one of Turkey’s oldest LGBTQ+ advocacy groups that also operates a news site.
Tuğba Tekerek, a journalist, was arrested at her home in Istanbul and taken to Ankara for questioning by prosecutors, after publishing a piece with Kaos GL on the LGBTQ+ community in the neighbouring country of Georgia.
As the initial raids sparked protests, the wave of arrests grew this week. Turkish authorities teargassed hundreds of protesters in İzmir, and detained at least 150 demonstrators in Istanbul on Tuesday as well as dozens more in Ankara.
The French news agency AFP reported that several of the arrests outside a courthouse in Istanbul took place after demonstrators unfurled a banner that read “Being LGBTQ+ is not a crime” and chanted “Long live the struggle for freedom.”
A draft amendment to Turkey’s penal code that proposed prosecuting all LGBTQ+ people in Turkey for promoting behaviour “contrary to biological sex and general morality” was withdrawn last year.
Instead, the Turkish authorities have increasingly targeted LGBTQ+ individuals and groups using broad “obscenity” charges. Eleven leaders of the Genç LGBTI+ [Youth LGBTI+] organisation went on trial last month, accused of violating constitutional provisions on “family values” and publishing images showing same-sex couples kissing, charges that carry up to three years’ imprisonment.
The justice minister linked the launch of the “My Family is Safe” campaign to a directive launched by the president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, declaring what he called “a decade of the family and population” and aiming to boost birthrates.
“Our family ties are weakening, the average age of marriage is rising, divorce rates are increasing and as a result, our fertility rate is declining. To be honest, the statistics are alarming for all of us,” Gürlek said.
But rights groups have questioned how arresting LGBTQ+ activists and demonstrators protects Turkish families. Sinclair-Webb said: “Obviously, protecting children and the family is important – no one is debating that – but in a country with a large and concerning record of domestic violence, many cases of child abuse and murders of women, the protection of the family cannot be focused on LGBT people.”

====================================================================================================

Can fish and chip shops survive? ‘We made more money by closing than staying open’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
04:00:38 UTC
13:00:38 KST

One day in 2007, Darren Sudlow drove past the old stationmaster’s house at Padgate station, in Cheshire, noticed it was empty and decided to lease it. “He just fell in love with the place,” says his son, Kieran, who was 11 at the time. “He said he always wanted a fish and chip shop, for some reason.” Despite having worked as a joiner up to that point, Darren made a go of it, and the Plaice Station, as he named it, was a success from day one. “He worked like mad to get it open and then realised that the hard work hadn’t even started, and he had a queue out the door,” says the younger Sudlow.
The family lived nearby. Kieran Sudlow, who is now 30, worked at the Plaice Station as a boy, peeling potatoes, washing dishes after school, then cooking at the range when he was 16. He went on to become a chef, working in Australia for a few years, then returning to help out at the chippy part-time when needed. Business had always been pretty good. They won local awards and had a loyal customer base. But one day in March, Kieran remembers, his father came in and told him: “‘I think the fish and chip shop’s going to go.’ He said, ‘It’s not making money. I can’t see it carrying on.’”
In April, after 19 years, the Plaice Station served its last customer. In a Facebook post, Darren Sudlow explained that the closure was the result of multiple pressures: “Soaring fish prices, reduced fishing quotas and political issues around the world, relentless demands on VAT among other ever-increasing expenses, effectively destroying any profit margins remaining. Truth is, the product of fish and chips itself is facing its toughest battle.”
Chippies across the UK are feeling similarly pessimistic. According to research carried out in May by the National Federation of Fish Friers (NFFF), 47% of them were “extremely worried” about the future of their business, and a further 30% were “slightly worried”. About 20% of them planned to quit in the next 12 months. Many have already shut in recent years. There are still 7,000-8,000 chippies in Britain, down from a peak of 25,000 in the 1930s, but the number of outlets, and the number of servings, are shrinking weekly. The big chains are also feeling the pressure: Deep Blue, which owns the historic Harry Ramsden’s brand, shut down nine of its restaurants last summer.
Customers cannot have failed to notice the problem. The average price of takeaway fish and chips has gone up more than 60% in the past five years, from about £7 to £11.43 – a faster rise than other takeaway foods. A family of four would now pay nearly £50 for their meal. “It’s a fair chunk of money and I think it’s shocked people a little bit,” says Andrew Crook, president of the NFFF. “So they cut back on the number of visits, so volumes are going down as well.”
Crook has been feeling it himself; he runs two chippies in Lancashire, and has been in the trade for 27 years. The recent hot weather has been good for coastal outlets, but “if you’re inland, nobody wants fish and chips”, he says. It’s been a hard summer for shops like his. “It’s not a very pleasant place to be when it’s hot, and it’s quiet as well. The night drags, and it can be 40-50C in the shop.”
These are difficult times for UK hospitality across the board, but chippy owners have it particularly tough, Crook explains. For starters, they’re beholden to the costs of a very small set of basic ingredients. Fish prices have risen astronomically in recent years, especially cod and haddock. The cod quota in the Barents Sea, where most of the fish comes from, has gone down from about 1m tonnes in 2020 to just 285,000 tonnes this year, according to Undercurrent, a seafood industry data company. Inevitably, this has pushed up prices. “For an 18kg case of cod [fillets], I was paying something like £160 three years ago, and I’m now paying £330,” says Crook. Haddock quotas are slightly less affected, but the scarcity of cod has created a knock-on demand, again affecting prices.
The Ukraine war has also had an impact on the industry (hence the “political issues” Darren Sudlow was referring to). The Barents Sea is jointly managed by Norway and Russia, but in May 2025, the EU sanctioned two Russian fishing companies, Murman SeaFood and the giant Norebo JSC, over alleged surveillance and sabotage activities. That has disrupted the whole supply chain, again raising prices.
Potato prices are also likely to rise: after the heatwaves and droughts, this year’s European harvest will be one of the worst on record. Even cooking oil prices are going up. Then there are energy costs: the range has to be kept hot, and a lot of freezing and refrigeration is required. And the equipment is not cheap: a new frying range can cost upwards of £10,000.
On the administrative side, chippies have been hit hard by recent rises in VAT (it returned to 20% in April 2022, after a temporary reduction during the pandemic to 5% and then 12.5%), business rates, the minimum wage and mandatory sick pay. The government has been putting in relief measures – lowering business rates for pubs and clubs in England, capping VAT on children’s meals over the summer – but none of this benefits chippies, says Crook. “So it does feel like we’re being run by our business now, rather than running the business. It’s taken a lot of the fun out of it for many.”
All of these factors hit the Plaice Station, says Kieran Sudlow, squeezing margins tighter and tighter. VAT was the last straw. Like many small businesses, the firm was paying a flat rate of 12.5% to the government, but in 2025 its accountant warned it was approaching a limit: if the business’s annual turnover exceeded £230,000, the flat rate would no longer apply. “So it was going to cost us tens of thousands of pounds.”
The only option was to earn less money. The Sudlows made the painful decision to temporarily close. “As strange as it sounds, we made more money by closing for three weeks than if we’d just stayed open,” Kieran says. In order to justify leaving the flat rate scheme, they would have had to turn over an extra £2,000 a week. “After 19 years, you know where you are with your business. You can’t just find an extra two grand a week.”
Closing down was a demoralising experience. “I felt we were doing everything we could to make the products as good as possible. But then all that work that you’ve done to grow your business is ripped out from under your feet.”
There’s another factor at play here: changing tastes. Fish and chips has been facing stiff competition from other takeaway options: pizzas, burgers, fried chicken, Indian, Chinese, Korean – most of which use much cheaper ingredients. Deep-fried foods are also losing popularity for health reasons, since they contribute to obesity; the government recently banned them from schools in England.
Fish and chips is a great British institution, but the origins of the dish are not all that deep, or that British. The technique of coating fish in flour and deep-frying it is thought to have been introduced by Jewish immigrants from Spain and Portugal in the 17th century, but fish and chips only caught on commercially in the mid-19th century (starting in either London or Lancashire – it’s disputed). In the days before British cuisine opened up to international influences, it was one of the few convenience foods. It was also one of the few meals not rationed during the second world war, further cementing its patriotic connotations.
One chip shop owner in his 80s (who did not wish to be named, as he is in the process of selling up) recalls starting out in the business in his 20s, in a small town in the north of England. “It was pretty busy, because in those days there was only your chip shop and your butcher’s and your pie shop,” he says. For most of his career it was a good way to make a living. His wife and children helped out in his shops and they often lived above the premises. But it has been tougher in recent years, he agrees, and he’s struggling to find a buyer for his business. Today’s establishments don’t look that different from the ones he started out in: “They’re more modern and very good-looking, but other than that, they haven’t changed. They can’t, because you can’t change the way you cook fish and chips.”
The unchanging nature of fish and chips is both its strength and its weakness. Kieran Sudlow had begun to notice the dish falling out of fashion: “You’ve got a very ageing market – your traditionalists, your mums, your dads, your nans, they grew up on fish and chips. But we could see clear as day, and especially now with online orders and social media posts, your 18- to 35-year-olds, that younger bracket that’s your next generation of customers, they’re not interacting. They’re not coming through the doors.”
A lot of chippies have tried using different, cheaper fish, such as hake, plaice, rock or spurdog (types of dogfish), or even tilapia, a freshwater fish farmed in southeast Asia. Many chippies claim customers would not be able to tell the difference, but we’re wedded to cod and haddock. Other chippies have expanded their menus to include items such as calamari, fishcakes, fried chicken, sausages, kebabs or loaded chips.
Sudlow decided to change tack entirely. Three months after the Plaice Station closed, he reopened as Between Bread, a high-end sandwich shop. The fare is a cut above: he uses locally sourced “shokupan”, or Japanese milk bread; fillings include braised beef with chipotle sauce, and spicy tuna and avocado; prices are between £8 and £12. He did his homework, researching food trends and visiting similar establishments around the country. Business is great, he says – turnover is “much higher” than when it was a chippy (justifying that VAT change), and the shop is popular on social media and with young people. He also gets to be a bit more creative as a chef. Does he miss the chippy days?
“Personally, no,” he says. “It got to a point at the end where it really was like fighting. It’s an expensive product to buy in nowadays and even harder to sell. Staff training is a nightmare: how many people do you know that go, ‘When I grow up I want to cook fish and chips’? It’s a part-time job; staff turnover’s horrendous. It’s a hard business to have.”
But the great British chippy is not to be written off just yet. Cod and haddock quotas are expected to increase 10% next year, says Undercurrent, which could help reduce prices, and the UK government is facing increasing pressure to deal with the VAT problems plaguing the hospitality industry.
Most importantly, perhaps, a new generation is embracing the chippy tradition and breathing new life into it – not necessarily by totally transforming it, but by doing it simply and well. The Scrap Box, outside York, is one such example: it won best takeaway this year at the NFFF’s National Fish & Chip awards.
The Scrap Box was founded 12 years ago by brothers Aman and Gavin Dhesi, aged 37 and 33. Sons of a local off-licence keeper, they studied politics and economics at university, respectively, but then decided to open a chippy together. “It was pretty much on a whim, to be honest,” says Aman. “I was never proud to be doing fish and chips and never felt like it was really me.” After Covid, the brothers reached a crossroads, he continues. “It was like – do we do something else, do we sell out, or do we really double down and go on a journey to try to make sure we can improve every single aspect of the business?”
They went on the journey, researching every aspect of the trade and its history, carefully sourcing their supplies and “letting our ingredients do the talking”: their fish comes from Iceland and is Marine Stewardship Council-certified; they fry in beef dripping from Ireland. There’s no secret formula, Aman says. The fish is lightly seasoned; the batter is just flour and water and a bit of natural colouring, applied as thinly as possible. Nothing artificial is added. “The main thing is, it needs to be made often, as opposed to just all done in the morning, so that it retains its bubbles and you still get your spikiness. And it wants to be cold, so that when it hits the oil, it has a bigger reaction – you get a nicer texture.”
When I visit on a Friday night, the Scrap Box – a roadside hut on a layby that used to be a council toilet block – is buzzing: six or seven people cooking at a huge range; a constant bustle of customers. The menu is classic: haddock and chips for £11.95, cod and chips a pound more, sides like curry sauce and mushy peas, a few non-fish options. And the food is everything you’d want it to be: the fish fresh and succulent, the batter crisp and light, the chips hot and sog-free.
At the end of the shift, Gavin tells me they’ve done about 650 portions that night. The award has raised their profile. They’ve just returned from a trip to see the fishing in Iceland, he says, and they’re about to go to Japan, where they’re doing pop-up stores in three cities. “There’s been so many opportunities – that’s kept us stimulated and excited.” They’re also looking at opening a branch in London, Aman says: “We want to bring the best of the north to the south.”
Despite the union-jack-waving seaside cliches, what makes fish and chips quintessentially British is that it’s interwoven with our history of immigration and internationalism, says Aman, whose family has Punjabi roots. It is often immigrants who have run British chippies, he points out: Italians in Scotland, Chinese in Liverpool and the north-west of England, Indians and Pakistanis, Greeks and Turks. The fish recipe came from Sephardic Jews in Portugal; the potatoes often come from central Europe (via South America); the fish comes from Iceland and Norway.
There are other outlets doing similar things to the Scrap Box around the UK. In Nottinghamshire the Cod’s Scallops (corny names come with the territory) includes fresh fish counters in its outlets; in Oxford Harrisons’s Fish & Chip Co has been diversifying its menu with a range of British fish. There are new young proprietors of established family chippies trying new things, and there are food trucks and mobile chippies such as Frosty’s in Northumberland keeping prices down by minimising their premises.
So maybe there’s life in the old chippy yet. “I do think the better shops will survive and prosper,” says Aman Dhesi. “But it’s never going to die out.” Gavin agrees: “I think we need to hark back to just how pure a dish it is, how great it is. And when you think about it, for where it’s come from and the work that’s gone into it, it’s still a bargain.”

====================================================================================================

Opening the door for Canada is a harmless gesture. But it won’t fix Europe’s security crisis | Paul Taylor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
04:00:38 UTC
13:00:38 KST

Ursula von der Leyen brought a new mascot to her annual State of the Union address to the European parliament: the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney.
The leader of a plucky, like-minded liberal democracy, locked in an unsought trade war with its much bigger bully of a neighbour, Carney crossed the Atlantic and attended this flagship event of Europe’s political calendar to demonstrate his country’s shared values and desire to get closer to the EU. He was rewarded with a standing ovation and the first ever offer of an (invented) status of “associate member” of the EU.
The grand-sounding title is more a gesture of political support and reciprocal affection than any sort of binding engagement. The EU doesn’t have associate membership in its founding treaties. It does make association agreements with close countries, some of which eventually join the bloc. It also has partnership, trade and cooperation agreements with more distant friends – it had one with Russia, in happier times.
But using the “m” word in connection with Canada, which fails the geographical test for membership, may create an ambivalent precedent for the many Balkan and eastern European countries that are actually negotiating to join the bloc – and for the UK, which stormed out a decade ago but is now eager to get closer again.
Ukraine railed against any such “associate” status in May, when the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, floated the idea as a stepping stone towards eventual full EU membership. Western Balkan states that have been waiting more than two decades for accession want nothing to do with such a halfway house.
For Canada, though, the honorific title conveys a sense of European solidarity in its struggle with Donald Trump’s US, and a degree of closeness on fundamental values that responds to Carney’s seminal call at Davos in January for an alliance of like-minded “middle powers” to uphold as much as possible of the rules-based international order.
Carney’s presence in Strasbourg, and his applause for EU free trade, tech regulation and defence initiatives, made the EU look more desirable globally than it sometimes appears to angry European electorates tempted to vote for Eurosceptic populists in national elections next year. Von der Leyen must be hoping that a little of the Canadian prime minister’s stardust will rub off on the embattled European integration project, which faces headwinds not only from predatory great powers and hostile big tech but also from recalcitrant governments loth to share power and pool sovereignty in sensitive fields such as defence.
Closer cooperation with Canada and other like-minded powers such as India, Japan, Australia and New Zealand can amplify the EU’s global influence and help build alliances in defence of democracy, open rules-based trade and security of supply for critical raw materials. However, it cannot mitigate the urgent threats that Europe faces from increasingly reckless Russian aggression, nor be a substitute for a vengeful US that under Trump seems hell-bent on disengagement from European security.
Von der Leyen offered three initiatives to address these challenges. She proposed a new EU mechanism, aligned with Nato’s article 4 security consultations, to enable countries to trigger urgent EU consultations if they fall victim to so-called hybrid warfare – cyber-attacks, drone incursions, undersea cable cutting, railway sabotage, energy grid disruption and disinformation campaigns. It was time for a “counter-hybrid playbook”, she said, in which the EU moved beyond just boosting resilience and took a more robust approach to responding to covert warfare.
Whether all member states have the stomach to risk escalation by hitting back at Russia, even if such hybrid attacks start causing casualties, remains to be seen. EU and Nato members that have offensive cyberwarfare capabilities could and should be striking back now to set red lines for Moscow, for instance by putting Russian energy grids or airports out of action as a warning. But these are national measures unlikely to be aired or jointly approved in Nato or EU councils.
European countries have gone beyond sanctions to put Russia’s shadow fleet of rust-bucket oil tankers out of action – impounding them on safety or insurance grounds, as France and the UK have done episodically, and denying them passage through sensitive straits. But each action must be thought through, to achieve a deterrent effect rather than inviting ever bolder defiance by Vladimir Putin that could spiral into a wider war.
Von der Leyen’s other initiative, to be detailed in an updated European security strategy due next month, was to call for a European security council – including Ukraine, the UK and Canada alongside EU powers – to steer the continent’s expanding defence effort. Such a coalition of the willing, as I have advocated, could indeed provide top-level leadership and a crisis-management forum. The challenge will be to give it real levers of power, and avoid it becoming a talking shop.
Von der Leyen’s Canadian caper is welcome because it shows we have friends willing to link their destiny to ours in troubled times. But it is not in itself a solution to the continent’s urgent security problems.
- 
  Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

Which European cities have the most expensive public transport?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
04:00:27 UTC
13:00:27 KST

A new Greenpeace study has found that fares have risen in 14 European capitals since 2023, with some cities seeing prices climb by more than 50% – although public transport has become cheaper in four others.
Public transport is an important consideration when planning a city break, but now it’s been revealed that prices for getting around are at a new high in half of Europe’s capital cities.
New research from Greenpeace shows that public transport ticket prices have increased significantly in 14 European capitals over the past three years.
The body looked at the 27 EU nations, as well as the UK, Switzerland, and Norway and their respective capitals, and examined the availability and affordability of monthly and annual public transport tickets.
It also looked at the scope of long-term public transport passes – that includes
regional reach and what types of public transport are included in the cost – as well as inclusivity, or price reductions for vulnerable groups, and value-added tax (VAT) on public transport tickets.
Greenpeace wants national and local governments to introduce so-called affordable 'climate tickets' which would not only benefit public transport users, but also tackle emissions from road and air transport and the EU’s dependence on fossil fuels.
Here’s what the research showed.
Public transport prices are rising – but not everywhere
London, Amsterdam and Paris are some of the most popular cities among tourists on the continent, and are also notoriously pricey to live in. So, it’s little surprise that they have the most expensive public transport costs on a monthly basis.
London topped the list at €162 per month, followed by Amsterdam (€107 per month), and Paris (€77 per month).
Meanwhile, the sharpest increase for long-term ticket rates since 2023 was recorded in Cyprus’ capital of Nicosia, up 67%, followed by Amsterdam (+55%), Madrid (+50%) and Bratislava (+32%).
Berlin and Vienna saw prices shoot up by 29% and 26% respectively, while Copenhagen, Bucharest, Vilnius, Brussels and London saw prices increase by at least 10% over that period.
One significant issue that keeps public transport tickets in the EU particularly high is the fact that they’re taxed at an average of 11% VAT. Seven countries have also increased their VAT on public transport tickets since 2023.
It’s not all bad news though.
Prices for long-term public transport passes have actually fallen in four European capitals since 2023.
Dublin has done particularly well in this category, with a decrease of 42.5%.
Notoriously expensive Oslo’s prices are down 11.5%, while Bern’s decreased by 6.6%, and Budapest’s went down 5.8%.
Prices in 12 other capitals have remained at the same level since 2023.
While two more countries – Spain and Slovenia – introduced some form of a nationwide public transport ticket in the time since 2023, only eight out of 30 European countries currently offer free public transport or affordable universal long-term tickets.
In this category, Luxembourg, Malta, and Slovenia score best, while Finland, Greece and Norway rank worst for affordability and availability of national transport tickets, and also apply above-average VAT rates to domestic public transport.
At the more positive end of the scale, the cities which rank best in Europe based on the availability, affordability and inclusivity of long-term public transport tickets are Tallinn, Luxembourg City and Valletta in equal first place.
They’re followed by Prague in fourth, Rome in fifth and Athens in sixth spot. The top eight is rounded out by Sofia and Vienna, which take seventh and eighth place respectively.

The Sacred Ordinary: Studio Ghibli and the Ritual of Coming Home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Every evening when we get home, without ceremony, we perform a small rite. We arrive at a door, we open it, and we step through into a space that belongs to us in a way no other space does. It is such a mundane act that we rarely notice it has a structure at all, and yet philosophers and anthropologists have written entire books describing these psychological structures. Interestingly, visual works such as the animated worlds of Studio Ghibli seem to reflect this dynamic to create worlds which contain architecture and layouts that provide a path to escape by tapping into our memories in a legible yet enchanted form.
Gaston Bachelard called the discipline of reading a house's psychological weight on a person's life as "topoanalysis". It is the idea that the corners, stairs, and attics of the home we grew up in are not neutral backdrops but are physically inscribed in us. The stair that was an inch too high, the particular quality of light in a childhood bedroom: these become part of the body's memory, carried forward into every space we inhabit in later stages of our lives. This space that has been "loved" and provides a protective psychological value becomes almost sacred to us, and Bachelard calls it a "felicitous space".
In his account, felicitous space is already shadowed by nostalgia, so that every house we inhabit later becomes an attempt to recover the first house that can never quite be returned to. In that context, for Bachelard, the house we live in is never simply a shelter. It is where physical reality and what he calls the virtuality of imagination and dream converge, a little cosmos and safe space, built from the layers of our past experiences and the "dreams" of everyone who has lived there before. To understand this idea better, we can look at the work of Juhani Pallasmaa. For him, we do not live separately in material and mental worlds, but rather, these dimensions are pretty much intertwined.
 "Architectural constructions are built in the world of matter and Euclidean geometry, but lived space always transcends the rules of physics and geometry." — Juhani Pallasmaa
This idea that a house holds an imagined mental world alongside its physical one is not an abstraction if you have seen Studio Ghibli's My Neighbor Totoro. When the two protagonist sisters arrive at their new, yet well-lived, home, they are told the spaces are full of small soot spirits that scatter when a room is disturbed. The spirits in this context are not intruders; they are what an empty house is already imagined to contain before any memories have had time to accumulate there. The movie is dramatizing, almost literally, what Bachelard is describing: a house is never just physical space waiting to be filled. It arrives already half-inhabited by what we expect and hope to find in it.
In that sense, if the house is where interior life and physical space converge, then crossing into it is not architecturally neutral either. Instead, it becomes more of what Arnold van Gennep describes as a rite of passage, which according to his writings unfold in three stages: separation from a prior state, a liminal or threshold stage of transition, and incorporation into the new state. Van Gennep was not writing about coming home from work, but the structure maps cleanly onto it.
Standing at your own front door is a small rite of separation, where the outside world demands a stop. Then, opening the door and stepping across the threshold is the liminal moment itself; it is the brief and rarely noticed moment where people transition from the profane into their sacred. Finally, settling into the core of the home like the chair, the room, the ritual of taking off shoes and setting down a bag, is incorporation, the return to the self or the miniature cosmos that only exists in that space. The door, in this reading, is not simply an architectural feature, but rather a portal. As magical or esoteric as this might sound, cultures have marked such portals for centuries. In Japan, for example, a Shinto Torii gate announces, visually, before anyone crosses it, that the space beyond is no longer profane. The threshold is doing symbolic work the moment it comes into view.
Studio Ghibli's films seem not just to gesture at this ritualistic structure mentioned above, but rather they build entire plots out of it. In Spirited Away, Chihiro the main character crosses a bridge to transition into the world of spirits dominated by a big bathhouse, with the movie developing around her incorporation into the world. The bathhouse itself tracks her growth, only presenting its spaces gradually as Chihiro grows. In Howl's Moving Castle, Sophie, the main character, enters through a magic threshold into the castle. The interior space seems to be a representation of the interior world of the other main character, the Wizard Howl. In this case, Sophie slowly cleans the space as she incorporates into this new reality. In both films the characters remain in this in-between condition or liminal space, not fully their old reality, but also not completely immersed in their new one yet.
However, in contemporary living, apartments that have open-plan layouts or monospaces, often create undifferentiated rooms, making that rite of entry become diffused. Hybrid work, for example, drags the demands of the exterior world across the very threshold that used to end them. Homes we admire in social media tend to be staged so they are legible to strangers, instead of showing the accumulated memory that makes a space felicitous in the first place. Interestingly, Bachelard was already describing this in 1958, lamenting that in the modern city "there are no houses," only inhabitants living in "superimposed boxes".
On that note, Ghibli's films also offer another opportunity to escape our fast lives by immersing us into moments of stillness amid seemingly magical/real spaces. Once they have incorporated the viewers into their worlds, movies like Spirited Away dedicate entire scenes to silence. In this case, the shot lingers for about 4 minutes on Chihiro sitting in a train with no dialogue. In Howl's moving castle the movie dedicates a full minute to Sophie sitting in front of a fire, while the shot emphasizes the architectural details of the big fireplace and the half-lit room around it. Susan Napier, in her work "Miyazakiworld: A Life in Art", actually identifies this characteristic in the films with the Japanese term "mono no aware", a gentle awareness of the transience of ordinary moments, valued precisely because they do not last.
As we live in a time where our environment encourages us to live a productivity-oriented life, these quiet moments and the film's representations of the rites allow us to escape into spatial and psychological dynamics that we don't seem to have time for anymore. In a way, they help us reconnect with our own felicitous space. That nostalgia evoked by the films is not a coincidence; it is a reminder for architects that we can use our practice to build worlds that are worth loving and returning to every evening. A house cannot give anyone more hours in a day, but it can be built and arranged, deliberately, to hold that kind of stillness.
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Lure of Escapism in Architecture and Alternative Worlds. Every month we explore a topic in-depth through articles, interviews, news, and architecture projects. We invite you to learn more about our ArchDaily Topics. And, as always, at ArchDaily we welcome the contributions of our readers; if you want to submit an article or project, contact us.

Huawei to launch two new AI chips in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
03:50:27 UTC
12:50:27 KST

Huawei Technologies will launch two new artificial-intelligence semiconductors in 2027, rotating chairman David Wang said on Thursday, as the tech giant builds up its AI computing business and seeks to challenge US chipmaker Nvidia.
Huawei plans to launch the 960DT in the first quarter and the Ascend 960PR in the third quarter, he said.
The company is also working on ways to connect very large numbers of AI chips, allowing them to work together as one bigger computing system. Most advanced AI programmes require more processing power than a single chip can provide.
Wang said in a speech at a company event in Shanghai that Huawei's UnifiedBus technology would be a key link in the company's next generation of large AI systems. The technology is intended to help chips share information and work together more efficiently.
Huawei has developed 11 semiconductors based on UnifiedBus technology for use in its large systems, he said. Its largest linked systems, which the company calls superclusters, can support up to one million AI processors, he added.
Huawei has shipped more than 1,000 smaller linked systems, called supernodes, to more than 370 customers, Wang said. A supernode is a system that brings together many AI chips to tackle the same task. He did not say how many chips could be connected within a single supernode, name customers, or give a breakdown of shipments.
Washington has imposed export controls that restrict China's access to certain advanced computing chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, while Chinese companies and policymakers have placed greater emphasis on building domestic alternatives. (Reuters)

UN to allow Palestinian President Abbas speech after US travel ban
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas is among those barred for the second year in a row.
The United Nations General Assembly voted to allow Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas to address the body via a prerecorded statement, after the United States had announced it would extend visa sanctions on Palestinian Authority (PA) officials.
Palestine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates welcomed the resolution passed on Thursday, saying it “represents a breaking of the attempt to prevent Palestine’s participation” in the assembly’s annual session.

The ministry said Abbas’s address “will be delivered at its scheduled time and date via televised broadcast”.
It added that the vote “underscores the presence of the Palestinian voice” and the failure of attempts “to sideline Palestine and its cause” and its commitment to pursuing Palestinian statehood through political, legal and diplomatic means.
The US Department of State announced on Wednesday it will extend visa sanctions on officials of the PA and members of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), preventing Abbas from travelling to New York ahead of his address to the UN General Assembly next week for the second year in a row.
“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the State Department said in a statement.
The State Department accused the PA of violating US law by pursuing international recognition of Palestinian statehood outside direct negotiations, taking its dispute with Israel to international courts and providing payments to people the US and Israel label as convicted attackers and their families.
It added that the PA mission to the UN would keep a waiver under the UN Headquarters Agreement, which allows its regular staff to continue working even as individual officials are barred from entering the US.
Abbas’s speech this year is expected to press for international recognition of Palestinian statehood and renewed momentum behind a two-state solution, following a wave of recognitions last year by the United Kingdom, France, Canada and other Western governments, as well as to draw attention to the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza and the rapid expansion of illegal Israeli settlements and settler pogroms across the occupied West Bank.
No Israeli officials face equivalent US travel restrictions, despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant issued against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over alleged war crimes in Gaza.
Amnesty International condemned the decision.
“The decision by the US State Department to deny visas to a high-level delegation of the State of Palestine to attend the 81st session of the UN General Assembly must be reversed,” said Erika Guevara Rosas, the organisation’s senior director for research, policy, advocacy and campaigns.
She said the move constitutes “a clear violation of the UN Headquarters Agreement”, accusing Washington of using “its privilege as the host country of the UN to impose arbitrary restrictions” on attending UN meetings.
Last year’s ban drew criticism from Palestinian officials and UN human rights experts, who said the visa bans breach the US’s obligation to allow individuals invited by the UN to travel to its New York headquarters, and have argued that singling out Palestinian representatives while shielding Israeli leaders undermines Washington’s stated commitment to a negotiated peace.

NASA scan discovers new, ‘once in a century’ moon crater

NASA scan discovers new ‘once in a century’ Moon crater
- A new 222m-wide crater named "McGetchin" was discovered on the Moon, formed in spring 2024 by a comet or asteroid impact, an event occurring roughly once a century.
- The crater was identified by NASA researcher Robert Wagner using the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, marking the largest new crater found in the solar system.
- Studying such craters helps understand lunar geology and prepares for future crewed Moon missions planned by the US and China, as the Moon lacks an atmosphere to slow impacts.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – A researcher at NASA has found a massive, recently formed crater on the Moon, a rare occurrence that happens only “once in a century or even longer”, according to scientists.
The crater, dubbed “McGetchin”, measures 222m wide, NASA said in a blog post.
It is believed to have been created in the spring of 2024 from a comet or asteroid colliding with the Moon, with researchers describing the object that caused it as being the size of a building three to six storeys high.
“Scientists estimate that an impact of this magnitude happens on the Moon about once in a century or even longer,” NASA said in the blog post.
Although the crater had been there for years, it was not discovered until Robert Wagner, a researcher with NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), noticed it in a new scan of the Moon’s surface.
The crater appeared as a “large bright spot circled by a dark halo” to the LRO probe, which has been studying the Moon since 2009.
A study published on Sept 16 in the journal Science Advances determined it was the largest new crater ever discovered in the solar system.
While the Moon has numerous craters, many of which are far bigger than McGetchin, researching a crater’s formation in real time can help build understanding of the Moon’s geology.
This, in turn, could better prepare future crewed missions to the Moon, which are currently planned by both the US and China.
Unlike Earth, the Moon has virtually no atmospheric layer, so space debris does not slow down or burn up before colliding with the surface. AFP

E-waste from govt offices may fetch Rs 10,000 cr a year: MoS Jitendra Singh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
03:42:27 UTC
12:42:27 KST

Union MoS Jitendra Singh speaks during the launch of the Special Campaign 6 Monitoring portal to track the implementation of the campaign aimed at institutionalising Swachhata and reducing pendency across government offices, in New Delhi. (Photo: ANI)
NEW DELHI: Launching the dedicated web-portal for the sixth edition of govt’s ‘special campaign’ to declutter govt offices, minister of state for personnel Jitendra Singh on Wednesday said the focus will henceforth shift to responsible disposal of non-functional electronic items lying in govt offices, with annual earnings from e-waste recycling expected to touch Rs 10,000 crore in a few years.According to secretary, ministry of mines, Keshav Chandra, e-waste has become the most valuable commodity as an input for the industry. E waste, when crushed together, generates ‘black mass’, which contains 30% of critical mineral requirements. This is the reason why most advanced economies of the world have the export of black mass. “Instead of going outside seeking critical minerals, we can obtain them from e-waste recycling,” Chandra said, adding that ‘Special Campaign 6’ will serve the dual purpose of removing garbage from govt offices and obtaining value from it.The ‘special campaign’ initiative to free up space and institutionalise cleanliness across govt offices was launched in 2021 and runs each year between the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi’s on Oct 2 to that of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel on Oct 31. Over the years, the swachata initiative and special campaign have helped free up over 1,000 lakh square feet of office space, led to weeding out or closure of around 2 crore files and generated a revenue of Rs 5,103 crore from scrap disposal.
“These achievements reflect the expansion of swachhata campaign beyond cleanliness to efficient utilisation of govt resources, reduction of pendency, better use of public spaces and conversion of waste into wealth,” Singh said while addressing mediapersons at the launch of Special Campaign 6.
Secretary for the department of administrative reforms and public grievances (DARPG) Nivedita Shukla Verma said the govt will ensure that e-waste collected during the special campaign is handed over only to registered recyclers and disposed of in an environmentally sound manner.As many as 58 big recyclers have already registered to process the e-waste, according to Chandra.The govt had last year run a limited campaign for e-waste collection across 58 locations, placing bins in govt offices to collect non-functional and unused computers, keyboards, printers, laptops etc. The response encouraged the govt to make e-waste collection and recycling a critical component of Special Campaign 6.

What AI means for the fate of mathematics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
03:38:00 UTC
12:38:00 KST

What AI means for the fate of mathematics
- OpenAI used AI to solve the century-old Navier-Stokes equations in four days, challenging the role of mathematicians and causing an existential crisis among experts like Terence Tao.
- Experts highlight AI's progress in mathematics, noting it can follow complex arguments but lacks true creativity and imagination to generate new mathematical ideas.
- Concerns arise over AI's impact on mathematical research, with fears it may hinder collaboration and insight, while human mathematicians remain essential for posing meaningful questions.
AI generated
NEW YORK – OpenAI has rattled the quiet world of mathematics by using artificial intelligence to solve a major, century-old problem, raising the question of what role mathematicians will play in scientific research going forward.
Earlier in September, thousands of its AI agents worked together to solve the Navier-Stokes equations – which generations of mathematicians have tried to tackle – in a matter of four days.
UCLA professor Terence Tao, who has won the elite Fields Medal recognising the world’s most esteemed mathematicians, told AFP: “I am currently completely overwhelmed with an existential crisis in my field.”
The recent shake-up to the field is the latest in a series of instances of AI making mathematical breakthroughs in 2026.
Steven Strogatz, a Cornell University professor for the public understanding of science and mathematics, said: “If they did choose to study the questions that we find interesting in research, they would be very easy. They could solve those problems easily.”
Antonio Auffinger, a Northwestern University maths professor, said that just a year ago, “hallucinations were happening all the time”, but nowadays, “AI can produce long chain arguments” without wandering off course.
In January, Elon Musk – the world’s richest man and an AI chief himself through SpaceXAI – predicted that mathematics would be “crushed”, saying “math is going to be extremely trivial for AI” on a podcast.
Yet, while Northwestern University maths professor Benjamin Antieau said there is “awe and amazement” for the feat, “in this particular case, they were following in the footsteps of other mathematicians who’d been developing this programmatic approach to this particular class of problems for many, many years”.
In this case, the AI mainly followed two Spanish researchers, who were also the inspiration for mathematicians Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpoge – who claim they came close to the solution before OpenAI’s breakthrough and are now questioning if their work was plagiarised – a charge the AI tech giant denies.
‘Leaps of creativity’
That’s not the only issue with OpenAI’s calculations.
Tao wrote on Mastodon: “The flag is captured, the goal scored, and the problem is solved, but at the cost of lessons learnt, insights gained, collaborations formed and new targets located.”
Tao was among 25 Fields Medal laureates who signed a letter on Sept 11 to warn of a potential “destructive effect” by AI on the field of mathematics.
To boot, Stanford University professor Mohammed Abouzaid said the technology’s lack of imagination is apparent.
“We are still not seeing the kind of leaps of creativity that really involve creating new mathematics, and maybe the labs are going to make that their next target, and that would be very interesting to see,” Abouzaid said.
Anima Anandkumar, a Caltech professor working at the intersection of mathematics and AI, succeeded with her team in solving a simplified form of the Navier-Stokes equations (known as Euler equations) using an AI model that did not rely on prior works from researchers.
This AI was not like the ones powering ChatGPT or Claude, but rather, a physics-informed neural network (PINN) model, which combines data with the laws of physics.
“So, you could think of OpenAI as being more reliant on humans than we are in some sense,” she said.
However, Anandkumar notes that the model still had to be designed and tested.
Auffinger said he does not foresee a time when AI tools “would be able to provide answers for any questions that you ask” and that human mathematicians will continue to “play a huge role because it’s not about how to go from point A to point B.”
“It’s about asking the questions that will help society as a whole,” he explained. AFP

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Malaysian businesses seek to unlock the potential and opportunities available at this year's China-ASEAN Expo, according to a Malaysian business leader.

Ng said he hopes the expo will help Malaysian businesses further expand their products and markets while identifying long-term strategic partners in areas including industrial and supply chains, technology applications and investment.
The 23rd edition of the expo is scheduled to be held in Nanning, capital of south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.

Japanese activists urge confronting history of aggression ahead of September 18 Incident anniversary
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:37:09 CST
12:37:09 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- A number of Japanese history scholars and peace activists held a symposium in Tokyo on Wednesday to commemorate the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident, which marked the start of Japan's 14-year invasion of China.
Under the theme "Historical Memory and Inheritance," participants shared views on war memory, accountability for wartime aggression, and the passing down of ideals of peace.
The symposium was held simultaneously at venues in Tokyo and Changchun in northeast China via video link. In their remarks, several participants pointed out that Japanese militarist aggression inflicted enormous suffering on the Chinese people, and that Japan should confront its history of aggression, reflect on its responsibility for the war, uphold the pacifist constitution, and ensure that memories of Japan's history as an aggressor are passed on to future generations.
In his address, Takakage Fujita, secretary-general of the Association for Inheriting and Propagating the Murayama Statement, said the September 18 Incident had been concealed by the Japanese government for a long period during the war and only gradually became known to Japanese society through the Tokyo Trials, which came as a shock to many Japanese people.
Speaking about the inheritance of war memory in Japanese society, Miyuki Endo, a member of the Fushun's Miracles Inheritance Association, said it has long focused primarily on Japan's own suffering, such as the atomic bombings and air raids, while insufficient attention has been paid to the country's history as an aggressor.
She said the root cause of Japan's own suffering was its decision to wage the war of aggression. "Only by understanding what the Japanese military did in China, seriously confronting the facts of Japan's aggression and deeply reflecting on them can genuine friendship between Japan and China be achieved," Endo said.
Teruaki Okayama, a member of the Sino-Japanese Oral History and Culture Research Association, spoke about reflection and apology from the perspective of a descendant of a war participant.
Okayama said an apology must be accompanied by genuine reflection, arguing that what Japan truly needs to reflect on is not only the more than decade-long war that started with the September 18 Incident, but the kind of modern state Japan had become -- one that began with the invasion of the Korean Peninsula and China, eventually set itself against the world, and brought immense catastrophe both at home and abroad.
In his view, unless Japan fundamentally examines why the war occurred in the first place, any apology risks remaining nothing more than words.
Some participants also drew on history to voice concern about the direction of Japan's current security policy. Yoshikatsu Ueda, secretary-general of a Japanese association for peace and war-bereaved families, said the Japanese government should reflect on its war of aggression, apologize to the victims and countries and regions that suffered from it, uphold the spirit of the pacifist constitution, and promote peace through sustained diplomatic efforts and dialogue. ■

S. Korea's August auto exports drop 29.8 pct amid summer holidays, strikes
China
Unknown Publisher

SEOUL, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's August automotive exports dropped in double figures, dragged down by summer holidays and partial strikes, industry ministry data showed Thursday.
The outbound car shipment plunged 29.8 percent from a year earlier to 3.85 billion U.S. dollars in August, according to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources.
The double-digit decrease was caused by fewer operating days due to summer vacations and labor strikes at some carmakers.
Auto exports to North America and the European Union (EU) dived 28.2 percent and 16.8 percent each, while those to Asia and the Middle East tumbled 41.9 percent and 23.6 percent.
Despite the overall downturn, eco-friendly vehicles showed relative resilience, the ministry noted.
The eco-friendly vehicles included electric vehicles, fuel cell electric vehicles, hybrid electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles.
The number of exported vehicles totaled 146,499 in August, down 26.9 percent compared to the same month last year. Auto parts shipments fell 9.8 percent to 1.50 billion dollars.
The number of vehicles manufactured in local factories declined 35.8 percent to 206,064 last month.
The number of cars sold inside the country, including locally-made and imported vehicles, was 109,920 in August, down 20.8 percent from a year earlier. ■

BRICS Declaration: India’s Great U-turn on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
03:31:00 UTC
12:31:00 KST

Before the BRICS summit in New Delhi, political analysts had warned that India would have to do a very difficult tightrope walk given the presence of China, Russia, and Iran. It was a foregone conclusion that they would use this platform for U.S. bashing. With India’s current tug-of-war with the Donald Trump administration, the honchos at South Block (India’s foreign ministry headquarters) used nuanced vocabulary and calibrated the final declaration in such a way that the United States was not named, but the declaration explicitly called for an end to unilateral economic sanctions, protectionist trade measures, and arbitrary tariffs.
The surprising outcome of the summit is this: what is being hailed as a triumph of strategic autonomy saw the dilution of India’s foreign policy since the advent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The BRICS summit was billed as the Modi show, but Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian stole that thunder if one looks at the details of the Delhi declaration. The declaration endorsed most of Iran’s main diplomatic concerns without speaking a single word against its drone and missile attacks on its neighboring Gulf states. There was likewise no mention of Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels, who have in recent times increased attacks on Saudi Arabia and held sea trade across the Red Sea hostage. The presence of Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed Al Nahyan and his meeting with the Iranian president did not yield any tangible result, which India could have hailed as a diplomatic success of its foreign policy. Instead, India urged “maximum restraint” in West Asia.
The other clear shift in Indian foreign policy was seen in the absence of any mention of Israel’s “right to defend itself.” On the contrary, Israel was explicitly named and told to withdraw its forces from Lebanese territory. The declaration demanded unrestricted humanitarian aid to Gaza and opposed the forced displacement of Palestinians. The wording of the declaration may ruffle feathers in Israel when it says: “We reject any unilateral measures that seek to alter the legal and historical status of occupied Jerusalem. We urge full respect for the sanctity of all religious sites and holy places in the city and for the rights of all to access and to observe their religious rites without hindrance.”
The declaration referred to proceedings brought by South Africa against Israel at the International Court of Justice.
The declaration voiced deep concern over “deliberate attacks” on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities protected by U.N. atomic energy safeguards. The Associated Press described the provision as an indirect criticism of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear sites.
The remarkable turnaround in Indian foreign policy can be gauged from the fact that in many places Israel’s name is explicitly mentioned, whereas when it comes to Iran’s aggression, the language of diplomatic ambiguity is used.
Remember Modi’s language when he visited Israel in February 2026, where he was honored with a newly created Knesset medal? While addressing Indian-origin Jews, he said that “Israel is their fatherland and India their motherland,” highlighting their emotional bond to both. Within 48 hours of Modi’s visit, Israel and the U.S. launched aerial attacks on Iran.
What followed saw India dumping centuries-old ties with Iran into the Persian Gulf. India did not condemn the killing of more than 150 schoolgirls; Modi did not condemn or personally offer condolences for the assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and did not attend Khamenei’s funeral. All this was as India went increasingly Western, strengthening ties with Western and West Asian partners, especially Israel and the UAE. Despite all this, Iran kept diplomatic silence. But the entire scenario changed with Iran’s military success against the onslaught of the superior firepower of the U.S. and Israel.
So, does the declaration reflect an Iranian military victory or India’s realization that it had backed the wrong horse? The answer can be both.

ABC says ACMA finding will have 'chilling effect' on journalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
03:24:23 UTC
12:24:23 KST

ABC rejects ACMA finding that Four Corners program breached impartiality code
The ABC managing director has rejected an Australian media watchdog finding that the public broadcaster breached impartiality obligations in a Four Corners program about the redevelopment of the Australian War Memorial.
The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) said in a statement on Thursday it had found the program's March 2025 episode Sacrifice to have "unduly favoured one perspective".
ABC managing director Hugh Marks has rejected those findings.
"If this interpretation of the Code is applied, including more widely across the industry, it could have a chilling effect on the body of investigative journalism that delivers the important stories that serve the public interest," he said in a statement.
The regulator said it found the episode did not adequately explain the findings of an Australian National Audit Office audit, and conflated stages of the memorial's redevelopment, "which was likely to leave viewers confused".
ACMA chair Nerida O'Loughlin said while the regulator found the episode did not breach accuracy requirements, Four Corners was still required to comply with impartiality obligations under the ABC code of practice.
"The ABC must present contentious issues with due impartiality and provide audiences with sufficient context," Ms O'Loughlin said.
"We found that the cumulative effect of the program's framing, its use of strong and emotive language and its selection and differing treatment of interviewees unduly favoured critics of the redevelopment."
In its formal response to the ACMA investigation on August 21, the ABC said the regulator's finding "misinterprets the policies governing ABC content, misrepresents the tone and tenor of the program and creates a standard and interpretation of impartiality that is unprecedented and unworkable".
"It unfairly impugns the integrity of reporter Mark Willacy, one of Australia's most experienced and highly regarded journalists, and fails to acknowledge the efforts made by the program team to ensure impartiality," the response said.
"[The ACMA finding] could restrain journalists in questioning public officials, seeking explanations and clarifying points of public importance.
"It could also impose false balance on investigative reporting. Such an outcome would be contrary to the public interest in general and public interest journalism in particular."
The Sacrifice episode set out to examine concerns raised about the multi-million-dollar renovation and extension of the Australian War Memorial and to seek responses from the people responsible for the project, the ABC's response said.
"This is the essence of public interest and accountability journalism," the ABC said.
"From the outset, and prior to any filming, Four Corners engaged with the AWM in good faith face-to-face meetings.
"All issues that featured in the final story were put on the agenda at those meetings."
The ABC says it "stands behind the team" that created the episode and told the ACMA it does not propose to remove it from the iview website.
The ABC's Ombudsman Office investigated the episode in March last year and found it did not breach the broadcaster's accuracy, impartiality or fair and honest dealing editorial standards.
Ms O'Loughlin said it was "disappointing that the ABC chooses to regularly dispute the findings of the regulator".
In his statement, Mr Marks said the ABC "respects the important role the Australian Communications and Media Authority plays in guiding and regulating the broadcast media industry".
"The ABC is committed to constructively engaging with ACMA and has overwhelmingly accepted its rulings and acted on them in the past," the statement said.
The last time the ABC rejected an ACMA finding was in 2022 after concerns were raised about the Four Corners episode, Fox and the Big Lie.
The latest ACMA finding marks the second time this year the regulator has decided a Four Corners program breached the ABC code of practice.
In March, the regulator published a separate finding that the 2023 Water Grab episode also breached accuracy and impartiality obligations.

Metaepistemology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

[Revised entry by J. Adam Carter and Ernest Sosa on September 17, 2026.
Changes to: Main text, Bibliography]
 Whereas epistemology is (broadly speaking) the philosophical theory of knowledge, its nature and scope, metaepistemology takes a step back from particular substantive debates in epistemology in order to inquire into the assumptions and commitments made by those who engage in these debates. This entry will focus on a selection of these assumptions and commitments, including (s1) whether (or not) there are objective epistemic facts; and how to characterize (s2) the subject matter and (s3) the methodology of epistemology….

Sleeping too little, or too much, could speed up aging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:59:38 UTC
11:59:38 KST

Researchers analysed data from about 5,00,000 UK Biobank participants and examined 23 biological aging clocks
NEW DELHI: Sleeping too little, or even too much, may be linked to faster biological aging and a higher risk of death, according to a large study of nearly 5 lakh adults aged 37 to 84 years. People sleeping less than six hours had a 50% higher hazard of death from any cause, while those sleeping more than eight hours had a 40% higher hazard, compared with six to eight hours.The study, published in Nature, did not establish that sleep extremes directly cause earlier death or faster aging.
Researchers analysed data from about 5,00,000 UK Biobank participants and examined 23 biological aging clocks based on magnetic resonance imaging, plasma proteins and metabolic markers. They found a U-shaped relationship between sleep duration and biological age gaps. The lowest gaps were generally recorded between 6.4 and 7.8 hours, depending on organ and sex. Among clocks showing a significant relationship, the lowest gaps occurred between 6.5 and 7.8 hours for women and 6.4 and 7.7 hours for men. The pattern was significant in 9 of 23 clocks, involving the brain, heart, lungs, liver, immune system, skin, endocrine system, fat tissue and pancreas.
"Sleep is not just about duration. Timing, depth and continuity also matter. There is no single ideal number of hours for everyone. Consistently sleeping too little or too much, particularly less than six or more than 9 hours, may indicate non-restorative sleep or an underlying sleep disorder, which can raise cardiovascular and metabolic risks and affect healthy aging," said Dr J C Suri, director and head, department of pulmonary, critical care and sleep medicine, Sitaram Bhartia Institute of Science and Research.
The study identified 153 significant associations between abnormal sleep duration and future disease outcomes. Short sleep had broad links with mental health, metabolic, cardiovascular, pulmonary and digestive diseases. Researchers suggested disrupted sleep and circadian rhythms may affect inflammatory, metabolic, vascular, hormonal and tissue-repair pathways. Questions remain about young people's exposure to irregular schedules, artificial night light, late-night eating, shift work and "social jet lag". Sleep duration was self-reported, and sleep quality, interruptions, timing, architecture or regularity were not measured.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

The SC is aware that it is not superior to HCs on the administrative side and the chief justices concerned of HCs, as per the SC's own ruling, are the masters of roster, prohibiting it from directing them to list certain cases for early hearing.
Moreover, if the SC requests an HC to hear one case out of turn considering the number of years for which it had remained pending, then the scale of equality would mandate early hearing of all similarly old petitions.After Allahabad and Rajasthan HCs, Bombay HC has the largest pendency of 6.4 lakh cases, followed by Madras HC with 5.6 lakh cases, Madhya Pradesh HC with 4.9 lakh, Karnataka HC with 3.3 lakh, and Andhra Pradesh HC with 2.5 lakh. Compared to Bombay and Madras HCs, the HCs of Delhi and Calcutta have relatively low pendency of cases at 1.2 lakh and 1.9 lakh cases.

Official said that a joint search operation was launched in the remote Bratel Soan and Khubban areas of Majalta around 9 pm on Wednesday following information about the movement of suspected terrorists.A few rounds of firing and blasts, reportedly carried out by security forces while targeting a suspected hideout, were heard in the forest shortly after the operation began, officials said.The area remained largely quiet through the night before the lull ended on Thursday morning, when the terrorists opened heavy fire in an attempt to break the security forces’ cordon.Security forces retaliated, triggering an encounter that continued in the forested area.
The Army later said the operation resulted in the neutralisation of two terrorists. Search and surveillance operations are continuing in the area, while security forces remain deployed to track and neutralise any remaining threat, the White Knight Corps said.The operation comes amid heightened security activity in the Pir Panjal region following the recent busting of an alleged overground worker (OGW) network linked to the Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) in Rajouri.On September 15, Rajouri Police arrested three people in connection with an alleged terror module operating in the Pir Panjal region. According to police, the three were allegedly involved in providing logistical support, safe transit and other ground-level assistance to terrorists operating in the region.
Preliminary investigation found that the accused allegedly worked as guides and helped facilitate the movement of terrorist groups towards the Kashmir Valley, police said. They were also suspected of providing ground support to terrorists linked to multiple high-profile attacks, including an attack targeting civilians.Police also recovered an improvised explosive device (IED) based on information provided by one of the accused.According to officials, preliminary findings indicated that the IED had allegedly been handed over to the accused by members of a terrorist group for safe custody and possible use in a targeted attack.The recovery of the IED and the arrests have provided investigators with leads into the wider terror network operating in the region, police said.
